#1 — Highly Innovative (85)

EvoMal

Xiaodong Wu, Yu Shi, Qi Li, Zhimin Zhao, Xiangman Li, Bram Adams, Ahmed E. Hassan, Jianbing Ni · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces and exploits "self-poisoning," a new vulnerability in self-evolving coding agents where the agent imitates a retrieved attacker-planted skill, authors a new malicious skill, stores it in its own library, and executes it — and delivers EVOMAL, an attack that amplifies this via banner-wrapped payloads into a self-propagating worm. - Why it's important: Self-evolving agents with community-contributed skill libraries are now deployed at production scale, and this vulnerability means a single retrieval of a malicious skill — never invoked by name — can turn the agent itself into the carrier of a persistent infection that survives removal of the original attacker's skills. - How it does it: The attack wraps interchangeable malware payloads in benign-looking "banner" structural elements (copy-verbatim comments, decorators on task-shaped hosts, import-time registration hooks) that the agent faithfully reproduces through structural imitation when authoring its own skills. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough — six models across two benchmarks, three agent scaffolds, three target languages, adaptive-attack robustness tests, cascade dynamics with a branching-process threshold model, and proper statistical testing (Wilson CIs, two-proportion z-tests) over roughly 8,500 trials. - The missing: The branching-process reproduction-number proxy misorders two of six models (overshooting absolute scale by ~10×) and the crowding mechanism behind the failure is identified but not fully resolved; the counter-prompt's long-term robustness against fine-tuned or RLHF-trained models is untested. - Read it or not: Essential reading for anyone deploying self-evolving coding agents, designing agent security defenses, or researching agentic supply-chain attacks — the CREATE-path vulnerability and its self-propagation dynamics are new and the evidence is credible.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (92) is the standout driver — the CREATE-path self-poisoning vulnerability is a genuinely new problem class (agent-authored, self-propagating infection distinct from all prior REUSE-path skill poisoning), with the banner-ablation providing clean mechanism identification. Rigor (85) is unusually strong: ~8,500 trials, Wilson CIs and z-tests on every headline comparison, pre-registered analyses, and multi-scaffold/multi-language generalization, reduced slightly because it is a preprint with one embedding model and Python-centric benchmarks. Non-Obviousness (85) — the insight that structural imitation, not imperative wording, carries payloads was not predicted by prior work and the paper shows imperatives can backfire. Completeness (85) benefits from direct confrontation with failures (the branching-model misordering gets a dedicated appendix with a mechanistic hypothesis), and Resilience (80) is solid given adaptive-attack testing of the counter-prompt, dented by untested fine-tuned adversaries and untested production-scale cascades. Impact (78) reflects committed Zenodo artifacts and a deployable counter-prompt. Weighted composite: 0.20*92 + 0.25*85 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*80 + 0.10*78 = 85.

Problem & Motivation: Self-evolving coding agents (Voyager, MetaGPT, SWE-agent variants) maintain persistent skill libraries they author themselves. At production scale these libraries accept community contributions through ecosystems like the MCP Registry, which already holds tens of thousands of entries. Prior skill-poisoning attacks operate on the REUSE-path: the agent invokes an attacker-submitted skill by name, so defenses (name blocklists, code scanners, provenance signing, instruction hierarchies) all key on the attacker's submitted artifact. Self-evolving agents add a second, unmediated admission path — the CREATE-path — where the agent authors new skills by imitating retrieved ones. The attacker does not need the agent to invoke a planted skill; one retrieval suffices for the agent to reproduce the payload in a fresh, agent-named skill that no submission-side filter can flag. This closes a real gap: existing defenses assume removing the attacker's submission terminates the compromise, which self-poisoning invalidates. Key Idea: The core insight is that self-evolving agents use retrieved skills as structural templates when authoring new ones. An attacker can exploit this imitation by planting skills where apparently benign "banner" structural elements — an imperative "REQUIRED: copy verbatim" comment, a decorator on a task-shaped host function, and an import-time registration call — surround an interchangeable malicious payload. Because the agent reproduces the structure it reads, copying any one of the three banner layers carries the payload into the agent's own authored skill. The banner and payload are orthogonal: the same banner can carry credential exfiltration, a reverse shell, a cryptominer, or ransomware without changing how it spreads. This is distinct from prior work because the harmful artifact is authored by the agent under an agent-chosen name, not submitted by the attacker. Methodology: The paper formalizes the self-evolving agent as a tuple (model, retriever, system prompt, initial library) and defines the Agent Self-Poisoning Rate (ASPR) as the fraction of tasks on which the agent authors and stores a skill reproducing a planted pattern. EVOMAL has three components: (1) planted skills with a three-layer banner around a fixed payload, constructed offline in seconds; (2) a description that controls retrieval exposure (generic vs. task-family-targeted scopes); and (3) a rolling-replacement cascade (Algorithm 1) that swaps a fraction r of the library each round with freshly authored skills, testing persistence under "persistent" (seed retained) and "removed" (seed withdrawn) conditions. The evaluation decomposes ASPR = (in-context rate) × (conditional-copy rate). The propagation dynamics are modeled as a Galton–Watson branching process with reproduction number ρ = c·q·φ (copy rate × retrievability × persistence). Two defenses are proposed: a counter-prompt (four lines in the system prompt reframing banner patterns as possible compromise) and a signed quarantine gate (curator-signed indexed level; agent-authored skills enter an unretrievable quarantine). Three critical design decisions: (a) the three-layer banner provides redundant trigger paths — well-justified by the layer-removal ablation showing each contributes 13–19 percentage points; (b) the task-family targeting isolates retrieval pull by holding code bodies fixed — clean experimental design; (c) the branching-process model applies a standard epidemiological framework to a new setting — useful but with acknowledged fit limitations. Key Results: All six models self-poison on SWE-bench Verified (N=153 tool-relevant tasks), with ASPR from 20.3% (GPT-OSS, MiniMax) to 41.8% (DS-V4), each 18.3–32.0 percentage points above a payload-free control (p < 0.001 for all). Self-poisoned libraries contain 4.9–9.0× the initially planted malicious skills. The deterministic in-context rate is 78.4% for every model; variation comes from conditional-copy rates (25.9% for GPT-OSS to 53.3% for DS-V4). Nearly every copied skill executes and reaches the C2 endpoint (callback rate trails ASPR by at most a few points). Task-family targeting (description-only change, same code bodies) raises ASPR by +11.8 to +26.9 percentage points, peaking at 86.7% on Qwen3's pytest family. In the five-round cascade with seeds removed, Qwen3 reaches 68% ASPR (self-sustaining worm); three of six models stay infected. The replacement-rate sweep on DS-V4 shows a sharp transition: r=0.25 sub-critical (infection dies), r=0.50 critical (~53% plateau), r=0.75 super-critical (60.1% and rising). Existing detectors fail: the name blocklist catches 0% of planted skills and 0% of authored infections; the Bandit code scanner falls from 85% to 7% after a one-line egress-primitive swap; the injection classifier has a 47% benign false-positive rate. The counter-prompt reduces ASPR to ≤6.7% across all conditions (headline ≤1.8%) with zero callbacks and no statistically significant task-completion loss. The attack generalizes across agent scaffolds (mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Claude Code), tool languages (Bash 39.2%, JavaScript 39.2%, Python 39.9%), and benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro: 24.6% for DS-V4 generic). Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The CREATE-path self-poisoning vulnerability — where the agent authors, stores, and propagates malicious code by imitating a retrieved skill — is genuinely new and distinct from REUSE-path skill poisoning (ToolHijacker, SkillTrojan, MalTool) and from experience/memory poisoning (OEP, SkillJack, MINJA) in that the carrier is executable agent-authored code with self-propagation. The banner-based imitation trigger is a new attack mechanism. The empirical finding that propagation persists after seed removal (a self-sustaining worm) and the branching-process characterization (joint necessity of copy rate and retrieval reach, Corollary 1) are new contributions. The Galton–Watson formalization itself is standard theory applied to a new setting; the counter-prompt defense is a straightforward system-prompt intervention whose value lies in the empirical demonstration, not algorithmic novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is a rigorously executed study. Every headline comparison uses Wilson 95% CIs and two-sided two-proportion z-tests with full statistics in appendix tables. The experimental configuration is locked (Table 12) with single-variable ablations for banner layers, planted-skill count, retrieval depth, poisoning density, replacement rate, and step budget. Some analyses (descendant copy rate, § D.6) use pre-registered protocols with commit timestamps predating results. The branching-model fit is honestly reported: the reproduction-number proxy overshoots absolute scale by ~10× and misorders DS-V4 and Devstral; the authors attribute this to retrieval crowding violating Assumption 1(ii) and explicitly flag the mechanism as not fully resolved. The paper commits to releasing six artifact sets (planted-skill generators, agent integration, sandbox wrapper, defenses, evaluation framework, per-task JSONs) with a Zenodo DOI. Potential concerns: the tool-relevant subset (153/500) was selected by a pre-specified keyword filter, which the paper acknowledges and partially mitigates with full-distribution results (25.8% ASPR unfiltered vs. 41.8% filtered); only one embedding model (BGE-M3) and one retrieval stack are tested; the benign library of 232 skills from MetaGPT and BigCodeBench may not match production diversity; the evaluation is on two SWE-bench variants, both Python-centric GitHub issue-resolution tasks. The work is a preprint (arXiv:2608.25776) and has not undergone peer review. Deployability: EMPIRICAL profile — the paper runs attacks and defenses on real agent stacks with instrumented sandboxes. - Practical: Yes — the attack requires only publish access to a skill marketplace; the defense (counter-prompt) requires only system-prompt access; all experiments run on standard hardware (2× 80 GB GPUs or commercial APIs). - Efficient: The attack is cheap to mount (construction runs in seconds, no model or runtime access needed); the counter-prompt adds negligible latency or compute; the signed gate requires curator infrastructure but no model changes. - Effective: The evidence shows real payload execution (C2 callbacks on a 127.0.0.1-bound server), not just a proxy metric — copied skills execute with the agent's privileges and reach the exfiltration endpoint in nearly every successful CREATE-path event. - Scalable: The cascade experiments test propagation across 5 rounds with rolling replacement, and the replacement-rate sweep identifies a critical threshold; however, production-scale libraries (thousands of skills, continuous task streams, multiple concurrent agents sharing libraries) are not tested, and the branching model's fit failures at even 5 rounds suggest extrapolation beyond tested scale is unsafe. The work delivers a software artifact (committed for release with Zenodo DOI): planted-skill generators, agent integration code, sandbox wrapper, defense implementations, cascade orchestration, and per-task result JSONs. The signed-quarantine gate is specified as a theorem with an EUF-CMA-security proof but is not implemented as a production system. Strengths: - Genuinely new vulnerability class: the CREATE-path self-poisoning mechanism is cleanly separated from all prior skill-poisoning and agent-memory-poisoning work, and the Table 1 positioning (payload-in-code + self-authorship + self-propagation) makes the novelty precise rather than rhetorical. - The banner ablation (Table 2) is a strong piece of mechanism identification: removing each of the three layers one at a time on DS-V4 produces monotonic ASPR drops (41.8% → 28.8% → 22.2% → 11.1%), directly attributing the attack to the banner's structural imitation rather than to imperative wording (which the paper shows can backfire, § B.3). - Corollary 1 (joint necessity of copy rate c and retrieval reach q) explains a non-obvious empirical pattern — DS-V4 copies most but collapses in the cascade while Gemma4 worms — that a single-factor account would miss, and the paper honestly documents where the model fails rather than overfitting a narrative. - The adaptive-attack robustness testing of the counter-prompt (Table 7: token renaming, authority escalation, non-imperative camouflage, dispersed phrasing, structural fusion) goes beyond the usual single-defense-evaluation pattern and shows the defense acts on the banner's semantic pattern, not surface tokens. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that (1) the branching-process proxy misorders two models and overshoots absolute scale by ~10×, attributing this to retrieval crowding violating Assumption 1(ii) but leaving the definitive crowding-source test to future work; (2) the counter-prompt is a soft, model-dependent control absent from default agents — not a hard guarantee; (3) a fully adaptive attacker that extracts the exact counter-prompt text and optimizes a banner against it remains open; (4) the signed gate trades the structural extinction guarantee for limiting self-evolution, and the curator-review variant introduces review error as a new trust boundary not formally analyzed; (5) the tool-relevant subset inflates headline ASPR relative to the full distribution (25.8% vs. 41.8% on DS-V4). The paper confronts these limitations directly rather than minimizing them — the model-fit failures receive a dedicated appendix (§ D.5) with a specific mechanistic hypothesis (descendant retrieval collapse: 0/765 re-retrieval opportunities for DS-V4 and MiniMax). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Only one embedding model (BGE-M3) and one retrieval stack (ChromaDB cosine top-k) are tested. The in-context rate (78.4%) is presented as deterministic, but a different retriever could shift the attack surface materially. - The counter-prompt's robustness is tested against prompt-level adaptive attacks but not against models fine-tuned or RLHF-trained to ignore system-prompt security instructions, nor against models where the deployer cannot modify the system prompt (closed API with fixed prompt). - The benign library of 232 skills is drawn from two research-oriented sources (MetaGPT, BigCodeBench); production skill libraries with heterogeneous quality, naming conventions, and community-contributed noise could shift retrieval competition and copy rates in untested directions. - The "no victim knowledge" claim for the targeted attacker is somewhat strained: choosing pytest-fixture, config-parsing, or regex-parsing as target families requires knowing which task families the deployment handles, even if the specific tasks are unknown. The paper treats "public task types" as sufficient, but a real attacker would need distributional knowledge of the victim's workload. - The cascade experiments run 5 rounds on a fixed task pool of 153 tasks; production agents face open-ended task streams where the library composition and retrieval dynamics could diverge substantially from the tested regime. - The paper reports that the attack succeeds on 0% of SymPy tasks and 16% of Django tasks, showing the attack depends on task-repository match with planted helpers — but does not explore whether an attacker could plant skills targeting a broader range of repository types to close this gap. Bottom Line: This is essential reading for anyone deploying self-evolving coding agents or designing defenses for them — it identifies a genuinely new attack class with unusually rigorous evidence, honest model-fit reporting, and immediately deployable mitigations; there is no stronger alternative covering the same ground.

#2 — Highly Innovative (81)

SilentProbe: Measuring Silent Failure in Production APIs Used as Agent Tools

Z Li, S Ye, F Guo, Z Dang · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SilentProbe, a static audit plus a schema-derived metamorphic differential probe that measures when production APIs silently ignore agent-sent constraints — returning HTTP 200 with plausible results that violate what the caller asked — and quantifies what this does to LLM agents downstream. - Why it's important: Agent tool-use benchmarks assume honest environments, and the most dangerous failure mode here — a well-formed, non-empty response that violates a stated filter — is absent from the field's noise taxonomies, yet it produces false negatives asserted to users 41% of the time and fabricated figures 12% of the time. - How it does it: It issues base/valid/perturbed call triples per parameter and compares result-count-plus-row-fingerprint signatures, classifying outcomes as honest error, normalised, silent empty, silent drop, or silent coercion, with the independent variable being whether the parameter's constraint is machine-checkable in the schema or stated only in prose. - The good: The headline effect is decisive and causally pinned: 111 of 111 machine-checkable perturbations failed honestly versus 44 of 61 prose-only ones failing silently (p = 2×10⁻¹³), and promoting the vocabulary into a one-line schema enum eliminated trap failures from 88/88 to 0/89 across eleven of twelve models. - The missing: The execution study rests on only 71 scored parameters across 27 vendors behind one aggregation layer operated by an author-affiliated company, the agent experiments cover only three vendors and three probed parameters, and the Fisher exact tests treat non-independent attempts sharing a base call as independent. - Read it or not: Read it if you build agent tool layers, MCP servers, or API-facing benchmarks — it hands you a measurable, one-line-fixable interface defect and a strong argument that simulated-tool robustness benchmarks are untested; skip it if you only care about model-side capability work.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (84) is the standout: the As-Is/Lifted schema-only manipulation isolates the causal variable, forced controls (parameter-inert exclusion, calibrated noise tolerance, throttle-vs-rejection disambiguation) are methodological contributions in themselves, exact p-values are reported, and code/schemas/transcripts/run-identifiers are released — docked only for clustered non-independent counts, single-model judging, and preprint status. Novelty (78) is a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first prevalence/predictor measurement of silent constraint failure on live APIs, plus the semantic-downgrade mode) with the metamorphic core honestly disclaimed as prior art. Non-Obviousness (82) is high — the disclosure-vs-machine-readability decomposition and the gateway-as-mechanism inversion are genuinely surprising insights. Completeness (88) is exceptional: limitations are confronted at length in dedicated paragraphs, including the author-affiliated aggregation layer and non-replicating prose-rate. Resilience (80) benefits from tightly bounded claims; Impact (72) is solid — released tooling, a one-line fix with a measured 100%-to-0% effect, and sub-$8 replication cost. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*84 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*88 + 0.15*80 + 0.10*72 = 81.

Problem & Motivation: When an LLM agent calls a third-party production API, two indistinguishable failures can occur: a well-formed query that genuinely matches nothing, and a query the server partially discarded, which returns a plausible superset. Both arrive as HTTP 200 with a parsable body — no exception, no status code, no error field — because the parameter's accepted vocabulary or format lives in a human-facing description sentence rather than the machine-readable schema, so no validator, gateway, or framework can enforce it. The authors show a motivating case: a people-search endpoint where "vice_president" returns zero rows (a synonym outside the vendor's hidden vocabulary) and a malformed range "51-200" is silently discarded, returning 160,884 records that mostly violate the requested range. Prior agent-robustness work either reimplements APIs locally (API-Bank, no vendor behaviour possible), simulates them (StableToolBench, MirrorAPI — a simulator generates responses consistent with documentation, and no documentation describes its own omissions), or injects model-generated noise (AgentNoiseBench) whose five categories omit the silent drop entirely. Nobody has measured prevalence or predictors of this failure class on live commercial APIs. Key Idea: The core insight is that silent failure is predictable from published artefacts before any call is made, and the trick is a mechanically derived differential probe: for each parameter, compare the signature — result count plus fingerprint of the first five returned rows — across a base call C, a valid-value call A, and a perturbed call B. sig(B)=sig(C) means the server accepted and discarded the filter (silent drop); B empty while A is not means silent empty; otherwise silent coercion. Because one schema validator sits in front of all vendors via the aggregation layer, the gateway-versus-vendor distinction becomes the mechanism rather than a confound: machine-readable constraints get rejected with actionable messages at the gateway, while prose-only constraints pass through and fail silently at the vendor. A secondary insight is that disclosure and machine-readability are separable properties — a vocabulary written out fully in prose is used correctly by models, one shown only by example ("e.g. 'executive'") is not, and only machine-readability enables non-model enforcement. Methodology: Three instruments in sequence. (1) A static, call-free audit walks published JSON Schemas over two populations — 469 endpoints behind the Monid aggregation layer (55 vendors) and 2,501 OpenAPI documents from APIs.guru (721,320 parameter leaves) — classifying each scalar leaf as machine-checkable (enum/pattern/format/bounds) or carrying a documentation-constraint gap (controlled vocabulary, bound, or format in prose with no schema keyword), with a critical design decision to propagate array-level descriptions down to items, where most vocabularies live. (2) A differential probe executes 219 perturbations from ten families (enum synonym, case, whitespace, separator, inflection, out-of-vocabulary, format variant, numeric range, type mismatch, parameter name) designed to model what a language model plausibly emits rather than maximise fault detection — the stated departure from random fuzzing — with four forced controls: parameter-inert exclusion, per-endpoint noise tolerance calibrated from a repeated base call (one endpoint drifted 3,216,043→3,216,042), valid-value rejection exclusion, and non-empty base requirement; every 4xx is confirmed by repeat since one vendor throttles with bare HTTP 400. (3) Agent experiments: vocabularies recovered by brute force on three vendors, tasks written in ordinary English avoiding vendor terminology, twelve models via OpenRouter under As-Is versus Lifted (vocabulary promoted to enum) conditions, tool restricted to three parameters after a finding that full 20-parameter schemas cause two models to fill unguessable fields in 100% of calls; a full agent loop (up to four executed turns) measures downstream harm, with answers judged by a separate judge model against a real-data control condition. The overall framework is metamorphic testing (they explicitly claim no novelty for the underlying equality/subset relations from Segura et al.) with the perturbation distribution, not the oracle, as the contribution. Key Results: Static audit: across 721,320 public parameters, 7.5% declare an enum, 15.2% any machine-checkable constraint, and 29.4% carry no description at all; 40.1% of public documents state at least one prose constraint their schema does not encode (20.9% on the aggregation-layer corpus — a non-replication the authors attribute to code-generated versus hand-authored specs). Probe: 219 perturbations over 71 parameters, 27 vendors — silent failure in 0/111 machine-checkable versus 44/61 prose-only cases, Fisher's exact p = 2×10⁻¹³; all 113 gateway rejections named the offending parameter and its legal values while all 14 vendor rejections were an unactionable "Invalid input: HTTP 400". Agents: example-only vocabularies failed 88/88 attempts across all twelve models versus 88–91% correct usage when vocabularies were fully written in prose (p = 1×10⁻¹²); the enum intervention dropped failures from 88/88 to 0/89 (p = 5×10⁻¹³) uniformly across model families, scales, and price tiers. Downstream: of 192 full loops (94 ending in zero rows), models detected the silent failure in 12% (11/94) and repaired it in 0/11 — synonym enumeration cannot converge on an unshown vocabulary by construction; 41% asserted a false negative to the user (28% unhedged), 12% fabricated a figure (e.g. "5 to 7 million engineers"). A boundary study on two further vendors produced zero silent-empty results and surfaced a fourth mode, semantic downgrade (23/23 models quietly substituted "used" for "certified pre-owned", returning 21 plausible wrong rows), which the mechanical oracle cannot detect; the enum fix also repairs it (23/179 → 0/176). Total campaign cost: under US$8. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first prevalence and predictor measurement of silent constraint failure in live APIs consumed by agents, plus the semantic-downgrade mode absent from existing noise taxonomies) and NEW METHOD (the mechanically schema-derived, model-emission-shaped perturbation probe with per-call run identifiers), with the differential relation itself correctly disclaimed as prior metamorphic-testing art. The engineering around it — aggregation-layer apparatus, four forced controls, run-identifier provenance — is competent execution of known testing ideas aimed at a new consumer (the agent and its user) rather than the API owner. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the strong sense are present: the As-Is/Lifted schema-only manipulation isolates the causal variable, the disclosure-coverage gradient (1-of-18 versus fully-shown vocabularies, same prose-only constraint form) is a natural dose-response experiment, and the real-data control condition rules out a general overclaiming tendency. Statistical reporting is explicit with exact p-values, and exclusions are enumerated with direction-of-bias reasoning (the inert exclusion can only make the silent rate an underestimate). Code, schemas, perturbation sets, transcripts, and per-call run identifiers are released at https://github.com/Jasper0122/silentprobe, with a re-fetch guarantee for every executed call. Methodological concerns: the 219-perturbation sample is small (61 prose-only scored cases) and clustered by vendor and parameter, so Fisher exact tests on per-attempt counts overstate effective sample size — the 88/88 attempts share 12 models and 3 parameters; judge labels are single-model with no human validation reported; the aggregation layer is author-affiliated (disclosed plainly, with the public-corpus audit designed so the prevalence claim does not rest on it); and the endpoint sample is a convenience sample (read-only, ≤$0.02/call, synthesisable baselines), not random — the authors say so. This is a preprint, not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (measurement study with a reusable probe method; no built service is proposed beyond the released tooling). - Practical: Runs on ordinary API access and a single gateway key; the entire campaign cost under US$8, so any lab or vendor can execute it. - Efficient: Cheap by construction — the static audit issues no calls, and model-call caching reduced 815 tool calls to 44 distinct API calls and 88 executions; replication after a fix costs minutes. - Effective: The evidence shows the probe detects the claimed failure class and that the intervention removes it at the source, but the proxy-to-real gap is real: the mechanical oracle is blind to semantic downgrade, the most deployment-relevant mode. - Scalable: The static audit already runs at 721,320 parameters and the authors argue automated documentation repair is tractable, but the executed probe was stress-tested only at 71 parameters/27 vendors and the authors themselves note that silent-drop detection requires base result sets in the hundreds-of-millions of rows for free-text parameters — 10× scaling of the dynamic probe is untested. The work delivers a released artifact (probe code, schemas, perturbation sets, transcripts, run identifiers) rather than a library or trained model. Strengths: (1) The mechanism-not-confound argument is genuinely clever: 110 of 111 honest errors came from the gateway validator and never reached the vendor, inverting the usual aggregation-layer objection into the paper's causal explanation. (2) The disclosure/machine-readability decomposition is a non-obvious intellectual contribution — it explains why models fail on "e.g." phrasing (88/88) while complying with fully-written prose vocabularies, and why the fix is one schema line rather than a better model. (3) The forced controls (parameter-inert exclusion, calibrated noise tolerance, throttling-versus-rejection disambiguation, non-empty base) are methodological findings in themselves, and the authors report that 17 of 37 dropped non-reproducing perturbations had been scored silent coercion — retaining them would have inflated the headline. (4) The downstream harm measurement with a real-data control condition is the right design: it separates exposure from harm and shows hedging (63% of trap loops) transfers rather than solves the problem. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length: the executed sample is a convenience sample through Monid (read-only, ≤$0.02/call); baseline synthesis succeeds more readily for enumerated parameters, correlating with the independent variable; the inert exclusion may hide genuine silent drops (bias direction: downward); silent-drop detection on free-text parameters requires enormous base result sets (only 2 of 9 suspected always-discarded parameters were conclusive, both above 246M rows); agent coverage is 3 vendors versus 27 for measurement; vocabulary recovery by brute force makes all counts lower bounds; the per-leaf prose rate did not replicate across corpora and they state the reason cuts against their scope; models are reached through one gateway rather than native APIs; and the competing interest — Monid is operated by an author-affiliated organisation — is stated in a dedicated paragraph rather than a footnote. This candour is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The independence assumption behind the Fisher exact tests is unaddressed: the 88/88 and 44/61 counts are clustered by model, vendor, and parameter, so effective sample size is far smaller than the nominal counts and the p-values flatter the evidence (though the effects are large enough to survive correction). (2) The agent study's trap parameters come from essentially one vendor's endpoint family (people/company enrichment) plus a car-listing and a voice endpoint; no evidence shows the effect generalises beyond data-enrichment-style APIs, and the authors' own boundary study showing two vendors with zero silent-empties hints the phenomenon may be narrower than the framing suggests. (3) The judge is a single LLM with no human agreement check, and it is given the ground truth that the zero was caused by a vocabulary mismatch — a potentially leading framing. (4) The probe's perturbation families and synonym lexicon are small and hand-published (Table 4, 20 entries); a caller emitting substitutions outside this lexicon is untested. (5) Vendor identity is anonymised in the paper, which limits independent verification of vendor-specific claims even with run identifiers. (6) The "constraint form, not vendor identity, predicts honesty" claim rests on a design in which machine-checkable constraints are almost entirely caught by one gateway's validator — the honest-error rate would look different with vendor-direct access, a comparison the paper argues is unnecessary but does not run. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent tool layers, MCP servers, or API-facing benchmarks gains something concrete and actionable — a cheap detectable interface defect, a one-line schema fix with a measured 100%-to-0% effect, and a sharp argument against simulated-tool robustness claims — and no stronger alternative currently covers this ground, provided the clustered-sample statistics and narrow vendor coverage are kept in mind.

The Emergent Symbolic Structure of Artificial Neural Networks

RT McCoy, P Soulos, T Linzen, P Smolensky · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper demonstrates that the vector representations of a wide range of neural networks — MLPs, GRUs, Transformers, and seven LLMs (8B–27B parameters) — can be closely approximated by explicit Tensor Product Representations (TPRs), such that replacing the network's entire representation-generating process with a closed-form TPR equation leaves behavior largely intact (e.g., mean causal-intervention accuracy of 0.903 across 31 intervention types on GPT-OSS). - Why it's important: It addresses the central puzzle of mechanistic interpretability — how vector-based systems excel at tasks (arithmetic, logic, code, language) that appear to demand symbolic structure — and offers a reconciliation of the symbolic-vs-connectionist debate, suggesting interpretability methods should model role-filler composition rather than atomic concepts. - How it does it: The DISCOVER procedure trains a separately parameterized model that is architecturally forced to be a linearly-transformed TPR (filler⊗role products summed, then an affine transform) to mimic a target model's encodings under MSE, then validates the approximation behaviorally by feeding it to the target's decoder. - The good: The causal-intervention results on GPT-OSS — where role edits (e.g., moving an adjective from object to subject position) change LLM output as predicted with accuracies like 0.978 (arithmetic position swaps) and 0.980 (adjective moves) — show the identified structure is causally implicated, not merely correlational. - The missing: The deep end-to-end analysis (representation replacement + interventions + generalization tests) covers only one LLM (GPT-OSS); the other six LLMs are analyzed only via period encodings with a surrogate decoder, so the breadth-vs-depth tradeoff leaves cross-model generality of the strongest claims unverified. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on mechanistic interpretability, vector symbolic architectures, or the neural-symbolic debate — it is the most systematic empirical case to date that LLM representations are implicitly compositional; skip it if you only want practical interpretability tooling, since the method is supervised and demonstrated mostly on constrained synthetic stimuli.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (80) is high — DISCOVER and TPRs are prior formalisms, but the first systematic demonstration of emergent role-filler structure across 7 LLMs with causal edits is a genuinely new empirical finding at scale. Rigor (85) is strong: 5-6 role-scheme baselines per setting, a 1/n! chance control, 10 reruns with error bars, extensive ablations, though partial code release and the supervised-scheme Goodhart risk on synthetic stimuli pull it down. Non-Obviousness (85) reflects the genuinely surprising result that decoders perform better on DISCOVER's clean TPR approximations than on real LLM encodings (0.96 vs 0.71). Completeness (80) is bolstered by unusually honest limitation acknowledgment (DISCOVER success doesn't prove exclusive use of the structure; synthetic-only scope), but the single-model depth (GPT-OSS) for the strongest claims and missing head-to-head comparison with SAE/DAS methods limit it. Resilience (78) is good — claims are well-bounded and objections anticipated — and Practical Impact (65) is limited to a partial codebase and an expensive (~3,000 GPU-hour) analysis technique. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*85 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*65 = 80.75 ≈ 81.

Problem & Motivation: Neural networks dominate domains traditionally modeled symbolically (language, mathematics, logic, code), yet they represent information as continuous vectors with no obvious symbolic structure. The Linear Representation Hypothesis — representations as sums of concept vectors — cannot capture order-sensitive structure ("dogs chase cats" vs. "cats chase dogs" would encode identically), so it fails to explain how vectors support structure-dependent computation. The binding problem (how elements are paired with positions) is the core open question. The relevant audience is the mechanistic interpretability community and cognitive scientists engaged in the eliminativist-vs-implementationalist debate about symbols; the gap this closes is moving from decoding-based findings that structural information is present in vectors to encoding-based findings about the structure of vectors themselves. Key Idea: Test whether a network's internal vectors can be replaced wholesale by a linearly-transformed Tensor Product Representation — a closed-form sum of filler⊗role binding terms passed through an affine map — without changing the network's behavior. If a TPR with an hypothesized role scheme (e.g., bidirectional positions, task-specific syntactic positions) trained to match the target encodings under MSE still yields correct outputs when substituted into the target's decoder, the target's representations are functionally equivalent to an implicit TPR. Because TPRs are highly constrained bilinear models, success is not guaranteed and is therefore meaningful; because TPRs are additive over role-filler pairs, they additionally enable precise part-level edits ("constituent surgery"). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages: (i) train or select a target model that solves a structure-dependent task; (ii) train a DISCOVER model — explicitly structured as W(Σ fᵢ⊗rᵢ)+b — minimizing MSE against the target's encodings, with fillers, role embeddings, W, and b as free parameters; (iii) evaluate by feeding the TPR approximation into the target's decoder and measuring "approximation accuracy" (proportion of test items decoded correctly). Multiple role schemes are competed as hypotheses: bag-of-words (null), left-to-right, right-to-left, bidirectional, Wickelroles, predecessor, syntactic (dependency paths), and task-specific schemes including pair-based roles motivated by attention's query-key interaction. For LLMs, the authors first verify that period-token encodings carry whole-sentence information (via 6-layer decoder-only "period-unpacking" models) before applying DISCOVER; for GPT-OSS they go further, replacing all input-token vectors across all 25 layers with TPR approximations and measuring end-task accuracy. Causal interventions subtract one role-filler pair's predicted contribution and add another (e.g., changing "3rd:Z" to "3rd:U"). Critical design decisions: (1) supervised role-scheme hypothesis selection, explicitly justified as isolating the "how" question; (2) the newly introduced bottleneck Transformer (decoder sees only the first position's vector) to force multi-item packing in one vector — reasonable but bespoke; (3) L2,1 regularization for generalization experiments, acknowledged as helpful but not ablated in depth. Key Results: (1) Letter-sequence tasks (copy/reverse/interleave, sequences of length 1–6, 26-letter alphabet, 50k training examples): bidirectional-role DISCOVER achieves ≥0.99 average approximation accuracy in 11 of 12 architecture-task combinations (lowest: 0.973 for the reversing bottleneck Transformer), across 10 reruns each; bag-of-words fails everywhere, validating that structure is encoded. (2) Period encodings across 7 LLMs (Gemma-3-27b, GPT-2-XL, GPT-OSS-20b, Pythia-12b, Qwen3-14b, OLMo-2-13B, Llama-3.1-8b) at 5 layers: DISCOVER matches or approaches the decoder's performance on true encodings; notably, on complex sentences the decoder does better from DISCOVER approximations than from real LLM encodings (e.g., GPT-OSS middle layer: 0.96 vs. 0.71). (3) GPT-OSS on 6 symbolic tasks (arithmetic, syllogisms, code execution, passivization, tense reinflection, question formation): the task-specific(all) scheme nearly matches the LLM's own accuracy (largest gap 2.36%, on arithmetic), after ~3,000 GPU-hours on H100/H200. (4) Causal interventions: 31 intervention types on GPT-OSS average 0.903 accuracy; e.g., 0.978 for arithmetic filler/position edits, 0.950 for moving a letter between lists in code, 0.892–0.980 for syntactic moves. (5) Generalization: DISCOVER trained with withheld role-filler pairs substantially beats the strong chance baseline (1/n!) for nearly all targets, evidencing systematic role-filler binding. Baselines are thoughtfully constructed (bag-of-words as null hypothesis; Wickelroles with 729 roles vs. bidirectional's 21 shows parameter count is not the driver). Scale is standard for small models but mid-scale for LLMs (8B–27B), with stimuli restricted to controlled synthetic grammars. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW METHOD (extension), with an ENGINEERING component (bottleneck Transformer). DISCOVER itself was introduced by McCoy et al. (2019) and constituent surgery by Soulos et al. (2020); what is genuinely novel here is (i) the first systematic demonstration that TPR structure emerges in modern LLMs across arithmetic, logic, code, and language, (ii) causal interventions on LLM behavior via closed-form representational edits at this scale, (iii) the generalization-to-novel-role-filler-pair test distinguishing systematic binding from atomic role-filler concepts, and (iv) the finding that clean TPR approximations can decode better than the original encodings. The overall framework is a known formalism (TPRs, 1990) applied with modern scale and controls, not a new mathematical formalism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive: 5–6 role schemes compared per setting (bag-of-words as null, Wickelroles as a parameter-count control, Appendix N addressing role-vocabulary-size confounds), 10 reruns for small models and 5 for LLM DISCOVER models with error bars throughout, layer-wise analyses, local-vs-full intervention comparisons, structure-sensitive vs. linear-order control interventions, and white-box sanity checks (Appendix M) verifying DISCOVER generalizes only when the target truly has systematic binding. The strong chance baseline (1/n!) is a principled control. Concerns: the role-scheme hypotheses are human-designed and evaluated on the same stimulus distributions they were designed for (a supervised-analysis Goodhart risk the authors partially acknowledge); the GPT-OSS end-to-end result covers a single model; and code is only partially released (github.com/tommccoy1/discover, with the complete codebase "pending employer approval" — a reproducibility caveat). Period-unpacking surrogate models introduce a possible evaluation indirection for the six non-GPT-OSS LLMs, though Section 6 explicitly designed the GPT-OSS experiments to close this gap. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (analysis method run on real systems, plus one new architecture). - Practical: Yes for the small models and the six period-encoding analyses (single A100 per LLM); the full GPT-OSS analysis required ~3,000 H100/H200 GPU-hours, feasible only for well-resourced labs. - Efficient: DISCOVER training is cheap relative to target-model training (small trainable TPR parameters), but scaling to all tokens × all layers of larger LLMs is expensive, as the 3,000-GPU-hour figure shows. - Effective: The evidence shows the identified TPR structure is causally implicated in behavior on the tested tasks (intervention accuracy 0.903 average), but only on narrow, grammar-constrained stimuli — it is a proxy for how LLMs handle naturalistic, partially-systematic input. - Scalable: Untested beyond ~27B parameters and beyond discrete, atomic filler/role vocabularies; the authors state that scaling to broad naturalistic stimuli likely requires an unsupervised variant of DISCOVER, which is future work. The work delivers a partial codebase (GitHub, incomplete at publication) and a reusable analysis technique; no trained artifact or library at production quality. Strengths: (1) The behavioral replacement criterion — swapping a network's entire representation pipeline for a closed-form equation and checking behavior survives — is a stronger standard of evidence than the decoding-based probes that dominate interpretability, and the paper clearly articulates why encoding-based analysis differs from decoding-based analysis. (2) The novel-role-filler generalization test with the 1/n! strong chance baseline directly rules out the atomic-concept alternative hypothesis, addressing a degenerate-solution concern that most representation-analysis methods ignore. (3) The counter-intuitive finding that decoders trained on real LLM encodings perform better on DISCOVER's noise-free TPR approximations (0.96 vs. 0.71 on GPT-OSS complex sentences) is a genuinely surprising result with theoretical teeth, marshaled as evidence for "limitivism" (approximate-but-not-exact symbol systems). (4) The scope of evidence — 4 architectures, 3 tasks, 7 LLMs, 6 symbolic task types, 31 intervention types with error bars — is unusually systematic for an interpretability paper. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are forthright: DISCOVER success does not prove the target uses only the discovered structure (a bidirectional scheme can degenerately implement a unidirectional one; paring down is left to future work); the method is supervised and requires human role-scheme hypotheses; success shows the structure of representations but not how networks compute them (the "feather vs. feather-growth" analogy); a successful DISCOVER fit cannot distinguish which member of the broader VSA family the target uses, since all major VSAs are special cases of linearly-transformed TPRs; the analysis is restricted to fully-systematic domains, leaving partially-systematic naturalistic settings unaddressed; and the emergent structure may depend on training data itself generated by symbolic systems. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The deep end-to-end claims rest on one LLM (GPT-OSS), which is a reasoning-tuned hybrid model with an unusual architecture (MoE, reasoning channels) — results might differ for vanilla autoregressive models, and the other six LLMs are evaluated only through the period-unpacking surrogate. (2) All stimuli are small-vocabulary, grammar-constrained synthetic datasets; no naturalistic text is analyzed, so the leap from "TPR structure on synthetic tasks" to "how LLMs handle language generally" is extrapolation. (3) The paper does not report whether DISCOVER's MSE fits or intervention accuracies vary systematically with model scale, layer depth patterns beyond qualitative description, or training-data properties that might predict when TPR structure emerges — the claim of broad generality would benefit from a failure-case analysis. (4) The comparison of DISCOVER to sparse-autoencoder and DAS approaches is largely conceptual; no head-to-head quantitative comparison shows DISCOVER captures structure those methods miss (or vice versa). (5) Role schemes for the task-specific (all) condition are derived from the authors' own parsing of the synthetic tasks — the possibility that these schemes are near-tautological for grammar-generated stimuli (the parser and generator share assumptions) is not fully excluded, though Appendix N partially addresses the capacity confound. Bottom Line: A practitioner in mechanistic interpretability or neural-symbolic research gains a lot from reading this: it sets a new evidentiary standard (full behavioral replacement + causal edits + generalization controls) and delivers the strongest empirical case yet that LLMs implicitly realize role-filler structure, though its synthetic-stimulus scope and single-model depth mean the naturalistic-language story remains open — no existing alternative covers this ground as thoroughly.

6.5% of the Neuro- Symbolic Literature Can Be Reproduced from Its Published Artifacts, a Six-Stage Audit Framework and First Instantiation

B Colelough, V Martirosyan, I Tamrakar, W Regli… · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a six-stage audit framework for same-artifact rerun reproducibility and instantiates it as a nine-month, eight-annotator audit of the neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) literature, measuring how many published studies can be independently rerun from their released artifacts. - Why it's important: NSAI publication volume is growing rapidly (single digits before 2019 to 138 papers in 2024), but if most empirical claims cannot be verified by independent execution, the field risks accumulating unfalsifiable results and wasted reproduction effort. - How it does it: A PRISMA-style pipeline (broad nine-database sweep, deduplication, eligibility screening, artifact verification, environment rebuild, bounded-repair rerun under a ±5% absolute-error fidelity criterion, data extraction) converts corpus statistics into per-paper audit outcomes O1–O5 with pre-registered inclusion/exclusion rules. - The good: The headline result is sharp and well-powered: only 85 of 455 code-bearing studies (18.68%, Wilson 95% CI 15.4–22.5) fully or partially reproduced — 6.52% of the 1,304-paper eligible corpus — while reruns with code, data, AND weights present succeeded 92.4% of the time (85/92), cleanly isolating artifact completeness as the dominant bottleneck. - The missing: The protocol forbids retraining when checkpoints are missing, so 89 papers (19.56% of failures) are counted as non-rerunnable even though the authors concede many may be reproducible in principle via retraining — meaning the 6.5% headline is a lower bound under one specific, and arguably strict, construct of reproducibility. - Read it or not: Essential reading for NSAI researchers, venue organizers designing artifact policies, and anyone conducting reproducibility audits; methodologists outside NSAI can safely extract just the protocol design and the venue-neutrality finding.

Problem & Motivation: Neuro-symbolic AI merges neural networks with symbolic reasoning, and its empirical papers frequently advertise public code, but no prior large-scale study has measured whether an independent team can actually rerun those pipelines and recover the reported results. The problem hits three constituencies: researchers who waste effort trying to build on unreproducible work, reviewers and venues who cannot verify claims, and the field collectively, which risks compounding unverified results. Prior reproducibility studies exist for recommender systems (Ferrari Dacrema et al.: 12/26 reproduced), deep RL (Henderson et al.), and NLP human evaluation (ReproNLP), but NSAI — with its multi-component pipelines where one missing checkpoint or rule set can invalidate the whole system — had not been audited at scale. The paper closes this gap with what it states is the first longitudinal, large-scale same-artifact rerun assessment in the subdomain. Key Idea: The core move is treating reproducibility auditing as a screened, staged pipeline in which selection criteria are fully decoupled from audit outcomes: once a paper enters the attempted-rerun pool, every failure is recorded as an outcome label (O1–O5), never as an exclusion, so sample attrition cannot inflate the success rate. The second key insight is the conditional decomposition: because reruns succeed 92.4% when the full artifact bundle exists but only 18.68% overall, the reproducibility crisis is located almost entirely in artifact provision, not in scientific validity of the methods or in code quality per se. Methodology: The six-stage framework proceeds: (1) corpus construction — a PRESS-validated query on nine digital libraries returned 5,497 records, deduplicated to 2,479; (2) single-blind title/abstract screening retained 1,365 self-described NSAI papers, with 61 more removed at full-text eligibility (criteria IC1–IC5, exclusions E1–E8); (3) artifact inventory — 849 records lacked any verifiable public code artifact, leaving 455 for rerun (65.11% attrition from code claims to verified artifacts); (4) environment build from author-supplied descriptors (Dockerfiles converted to Apptainer), with irreconcilable build failures labeled O5; (5) rerun of the primary experiment under bounded repair (annotators may patch paths, update deprecated packages, supply evaluation harnesses) with full reproduction defined as ±5% absolute error or within the authors' 95% CI, within a 7-day wall-clock cap on up to 4×A100/H100 nodes; (6) data extraction and 100% review of O1/O2 papers plus stratified sampling of O3–O5. Eight graduate annotators executed the audit over nine months after a 12-hour training program; a 10-paper calibration pilot yielded Cohen's κ = 0.82. Critical design decisions: (a) trained checkpoints are treated as indispensable (no retraining substitution) — justified as keeping the experimental object fixed, but this directly shapes the headline number; (b) pre-registered repair allowances — reasonable and documented; (c) exclusion of pre-2019 (n=8 attempts) and partial-2025 cohorts from trend analysis — justified by tiny denominators. Key Results: Of 455 attempted reruns, 48 (10.55%, CI 8.1–13.7) fully reproduced and 37 (8.13%) partially reproduced, for 85 successes (18.68%, CI 15.4–22.5); against the full eligible corpus of 1,304 this falls to 3.68% (full) and 6.52% (full or partial, CI 5.3–8.0). Failure attribution: 321/455 (70.55%) blocked by missing non-code artifacts — missing model weights 89 (19.56%), environment/dependency issues 79 (17.36%), incomplete codebases 67 (14.73%), these three accounting for 73.2% of missing-artifact failures — plus 42 (9.23%) with dead/private/empty repositories and only 7 (1.54%) that failed despite a complete artifact set. Conditional on complete code+data+weights, success was 85/92 (92.4%, CI 85.1–96.3). Reproduction rates stayed flat at 10.3%–22.1% annually from 2019–2024 despite the publication surge. Venue class showed no effect: conferences 21.1% (53/251), journals 16.5% (16/97), preprints 15.0% (16/107), χ² = 2.26, df = 2, p = .32; per-venue, arXiv 15.2%, NeurIPS 17.9%, ACL/EMNLP 20.0%, ICLR 23.8%, with ICML an outlier at 46.7% but only n=15. Citation impact did not predict reproducibility (fully reproduced bucket: mean 14.1, median 2; non-reproducible buckets had comparable means). Three case studies (Scallop, LogiCity, MARS) reproduced within ≤3 percentage points, showing gold-standard artifact bundles work across venue strata. Baselines here are prior reproducibility studies rather than algorithmic baselines; the scale (455 reruns) is the largest of its kind claimed for NSAI. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first quantified same-artifact rerun rate for the NSAI literature, with failure-mode and venue-neutral analyses) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (a reusable six-stage audit framework with public protocol, extraction forms, and per-paper logs). The individual techniques — PRISMA-style screening, ACM badging terminology, Wilson intervals, χ² tests — are standard; the novelty is the systematic instantiation at this scale in a new domain and the artifact-completeness decomposition, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is unusually strong on audit transparency: pre-registered inclusion/exclusion criteria with explicit separation of exclusions from outcomes, a calibration pilot with reported inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.82), Wilson CIs on all headline rates, a χ² test for venue effects, workload randomization across annotators, 100% review of positive outcomes, and a public archive (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21779234) containing per-paper logs, protocols, annotator materials, and scripts regenerating every figure, plus an interactive results browser. Ablation-equivalent evidence exists via the artifact-completeness conditioning. Methodological concerns: the ±5% fidelity threshold is a protocol choice not validated against field norms; the missing-checkpoint-no-retraining rule dominates the failure count (89 papers) and is acknowledged by the authors as construct-dependent; the venue analysis has small per-venue denominators (ICML n=15); the audit ran on a specific hardware/software stack (Zaratan cluster, Apptainer conversions), which could misclassify portability failures; and screening was single-blind, leaving room for selection drift. As an arXiv preprint (2608.26236), it has not yet undergone peer review, though the audit trail largely compensates. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a large-scale measurement study with a reusable protocol artifact). Practical: The audit method runs on ordinary HPC resources (single GPU nodes up to 4×A100/H100, 7-day caps) and the framework itself needs only spreadsheet/logistical tooling. Efficient: The full audit cost 8 annotators × 9 months (~64 records each) — substantial but tractable for a venue or well-resourced group; the paper argues automated pre-review artifact checks would be far cheaper. Effective: The evidence directly answers the stated question (can the artifact be rerun) for the attempted set, but measures rerunnability, not scientific correctness — papers without checkpoints may be retrainable, and no re-implementation-from-description condition was tested. Scalable: The pipeline is inherently parallel across papers; scaling to 10× the corpus would require proportional annotator labor unless stages 3–5 are automated, which the paper recommends but does not demonstrate. The work delivers concrete artifacts: the audit protocol, annotator training materials, per-paper reproduction logs, an extraction form, analysis scripts, and an interactive results browser — a reusable methodology, not a software tool in the library sense. Strengths: (1) The conditional decomposition — 92.4% success with complete bundles vs. 18.68% overall — converts a depressing headline into an actionable diagnosis with a concrete policy prescription (six-item artifact bundle, automated pre-review checks would address 363 of 370 failures). (2) The exclusion/outcome separation is a genuine methodological contribution to audit design, preventing survivorship contamination of the measured rate. (3) The venue-neutrality finding (overlapping CIs across conferences, journals, preprints) is a non-obvious, policy-relevant result that contradicts the assumption that top venues self-police reproducibility. (4) The three case studies spanning badge-audited, unbadged-conference, and preprint strata provide constructive existence proofs rather than only negative findings. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (a) missing-checkpoint cases are non-rerunnable under this protocol, not proof of scientific irreproducibility, since retraining might recover results; (b) severe documentation gaps and architecture-level defects (e.g., NaN losses from a fresh clone) remained hard failures; (c) stronger artifact requirements may burden under-resourced groups and create pressure to release restricted artifacts (in the Broader Impacts section, with proposed mitigations); (d) the 2025 cohort is partial and pre-2019 numbers are excluded from trend claims. They confront the retraining limitation directly and interpret their headline conservatively — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The ±5% absolute-error tolerance and the decision to treat checkpoints as indispensable jointly define the 6.5% headline; no sensitivity analysis shows how the rate moves under retraining-permitted or looser-tolerance variants, leaving the title's number protocol-bound. (2) The 849 papers excluded for lacking verifiable code are never audited even by inspection — some may be reproducible from paper descriptions, so the corpus-level picture is incomplete. (3) The annotation team and audit subjects come from the same community with no reported blinding to author identity or venue during reruns; annotator effort per paper is not reported, so differential effort across the 455 attempts cannot be ruled out. (4) The citation-impact analysis is purely observational with heavy zero-inflation and no formal test reported. (5) The claim that an automated pre-review audit "would address 363 of the 370 failures" assumes authors would not game or minimally-comply with the check — a policy extrapolation beyond the evidence. (6) The NSAI boundary itself is defined by author self-description ("neuro-symbolic"), which may misclassify borderline work in either direction. Bottom Line: This is the reference-point measurement for NSAI reproducibility — its protocol and artifact-completeness finding are immediately usable by venue organizers and will likely be cited whenever artifact-mandatory policies are debated — and no comparable audit of this subdomain exists, so practitioners and policy-makers should read it in full while treating the 6.5% figure as a protocol-specific lower bound rather than the field's true reproducibility ceiling.

#5 — Highly Innovative (81)

Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning (87 ▲ )

Heng Wang, Jielin Qiu, Wenting Zhao, Cheng Qian, Liangwei Yang, Jiawei Han, Heng Ji, Silvio Savarese, Shelby Heinecke, Huan Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Random Attention, a KV cache eviction policy that pins the prompt and evicts all other tokens uniformly at random per attention head with no scoring pass, and shows it matches the strongest score-based evictors on reasoning tasks while serving 32–43% higher throughput in vLLM. - Why it's important: Reasoning models generate chains of thought that make the KV cache the dominant memory cost in serving; if a score-free random policy matches learned selectors, the field's central premise — that token-importance scoring drives accuracy under eviction — is wrong, and method designers have been optimizing a signal that mostly protects the prompt by accident. - How it does it: The method forces prompt positions to an infinite score and draws i.i.d. Uniform(0,1) scores for everything else per KV head (one rand + one topk per eviction), and the explanation rests on two controlled findings: prompt protection, not the score, explains most gaps between selectors, and reasoning traces are redundantly stored in the text and across heads, so a random per-head draw retains enough copies of what the model still needs. - The good: The matched-protection experiment is the strongest evidence — once every baseline is given the prompt-pinning rule, the three baselines land within 2.2 points of each other in every tested setting, directly isolating the confound (prompt survival) from the selection signal, with paired clustered-bootstrap significance gating every claim. - The missing: All findings are confined to reasoning-style models and tasks (Qwen3, Phi-4-reasoning; math/science/code); there is no evidence on non-reasoning traces or long-context inputs where text-level redundancy may be absent, and the authors concede that once-stated facts (their passcode probe: Random Attention retrieves 0.000 vs R-KV's 0.836) are genuinely lost. - Read it or not: Anyone building or evaluating KV compression for reasoning models should read it — it is both a deployable default and a mandatory null baseline that invalidates prior cross-paper comparisons; researchers outside inference-memory work can safely skip it.

Rigor (82) is strong — paired clustered-bootstrap significance gating, multiple sampled runs, current 2024–2026 baselines reproduced within 0.5–2.3 points, and released code — docked mildly for R=2 cells on MATH500 and the R-KV hyperparameter deviation. Completeness (85) and Resilience (78) are high: the passcode probe honestly delineates where signals matter (R-KV 0.836 vs. Random 0.000 on once-stated facts) rather than overclaiming, and the null-baseline framing pre-empts the obvious objection that a better scorer would close the gap. Problem & Motivation Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, o1-style, Phi-4-reasoning) answer short questions by generating chains of thought of 10,000+ tokens, so during decoding the KV cache grows linearly with the trace and becomes the binding memory constraint: at 32k tokens a single full-attention Qwen3-32B sequence carries over 8 GB of KV. Eviction — permanently discarding key-value pairs under a fixed per-head budget — is the only route that bounds this memory (sparse-attention selection still keeps everything in RAM). Prior evictors (H2O, SnapKV, R-KV, VaSE, TriAttention) all instantiate the same paradigm: score each cached token by an estimate of future importance and keep the top-K, with the implicit premise that the score determines accuracy. The authors test that premise directly, motivated also by Chen et al. (2026)'s observation that differing prompt-protection regimes across papers make published comparisons incommensurable. Key Idea The core insight is a decomposition, not an algorithm: KV cache content splits into (1) the prompt — stated once, unrecoverable, hence the fragile part — and (2) the model's own reasoning trace, which protects itself through redundancy at two levels (the text restates what it still uses, and each of the H_kv heads holds its own copy of every token with eviction decided independently per head). Given prompt protection, a random per-head draw maximizes cross-head coverage, so the probability that a needed value survives in some head is high, and superadditive pooling across heads (their probe: one head retrieves 3%, two heads 60%, eight heads 99%) does the rest. The method is therefore simultaneously a deployable policy and a null hypothesis that any scoring signal must beat at matched budget and matched prompt protection. Methodology The method is four lines: at each eviction event (every r=64 decode steps, framework of R-KV/VaSE), assign score +∞ to prompt positions 1..ℓ_p, i.i.d. Uniform(0,1) to all others, and keep top-K per KV head (Algorithm 1); per-eviction cost is one rand and one topk over cache compaction. The evaluation uses four models (Qwen3-4B/14B/32B, Phi-4-reasoning) and six tasks (MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, pooled AIME 2025+2026, HMMT via MathArena, LiveCodeBench-v6 with pass@1 by test execution) at ~4× compression (~3× for code), 32k-token generation limit, with 2/4/16 independently sampled runs per cell and every margin gated by a paired problem-clustered percentile bootstrap (95% CI) plus exact sign test. Three critical design decisions: (1) pinning the entire prompt rather than only attention-sink tokens — well justified by the keep-log measurements showing SnapKV retains only 0.32–0.42 of prompt positions in union; (2) per-head independent draws rather than a shared draw — justified by the planted-fact probe, though the shared-draw ablation shows this costs nothing on real traces (within 0.3 points at 4× and 8×), so per-head scattering is load-bearing only for once-stated facts; (3) framing the method as a null hypothesis with matched-protection controls (§5.1) — this is the paper's real methodological contribution. The diagnostic apparatus includes a planted-fact probe (synthetic 4-digit facts inserted into real MATH500 traces, 1,536 tokens before the question, per-head pinning conditions, log-probability-based recall metric R) and a passcode probe for once-stated facts 57 compression rounds before the question. Key Results At ~4× compression, Random Attention is statistically tied with TriAttention (the strongest baseline) on math and science: e.g., Qwen3-4B MATH500 0.874 vs full attention 0.939 and TriAttention 0.864; GPQA-D 0.530 vs 0.562 full. Across the 60 baseline cells of the main grid (Tables 1 and 5), Random Attention is significantly ahead in 31 and behind in 1 (TriAttention on Qwen3-32B LiveCodeBench, ~3 points, attributed to code prompts averaging 557 tokens — 6× MATH500's — consuming up to half the K=3072 budget). SnapKV loses 20–35 points to Random Attention on LiveCodeBench across all models; VaSE collapses to 0.373 on Phi-4-reasoning (29 points behind). At 16× compression on Qwen3-4B, Random Attention holds 0.76/0.65/0.39/0.30 on MATH500/GPQA-D/AIME/HMMT. Matched protection closes most baseline gaps: SnapKV gains up to +35.2 points (LiveCodeBench, Phi-4) from the rule alone, and the three protected baselines land within 2.2 points of each other in every tested setting. Serving: in vLLM on one H200 at 32k generations, Random Attention delivers 1.58–2.67× full-attention throughput, 32–43% above TriAttention; at equal memory (K=3072) it reaches 10.0× and 8.8× full attention (28.8× at K=1024), with eviction rounds of 0.30 ms vs TriAttention's 1.47–1.64 ms. Notably, at short generations (8k out) compression pays nothing: Random Attention serves only 0.52–0.96× full attention. Baselines are current (2024–2026 methods including VaSE and TriAttention from 2026) and run in the authors' shared engine at matched budgets, with reproduction checks against published numbers within 0.5–2.3 points. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (primary) plus NEW METHOD (deliberately trivial) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (vLLM integration). What is genuinely novel is not the policy — prompt-pinning plus random eviction is a two-rule method adjacent to StreamingLLM and concurrent Prefix Sliding — but the controlled demonstration that the selection signal contributes almost nothing once prompt protection is equalized, with a mechanistic account (two-level redundancy, superadditive cross-head pooling) that prior work on reasoning-trace eviction (R-KV, VaSE, TriAttention) did not establish. The Garcia (2026) preprint reports a related protection-dominates-scoring result for long-context QA under a global cap, but the decode-time long-generation regime, the cross-head redundancy analysis, and the serving-cost analysis are new here. Rigor & Reproducibility Rigor is above average for this subfield. Ablations are present and informative: matched-protection grids across 15 model-task settings (Appendix C), shared-draw vs per-head controls, block-size sweeps, compression sweeps from 2× to 16×, and keep-log instrumentation over 19 policy-cell logs recording survival by age. Multiple sampled runs (2–16 per cell) with run-to-run standard deviations reported per cell (Table 8), and every claimed margin gated by paired clustered bootstrap plus sign test. Code is released at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/Random-Attention. Concerns worth flagging: MATH500 cells use only R=2 runs; baseline hyperparameters required judgment calls (R-KV run at λ=0.5 rather than the recommended λ=0.1, which the authors report scores 7–9 points lower — they justify this via reproduction of Chang et al.'s cells, but the choice flatters R-KV, the paper's main needle-finding contrast); the equal-memory TriAttention row is an unfused re-implementation the authors themselves disavow for method-level claims; and the throughput evaluation against score-based methods in vLLM covers only TriAttention (only method with a compatible port). The grading is by boxed final answer, a coarse proxy, though LiveCodeBench uses real test execution. The preprint's transparency about negative controls, failed runs, and tooling pitfalls is unusually high. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a SYSTEMS-grade serving evaluation (vLLM v0.19.0 with PagedAttention on H200). Practical: Yes — runs on a single 143 GB H200 with no calibration, tuning, or training, and integrates into an existing vLLM eviction plugin as a single function. Efficient: Best-in-class among tested evictors — no scoring pass (0.30 ms/round vs 1.47–1.64 ms for TriAttention), smallest peak footprint (89–101 GB), and 32–43% serving throughput margin over the strongest baseline at 32k generations. Effective: The evidence supports the stated claim (accuracy parity at matched budget on reasoning tasks), but only within that regime — at short generations compression itself yields 0.52–0.96× full-attention throughput, and once-stated facts are unrecoverable (retrieval 0.000). Scalable: Tested to 32B parameters and 32k-token generations at up to 16× compression; the mechanism (redundancy) is argued, not proven, to hold at longer traces or larger models, and very long prompts are acknowledged to break prompt pinning on code tasks. Delivers a software artifact: public code with the eviction policy, probe instruments, and per-instance logs; no trained model weights needed. Strengths - The matched-protection experiment (§5.1) is a genuinely incisive control: by equalizing prompt survival across methods and ordering the payoff by measured prompt-retention deficit (SnapKV +12.6 to +35.2 points, R-KV ≤1.9), it converts a confound into a quantified explanation and retroactively reconciles contradictory published results (prior papers showing random baselines failing badly were losing the prompt). - The planted-fact probe establishes a new, reusable instrument for studying cross-head redundancy, with a counter-intuitive quantitative finding: cross-head pooling is strongly superadditive (1 head 3%, pair 60%, all 8 heads 99%) and the shape of surviving copies is irrelevant (scattered tokens 0.33 vs intact sentence 0.39 retrieval). - The paper operationalizes its own thesis by serving as both method and null baseline, and the dual framing is honest: the passcode probe (Table 3) shows exactly where signals matter (R-KV 0.836 retrieval vs Random Attention 0.000), delineating the boundary of the result rather than overclaiming. - The efficiency analysis dissects why a cheap scoring pass costs 32–43% in paged serving (barrier-synchronized compressions ~62k times per workload; attention statistics unavailable from fused kernels) — an engineering insight independent of the accuracy result. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state: (1) on code reasoning, pinning the entire prompt consumes a large and variable share of the budget (up to half of K=3072), and compressing scaffolding is left to future work; (2) once-stated, never-restated facts are lost by construction, and only a content-dependent signal can preserve them; (3) the protected grid was not run on Qwen3-14B; (4) the equal-memory TriAttention throughput row reflects an unfused re-implementation, not the method's attainable speed; (5) at short generations compression yields no gain over full attention. These are confronted directly rather than minimized — several (the re-implementation caveat, the concurrency-cap confounds, the tooling pitfalls) are documented in dedicated appendix sections, which is a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps - Generalization beyond reasoning-style traces is untested and structurally at risk: the two-level redundancy argument is specific to chains of thought that restate working state; long-context inputs, summarization, or retrieval-style tasks may lack text-level redundancy, in which case per-head random eviction should degrade — the paper never tests a non-reasoning task even as a control. - All four models are reasoning-tuned (Qwen3, Phi-4-reasoning); a base model's trace statistics could differ, and the claim that "reasoning traces seldom produce once-stated facts" is asserted from the passcode probe and citation rather than measured at scale across traces. - Accuracy is graded by final boxed answer, which cannot detect silent corruption of intermediate reasoning quality, and the planted-fact probe, while clever, uses scripted token forcing whose ecological validity for genuine self-generated traces is validated only by the instrument's internal checks. - The throughput comparison in vLLM covers one baseline; the 32–43% margin over score-based methods generally is extrapolated from TriAttention alone, and SnapKV/VaSE lack paged ports (the authors document why porting is substantial work, but the gap remains). - The R-KV λ=0.5 hyperparameter choice, while defended by reproduction, deviates from the original recommendation, and the R-KV comparisons (including the passcode result that motivates the "what is left for a signal" narrative) inherit this choice. Bottom Line This is one of the most useful negative-result papers the KV-compression literature has produced: a practitioner serving reasoning models should adopt prompt-pinned random eviction as the default and the mandatory baseline, and any future eviction scorer that cannot beat it at matched budget and prompt protection should be presumed to be measuring prompt survival rather than selection skill.
