Problem & Motivation: KGQA pipelines that couple GNN reasoning with retrieval-augmented generation process a question through four stages (entity linking, subgraph retrieval, GNN reasoning, answer generation), and standard robustness evaluation collapses all stage-level failures into one end-to-end metric. Practitioners deploying these systems cannot tell which stage fails first or how failures propagate, so they cannot target mitigation. Prior robustness work on RAG assumes corpus-side adversaries who can poison the KG or index — a strong, often unrealistic capability — and prior KGQA perturbation studies (e.g., Perçin et al., 2025) apply surface-form noise without per-stage attribution. This paper closes that gap with a query-only threat model: the adversary need only submit a reworded question. Key Idea: The core insight is answer presence ≠ answer reachability: a retrieved subgraph can contain the gold answer entity while its PPR-derived topology remains anchored to the original reasoning chain, making the answer unreachable under a restructured hop order. Operationally, the enabling trick is the stage-isolation protocol — three configurations (clean baseline, full pipeline on perturbed question, clean subgraph with only the question text replaced) whose pairwise gaps decompose total degradation into subgraph-attributable (δ_SG) and decoder-attributable (δ_DEC) components. Methodology: The paper formalizes GNN-RAG as a function composition q → E_q → G_q → c_q → â (ELQ entity linker, Personalized-PageRank subgraph retrieval, three-layer GAT/ReaRev reasoner, fine-tuned Llama-2-7B generator). Two primary attacks are generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and certified against a local Virtuoso Freebase endpoint: CR (one KG-safe structural operation — hop-order reversal, distractor constraint injection, or intermediate-entity alias substitution) and RS (predicate synonym replacement), both preserving SPARQL denotation with entity mentions unchanged, filtered by PPL < 50, BERTScore > 0.85, and verified denotation equality. Per-stage metrics include Δ_EL (SeedHit drop), Δ_SR (triple-level Jaccard drift), α_pert (answer presence in perturbed subgraph), and Δ_AG (EM drop with bootstrap 95% CIs, n=1000). Critical design decisions: (1) answer-preservation verified against the KG rather than trusted from the generator — well justified, with manual inspection of 500 samples per type; (2) swap-in of alternative retrievers (GraftNet-Orig, NSM, GraftNet with GEM oracle seeds, EPR-KGQA) under a fixed GNN checkpoint — well justified as an architectural control; (3) a MetaQA (non-Freebase) end-to-end replication — well justified as it converts a claimed mechanism into a tested one. A key honest caveat: GEM seeds are gold SPARQL entity MIDs unavailable at deployment, and the paper carefully reports the deployment-realistic ELQ+cosine configuration (14.98% CWQ CR) alongside the oracle upper bound (29.82%). Key Results: On CWQ (3,531 test questions) and WebQSP (1,639), clean GNN-RAG achieves 52.9% and 74.3% EM. Under CR with ELQ retrieval, EM collapses to 0.68% (CWQ, Δ_AG = 52.2 pp [50.5, 53.8]) and 0.49% (WebQSP), despite 74.0%/94.6% answer presence and ≤0.3 pp SeedHit degradation. Stage isolation attributes 52.08 pp of the 52.22 pp CWQ CR drop to subgraph failure (clean-subgraph + CR question: 52.76% EM). GraftNet with oracle GEM seeds reaches 29.82% CWQ CR at 63.3% answer coverage — lower coverage but higher EM than ELQ, because question-weighted PPR reorients mass toward the restructured chain. RS is milder (20.31% CWQ, 50.95% WebQSP with ELQ), measuring decoder sensitivity in isolation. Architectural controls: EPR-KGQA (single-shot pattern retrieval) retains 59.22% CWQ Hit@1 under CR and GMT-KBQA (S-expression generation) drops ≤5 pp, while ExplaiGNN (iterative, Wikidata) collapses >70% relative on ConvMix. Inference-time path injection into RoG recovers 51.43% CWQ Hit@1 without fine-tuning, matching path-augmented training within 1 pp. Across a 24-cell ablation grid, α_pert correlates with EM at Spearman ρ = 0.91, but the ELQ-CR cells are the informative exception that inverts the relationship. MetaQA replication confirms the vulnerability tracks the retrieval algorithm: CR costs only 6.91 pp on MetaQA-3 vs. 52.22 pp on CWQ, and end-to-end re-execution changes Hit@1 by ≤0.6 pp under CR. Baselines (GraftNet-Orig, NSM, EPR-KGQA, GMT-KBQA) are current published systems with authors' checkpoints. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus NEW METHOD (evaluation methodology, not a defense). The genuinely novel elements are the stage-isolation protocol with KG-verified answer-preserving perturbations, and the presence-vs-reachability finding that inverts the assumed relationship between subgraph coverage and accuracy. The components — LLM-based question rewriting, PPR retrieval, existing checkpoints — are standard; the contribution is the attribution framework and the resulting diagnosis, not a new model. Concurrent work (Zhou et al., 2026) arrives at the subgraph bottleneck from the corpus side, which the authors cite. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Ablations are extensive: seeds × PPR-flavor decoupling (Table 11), NSM-LSTM decoder replication of the robustness finding (ruling out a ReaRev artifact), seven perturbation types, Bonferroni-corrected 99.8% CIs that all five primary conclusions survive, and manual validation of 500 perturbations per type. Bootstrap CIs are per-comparison and the authors say so explicitly. Code and perturbed datasets are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/atkgrag-E85C under CC BY 4.0. Concerns: (1) the headline collapse is established on one production pipeline and two Freebase benchmarks, with the cross-KB generalization carried by MetaQA and a qualitatively-scoped ExplaiGNN run rather than a full Wikidata replication of GNN-RAG; (2) the GraftNet headline number uses oracle GEM seeds — the paper flags this transparently, but the 29.82% figure could be quoted out of context; (3) perturbation pass rates imply fallback-to-original for 4–14% of questions, which the authors handle by noting severity is a conservative lower bound. The evaluation uses the authors' own perturbations but verifies them against an independent SPARQL endpoint, avoiding self-certification. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored released artifact). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on 4×A100-80GB with public checkpoints (GNN-RAG, ELQ, RoG, Llama-3.1-8B); the attack itself is a single submitted question. - Efficient: Inference is cheap (≈2 s per perturbation via API; total ≈800 A100-hours for all experiments); the expensive component is the certification infrastructure (70B rewriter + local 140 GB Freebase endpoint), which the authors correctly assign to the evaluator, not the adversary. - Effective: The evidence shows the diagnosis works — path injection recovers 51.4% CWQ EM without retraining, directly validating the attribution — but the proposed partial mitigations do not restore clean baseline accuracy (best deployment-realistic CR result is 14.98% vs. 52.9% clean). - Scalable: Not tested beyond these benchmarks; Freebase is a static 2015 dump and the paper does not examine how PPR topology fragility behaves on larger or dynamically updated KGs. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: perturbed datasets, evaluation code, and the stage-isolation harness. Strengths: - The presence-vs-reachability decomposition (74.0% α_pert → 0.68% EM, with the 2,588-question "present-but-unreachable" bucket) is a genuinely counter-intuitive, precisely quantified finding that end-to-end evaluation structurally cannot produce. - The isolation design is unusually clean: swapping retrievers under a frozen GNN checkpoint, and swapping question text under a frozen subgraph, gives two independent attribution paths that agree (52.08 pp subgraph-attributable from both directions). - The MetaQA replication converts what could have been a Freebase-specific anecdote into a tested mechanism claim — CR costs 0.11–6.91 pp where PPR is absent vs. 52.22 pp where it is present, with generator and filters held fixed. - Statistical hygiene above the norm for this area: Bonferroni-corrected CIs reported in an appendix with explicit statements of which conclusions survive, and sub-1 pp differences explicitly treated as ties. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: single system (GNN-RAG/ReaRev) and two Freebase benchmarks; uncorrected per-comparison CIs (mitigated by Appendix M); no UniKGQA checkpoint; Freebase deprecation with only partial Wikidata evidence (ExplaiGNN) and a full GNN-RAG Wikidata replication deferred; GEM oracle seeds unavailable at deployment; and that the threat model is an offline diagnostic stress test rather than a resource-constrained attacker model, since certification requires infrastructure the attacker does not need. They confront these directly and quantify the deployment-realistic vs. oracle gap rather than minimizing it — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged single-pipeline scope, a reviewer would flag: (1) the RS residual drop (32.6 pp CWQ) is attributed to "subgraph divergence between GEM and ELQ seeding" (triple Jaccard 0.041), but the mechanistic explanation of why identical seeds under RS preserve topology while CR does not, given identical SeedHit, is asserted through the PPR-anchoring story more than directly measured across many examples (only 4 in the visualization; only 2 case studies per failure mode); (2) the path-injection defense is evaluated only via RoG's own path predictor on the same clean training distribution, so its robustness under adaptive attacks (attacker aware of path injection) is untested; (3) perturbation naturalness is validated by PPL/BERTScore thresholds calibrated on Freebase-backed questions only — the authors note the multilingual transfer caveat but not the possibility that these filters systematically select perturbations of one stylistic family, narrowing the effective attack diversity; (4) all perturbations come from a single generator model (Llama-3.3-70B), so generator-specific artifacts cannot be ruled out. None of these undermines the headline attribution, which is multiply corroborated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or hardening GNN-based KGQA systems should read this — it converts an invisible 52-point fragility into a specific, actionable target (PPR subgraph topology, not the GNN or the linker) backed by released tooling, and it is the first work to make stage-level robustness attribution on these pipelines measurable rather than assumed.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper reports a pre-specified case study showing that a conformal test martingale monitor gating the online updates of a Kalman adapter on frozen time-series foundation models fires on 135 of 135 real clean-stream runs at α = 0.05 (where Ville's inequality would cap expected fires near 7 of 135), and that the gate's drift response amplifies the very transient it was designed to prevent. - Why it's important: Anytime-valid monitoring is moving from theory into deployed ML systems, but its finite-sample false-alarm guarantee holds only under exchangeability of the monitored score stream — a premise that fails inside feedback loops where the monitor modifies the learner whose scores it reads, turning a "safe" monitor into a source of catastrophic interventions. - How it does it: The authors run a three-arm gated deployment (full gate, Huber-only, SGD surrogate) across 5 streams × 3 backbones × 3 seeds, then use exchangeable null controls, drift-free synthetic pipeline controls, component ablations, and single-step mechanism traces to attribute the pervasive firing and the amplification to specific components. - The good: The attribution chain is unusually clean: the identical implementation fires at most 1 of 60 runs on exchangeable inputs (so the construction is not at fault), 60 of 60 on drift-free synthetic scores produced by the pipeline's own adaptation (so the loop is), and a soft-reset-only ablation reproduces the weather-stream divergence in 6 of 6 runs while a boost-only arm diverges in 0 of 9. - The missing: Every claim is scoped to one gate configuration on one deployment; no second monitor architecture, no theoretical account of the firing mechanism under loop dependence, and no demonstration that the recommended fixes generalize beyond these five datasets and three backbones. - Read it or not: Read it if you deploy or build sequential change-detection or anytime-valid monitors on dependent data — it is a concrete, well-controlled existence proof of premise failure — but skip it if you only want new methods, since it deliberately delivers a negative result.

Problem & Motivation: Operators of online ML systems increasingly delegate intervention decisions to statistical monitors, and anytime-valid inference (conformal test martingales under Ville's inequality) is the advertised instrument because its false-alarm guarantee holds at every stopping time. That guarantee is conditional on exchangeability of the monitored score stream — a premise that is hardest to satisfy exactly where these monitors are most attractive: on dependent real data and inside loops where the monitor's actions change the learner producing the scores. Prior work (Ramdas et al., Vovk et al., Shin et al.) establishes the theory and proposes e-detectors and e-processes but does not measure whether deployed implementations keep the premise on real streams, nor what happens downstream when the premise fails. This paper measures both, in one frozen, pre-registered deployment. Key Idea: The core insight is an attribution result, not a technique: pervasive martingale firing on real streams originates in the monitored score stream itself — the adaptation loop's own serially dependent innovations break exchangeability even with zero drift in the data — and the damage comes from what fires trigger, not from the martingale: repeated re-fires hold the drift response's Q-boost permanently active (measured 9.6× at the event step), so the gated filter amplifies a self-excited transient up to 12× the ungated error, with the covariance soft reset plus immediate full-vector label reveal identified as the sufficient cause of divergence. The methodological corollary — pair any anytime-valid claim with a null-calibration control of the deployed implementation at its horizon, raw clean-stream fire counts, and mechanism traces — is the paper's transferable "trick." Methodology: The deployed object is a per-step linear black-box stacking adapter (horizon 96, state dimension 192) maintained by a Kalman filter with online Adam-tuned hyperparameters (λ, Q, R), correcting three frozen backbones (TiRex, Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5) on five standard forecasting streams (ETTh2, ETTm1, weather, electricity, traffic; test blocks 12,922–52,117 steps). The gate's nonconformity score is the filter's standardized innovation; the monitor is a simple-mixture conformal test martingale (K=19 grid values ε ∈ [0.05, 0.95]) over randomized conformal p-values from a 250-step sliding calibration window, threshold 1/α, reset on fire. A decision table maps each step to normal / huberize / skip / sustained drift; drift declares on M_t ≥ 1/α and triggers a 10× Q-boost decaying over 50 steps, a covariance soft reset, and a forgetting-factor switch. Three arms isolate components (full gate; Huber-only with drift response disabled; SGD surrogate driven from a trailing mean-square score). Protocol: deterministic cached-forecast replay, immediate-reveal streaming (consecutive 96-step labels overlap in 95/96 entries — a mechanical source of serial dependence the authors flag), fraction-pinned contamination injectors (spike, level-shift, stuck at 1/5/10% of steps applied to the update channel only), a magnitude divergence guard, three seeds, and version-stamped pre-specified verdicts with a composite pass criterion (gated arm must beat ungated per contamination kind on ≥3 of 5 comparable cells for every kind). Controls include exchangeable i.i.d. score streams (pre-filled vs deployed empty-window initialization, T = 20,000 and 52,117), drift-free synthetic streams fed through the full deployed pipeline, delayed-feedback (96-step) ablations, soft-reset-only/boost-only/forgetting-only component ablations, a martingale-free fixed-threshold cutoff arm, and SR/CUSUM e-detector replay on the committed p-value streams. Key Results: On exchangeable synthetic streams the deployed construction is quiet: 0 of 60 fires (pre-filled window), 1 of 60 (deployed empty-window start), 0 of 60 (heavy-tailed scores), at both horizons. On the five real streams at α = 0.05, all 135 clean runs fired (first fires at steps 6–4,274, median 460; 18–1,340 total fires per run), against Ville's implied cap near 7 of 135. Ljung-Box rejects whiteness at p < 0.01 in 119 of 135 runs, though the authors show the portmanteau over-rejects under heteroskedasticity and is inconclusive. On drift-free synthetic data passed through the full pipeline, 60 of 60 runs fired (33–42 fires each, first fires within 67 steps), while an i.i.d.-score control with the same empty-window start fired 1 of 60 — the loop's own adaptation breaks the premise. The weather transient: full-gate per-step MSE reaches 1.155 × 10^5 versus 9.8 × 10^3 ungated; final cumulative MSE rises from 0.36 to 2.6–3.1; on TiRex and Chronos-2 the clean stream itself diverges in 6 of 6 runs at step 18,536, and in 54 of 54 contaminated weather runs; the soft reset is sufficient for divergence, the boost alone is not, and the catastrophe requires immediate full-vector reveal (with 96-step delay, 0 of 9 diverge). The useful half: Huber-only gating cuts isolated-spike degradation roughly an order of magnitude — +3.32→+0.15 (ETTh2), +3.73→+0.11 (traffic), +2.68→+0.63 (ETTm1) versus ungated Kalman — and a martingale-free fixed-threshold cutoff holds spike degradation to ≤ +0.05 everywhere (at a backbone-dependent clean-weather cost up to 9.5× on TimesFM 2.5). Negative results: level-shift contamination degrades every arm by +7.8 to +19.3 (ETTh2/ETTm1) and +9.5 to +18.3 on traffic; stuck injectors degrade the full gate by up to +14.2 versus ≤ +1.8 ungated; on synthetic piecewise drift the full gate adapts more slowly than the ungated filter on all three seeds (latency 154.8/137.5/128.0 vs 126.8/128.0/95.2 steps) with ~4× worse final MSE; the pre-specified composite criterion fails on 3 of 3 backbones. E-detectors replayed on the committed p-streams alarm in 135 of 135 runs at every tested threshold (SR at A = 10^4: 193/320/1,464 min/median/max alarms vs expected 1.3–5.2), so a detector swap does not repair the premise. Baselines are the ungated Kalman and SGD learners plus ablated gate variants — appropriate for a case study, but no external gating methods are compared. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, plus a methodological recommendation (null-calibration controls and mechanism traces as mandatory companions to anytime-valid deployment claims). The building blocks — conformal test martingales, Ville's inequality, Kalman filtering, Huber robustification, e-detectors — are all standard; what is genuinely new is the measured quantification that a deployed martingale monitor breaks its premise on real score streams inside a self-modifying loop, the causal decomposition of the resulting amplification, and the honest quantification that the benefit lives entirely in the guarantee-free robust-update half. There is no new method, dataset, or formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for its genre: all verdicts, exclusion rules, and contamination severities were version-stamped before runs, with an errata trail and a pre-specified composite criterion that the authors report failing against their own gate; deterministic cached-forecast replay, three seeds per cell, and component/feedback ablations (Appendices B–C) trace specific mechanisms (soft reset sufficient for divergence; immediate reveal necessary). Null controls at 60 runs per condition are acknowledged as unable to certify strict conservatism, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported beyond per-cell ranges across 3 seeds. Code and artifacts are stated to be released (anonymized during review); no public URL is yet given. Methodological concerns: every quantitative claim is about a single gate configuration on a single deployment (the authors say so explicitly); the immediate-reveal protocol is optimistic relative to real deployment; divergence-table cells losing runs are survivor-only and read qualitatively; and the study develops and evaluates on the same five benchmarks, so there is a mild risk the conclusions are configuration- and benchmark-bound rather than general. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — a built gating pipeline evaluated by deployment replay). - Practical: Yes — pinned public checkpoints (google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch, TiRex, Chronos-2) and a filter costing 0.163× one-step SGD; the gate's conformal/martingale path is not counted in that figure, but nothing suggests exotic hardware. - Efficient: The kept component (Huber-style update gating) is essentially free relative to the base filter; the martingale path's cost is unquantified. - Effective: Split — the robust-update half demonstrably solves isolated-spike degradation on the three affected datasets, but the full deployed gate fails its own pre-specified composite criterion on all three backbones and actively causes divergence on clean data, so the headline object does not solve the stated problem. - Scalable: Not tested and not claimed — results cover five datasets, three backbones, three seeds, and streams up to 52,117 steps; the authors scope every claim to this single deployment rather than projecting to larger scale. The work will deliver a software artifact (deterministic replay code, null-control scripts, run artifacts with raw counts), currently stated as forthcoming; no trained model weights are contributed beyond pinned third-party checkpoints. Strengths: - The attribution chain is genuinely rigorous: three independent controls (exchangeable i.i.d. scores, drift-free synthetic data through the full pipeline, i.i.d.-score control sharing the deployed window initialization) jointly isolate the adaptation loop's score stream as the premise-breaking element, something most anytime-valid papers never test at all. - Pre-specification is real, not decorative — the composite gate criterion was committed before runs, and the paper reports its failure on 3 of 3 backbones, a self-incriminating negative result. - The single-step mechanism trace (Figure 2) of a self-exciting feedback loop — re-fires every 5–10 steps holding the Q-boost at 8–10× through an elevated-error episode, culminating in a 12× per-step MSE amplification — is a rare, concrete demonstration of how a statistically "safe" monitor becomes harmful through its response policy. - The practical salvage is quantified honestly: the guarantee-free Huber/fixed-threshold gating delivers the measurable benefit (+3.32→+0.15 spike degradation on ETTh2), and the paper explicitly warns against crediting it to the anytime-valid framing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and extensively. They state that all claims concern one gate configuration on one deployment; that 60-run null controls cannot certify strict conservatism; that the Ljung-Box diagnostic over-rejects under conditional heteroskedasticity (with a shipped counterexample) and that the weather portmanteau value is a lower-tail degeneracy artifact; that the immediate-reveal convention is optimistic for real deployment and itself mechanically induces serial dependence; that "clean" means uncontaminated replay with no stationarity claim; and that survivor-only cells in divergence tables favor arms that lose runs. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Generality is untested beyond one monitor architecture, one score type (filter innovations), and five long-horizon forecasting datasets; the paper's recommendations are framed generally but supported by a single deployment, and no second monitor design is tried to see whether the premise failure is structural or idiosyncratic. - There is no theoretical account of why the loop's scores break exchangeability so severely (e.g., whether the overlap in 95/96 labels, the adaptive window, or the hyperparameter dynamics dominate) — the i.i.d.-score versus pipeline-score controls bound the locus but do not isolate the responsible element, as the authors concede. - The proposed remedy space is thin: the martingale-free cutoff has a 9.5× clean-weather cost on TimesFM 2.5 that the authors report but do not resolve, and no repair restoring score exchangeability is proposed or tested. - No statistical uncertainty quantification beyond per-cell ranges over three seeds; the 60-run null controls bound rather than certify conservatism, so the "construction is quiet" conclusion rests on point estimates. - The e-detector replay is confined to the authors' own p-value streams from this deployment; whether other detector families would also inherit the failure is untested. Bottom Line: For anyone planning to put conformal test martingales, e-detectors, or any anytime-valid monitor in an online control loop, this paper is essential reading — it is the most concrete controlled demonstration I know of that the exchangeability premise fails on real score streams and that guarantee-triggered responses can amplify the exact anomaly they guard against — while readers seeking methods or generalizable theory will find only a well-executed, deliberately narrow negative result.

What's in Your Agent's Context? Context Privilege Escalation Attacks against AI Agent Harness

Z Li, J Cui, A Chen, X Liao, L Xing · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the first systematic security analysis of context-assembly mechanisms in 12 real-world AI agent harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, etc.), and introduces two new attack classes — Message-Role Context Privilege Escalation (M-CPE) and Cross-Scope Context Privilege Escalation (X-CPE) — with a taxonomy of 16 attack vectors and end-to-end exploits against all 12 harnesses. - Why it's important: Agent vendors rely on message-role privilege hierarchies (system > developer > user > assistant > tool) as their primary defense against indirect prompt injection, and this paper shows that harness-level design flaws silently break that hierarchy, enabling persistent injection, sandbox escape of instructions, and remote code execution on widely deployed tools with millions of users. - How it does it: The core move is formalizing every piece of agent context as a source tuple (content, privilege role ρ, scope σ) and showing that harness logic (memory-file discovery, skill-path precedence, self-modifiable configs, XML markup wrapping) lets attacker content propagate from low-ρ/low-σ sources into higher-ρ/higher-σ sources, validated automatically by the CORA pipeline using static analysis plus canary-instrumented runtime verification. - The good: The evidence is grounded in real systems, not simulations: CORA verified 282 context sources across 12 harnesses, enumerated 1,761 candidate escalation paths, and achieved 58–78% end-to-end behavioral verification with real frontier models, including a demonstrated Claude Code RCE and a Codex pull-request-review bypass that approved injected command-injection code. - The missing: No defenses are built or quantitatively evaluated — the paper stops at disclosure and qualitative mitigation lessons (e.g., a proposed "context manifest" SBOM analog), so practitioners get no measured answer on how much the attacks can actually be blunted. - Read it or not: Essential reading for agent-harness developers, security engineers assessing agent deployments, and prompt-injection researchers; general ML practitioners can skim the taxonomy tables, which are the reusable contribution.

Problem & Motivation Real-world AI coding and task agents (Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, Cline, and others) defend against indirect prompt injection primarily through instruction-hierarchy training: LLMs are trained to prioritize higher-privileged message roles (system/developer) over lower-privileged ones (tool outputs, retrieved content). But the harness software — not the model — decides which files, configurations, skill descriptions, and environment metadata get loaded into context and at which role, and these designs are vendor-proprietary, opaque, and undocumented. Users and defenders therefore cannot know which content sources an agent loads, when, or with what privilege. The paper identifies the gap: prior prompt-injection work studied malicious content from particular sources (tool outputs, web pages), but nobody had systematically analyzed whether harness context-assembly logic itself creates privilege-escalation channels — attacker content entering context in a higher-privileged role or a more persistent scope than the source it originated from. This matters to anyone running community-contributed skills/MCP servers, or using agents to review untrusted pull requests. Key Idea Model every context input as a source Sk = (content, role ρ, scope σ) with ρ ∈ {r0..r4} (privilege hierarchy) and σ ∈ {user > project > session} (persistence/breadth), then define privilege escalation as any propagation of attacker-controlled content from a lower-ρ source into a higher-ρ source (M-CPE) or from a lower-σ source into a higher-σ source (X-CPE). Once this abstraction is in place, the attacks become systematic: any harness feature that lets low-trust content (tool output, git commit messages, file names, zip archives) get written into, discovered by, or supersede higher-trust, more persistent sources (memory files, skills, configuration) is an escalation primitive — and the paper shows 12 real harnesses are full of them. Methodology Three components. (1) Formal modeling: the agent loop C_{i+1} = C_i ∪ exec(T_i; E) is extended with role/scope-tagged context sources, lifecycle (launch-time vs. runtime loading), and vendor role mappings (Appendix Table VIII normalizes OpenAI/Anthropic/Google role schemes). (2) Taxonomy: 16 attack vectors in three categories — diverse context sources (A-1..A-7: agent-specific memory files, memory search directories including Gemini CLI's downward BFS, runtime memory/skill loading, environment context like file trees and git logs, recursive memory imports), context markup (B-1/B-2: injecting fake XML closing tags like </skill> to escape skill-description boundaries; echoing model-output tags like Cline's <write_to_file> to forge tool calls), and assembly logic (C-1..C-7: file-precedence overrides like Codex's AGENTS.override.md, skill-directory priority and last-one-wins duplication resolution, self-modification of config files under YOLO mode, inline shell execution in Claude Code skill bodies and Aider AI! comments, context refreshing, and unsandboxed memory tools escaping sandboxes). (3) CORA, an LLM-assisted analyzer: static analysis with an LLM agent identifies candidate context sources and markup from harness source code (language-agnostic semantic reasoning); a deterministic runtime stage instruments the LLM endpoint, injects random canaries into candidate sources, differentially relaunches the agent across three directories to classify scope, and verifies role placement from captured endpoint requests; finally, CORA enumerates low→high (ρ,σ) source pairs, stages injection instructions in the low source, runs a two-round protocol (inject + cleanup + benign relaunch) and verifies propagation and behavioral effect in isolated containers. The analyzer backend is Codex with GPT-5.5 (medium reasoning); targets run GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini, Claude Sonnet/Opus 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro. Key Results - CORA identified 463 candidate context sources across 12 harnesses and verified 282 at runtime (93.4% of eligible); 64.9% of verified sources enter the highest r0 role and 64.2% carry project scope; configuration-file sources (34.4%) and third-party components (28.0%) dominate. Verified sources per agent range 15–41 (mean 23.5). - 1,761 candidate CPE paths (940 M-CPE, 640 X-CPE, 181 both); under GPT-5.5, 1,315 paths (74%) loaded the injected instruction into the higher-privileged source and 1,034 (58%) produced the verified behavioral effect; GPT-5.4-mini: 73%/58%. Per-agent spread is large (e.g., Qwen Code 100% loaded/76% verified under GPT-5.5 vs. Kimi CLI 53%/46%). - CORA accuracy against 40 person-hours of manual ground truth: Codex 100% precision / 93% recall (28/30 sources), Gemini CLI 97% precision / 91% recall (38/42). - Five end-to-end attacks on real harnesses: Claude Code RCE via chained dynamic skill discovery + inline shell commands in SKILL.md (payload restricted to already user-approved commands, e.g., node); Cline manipulated tool invocation chaining XML tag interpretation + .windsurfrules implicit memory + unrestricted self-configuration modification; Gemini CLI sandbox escape where a deep nested GEMINI.md instructs save_memory(scope=global), persisting instructions into user-scope memory across projects; Codex PR-review bypass where an AGENTS.override.md suppresses review of a directory containing a popen() command-injection backdoor (the identical code without the override is correctly flagged); and a cross-agent attack where a malicious git commit message (auto-loaded into Claude Code's r0 context) forges CLAUDE.md-style markup, causing Aider's file watcher to modify Claude Code's execution policy. - Vendor response: Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cline shipped mitigations; OpenAI and Anthropic acknowledged findings. Baselines here are prior prompt-injection taxonomies (AgentDojo, InjecAgent, cross-tool work), which the paper argues are source-specific rather than harness-systemic — no quantitative head-to-head comparison is run. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM + NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the (ρ, σ) source formalization and the framing of privilege escalation at the harness/context-assembly layer rather than the content layer; the 16-vector taxonomy derived from real implementations; and CORA as the first automated source-identification + canary-validated exploit pipeline for this surface. The individual primitives (prompt injection, malicious skill registries, config tampering) build on known ideas, but their composition and the systematic measurement across 12 harnesses is new. The markup tag-injection vector (B-1) is a known LLM weakness applied to a new, concrete harness surface. Rigor & Reproducibility Strong for a measurement/attack paper: the identification (LLM-based, fallible) is deliberately separated from validation (deterministic canary matching and differential relaunches), addressing the classic hallucinated-finding problem. Ground truth for two agents was built with 40 person-hours of manual analysis; all 161 statically filtered sources were manually reviewed (156/161 filtering decisions correct, 5 false negatives documented with a concrete Aider LANG-variable example). No multiple seeds or error bars are reported for behavioral verification rates, which are inherently model-stochastic — the authors acknowledge this by noting propagation (deterministic) vs. behavior (reference-only) are distinct outcomes. Code will be released (project site https://zichuan.li/LLMAgentCPE with demo videos; source code promised). Concerns: evaluation uses each agent's pinned version at analysis time (a moving target, though disclosure-triggered patches are noted); the behavioral-success metric partly measures model instruction-following rather than vulnerability, which the authors flag; and the candidate-path counts derive from CORA's own taxonomy, so recall of the attack space (as opposed to source recall on two agents) is unquantified. The authors honestly label CORA-confirmed paths a lower bound. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (security measurement with a built analysis tool). The artifact is CORA plus the exploit corpus — a reusable research tool, not a production defense. - Practical: Yes — it operates on open-source harness code and standard cloud LLM APIs in Docker containers; Claude Code analysis used the publicly distributed npm source map, handled under IRB-exempt protocol. - Efficient: Not stated in compute terms; the analysis is LLM-heavy (per-agent multi-stage LLM workflows) but bounded — 12 harnesses fully analyzed, with 40 person-hours of human effort only for ground-truth calibration. - Effective: The evidence shows the stated problem is real: every one of 12 harnesses has verified, behaviorally-confirmed escalation paths, with vendor-acknowledged patches as external validation. - Scalable: Untested beyond these 12; CORA's per-harness static analysis and environment construction may not generalize to harnesses with more opaque or dynamically generated assembly logic, and the authors note EnvSpec construction failures for 20 sources. The defense-space question (scaling to thousands of community harnesses) is unaddressed. Strengths - The (role, scope) source abstraction is a genuinely useful intellectual contribution: it converts an amorphous "prompt injection" space into a checkable escalation graph, and the role-assignment inconsistency findings across vendors (e.g., project memory is user-role in Codex/Claude Code but system-role in six other agents) are concrete, defensible evidence of a design-space problem. - The deterministic-validation methodology (canary injection, three-launch differential scope testing, two-round attack validation with cleanup) is careful experimental design that distinguishes this from typical LLM-only vulnerability scanning. - The end-to-end attacks are realistic and consequence-graded — the Codex AGENTS.override.md review-bypass attack, in which identical vulnerable code is approved only when the override file is present, is a clean controlled demonstration of security-relevant impact (vulnerable code reaching protected main). - Coordinated disclosure across 12 vendors with patches already shipped (Codex, Gemini CLI, Cline) converts the findings from theoretical to externally validated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly. They state: (1) behavioral verification depends on model instruction-following and security alignment, so verified path rates are a lower bound and the behavior metric is "a reference rather than a definitive measure"; (2) CORA's template instructions are simple — human experts could compose multi-vector payloads with higher success; (3) source validation fails when canaries cannot be staged (complex configs, runtime-discovered sources), causing 5 known false-negative filters; (4) some paths fail on payload-capacity mismatch (short-value sources like env vars/folder names) or conditional activation prerequisites; (5) end-to-end attack success is probabilistic (e.g., the model may not choose to invoke a planted skill). They also advocate, rather than implement, mitigations (context manifest, reduced sources, CPE filtering). Analyst-Identified Gaps - No defense is built or evaluated: the paper proposes a context manifest and CPE-content filtering qualitatively but provides no measurement of how well any mitigation (including vendors' shipped patches) reduces the 1,761-path attack surface — a dogs-not-barking omission given the disclosure timeline. - Behavioral verification conflates vulnerability with model compliance: a path "verified" under GPT-5.5 may fail under a better-aligned future model, and the paper does not break down failure by role level, so it cannot say whether instruction-hierarchy training actually resists r0-role injection specifically. - Snapshot evaluation: each harness is analyzed at one version; the measured surface will drift, and no longitudinal or patch-diff analysis is provided. - The threat model assumes a benign host OS and non-malicious vendors/users, but the demonstrated consequence is host RCE; the paper does not explore attacker-host collusions or multi-tenant settings where the host assumption weakens. - Ground truth for CORA's precision/recall covers only 2 of 12 harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI); identification accuracy on the other 10 — including the Rust and Python implementations — is unmeasured. - No statistical treatment of the behavioral rates (single runs per path, no seeds/confidence intervals), so per-agent differences (e.g., OpenClaw's 47% vs. Qwen Code's 76% verified) cannot be distinguished from noise. Bottom Line Any team building, deploying, or securing LLM agent harnesses should read this paper — it defines a new, formally grounded attack surface (harness context assembly), demonstrates it convincingly on the most widely used agents in the field, and ships an analysis methodology (CORA) that defenders can reuse; its main shortfall is that it stops at diagnosis, with no measured mitigations, but no existing alternative covers this ground with comparable depth.

Problem & Motivation: Post-training (SFT and RL) places acquired reasoning capability inside model weights, where it is opaque, unverifiable mid-trajectory, and bound to one checkpoint. For tasks whose intermediate steps are checkable—tool calling, policy-constrained dialogue, code generation—the authors argue reasoning should live outside the weights as an explicit program. The technical gap they attack: prior program/workflow optimizers (ADAS, AFlow, Trace, TextGrad) assign credit via coarse scalar trajectory scores or LLM-generated critiques, both stochastic and unverifiable, while RLVR's verifiable reward is terminal and sparse. The open question is how to assign credit through a discrete, non-differentiable program of mixed symbolic/neural primitives. Key Idea: In a typed, contract-verified program, credit assignment need not be estimated at all. Given the ontology a layer must produce, the declared type signatures of primitives deterministically induce (via first-order unification and composition) the ontology the layer below must supply—chain-rule credit assignment as derivation, not estimation—while per-step output contracts give a dense, programmatic (not learned) verification signal, the step-level analogue of RLVR's outcome-level check. Methodology: A program is N=4 layers of compositions from a typed DSL over 10 primitives (4 fully deterministic, 6 hybrid: small fine-tuned LMs of 3B–27B paired with symbolic correct-by-construction guards). A neurosymbolic tokenizer converts raw text to/from typed ontologies at both ends, with a verbatim-span constraint so nothing is invented at the boundary. The ontology loss is per-object, content-aligned (not key-aligned), scored lexicographically as (type-error count, L2 value error), with type-declared agreement measures (test pass rate for Code, partial credit for ToolCall). The backward pass propagates required ontologies: unification over signatures proposes compositions (depth dmax=3), leaf signatures induce required inputs, contract verdicts prune value assignments, and an availability filter at layer 1 (exact, 4–25× reduction) guarantees executable closure. A layer-wise beam (width 8) plus trust-region deviation term stabilize the search; the loop alternates program search under frozen primitives with primitive retraining using backward-pass signals as targets. Three notable design decisions: (1) lexicographic type-first scoring—justified and explicitly flagged as brittle by construction; (2) content alignment over key alignment—motivated by an observed failure case and load-bearing; (3) a trust-region ranking term (deviation from incumbent)—plausible but largely untested. Key Results: On τ²-Bench (Airline/Retail/Telecom) and LiveCodeBench v6 (Mar–Apr), every base model improves under PLVR: Gemma 12B 21.6→63.9 average, GPT-OSS-20B 30.0→78.4 (largest gain, +48.5), Muse Glimmer 30B 61.4→80.6, Inkling 975B 53.9→83.1. Against published RL checkpoints, PLVR on Muse Glimmer 30B leads by 27.8 points on shared columns (+30.7 over INTELLECT-3 106B-A12B, +30.0 over DeepCoder-14B on LCB, +22.6 over Nemotron-Cascade-2-30B on τ²), and by 13.6 over the mean of five frontier models under vanilla prompting. The pre-registered ablation: search pool median 65.6% vs null pool 17.5%; 96/213 vs 1/64 programs above 70% accuracy; best-of-N gap narrows from +40.2 (N=5) to +7.6 (N=60), which the authors correctly attribute to finite-pool exhaustion. Program identification of p* is reliable within 70 training examples over 10⁹ orderings (distinct from accuracy plateauing at n≈10); transfer to 73 unseen examples costs 4.7 points, tracking the pool-wide 7–8 point difficulty drop, with BFCL tool-calling transfer of only −0.1 points vs pool average −8.3. The search space is ~10²⁷ type-correct programs; ~14,400 candidates scored. Baselines are current and strong (DeepSeek-R1-lineage checkpoints, frontier models), though comparisons are not training-controlled. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (symbolic backpropagation—deterministic type-inference backward signal, distinct from TextGrad/Trace/GEPA where the gradient analogue is stochastic LLM-generated text) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDINGS (types make candidates well-formed but not tractable—the beam does; discovery continues after best-in-pool plateau; type-first loss may select for robustness). The surrounding machinery—beam search over program compositions, small fine-tuned primitives, verifiable rewards—is a competent combination of known ideas; the genuinely new element is the deterministic typed backward pass and the step-level contract reward extending RLVR's verification inward. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually strong for a preprint: a pre-registered ablation (null hypothesis and three design choices fixed in advance), bootstrap and Wilson intervals over problems as primary uncertainty, paired resampling for comparisons, an 'indifference class' analysis distinguishing statistical noise from real program differences, distribution over 10⁹ training orderings, explicit reporting of both marginal and paired intervals, and candid self-assessment of weak cells (Airline's 50-task set cannot resolve <13-point margins; Telecom gains reflect collapsed baselines). No code released at time of writing—library and conformance checker promised 'following peer review.' Methodological concerns: baselines are published checkpoints (no training seed variance; the authors acknowledge this trade-off); no empirical comparison against workflow optimizers (AFlow, ADAS, GEPA) despite them being the closest methods; the loss and backward pass are held fixed across all arms, so the loss design is never independently ablated; scoring during search uses cheap lookahead (3-test prefixes, assumed reachability) versus full evaluation at report time—disclosed, but the selected program is partly a product of the cheap scorer. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method and search procedure actually run, with a released-at-peer-review library). Practical: Yes—primitives are 3B–27B open-weight models plus a base model, all commercially available hardware. Efficient: Not clearly favorable—composed programs spend many more inference tokens than a single forward pass, input tokens dominate (context re-sent per primitive), ~57B total parameters with 3–27B active; the paper reports token counts honestly but no latency and no FLOP-matched training comparison. Effective: Strong evidence on two benchmarks with distinct verification characters, including held-out transfer; but effectiveness is proxy-bounded—the contracts are 'contract checking plus empirical validation,' not formal correctness, and the tokenizer's learned component is the one unverified boundary. Scalable: Untested beyond 109 examples and a 10-primitive library; a third task has never been attempted, and the 10²⁷ program space plus max-plans cost (raising 60→200 made search unfinishable) suggests search cost grows sharply with library width. Delivers a software artifact (symbolic backpropagation library + conformance checker, pending release). Strengths: (1) The core mechanism is a real conceptual move: replacing estimated credit assignment with a deterministic type-theoretic derivation, which the paper carefully distinguishes from the LLM-critique backward passes of TextGrad/Trace. (2) The ablation is the right ablation—uniform sampling over the identical type-admissible space with identical closure constraints isolates the backward pass, and the distributional (median) evidence is robust to the best-of-N artifact the authors themselves identify. (3) Statistical hygiene well beyond field norms: indifference classes rather than false precision, identification separated from accuracy convergence, permutation distributions, paired bootstrap intervals, pre-registration. (4) Honest self-refutation: two findings run against the authors' initial expectations (types don't make search tractable; discovery continues after plateau) and are reported as such. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly that (a) the method applies only where intermediate outputs admit checking—no claim on summarization or open generation; (b) no claim relative to SFT, only RL post-training; (c) the held-out split is not i.i.d. (difficulty effect, not generalization gap); (d) the loss and backward pass are not separately isolated—shown is 'derivation beats other proposals under this loss,' not that loss design is independently responsible; (e) Telecom's +80.7 on Gemma measures recovery of a collapsed 5.2% baseline; (f) Retail's 2.6-point margin is unresolvable at three runs; (g) type errors on unexercised branch paths carry no static guarantee (though contracts localize them at runtime); (h) the robustness-from-type-first-loss observation is flagged as untested and explicitly named as the one ablation not run. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations—a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No empirical baseline from the nearest competing methods—AFlow, ADAS, GEPA are discussed but never run, so 'per-step structural attribution beats reflective scalar search' is asserted, not measured. (2) The frontier comparison is against vanilla prompting only; the one harness arm (GPT-OSS-120B + RLM) is weaker than PLVR, but a frontier model with a strong scaffold—the authors themselves call this 'a different and fairer opponent'—is absent, and PLVR's inference-token cost against such harnesses is not compared. (3) The tokenizer's learned component is a silent failure surface: its errors are invisible to all downstream contracts by construction, and no tokenizer accuracy/error rate is reported. (4) The 10-primitive library was designed by the authors for these task families; the claim that marginal cost of a new task is ~100 examples is untested on any third task, and the 'substrate conjecture' (typed programs beat raw model calls for any construction procedure) is admitted as untested with third-party methods. (5) Search-time scoring differs from reported scoring (3-test prefix, assumed reachability); no sensitivity analysis of how the cheap scorer shaped the selected program. (6) Primitive corpora are synthetic and screened for overlap, but the generating model for those corpora is not identified in the main text. Bottom Line: A practitioner in program synthesis, agentic scaffolding, or post-training gains real substance here—a genuinely different, deterministic credit-assignment mechanism backed by unusually disciplined evidence and self-critique—despite the missing empirical comparison against workflow optimizers and the as-yet-unreleased code making independent validation a wait-and-see matter.

#10 — Highly Innovative (79)

Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models II: One Training Example (65 ▲ )

Zixuan Fu, Bingxiang He, Yuxin Zuo, Haohuan Huang, Jinqian Zhang, Ruhang Xiao, Cheng Qian, Qinyu Luo, Huan-ang Gao, Yudong Wang, Zhiyuan Liu, Ning Ding, Chaojun Xiao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that on-policy distillation (OPD) of LLMs trained on a single query keeps improving for hundreds of steps and recovers 72% of the gain of full-data OPD (68.4 vs 72.1 average accuracy at step 1000), and explains this via a state-coverage measure (one query reaches 71.5% of the state space full-data OPD visits; 16 diverse queries reach 98.9%) plus a declining absorption-rate dynamic that is independent of dataset size. - Why it's important: OPD is now used in frontier post-training stacks (Qwen3, GLM, DeepSeek), and if 16 diverse queries per domain match 17k-query full-data training, the field's attention should shift from collecting problems to curating teachers and the reasoning states data induces, potentially collapsing data-collection costs. - How it does it: The core move is an extreme controlled experiment (one query) that decouples data supply from algorithmic absorption, combined with two diagnostics: state coverage (clustering teacher hidden-state signatures of visited prefixes with PCA + K-means, K=200) and absorption rate (fraction of remaining teacher-student token-level gap closed per update). - The good: The causal ablations are unusually strong for this literature — holding everything fixed, adding distinct trajectories (off-policy) or semantically distinct queries (on-policy) monotonically raises both state coverage and accuracy, and 16 diverse queries reach 98.9% coverage and match full-data OPD (and full-data multi-teacher OPD at 101% recovery), while 16 same-cluster queries stall at 76.8% coverage. - The missing: All results are on 1.5B–7B students distilled from same-family teachers of the same scale; no experiment tests whether the state-coverage account or the 16-query result transfers to larger students, and validation accuracies lack multi-seed error bars (uncertainty is only quantified for coverage subsampling). - Read it or not: Read it if you design post-training data pipelines or study distillation/RL dynamics — it is the first data-side account of OPD and directly actionable; skip it if you only need another OPD recipe, since it changes no algorithm, only the interpretation of what data is for.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (90) and Novelty (85) lead: the one-query extreme experiment cleanly decouples data supply from algorithmic absorption, and the state-coverage formulation — validated by the 16-same-cluster vs 16-diverse contrast (76.8% vs 98.9% coverage at equal count) — is a new, falsifiable way to value distillation data. Rigor (72) is strong on ablation design (frozen-state runs, query-order scheduling, learning-rate rescaling, coverage-robustness checks) and benefits from a released code artifact, but is capped by single-seed training runs where headline gaps of 1–3 points are within plausible run variance, plus preprint status. Completeness (78) and Resilience (78) are lifted by the authors' unusually honest self-measurement, including reporting the AUROC-0.552 diagnostic that exposes their own metric's circularity. Impact (70) reflects public code and an analysis recipe, though no weights or data-selection tool. Weighted composite: 0.20*85 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*90 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*70 = 79.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners running frontier LLM post-training use on-policy distillation — the student samples its own rollouts and the teacher supplies dense token-level supervision (full next-token distributions at every visited prefix) — but prior work has studied OPD's algorithmic mechanics while treating the training set as given. Nobody knows how much data OPD actually needs or how data and algorithm interact, which matters because curating tens of thousands of domain problems is expensive and because data-efficiency findings for RLVR (one-shot RLVR, Wang et al. 2026a) might not transfer to a dense-signal objective. The paper closes this gap by asking the data-minimal question: can OPD train on a single query, and if so, why does that work? Key Idea: The central insight is that OPD is "data-overfed but algorithm-starved": a training query acts on the student only through the states (prefixes) its rollouts reach, and because each rollout generates thousands of supervised states, even one query covers most of the state space full-data OPD visits (71.5% coverage) — while the student's absorption rate, the fraction of remaining teacher-student gap closed per update, declines identically whether training on 1 or 17,000 queries. Once understood, this reconstructs the whole approach: query count is the wrong unit of data value; state coverage is the right one, and the input's job is merely to start the student reasoning (hence even content-free templates work). Methodology: The paper runs one-shot OPD (single query, 64 rollouts per update) using the standard OPD objective — per-token KL between student and teacher on student-visited states, estimated either by a sampled-token advantage (log-teacher minus log-student at the emitted token, Eq. 2) or a top-k advantage over the student's 16 most likely tokens (Eq. 3) — implemented in veRL with AdamW, lr 1e-6, temperature 1.0. The analysis has three phases. (1) Phenomenology: one-shot OPD across math, code, instruction following, and agentic tool use, on three student-teacher families, with ablations over query difficulty (pass rates 8/8, 4/8, 0/8), response-length caps, and sampling temperature. (2) Data-side explanation: state coverage is defined as the fraction of K=200 K-means clusters (over teacher final-layer hidden signatures, PCA to 50 dims) reached by a setting's rollouts, with the reference space built from full-data OPD rollouts; diversity is then manipulated two ways — a fixed off-policy pool of 1/4/16/64 trajectories from one query, and on-policy query ladders of 1/4/16 semantically distinct queries selected via BGE-M3 clustering. (3) Algorithm-side explanation: distance (mean |log-ratio| over visited tokens, Eq. 6) and absorption rate (relative distance reduction per update, Eq. 7, estimated over a geometric window) are tracked for 1/4/16/full-data runs, plus an off-policy ablation that freezes the state set, learning-rate rescaling experiments, extension to multi-teacher OPD (3 domains, query-routed teachers), and stress tests with content-free templates and off-domain WildChat prompts. Critical design decisions: measuring coverage against a full-data-anchored reference (justified by stability checks across K, reference construction, and state positions); normalizing gains as gap-recovery ratios for cross-setting comparability; and reporting the held-out full-data split as the 100% ceiling. Each is reasonably well justified, though the coverage metric's circularity (reference defined by the full-data run) is only partly mitigated. Key Results: One-shot OPD on mathematics reaches 68.5 average accuracy (MATH-500/AMC 2023/AIME 2025, avg@16) vs 69.8 for full-data OPD at step 300 — 87% of full-data's gain and 69% of the teacher-student gap — and 68.4 vs 72.1 at step 1000 (72% recovery). The effect holds across families (R1-Distill-1.5B: 77.1→85.5; Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct: 28.2→40.2; OLMo-3-7B-DPO: 70.8→82.4 on MATH-500+AMC average) and domains (73%, 66%, 64% of teacher-student gap recovered on LiveCodeBench v6, Multi-IF, BFCL v3 respectively), and works even on a query the student never solves (0/8 pass rate). One query covers 71.5% of full-data's state clusters (65.9% within 100 steps); 16 semantically distinct queries reach 98.9% coverage and match full-data accuracy (70.9 vs 70.8), while 16 queries from one semantic cluster stall at 76.8% coverage and ~69.9 accuracy. Absorption-rate decline is nearly identical across 1/4/16/17k queries (each removes 78–84% of its step-30 distance by step 300; rate falls 4.2–6.4× between steps 50 and 200), and a frozen off-policy state set still improves for ~200 steps, so fresh states are not what sustains training. In multi-teacher OPD, 16 queries per domain match full-data MOPD (52.9 vs 52.8 average; 101% recovery). Content-free templates and WildChat prompts (0.17% math-related) approach the real-query baseline at one-third to one-half the rollout tokens; against one-shot RLVR on the same query, OPD's validation gain over 1000 steps is more than twice RLVR's, closing 72% of its teacher gap. Baselines are current and appropriate (the paper's own full-data OPD runs, teacher ceilings, one-shot RLVR); the scale is standard research scale (1.5B–7B models, 300–1000 steps), not frontier scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (one-shot OPD works, and OPD's pace is data-independent) plus a NEW FORMULATION of OPD data value in terms of induced state coverage rather than query count; the experimental lens is adapted from one-shot RLVR, and the OPD objective itself is standard (GKD/MiniLLM-style), so the genuinely novel part is the data-side explanation and the coverage/absorption decomposition, not the training algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a real strength: the causal claim that states, not queries, carry the signal is tested by holding count fixed while varying diversity (16-from-16-clusters vs 16-from-1-cluster), by an off-policy fixed-state run, by query-order scheduling (no effect: 68.8 vs 69.1), and by learning-rate rescaling (curves collapse onto one axis). Coverage robustness is checked across K ∈ {50, 100, 200, 500}, alternative reference constructions, and state-extraction positions, with standard deviations over 30 subsampling repetitions; distance/absorption-rate estimation conventions (windowing, step-30 start due to gradient clipping) are documented with justifications. Code is released at github.com/Thinking-Space/One-Shot-OPD. Concerns: validation accuracies have no multi-seed error bars or significance tests (single training runs per condition appear to be the norm, and the one-shot/full-data differences of 1–3 points are within plausible run-to-run variance); the instruction-following teacher was trained by the authors themselves for this study; the coverage metric is defined against a reference space built from the very full-data run it explains (partially addressed by a pooled-reference robustness check and an AUROC-of-0.552 separability diagnostic the authors report honestly); and the paper is a preprint (arXiv:2609.04172), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (diagnostic/experimental study of a training method, with a reusable analysis methodology rather than a deployed system). - Practical: Yes — all experiments run on 1.5B–7B open models in veRL with batch size 64, well within commodity multi-GPU budgets. - Efficient: The finding itself is an efficiency claim — 16 queries match 17k with identical rollout/optimization budgets, and template-based inputs reach comparable accuracy on 18M vs 277M rollout tokens — but the 300–1000-step runs mean savings appear in data collection, not compute per run. - Effective: The evidence shows OPD recovers most of the teacher-student gap on standard benchmarks, but the ceiling is the teacher's own distribution; it solves style/capability transfer from a matched teacher, not acquisition of abilities the teacher lacks. - Scalable: Untested beyond 7B students and 3 teacher domains; the authors flag larger students, more teachers, and long contexts as open, so the 10×–100× story is a claim, not a measurement. The work delivers a public code artifact and an analysis recipe (coverage + absorption-rate instrumentation); it does not ship trained model weights or a data-selection tool (estimating coverage without a full-data reference run is explicitly left open). Strengths: - The one-query experimental design is a genuinely sharp instrument: by driving data to its minimum it cleanly separates "how much supervision is available" from "how fast the student absorbs it," and the answer (absorption-rate-limited, data-independent slowdown) is a non-obvious, falsifiable claim backed by matched comparisons. - The state-coverage causal chain is closed with controls most empirical LLM papers omit — the 16-same-cluster vs 16-diverse-query contrast (76.8% vs 98.9% coverage at equal count) is the single most convincing experiment, directly isolating diversity from count. - Honest self-measurement: the authors report the off-reference-distance diagnostic (one-shot's heavier tail, AUROC 0.552 ≈ not separable) and the coverage metric's circularity themselves, which raises confidence in the rest. - The template/WildChat result (a content-free input reaching within ~1 point of a 17k-problem baseline) is a striking, decision-relevant finding for anyone curating post-training data. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that state coverage is a semantic-level proxy measured against a full-data reference (so it reports reach relative to that run, weighting every cluster equally regardless of visitation frequency or remaining teacher signal); that what sets the absorption rate remains open; and that MOPD results cover only three domains with one teacher each, leaving the diversity result's reach at larger teacher counts untested. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-seed training runs: headline one-shot vs full-data gaps of 1–3 accuracy points (68.5 vs 69.8) come with no cross-seed variance, so "most of the gain" claims at that margin are not statistically grounded. - Scale confinement: all students are 1.5B–7B and all teachers are same-scale or same-family; the state-coverage account could behave differently for frontier-scale students whose rollout distributions are broader, and the paper does not test this. - Possible evaluation-alignment confound: math training and evaluation share the DAPO/competition-math distribution, and one-shot OPD may partly be transferring teacher style/format rather than reasoning; the content-light results intensify this concern — if a bare template works, what exactly is being measured on MATH-500? - The coverage reference is constructed from the full-data run being explained, so high coverage of 1-shot is partly guaranteed by the student's rollout distribution spanning broadly; the pooled-reference robustness check mitigates but does not eliminate this circularity. - No comparison against a one-shot SFT or one-shot reverse-KL off-policy baseline (beyond the fixed-trajectory ablation), so the reader cannot tell how much of the advantage comes from on-policyness versus dense supervision alone. - Missing dogs-not-barking: the absorption rate is measured but no intervention raises it (the proposed trust-region/epoch-reuse ideas are future work), so the "algorithm-starved" diagnosis yields no fix in this paper. Bottom Line: For anyone building post-training data pipelines or studying distillation, this is a must-read — it is the first credible demonstration that OPD's binding constraint is absorption rate rather than data, backed by unusually careful ablations — though its small-model scale and single-seed results mean the 16-query prescription should be re-validated before being trusted at production scale.

ASIL: Replacing Screenshot-and-Click with Structured State and Semantic Actions

R Xie, L Chen · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ASIL, an agent-software interaction layer that replaces screenshot observation and coordinate-level GUI clicks with structured JSON state observations and code-executable semantic actions, instantiated across 15 desktop applications with a 380-task benchmark and SFT/RL training studies. - Why it's important: Most desktop software is still only operable through GUIs, and screenshot-and-click agents pay heavy per-step vision/grounding costs, need 50–100-step budgets, and fail from brittle coordinate actions;
