Problem & Motivation: Agents that operate real desktop software (creative tools, office suites, service-backed apps) currently do so through a human-native loop: read a screenshot, ground UI elements, emit clicks and keystrokes. The observation side is incomplete (screenshots omit hidden panels, document structure, background state) and the action side is brittle (one semantic intent expands into many coordinate-sensitive motor events that break on layout changes). The authors argue the bottleneck is the interface itself, not grounding quality, and that code agents succeeded precisely because they read machine-readable state and act through executable tools — a lesson that has not been transferred to GUI software. Who has this problem: anyone building computer-use agents, and users who want automation over the large body of functionality trapped behind GUIs. Key Idea: Treat software operation as state-based interaction: make the observation a near-injective structured projection of latent software state (Φ) and the action a schema-constrained semantic operation, so one semantic action realizes what would otherwise be a long GUI event sequence — shortening trajectories, shrinking the RL credit-assignment horizon, and making success checkable against state rather than action history. The companion idea is 'deepest feasible access path': the same protocol is realized through whatever backend exposes stable state (file parsing, native scripting, service API) rather than through one fixed mechanism. Methodology: Three pipelines. (1) ASILization: a semi-automatic onboarding pipeline maps each of 15 applications to an adapter implementing observe()/execute(action)/validate_action(); observations are typed JSON with six fields (metadata, app state, interactive elements with stable IDs, environment, navigation, data summary); actions are typed (set_value, invoke_function, modify_file, api_call, navigate, batch). Six adapters are file-backed, four native-script, five service/API. Onboarding is automated after a human-reviewed interface profile (one GPT-5.4 call compiled a 97-line Gitea profile in 24.8s with zero audit errors). (2) Benchmark: 380 tasks (300 single-app across 15 environments × 20, 80 multi-app) sharing task definitions, initial artifacts, and final-state validators between ASIL and GUI modes; the evaluator checks typed checkpoints on final software state and returns a max-path score in [0,1]. (3) Training: SFT from known-correct replayed actions plus verified GPT-5.4 rollouts (~2.9k merged rows for 9B), then GRPO-style on-policy RL (Verl, vLLM policy server, external ASIL rollout service) on a 320/80 task curriculum with an overlap audit against held-out tasks. Critical design decisions: state-checking evaluators shared across scoring/SFT/RL (justified, with an independent raw-validator check on 60 states), evaluator-derived success hints in main ASIL prompts (acknowledged as a confound), and 'deepest feasible access' selection (justified by the path-restriction study: 98.6 vs 98.6 for GPT-5.4 file vs script paths on LibreOffice). Key Results: On the 380-task benchmark, ASIL/15max reaches 81.6 (GPT-5.4), 84.8 (Kimi K2.5), 81.2 (sonnet4.6), 81.1 (Qwen3.6-plus) strict success, with trajectories averaging under 5 actions. Repaired GUI/50max rows yield 6.6 (GPT-5.4) and 26.6 (sonnet4.6) strict; truncating sonnet4.6 to 15 steps gives 17.9. On an OSWorld-comparable easy60 band, GUI rises to 15.0 and 53.3 strict. Against native interfaces on matched tasks, ASIL beats LibreOffice UNO by 28–38 strict points (e.g., sonnet4.6: 98.3 vs 60.0) but only matches draw.io MCP for GPT-5.4 (55.0 vs 55.0) and trails it for sonnet4.6 (25.0 vs 55.0). Training: Qwen3.5-2B goes 58.0 → 72.1 (SFT) → 74.4 (RL); Qwen3.5-9B goes 66.6 → 80.4 → 82.2, using only thousands of SFT rows and 4–8 A800 GPUs. On the held-out 80-task hard suite, 9B gains grow to +17.1/+19.8 while 2B gains shrink to +6.0/+3.6 with the RL checkpoint trailing SFT. GIMP real-photo editing is the residual bottleneck (best 15.2 average; GPT-5.4 gets 0/24 full passes). The 75-point aggregate GUI gap is striking but partly reflects deliberately hard 'no pre-staged progress' tasks and the hint asymmetry; the authors themselves surface the easy60 band showing GUI doing materially better on easier tasks. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. Genuinely novel: the framing of GUI-agent failure as an interface (not grounding) problem, formalized as substituting (Pix, Mk) with (Φ, A); the ASILization methodology with its three realization patterns; and the shared evaluator serving benchmark scoring, SFT filtering, and RL reward. The individual ingredients — structured state, code actions, API-first interaction (AXIS, OS-Copilot, UFO2, DynaSaur, CLI-Anything, MCP servers, SWE-agent's ACI lesson) — are established; the contribution is the unified contract (observation + schema-constrained action + stable IDs + final-state validation + trajectory reuse for SFT/RL) instantiated at benchmark scale with matched native-interface baselines, which no cited prior work evaluates. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and load-bearing: realization-pattern audit (interface effect holds in all three buckets: +89.5/+84.5/+77.1 for GPT-5.4), within-application path-restriction study (file vs script-dispatch differ by ≤1.3 points), GIMP visual-supplement ablation (44.1 vs 43.7, showing screenshots don't help ASIL), and hint-off arms. No multi-seed runs or error bars are reported for benchmark scores; single-run point estimates throughout. Evaluation-only-on-own-benchmark is partially mitigated by the OSWorld-calibrated easy60 band and native-interface baselines, but the benchmark is author-designed and the same evaluator supplies RL rewards (Goodhart risk, explicitly acknowledged with a 60/60 independent raw-validator check as partial mitigation). The training-task overlap audit is unusually detailed (fingerprint scoring, GPT judge, hard rejects; the authors still self-label the pool as 'engineering-valid low-leakage' with many tasks in the warn band). Reproducibility is strong on paper: the release covers adapter code for all 15 apps, all 460 task definitions, Docker runtime images, SFT/RL datasets, selected checkpoints, and baseline scripts, with a one-command smoke test. Two concerns: the submitted main table ran ASIL with success hints and GUI without (quantified on only 30 tasks), and the headline GUI baselines were 'repaired' post-review — the camera-ready numbers are the ones to trust. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (built benchmark, adapters, training stack; evaluated by deployment across 15 live software environments). Practical: Yes — runs on x86_64 Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 via Docker with open-source apps; no exotic hardware beyond standard GPUs for training. Efficient: Substantially cheaper than GUI agents — under 5 actions per task versus 15–100-step GUI budgets, and RL on 320 tasks with 4 A800s; but each application needs an ASILization onboarding cost (partly automated, partly human-reviewed). Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated problem for software with at least one open access path (81–85 strict for strong closed models), but fails on intrinsically perceptual tasks (GIMP hard-suite best 15.2) and cannot cover fully opaque applications. Scalable: Not tested beyond 15 applications and 380 tasks; the 24.8s Gitea onboarding suggests per-app cost is dropping, but coverage of the broader software ecosystem (closed-source apps with no file/script/service surface) is claimed to require fundamentally different access strategies. Delivers a concrete software artifact: adapter library, benchmark, runtime images, datasets, and released Qwen3.5-2B/9B SFT+RL checkpoints. Strengths: (1) The reframing is intellectually sharp and falsifiable: the paper commits to a compositional claim (one cross-application contract) rather than per-application dominance, and then actively hunts for counter-evidence (draw.io MCP matching/beat, easy60 GUI recovery to 53.3). (2) The evaluator-as-reward design closes the loop between benchmark, SFT data filtering, and RL, and the paper demonstrates its payoff with double-digit training gains from ~3k SFT rows and 4–8 GPUs — a credible efficiency argument that screenshot-based training cannot currently match. (3) The camera-ready validity work (repaired GUI re-tests, hint-off arms, independent raw-state validator, native-interface matched baselines, path-restriction study) is a model of post-review hardening; most papers would not have added Table 2. (4) The overlap-audit appendix (Table 10, fingerprint scoring, calibrated GPT judge, explicit self-labeling of residual warn-band leakage) sets a standard for RL-task-generation hygiene. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Four, stated directly and with unusual candor: (1) prompt asymmetry — main-table ASIL prompts contained evaluator-derived success hints while GUI prompts did not, and the same evaluator filters SFT data and supplies RL rewards, so the main table does not isolate the interface variable (hint effect measured at 29/30 vs 26/30 on balanced-30); broader independent validation is future work. (2) 2B RL instability on long-horizon tasks — hard-suite gains shrink to +3.6 and the RL checkpoint trails SFT by 2.4 points. (3) Coverage gaps — applications that are simultaneously closed-source, hard-to-unpack, and lacking scripting/service interfaces are out of scope entirely. (4) Intrinsically perceptual tasks — GIMP real-photo editing fails under the semantic action vocabulary (GPT-5.4: 0/24 full passes), and adding screenshots back does not help (44.1 vs 43.7), so hybrid interfaces are needed for aesthetic criteria. This is direct confrontation, not minimization, and is a major credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The repaired GUI baselines, while far more careful than typical, are still tuned by the authors of the benchmark that defines success; no fully independent lab has replicated either side, and the paper concedes independent validation remains future work. (2) The hint-off repair was applied to the added baselines (balanced-30, native-interface, visual-supplement, easy60 arms) but not to the full 380-task main table, so the most-quoted numbers (81.6 vs 6.6) still carry the hint asymmetry and were never re-run hint-off at scale. (3) The benchmark's task distribution — complete workflows with no pre-staged progress — structurally disadvantages GUI control; the paper admits this and offers easy60 as calibration, but 60 tasks is thin for calibrating a 75-point headline gap. (4) The GUI baseline side appears to use only two models (GPT-5.4, sonnet4.6) despite five closed models evaluated under ASIL; missing GUI rows for Kimi K2.5 and Qwen3.6-plus leave the cross-model interface-effect claim partially unevaluated. (5) No comparison against third-party GUI+script hybrid systems (UFO2, DynaSaur, OS-Copilot) on the same tasks, so the incremental value of ASIL over 'GUI agent plus generated scripts' is argued by contract comparison (Table 5) rather than measured. (6) Single-seed benchmark scores with checkpoint selection by downstream benchmark performance (SFT step 543, RL step 140/8) introduce selection-overfitting risk that multi-seed or a dev/test split would address; the hard suite is held out, which helps, but main-table checkpoint selection is on the reported benchmark. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous and honest version of the 'stop clicking, start calling' argument for desktop agents that I have seen, and its benchmark, adapters, and training artifacts are directly reusable — but read the easy60 and native-interface numbers rather than the 81.6-vs-6.6 headline, and treat the interface-vs-model conclusion as established only for software that already exposes an access path.

From Production Traffic to Post-Training: Building a Self-Hosted LLM That Covers the Corporate Request Mix (31 ▲ )

Olga Tsymboi, Dmitrii Stoianov, Ramil Latypov, Danil Taranets, Daniil Dryabin, Mikhail Gashkov, Viktor Zelenkovskiy, Aleksandr Fida, Gleb Alektorov, Nikita Gulyakov, Arthur Babkin, Aleksandr Medvedev, Pavel Gein, Anatolii Potapov · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 2 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a production-driven post-training recipe that consolidates traffic from 200+ internal applications onto a single self-hosted Qwen3-32B-based model, built from a shared SFT checkpoint forked into three GRPO experts (instruction-following, function-calling, general chat) merged via two-stage sequential SLERP. - Why it's important: Data-residency constraints force enterprises to self-host LLMs, and per-team model selection fragments a finite GPU pool as new generations arrive quarterly and old models cannot be retired, inflating effective per-token cost. - How it does it: Rather than joint multi-objective RL, which the authors show suffers cross-domain reward interference, each weak capability axis gets its own GRPO run with a domain-specific reward (with per-axis fixes for reward hacking: semantic collapse, over-calling, verbosity), and the experts are combined in weight space with layer-wise SLERP coefficients chosen by grid search. - The good: The deployed 32B model matches or beats the ~7×-larger Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 on in-house Arena (69.57 vs 65.83) and in-house BFCL (0.79 vs 0.77) in non-reasoning mode, and a public checkpoint trained without internal data reproduces most gains, arguing the recipe—not proprietary data—drives them. - The missing: The in-house Arena win over the 235B baseline rests on an LLM judge with κ≈0.72 on open-ended subtasks and a benchmark drawn from the same traffic distribution the model was tuned on; no statistical significance is reported for headline single-run comparisons (only merge-order ablations have error bars). - Read it or not: Worth reading for ML engineers building self-hosted, non-English enterprise LLM platforms—it is one of the few reproducible accounts of traffic-stratified benchmark construction, per-axis reward hacking, and expert merging at deployment scale—but skippable if you only work on English-first, API-based systems.
Why this rank

Practical Impact (90) drives the score — a deployed production model serving 116M requests/month, open-weight checkpoint released, and 2.8-3.9× per-token cost reduction against a 7×-larger baseline. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (72) reflect the per-axis reward-hacking taxonomy with targeted, ablated fixes — a genuinely transferable empirical finding — though individual techniques are standard. Completeness (78) benefits from unusually honest limitation acknowledgment, and Resilience (70) survives scrutiny modulo the distribution-fit concern. Problem & Motivation A large enterprise operating under data-residency regulation must self-host LLMs on a finite GPU pool shared by hundreds of internal applications. Each team independently picks a model; model churn (new generations quarterly, no decommissioning of predecessors) fragments the fleet and raises effective price per token. The authors need one model that covers the corporate request mix—instruction following (37.9% of production failures), function calling (~12% of traffic), and alignment to the internal task distribution—without regressing general capabilities, because the long tail of applications changes faster than any single one accumulates traffic for reliable A/B testing. Prior Russian-language LLM work targeted fluency or pre-training, not reproducible post-training for agentic skills, and English-centric IF/FC verifiers and datasets break down in Russian due to morphology, free word order, and fixed API schema fields. Key Idea The core move is modularity under reward interference: diagnose weak axes from production error analysis, train one independently-rewarded GRPO expert per axis from a shared SFT checkpoint, and combine them via two-stage sequential SLERP instead of joint multi-objective RL—paired with the observation that each verifiable reward admits a distinct shortcut (empty-but-compliant completions for IF, call-when-in-doubt for FC, verbosity for the RM-based general reward) that is fixed per-domain via reward-model quality penalties or data-mixture injection rather than a unified reward. Methodology The pipeline has four phases. (1) Benchmark construction: a template-aware sampler masks variable tokens, groups near-duplicate prompts via LSH, runs greedy max-min within templates over variable spans with √count budget allocation, achieving the highest lexical diversity (0.953 mean pairwise TF-IDF distance) while keeping Jensen-Shannon distance to the production pool low across model, length, service, and task dimensions. Judging routes requests through an LLM task classifier (90.6–99.6% agreement with human consensus) and applies task-specific schemes: reference-based scoring for classification/extraction (63.2% of traffic) and pairwise SBS augmented with RubricHub-style checklists for open-ended tasks, lifting judge–human Cohen's κ from 0.63 to 0.88 (reference-based) and 0.57 to 0.72 (open-ended). (2) Shared SFT on a mixture of general Russian instruction data (~80%), in-house production data (20%, decontaminated via Min-Hash), IF, and FC data; an ablation shows shared SFT matches per-domain SFT quality. (3) Three GRPO branches from the shared checkpoint: a general expert (RM reward with a multiplicative length penalty against Qwen3-235B-completion baselines and KL coefficient raised from 0.001 to 0.01 to stop verbosity hacking); an IF expert (AutoIF-style synthetic pipeline expanding 54 seed constraints to 43K verified constraints / 26K examples, GRPO with a VerIF-style verifier reward plus a prompt-specific RM-quality penalty against the 235B teacher's mean score to prevent semantic collapse); an FC expert (native-language synthetic generation of 1.2M English and 300K Russian samples via a planner-plus-three-agent-asymmetric-visibility simulation, binary Tool-N1 exact-match reward, with over-calling fixed by injecting 10% synthetic irrelevance cases into the data mixture rather than the reward). (4) Two-stage sequential SLERP merging—IF+FC first at layer-wise coefficients (attention {0,0.3,0.5,0.7,1} per block, MLP complementary, others 0.5), then the general expert at t₂=0.8—chosen by enumerating all orderings and grid-searching coefficients on validation splits; a post-merge SFT polish pass was tried and dropped for causing IF/FC regressions. Key Results The deployed model (Qwen3-32B, non-reasoning, Cyrillic-adapted tokenizer) reaches in-house Arena 69.57 vs 65.83 for Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 (~7× total parameters), ruBFCLv3 65.96 vs 64.42, AceBench 73.50 vs 70.20, and in-house BFCL example pass 0.79 vs 0.77; ruIFEval is 0.799 vs the 235B's 0.803, and ruMultiChallenge/SmartSearch remain below the 235B (34.1 vs 46.2; F1R&G 0.557 vs 0.669), though SmartSearch beats both 32B thinking-mode baselines. Joint GRPO baselines: at 8B, joint optimization from mixed SFT lifts ruIFEval (0.731→0.801) but collapses BFCLv3 EN below start (61.2→54.5); the best joint config needs a general-GRPO warm start and 1.7× budget to reach parity (32B: 70.45 ruIFEval, 65.29 in-house BFCL vs merge's 69.57/65.96). Production: 116M requests/month from 200+ services, 45 average/110 peak RPS, FP8 single-GPU vLLM replicas (16–48 pods), p95 latency 3.2 s, TTFT 0.3 s, per-token cost 2.8–3.9× lower than the 235B baseline and up to 4–9× versus the largest prior platform models. Baselines are current (Qwen3 family, T-Pro 2.0, DeepSeek-derived judges), and the evaluation spans the authors' own benchmarks plus localized public ones (ruIFEval, ruBFCLv3, ruMultiChallenge, Arena Hard Ru, WildChat Hard Ru) and original English AceBench/τ²-bench. Judge-ordering robustness is checked across four judges; the deployed model ranks first under all four. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK component (traffic-stratified in-house Arena/IFEval/BFCL/SmartSearch and Russian localizations). The genuinely novel elements are the documented per-axis reward-hacking taxonomy with domain-specific fixes at production scale, the empirical demonstration that joint GRPO interference justifies expert merging for this setting, and the validated traffic-sampling methodology; the individual techniques (GRPO, AutoIF, Tool-N1 rewards, SLERP merging, task-arithmetic) are standard components combined competently in a new setting (Russian enterprise self-hosting). Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are unusually thorough: shared-vs-domain SFT (Table 3), RM adaptation (Table 4), cross-domain transfer of each expert (Table 5), merge orderings with mean±std over five checkpoint combinations (Table 7), joint-vs-merge at both 8B and 32B (Tables 8, 23), merging-operator comparison including TIES (Table 24), per-stage FC decomposition (Table 18), mixture sweeps (Tables 16, 17, 19), and judge sensitivity across four models (Table 27). However, headline model comparisons are single runs without error bars or significance tests; several mixture-sweep decisions are explicitly read only at sign level. An open-weight checkpoint is released (https://huggingface.co.co/t-tech/T-pro-it-2.1), and the in-house benchmarks are decontaminated against training data via Min-Hash, with weak-axis experts trained on synthetic data only. Methodological concerns: the in-house benchmarks and the deployment tuning loop come from the same traffic distribution (development decisions were made on BFCLv3 and in-house benchmarks), so in-house wins partly reflect tuning to the eval distribution; judge κ of 0.72 on open-ended subtasks leaves meaningful judge noise; and merge coefficients are grid-searched with "no general rule" for transfer. This is an arXiv-style preprint, not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS (a deployed production model evaluated by live traffic, with an empirical training-recipe core). - Practical: Yes—runs on single-GPU FP8 vLLM replicas behind standard infrastructure, far below frontier-model hardware. - Efficient: 2.8–3.9× cheaper per token than the ~7×-larger 235B baseline it matches on target metrics, and up to 4–9× versus the largest prior platform models. - Effective: Evidence covers both offline benchmarks calibrated against human annotators (κ 0.85 average) and 116M monthly requests in production, though the arena-based effectiveness signal is judge-mediated and residual gaps persist on knowledge/memory-heavy tasks. - Scalable: Tested only at one organization's scale (45/110 RPS); the recipe's modularity is claimed to extend ("one new expert per capability"), but 10–100× traffic or a new model family is untested. The work delivers a deployed production system, an open-weight checkpoint, and reusable benchmark/recipe artifacts (ruIFEval, ruBFCLv3 localizations referenced via Hugging Face). Strengths - The reward-hacking taxonomy is the paper's most transferable contribution: three distinct, empirically documented failure modes (semantic collapse under verifier rewards, over-calling under exact-match FC rewards, verbosity under RM rewards), each with a targeted, ablated fix (prompt-specific RM-quality penalty, data-mixture irrelevance injection, length penalty + raised KL). - The evaluation infrastructure is validated against humans rather than asserted: the template-aware sampler is compared quantitatively against random, greedy max-min, and #InsTag on diversity-representativeness trade-offs (Table 1), and the task-routed judging pipeline's κ improvement (0.62→0.85 average) is measured, not claimed. - The public no-internal-data checkpoint scoring close to the deployed model (e.g., Arena Hard Ru 66.8 vs 69.57; ruBFCLv3 66.84 vs 65.96) is a clean control attributing gains to the recipe rather than proprietary data memorization. - The merge-vs-joint-GRPO comparison is done at both 8B (sweep) and 32B (replication) scales, and the non-associativity of SLERP is handled by exhaustive ordering enumeration with error bars—the kind of diligence most merging papers skip. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and credibly: evaluation covers only Russian and English with in-house benchmarks from a single deployment; LLM-judge scores require re-calibration against human annotations if the distribution changes; all experiments use only the Qwen3 model family from one organization, so cross-family and cross-organization generality is unverified; and the paper explicitly instructs that all quantitative claims be read as validated for Russian and English only. They also acknowledge within appendices that merge coefficients have no general transfer rule, that the in-house BFCL metric excludes free-text argument quality and text-reply content by construction, and that τ²-bench session-level success is not aligned with their per-turn reward. Analyst-Identified Gaps - Circularity pressure on the headline claim: the in-house Arena benchmark is built from the same traffic used to tune the model, and the 235B baseline was never adapted to this distribution; the judge-sensitivity table mitigates but does not eliminate the concern that the deployed model wins partly by distribution fit. The public-checkpoint control helps, but the public checkpoint is not the deployed one and lacks the in-house data increment. - No comparison against the obvious alternative consolidation strategy—routing across a small curated model set—or against cheaper adaptation baselines (e.g., a single joint SFT+DPO checkpoint without any RL), so the reader cannot tell how much of the gain requires the three-expert machinery versus any competent post-training on the same data. - Error bars are absent for all headline single-run numbers (Table 6); several margins over the 235B (in-house BFCL 0.79 vs 0.77, AceBench 73.50 vs 70.20) could plausibly sit within judge or seed noise given the open-ended κ ceiling of 0.72. - The IF expert's generalization claim rests on ruIFEval and in-house IFEval, both built with AutoIF-derived verifier machinery that overlaps the training pipeline's verifier-generation procedure—there is no held-out IF evaluation from an independent constraint family. - Cost figures (2.8–3.9×) are self-reported without a published cost model, and no throughput/latency comparison table against actually serving the 235B is provided. Bottom Line For teams building self-hosted, non-English enterprise LLM platforms this is one of the most complete and honestly ablated public accounts of the full loop from traffic analysis to deployment, and the per-axis reward-hacking fixes alone justify reading it; for everyone else, Tulu-style recipes plus model merging literature cover the same techniques, though not the production validation.

The Mask Is Not the Model: Auditing Prefix Invariance in Attention, State-Space, and Hybrid Sequence Models

T Kim, Y Hong, M Kim, S Choi, J Jang, M Kim · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a two-forward-pass, gradient-free audit for prefix invariance in autoregressive sequence models that both detects causal leakage and localizes it to the exact offending layer, and uses it to find and root-cause a real causality bug in two released hybrid models (Zamba2-1.2B, Nemotron-H-8B). - Why it's important: Causal leakage silently improves the very metrics (teacher-forced perplexity, benchmark likelihoods) used to select models while breaking autoregressive inference, and the field's default check — reading the attention mask — detected 0 of 192 injected faults and has no object to inspect at all for mask-free architectures like Mamba and RWKV. - How it does it: Perturb the final token of a length-T sequence, run two uncached forward passes with per-layer hooks, and report the first layer whose prefix outputs (positions 0..T−2) differ from exact zero; in a correct implementation the delta is bitwise zero, making the verdict threshold-robust. - The good: The audit localized all 192/192 injected faults to the exact layer across 8 checkpoints and 5 architecture families, and the discovered Zamba2/Nemotron-H defect was predicted by a static code census, reproduced across 4 seeds and random weights, onset exactly at the declared chunk boundary (256/128), and driven to exact zero by a 2-line patch. - The missing: The gradient-based baseline (B5) matches their localization exactly (96/96), so the contribution over existing practice is cost and applicability, not accuracy; and the headline defect is a single shared code lineage found in two models, not evidence about defect prevalence (which the authors explicitly disclaim). - Read it or not: Read it if you build, release, or evaluate hybrid/state-space sequence models — the test costs seconds and the two methodological gates (positive-control liveness check, chunk-exceeding test length) are directly actionable; skip it if you only need detection rather than localization, since a logits-only perturbation check already gives you that for free.

Novelty (70) reflects a deliberately trivial audit method elevated by a new incompleteness argument and a real traced defect in released models; Non-Obviousness (65) is moderate because the core test is standard metamorphic testing on an intrinsic oracle. Problem & Motivation: Autoregressive language models are meaningful only if position t's output depends solely on inputs at positions ≤ t, yet released models report parameter counts, context lengths, and benchmarks while providing no evidence that the implementation is causally correct. Practitioners historically audited causality by inspecting the attention mask, but modern stacks mix heterogeneous mixers (local/sparse attention, Mamba-style SSMs, RWKV recurrences, convolutions, hybrids) where masks govern only a subset of layers or none. Leakage is a dangerous failure mode because it is silent and asymmetric: it lowers training loss and validation perplexity, improving the metrics used for model selection, while surfacing only at generation time — by which point architecture comparisons are contaminated. The authors were motivated by three distinct causal faults they hit while building an internal hybrid stack, each requiring manual debugging despite violating the same underlying property. Key Idea: Prefix invariance — that per-layer representations at position t must be identical under any perturbation strictly in the future — is a graph-level property with an intrinsic oracle, testable in two forward passes; because a correct implementation performs bitwise-identical arithmetic on all compared positions, the clean delta is exactly zero, not merely small, which converts the audit from a calibrated-threshold heuristic into a threshold-free exactness check whose only output that matters is the first layer where exactness breaks. Methodology: The method (printed in full in §2.2): take a random length-T sequence x₁, copy it with the final token replaced (x₂), attach forward hooks to every layer, run two forward passes with caching disabled, compute Δ_ℓ = max|h₁_ℓ[0:T−1] − h₂_ℓ[0:T−1]| per layer, and report LEAK plus the first layer with Δ_ℓ > τ. Four design choices are justified: per-layer hooks (logits-only detects but cannot localize), excluding position T−1 (the perturbation site), disabling caching (so both passes traverse the same graph), and deterministic single-precision evaluation (enables exact-zero clean deltas). Validation uses 8 executable injected-fault patterns in four leakage classes (shift, aggregation, normalization, scan-direction), applied at 3 depths per model. Two methodological gates are derived from the paper's own failures: (1) a CLEAN verdict is admissible only if 24 positive-control injections localize on the same loaded checkpoint (this caught three Falcon-H1 checkpoints whose loaded state produced bit-identical outputs for different inputs); (2) the audit sequence length must exceed the model's chunk/window/kernel parameters, since a chunked scan below one chunk degenerates and hides an entire defect class. The root-cause analysis of the Zamba2/Nemotron-H defect combines a static census of chunked-scan code in transformers 5.7.0 with dynamic confirmation, alternative-explanation controls, and an on-checkpoint patch-to-zero sole-cause test. Key Results: On 8 public checkpoints × 8 patterns × 3 depths = 192 injected-fault trials, the audit localized all 192/192 to the exact injected layer, uniformly across attention (SmolLM2-135M, Qwen3-0.6B, pythia-1.4b, gemma-3-1b-it), state-space (mamba-130m-hf), linear-recurrent (rwkv-6-world-1b6), and hybrid (recurrentgemma-2b, LFM2-1.2B) families. Against six baselines on 96 trials: static mask inspection detected 0/96; shuffled-suffix perplexity missed 25/96 (structurally, with loss difference exactly 0 for radius-1 leaks); logits-only perturbation and future-token resampling detected 96/96 but localized 0/96; gradient-based checking matched 96/96 detection and localization at higher cost. Clean checkpoints (4 models, 106 layers checked) showed exactly 0.0 maximum delta and bitwise-identical outputs. The census found real defects: Zamba2-1.2B leaks with prefix contamination beginning exactly at its 256-token chunk boundary (max |Δ| = 1.12×10⁻² at T=512) and Nemotron-H-8B at its 128-token boundary (prefix delta jumping from 0.0 at T=128 to 7.445×10⁻¹ at T=192); a byte-identical three-line inter-chunk recurrence block in both files reduces over the output-chunk axis instead of the input-chunk axis, and replacing it with the Mamba-2 reference orientation drives the prefix delta to exact zero on both released checkpoints (e.g., Nemotron-H: 0.745/0.320 → 0.0000 at T=192/384). Four conformant implementations and a from-config random-weight reference build stayed bit-exact clean up to several multiples of chunk size, tested at lengths up to 3× the sliding window (T=1536 for gemma-3-1b, T=3072 for recurrentgemma-2b). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a formalized, trivially simple audit — the paper itself emphasizes it fits on one page — whose value lies in the localization output and the exact-zero property, not algorithmic sophistication), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a traced, patched causality defect in two released 1B–8B models from major providers, predicted by static analysis), and a methodological contribution in the form of two auditing norms (positive-control gating, chunk-exceeding test length). The genuinely novel elements are the incompleteness argument against mask inspection, the static-census-predicts-dynamic-leak demonstration, and the self-audit methodology; the core test is a straightforward application of metamorphic testing (which the authors cite) to a property with an intrinsic oracle, and the defect itself is an axis-orientation bug. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and controls are unusually thorough for this kind of paper: 6 baselines implemented and compared on identical faults, bit-level verification of clean deltas, a precision/threshold operating-range sweep across 15 orders of magnitude of injection strength (float64 floors of 1e-13–1e-14 at τ=1e-14; float32 has a hard floor at ε≈1e-11), a 6-way alternative-explanation table for the Zamba2 defect, 4-seed replication, a random-weight from-config structural control, and an ε-sweep discriminator that correctly separated a real leak (Zamba2, log-log slope 0.63±0.07, t≈8.6) from two numerical-floor candidates (Granite-4.0-h, Jamba-tiny, slopes ≈0) that the authors explicitly declined to report as findings. No error bars in the classical sense, but the deterministic nature of the test makes most measurements exact. Reproducibility is deliberately package-free: the method is 5 lines the authors argue is better reimplemented than run from a binary, and they release audit logs, per-layer delta arrays, fault specifications, and scripts (leak_cpu_suite2.py, baseline_e2.py, fp64_sens.py) with a raw-data index mapping every table to a JSON file — though no public URL or repository is given in the text, and the listed paths are on the authors' compute host. A superseded harness with a float32-cast defect is disclosed and marked rather than hidden. Methodological concerns are minimal and largely self-flagged; the main one is that the census is small (~20 checkpoints) and non-randomly selected, and one model's sensitivity anomaly (LFM2-1.2B) is reported without a mechanism. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a lightweight audit procedure as the delivered tool). Practical: Runs on commodity CPU — 0.1–0.5 s per scan of a 135M model after loading; GPU used only for memory capacity on ≥1B-parameter checkpoints. Efficient: Two forward passes, no gradients, no training data, no labels; the gradient-based alternative (B5) with equal localization requires a backward pass, full activation-graph retention, and differentiability of every op on the path, which excludes quantized weights and custom kernels. Effective: Evidence shows it detects and localizes injected faults and two real released-model defects, but only structural (input-independent) faults in the reference PyTorch execution path — the fused-kernel paths of the leaking models were not auditable and remain open. Scalable: Untested above 9B parameters and above lengths that exercise single chunk boundaries; the paper claims no scaling limitation but also runs no stress-scale experiment, and the exact-localization floor is shown to be model-dependent. The deliverable is paper form plus released measurement artifacts and a specified 5-line procedure; no library, CLI, or package is shipped (a deliberate, argued choice), and the authors propose rather than produce a causal-correctness certificate standard. Strengths: (1) The most credible single result is the closed loop from static code census to dynamic confirmation to patch-to-zero: the inter-chunk axis error was predicted from source alone, confirmed at exactly each model's declared chunk boundary (256/128), and eliminated by a 2-line fix on the released checkpoints — a complete causal chain, reported upstream (transformers issue #47475 / PR #47476) for Zamba2. (2) The paper treats its own instrument as a suspect: the positive-control gate arose from three checkpoints that returned Δ=0 everywhere while being inert (bit-identical outputs for different inputs), and the sequence-length rule arose from the authors' own census at T=48 being blind to the defect they later found — both negative results about their own procedure are reported as headline findings, which is rare and valuable. (3) The baseline comparison is unusually honest: it states plainly that logits-only checks already detect everything, that gradient-based checking matches localization exactly, and that the paper's delta over existing practice is localization plus cost/applicability. (4) The ε-sweep discriminator (does the prefix delta scale with perturbation magnitude?) is a reusable, non-obvious tool for distinguishing genuine sub-threshold leaks from numerical floors, and it was used to reject two findings the authors could have published. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The limitations section is among the most candid this reviewer has seen, ranked by confidence impact: (1) the two leaked models share one byte-identical code lineage — an existence proof with a traced lineage, not a base rate, and Nemotron-H's validation is slightly asymmetric (no random-weight build, no 6-way alternative-explanation table); (2) no improvement over existing practice at detection — the contribution is localization only; (3) B5 matches localization exactly, so the case against it rests on cost, differentiability requirements, and the zero-gradient interpretive caveat; (4) the authors' own releases are only partially audited (the primary Aether-7B checkpoint passed both controls at 49 layers clean / 16/16 localization, but the instruction-tuned variant has a negative control only and two internal checkpoints remain unaudited); (5) the ~20-checkpoint census is small and non-random; (6) four checkpoints requiring GPU-only compiled kernels plus one gated and one unloadable model make part of the hybrid ecosystem unauditable by third parties; (7) several conformant-checkpoint clean verdicts are provisional, not positive-control-gated, because layer return signatures reject their injection harness; (8) the LFM2-1.2B localization anomaly is unexplained; (9) single length/seed/batch-size configuration in the main suite, and one unexamined dimension (sequence length) already hid a real defect; (10) only static, structural faults are covered — data-dependent leakage requires a different search; (11) the B6 false positive is a single observation; (12) the no-prior-work claim is a keyword search, not a proof. The authors confront limitations directly and repeatedly minimize nothing. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations: (1) the released raw data is described as on the authors' compute host with no public URL, repository, or DOI given in the text — as printed, the promised reproducibility artifacts are not independently accessible; (2) all clean-delta exactness arguments assume deterministic float32/float64 evaluation, but deployment stacks increasingly run bf16/fp16 or quantized inference where bitwise-identical prefix arithmetic may not hold, and the paper does not test whether the exact-zero property survives reduced-precision serving; (3) the defect is demonstrated only in the reference PyTorch path — the authors note fused-kernel paths are unaudited, which means the practical production exposure of the finding is unknown in both directions; (4) the injected-fault taxonomy consists entirely of additive/structural output transforms, so the 192/192 localization result overstates what is known about detection of subtler leak classes (e.g., leaks that pass through the residual stream in a way the C1–C4 patterns don't model); (5) the Aether-7B self-audit uses a reduced grid (16 trials at 4 pinned sites) with the positive-control sites chosen by the authors, a weaker guarantee than the 24-trial census applied to public models; (6) there is no measurement of audit cost versus B5 beyond the qualitative backward-pass argument (e.g., wall-clock or memory on equal footing), so the claimed cost advantage is asserted rather than benchmarked. None of these undermines the core findings. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or releasing hybrid or state-space sequence models gains something concrete and cheap from this paper — a seconds-cost test, two methodological gates, and a sobering demonstration that the field's default causality check is unsound — and the honest, defect-tracing execution makes it worth reading despite a core method that is, by design, almost trivially simple.

Capability Provenance in Language Models: A Case Study in Social Reasoning

G Matlin, C Chakraborty, S Eom, M Okamoto, R Castilla… · openreview.net · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a corpus-scale training-data attribution pipeline that maps which pretraining corpus regions support social reasoning versus STEM reasoning in OLMo3-7B, validated by targeted machine unlearning. - Why it's important: Data curators and auditors currently lack evidence for which parts of a web-scale pretraining corpus drive specific capabilities; a capability-to-corpus map makes auditing and data reweighting actionable rather than guesswork. - How it does it: Gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) scores document influence on benchmark queries, aggregated over WebOrganizer's 576 topic×format bins, with causal confirmation by unlearning high-influence topics via NGDiff LoRA and comparing against in-topic random controls. - The good: SocialIQA's attribution profile is a strong structural outlier (r ≤ 0.21 to comparison benchmarks vs r = 0.76–0.86 among them), and influence-targeted unlearning of Literature × Customer Support degrades SocialIQA significantly more than random controls (Wilcoxon BH-adjusted p ≈ 10⁻⁵). - The missing: The causal validation succeeds cleanly only for SocialIQA; it weakens, nullifies, or reverses on the three comparison benchmarks, and the paper tests only a single 7B model from a single ecosystem. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on data attribution, corpus curation, or AI auditing; skip it if you need generalizable laws about capability provenance beyond one model-family at one scale.

Problem & Motivation: Training-data attribution (TDA) produces noisy per-document influence scores that are hard to interpret at scale. Prior corpus-scale provenance work either characterizes top-k documents post hoc (Ruis et al., 2025; Razeghi et al., 2024) or unlearns dataset components on closed-data models with proxy datasets (Zhao et al., 2024). Neither approach yields a reusable map from capabilities onto semantically named, inspectable corpus regions. Practitioners who curate pretraining data need to know: which regions of the corpus support which capabilities, so they can audit, reweight, or intervene. This paper closes that gap by operating on a fully open ecosystem (OLMo3-7B / Dolma3) where document-level attribution is possible. Key Idea: Aggregate noisy document-level influence scores over a fixed, semantically interpretable taxonomy (WebOrganizer 24-topic × 24-format = 576 bins) before interpretation, then validate the strongest attribution findings causally via targeted unlearning. The taxonomy, not the individual documents, is the unit of analysis that makes corpus-level claims stable. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Corpus construction: De-duplicate the 6T Dolma3 mix (1,263,587,168 unique documents after removing upsampled duplicates), classify the Common Crawl + olmOCR portion (1,098,646,162 docs) with WebOrganizer classifiers into 576 bins, then draw a stratified working set of 5,678,621 documents (10,000/bin; 10.5B tokens) to equalize bin representation. (2) Attribution: Compute per-document gradients on OLMo3-7B Base via TrackStar (Rademacher projections, d=16, 256 per module, fp32, mixed preconditioner), reduce query gradients from OLMo3-7B Instruct on four benchmarks in a 2×2 design (SocialIQA, MMLU Social Sciences, ARC-Challenge, MMLU STEM; crossing domain × capability type), and compute signed influence as preconditioned gradient dot products. (3) Aggregation: Compute per-bin mean influence, z-score within each benchmark, derive pairwise benchmark contrasts and a correctness differential (influence on correctly vs incorrectly answered queries). (4) Validation: Unlearn top-200 influence-guided documents per topic vs 1,000 random in-topic documents using NGDiff with rank-8 LoRA on OLMo3-7B Base, 3 seeds per condition, 24 topics swept. Critical design decisions: (a) stratified (not proportional) sampling is justified by the corpus's extreme skew (Gini = 0.68 for documents; top-20 bins carry ~36% of tokens) and enables per-bin estimation, though it changes the estimand from population contribution to per-bin conditional signal; (b) the Base-document/Instruct-query split follows Ruis et al. (2025) and treats the instruction-tuning second-order term as identity — an acknowledged approximation; (c) mean aggregation over documents within bin (not median) is chosen because the influence distribution's tail carries the signal that drives unlearning forget sets, while paired unlearning statistics use medians to resist outlier runs. Key Results: SocialIQA's 576-bin influence profile correlates with the three comparison benchmarks at r = 0.06, 0.21, and 0.09, while those three correlate at r = 0.76–0.86 among themselves (outlier statistic Δ = +0.68, 95% CI [+0.34, +0.96], permutation p ≈ 10⁻⁴). The strongest single cell, Literature × Customer Support, reaches +16.0 for SocialIQA and −7.31 for MMLU Social Sciences. The reasoning contrast (SocialIQA − ARC-Challenge) spans top-3 topic differences up to |Δz| = 0.91 versus ≤ 0.63 for the knowledge contrast (MMLU SS − MMLU STEM), a 1.4× dynamic-range ratio. Influence-targeted unlearning produces significantly larger SocialIQA accuracy drops than random in-topic controls (Wilcoxon BH-adjusted p ≈ 10⁻⁵); MMLU STEM reaches significance on the pooled test but not the paired t-test; MMLU Social Sciences does not reach significance; ARC-Challenge shows a negative median paired difference (influence-targeted forgetting is slightly less damaging than random). A held-out suite of nine social-reasoning probes shows seven sharing a provenance block (mean within-block r = 0.70) with a formal-register signature, while SocialIQA sits outside it (r = 0.22 to the block). The full pipeline consumed ~37,000 H200-equivalent GPU-hours. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (taxonomic aggregation of gradient-based TDA over WebOrganizer bins for corpus-scale capability provenance) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (social reasoning draws on qualitatively distinct corpus regions from STEM reasoning, with reasoning-level contrasts sharper than knowledge-level ones). The individual components — TrackStar attribution, WebOrganizer taxonomy, NGDiff unlearning — are existing tools; the contribution is their combination into a validated, interpretable pipeline on a fully open ecosystem, which the authors state is the first such application. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and robustness checks are extensive: format/topic marginal decompositions, negative-control bins (Creative Writing, Transportation), a label-permutation null, three bootstrap schemes with different assumptions, base-model query-gradient re-scoring as a register-robustness control, and a correctness-partition analysis with bootstrap CIs. Multiple seeds (3 per unlearning condition) and paired statistical tests are reported. All code, data artifacts, influence scores, and checkpoints are open-sourced at https://github.com/HCAI-Lab-GT/capabilibara and https://huggingface.co/HCAI-Lab-GT. Methodological concerns: (a) attribution is computed against Instruct query gradients but unlearning is applied to Base, so the associational and causal measurements target different checkpoints; (b) ARC correctness partitions are reconstructed positionally rather than from verified per-query identifiers, weakening that specific analysis; (c) the Literature × Customer Support bin has only 34K documents in the full corpus (one of the corpus's bottom-20 bins by token mass), so its extreme z-score comes from a small population; (d) no comparison against alternative attribution methods (e.g., TRAK, TracIn) is performed. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile. - Practical: Requires H200-class GPUs (~37,000 GPU-hours for the full pipeline), placing it in the range of well-funded academic labs rather than individual practitioners. - Efficient: Once the gradient index is built, scoring new queries is a parallel CPU pass; the expensive part is one-time index construction over 5.68M documents. - Effective: The evidence shows the pipeline identifies corpus regions that are functionally necessary for SocialIQA specifically; for the other three benchmarks the causal validation is weak, null, or reversed, so it solves the stated problem only for a subset of capabilities. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 7B; the authors explicitly state that repeating the pipeline on a larger model is a separate follow-up study given the ~37K GPU-hour cost. The work delivers a reusable software pipeline (Bergson-based attribution + unlearning protocol), a released 576×4 influence matrix, unlearning checkpoints, and analysis notebooks. Strengths: - The 2×2 contrastive benchmark design (domain × capability type) is a genuinely controlled comparison that lets the paper separate domain effects from capability-type effects, rather than confounding them. - Causal validation via targeted unlearning with proper in-topic random controls and paired significance testing moves the work beyond purely associational TDA claims, which is rare in this literature. - The corpus characterization (Gini coefficients, fill rates, token-mass distributions across all 576 bins) is unusually thorough and directly motivates design choices rather than being decorative. - The held-out probe suite with a tiering policy and register-robustness control (base-model query-gradient re-scoring) demonstrates genuine concern for confounds that most TDA papers ignore. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (a) TDA estimates influence but does not prove causal necessity for individual documents, and influence-function approximations are strained on heterogeneous web corpora; (b) results characterize the stratified working set, not the full 1.26B-document population; (c) the core causal validation covers only four benchmarks, with held-out probes being attribution-only except for one ToM unlearning test; (d) unlearning establishes functional necessity without decomposing mechanisms; (e) the analysis uses a single open-data ecosystem, and extending to other families is a separate study. The authors confront these directly and scope claims accordingly — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The Base-document/Instruct-query split introduces a systematic mismatch: document gradients and query gradients come from different checkpoints, and the identity approximation for the instruction-tuning second-order term is unquantified in its error. - No ablation compares the WebOrganizer taxonomy against alternative aggregation schemes (e.g., k-means clusters, source-level labels), so the claim that the fixed taxonomy is what makes interpretation stable is asserted, not demonstrated comparatively. - The Literature × Customer Support bin's extreme SocialIQA score (+16.0) derives from a bin with only ~34K documents in the corpus — the result may be fragile to the specific documents sampled from that bin, and no leave-bin-out sensitivity analysis is reported for this cell. - Only one model size and one corpus are tested, so the central finding (social reasoning draws on distinct regions) cannot be separated from OLMo3/Dolma3-specific data composition. - The correctness-differential analysis for ARC-Challenge relies on positionally reconstructed correctness labels, which the authors flag but then still interpret in the reasoning-vs-knowledge sign-flip narrative. - The unlearning uses rank-8 LoRA merged into the base checkpoint; no check is reported that the unlearning procedure itself is not causing collateral damage that differentially masks or mimics the influence signal across benchmarks. Bottom Line: This is the most methodologically careful corpus-scale capability-provenance study to date on a fully open ecosystem, and it delivers a genuine (if narrow) empirical finding — but its causal validation holds for one benchmark out of four, so practitioners should read it as a well-executed case study with a promising pipeline, not as a general law about how capabilities map to pretraining data.

#15 — Highly Innovative (76)

Safe to Resume? Breaking Execution Continuity of Agent Execution via Rollback

G Wu, D Li, K Jiang, J Niu, C Wang, Y Zhang · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces "execution continuity" as a security property of agent checkpoint/rollback (C/R) systems, derives five failure classes (SF1–SF5) from a Chandy-Lamport-style execution model, and demonstrates three end-to-end attacks (malware-verification bypass on Hermes, unauthorized mail forwarding on Cline, duplicate payment on LangGraph) plus a multi-agent trace-analysis pipeline that detects and validates these failures across five frameworks. - Why it's important: Agent systems are becoming persistent and stateful (Tata Steel: 300+ agents; Cognizant: 200+ agents serving 350,000 employees), and C/R is becoming their default recovery mechanism — yet a faithfully restored checkpoint can rebind a genuine security judgment (a validation, approval, or authorization) to an artifact it never judged, without any checkpoint corruption or compromised recovery code. - How it does it: The core move is modeling each agent framework's recovery boundary (framework-state, workspace-state, or OS/VM-state) against an execution model with independently evolving internal processes and an outside world that does not roll back, then systematically enumerating how rollback breaks causal cuts, external assumptions, nondeterministic replay binding, and effect records. - The good: The empirical validation is unusually thorough: 347 traces / 1,735 framework-task executions over TerminalBench and AgentBench with native-rollback confirmation, 98.7% precision / 99.9% recall against fully manual ground-truth labeling, and 30 of 30 sampled findings converted to successful attacks under a malicious-skill adversary. - The missing: The paper validates failures at a single randomly selected checkpoint per trace under its own task distribution, and its prevalence numbers (e.g., SF5 at 2.3%) are admitted to be artifacts of benchmarks where few tasks produce persistent external effects — so headline prevalence figures are not directly transferable to production agent deployments. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or secure agent frameworks, tool-calling infrastructure, or agent-facing transaction systems (payments, credentials, mail); skip it if you only need classic anti-rollback state-continuity work (Memoir, Narrator), which this paper is the agent-era descendant of.

Problem & Motivation: Long-running AI agents accumulate execution state and external effects (paid invoices, forwarded mail, credentials) that are costly to reconstruct, so checkpoint-and-rollback is becoming standard recovery infrastructure: frameworks checkpoint graph state (LangGraph, CrewAI), coding agents snapshot workspaces via shadow Git (Hermes, Cline, Gemini CLI, Claude Code), and sandboxes snapshot full VM state (E2B, CRAB, DeltaBox). The unstudied gap is that correct rollback does not imply secure recovery: security-relevant facts carried across recovery (an artifact passed verification, an approval was given, a binding held) depend on state, assumptions, and effects distributed across framework state, files, nondeterministic decisions, and external services that do not share the checkpoint's recovery boundary. A 2026 enterprise survey (79% of respondents reversed an agent action; 42% reported revenue loss from agent failures) indicates the pain point is real, and prior agent-recovery security work (Resume Means Resume, DART, ACRFence) covers only fragments of this space. Key Idea: The single core insight is the distinction between correct rollback and secure recovery: a checkpoint's recovery boundary K (the set of processes it covers) almost never covers the full dependency closure of the security-relevant facts it carries, and the outside world W does not roll back with the agent. Once formalized — rollback reconstructs the configuration X̂ = (checkpointed states for Pi ∈ K) ⊕ (recovered states ρj for Pj ∉ K) ⊕ W^tr — the five failure modes (incomplete internal coverage, causally inconsistent cuts, external-state mismatch, unbound nondeterministic replay, unrecorded external effects) fall out as the combinatorially distinguishable ways this recombination violates either the recovered state or the recovery transition. Methodology: The paper proceeds in three stages. (1) Characterization: 12 agent C/R systems are classified into three recovery-boundary categories — framework-state (LangGraph superstep snapshots, CrewAI event-driven checkpoints), workspace-state (Hermes shadow-Git with /rollback and a 20-checkpoint/500 MB retention policy, Cline's independent workspace/task-history restore), and OS/VM-state (E2B explicit create_snapshot of filesystem and memory) — summarized in Table I. (2) Formal model: processes P with local states, events e = (a, ξ) with nondeterminism factors, causal precedence ≺, checkpoints C_K = (s_i^{k_i})_{Pi∈K}, and a compatibility predicate Γ(s_i, W) for external assumptions; execution continuity is violated either via an invalid recovered state or an invalid recovery transition. (3) Detection pipeline: a four-agent pipeline (collector → analyzer → checker → validator) where the analyzer reconstructs structured events ei = ⟨op_i, In_i, Out_i, ND_i⟩ with versioned states and dependencies, the checker applies five SF-specific rules to flag candidates, and the validator performs actual native rollback and re-execution (three replays for SF4 candidates) to confirm security-relevant invalidation; all security-relevance annotations are fixed before rollback validation. Critical design decisions: (a) using each framework's native recovery mechanism for validation rather than a simulated rollback — well-justified, prevents framework-external artifacts; (b) freezing analyzer annotations before validation — well-justified against circularity; (c) LLM-based (DeepSeek-v4) semantic trace reconstruction — weaker justification, though partially compensated by the 98.7%/99.9% manual-precision/recall audit of every trace-recovery-point instance. Key Results: Across 347 traces (241 TerminalBench, 106 AgentBench across OS/DB/ALFWorld) yielding 1,735 framework-task executions over five frameworks, validated failure rates per execution were SF1 67.2%, SF4 67.7%, SF2 489 executions (~28%, concentrated in Hermes/Cline: e.g., Hermes/TerminalBench 143 SF2 occurrences), SF3 198 (~11%, zero for CrewAI which checkpoints at task start, zero for E2B in AgentBench), and SF5 2.3%. E2B's OS/VM snapshots eliminated SF1/SF2 entirely but left SF3–SF5 possible. The pipeline achieved 98.7% precision, 99.9% recall, 99.5% accuracy against exhaustive manual labeling (Table V); all 30 sampled validated findings converted to successful malicious-skill attacks, and the Case-1 malicious skill evades a recent neuro-symbolic malicious-skill detector. A 96-workflow microbenchmark on persistent external actions (payments, messages, resource changes) shows neither execute→commit (90/96 = 93.8% failure) nor commit→execute (93/96 = 96.9% failure) ordering closes the external-effect gap. Tested scale: standard benchmark tasks on a 16-core/32 GB Linux server; no stress-scale testing. Baselines are contemporary (current framework documentation, AgentDojo, SWE-bench trajectories, OSWorld-Human), though comparisons are qualitative since no competing detection systems exist. Surprising finding: broader snapshots do not imply safety — full-sandbox E2B still fails on external dependencies, and the most complete checkpoints leave the structurally unavoidable SF3–SF5 open. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM + NEW FORMULATION + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the systematic cross-boundary security framing of agent C/R (the execution-continuity property and the SF1–SF5 taxonomy derived from a general recovery model) and the first cross-framework prevalence measurement with native-rollback validation. The underlying formal machinery is a competent adaptation of Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshots and classic rollback-recovery/anti-rollback theory (Memoir, Narrator) to agent systems; the attacks use known adversary primitives (malicious skills, poisoned MCP servers) in a new role — as rollback-timing triggers rather than as direct state manipulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence exists at the design-space level (each framework's failure profile traces to its recovery-boundary choice), and the ordering microbenchmark ablates commit ordering. Unusually strong validation hygiene: every trace-recovery-point instance was manually labeled to establish ground truth, per-SF precision/recall is reported (SF1: 96.6%/100%; SF2–SF4: 100%/100%; SF5: 100%/90%), and all annotations were frozen pre-validation. Weaknesses: single LLM backend (DeepSeek-v4) for both agent execution and analysis; one random checkpoint per trace as the fixed recovery point; three-replay protocol for SF4 is small; no error bars or significance tests; failure modes were characterized on the same framework behaviors then evaluated on the same frameworks (inherent to the problem, but prevalence numbers should be read as descriptive of the tested configuration — the authors themselves disclaim framework ranking). The paper states that attacks, execution traces, and artifacts are "included in our artifact," but no URL or repository is given in the provided text. Preprint, not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the detection pipeline). Practical: Yes — the analysis pipeline runs on a single 16-core/32 GB Linux server with a commercial LLM backend; the attacks require only documented C/R interfaces and a malicious skill/MCP server. Efficient: Cost is not reported in compute terms; the pipeline adds LLM-based trace reconstruction per execution, and the validator's native-rollback + re-execution (×3 for SF4) is inherently per-candidate. Effective: The evidence shows the failures manifest under native rollback on the tested benchmarks with 98.7% detection precision and 30/30 exploitability confirmation, but effective prevention is not delivered — the paper stops at detection and design takeaways (deterministic references, recovery-state specification, external coordination mechanisms), not a deployed defense. Scalable: Not tested at 10×–100× scale; production workloads with heavy external-service interaction (where SF5 concentrates) are underrepresented in the evaluated benchmark mix by the authors' own admission. Delivered artifact: analysis pipeline and attack traces (claimed in artifact, no public URL given); no hardened C/R tool or patch set ships with the paper. Strengths: (1) A crisp, reusable conceptual contribution — the recovery-boundary-versus-dependency-closure gap — that immediately generalizes: it explains why E2B's full-sandbox snapshots still fail and why no commit ordering fixes external effects (93.8%/96.9% failure both ways). (2) End-to-end attack realism without checkpoint corruption: all three attacks work within documented C/R behavior and trusted components, and evade a recent malicious-skill detector, making the threat credible rather than hypothetical. (3) Validation discipline rarely seen in agent-security papers: exhaustive manual labeling (all instances, both error directions), pre-frozen security-relevance annotations, and native-mechanism rollback validation rather than simulation. (4) The three design observations (semantic references to external context — 1,357 instances counted; under-specified recovery state; commit-ordering insufficiency) are concrete, quantified, and actionable for framework designers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the five failure modes do not cover all agent security failures, that identified hazards are not necessarily exploitable in every deployment, that the methodology exposes and validates recovery violations but does not certify system security, and that framework-level prevalence numbers should not be read as a security ranking (checkpoint policies differ). They also acknowledge SF5's 2.3% rate is largely a task-distribution artifact and that exploitability depends on surrounding application and adversarial capabilities. This is a direct, non-defensive treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Prevalence extrapolation risk: TerminalBench/AgentBench tasks are local-file, database, and simulation workloads; production agents in payments, mail, and cloud provisioning (the settings of the three motivating attacks) are precisely the ones the benchmark mix underrepresents, so "67% of executions fail" should not be read as a deployment statistic. (2) One checkpoint per trace: testing only a single randomly selected recovery point per trace may understate or misallocate per-SF prevalence relative to all checkpoints (LangGraph imposes no default retention limit; Cline has none either). (3) LLM-in-the-loop dependency: trace semantics, security-relevance annotation, and failure judgment all flow through DeepSeek-v4; no cross-LLM robustness check is reported, and the manual validation — while exhaustive — was performed by the same team. (4) No defense is built or even prototyped, so the practical remedy (durable effect records, idempotency, dependency-preserving checkpoints) is asserted rather than evaluated; the related-work-adjacent systems (Atomix, Cordon, ACRFence) that address subsets are not empirically compared. (5) The "first systematic security study" framing is contested by the paper's own related work (DART, ACRFence, Resume Means Resume each cover a slice); the novelty is in breadth, not in being first to any single failure mode. (6) No public artifact URL, limiting reproducibility despite the artifact claim. Bottom Line: For anyone building agent frameworks, sandbox infrastructure, or security tooling for stateful agents, this is the reference point for agent-rollback security and worth reading in full; for readers seeking a solution, it diagnoses thoroughly but prescribes only design lessons, and no deployed alternative yet covers the same cross-boundary ground.

Does Reasoning Mitigate Backdoor Attacks? A Neuro- Symbolic Perspective

MA Corallo, A Agiollo, M Conti, A Giaretta · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the first systematic empirical evaluation of backdoor attacks against neuro-symbolic (NeSy) models, comparing DeepProbLog against matched neural baselines across 4 attacks, 4 reasoning tasks, and targeted/untargeted settings, and introduces a 'reachability' metric that predicts when attacks will succeed. - Why it's important: NeSy models are frequently marketed as robust-by-design for safety-critical deployment, and this paper shows that claimed robustness is real only for logically unsatisfiable attack targets — for everything else, backdoors succeed nearly as well as on plain neural networks. - How it does it: It runs dirty-label data-poisoning backdoors (BadNet, WaNet, FTrojan, ReFool) identically against a DeepProbLog model and a neural model sharing the same encoder and training data, then shows the targeted attack success rate is bounded above by the fraction of inputs for which the attacker's target label is logically derivable from the symbolic program (target reachability R(y_t)). - The good: The reachability analysis is validated tightly: observed ASR tracks predicted reachability across all tasks (e.g., ASR ≈ 0 for unsatisfiable targets like y_t=13 in multiplication and Forward+Stop in SDDOIA on DPL, ASR ≈ 1 for fully reachable ones), turning an empirical observation into a training-free, attack-agnostic prediction rule. - The missing: Only one NeSy framework (DeepProbLog) is tested, so the central claim about NeSy robustness rests on a single probabilistic-logic architecture whose compile-based inference may behave differently from constraint-based or semantic-loss NeSy methods. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or trust NeSy/concept-based systems in security-sensitive settings — it is the only concrete evidence base on their backdoor behavior — but skip it if you only care about backdoor attacks on standard neural networks, where existing literature already covers the baselines used here.
