Problem & Motivation: Neuro-symbolic AI combines neural perception with symbolic reasoning and is increasingly motivated by claimed robustness benefits, but that evidence comes exclusively from naturally occurring noise and distribution shift — not from an adaptive adversary who deliberately poisons training data. The authors ask whether symbolic constraints genuinely prevent trigger learning, or whether the neural-symbolic interface is an additional attack surface. Prior work (reasoning-shortcut analyses, position papers like Parmar 2026) argued NeSy systems may not be inherently safe, but no study had empirically measured how established NeSy frameworks behave under training-time backdoor attacks. This matters for anyone deploying concept-based NeSy pipelines where data collection is outsourced and a malicious data provider is realistic. Key Idea: The core insight is that a backdoor against a NeSy model succeeds exactly to the extent that its target label is reachable under the symbolic program: the attacker's trigger need only force some concept z such that K(z, c) = y_t for the contexts c seen at inference, so the symbolic layer acts as a sharp logical gate on targeted attacks while providing essentially no protection against untargeted corruption (any logically consistent wrong answer suffices). The latent-space analysis confirms the encoder always learns the trigger cluster — even at 1% poisoning — so mitigation happens entirely at the reasoning layer, never in perception. Methodology: The threat model is a dirty-label data-poisoning adversary who modifies a fraction (ρ = 0.1 default) of training images and task labels but cannot touch the clean context, the symbolic program, or the training procedure. Four concept-based tasks are used: MNIST addition and multiplication (single-image operand plus integer context c), a newly introduced FashionMNIST 'binding' task with compatibility rules over season and body-part attributes, and the SDDOIA autonomous-driving multi-label task from RSBench (21 binary concepts mapped to 4 action labels). For each task, DeepProbLog (neural predicate distributions propagated through compiled probabilistic inference, per Equation 8) and an NN baseline (same encoder, FC classification head) are trained on identical poisoned data from four attacks: BadNet (patch), WaNet (elastic warping), FTrojan (frequency-domain), and ReFool (reflection blending, re-implemented as dirty-label). Metrics are clean accuracy/F1 and Attack Success Rate computed only over initially-correct predictions (Equations 19–20). For targeted attacks they define reachability R(y_t) = max_z Pr_c[K(z,c) = y_t] under the empirical context distribution (Equation 21), proving ASR_t ≤ R(y_t), plus a black-box attacker variant R_u using a uniform context distribution. Critical design decisions: (i) collapsing two-image arithmetic to single-image-plus-context to fit the standard backdoor setting — reasonable but changes the benchmark; (ii) attack hyperparameters tuned on a held-out validation set (ablations for poisoning ratio and WaNet grid/warp strength in Appendix A.2) — good practice; (iii) restricting the attacker from poisoning contexts or concepts — justified on threat-model grounds, though it is what makes the reasoning layer protective at all. Key Results: On MNIST Addition, DPL caps targeted ASR at 0.101 across BadNet/WaNet/ReFool and all targets, versus 0.840–0.999 on the NN baseline, with clean accuracy unchanged (~0.987 both). On MNIST Multiplication, DPL robustness collapses exactly where the logic permits it: ASR = 0.999 for the absorbing-element target y_t = 0 but 0.000 for unsatisfiable prime y_t = 13, while NN reaches ASR ≥ 0.84 even on 13. On FashionMNIST Binding, symbolic constraints help but do not suppress: highly compatible targets (bag, trouser) achieve ASR ≥ 0.80 on DPL; constrained targets (ankle_boot, tshirt) drop to ~0.56–0.59. On SDDOIA, DPL fully suppresses only the logically contradictory Forward+Stop target (ASR 0.000 vs 0.997 on NN); all satisfiable targets yield ASR 0.42–0.98 on both models. Untargeted attacks mostly bypass the logic: DPL ASR_u is 0.73–0.96 on Addition, Binding, and SDDOIA (roughly matching NN), with the sole exception of Multiplication (e.g., WaNet ASR 0.006 on DPL vs 0.833 on NN), attributed to the large output space rather than intrinsic robustness. Observed ASR closely matches computed reachability across all tasks (Table 6), e.g., multiplication y_t=0: R = 1.000, ASR = 0.766; y_t=13: R = 0, ASR = 0. Experiments comprise ~7,780 runs over 5 random seeds with reported mean ± std, ~650 GPU hours on consumer GPUs. FTrojan consistently failed on the MNIST arithmetic tasks despite succeeding on standard MNIST classification with the same hyperparameters — reported honestly but not theoretically explained. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first systematic backdoor evaluation of NeSy models) plus a NEW FORMULATION (the target-reachability bound R(y_t) linking symbolic satisfiability to attack success). The individual components — DeepProbLog, standard backdoor attacks, dirty-label poisoning — are all existing techniques; the novelty lies in the controlled DPL-vs-NN experimental design and in the reachability analysis that explains and predicts the empirical pattern, not in any new attack or architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: The controlled comparison (shared encoder, data, and optimization; only the output mapping differs) is a genuine strength, and ablations cover poisoning ratio (0.005–0.1) and WaNet parameters, with attack hyperparameters tuned on a separate validation set rather than the test benchmark. Five seeds with mean ± std are reported throughout, and the FTrojan failure was verified against the original MNIST classification benchmark to rule out implementation error. Code is released at https://github.com/marcoantoniocorallo/NeSy-Backdoor. Concerns: no significance tests beyond std; results are confined to small 28×28-image benchmarks (MNIST-scale), so the reachability–ASR correspondence is demonstrated only at toy scale; the FashionMNIST binding task is the authors' own construction; and no defensive baselines (e.g., STRIP, activation clustering) or detection methods are evaluated, so the paper measures vulnerability but not whether known defenses change the picture. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an experimental security evaluation, no deployed system). Practical: Yes — all experiments run on consumer GPUs (RTX 5070 8GB, RTX 4080 Super 16GB). Efficient: Cheap relative to typical poisoning studies (~650 GPU hours total, 5–20 epochs per run); the reachability metric itself is training-free and computable from the symbolic program alone. Effective: The evidence convincingly shows the reasoning layer suppresses only logically unsatisfiable targets — it solves the stated diagnostic question, not a general defense problem, and the paper does not claim otherwise. Scalable: Untested beyond MNIST-scale tasks with ≤21 concepts; the paper itself flags single-input restriction, and the reachability computation for multi-concept inputs reduces to satisfiability checking that could grow combinatorially — no 10×–100× evidence exists. Deliverable: a reusable evaluation codebase and the reachability analysis method; no model weights or dataset release beyond code is stated. Strengths: (1) The reachability metric is a genuinely useful contribution: a training-free, attack-agnostic upper bound on targeted ASR that a defender can compute from the knowledge base alone, validated by ASR tracking R(y_t) within a few points across every task (Table 6). (2) The controlled DPL-vs-NN design cleanly isolates the effect of symbolic integration, avoiding the confounds that plague most robustness comparisons. (3) The mechanistic finding — trigger clusters form in the DPL latent space at 1% poisoning regardless of eventual ASR, and untargeted attacks shift predictions along the diagonal to stay logically valid — correctly localizes where protection does and does not occur. (4) Honest treatment of the FTrojan anomaly, including cross-benchmark verification rather than silent omission. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three directly: experiments cover only single-input reasoning tasks (multi-perceptual-input NeSy is untested); enriching tasks with trusted context could shrink reachable output sets (a defense direction, not tested); and the threat model permits poisoning only task-level labels — a stronger grey-box attacker poisoning intermediate concepts could bypass the reasoning layer with logically consistent malicious concepts. These are confronted candidly in Section 8 rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Generalization beyond DeepProbLog is unstated but critical — the paper's framing is about 'NeSy models' broadly, yet constraint-based or semantic-loss NeSy methods (cited but untested) may admit partial satisfiability where compiled ProbLog semantics give binary gates, so the sharp satisfiable/unsatisfiable dichotomy may be a DeepProbLog artifact. (2) All targeted-attack analysis assumes the attacker knows or can estimate the context distribution π; the black-box relaxation R_u exists, but no experiments quantify attacker performance under genuinely unknown context distributions. (3) The untargeted result is arguably underexplored: the cyclic +1 mod |Y| mapping is the only untargeted strategy tested, and smarter untargeted mappings might behave differently on Multiplication, where DPL appears robust. (4) Clean accuracy under poisoning is reported but the utility cost of symbolic constraints at higher poisoning ratios is only partially covered by the Appendix ablation. (5) No comparison against any backdoor defense, so practitioners cannot judge whether adding symbolic reasoning is more or less cost-effective than established poisoning defenses. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying or designing NeSy systems should read this: it delivers the first concrete evidence that symbolic reasoning is a narrow, exactly-characterizable safeguard (blocking only logically unsatisfiable targets) rather than a general backdoor defense, and its reachability metric is a cheap tool any NeSy system designer can apply to their own knowledge base — though its single-framework, toy-scale evidence base means broader conclusions about 'NeSy robustness' should be held loosely.

Problem & Motivation: Hybrid LLMs like Qwen3.8-27B (48 GDN layers + 16 softmax-attention layers) replace most attention with a fixed-size recurrent state updated by the gated delta rule. Every public 4-bit checkpoint of this model, and the model authors' own FP8 release, protect the GDN block — especially the decay gate (a) and write-strength gate (b) projections — on the intuition that a recurrence carrying state across tens of thousands of tokens must accumulate per-step quantization error. Nobody had tested this; the exemptions cost memory, KV budget, and prefill throughput on the very layers that dominate the model (75% of layers). The paper closes this gap: is the protective precision map justified, and if not, why not? Key Idea: The core insight is that three architectural properties — not luck — make the GDN block the easiest part of a hybrid to quantize: (1) NVFP4's 16-element block scaling confines each residual-stream outlier to 15 neighbors, equalizing activation error (~7.5–9.2%) across all layer roles; (2) the log-space gate parameterization g = −exp(A_log)·softplus(a+dt_bias) and β = σ(b) compresses ~11% pre-activation GEMM error before it reaches the control signals, whereas the same relative noise applied directly to α produces 22% state error; (3) the delta rule's write term overwrites the state along each new key direction, so injected noise plateaus (12.6% over 32K tokens) and a 1% state impulse decays to 1/e within 80–1,382 steps — far faster than the decay-implied horizons of 44K–62K tokens. The projections the community protects are exactly the ones the architecture already protects. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Checkpoint construction: llm-compressor NVFP4 W4A4 (E2M1 values, E4M3 scale per 16-element block) applied to all 496 linear layers (240 GDN, 64 attention, 192 MLP), calibrated on a frozen 128×32K-token set, excluding lm_head, embeddings, convolutions, and norms; a checkpoint-side repair harmonizes global scales for vLLM's fused GEMMs. (2) Evaluation under one fixed serving regime: vLLM 0.27.1, TP=1, one RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), FP8 KV cache, chat-template harness with per-sample validity gates; suites are WikiText-2 PPL at 4K/32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25 (pass@1, 4 seeds), GPQA-Diamond (4 seeds), LiveCodeBench v6, and RULER NIAH at 32K/64K, against BF16 and two community NVFP4 recipes (Unsloth Dynamic v3, RadixArk ModelOpt) that keep GDN/attention at FP8. (3) Mechanism study: real 32K-token activations captured from all 48 GDN layers; NVFP4 fake quantization to inject pure 4-bit rounding; per-projection sensitivity replays (96 layer-sequence runs); FP32 lockstep recurrence — one clean trajectory vs. eleven perturbed ones over 32K tokens on five layers across depth — plus synthetic-noise and impulse arms; and a per-position decomposition of 32K NLL. Critical design decisions: fake quantization isolates rounding error from kernel numerics (well-justified, with kernel-vs-reference floors characterized in Appendix A); the within-path FP32 comparison sidesteps the BF16 kernel's 3.8×10⁻³ floor exceeding the smallest measured perturbation (well-justified); inheriting Minima+scales task scores from Minima based on the KV ablation (partially justified — PPL/RULER/throughput re-measured, task scores not). Key Results: Under one serving regime, no pair of models is CI-separated on any task: Minima scores 85.10 on the 5-task average vs. BF16's 85.62 (−0.52), Unsloth 85.34, RadixArk 84.80; AIME'25 is exactly 86.7 for both BF16 and Minima (all four Minima seeds 26/30) and mean AIME generation length matches BF16 to one token (14,531 vs. 14,532). Minima is the smallest (17.53 GiB vs. BF16's 50.13; 7–13% smaller than community builds) and fastest at prefill (TTFT at 32K: 4.03 s vs. 6.90 s BF16; +14–19% prompt throughput at 8K over Unsloth/RadixArk), with decode within 4% of other 4-bit recipes (RadixArk leads by 2–4% due to small-batch activation-quantization overhead). Perplexity is the one metric that orders recipes as expected (Unsloth < RadixArk < Minima), but Minima's gap shrinks with position: +0.72 at 4K vs. +0.49 at 32K, with the weight-quantization NLL gap falling from +0.081 nats (first half) to +0.011 (second half) and turning negative (−0.053) in the final 2K. The serving-stack findings are individually notable: the fused-GEMM scale mismatch (per-module scales differing 1.82×–2.75× across all 48 layers) produced a deceptively better-than-BF16 long-context perplexity (6.86 vs. true 10.84) while degrading AIME by ~6 points; raw-completion harnesses on this thinking model produced ±40–60-point per-subject swings (66.3 vs. valid 80.4 for BF16 MMLU-Pro); calibrated FP8 KV scales recover 83% of the 32K PPL penalty at zero throughput cost. Baselines are current community checkpoints of the same model, though all evaluated on the authors' own harness. RULER is 100/100 for all four models at 32K/64K — a saturated benchmark providing no discrimination. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (recurrent-state mixers in large hybrids survive full W4A4 PTQ, inverting the protective consensus) plus a NEW METHOD in a narrow sense (first shipped fully-W4A4-GDN NVFP4 checkpoint via calibration-only PTQ) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (released checkpoint and repaired serving recipe). The genuinely novel part is the mechanistic account linking block scaling, gate parameterization, and delta-rule error erasure to the end-to-end result; the quantization machinery itself (llm-compressor, NVFP4, vLLM) is standard, and the concurrent QUASAR QAT checkpoint shows the same configuration is reachable by a different (training-based) route — though QUASAR offers no explanation and no controlled comparison, so the causal study here remains the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a quantization paper: per-projection sensitivity, synthetic-noise arms locating the actual fragility (α-noise vs. β-noise), impulse-response runs across five depths, and a position-binned NLL decomposition that separately tracks weight cost and KV cost. Statistics are reported: 4-seed pass@1 with 95% CIs for AIME/GPQA (with the honest note that Minima's degenerate all-identical AIME seeds make its interval uninformative), truncation rates, per-seed scores, and the explicit statement that no pair is CI-separated on any task. The standalone GDN reimplementation is verified against the reference to 6×10⁻³ and FP32 kernel numerics are characterized in an appendix, including a reproducibility trap (the 1/√K query scale). The quantized checkpoint is released at https://huggingface.co/minima-ai/mnma_qwen3.8_27b_nvfp4; harness code and captured activations are not stated as released. Methodological concerns: single-model evidence means the title's general claim ("Gated DeltaNet") is supported by one architecture; perplexity development and evaluation both center on WikiText-2 within one serving path (mitigated by the fixed-regime discipline and by task-score corroboration); RULER saturation means retrieval robustness is weakly tested. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — a released, servable checkpoint and serving-stack repairs). - Practical: Runs on a single commercially available GPU (RTX PRO 6000, 96 GB, native NVFP4 tensor cores) at TP=1; 17.53 GiB weights leave the largest KV budget (1.81M cacheable tokens on one card). - Efficient: 2.9× smaller than BF16, decode 1,154 tok/s at concurrency 32 (1.86× BF16's 621), TTFT at 32K nearly halved (4.03 s vs. 6.90 s); trails RadixArk by 2–4% on decode due to kernel-level activation-quantization overhead. - Effective: Evidence shows task parity with BF16 across six suites plus a mechanistic account of the residual perplexity gap; this is a direct evaluation of the stated problem, not a proxy, though only for this model. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 64K contexts and one 27B model; the flat-plateau mechanism predicts bounded error at longer contexts, but 128K+ behavior is explicitly acknowledged as extrapolation. Delivers a software artifact: a released Hugging Face checkpoint (Minima+scales); the scale-harmonization repair is described precisely enough (94 scale sets, worst ratio 2.81×, re-rounding error ≤6.2%) to reimplement, but no standalone tool or library is stated as released. Strengths: - The paper refutes a widely held intuition with a causal mechanism rather than a spot check: the four-link chain (block scaling → gate nonlinearities → delta-rule error erasure → positional PPL decomposition) makes each layer of the explanation independently testable, and the pieces cross-validate (the lockstep plateau predicts the shrinking end-to-end gap, which is then measured). - The finding that the community's most protected projections (a, b) are the two least sensitive (2.1%/2.6% output effect vs. 10–13% for the plain GEMMs) is a sharp, counter-intuitive, actionable result. - The serving-stack forensics are genuinely valuable and would not appear in a typical quantization paper: the fused-GEMM scale mismatch that improves long-context perplexity while silently corrupting the gates is a trap any future GDN-quantizing practitioner would hit, and the paper diagnoses and repairs it. - Measurement discipline throughout: one fixed serving regime, per-sample validity gates, truncation statistics, CI reporting, and honest flags (degenerate seed interval, RULER saturation implied by uniform 100s). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: single model family/size and single format (NVFP4); no 128K+ stress tests, with longer-context behavior flagged as extrapolation; the concurrent QUASAR QAT checkpoint is acknowledged but not benchmarked (released after their campaign closed, different recipe class); Minima+scales task scores are inherited rather than re-measured; a 2–4% decode deficit vs. RadixArk attributed to kernel overhead; and the gate-shielding argument is parameterization-specific — linearly-parameterized decay gates may not be shielded, with their own 0.1% α-noise result demonstrating the fragility. This is a direct, well-confronted limitations section; nothing is minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Generalization is the headline gap the authors underplay in the title: the mechanism depends on Qwen3.8's specific log-space gate parameterization, head sizes (K=V=128), and outlier structure; "Gated DeltaNet survives 4-bit quantization" is demonstrated for one checkpoint, and recurrent mixers with different gating (e.g., Mamba2-style linear decay, different A_log initialization distributions) are untested. - The mechanism study uses a standalone reimplementation of one GDN layer fed by captured activations, not the fused chunkwise kernel in the served model; the within-path FP32 discipline is sound, but the bridge from replay to serving rests on the appendix numerics verification rather than an end-to-end fake-quant study. - No comparison against a stronger PTQ baseline (e.g., GPTQ-style or SmoothQuant-family variants applied to GDN), so it is unknown whether plain RTN-style NVFP4 calibration is even the right PTQ method or whether the result would hold for harder calibration regimes (shorter/diverse calibration data is not ablated — calibration is one frozen 128×32K set). - The evaluation GPU (SM120 with native NVFP4) means the throughput story is tied to one hardware generation; no cross-vendor or older-GPU numbers. - The claimed KV-scale interaction (3× PPL penalty for W4A4 weights) has a stated hypothesis ("less headroom") but no direct experiment isolating the cause. Bottom Line: Any practitioner quantizing or serving hybrid linear-attention LLMs should read this — it is the first controlled evidence that the recurrent half is safe to quantize, a released checkpoint to use, and a set of serving-stack traps (fused-scale mismatch especially) that will otherwise silently corrupt results — with the caveat that its generality claim awaits replication on a second architecture.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StudentSim, a two-stage training framework (pooled training followed by per-student LoRA specialization) that turns sparse per-student records into individualized LLM student simulators that are both behaviorally faithful to a specific student and responsive to natural-language tutor guidance, plus a standardized 60-student evaluation protocol (StudentSimEval) spanning chess, L2 English writing, and mathematics. - Why it's important: Collecting per-student feedback on which teaching approaches work is slow, costly, and sparse, so AI tutor evaluation and training lag behind frontier model progress; a simulator that faithfully stands in for teachable students supplies that feedback signal at machine timescales. - How it does it: A base Qwen3-4B-Instruct with a domain LoRA is first fine-tuned on records pooled across 100–200 students to learn shared response patterns and guidance-following, then that adapter is further fine-tuned on each individual student's own records (e.g., 1,000 chess records) to specialize. - The good: Across all three domains the specialized simulators beat prompted GPT-5.4 and the state-tracking Maia2 baseline on both metrics — e.g., chess F=0.5150/R=0.9067 vs. GPT-5.4 F=0.2316/R=0.7186 and Maia2 F=0.4535/R=0.2721 — and a frozen simulator used as the RL reward for a chess tutor yields the tutor that expert humans rate best on all three axes (90.5% accuracy vs. 75.7% no-RL). - The missing: The chess fidelity prompt for StudentSim includes a Maia2-derived top-5 candidate-move list that is deliberately withheld from the LLM baselines, so part of the headline F gain may come from a stronger input rather than from per-student training; the tutor-RL claim is also validated only in chess with a Stockfish-defined reward. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on simulated students, tutor RL, or learner-model evaluation in education NLP — it is the first per-individual, weight-level simulator framework with a reusable benchmark — but skip it if you need multi-turn learning dynamics or evidence beyond a single-domain tutor proof of concept.

Problem & Motivation: Adaptive AI tutors need feedback on which guidance works for which student, but real-student feedback is sparse (median L2 learner has 3 essays; >71% write five or fewer), slow, and costly to collect. Existing student simulators split into two families, each satisfying only one requirement: state-tracking/knowledge-tracing models and behavior cloners (e.g., Maia2) fit real learner behavior but have no input pathway for natural-language tutor guidance, while prompted LLM role-play follows tutor guidance fluently but does not reproduce a target student's competence (GPT-5.4 reaches only F=0.23 on chess). The gap is per-student simulators that are jointly faithful to an individual's behavior and updatable under guidance — the two properties tutor training needs (a personalized starting point and the capacity to be taught), mirroring the educational-measurement distinction between independent performance and the zone of proximal development. Key Idea: Cast student simulation as a jointly optimizable two-metric target — behavioral fidelity (F: match the student's own held-out responses) and guidance responsiveness (R: update to the canonical corrected response after reading tutor guidance) — and satisfy both simultaneously via pooled-then-specialized fine-tuning: Stage 1 learns what is shared across students in a domain (common mistakes, response format, guidance→revision pathway) from pooled records, and Stage 2 adapts that shared LoRA adapter to one student's sparse records, so per-student specialization starts from a population-level foundation instead of overfitting from scratch. The F/R decomposition itself is the conceptual move that turns a previously fuzzy simulation-quality debate into a measurable, comparable objective. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) cast public learner corpora (Lichess May 2025 chess games; EFCAMDAT L2 essays with teacher corrections; FoundationalASSIST math interactions) into a per-student record schema of single-turn records S_i=(problem, student response) and multi-turn records T_i=(problem, wrong response, tutor guidance, canonical corrected response m*); (2) Stage 1 trains one domain LoRA (rank 128, AdamW, lr 1e-4, bf16, 8×A100, ms-swift) on pooled records with a 0.2 multi-turn mixing ratio; (3) Stage 2 continues training that adapter on each Stage-2 student's own records (30 chess / 15 L2 / 15 math students), producing 60 simulators; (4) evaluate on frozen chronological held-out splits scored identically for every method. F is top-1 move accuracy (chess), LanguageTool error-density profile match (L2), or top-1 accuracy on a four-way multiple-choice form built from real other-student distractors (math); R is exact-match/top-1 against the canonical correction (Stockfish best move, teacher-corrected fragment, correct answer letter). Tutor RL (chess only): a Qwen3-VL-8B tutor trained with GRPO, where each episode replays a real student's wrong move, the tutor proposes guidance, a frozen Stage-1 simulator revises, and reward is the Stockfish centipawn improvement, gated multiplicatively by two lightweight linear heads (personalization, board-state perception) mounted on the simulator's backbone. Critical design decisions: (i) pooling in Stage 1 is ablated directly (replacing pooled records with one student's repeated records at matched optimizer budget drops F 0.5131→0.4602 and R 0.9003→0.8276), justifying the two-stage split; (ii) the multi-turn ratio ρ=0.2 sits inside a broad plateau (R>0.8 for any ρ≥0.025, F invariant within ±0.004), well-justified; (iii) chronological train/held-out splits per student are a sound choice; the Maia2-derived candidate list included in StudentSim's chess prompt but withheld from LLM baselines is the least well-justified design choice. Key Results: Chess (30 players, 5,000 single-turn + 4,000 multi-turn held-out records per player): StudentSim F=0.5150 vs. Maia2 0.4535, GPT-5.4 0.2316, GPT-4o 0.2163; R=0.9067 vs. GPT-4o 0.7655, GPT-5.4 0.7186, Maia2 0.2721 (Maia2's R is a zero-guidance floor). L2 (15 learners, 26 essays/40 corrections held out each): F=0.5624 vs. GPT-5.4 0.5141; R=0.6417 vs. GPT-5.4 0.5950 and untrained Qwen3-4B 0.0200. Math (15 students, 66/mean-59 held-out each, 879-record R set): F=0.6384 vs. GPT-5.4 0.6121; R=0.9181 vs. GPT-5.4 0.7099. The gap is largest on open-ended guidance modes (chess Socratic R: 0.7649 vs. GPT-5.4 0.5174; math Socratic 0.8783 vs. 0.655). Headline numbers are cross-seed means over 3 training runs with standard deviations in the appendix. Tutor RL human study (8 competitive-chess annotators, 74 annotations): StudentSim-reward tutor rated 90.5% accuracy / 3.31 guidance / 3.93 personalization vs. 75.7 / 2.99 / 2.80 (no RL) and 71.6 / 3.08 / 2.42 (GPT-5.4-simulator reward, which shows a markedly higher severe-factual-error rate). Surprising finding: a 4B fine-tuned model solves the Socratic chess case (guidance never names the move) where prompted GPT-5.4 picks a wrong square. Tested scale is standard (60 students, ~100K pooled chess records), not stress-scale; F=0.51 top-1 chess accuracy is solid but not near ceiling. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the F/R decomposition formalizing per-student simulation as a measurable, optimizable target), NEW METHOD (per-individual, weight-level simulators trained on real learner data that jointly achieve fidelity and guidance responsiveness), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (StudentSimEval, a frozen 60-student protocol with released construction code), and a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a trained simulator as tutor-RL reward beating a frontier-LLM-simulator reward in expert human evaluation). The underlying mechanism is a standard combination — pretrain-then-finetune transfer learning with LoRA, essentially a meta-learning/cold-start recipe — applied to a genuinely new problem setting; the benchmark and the F/R objective, not the training algorithm, carry the novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: cross-student pooling at matched optimizer budget (App. D.1), text vs. vision modality (image adds 0.001 F at 2× cost), multi-turn-ratio robustness sweep (ρ∈[0,0.8]), and guidance-mode leave-one-out/single-mode/weight-scaling sweeps showing modes are largely substitutable except strategic. Headline numbers are 3-seed means with per-seed standard deviations in App. E.4. Code, splits, and evaluation pipeline are released (https://github.com/microsoft/StudentSim); Lichess is CC0, but EFCAMDAT and FoundationalASSIST require gated academic access, so those two domains are only partially reproducible. Methodological concerns: (1) the chess fidelity prompt for StudentSim includes Maia2-derived candidate moves that LLM baselines are denied, creating an input-asymmetry confound on the headline F comparison; (2) L2 held-out sets are tiny (26 essays, 40 multi-turn records per student), so per-student F/R estimates there rest on thin data; (3) the authors themselves disclose severe bf16 nondeterminism on small math subsamples (R=0.565 vs. 0.952 on the same 315-record checkpoint re-run), though the full 879-record set is stable; (4) R is scored against a canonical correction (engine/answer key) rather than the student's actual post-guidance behavior, so R is a proxy for the counterfactual quantity a tutor cares about — the authors acknowledge this as a complementary question; (5) chess/math guidance text is LLM-generated under fixed templates (only wording is synthetic; targets are engine/answer-key fixed), so R partially measures following a templated guidance distribution. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods, benchmarks, and a small RL system actually run), with a SYSTEMS component in the released evaluation pipeline. - Practical: Yes — Qwen3-4B + LoRA trained on a single 8×A100 (40GB) node; the tutor-RL reward simulator is small, open, and served locally, unlike the GPT-5.4 API baseline. - Efficient: Stage-2 specialization is 12 optimizer steps per chess student and ~73–153 records in the other domains, so per-student cost is trivially low; the tutor loop avoids per-rollout frontier-API calls. - Effective: Evidence supports fidelity and one-step guidance responsiveness on held-out records, and the chess tutor study supports the reward use case; but the R target is a canonical endpoint, not verified real-student post-guidance behavior, so effectiveness for the true use case (predicting real students' reactions) is demonstrated only indirectly. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the evaluation covers 60 students; scaling to thousands of students requires a per-student Stage-2 run each, which is cheap per student but is never stress-tested, and Stage-1 pooling must be re-done per domain. Delivers a software artifact: released code/splits/evaluation harness plus the training recipe; no model weights release is stated. Strengths: (1) The F/R decomposition is a genuinely useful formalization — it turns an amorphous "is the simulated student valid?" debate into two separable, measurable properties and makes the known failure modes of both prior families (state-tracking has no guidance channel; prompted LLMs are unfaithful) quantitative and directly comparable. (2) The pooled-then-specialized recipe is validated by a properly matched ablation (same optimizer budget, repeated single-student data), so the two-stage claim rests on evidence, not intuition. (3) The benchmark protocol is methodologically careful: chronological per-student splits, frozen held-out files shared by every method, per-domain metric operationalizations with explicit rejections of plausible-but-wrong metrics (BLEU on L2 essays, centipawn-loss credit in chess). (4) The tutor-RL proof of concept closes the loop end-to-end and includes the right control (a frontier-LLM-simulator reward under an identical GRPO setup), isolating the reward model as the only varying factor. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state explicitly that the tutor-RL result is a proof of concept, not a best-tutor claim, and that transfer to non-chess domains requires per-domain reward functions on free-form responses (untested). They acknowledge that R measures update toward a canonical endpoint rather than the student's literal post-guidance behavior, calling the latter a counterfactual question for controlled studies with real students. They note the per-domain reward-head setup depends on their simulator's backbone. They conclude by naming the deeper unsolved problem: reproducing multi-interaction learning dynamics (acquisition, retention, forgetting) rather than one-step state updates. These limitations are confronted directly, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The chess F comparison is confounded by the Maia2-derived candidate-move list present in StudentSim's prompt but withheld from GPT-4o/GPT-5.4; a StudentSim variant without that list (or baselines given it) is not reported, and given Maia2's F=0.45 the margin of 0.06 over Maia2 could shrink substantially. (2) No baseline fine-tunes the base model without the pooled stage in L2 and math, so the two-stage claim is ablated only in chess. (3) L2 R gaps over GPT-5.4 (0.6417 vs. 0.5950) rest on 40 records per learner with seed standard deviations up to ±0.0557 on one mode — the L2 advantage is within roughly one to two standard errors and should not be treated as settled. (4) The tutor study's GPT-5.4-reward condition scoring below even no-RL on accuracy (71.6% vs. 75.7%) is anomalous and explained only by severe-error rate; with 74 annotations from 8 annotators and no significance testing, the ordering rests on thin evidence. (5) The 60-student roster is selected from the most active learners in each corpus (Stage-2 L2 learners average ~92 essays vs. a 3-essay median), so the evaluated population over-represents high-volume users — exactly where per-student data is least sparse. (6) Whether R-trained simulators would actually predict a real student's idiosyncratic reaction to a given guidance style (vs. converging to the canonical answer) is untested, and the RL reward's move-quality term comes from Stockfish lookups that exist only in chess. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating student simulators or simulator-grounded tutor RL, this is worth reading for the F/R formulation and the reusable 60-student benchmark alone — the training recipe is competent but conventional — though the headline chess-fidelity comparison should be treated as provisional until the Maia2-hint confound is removed.

#19 — Highly Innovative (76)

Advancing Generative AI via the Science of Data

Y Hu · mirnegg.github.io · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This PhD dissertation (UIUC, 2026) compiles four research contributions unified by the thesis that data is a first-class object of study in generative AI: (1) a unified theory of when random projection provably preserves influence-function attribution, (2) the first local data attribution framework for online RL (PPO) that yields an iterative influence-based filtering (IIF) algorithm, (3) the discovery and characterization of "empirical privacy variance" — DP-SGD models with identical (ε,δ)-DP guarantees exhibiting wildly different memorization-based privacy — with hyperparameter-selection heuristics, and (4) ACTG-ARL, a hierarchical framework for differentially private conditional text generation with anchored RL post-training. - Why it's important: Influence-function attribution is used at scale with sketching but lacked any correctness theory (JL-style justifications are provably misaligned), online RL wastes sample efficiency on harmful rollout records, ε-based DP certification breaks down when identical ε yields divergent empirical privacy (a standardization/policy problem), and DP synthetic text unlocks sensitive user data for reuse without added privacy cost. - How it does it: The unifying mechanism is analyzing how individual training examples influence a model — measuring it (influence functions, TracIn-style gradient alignment restricted to one PPO round's rollout buffer) versus limiting it (DP-SGD/DP-Adam), with the theory chapter reducing influence preservation to subspace embedding of the λ-whitened curvature operator and showing the effective dimension d_λ(F) = tr(F(F+λI)^{-1}) — not rank — governs required sketch size. - The good: The theory chapter delivers matching upper and lower bounds (sketch size m = Ω((d_λ(F)+log(1/δ))/ε²) with a worst-case converse for Gaussian sketches), and the RL attribution work is a NeurIPS 2025 oral showing IIF cuts training rounds by 20–67% across six RL environments and achieves ~4× runtime reduction in RLHF detoxification of gpt-neo-2.7B. - The missing: The theory chapter is validated only at toy scale (MNIST/CIFAR-2, ≤5000 training examples, LR/MLP/ResNet9), never at the LLM scale where projection-based influence is actually deployed, and empirical privacy is measured only via memorization probes (ACR/VMR/AIR), not adaptive extraction or membership-inference adversaries. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in data attribution, DP training, and DP synthetic data who want the state of each subfield plus a unifying attribution↔privacy framing; anyone needing a single deep treatment of one topic should go to the underlying published papers (NeurIPS 2025 oral, ICML 2025, and the Google collaboration).
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with one theoretical chapter). Novelty (78) is the strongest dimension — the effective-dimension characterization of sketched influence with matching lower bounds, the first attribution framework for online RL, and the named 'empirical privacy variance' phenomenon constitute new formulations, not just new methods. Rigor (78) is solid: NeurIPS 2025 oral and ICML 2025 backing, multi-seed experiments with error bars, matching upper/lower bounds with full proofs, and public code for the privacy work — docked for toy-scale validation of the theory and memorization-only privacy probes. Non-Obviousness (78) is high: identifying d_λ(F) rather than rank as the governing quantity, and showing utility-oriented DP tuning systematically worsens empirical privacy, are genuinely surprising. Completeness (75) is helped by candid limitation acknowledgment throughout; Resilience (72) is limited by the scale mismatch between the LLM-motivated theory and ResNet9-scale validation and by extrapolating memorization probes to certification claims; Impact (70) reflects the released empirical-privacy code and the practical ~4× RLHF runtime reduction from IIF. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*78 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*70 = 76.

Problem & Motivation The dissertation addresses the growing dependency of generative AI on data quality, provenance, and privacy: scaling laws make data composition decisive, high-quality corpora are depleting, extraction attacks expose memorized PII, and sensitive user data (emails, chat logs, medical records) cannot be used freely. The author identifies a conceptual duality — data attribution asks how individual examples influence a model (measurement), while differential privacy limits that influence (control) — and argues both must be treated rigorously rather than heuristically. Specific gaps closed: (a) practitioners use random projection to scale influence functions based on a JL-lemma analogy that does not actually apply to inverse-sensitive bilinear forms g⊤(F+λI)^{-1}g′; (b) no existing attribution method handles online RL's circular data-model dependency (policy shapes data, data shapes policy); (c) prior DP-SGD hyperparameter tuning optimizes utility alone, implicitly assuming the privacy budget ε fully determines practical privacy risk; (d) DP synthetic text work rarely supports conditional (controllable) generation. Key Idea Three distinct core insights, one per research pillar: (1) For projection-based influence, ridge regularization changes the governing complexity measure from rank(F) to the effective dimension d_λ(F), because the sketch need only be an approximate isometry on the λ-whitened subspace F^{1/2}(F+λI)^{-1/2} rather than on range(F) — with an unavoidable barrier (m ≥ r needed for exactness) in the unregularized case and a quantifiable leakage term when test gradients leave range(F). (2) For online RL, restrict attribution to a single PPO round — attributing the checkpoint update θ^(k)→θ^(k+1) to rollout-buffer records via TracIn-style gradient inner products against two well-designed target functions (f_action = log π_θ(a|s) and a REINFORCE-with-baseline surrogate f_return anchored at the round-start policy), which sidesteps the non-differentiable cascading influence through future data collection. (3) For DP, the composition structure of DP-SGD creates a one-to-many ε-to-risk mapping, so hyperparameters (b, T, η) — not just ε — determine empirical memorization, and utility-oriented tuning systematically worsens empirical privacy (a no-free-lunch result). Methodology Chapter 3 (theory): For F ⪰ 0 (empirical Fisher or GGN) and oblivious sub-Gaussian sketches P, it analyzes the bilinear form τ_λ(g,g′) = g⊤(F+λI)^{-1}g′ versus its sketched version. Proofs proceed by controlling ‖B⊤(P⊤P−I)B‖₂ on the whitened subspace B = F^{1/2}(F+λI)^{-1/2}, yielding a PSD sandwich on F+λI and a resolvent-perturbation bound; the Kronecker case (F = A⊗E, P = P_A⊗P_E) requires a dedicated factorized covariance-deviation theorem; out-of-range leakage is bounded via a deterministic reduction plus subspace/union-bound concentration arguments. Chapter 4 (RL attribution): per training round, compute influence I_i = Σ_{j: z_i∈B_j} ⟨∇f(θ_j^(k)), ∇L_PPO(θ_j^(k), z_i)⟩ for f ∈ {f_action, f_return}; f_return uses a reference-policy surrogate E[log π_θ(a|s)·Â_ref] (REINFORCE-with-baseline structure) with π_ref = π^(k), reusing the rollout buffer as the validation set so attribution adds zero sampling overhead. IIF then drops the bottom p% of records by influence each round and re-trains. Chapter 5: fine-tune GPT-2-S/L on Enron (33k samples, 23/15 configurations) and Llama-2-7b/13b on TOFU (60-configuration grids) with DP-Adam+LoRA under ε ∈ {1,2,4,8,16}, δ = n^{-1.1}, PRV accountant; measure ACR, VMR, and a proposed AIR metric; multivariate log-space regression of privacy scores on (b, T, η), plus composite quantities compute C = b·T and updates U = C·η; derive pairwise-comparison heuristics and a sequential selection algorithm. Chapter 6: hierarchical DP text generation splitting feature learning (LLM-assisted schema, DP tabular synthesizer) from conditional generation (DP fine-tuned generator), with Anchored RL post-training combining a PPO control objective with SFT on best-of-N data to anchor to the private distribution and mitigate reward hacking. Critical design decisions: the λ-whitened (not OSE) embedding condition in Ch.3 is well-justified and yields the sharper d_λ bound with a matching lower bound; the round-local reference policy in Ch.4 is justified by buffer-as-validation reuse and the alignment of f_return with the PPO objective; the fixed clipping norm c in Ch.5 is justified empirically (minimal sensitivity). The utility/privacy-tuning trade-off in Ch.5 is honestly framed as exploratory regression, not causal proof. Key Results Chapter 3: sharp dichotomy — unregularized projection preserves influence iff P is injective on range(F) (forcing m ≥ r ≈ n in overparameterized regimes), while regularized projection needs only m = Ω((d_λ(F)+log(1/δ))/ε²) with a worst-case converse at m = o(d_λ(F)/ε²) for Gaussian sketches; factorized (K-FAC) sketches incur a worse ε^{-4} total-sketch-size dependence (m = m_A·m_E); leakage from out-of-range test-gradient components decays at O(m^{-1/2}). Experiments (MNIST-10+LR, MNIST-10+MLP, CIFAR-2+ResNet9; 5000 training examples; 5 sketch draws; dattri library) confirm error decays once m ≳ d_λ(F) and a two-stage λ/m selection procedure suffices with constant C ∈ (10,100)·d_λ*. Chapter 4: IIF reduces training rounds to match standard PPO by 20–67% (SE_ave 26.0–65.8% with ±1.8–8.7% error bars across FrozenLake, Acrobot, MiniGrid, Highway, LunarLander, BipedalWalker; 5 seeds), with negligible overhead (runtime reductions 29–69% at peak); random filtering underperforms, isolating attribution as the active ingredient. RLHF detoxification on gpt-neo-2.7B: IIF filters ~50% of records, halves optimization time, needs fewer than half the rounds to surpass standard training, totaling ~4× runtime reduction; lower test toxicity on a held-out set with a different detector. Chapter 5: empirical privacy variance is substantial — e.g., Llama-2-7b on TOFU-4 at ε=8 spans AIR from near 0 to >0.8 across hyperparameter configurations; variance grows with model size, dataset size, secret density, and ε; regression coefficients all positive and significant (p < 0.001); selection procedure's relative privacy risk is markedly lower than best-utility practice across ε ∈ {1,...,16}. Chapter 6: claims +20% MAUVE and +50% attribute-distribution-matching over prior DP text-generation methods, with ablations on schema richness, a larger gemma-3-4b-pt model, oracle-choice robustness, and significance tests (per the table of contents). Baselines: Chapter 4 compares against standard PPO, random filtering, and advantage/TD-error/difficulty heuristics — reasonable but not the strongest modern filtering baselines; Chapter 6 compares against DP-FT and PE-line methods; no baseline weakness is fatal but the influence-filtering space has competing approaches not exhaustively compared. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. Genuinely novel: the effective-dimension characterization of sketched influence with matching lower bounds (prior work appealed heuristically to JL); the round-local attribution formulation for online RL with the f_return target function (claimed first data attribution framework for online RL); empirical privacy variance as a named, systematically characterized phenomenon with the C/U hyperparameter hierarchy; the anchored-RL post-training for DP conditional generation. Standard components reused competently: TracIn gradient inner products, DP-SGD/LoRA, PPO, best-of-N data, K-FAC structure — the contributions lie in the analysis, formulation, and empirical discovery, not in inventing these primitives. Rigor & Reproducibility Strong for a compilation of this breadth. Chapter 3 states theorems with full proofs across ~130 pages of appendix, including a matching worst-case lower bound and anti-concentration arguments; experiments report 5 runs with different sketches and 95th-percentile statistics. Chapter 4 reports 3–5 random seeds, boxplots for single-round interventions, and dedicated appendix sections on statistical significance, multiple filtering percentages, Adam compatibility, and runtime breakdowns. Chapter 5 releases code (https://github.com/empvv/empirical-privacy-variance), verifies fine-tuning data exclusion from pre-training corpora, and quantifies hyperparameter-vs-seed effects (Appendix C.3.3); regression p-values are reported. Chapter 6 includes significance testing, ablations, and documents an identified flaw in MAUVE evaluation in prior literature (a credibility positive). Methodological concerns: hyperparameter tuning in Chapter 5 is performed without accounting for its privacy cost on private data (following prior work, explicitly acknowledged); Chapter 3's empirical validation is toy-scale (≤ ResNet9, 5000 examples) relative to the LLM-scale motivation; Chapter 6 results come from Google internship work with vendor-adjacent resources; the dissertation itself is not peer-reviewed as a whole, though Chapters 4 and 5 correspond to NeurIPS 2025 (oral) and ICML 2025 papers. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (with one theoretical chapter). - Practical: Yes — IIF adds only per-record gradient dot products to standard PPO pipelines (a "ghost dot product" trick reduces cost), and DP-SGD hyperparameter heuristics run on standard LoRA fine-tuning stacks; all experiments used commercially available models (GPT-2, Llama-2-7b/13b, gpt-neo-2.7B, gemma-3-4b). - Efficient: IIF's attribution overhead is reported as negligible and offset by halved optimization time (~4× total runtime reduction in RLHF); the two-stage λ/m procedure makes influence sketching operational with C ∈ (10,100)·d_λ; DP synthetic generation inherits DP-Adam's standard cost. - Effective: Attribution-guided filtering demonstrably improves RL performance beyond random filtering (so the signal is real, not mere data reduction), and heuristics outperform best-utility selection on empirical privacy — though effectiveness is measured on memorization proxies, not realized attacks. - Scalable:* Not stress-tested: RL experiments top out at 2.7B parameters and small MDP environments; influence theory is validated on models with ≤ ResNet9 scale; the paper claims, but does not demonstrate, applicability to frontier-scale attribution. Deliverables: public code for the empirical privacy work; the other chapters stop at paper form within this document (Chapter 6 is Google-internship work, artifact release not stated in the provided text). Strengths - The random-projection theory is genuinely new intellectual territory: it proves JL-style distance preservation is provably misaligned with influence computation and identifies the effective dimension d_λ(F) as the tight complexity parameter, with both upper and lower bounds — this converts a folklore heuristic into a principled sketch-size selection rule. - The RL attribution framework sidesteps a real conceptual obstacle (endogenous, non-differentiable data-model feedback) by localizing to one PPO round, and the payoff is concrete and measured: 20–67% sample-efficiency gains and ~4× RLHF runtime reduction, with an ablation battery separating attribution signal from data-reduction effects. - Empirical privacy variance is a non-obvious, policy-relevant empirical finding: the paper controls for data, architecture, and algorithm and still finds large variance among high-utility models, then extracts an interpretable hyperparameter hierarchy (C = b·T, U = C·η) with statistically significant regressions rather than mere observation. - The dissertation-level synthesis — attribution as measurement of individual influence, DP as its control — is a genuinely clarifying conceptual framing that suggests concrete future coupling (attribution as a probe for DP effectiveness). Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive: Chapter 5 explicitly states hyperparameter tuning on private data is not accounted for in the privacy budget (following common but flawed practice), that linear regression is an exploratory rather than definitive tool, that empirical privacy is task- and metric-dependent (ACR/VMR/AIR are memorization-based proxies), and recommends application-specific upper bounds alongside formal ε. Chapter 6 documents MAUVE evaluation issues in the literature, a failure mode of the CTCL baseline, reward-hacking examples, and the suboptimality of filtering all negative records (p = 100%) due to non-additivity of influence. Chapter 4 discusses the assumption underlying f_return (on-policy advantage noise averaged out) and non-additivity of influence in subset selection. The unregularized/factorized sketch barriers are presented as fundamental rather than analysis artifacts. Analyst-Identified Gaps - Scale mismatch between theory and practice in Chapter 3: the projection theory motivating LLM-scale attribution is empirically validated only on LR/MLP/ResNet9 with 5000 examples; no experiment shows d_λ-based sketch sizing on a language model, where Hessian/Fisher spectra may behave differently. - Empirical privacy in Chapter 5 is measured against non-adaptive memorization probes; the gap to adaptive extraction attacks, membership inference, or reconstruction (the threat models DP is designed against) is not bridged, so "empirical privacy variance" may partly reflect metric idiosyncrasy rather than actionable risk — the related-work comparison to Hayes et al. and Kaissis et al. partially mitigates this but the practical certification claim (ε unusable for certification) extrapolates beyond the memorization probes tested. - Chapter 4's RLHF evaluation uses one task (detoxification) and one base model (gpt-neo-2.7B, 2021-era); no evaluation on modern instruction-tuned models or reward-model-driven tasks beyond toxicity, and comparison to learned data-filtering baselines beyond advantage/TD-error heuristics is thin. - Chapter 6's headline MAUVE/attribute-matching gains (+20%/+50%) are relative to specific baselines under a fast-moving evaluation landscape the authors themselves criticize (MAUVE reliability); absolute quality versus non-DP generation is not the framing, which is appropriate, but the practical utility of the synthetic data for downstream model training is only partially evaluated (per appendix listing "utility evaluation of synthetic data"). - As a dissertation, the document is a compilation; cross-chapter integration (e.g., attribution probes of DP effectiveness, promised in Fig. 1 and Chapter 7) remains future work rather than demonstrated results. Bottom Line A practitioner working on data attribution, DP training, or DP synthetic data gains real value here — the Chapter 3 theory alone replaces a folk justification with a usable sketch-size rule, and Chapter 5's findings should change how anyone tunes DP-SGD — while readers seeking a single-topic deep dive are better served by the underlying NeurIPS/ICML papers that this dissertation competently unifies.

Foundational Verification of Hardware Against Timing-Channel-Aware Contracts

TL;DR - What it does: This PhD thesis introduces two machine-checked verification methodologies — MTIsolation (proving strong timing isolation between colocated security domains) and Granite (proving functional correctness plus secret-independent timing of RTL processors against hardware-software leakage contracts) — built on a shared specification technique the author calls leakage-aware refinement via determinism. - Why it's important: Timing side channels (Spectre/Meltdown and successors) have defeated a decade of whack-a-mole mitigations and dismantled SGX-class enclave guarantees, so a method that rules out entire classes of timing leakage — including undiscovered attacks — by machine-checked proof addresses a persistent, unsolved security problem for cloud and confidential-computing hardware. - How it does it: Both methodologies formulate security as trace equivalence against a family of deterministic, cycle-accurate specification state machines existentially parameterized by untrusted "black box" functions that constrain which inputs (public vs. secret) may influence nondeterministic behaviors like latency, enabling single-cycle simulation-relation proofs instead of state-space exploration. - The good: The core spec style is demonstrated on synthesizable RTL: MTIsolation delivers what the author states is the first machine-checked proof of strong isolation for an enclave system (a multicore pipelined RISC-V design in Kôika), and Granite composes hardware proofs with a verified constant-time static analysis into a single end-to-end RTL confidentiality theorem (Salsa20 case study) that removes even the hardware-software contract from the TCB. - The missing: Case-study designs are deliberately small in-order pipelined cores with partial feature coverage (the text available cuts off before Granite's evaluation chapters, so no quantitative Granite verification results are visible), and the gap between these prototypes and commodity out-of-order superscalar processors — where real attacks live — is acknowledged but not bridged. - Read it or not: Worth reading in full if you work on formal hardware verification, secure processor design, or TEE security; skimmable if you only need the specification technique (leakage-aware refinement via determinism), which is the transferable core idea.

Problem & Motivation: The thesis targets the problem of running security-critical code on hardware shared with untrusted code without leaking secrets. Modern processors leak secrets through how long computations take, not just what they compute: the ISA contract specifies functional behavior but deliberately abstracts over timing, leaving microarchitectural state (caches, predictors, interconnects) free to leak. The author decomposes the problem into (1) isolation — colocated domains must not observe or interfere with each other via interdomain channels (cache contention, predictor pollution), threatening cloud tenants, VMs, and enclaves — and (2) secret-independent timing — a program's own wall-clock timing must not depend on its secrets (intradomain channels), threatening constant-time cryptographic code broken by transient execution. The motivation is that point defenses (cache partitioning, per-attack mitigations, SGX/SEV-SNP/TDX/CCA) have repeatedly proven insufficient: each closed one channel while attacks exploiting other structures kept appearing, from Kocher's 1996 timing attacks through Foreshadow and microarchitectural data sampling. The thesis argues the root cause is a semantic gap between architectural specifications and cycle-level microarchitectural reality, and that closing it requires timing-channel-aware contracts enforced by machine-checked proof rather than informal argument or testing. Key Idea: The single core insight is leakage-aware refinement via determinism: reduce both functional correctness and noninterference to trace equivalence against a family of deterministic, cycle-accurate specification state machines, where the nondeterminism that real hardware legitimately exhibits (variable latency, interrupt timing, MMIO) is determinized by existentially quantified, untrusted parameters. Two kinds of parameters encode the information-flow policy: deterministic "drivers" that receive only public information (public inputs, the program, declassified leakage events) resolve secret-independent choices, and unconstrained "witnesses" absorb choices that may legitimately depend on secrets. Because the specification admits no behavior that cannot be explained by a public-information-driven machine, a leaking implementation cannot hide behind adversarial resolution of spec nondeterminism — the classical unsoundness of refinement under nondeterminism. The existence of a "leakage transformer" mapping public-input traces to adversary observations then implies classical noninterference. For isolation specifically, the spec models enclaves as running on separate air-gapped machines, with context switching modeled as throwing away the old machine and booting a fresh one, preserving only explicitly allow-listed state. Methodology: Both parts follow the same proof skeleton. The specification is a family of deterministic cycle-accurate Mealy machines written in Gallina (Rocq/Coq); security is stated as: for all external-world oracle state machines, implementation and specification traces are observationally equivalent. Implementations are written in rule-based HDLs with cycle-accurate semantics mechanized in Rocq — Kôika for MTIsolation, Quartz (a new deterministic HDL introduced here for combinational circuits) for Granite — with verified compilers lowering to circuit level. Proofs reduce unbounded-horizon trace equivalence to preservation of a simulation relation across a single clock cycle, sidestepping state-space explosion. MTIsolation (Part I): the security obligation is decomposed into (a) enforcing simulation between colocated enclaves via spatial/temporal resource partitioning (security monitor filters out-of-region accesses; round-robin arbiters time-partition shared ports) and (b) purging microarchitectural state at context switch to reach a state equivalent to a freshly initialized machine. Crucially, the methodology sidesteps full functional-correctness proof: specification parameters are instantiated by erasing the other core's circuitry from the implementation. A hybrid Rocq–SMT toolchain extracts a deeply embedded symbolic assertion language to OCaml/SMT-LIB and discharges single-cycle obligations with Z3, with metatheory soundness proofs kept in Rocq. Granite (Part II): an ISA leakage contract (RISC-V-COQ-style, extended with a leakage model emitting declassified events — memory addresses, branch conditions, variable-latency instruction operands) is lowered into a cycle-accurate machine whose nondeterminism is constrained by existential parameters, instantiated by running a public "shadow" copy of the implementation. Modular proofs are organized along two axes: vertical layering decoupling ISA from microarchitecture, and horizontal per-component specifications with a substitution principle. Granite composes with a certified software static analysis for constant-time programming to yield a single theorem connecting source-level discipline to RTL cycle-by-cycle confidentiality. Critical design decisions: (1) existentially parameterized rather than fixed specifications — well-justified by the need to permit performance optimizations without trusting the implementation; (2) avoiding functional-correctness proof in MTIsolation — justified by the argument that security and functionality decouple; (3) academic HDLs rather than Verilog — acknowledged as a deliberate trade-off prioritizing modular reasoning over industry compatibility. Key Results: The available text (truncated mid-Chapter 8) fully reports MTIsolation results but not Granite's evaluation chapters. MTIsolation: a two-core pipelined RISC-V enclave system (security monitor, memory subsystem with round-robin arbiter, later extended with BTB/BHT branch prediction and four L1 caches) verified in Rocq; the design is ~2,850 lines of Kôika, spec 280 SLOC, proofs 17,750 SLOC Rocq for the full configuration; most SMT queries discharge in under 1 second, with worst-case per-query time reduced from 360 s (monolithic proof) to 95 s (modular proof). Adding a branch predictor required zero spec/proof changes and about one day; adding caches took 3–4 weeks with core and monitor proofs unchanged, modifying only memory invariants. Functionality was validated by running RISC-V/C tests under Cuttlesim and Verilator and a toy password-manager enclave application. The author claims this is the first machine-checked proof of strong isolation (or absence of timing side channels) for an enclave system. Granite: a machine-checked proof of a synthesizable pipelined RISC processor with branch prediction, exceptions, interrupts, and MMIO against a constant-time ISA contract, plus an end-to-end Salsa20 confidentiality theorem — quantitative verification costs are stated as "Not stated" in the available text. A notable empirical byproduct: the Granite case study exposed a real specification bug (writes to interrupt-related system registers must be declassified as public). The underlying CCS 2024 paper (MTIsolation) is peer-reviewed; the Granite paper is an in-submission preprint (arXiv:2607.27480). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD, with components of NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel contribution is the leakage-aware refinement via determinism technique — existentially parameterized deterministic specifications that make refinement sound for noninterference under declassification at cycle granularity — and its instantiation as (a) an air-gapped-machine formalization of strong isolation supporting dynamic context switching and (b) a composable hardware-software leakage contract that eliminates the contract itself from the TCB. The building blocks (refinement, noninterference, rule-based HDLs, simulation relations, MI6-style partitioning/purging mechanisms, leakage transformers from prior compiler-verification work) are standard; the novelty is their composition into a sound, auditable, cycle-accurate security specification and the first machine-checked enclave-isolation proof for synthesizable RTL. Quartz is a new HDL/tool contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is high by construction: all security claims are machine-checked in Rocq, and specifications are designed to be auditable from theorem statements alone. Ablation-style evidence is present in an unusual form: the thesis demonstrates proof-modularity empirically (BTB addition: no proof changes, ~1 day; cache addition: localized invariant changes, 3–4 weeks; modular SMT decomposition cutting worst-case query time 360 s → 95 s), which directly supports the claim that non-security-critical design changes do not trigger proof avalanches. Verification cost tables report SLOC and Rocq/SMT times per configuration. Error bars and multiple seeds are not applicable to proof artifacts. All code is open-sourced: MTIsolation (github.com/mit-plv/isolation), Granite (github.com/mit-plv/granite), Quartz (github.com/mit-plv/quartz). Methodological concerns to flag: (1) Z3 sits in the TCB for MTIsolation's SMT discharge, and the Kôika-to-δKôika transpiler is unverified (validated via Z3-checked assumptions) — the author flags TCB membership honestly; (2) the case studies are the authors' own designs in academic HDLs, so external validity to industry Verilog designs is argued, not shown; (3) the Granite preprint component is not yet peer-reviewed; (4) no external independent replication is cited. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (built proof artifacts, HDLs, and a toolchain, evaluated on synthesizable designs) with a strong THEORETICAL component. Practical: The designs are synthesizable RTL (Verilog generated by verified compilers) targeting modest FPGA-class hardware, but deployment requires rewriting designs in Kôika/Quartz rather than annotating existing Verilog — a substantial adoption barrier. Efficient: Isolation costs real performance (round-robin time partitioning, cache flushing, purge drains at context switch); the thesis itself shows a plausible epoch-based cache invalidation optimization is insecure under its spec unless purge time is padded. Effective: The evidence shows the methodology solves the stated problem for the case-study designs — proofs, not proxies — but only for in-order pipelined cores with partial ISA coverage. Scalable: Not tested at commodity-processor scale; the single-cycle simulation approach and modular abstractions are designed for scalability, and modularity demonstrably cut SMT times ~4×, but out-of-order superscalar designs remain unproven territory. The work delivers real software artifacts (open-source Rocq developments, two HDL toolchains, verified compilers) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: - The specification technique (leakage-aware refinement via determinism) is a genuine conceptual contribution: it resolves the known unsoundness of refinement-based noninterference under nondeterminism in a way that is simultaneously auditable (specs stand alone, implementations outside the TCB) and permissive (allows latency variation that legitimate optimizations require). - The MTIsolation result — first machine-checked strong-isolation proof for an enclave system at RTL, with a spec whose audit does not require reading pipeline internals — is a concrete, verifiable milestone, and the existential-parameter instantiation-by-erasure trick that avoids full functional-correctness proof is clever and well-motivated. - The end-to-end Granite theorem (verified constant-time static analysis composed with processor correctness/nonleakage down to RTL, eliminating the HW/SW contract from the TCB) is the kind of full-stack composition that few verification efforts achieve, and the discovery of a real spec bug during the case study is credible evidence the methodology catches subtle leakage-corner cases. - The evaluation honestly quantifies the human and computational cost of verification (SLOC, SMT times, days-to-weeks per design change), which is rare and valuable for anyone planning a similar effort. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The thesis is explicit and direct about limitations (a credibility positive): it targets the digital abstraction within a single clock domain and excludes physical side channels (power, EM, temperature); case-study processors are in-order pipelined cores chosen to demonstrate the methodology, not to cover full ISAs or commodity-system complexity; designs must be expressed in HDLs with sequential semantics (Kôika/Quartz), with no direct path for Verilog/VHDL designs; only safety properties are treated (no liveness — "a brick does not leak secrets"); specification errors remain trusted (mitigated partially by broadening proofs); MTIsolation does not protect against remote timing channels like NetSpectre and does not itself give constant-time purge (constant-time purge is shown to be specifiable but potentially costly); the MTIsolation threat model assumes cooperative enclave yielding, an attacker who can only send/observe MMIO, and no availability guarantees. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The elephant not addressed by case-study evidence: the methodology's applicability to out-of-order, deeply speculative superscalar designs — precisely where the motivating attacks (Spectre-class) live — is argued via modularity but never demonstrated, and the state of the available text gives no quantitative Granite results to assess how far the pipelined case study stretches the technique. - The Granite end-to-end guarantee covers programs accepted by the constant-time static analysis; the acceptance rate, false-positive burden on real cryptographic codebases (beyond one Salsa20 program), and the analysis's completeness on realistic code are not evaluated in the available text. - The MTIsolation programming model is cooperative with statically partitioned address spaces; dynamic resource allocation, preemption, and shared read-only memory (noted as missing) all leak or complicate the model, and the gap between this model and production enclave systems (SGX-style dynamic paging) is large. - Two unverified components in the MTIsolation TCB (Kôika-to-δKôika transpiler; Z3 for SMT discharge) mean the "foundational" guarantee is foundational relative to those tools — the author flags this but its practical audit burden is not quantified. - Performance cost of the isolation mechanisms (purge latency, time-partitioned bandwidth) is not benchmarked against unprotected execution, so the practical overhead a deployer would accept is unknown from the available text. Bottom Line: For researchers and practitioners in verified hardware and secure computer architecture, this thesis is essential reading — it delivers the first machine-checked enclave-isolation proof for synthesizable RTL and a reusable, sound specification idiom for timing security — but anyone expecting a recipe for verifying commodity out-of-order processors, or a deployable low-overhead design, will have to wait for the follow-on work the author correctly charts as future work.

#21 — Highly Innovative (75)

HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness? (225 ▲ )

Yuhao Wu, Jingyuan Zhang, Jiajun Shi, Xinping Lei, Qingshui Gu, Yuxuan Zhang, Zexuan Wang, Chen He, Chen Huang, Maojia Song, Zhiyuan Zeng, Shaowen Wang, Jinkai Liu, Yunfeng Shi, Jiaheng Liu, Shen Yan, Wenhao Huang, Ge Zhang, Wenxuan Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 3 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HarnessDev, a benchmark that evaluates whether an LLM can build a runnable agent harness from a zero-scoring seed (Creation) and then iteratively improve it from downstream execution feedback (Evolution), scoring the frozen harness on held-out tasks and token cost rather than a single answer. - Why it's important: Agent performance depends heavily on the model-external execution scaffold (e.g., GPT-5 scores 35.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 under Terminus 2 vs 49.6% under Codex CLI), yet current evaluations treat the harness as fixed configuration while humans do the harness engineering that turns a model into a deployed system. - How it does it: A creator LLM works inside Claude Code/Codex from a deliberately weak, runnable seed (no loop, tools policy, state, verifier, or stopping rule) with 1–3 dev cases; the frozen harness is then run by a fixed executor on five benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1, MLE-bench, EQ-Bench3, BrowseComp; 2,207 instances total), with Creation scored under both creator-as-executor (Self-Eval) and a fixed Gemini 3.1 Pro executor (Unified-Eval), and Evolution trajectories frozen per version and re-scored post-hoc on a disjoint 630-instance SWE-Pro split. - The good: The evaluation design is unusually careful — score paths are isolated from harness self-reports (SWE-Pro credit comes only from real repo diffs, Terminal credit from environment state), every run's source and artifacts are audited for prohibited benchmark-gaming (zero violations found), and held-out generalization is measured separately from feedback-set adaptation. - The missing: Evolution results come from a single trajectory per creator–runtime cell (9 lineages, 73 versions) with no uncertainty estimates, held-out evaluation covers only SWE-Pro, and the human-engineered references are external system reports with different paired executors, not controls under one runtime. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building agent benchmarks, harness-optimization methods, or forward-deployed agent tooling — it defines the evaluation protocol that concurrent harness-evolution benchmarks (HarnessOpt-Bench, Evo-Bench, SEAGym) compete against; model-lab researchers can skim the results tables.

Novelty (74) is anchored by a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK defining the Creation-and-Evaluation-of-harnesses problem class, with the co-adaptation finding (Opus losing 36 points under a swapped executor) driving Non-Obviousness (76).
