Problem & Motivation Agent capability depends as much on the surrounding execution infrastructure — loop, tools, context management, state, recovery, verification — as on model weights, and industry pays for this gap through forward-deployed engineers. Existing agent benchmarks fix the harness and report task outputs, so the harness is experimental configuration rather than a developable artifact; whether models can create and continually improve the systems they run inside is unmeasured. Harness development is also argued to be harder than ordinary code editing: the model edits the substrate through which it itself acts, must diagnose its own behavioral limits from execution traces, and must accumulate changes that generalize rather than produce one-off fixes. The gap the paper closes is the absence of a benchmark whose unit of evaluation is runnable, persistent infrastructure, evaluated for both capability (held-out task success) and efficiency (executor tokens). Key Idea Shift the evaluated artifact from a task answer to a frozen, runnable harness: give the creator only a policy-free seed and public dev feedback, then measure what the creator built by running it on hidden tasks — separating creator LLM from executor LLM, adaptation-to-feedback from held-out generalization, and capability from token cost. The weak-seed design is the crux: an empty repo would conflate harness design with boilerplate, a mature scaffold would give away the planning/verification logic under test, so the seed scores zero everywhere and any nonzero score must come from the creator's added control layer. Methodology The pipeline formalizes (creator LC, dev environment D) → harness H → (H, executor LE, task x) → evaluator J → score. Creation (RQ1): six creators (Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen 3.7 Max, Seed 2.0 Pro) build harnesses for four domains/five benchmarks from a common seed, spec, and 1–3 dev cases; three independent creations per creator–benchmark pair (avg@3) under Self-Eval and under a fixed Gemini executor. Evolution (RQ2): creators improve their own RQ1 code harness from results on a 100-task SWE-Pro feedback set and all 89 Terminal-Bench tasks, with a budget of ten frozen two-benchmark evaluation pairs and at most two 5-task probes per round, terminating in a creator-declared final commit; afterwards every official version is re-scored on a 630-instance held-out SWE-Pro split never shown to the creator. Metrics are native benchmark scores plus executor tokens per task (creator tokens excluded); constraint compliance (no hard-coded answers, no scorer access) is enforced by score-path isolation and post-hoc audit of source plus recorded trajectories. Critical design decisions: (1) the zero-scoring seed — well justified against both extremes; (2) creator–executor separation with Self/Unified-Eval — well justified, and it surfaces co-adaptation (e.g., an Opus code harness that hard-codes a 120-step limit collapses from 69.3 to 33.0 under Gemini); (3) human references taken as verified external leaderboard results rather than re-run paired controls — a practical necessity but a comparability weakness the authors flag. Key Results Creation: under Self-Eval, Opus 4.8 leads with avg 67.8 vs the human-engineered reference aggregate of 86.2; GPT-5.5 55.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro 55.6, DeepSeek 45.2, Qwen 44.0, Seed 2.0 Pro 22.8. Per benchmark (Self-Eval, Opus): SWE-Pro 69.3 vs human 80.0, Terminal-Bench 64.8 vs 88.8, MLE-bench 32.9 vs 24.0 (Opus and Gemini exceed the reference), EQ-Bench3 84.6 vs 83.7 (at parity), BrowseComp 52.4 vs 92.2 (largest gap). 77.8% of failed Data tasks are attributed to harness defects, not executor capability. MLE-bench token cost spans ~19× (GPT-5.5: 19.1 medal rate at 29.3M tokens; DeepSeek: 19.6 at 208.4M). Dead code is pervasive: 124 of 587 Writing features and 18 of 108 Code component instances never execute; only 1 of 18 code harnesses implements checkpointing, and no checkpoint event appears in 26,679 trajectories. Edit volume does not predict performance (Gemini adds 1,006 LOC but scores best on Terminal-Bench at 68.8). Evolution: feedback-set gains (up to +13.9 pair points for Qwen, +13.4 DeepSeek) shrink on held-out-630 (self-runtime mean +3.11, max +4.44 for Opus); under a fixed Gemini executor, three of four lineages regress on held-out (GPT-5.5 −10.32) and one declared version's final gap reaches 16.51 points. Same-commit reruns vary by ±4.75 pair points; feedback and held-out scores co-move in only 53.1% of the 64 version switches; only 2 of 9 creator-declared finals are held-out optimal. Tested at standard benchmark scale with hidden-task splits; no stress-scale claims. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the Creation-and-Evolution protocol connecting both stages in one artifact, the creator–executor separation with paired Self/Unified-Eval, per-version frozen trajectories re-scored post-hoc on a disjoint split, and the token-cost axis. The finding that harness gains fail to transfer across executors and that feedback-set gains overfit is a substantive empirical contribution. Relative to concurrent work (Meta-Agent Challenge covers creation-like evaluation; HarnessOpt-Bench covers optimization; Evo-Bench covers evolution with fixed runtime), the combination of both stages, cross-executor transfer, and cost measurement is the distinguishing increment; the individual evaluation techniques (held-out splits, budgeted evaluation, version freezing) are standard ideas composed carefully. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are partial but informative: Unified-Eval isolates executor effects; three independent creations per cell (avg@3) address creation variance; the fixed-Gemini Evolution arm is a deliberate control. Correlation analyses are reported with statistics (revision-call Spearman 0.57, p≤.0005; self-test count 0.13–0.26, n.s.), and the ±4.75 noise band is empirically estimated — but Evolution has one trajectory per cell, so no error bars or significance tests on the headline evolution deltas are possible, and the authors say so. No multiple-seed reruns of full evaluations are reported beyond the avg@3 creation replicates. The compliance audit (source + execution artifacts for every run, reported as a null result) is a rigor positive. A project page is given (self-developing-agents.github.io); the seed reference implementation, audit script, and held-out splits are stated to be released with the benchmark, but no repository URL is confirmed in the text. Methodological concerns: human baselines are external, self-reported vendor leaderboard numbers with different executors (marked *); the Evolution feedback and held-out tasks come from the same benchmark (SWE-bench Pro public split), a residual Goodhart surface; benchmark choice and reference selection are not exhaustive of deployment settings. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark instantiation with extensive executed experiments). - Practical: Yes for the harness-creation protocol (commercial API access plus standard containers; MLE-bench legs use one A800-80GB per task, which is non-trivial but available). - Efficient: A single full Evolution lineage consumes substantial compute (10 two-benchmark full evaluations plus held-out re-scoring of 73 versions), and generated harnesses differ up to ~19× in executor-token cost at comparable quality. - Effective: The benchmark demonstrably measures what it claims — it separates harness quality from executor capability and detects co-adaptation and overfitting that task-level evaluation would miss. - Scalable: Not tested at 10× scale; Evolution is limited to code-domain harnesses with one trajectory per cell, and scaling trajectory counts or domains is asserted as future work rather than demonstrated. The deliverable is a benchmark artifact (seed harness, interface spec, audit script, held-out splits, released audit artifacts) rather than a method or tool. Strengths - The evaluation-protocol engineering is the real contribution: score-path isolation, per-version freezing, honest-status contracts, and a source-and-artifact audit for every run make cheating checkable rather than advisory — most agent benchmarks lack this. - The creator–executor separation yields a genuinely non-obvious finding: harness quality is not monotone in executor strength (Qwen gains +17.6 on BrowseComp under Gemini; Opus loses 36 points on SWE-Pro), establishing harness–model co-adaptation as a measurable phenomenon. - The Evolution analysis is unusually honest about noise: it decomposes 64 switches into gains inside/outside the noise band (27 vs 2), documents dead code and unreachable mechanisms, and shows only 2/9 creator-declared finals are held-out optimal — evidence that cuts against the benchmark's own optimistic framing. - Diagnosing harness defects as the bottleneck (77.8% of Data failures) and the concrete finding that targeted read-fail-fix-reverify loops work while test-count does not (Spearman 0.13–0.26) give practitioners actionable signal. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors directly state: the four domain categories do not cover all deployments; human baselines are uneven and not guaranteed optimal; Unified-Eval cannot fully remove executor-model interaction effects; behavioral analyses are descriptive with incomplete coverage; Evolution has one trajectory per cell (one unfinished), no uncertainty estimates, and held-out evaluation on SWE-Pro only; the development environment is fixed across stages; and the benchmark measures model-external learning, not a replacement for weight training. This is an unusually candid limitations section and a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The headline "distance to human-engineered reference" comparison is not a controlled experiment: reference numbers come from different harness–model pairs (e.g., GPT-5.6 Sol for Terminal-Bench and BrowseComp), some from vendor release reports the authors did not re-run, so the 67.8 vs 86.2 aggregate conflates harness and executor differences in unknown proportion. - Evolution's budget (10 evaluation pairs) and feedback-set design are single fixed choices; there is no matched-budget baseline (e.g., random search or a simple meta-prompt), so the observed instability cannot be attributed to the models rather than the protocol — the related-work section admits matched-search evaluation is future work. - The Evolution held-out split is drawn from the same SWE-bench Pro distribution as the feedback set, so "held-out generalization" here means task-level, not distribution-level, generalization; no transfer to Terminal-Bench is evaluated post-freeze. - Three of the six creators are from or affiliated with the lead organization's ecosystem (Opus, Seed 2.0 Pro is ByteDance's own model, and the paper is ByteDance Seed-led); selection of which models participate in which stages is not justified. - The seed and six-module harness abstraction (E/T/C/S/L/V) embeds a particular architecture prior; creators that reject it (e.g., GPT-5.5's monolithic agent) are evaluated within that frame, and no sensitivity analysis of seed design is provided. - Beyond the acknowledged single-trajectory issue, the Evolution conclusions rest on 9 lineages whose version-to-version differences are mostly within the measured ±4.75 noise band — the strongest claims in Section 4.3 are descriptive at n=1 per cell. Bottom Line For anyone building or benchmarking self-improving agent systems, this paper is the current reference protocol for evaluating harness development and its negative results (unstable evolution, executor-locked gains) are as valuable as the benchmark itself; for a general agent researcher, the tables alone justify a skim.

Hi-Q: Hierarchical Evidence-guided Query Refinement for Multi-Hop Question Answering (24 ▲ )

Jueun Kim, Sungho Park, Wook-Shin Han · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 2 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Hi-Q, a training-free framework for multi-hop QA that grows a binary query decomposition tree at run time, expanding a query node only when a resolution operator finds the retrieved evidence does not support answering it. - Why it's important: Multi-hop questions are asked at a coarse granularity while their evidence lives at finer granularity, and existing fixes (pre-built graphs, blind iterative rewriting, question-complexity routers) either fix granularity before seeing evidence or never check whether a query was retrievable, causing error propagation; Hi-Q avoids corpus-wide graph construction costs that can exceed $2,500 in API calls for a 5.2M-passage corpus. - How it does it: Each node runs a resolution operator (refine-from-history → retrieve top-k → reader answers or abstains with ⊥); resolved nodes stop, unresolved nodes are split by a dependency-preserving binary operator (prerequisite branch resolved and written to history before the dependent branch) and gated by a round-trip semantic-coverage verifier, which the paper frames as a cost-sensitive threshold on unresolved-support probability. - The good: Gains hold under full-corpus retrieval (139K–5.2M passages), where Hi-Q averages 52.3 EM / 64.0 F1 over three benchmarks, beating IRCoT by 15.1 EM / 18.2 F1 with 19 of 22 paired-bootstrap EM/F1 tests at p < 10⁻⁴, and the paper diagnoses the abstention trigger itself (≈90% correct-fire rate, FRR = 11%, FAR = 2% on adversarial unanswerable queries). - The missing: PropRAG — the strongest graph baseline — is omitted from HotpotQA-full (5.2M passages) for budget reasons, the trigger-precision analysis is a 100-question manual sample, and everything is a single temperature-zero run with no seed variance, so run-to-run robustness of an LLM-orchestrated pipeline is unmeasured. - Read it or not: Read it if you build RAG or agentic retrieval systems and care about when to decompose versus when to just retrieve — the control-policy framing, trigger diagnostics, and cost-matched comparison are directly usable; skip it if you need evidence beyond English Wikipedia short-answer QA.

Problem & Motivation: Multi-hop QA requires chaining dependent facts, but the query's granularity rarely matches the granularity at which corpus evidence is retrievable. The paper identifies three failure modes: single retrieval matches surface terms and misses the chain; Graph RAG fixes granularity at corpus pre-computation time, query-agnostically; iterative retrieval (IRCoT, Self-Ask, ReAct) rewrites queries without ever testing whether the reformulated query was actually retrievable, so an early wrong bridge entity propagates. Query-decomposition methods (Least-to-Most, TRQA) commit to a full decomposition before any evidence is seen. The gap: no prior method explicitly decides, per query unit and per evidence state, whether the query is already answerable or should be refined. Practitioners deploying RAG over large open corpora have this problem whenever questions require multi-step chains. Key Idea: Condition the decompose/stop decision on the realized evidence state, not the question: run retrieval-and-reading at the current granularity first, and expand only when the reader abstains (a = ⊥), treating reader failure as an operational test of granularity misalignment. The paper formalizes this as a cost-sensitive threshold rule (expand iff Pr[unresolved | state] ≥ Δ_R/(Δ_R + Δ_U)) and proves a separation argument (Appendix B): two states with identical queries but different retrieved evidence can demand opposite actions, so any policy measurable on the query alone incurs irreducible regret — which is why question-complexity routing (Adaptive-RAG) is structurally insufficient. Dependency-ordered binary splits with execution-order enforcement (prerequisite answers enter history before the dependent branch retrieves) keep dependent sub-queries grounded. Methodology: Evidence-conditioned recursive search. State x = (query node q, interaction history H, depth d). At each node, a resolution operator G refines q using H, retrieves top-k = 5 passages (NV-Embed-v2, dot product), and has a retrieval-grounded reader answer or abstain. Policy π: STOP if resolved, FAIL if depth d_max = 4 or non-decomposable, otherwise EXPAND. A binary expansion operator B proposes (q_left, q_right) with q_left as the bridge/prerequisite; a semantic-coverage verifier V checks the split recovers the parent's intent and repairs it at most once. The left branch is fully solved first, its answer/evidence written to H, then the right branch runs. A synthesis step aggregates leaves into a final answer. All operators are prompted GPT-4o-mini modules; no fine-tuning, no corpus pre-computation. Critical design decisions: (1) binary rather than N-ary splitting — justified by a controlled 400-question high-arity study (Appendix L: binary holds 95–99 EM from 2 to 5 leaf needs, flat N-ary aggregation loses 27.5 EM); (2) hard reader-abstention as the trigger rather than a learned classifier — justified by Appendix C, where a Platt-calibrated logistic head trained on 3,060 labeled decision states changes accuracy by a non-significant −0.30 to −1.40 EM and increases LLM calls; (3) full-corpus evaluation as primary rather than the annotated supporting/distractor pools prior work uses — well justified as the deployment-realistic regime. The threshold derivation (Appendix B) is explicitly characterized as a decision characterization, not a global-optimality claim. Key Results: Full-corpus (primary): Hi-Q averages 52.3 EM / 64.0 F1 over MuSiQue-full, 2Wiki-full, HotpotQA-full (1,000 questions each, corpora of 139,416 / 430,225 / 5,233,235 passages), beating IRCoT by +15.1 EM / +18.2 F1 on average (+27.0 EM on 2Wiki-full; +5.4 EM on HotpotQA-full) and PropRAG by +11.5 EM / +12.0 F1 on MuSiQue-full and +9.9 EM / +12.1 F1 on 2Wiki-full; PropRAG omitted on HotpotQA-full because graph construction would exceed $2,500. Controlled supporting/distractor setting: 57.9 EM / 69.3 F1 average, +5.6 EM / +3.9 F1 over PropRAG, +13.7 EM over IRCoT. Agentic baselines under a standardized setup: +30.8 EM over a coding agent and +24.4 EM over a Recursive Language Model; PyRAG on MuSiQue-full with a shared Qwen3.6-27B reader: 47.9 vs 41.2 EM. Cost: full Hi-Q uses 70.5% fewer tokens than IRCoT but 2.11× latency and 1.95× LLM calls; a cost-matched variant (depth capped at 1) runs at 2.93 vs IRCoT's 2.92 calls, 9.4× fewer input tokens, 25% faster, and +10.4 EM macro-averaged. Trigger diagnostics: decomposition fires on 10.7% (HotpotQA) to 48.6% (2Wiki) of nodes; on triggered MuSiQue cases, leaf retrieval lifts all-gold cover from 7.0% (root@5) to 47.7% (leaf-union) at matched budget 42.7% vs 7.9% on the clean subset. Depth stratification: at 4 hops Hi-Q reaches 39.2 F1 vs PropRAG's 26.9. Robustness holds across Llama-3.3-70B (60.2 avg EM) and Qwen3-30B-A3B (58.3) readers and three embedding models. Baselines are current (HippoRAG 2, PropRAG from 2025, IRCoT, agentic 2025–26 work); some are quoted from prior work, key competitors reproduced. Gains are large, but the evaluation is 1,000-question samples per benchmark with a single decoding run. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (multi-hop RAG as retrievable-granularity discovery conditioned on evidence state, with a formal threshold-rule and query-only-regret separation argument) plus NEW METHOD (the resolution-operator-gated dependency-ordered binary refinement loop). The components are individually standard — query rewriting, binary decomposition, round-trip verification, reader abstention all exist — and the genuinely new element is conditioning the when-to-decompose decision on retrieved evidence rather than question complexity or a fixed template; the appendices' demonstrations that learned routers and calibrated controllers add nothing over the training-free trigger strengthen this framing rather than dilute it. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and each component earns its cost: static one-shot decomposition drops average to 51.5 EM, removing dependency awareness to 47.1 EM, always-decompose costs 3.4 EM (sampled 100 queries), and verification removal widens with hop depth (−1.0 F1 at 4 hops). Statistical protocol is explicit: paired question-level bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, 95% percentile intervals, all IRCoT/PropRAG comparisons significant, smallest at p = 0.0033. The trigger itself is audited (100-sample causal taxonomy, FRR/FAR on normal and adversarial queries), a closed-book control, a strict evidence-grounding variant, and a backbone-sensitivity analysis (GPT-5 closed-book reaches 25.0 EM on MuSiQue, and the authors honestly note stronger readers partially bypass retrieval) are all included. Concerns: temperature-zero single runs — the bootstrap quantifies population uncertainty, not pipeline stochasticity; the trigger-precision audit is a 100-question manual sample; 366 of 836 triggered MuSiQue cases were excluded as annotation errors; baselines are a mix of quoted and reproduced numbers (source table provided, mitigating this); and a project page (https://hi-q-project.github.io/) is linked but no code repository or artifact release is explicitly stated in the provided text. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — a fully prompted pipeline over commercial APIs). - Practical: Yes — GPT-4o-mini or open 70B/30B readers, NV-Embed-v2 on a single Tesla P40 (four A6000 for the 5.2M-passage corpus), no fine-tuning or graph construction required. - Efficient: Mixed — cost-matched configuration is cheaper and faster than IRCoT (8.6× lower token cost per question), but the full configuration costs 2.11× IRCoT's latency (13.5s vs 6.4s per question) and 5.7 LLM calls; it is uniformly cheaper than PropRAG-style graph pipelines at large corpus sizes. - Effective: Strong evidence on the stated problem — trigger diagnostics show decomposition recovers gold passages root retrieval misses (7.9% → 42.7% cover at matched budget), and accuracy gains survive reader, embedding, and grounding-strictness substitutions; evidence is answer accuracy plus recall proxies, not deployment outcomes. - Scalable: Partially tested — the 5.2M-passage HotpotQA corpus is the largest setting and gains hold there, but latency grows with recursion depth (worst case 31 nodes at d_max = 4) and no experiment probes corpora beyond 5.2M passages or concurrent deployment load. Delivers a method and protocol in paper form plus prompt templates (Appendix O); no released library, dataset, or trained model is confirmed from the text. Strengths: - The control-theoretic framing of when-to-decompose is a real conceptual contribution: the Appendix B separation result (query-identical states requiring opposite actions) gives a principled, testable reason why question-complexity routing must fail, and Appendix D confirms it empirically (Adaptive-RAG routes 959/1000 questions to one action and scores below the constant policy). - Rare self-auditing of the core mechanism: the abstention trigger is manually taxonomized (90% correct-fire), bounded above by the always-decompose ablation, and shown replaceable by a calibrated learned head without benefit — this pre-empts the obvious "is the trigger just a heuristic?" objection. - Evaluation honesty: full-corpus retrieval as the primary setting is a deliberate improvement over the field's small supporting/distractor pools, and the PropRAG omission is disclosed with a concrete cost figure rather than hidden. - The cost-matched configuration is a genuinely useful engineering result: same call count as IRCoT, +10.4 EM, 8.6× cheaper — the paper optimizes its own cost-accuracy frontier rather than only reporting its best number. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Appendix N): results cover only English, Wikipedia-derived, short-answer passage QA; dependency structures are assumed acyclic and sequentially resolvable, excluding mutually dependent prerequisites; the binary resolved/unresolved signal cannot represent partial, conflicting, or competing evidence; performance depends on LLM module reliability, with false abstention causing over-refinement and unsupported answers causing premature stopping. They also confront the backbone-sensitivity issue head-on: GPT-5 supplies bridge entities from parametric knowledge, weakening answer accuracy as a diagnostic of retrieval alignment, and they hold the reader at GPT-4o-mini for attribution. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No run-level variance: all results are single temperature-zero passes; for an LLM-orchestrated recursive pipeline, run-to-run variability across the bootstrap's population-only intervals is unknown. - The trigger audit is small: 100 manually sampled triggers, 50 adversarial queries, one dataset — the headline 90% correct-fire rate carries non-trivial sampling uncertainty that is not quantified. - PropRAG is missing on the largest corpus (HotpotQA-full), so the flagship table's strongest graph baseline is absent exactly where the paper's anti-graph argument is most pointed. - 366 of 836 triggered MuSiQue cases excluded as annotation errors before the recovery analysis; the Leaf@5 recovery numbers are reported on the filtered clean subset, and sensitivity to that filtering is not shown. - Dependency handling is enforced by execution order plus history, not correctness: a wrong left-branch answer still grounds the right branch, and the multi-decomposition voting study (Appendix K) shows only +1.6 EM at 3× cost, indicating residual split-error propagation the paper characterizes but does not eliminate. - Latency: full Hi-Q is 2.11× slower than IRCoT; the paper foregrounds the cost-matched variant but the full configuration's wall-clock cost in latency-sensitive deployments deserves equal billing. Bottom Line: For anyone building multi-hop RAG systems, this is worth reading — the evidence-conditioned control policy is a well-validated, cheap-to-adopt design point with unusually thorough self-diagnostics, and I know no paper that covers the when-to-decompose question with equal rigor, though its scope is confined to English Wikipedia short-answer QA and single-run evaluation.

Register Shifts Break LLM Safety: A Bengali Benchmark with Culturally Grounded Harms

N Islam, NJ Lia, SR Dipta, SB Sultan, AK Zehady · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BANGLASAFE, an 879-prompt Bengali safety benchmark spanning 17 statute-anchored harm categories and five language/register/framing conditions, and uses it to show that non-adversarial register shifts within Bengali — not the English-to-Bengali switch itself — drive LLM safety failures across 18 frontier models (15,822 responses). - Why it's important: LLMs are deployed in Bangladesh and other diglossic, non-English markets, but their safety alignment is trained almost exclusively on English norms and vocabulary, so ordinary, everyday writing styles can silently bypass safeguards for harms (yaba, hundi, bKash fraud, formalin adulteration) that English taxonomies do not even name. - How it does it: Each harmful act is rendered in five fixed conditions (English direct, English institutional, formal Bengali journalism, colloquial Banglish, institutional Bengali) with identical semantic content, enabling paired within-prompt ablations (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Holm-Bonferroni) that isolate language, authority, and register effects, plus a four-way LLM-as-judge rubric validated against human annotation. - The good: The headline finding is mechanistically clean and statistically solid — formal journalistic Bengali reaches 63.3% ASRloose vs. 45.8% for colloquial Banglish (a +17.0pp paired gap, r_rb = +0.573, p < 10^-15), present in 17 of 18 models, and the paper traces it to the PARTIAL bucket (models complying by writing mock investigative articles) rather than verbatim leakage. - The missing: The benchmark has no benign control set, so the paper cannot say whether hardening against the journalism register would cause over-refusal of legitimate Bengali investigative reporting; the proposed journalism-cover mechanism also rests on a single-author qualitative read of 200 responses. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on multilingual safety alignment, red-teaming, or safety evaluation infrastructure for low-resource languages; skip it if you only need the now-well-established point that non-English prompts weaken safety, since the genuinely new content is the register/genre dimension and the Bangladesh-specific taxonomy.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is strong — the register-within-language axis and the journalism-schema compliance mode are genuinely new relative to the well-worn multilingual-degradation backdrop, anchored by a NEW DATASET + NEW FINDING classification. Non-Obviousness (80) is the top dimension: the +17pp paired register effect (r=0.573, 17/18 models, stronger in capable models) was not predicted by prior work, and the five-condition within-prompt design cleanly separates language, authority, and register effects. Rigor (72) is solid — Holm-corrected paired tests, bootstrap CIs, cross-judge replication — but is held back by the absent benign control set, author-only annotation, low four-way inter-human agreement (κ=0.286) on the headline metric, and preprint status. Problem & Motivation LLM safety alignment is trained and evaluated predominantly on English harm categories, and multilingual safety benchmarks mostly operate by translating English taxonomies into other languages and measuring refusal rates. The authors argue this translation paradigm misses two things specific to Bengali (the seventh-most-spoken language globally): (1) culturally specific harms — yaba (methamphetamine-caffeine pills), hundi (informal value transfer), bKash/Nagad mobile-financial fraud, formalin adulteration, certificate forgery, acid attacks — that carry local statutory and institutional meaning flattened by generic English categories; and (2) diglossia, i.e., Bengali's rich register variation (formal journalism, colloquial Banglish, institutional officialese) that signals different authority and intent without any adversarial engineering. Prior multilingual jailbreak work (Yong et al. 2023's 79% success via low-resource translation; MultiJail; XSTafety) and prior Indic benchmarks (IndicSafe's ~500 Bengali prompts with Indian categories) leave Bengali-native, culturally grounded, register-controlled safety evaluation unoccupied. Practitioners deploying or auditing LLMs for Bangladeshi users currently have no instrument to measure these failures. Key Idea The core insight is that in a diglossic language, register is an independent safety axis from language itself: the same harmful request, in the same language (Bengali), phrased in the formal journalistic register of Prothom Alo/The Daily Star triggers an "investigative-news schema" — the model complies by embedding operational content inside a mock newspaper article — while the colloquial peer-help register triggers refusal. This interpretive reframing (task-level bypass, not content-level bypass) interacts with a measurable coverage gap: across 80,587 prompts in twelve English safety RLHF corpora, 239 of 240 (corpus × Bengali-term) probes return zero hits, so culturally specific Bengali harm vocabulary was likely never seen by safety training. The experiment design — five conditions crossed with paired within-prompt statistical tests — is the trick that makes the register effect separable from language and authority effects. Methodology The pipeline has three stages. (1) Dataset construction: 879 prompts across 17 statute-anchored categories (e.g., hundi anchored to FERA 1947/MLPA 2012, acid attacks to the Acid Crime Control Act 2002) built from a 309-prompt human-authored gold set (grounded in named Bangladesh cases from Prothom Alo, The Daily Star, NGO case files, each traceable to a primary-source URL) and a 570-prompt synthetic set from a four-agent Claude Opus 4.7 generation pipeline, line-by-line reviewed by native annotators; 57% of prompts are case-anchored, balanced across conditions. Each harm-act instance appears under all five conditions (ENDirect, ENInst, BNFormal, BNCollq, BNInst) holding semantic content fixed. (2) Evaluation: 18 models (open-weight <10B, 10–30B, 30B+, and closed-source, from Llama-3.2-3B to DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GPT-5-mini, Claude-Haiku-4.5) run at temperature 0 with no system prompt, producing 15,822 responses judged by a four-way rubric (REFUSE / POLICY / PARTIAL / HARMFUL) with 17 tie-breakers, yielding ASRloose (PARTIAL+HARMFUL) and ASRstrict. (3) Analysis: six paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on within-(model, base-prompt) pairs with Holm-Bonferroni correction (K=6), bootstrap CIs (B=10,000), a corpus-coverage probe, Latin-script-density analysis, and a cross-guard audit of LlamaGuard 4 and GPT-OSS-Safeguard. Critical design decisions: deterministic decoding to isolate policy from sampling noise (justified by cited evidence that decoding parameters swing safety rates by up to 95pp); a four-way rather than binary rubric because register-shift failures concentrate in partial compliance (well justified by the label distributions); and a gold-vs-synthetic split reported separately to mitigate judge/generator same-family bias (both use Claude Opus 4.7; gold-only ASRloose is 47.6% vs. 56.9% synthetic — a directionally consistent replication). Key Results Across 15,822 responses from 18 models, overall ASRloose is 53.6% and ASRstrict 14.7%. By condition, ASRloose: BNFormal 63.3% [0.617, 0.650], BNInst 55.7%, ENInst 53.4%, ENDirect 50.4% [0.487, 0.522], BNCollq 45.8% [0.442, 0.475]; ASRstrict: ENDirect 18.7% vs. BNFormal 13.5% — the journalism-register effect lives in the PARTIAL bucket (49.9% of BNFormal responses). The paired register ablation (ABL-3a: BNFormal vs. BNCollq, 3,132 pairs) yields +17.0pp [+0.152, +0.188], r_rb = +0.573; the language effect (ENDirect↔BNFormal) is +13.0pp (r = −0.411); authority effects are +2.9pp (English) and +4.4pp (cross-lingual) — significant but small. The register effect holds in 17 of 18 models (sign test p < 0.001, median gap +17.6pp) and is larger in the most capable models (Mistral-Medium-3 97.1%, DeepSeek-V3 95.4%, GPT-4.1-mini 91.4% in BNFormal); per-model ASRloose ranges from 17.1% (Claude-Haiku-4.5) to 89.5% (Mistral-Medium-3), with no size–safety correlation (ρ = +0.093). The coverage probe finds one hit ("dowry" in PKU-SafeRLHF) out of 240 cells over 80,587 prompts, vs. 290 hits for "methamphetamine," 177 for "money laundering." Cross-judge audit: LlamaGuard 4 agrees with the calibrated judge at κ = 0.014 (chance) and GPT-OSS-Safeguard at κ = 0.667; an independent Gemini-3.1-Pro judge reproduces overall ASR within 3.6pp (binary κ = 0.787, per-model rank correlation r = 0.989). Notably, prompt-level guard flagging rates (81.5%/89.1%) collapse on the very authority-cover conditions that bypass the target LLMs (LlamaGuard drops to 51.5% prompt-level, 3.3% response-level on ENInst). Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the first Bengali-native safety benchmark combining native authorship, Bangladesh-statute-anchored taxonomy, controlled register variation, and a human-validated four-way judge; and the finding that non-adversarial register variation within a single language dominates the language-switch effect — an interpretive (genre-reframing) failure mode distinct from prior persona/persuasion attacks. The statistical machinery (Wilcoxon paired tests, bootstrap CIs, LLM-as-judge with κ validation) is standard, competently applied; the multilingual-safety-degradation backdrop itself is well established. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are present and strong: six paired tests with Holm correction, condition-level label distributions, per-model and per-category breakdowns, a gold/synthetic robustness split, a second independent judge reproducing all conclusions, and a same-family bias check (Claude judge vs. GPT-OSS-Safeguard agree at κ = 0.856 on Claude-Haiku-4.5 rows). Uncertainty is handled via B=10,000 bootstrap CIs and cluster-aware inference. Judge validation: binary κ = 0.666 against the primary annotator on 300 responses, exceeding inter-human agreement (κ = 0.586); prompt-level register IAA is κ = 0.915. Concerns: (1) prompt-level IAA was performed by two annotators who are authors; (2) the cultural-authenticity IAA is only 51.7% raw agreement, attributed to a definitional split about code-mixing; (3) evaluation and generation both use Claude Opus 4.7, only partially mitigated; (4) no benign-prompt control set; (5) ASR is LLM-judged, a proxy — the PARTIAL/HARMFUL boundary has four-way inter-human κ of only 0.286, so the headline 53.6% number inherits judge subjectivity. Release: two-tier access — taxonomy, rubric, scripts, aggregates under CC-BY-4.0/MIT; the 15,822 prompt-response pairs gated on Hugging Face with manual use-case review ("upon acceptance" for full dataset — the paper is an arXiv preprint, arXiv:2608.22335, not yet peer-reviewed). Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark construction plus a large model-evaluation campaign; no trained artifact). - Practical: Yes — everything runs via commercial APIs or off-the-shelf open-weight models on commodity hardware; the audit tools (LlamaGuard 4, GPT-OSS-Safeguard) are open-weight. - Efficient: Inference-only cost; the 15,822-response sweep is trivially cheap by current standards, and re-running the benchmark on a new model costs 879 generations plus judge calls. - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark detects a real, robust behavioral difference that existing safety classifiers miss (κ = 0.014 for LlamaGuard 4), but "effectiveness" is self-referential — measured against the authors' own judge and rubric, with the strict-harm boundary subjectively graded (inter-human four-way κ = 0.286). - Scalable: Not tested and not really applicable — the open question is not scaling the benchmark but whether targeted Bengali safety alignment fixes the failures, which the paper only recommends without evaluating; the register gap widening in stronger models suggests the problem may worsen at frontier scale. The work delivers a concrete software/data artifact (879-prompt benchmark with provenance flags, judge rubric with 17 tie-breakers, evaluation framework, gated response corpus) rather than a reusable proof technique. Strengths - The controlled five-condition, within-prompt design is the real methodological contribution: it converts a confounded correlation ("Bengali is less safe") into three cleanly separated causal-style contrasts, and the register effect (+17pp, r = 0.573) survives correction, holds in 17/18 models, and strengthens with model capability — a genuinely non-obvious empirical finding. - The mechanism analysis goes beyond the number: the PARTIAL-bucket redistribution, the 97%-of-200 qualitative journalism-frame adoption, and the Latin-script-density dissociation (BNFormal bypasses at 2.9% code-mixing while BNInst uses 18.1%) distinguish two distinct failure routes rather than lumping them. - The cross-infrastructure audit (LlamaGuard 4 at chance-level κ, prompt-vs-response detection collapse under authority framing) is independently useful to anyone building multilingual moderation pipelines. - The corpus coverage probe is a clever, cheap piece of evidence — 239/240 zero hits across 80,587 prompts — that grounds the interpretive story in a training-data deficit, though it stops short of causation (as the authors concede). Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations unusually directly (a credibility positive): the coverage probe does not establish causality; the journalism-cover mechanism rests on single-author qualitative inspection of 200 responses and is "explanatory rather than quantitatively calibrated"; the judge is anchored to a single 300-response annotation session with no independent annotator cohort replication; 570/879 prompts and the judge share Claude Opus 4.7 lineage (mitigated by the gold-subset ASR of 47.6% and the Gemini cross-judge replication); and — most importantly — there is no benign control set, so the benchmark cannot measure over-refusal of legitimate Bengali investigative journalism if models are hardened against this register. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No benign control set is acknowledged, but its absence cuts deeper than stated: without measuring false-refusal rates on legitimate Prothom Alo-style requests, the 63.3% BNFormal figure cannot be interpreted as a deployable risk ratio — a model that answers all Bengali journalistic prompts (harmful or not) at high rates would look identical. - The cultural-authenticity IAA of 51.7% is explained away as a "definitional split," but a coin-flip agreement on one of the three validation axes weakens the claim that prompts are ecologically valid Bangladeshi usage, and annotators for both validation passes were authors or team-adjacent. - Judge dependence on the PARTIAL/HARMFUL boundary is understated: with four-way inter-human κ at 0.286, the paper's framing of BNFormal as "compliance" rather than hedged refusal partially rests on rubric choices (e.g., the journalism-cover-with-content tie-breaker) authored by the same team that benefits from the finding. - Model roster is fine-grained on capability but the paper does not test any mitigation (Bengali-targeted safety tuning, register-balanced RLHF), so the practical remedy remains speculation; the conclusion "points toward targeted safety alignment" without any supporting experiment. - Minor: register-condition prompt counts are unbalanced (173–190 per condition), acknowledged as inherited from the gold track and handled by paired tests, but the synthetic track's Claude generation means register fidelity is partially an artifact of one vendor's notion of Bangladeshi registers. Bottom Line For anyone building or evaluating LLM safety beyond English — especially in South Asia — this is a worth-your-time benchmark paper with a genuinely surprising and well-isolated register effect; readers seeking mitigation techniques or a causally established training-data account will find only the diagnosis here, not the cure.

C Kevin, N Raghavan, JF Puget, R Malani, M Puvvadi… · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ACES, a framework that evaluates agent skills (SKILL.md packages) by running paired live-agent trials with and without the target skill and reporting the marginal delta, called Skill Lift, instead of relying on static document scans. - Why it's important: Enterprise teams are shipping thousands of skills through CI gates that only inspect documents, and the paper shows these scans are statistically uninformative about runtime behavior (scan scores correlate with live lift at essentially zero), so a skill that passes review can silently degrade an agent in production. - How it does it: The core trick is differential measurement — run the same task, agent, model, fixtures, and decoy skills in two conditions that differ only in target-skill availability, normalize both trajectories into a shared trace format (ATIF), grade with six metrics, and report the paired difference. - The good: The strongest evidence is the direct static-vs-live disconnect on their own corpus: 94.5% of 145 skills pass the structural gate, yet Tier 1 and Tier 2 scan scores correlate with live lift at Spearman ρ = −0.0181 and −0.0266 (CIs spanning zero), while 947 paired cases show mean composite lift of 0.2134 (95% CI [0.1967, 0.2301]). - The missing: Live grading depends on LLM judges whose live inter-judge agreement, human calibration, and bias (e.g., behavior_check items that structurally favor the with-skill arm) are unmeasured, and no human-verified ground truth exists for the internal skill corpus, which is not released. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or gate agent skill/plugin catalogs or run agent CI/CD; skip it if you only care about agent benchmarks or judge methodology in the abstract, since the contribution is a domain-specific evaluation system rather than a general method.

Problem & Motivation: Agent skills — natural-language procedural-knowledge packages (SKILL.md plus optional scripts) loaded at inference time via progressive disclosure — have become the standard extension mechanism for harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, with registries hosting thousands of community skills. Existing quality gates (structural spec checks, LLM-as-judge document rubrics, linters, security scanners) all inspect the skill document without ever running it, so they cannot answer the deployment question: does the skill help a live agent discover, route to, and execute the right workflow? Document scanning cannot detect failure modes like non-discovery, wrong script invocation, misreported outputs, skill collisions, or silent regressions after model updates. The team operating NVIDIA's enterprise skill catalogs needs evidence, not prose, when reviewing skill changes at merge time. Key Idea: Treat a skill's runtime quality as a paired differential quantity — Skill Lift, the mean score delta between a with-skill condition and a baseline condition that withholds only the target skill while keeping every other variable (task, agent, model, fixtures, support/decoy skills, grader) fixed. Two refinements make this more than an A/B test: (1) staging reference decoy skills in the baseline so the delta isolates the skill's content value from the mere existence of any skill to discover, and (2) an isolation-vs-group decomposition where Lift_grp − Lift_iso measures a "routing premium" — how much value survives when the agent must discriminate the skill from plausible neighbors. A shared trajectory contract (ATIF) lets the same grading layer compare across harnesses. Methodology: ACES is a multi-tier pipeline. (1) Static tiers: ~50 deterministic structural rules across four weighted dimensions (Correctness 0.35, Discoverability 0.25, Reliability 0.25, Efficiency 0.15; gate at 70/100), a G-Eval-style 9+1-criterion LLM-judge rubric at temperature 0, plus linting and security scanning. (2) Evaluation assets: an evals.json dataset (prompt, expected_skill, expected_script, ground_truth, ordered free-form expected_behavior strings) that authors write directly, bootstrap via a four-bucket LLM generator (explicit / implicit / contextual / negative-control), or refine by lifting observed behaviors out of recorded ATIF trajectories; author intent in EVAL.md overrides generated content; BYOT tasks and BYOG graders extend the contract for product-specific needs. (3) Execution: a Harbor-based adapter emits paired Dockerized task environments per (skill, agent, case, condition), stages the target skill or its decoy/support set, and schedules agents in parallel; total container runs scale as 2·N·K·C·A. (4) Grading: six default metrics (trace-level security, skill_execution with four sub-checks, skill_efficiency with routing and tool-efficiency sub-checks, 5-criterion accuracy judge, RAGAS goal_accuracy, per-behavior LLM judge) mapped to five stakeholder dimensions, aggregated as a 1/6-weighted composite plus an outcome-only view averaging accuracy and goal accuracy. The composite lift formula and per-mode variants (Lift_iso, Lift_grp, routing premium) are fully specified. Well-justified decisions include the fixed-support baseline and the isolation/group split; the equal 1/6 metric weighting is explicitly offered only as an inspectable default, not a claim. Key Results: On the 145-skill corpus, 94.5% pass the 70-point structural gate (scores 61–98, mean 79.2), 86.2% pass the LLM-judge threshold, and the two scan tiers correlate at Spearman ρ = 0.14 (Pearson r = 0.08). The headline live result: across 947 scored paired cases from 58 of 64 production skills and four primary harnesses, mean composite Skill Lift is 0.2134 (95% paired-case CI [0.1967, 0.2301]); with-skill absolute score 0.7460 vs baseline 0.5326; outcome-only lift 0.1799; lift positive in 689 cases (72.8%), zero in 171, negative in 87. Per-metric lifts: skill_execution +0.3263, behavior_check +0.2983, skill_efficiency +0.2758 (positive in only 41.7% of cases — high variance), goal_accuracy +0.2167, accuracy +0.1431, security +0.020. Harness-mean lifts range from 0.3611 (OpenCode) to 0.0896 (Terminus-2) with uneven cell coverage (34–56 cells, 211–259 cases each). Critically, scan scores do not predict live lift (Tier 1 ρ = −0.0181, Tier 2 ρ = −0.0266 on 62 skills with matching metadata). A 25-variant routing stress test holds lift at 0.133–0.149 for 1–20 visible skills while wall time grows from 258 s to 451 s, and at 50 visible skills the with-skill pass rate drops to 0.55 and wall time hits 1,290 s. A same-harness Codex model sweep shows lift shrinking (Δ +0.09 to +0.05) as stronger model backends raise the no-skill baseline — a genuinely counter-intuitive, methodologically important observation. Baselines in Table 3 (SkillsBench, SkillTester, in-the-wild retrieval studies, Anthropic skill-creator) are recent but each covers at most two of the five capabilities ACES claims. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are: the first production-scale demonstration that document-scan scores carry no signal about live skill value (ρ ≈ 0 between scans and lift), the reference-decoy paired baseline that separates content value from discoverability value, and the isolation-vs-group routing-premium decomposition. The constituent techniques — G-Eval judging, RAGAS goal scoring, paired A/B evaluation, Harbor containerized execution, CI-native eval assets — are standard; the contribution is their skill-specific composition rather than any new algorithmic primitive. Related concurrent work (SkillsBench, SkillTester, AEVAL, SkillAudit) is cited and positioned honestly in Table 3 and Appendix C. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above average for a systems/eval paper. Ablation-style sensitivity checks are present: cluster bootstrap over skills [0.1898, 0.2350] and over skill–agent cells [0.1880, 0.2385], both consistent with the headline; a raw-row audit reconstructed 898/947 pairs and reproduced composite lift to 0.2153; a conservative imputation (every unscored with-skill case counted as failure) drops composite lift to 0.1840 but keeps it positive. Three-judge rotation on the document rubric quantifies judge spread (~1.5 points on a 10-point scale). An open-source implementation exists (github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator, v0.1.0, Apache-2.0), but raw trajectories, internal hostnames, and the enterprise skill corpus are withheld, so exact replication of the headline numbers is not possible from released artifacts. Methodological concerns: (a) live grading is LLM-judge-driven with no human calibration and live inter-judge agreement explicitly unmeasured; (b) behavior_check and skill_execution are process metrics the baseline arm can structurally fail when the target skill is withheld — the authors acknowledge this and report the outcome-only view, but the composite still embeds this asymmetry; (c) goal_accuracy is a lower bound for VPN-bound internal skills, which the paired design partially absorbs but which distorts absolute numbers; (d) the corpus is internal and skewed (System Access 49, Deployment 41, Platform 29, Data Infra 21). This is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2608.20614), not peer-reviewed, from a vendor with an obvious product interest — confidence should be tempered accordingly, though the paper is unusually candid about its own filtering and imputation choices. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL + SYSTEMS (a built, CI-deployed evaluation system with measurements from its own deployment). - Practical: Yes — runs on standard container infrastructure with any modern harness (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor/OpenCode, Terminus-2) and an Apache-2.0 public implementation; LLM-judge tiers need only API access. - Efficient: Scans are free and instant; live paired evaluation doubles container runs per case and costs real tokens (a 20-skill workspace run took ~451 s wall time), so the authors sensibly reserve live runs for release candidates, high-risk skills, and reviewer-triggered changes rather than every edit. - Effective: The evidence supports the central claim — live paired evaluation surfaces discovery, routing, workflow, and regression signals that scans provably cannot (zero scan-lift correlation), including 87 negative-lift cases debugged from trajectories. - Scalable: Cost is linear in N·K·C·A by design and 50-skill routing stress is tested (pass rate 0.55, 1,290 s), but the paper only claims, not tests, behavior at registry scale (thousands of skills) or across organizations; 64 production skills is a modest deployment footprint. The work delivers a real software artifact (SkillEvaluator library with CI hooks) plus a reusable evaluation protocol; the paired-lift methodology itself transfers beyond the NVIDIA corpus. Strengths: (1) The static-vs-live correlation result is a sharp, quantitative, falsifiable finding (ρ ≈ 0 with CIs spanning zero on 62 skills, against 94.5% gate pass rates) that directly quantifies the observability gap in current practice — this is the paper's intellectual core, not an afterthought. (2) The paired-decoy baseline design is a genuinely thoughtful measurement construct: holding decoy skills fixed in both arms separates what a skill contains from the fact that any skill exists to be found, an error most naive A/B evals would commit. (3) The isolation/group decomposition yields an actionable per-skill diagnostic (routing premium) that converts an aggregate metric into author guidance. (4) Unusual evidentiary hygiene: a frozen-evidence inventory (Table 6), a post-hoc raw-row audit with conservative imputation, explicit caveats that harness means are diagnostics not leaderboards, and an OpenClaw n=1 case showing a security failure invisible to scans despite 89/100 static quality — all reported against the paper's own interest. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront: corpus generalizability (145 skills, skewed toward four infrastructure categories, single organization, needs cross-organization replication); uneven harness coverage and the non-balanced nature of harness means; the causal-scope limit that Skill Lift is marginal under a declared workspace/baseline policy, not an intrinsic skill property; judge sensitivity (document-rubric spread measured, live grading agreement unmeasured); the model-update shrinkage of lift (stronger baselines need skills less); VPN-unreachable enterprise endpoints lowering absolute goal_accuracy; conflated timeout accounting in the raw audit; and the composite metric weighting being a default, not a calibrated claim. This is a credibility positive — the limitations section reads as self-audit rather than minimization, and the outcome-only view is introduced precisely to blunt the process-metric asymmetry objection. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No human ground truth anywhere in the live pipeline — accuracy, goal_accuracy, and behavior_check are all machine-judged, so the "runtime evidence" replacing doc-scans is itself judge-model output; a small human-annotated validation set would substantially strengthen the headline. (2) The behavior_check and skill_execution metrics partially encode the conclusion: a baseline arm without the skill cannot "read the expected SKILL.md," so ~2/6 of the composite is structurally biased toward positive lift; the outcome-only lift (0.1799) is the honest headline, and the paper buries it behind the larger composite number. (3) The 947-case aggregate clusters within 58 skills but per-skill lift variance is only partially characterized (88/201 cells with a second trial, median within-cell SD 0.0319); no per-skill significance testing is possible from released data. (4) Selection effects in which skills received live evaluation (58 of 64) are unexamined — if live evaluation was triggered preferentially for promising skills, mean lift is inflated. (5) Decoy/support skill sets are author-configured, so the routing-premium measurement depends on choices the framework itself does not standardize; the authors list automated decoy selection as future work but report routing results as if the decoys were neutral. (6) Vendor affiliation and withheld internal corpus mean the empirical claims are not independently replicable, only the method. Bottom Line: For anyone operating or gating an agent-skill catalog, this is required reading — it is the first paper to quantify, on production skills, that document-scanning is worthless as a proxy for runtime skill value, and it ships a working, open-source paired-evaluation protocol to replace it; for everyone else, concurrent benchmarks like SkillsBench cover the "do skills help" question on open data with fewer strings attached.

Does On-Policy Distillation Really Distill? From Noisy Teacher to Self-Improvement (100 ▲ )

Yi Ding, Ruqi Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 1 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that on-policy distillation (OPD) improves students largely by suppressing the student's own low-probability tokens rather than by transferring teacher knowledge, and builds On-Policy Self-Adaptation (OPSA), a teacher-free, reward-free method that assigns entropy-scaled negative advantages to the lowest-20%-log-probability sampled tokens. - Why it's important: OPD requires a teacher with shared vocabulary and white-box logit access, and if its gains come from a teacher-free mechanism, practitioners can get the same or better improvement with no teacher forward passes, no verifiable rewards, and no reference-answer hints. - How it does it: The core move is an ablation-driven diagnosis — training only on noisy teacher signals, only on clean signals, on top-logp tokens with random advantages, and with fixed negative advantages — which isolates negative advantage on low-logp tokens as the active ingredient, then modulates its magnitude by token entropy (A_dyn = −1/2 − (H_i − H_min)/(2(H_max − H_min))). - The good: The central controlled experiment is decisive: on Qwen3-1.7B, standard OPD, OPD trained only on noisy trajectories, and OPD trained only on clean trajectories all converge to comparable AIME24 Avg@4, and a fixed negative advantage of −0.5 on the bottom-20%-logp tokens matches full OPD — a clean falsification of the distillation story. - The missing: All results are on models up to 9B parameters evaluated on three small math benchmarks (~30 problems each) with best-checkpoint selection by validation Avg@4, no seeds/error bars, and the authors admit the method may not extend to large or heavily post-trained models. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM post-training or distillation — the negative result about OPD's mechanism and the teacher-free recipe that beats OPD by 16.77 Avg@32 points on AIME24 directly challenge a popular training paradigm; skip it if you need theorems, large-scale validation, or methods beyond math-reasoning RL.

Problem & Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision by computing reverse-KL advantages from a teacher on student-sampled trajectories, addressing the sparse, sometimes-vanishing outcome rewards of RLVR (GRPO/DAPO). But the teacher scores prefixes it would never generate, so the reliability of that off-policy supervision is questionable, and OPD additionally requires shared vocabulary and white-box teacher logits. Practitioners choosing between RLVR, OPD, and self-distillation (OPSD) currently lack an understanding of what part of OPD actually drives improvement. The paper closes this gap by quantifying teacher-supervision noise and isolating the true source of OPD's gains. Key Idea: The key insight is a mechanistic decomposition: reverse-KL advantages computed on student trajectories are almost always negative for off-policy tokens, gradient analysis shows high-logp student tokens receive near-zero advantages and contribute no learning signal, so OPD's improvement is driven by negative advantages on the student's low-logp tokens — an operation requiring no teacher — and the magnitude of the negative signal should scale with token entropy so that high-entropy "fork" positions get stronger updates without collapsing diversity. Methodology: The paper proceeds in two phases. Phase 1 (diagnosis): using Qwen3-1.7B as student and Qwen3-4B/30B-A3B/235B-A22B-Instruct as teachers on 500 DAPO-17k questions, it defines noisy supervision as an advantage sign that disagrees with the verifiable reward on \boxed{} answer tokens, measures noise rates, and runs controlled OPD variants (noisy-only, clean-only, top-logp-only with calculated vs. random advantages, fixed advantage of −0.5 vs. +0.2). Phase 2 (method): OPSA is a token-level policy-gradient objective over only the lowest-20%-logp sampled tokens per response, each assigned a negative advantage whose magnitude increases linearly with the token's entropy normalized within the response (A_fix = −3/4, δ = 1 in Eq. 4), implemented in the slime framework (Megatron + SGLang) on 8×H100/H200 GPUs, lr 1e-6, batch size 64, thinking mode disabled, trained on DAPO-17k questions without labels. Critical design decisions: (i) restricting updates to the bottom-20% logp tokens — justified by ablation showing bottom-10% over-sharpens and 20/30/40% perform similarly; (ii) entropy-proportional advantage magnitude — justified by the δ = 1 vs. δ = −1 comparison (50.0% vs. unstable/worse); (iii) defining noise only on verifiable answer tokens — reasonable but only a proxy for token-level supervision quality elsewhere in the trajectory. Key Results: On Qwen3-1.7B, OPSA lifts Avg@32 on AIME24 from 13.44 to 48.85 (+35.41 points, 263.5% relative), AIME25 from 9.69 to 35.31, and HMMT25 from 5.73 to 23.33, and more than doubles Pass@32 on all three (e.g., 40.00→80.00 on AIME24). Against baselines on Qwen3-1.7B (averaged over three math benchmarks): OPSA 35.83 Avg@32 vs. GRPO 24.79, OPSD 23.58, OPD 32.08, TTRL 11.81, and NSR 24.13 — beating the best baseline by 11.04 Avg@32 and 8.89 Pass@32. Gains transfer to Qwen3-4B (AIME24 23.33→62.08) and Qwen3.5-9B (76.35→87.81 AIME24), and to out-of-domain MBPP+ and GPQA-Diamond (+1.20 to +4.48 points). Diagnosis results: teacher noise rates of 30.6% (4B), 34.7% (30B-A3B), and 50.6% (235B-A22B); 29.2% of tokens get exactly zero advantage and 51.7% get |A| < 1e-4; fixed −0.5 advantage matches OPD while fixed +0.2 collapses. Training is 46.3 s/step vs. 61.2 s for OPD and 186.2 s for GRPO on Qwen3-1.7B. A token-budget-matched control (appending "wait" to baseline responses) shows OPSA's gains are not explained by longer responses. Baselines are current and relevant (GRPO, TTRL, OPD, OPSD, NSR). The most counter-intuitive finding is that supervision noise increases with teacher scale, yet students improve identically with or without it. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (OPD's gains survive removal of clean teacher supervision entirely, and larger teachers give noisier supervision) plus NEW METHOD (OPSA). The method itself is a recognizable combination of existing ideas — negative-sample reinforcement (NSR), the high-entropy-minority-token finding of Wang et al. (2026c), and bottom-p token selection — applied in a new teacher-free setting; the genuinely novel contribution is the falsification of the distillation narrative for K1-estimator OPD and the demonstration that internal entropy alone suffices as a learning signal. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is unusually strong on mechanism-isolating ablations: noisy/clean filtering, random-vs-calculated advantages, δ = ±1/0 sweep, bottom-10/20/30/40% token-fraction sweep, fork-token masking (which eliminates the length and accuracy gains), Jaccard-distance diversity analysis, and a token-budget-matched length control. A GRPO cold-start experiment (Appendix C.4) adds practical value. However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere, which matters given ~30-problem benchmarks; checkpoint selection uses Avg@4 on a "validation set" whose composition is not specified relative to the test benchmarks (the training-dynamics figures track AIME24 directly, raising a Goodhart-style selection concern); the noise definition covers only \boxed{} answer tokens, leaving per-token noise in the reasoning body unmeasured; and full training/evaluation hyperparameters are given but no explicit code or model release URL appears in the text (Hugging Face/GitHub icons on the title page suggest intended release). Results are self-reported by the authors; this is a preprint (arXiv 2608.31046, Aug 2026) and has not been peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong systems component via the slime implementation). Practical: Yes — runs on 8×H100/H200 with models up to 9B, well within commercial reach. Efficient: The cheapest of the compared methods (46.3 s/step vs. 61.2 for OPD, 186.2 for GRPO), since it needs no teacher forward passes and no group rollouts. Effective: The evidence shows it substantially improves math reasoning Avg@32 and Pass@32 and modestly helps MBPP+/GPQA-Diamond, though the authors themselves note it redistributes existing probability mass rather than expanding the exploration frontier (thinking-mode Pass@k gains are modest). Scalable: Untested beyond 9B dense models; the authors explicitly flag uncertainty about MoE and larger-scale behavior, and the mechanism (suppressing tail mass) may be inert or harmful for already-sharp, heavily post-trained distributions. The work delivers a described recipe and training configuration rather than an explicitly released library or checkpoint in the provided text. Strengths: - The noisy-supervision finding is a genuine, well-executed negative result: 50.6% noise from the 235B teacher, and identical convergence whether training on noisy-only, clean-only, or all trajectories — this credibly undermines the standard justification for OPD. - The gradient analysis (Eq. 3) connecting near-zero advantages to high-logp tokens turns an empirical observation into a mechanistic explanation, and the fixed-negative-advantage experiment then tests it directly rather than leaving it as a plausible story. - The fork-token masking ablation (Fig. 8) is a proper causal test of the proposed mechanism: removing reflective fork positions from training collapses both response length and accuracy gains. - The method's constraint profile (dense token-level signal, no teacher, no verifiable reward, no hints) genuinely dominates all four compared baselines on those axes (Table 1), and the token-budget-matched control in Appendix C.4 anticipates and defuses the obvious "it's just longer responses" objection. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Appendix A): experiments are limited to models up to 9B and it is unclear whether OPSA scales to larger or MoE models; OPSA primarily redistributes existing probability mass and may not help heavily post-trained models with already-sharp distributions; it may not expand the exploration frontier, as reflected in modest thinking-mode Pass@k improvements; and the true mechanism of OPD with the K1 estimator warrants further theoretical analysis. This is a direct, non-defensive limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No seed variance or confidence intervals on any benchmark; with 30 problems per AIME/HMMT split and Avg@32 estimated from 32 samples, several reported gaps (e.g., OOD gains of +1.20 on MBPP+) are plausibly within evaluation noise. - Checkpoint selection by validation Avg@4 with an unspecified validation set, while training-dynamics plots report AIME24 throughout — the possibility of indirect test-set selection is not addressed. - All training and evaluation is in-distribution math (DAPO-17k questions → AIME/AIME/HMMT); the OOD tests (MBPP+, GPQA-Diamond) show gains of only ~1–4 points, so the "generalizes across tasks" claim rests on thin evidence. - The noise metric covers only final-answer tokens; the paper's central claim about supervision quality would be stronger with noise estimates over reasoning tokens, even via a proxy. - Key hyperparameters (A_fix = −3/4, bottom-20%, advantage range [−3/4, −1/4]) are validated by ablation on a single student/teacher pair at 1.7B; sensitivity at other scales is not shown. - The insensitivity-to-noise experiment trains on filtered trajectory subsets, but both subsets still contain a mix of clean and noisy tokens within trajectories (noise was defined only at answer tokens), so "training only on noisy supervision" is an approximation the paper does not quantify. Bottom Line: For anyone training reasoning LLMs, this is worth reading: its falsification of the distillation story behind a widely adopted method, plus a teacher-free recipe that beats GRPO, OPD, OPSD, and NSR at lower cost, is consequential even granting the small-model scale, math-only in-domain evaluation, and missing statistical rigor — the diagnosis alone justifies the read, and OPSA is a credible, cheap addition to the post-training toolbox pending independent replication.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper identifies and formalizes an "edge spectrum" in choice-model-derived item–item graphs for graph collaborative filtering, proving that strong edges (MNL diversion weights) concentrate on in-slate clicked–unclicked competitor pairs that positive smoothing misaligns with the within-slate BPR ranking gradient, and delivers a diagnostic protocol plus an edge-partitioned operator whose pre-registered predictions match four-for-four on MIND and EB-NeRD. - Why it's important: Graph CF design effort on item-graph construction (KG-augmented, content, social, choice-derived) consistently moves headline NDCG@10 by less than 0.01 on impression benchmarks while consuming substantial research attention; knowing when a richer graph is structurally misaligned saves practitioners from a doomed drop-in deployment. - How it does it: The core move is a first-order perturbation argument (Proposition 1): symmetric positive smoothing shrinks the score gap on exactly the pairs where MNL diversion weights are top-K-dominant — in-slate competitors — while the within-slate BPR gradient grows it, and co-click graphs provably cannot concentrate weight on such pairs (Lemma 1). - The good: The evidence is a pre-registered pattern of interventions, not a tuned headline number: scalar fixes (sign flip, margin loss) fail as predicted, the regime boundary localizes at k=10 as diagnosed from the lift profile rather than by tuning, and the edge-partitioned operator's ordering matches the diagnosis on both datasets with 3-seed standard deviations. - The missing: The recommended Anchor-B operator beats co-click by only +0.0027±0.0019 NDCG@10 on EB-NeRD and ties on MIND (not claimed significant), the entire operator comparison runs in a framework that trails the locked LightGCN++ baseline by 0.054–0.083 NDCG@10, and the three dataset-level moderators of when the spectrum surfaces in headline metrics are explicitly left confounded on only two news datasets. - Read it or not: Read it if you build item-side graph operators or choice-aware recommenders and want a rigorous negative result plus a reusable pre-deployment diagnostic; skip it if you want a method that materially improves headline ranking metrics — the authors themselves predict (and measure) that it will not.
