Problem & Motivation: Graph collaborative filtering propagates over item–item graphs under a shared implicit assumption: a stronger edge encodes more of the same relation as a weaker edge, so the neighbor cutoff k is merely a sparsification knob. This assumption has never been stress-tested for graphs whose weights come from choice models — the natural way to encode in-slate competition in impression-rich domains like news recommendation (MIND, EB-NeRD). Practitioners fitting MNL diversion-weight item graphs — the translation of a long choice-modeling tradition (diversion ratios, Collaborative Competitive Filtering, MNL slate rankers) into graph CF — have had no controlled comparison against co-occurrence baselines and no way to predict in advance whether such operators help or hurt. The paper closes the gap of whether choice-derived edges, which by construction concentrate on clicked–unclicked competitor pairs, are compatible with the within-slate ranking losses that impression-aware training applies. Key Idea: The single core insight is the sign mismatch: on a choice-derived graph, the highest-weight edges connect clicked items to their strongest in-slate competitors (because MNL diversion weight is large precisely when both items are jointly plausible choices in the same slate), so positive smoothing over those edges pulls competitor scores toward clicked items — shrinking the score gap by factor (1 − αW_ij) — while the within-slate BPR gradient pushes the same gap apart. Co-click weights are built from disjoint event types (co-positivity, not co-candidacy-with-disagreement), so they cannot satisfy this misalignment by construction. Consequently the neighbor cutoff k on choice-derived graphs is a semantic switch separating two qualitatively different edge regimes, not a sparsification parameter. Methodology: The authors isolate the item-graph axis inside a LightGCN-style propagation polynomial: they identify the item-side even-hop operator (SᵀS) and swap it for one of four candidates — SᵀS, co-click, co-exposure, and MNL-substitution — holding the bipartite structure, layer combination, scoring rule, within-impression BPR loss with in-slate negatives, and hyperparameters fixed. The substitution operator is built by fitting a factorized MNL choice model (utility p_u·q_i + b_i, slate-level softmax, slate cross-entropy objective; dev NLL 3.22 MIND / 1.92 EB-NeRD), aggregating diversion weights Δ_{j→i} = P(i|u,C)·P(j|u,C)/(1−P(j|u,C)) over co-appearance impressions, symmetrizing, and applying top-K=50 pruning and symmetric degree normalization. A frozen-comparison protocol (following Dacrema et al. / Rendle et al.) locks data splits, evaluator (NDCG@10, MRR, Hit@1, gAUC), and a baseline pack (LightGCN, LightGCN++, BPR-MF, GFCF, ItemKNN variants, MNL-only slate ranker) before any operator variant runs. The structural analysis defines a within-slate lift Δ_o(k) (Eq. 6): the mean score difference between operator-neighbors and non-neighbors of clicked items among unclicked in-slate candidates, computed across cutoffs k ∈ {10, 20, 50, 100, all}. Critical design decisions: (i) swapping only the item-side operator for apples-to-apples comparison — justified by a parity decomposition (Appendix A) though it sacrifices numerical equivalence with locked LightGCN, honestly decomposed in Appendix B; (ii) pre-registering two anchor configurations for the edge-partitioned operator (K_strong=10 set by the diagnosed regime boundary, γ=1.0, β∈{0,1}) before evaluation, with the 27-cell sweep explicitly labeled exploratory at seed=1 — well justified against test-on-train selection; (iii) confining theory to a first-order perturbation under a top-K-dominance condition — appropriately scoped, with the paper acknowledging that beyond the strong-edge regime the first-order direction is no longer predicted. Key Results: On the headline metric, all four operators land in a narrow band: MIND NDCG@10 0.4036–0.4088 (spread 0.0052), EB-NeRD 0.5902–0.5985 (spread 0.0083), with co-click best on both datasets and substitution at or near the bottom across 3 seeds — despite the substitution graph indexing largely disjoint neighborhoods (mean Jaccard@50 vs. co-click: 0.014 MIND, 0.044 EB-NeRD). The best operator variant trails locked LightGCN++ by 0.083 NDCG@10 on MIND and 0.054 on EB-NeRD; the framework-axis ablation shows LightGCN-aligned axes (binary R, no pruning) explain under 0.002, localizing the ~0.04 residual outside the operator axis. The lift profile confirms both predictions: substitution lift at k=10 is +0.223±0.027 on MIND (largest) and +0.357±0.065 on EB-NeRD, flipping sign to −0.17 at k=all on EB-NeRD, while co-click stays flat (+0.14→+0.01 MIND; +0.60→+0.58 EB-NeRD). Scalar remedies fail as predicted: sign flip peaks at +0.0006 over co-click on EB-NeRD but −0.0082 on MIND; every margin-loss configuration trails co-click by ≥0.006. The pre-registered edge-partitioned Anchor-B (10, 1.0, 0.0) reaches 0.3941±0.0029 on MIND (vs. co-click 0.3928) and 0.6045±0.0019 on EB-NeRD (vs. 0.6018, +0.0027 outside seed std but not claimed significant). A learnable softmax layer mixer collapses onto the un-propagated user term (even-mass >0.9996, entropy <0.005), which the authors identify as the reason all operator-level effects are small. Tested scale is standard news benchmarks (MIND, EB-NeRD), not stress-scale; baselines are current and the comparison protocol follows the rigorous re-evaluation literature. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the edge spectrum — strong vs. weak edges of a choice-derived graph encoding opposite-sign relations relative to the ranking gradient — with a supporting proposition and lemma) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the first controlled comparison showing drop-in choice-derived operators never beat co-click, and that item-graph construction moves headline metrics by less than 0.01 on impression benchmarks) plus a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the four-step pre-deployment diagnostic protocol). The edge-partitioned operator itself is a straightforward combination of known ideas (signed propagation, magnitude partitioning); the genuinely novel part is the interaction analysis between graph weight distribution and the ranking gradient, and the pre-registered, diagnosis-guided evaluation design. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a diagnosis paper: a framework-axis decomposition (Appendix B) attributing the gap to locked baselines, mixer-collapse diagnostics (Appendix C), full sweeps for both scalar remedies (Appendix D), and an alternative-framework robustness check preserving the operator hierarchy. Three random seeds with mean±std are reported for all anchor comparisons; the authors explicitly decline to claim statistical significance at this seed count. Code and trained MNL models are stated to be released upon acceptance at https://github.com/kyomusso/Edge-Spectrum-in-CF. Methodological strengths: the frozen-baseline protocol and the pre-registration of the two anchor operator configurations before multi-seed evaluation directly guard against Goodhart-style benchmark gaming. Concerns: evaluation rests entirely on two news datasets both authored/curated by the same ecosystem lineage; the three moderators (in-slate neighborhood density, MNL predictability, candidate-pool construction) co-vary and cannot be disentangled; and the headline framing depends on an exploratory 27-cell sweep (seed=1) whose best cells slightly exceed the anchors. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small theoretical component). - Practical: Yes — all operators are sparse matrix operations on item–item graphs with top-K=50 pruning, plugging into a LightGCN-style pipeline on commodity hardware; the diagnostic costs one MNL fit plus a handful of inference passes. - Efficient: The choice-model fitting and diversion-weight aggregation add a pre-processing stage, but the training cost is identical across operators; the diagnosis is explicitly cheap by design. - Effective: The evidence shows the diagnosis correctly predicts which interventions fail and succeed (4/4 pre-registered predictions on both datasets), but headline-metric gains are +0.001 to +0.003 NDCG@10 — the paper argues this smallness is itself predicted by the attenuated propagation channel, which is honest but means the deployed benefit is marginal. - Scalable: Not tested beyond MIND/EB-NeRD scale; the authors claim the diagnostic transfers to non-parametric choice models, richer utilities, KG-augmented graphs, and hard-negative sampling, but none of these transfers is evaluated. The work delivers a reusable diagnostic protocol and a small signed-propagation operator in paper form, with a GitHub repository promised upon acceptance; it stops short of a packaged library. Strengths: - The edge-spectrum formulation is a genuine conceptual contribution: it reframes the neighbor cutoff k as a semantic switch and gives a crisp, falsifiable mechanism (Proposition 1 + Lemma 1) connecting MNL diversion structure to gradient conflict — an analysis absent from the choice-modeling-to-graph-CF literature the paper surveys. - The evaluation design is exemplary for a mostly-negative-result paper: frozen baselines, pre-registered anchor configurations with K_strong located by diagnosis rather than tuning, an explicit pre-registration table (Table 7) scored 4/4, and exploratory cells clearly separated from confirmatory ones. - Honest self-accounting throughout: the authors proactively decompose the 0.04–0.08 gap to LightGCN++, discover the mixer-collapse phenomenon that attenuates all operator effects, and explicitly frame their evidence as a pattern of predicted fail/succeed orderings rather than headline gains — the diagnosis predicts its own small margins. - The structural-overlap analysis (Jaccard@50 ≤ 0.05 vs. co-click) rules out the trivial "rediscovery artifact" explanation before the structural theory is introduced. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive. They explicitly state: absolute improvements over co-click are modest by the diagnosis's own prediction; the propagation channel is attenuated (mixer collapse), constraining all operator-level effects; the three moderators of headline impact co-vary and cannot be disentangled on two datasets; Proposition 1 holds only to first order under top-K-dominance, beyond which the lift decays or reverses; the diagnostic identifies misalignment but not its magnitude; the protocol assumes positive smoothing (hard-negative sampling is proposed but not evaluated); and external validity awaits additional choice-context datasets. They also disclaim statistical significance for the Anchor-B gain at the available seed count. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The operator comparison is conducted inside a framework whose absolute quality is far below the strongest baseline (best variant trails LightGCN++ by 0.054–0.083 NDCG@10, partly from embedding dim 32 vs. 64 and 5 vs. 20 epochs). The operator-axis findings may not transfer to a framework where propagation is not attenuated — i.e., in a well-trained model, the sign mismatch could be either worse or irrelevant, and the paper cannot say which. - The EB-NeRD asymmetry (spectrum present in lift but invisible in headline NDCG) is attributed to a bundle of three confounded moderators; with only two datasets, the diagnostic's "surfaces in NDCG?" step is effectively calibrated on one positive case (MIND) and one negative case (EB-NeRD) — near-circular validation of the Step-4 criterion. - Only MNL-derived substitution is tested; the claimed generalization to non-parametric choice models, richer utility functions, and KG-augmented graphs is asserted, not demonstrated, so the practical reach of the diagnostic is unverified beyond one weight family. - The lift profile Δ_o(k) is a post-hoc measure on trained embeddings; a skeptic could ask whether it is sensitive to training stochasticity beyond the 3 seeds reported, particularly for substitution whose lift std is an order of magnitude larger than co-click's (±0.027–0.065 vs. ±0.004). - The most promising remedy the paper itself identifies — hard-negative sampling biased toward strong-edge competitors — is left entirely unimplemented, so the practical payoff of the diagnosis remains confined to a nearly-null-magnitude operator fix. Bottom Line: A practitioner building choice-aware or graph-based recommenders gains a genuinely useful pre-deployment diagnostic and a well-earned caution about drop-in choice-derived operators, but anyone seeking a method that materially improves ranking metrics should look elsewhere — this paper's own diagnosis predicts, correctly, that its gains are marginal.

Evaluating Multimodal LLMs as Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agents for Drone Control: Commanding, Approaching, Tracking and Searching (21 ▲ )

Jaewoo Park, Minyoung Lee, Sukmin Seo, Moonbin Yim, Hyunwook Yoon, Dohoon Ryu, Daehee Kim, Myungseo Song, Jihyuk Byun, Seunggyu Chang, Taeho Kil, Jiseob Kim, Bado Lee, Geewook Kim · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 2 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DroneCATS-Agent, a model-agnostic drone agent whose action space (go / rotate / think / finished) is declared solely in the prompt with no fine-tuning, and DroneCATS, a 100-episode AirSim benchmark that holds the agent fixed and varies the MLLM across approaching, tracking, searching, and four-drone commanding tasks. - Why it's important: Prior drone-LLM systems progressively strip decision-making away from the model (external detectors, verifiers, distance-threshold termination), so the field has no measurement of what MLLMs can and cannot do when the action loop is actually theirs — including at the 2B–4B scale an onboard computer can serve. - How it does it: The core move is making termination (and search and deliberation) the model's own claim: a 'finished' action is logged and scored post hoc by a verifier against a δ = 5 m, visibility-checked criterion, so success cannot be earned by drifting through the goal region or by an external oracle. - The good: The headline finding is sharply localized with decomposition data — Qwen3.5-9B enters the success radius in 90% of approaching episodes (more than any frontier model) but converts only 35% to success, and Qwen3.5-2B declares arrival at 1.28× its start distance with 0% success, isolating protocol adherence, not navigation, as the small-model bottleneck. - The missing: Everything is in simulation (AirSim with the idealized SimpleFlight controller, no PX4 or physical airframe), and per-cell sample sizes of 20 episodes give 5-point granularity with measured run-to-run standard deviations of 9–13 points, so most between-model orderings inside tiers are unresolvable. - Read it or not: Read it if you build embodied agents, drone autonomy, or MLLM evaluation harnesses — the declaration-failure finding and the criterion audit are directly actionable; skip it if you need real-hardware results or a method rather than a benchmark and diagnosis.

Problem & Motivation: MLLMs are established image/video perceivers, but embodied drone control requires closing an action loop where camera pose is the action and errors compound. Existing systems (TypeFly, PIVOT, See-Point-Fly, Fly0, OnFly) answer 'can an MLLM close the loop?' only by progressively removing model responsibility — external detectors, LiDAR planners, verifiers, threshold-based termination — and report that this works. Because these papers vary systems while holding the model fixed, the converse question — which parts of drone control actually depend on the model, especially at deployable edge scales — is unmeasured. The relevant audience is embodied-agent and robotics researchers deciding whether an MLLM can serve as the pilot itself, and edge-deployment practitioners constrained to ~2B models on aircraft-carriable compute (Cosmos3-Edge-2B serving needs 10.5 GiB and runs ~2 Hz even on an H100). Key Idea: Make the model the independent variable by putting the entire action protocol — including termination — in the model's hands. The consequential single move is the 'finished' action: prior systems decide arrival by thresholding a distance the model never sees, while here the model self-declares arrival and a verifier judges the claim post hoc. This makes 'does the model know it is done?' a measurable quantity, and makes the agent composable (a fleet commander can only delegate to drones that report their own completion). Searching (rotate) and deliberation (think, a hover that buys extended reasoning for one call) become explicit actions for the same reason — they are decisions prior scaffolds made for the model. Methodology: The pipeline is: egocentric RGB frame (1280×720, 90° FOV) + instruction + last five actions → MLLM emits exactly one JSON action → rule-based controller → flight stack. 'go' carries a 0–1000-normalized pixel and a model-estimated depth in meters; a pinhole back-projection with known intrinsics turns it into a body-frame velocity setpoint (clamped to 3 m per 2.5 s step, ≤1.2 m/s, with near-target braking bands under 5 m and 2 m). 'rotate' is a 60°/s rate command; 'think' and 'finished' hover. Tasks span two binary axes (target stationary/moving × visible/out-of-view at start) giving four cells — approaching, searching, tracking, search-and-track — each scored by one criterion: success = ∃ declaration with dist ≤ 5 m and target visible. The commanding suite adds 20 episodes at N=4 with look-alike targets distinguishable only by close-range inscription (licence plate / sign), pooling fleet declarations. Episodes run in AirSim 1.8.1 on two Unreal maps (80 single-drone episodes: 10 per map per cell; 20 commanding: 10 residential, 10 Blocks). Nine models are evaluated: GPT-5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Gemini Robotics-ER 2, Qwen3.5 at 2B/4B/9B/27B, and Cosmos3-Edge-2B. Critical design decisions: (1) declaring the action space in the prompt rather than weights — justified as the only way to make swapping the model a clean intervention, though it changes what a failure can mean; (2) counting all declarations rather than the first — well-justified by a verifier audit showing single-declaration judging would flip 95 of 182 successes; (3) an admission that the earlier criterion mixed dwell-window and distance scoring, replaced by the unified rule after auditing that trajectory-proximity credit would inflate successes by a third. Key Results: Approaching is unsolved: the best model (Gemini 3.7 Flash) succeeds in 65% of episodes (13/20), and hiding the target from the first frame drops it to 40% — no model exceeds 40% on searching. Model ordering is task-dependent: GPT-5 approaches at 60% but tracks at only 15%, where Gemini 3.7 Flash reaches 80%. The central finding: Qwen3.5-9B enters the 5 m radius in 90% of approaching episodes (versus 65–70% for frontier models) yet succeeds in 35%, declaring at 0.63× start distance; Qwen3.5-2B declares at 1.28× start distance and succeeds 0%; Cosmos3-Edge-2B never declares at all. The Qwen3.5 ladder is monotone in scale (33.8/21.3/12.5/0% averages for 27B/9B/4B/2B). Embodiment specialisation buys nothing: Gemini Robotics-ER 2 averages 47.5% versus Gemini 3.7 Flash's 57.5%, within run-to-run noise. Commanding amplifies the protocol split: Gemini 3.7 Flash wins 80% of commanding episodes while GPT-5 (60% with one drone) wins 20% and Claude Opus 5 wins 0%; small models copy a single point across all four views (Qwen3.5-9B on 70% of all-go steps, 27B on 58%, frontier models 0–1%). The 'think' action is a measured null result: steps after a think gain +0.03 m/step over matched non-think steps, and stalls break less often after a think (1/230) than after ordinary steps (103/8401). A three-flight variance audit of Gemini 3.7 Flash shows per-cell standard deviations of 1.7–2.5 successes (9–13 points), matching binomial expectation, so tier structure survives but within-tier orderings do not. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the unified declaration-anchored closed-loop protocol across four task cells plus multi-drone commanding, covering axes no prior benchmark combines — the Table 1 coverage matrix is specific and credible), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the declaration-not-navigation localization of the small-model failure, and the coordinate-copying failure mode that only exists at N=4), and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (DroneCATS-Agent). The pointing interface itself derives from See-Point-Fly (the 'go' action is acknowledged as SPF's interface), and a prompt-declared JSON action space is a known technique; what is genuinely new is the model-as-independent-variable experimental design, self-declared termination as the scored quantity, and the commanding setting — to the authors' (plausible) knowledge, no prior work evaluates one MLLM controlling several drones from multi-view observations in a closed loop. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is unusually strong for a benchmark paper: a verifier audit re-derives all verdicts offline (agreement on 720 episode-runs) and quantifies how three alternative criteria would change conclusions; a three-flight variance audit bounds sampling noise; a per-model failure taxonomy over six modes partitions all 80 episodes; a stationary probe test shows inscription reading distance (6–13 m across the roster) cannot explain commanding gaps; and a throughput-sensitivity note documents that slowed control loops depress success, with affected runs re-measured under pinned serving conditions. Decoding settings, model identifiers, prompts (verbatim), controller constants, and back-projection math are all pinned in appendices. Code is promised at github.com/naver-ai/DroneCATS (stated as 'will be available' — not verified as released). No statistical significance tests are run beyond the variance audit. Concerns: results are simulation-only (SimpleFlight, not PX4); per-cell n=20 with 5-point granularity limits resolution; the commanding suite is not a matched control against the one-drone approaching cell (adds disambiguation and swaps maps), which the authors state plainly; frontier API models and locally served models differ in decoding constraints (schema-enforced for open models, free decoding for GPT/Claude/Gemini), an asymmetry the authors argue is neutral (2 of thousands of replies failed to parse) but do not ablate. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and agent evaluated in simulation; no hardware flights). - Practical: The small-model end targets exactly the deployable regime — 2B/4B models run on a single L40S via vLLM — but the frontier results require API models no aircraft can carry. - Efficient: The agent loop runs at ~2 Hz for the smallest model on an H100 (a ceiling no aircraft has), with 0.44 s per 30-token decode; the paper itself flags that onboard rates will be lower and that success is sensitive to loop rate. - Effective: The evidence convincingly diagnoses the problem (protocol/declaration failure) in simulation, but the stated end goal — a deployable onboard model that plans persistently and knows when it is done — is measured, not achieved. - Scalable: The N=4 commanding result is a protocol split, not a scale curve; hierarchy, larger fleets, and hardware transfer are explicitly future work, and the 100-episode benchmark would need expansion for finer-grained claims. The work delivers a promised code artifact (agent, runner, benchmark specification), though no trained model weights and no dataset of demonstrations. Strengths: (1) The experimental design is the paper's real contribution: holding the agent fixed and varying the model is the clean intervention the systems literature lacks, and the three additions to SPF's interface (rotate, think, finished) are each motivated by a decision prior scaffolds made for the model. (2) The declaration finding is a genuinely non-obvious, well-supported empirical result with a counter-intuitive inversion — a 9B model out-navigating every frontier model on radius entry while losing to protocol misuse — and the OSR/SR/declaration decomposition plus Table 4 diagnostics make it auditable. (3) The criterion audit (Appendix B) is exemplary: it shows the scoring rule choice flips 95 of 182 successes, 65 of 99 tracking successes, and would inflate results by a third under proximity credit — evidence most benchmark papers never provide. (4) Honest bookkeeping throughout: binomial noise quantified, within-tier orderings explicitly flagged as unresolvable, a simulator-fault episode class identified and re-flown, and the 'think' null result reported against the community's default lever. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly that results are simulation-only (SimpleFlight, not PX4 SITL), that hierarchical commanding is unevaluated and left to future work, that the commanding columns compare settings rather than matched tasks, that sample size at N=4 gives 5-point granularity, that within-tier model orderings sit inside the noise, and that the 'think' result is step-level observation rather than a controlled ablation of the action. They also flag throughput sensitivity as an open benchmark-design problem. This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted directly and quantified rather than minimized, and the conclusion proposes concrete follow-ups (training the action space into weights, flying the loop on hardware via the offboard velocity interface, evaluating hierarchy). Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The prompt-declared-versus-weights action space confound is acknowledged rhetorically but never tested — a fine-tuned or few-shot-conditioned variant on even a handful of episodes would establish that the protocol failure is not an artifact of zero-shot prompting, which the authors' own follow-up concedes is the fix. (2) The decoding asymmetry (JSON-schema-enforced for open models, free decoding for API models) is argued away with a two-reply parse-failure count rather than ablated, and temperature 0.4 on a closed-loop control task is unexamined. (3) Success is scored against the target centre while some targets are large vehicles; the paper reports oracle/diagnostic metrics to bound this but never quantifies the centre-versus-surface discrepancy. (4) The history representation contains a rescaling inconsistency (history pixels versus 0–1000 prompt coordinates, a 1.28×/0.72× distortion per round trip) documented in Appendix A.2 but not evaluated for its effect on small models that copy coordinates. (5) One simulator (AirSim/SimpleFlight) and two maps bound external validity; the near-0% uniform failure of the two 2B models across all cells suggests the regime may be below a floor where any protocol-level comparison is meaningful, yet those zeros carry weight in the scale-ladder monotonicity claim. (6) The paper is a preprint and, unusually for a benchmark, several of its baselines are contemporaneous or future-dated systems papers whose stability is unproven. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous model-controlled evaluation of MLLMs in the drone control loop available, and its declaration-failure diagnosis is worth any embodied-agent researcher's time — but it is a diagnostic benchmark in simulation, not a deployable capability, and practitioners wanting a flying system should treat the cited scaffolds (Fly0, OnFly) as the stronger engineering reference while using DroneCATS to understand what those scaffolds are hiding.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Packora, an all-atom variational flow-matching generative model that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and unit-cell lattices for molecular crystals from molecular graphs, plus a two-track generation/ranking evaluation protocol and an ablation-backed design recipe. - Why it's important: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) determines polymorph stability for pharmaceuticals and organic electronics, where traditional search-and-DFT pipelines are expensive and prior generative models require fixed inputs (e.g., mandatory 3D conformers) and lack flexible conditioning. - How it does it: It combines a condition-only Pairmixer pair-refinement stage whose output is cached across denoising steps (20.1× wall-clock reduction in a synthetic benchmark), a DiT trunk with pair-bias attention, L1 endpoint regression under variational flow matching, conditioning dropout (template dropout p=0.5) so one model handles any subset of conformer/stereochemistry/space-group inputs, and EDM–Heun sampling. - The good: Packora-M (88M) and Packora-L (187M) achieve the highest crystal-level solve rate on all six generation benchmarks at both 30- and 1,000-candidate budgets against CLARI-M/L/H and OXtal, and recover 19/26 and 21/29 experimental forms on the FastCSP ranking benchmarks versus 16/26 and 18/29 for CLARI-H (354M). - The missing: The strongest structural baseline (CLARI) is re-evaluated under the authors' own adapted protocol, and the ranking track uses a machine-learning interatomic potential (UMA-S-1.2) rather than dispersion-corrected DFT, so end-to-end ranking claims rest on a proxy evaluator; no public code/weights URL is stated in the provided text. - Read it or not: Read it if you build generative structure-prediction models or run CSP workflows — the design-space study (architecture, training, conditioning, inference, scaling) is transferable beyond molecular crystals; skip it if you only need a physics-based CSP pipeline, since the ranking evidence is MLIP-based and small-target-count (23–29 forms).
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (77) is strong — extensive one-factor ablations, bootstrap error bars, explicit data hygiene — but is pulled down by the re-evaluated CLARI protocol, the MLIP-only ranking proxy in place of DFT, and no stated code/weights release. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (75) are solid: the cacheable condition-only Pairmixer and the balanced single/pair width-scaling Pareto result are genuine contributions, though the machinery is a competent assembly of existing components. Completeness (72) benefits from honest acknowledgment of ablation-interaction and checkpoint-selection limits, while Resilience (70) suffers because the headline ranking claims (mean rank 102→47) rest on an unvalidated MLIP evaluator. Impact (70) reflects a strong trained model family and two-track protocol but no confirmed artifact release. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*77 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*70 = 74.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners predicting crystal structures of organic, multi-component, and organometallic molecules (drug polymorphism, agrochemicals, organic electronics) need to enumerate plausible packings and rank them by energy. Traditional workflows sample conformations and packings randomly or evolutionarily, then relax and rank with DFT — expensive and coverage-limited. Recent generative models (OXtal, MolCrystalFlow, PackFlow, CLARI) accelerate generation, but differ in required inputs and chemical scope, use heterogeneous evaluation protocols and candidate budgets that make results incomparable, and none supports a single model where conformer templates, stereochemistry labels, and space-group information can each be provided or omitted at inference. The effects of core architecture, training, conditioning, inference, and scaling choices in generative molecular CSP were also poorly characterized. Key Idea: The core trick is a cacheable pairwise-reasoning architecture: because the condition-only pair representation (refined by four triangle-multiplication Pairmixer blocks) does not depend on the noisy state, it is computed once and reused across all denoising steps, so the expensive pair refinement is amortized while the cheap DiT trunk re-attends over cached pair biases at each step. A secondary enabler is conditioning with dropout (template p=0.5, stereochemistry 0.5, space group 0.9), letting one model serve any subset of available prior knowledge without collapsing when inputs are absent. The lattice is canonicalized via Niggli reduction plus Cholesky of the Gram matrix into an unconstrained 6-vector, removing basis and rotation ambiguity. Methodology: Packora formulates molecular CSP as conditional generation p(X, ℓ | G, r, Z, O) over Cartesian coordinates and a canonical lattice latent. Training uses variational flow matching (Eijkelboom et al., 2024) with a linear interpolant; the posterior is a factorized Laplace with fixed scale, reducing to an L1 loss on predicted clean endpoints with a 10:1 coordinate-to-lattice weight ratio. The pipeline: (1) embed the condition into single and pair representations; (2) refine the pair representation with four Pairmixer blocks (triangle multiplication + gated transition, no triangle attention) — cacheable since it is condition-only; (3) inject noisy coordinates (Fourier features) and lattice into the single track; (4) run a 16-block DiT trunk where the cached pair representation supplies attention biases; (5) decode centered coordinates (mean-subtracted per molecule set) and mean-pooled lattice. Sampling uses the EDM–Heun stochastic sampler with churn (ρ=7, 200 steps) with template rotation/translation augmentation. The recipe was selected via five one-factor-at-a-time ablation studies (architecture, training, conditioning, inference, scaling), each trained 300 epochs on ≤300-atom crystals and evaluated on 8,192 validation crystals at 30 candidates. Key selected decisions: post-entry (cacheable) Pairmixer placement (SolC 0.474 vs 0.479 pre-entry, but 20.1× faster sampling), Beta–uniform mixture time sampling, random crystal translation augmentation (0.466→0.486), L1 over L2 (0.486 vs 0.407), Muon over AdamW (0.486 vs 0.447), EMA 0.9999, and balanced width scaling (768, 192) for Packora-L. Two-stage curriculum (≤300 then ≤512 atoms) on 912,807 CSD-derived training structures, bf16 on eight H200s. Design decisions are generally well-justified by the ablation protocol, though interactions between choices are not tested. Key Results: Generation: on six benchmarks (OXtal Rigid/Flexible, 50 targets each; CSP5, CSP6, CSP7 with 6/5/8 targets; CSD Teaching Subset, 773 targets), Packora achieves the best SolC in 23 of 24 settings and ties on saturated CSP5. At 30 candidates, Packora-L reaches 0.795 (Rigid), 0.530 (Flexible), 0.793 (CSP5), 0.433 (CSP6), 0.238 (CSP7), 0.663 (Teaching), versus CLARI-H's 0.740/0.396/0.598/0.412/0.134/0.590; at 1,000 candidates Packora-M/L hit 0.96–1.00 on CSP5–7 and 0.895–0.900 on Teaching versus CLARI-H's 0.869. Strict 15/15-molecule matching shows relative gains up to 188% (CSP6, 30-candidate). Ranking (FastCSP-derived, 26 single-polymorph and 29 multi-polymorph forms): Packora-L recovers 19/26 and 21/29 versus 16/26 and 18/29 for CLARI-H; mean recovered rank drops from 4.25 to 2.00–2.05 (single) and from 102.17 to 47.11–54.62 (multi). Packora candidates relax faster: 50% convergence at 98 BFGS steps vs 198 for CLARI-H; total relaxation takes 8.9–11.4 h vs 16.8 h on eight H200s. Baselines CLARI-M/L/H (88/173/354M) and OXtal (90M) are current, strong competitors; FastCSP itself is excluded because its random generator uses ~53,000–300,000 raw structures per target versus Packora's 1,000. Bootstrap error bars (5,000 resamples) accompany the 30-candidate generation results. The scaling study's finding that balanced single/pair width scaling (preserving ds/dp = 4) dominates isolated scaling is a notable non-obvious result. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the cacheable post-entry Pairmixer design with flexible subset conditioning as a single model) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (balanced single/pair width scaling reaching the Pareto frontier; conditioning dropout improving even unconditioned performance) plus a benchmark contribution in the NEW EVALUATION sense via the matched two-track generation/ranking protocol. The underlying machinery — variational flow matching, DiT, triangle multiplication, EDM–Heun sampling, Muon — is a competent combination of existing components; the novelty lies in the cacheable architectural arrangement, the unified conditioning design, and the systematic evidence-backed recipe for molecular CSP, not in a new generative framework. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive: one-factor-at-a-time studies across architecture (8 configurations with parameter counts and GFLOPs), time sampling, augmentation, loss form, loss weighting, auxiliary losses, optimizer, EMA, conditioning dropout (5 inference settings), sampler/NFE, autoguidance, and width scaling (6 configurations). The 30-candidate generation results carry bootstrap standard deviations (e.g., ±0.031–0.047 on Rigid); 1,000-candidate results are exact counts. Data hygiene is explicit: test refcode families and shared molecular components (>7 heavy atoms) are excluded from training, and multi-polymorph entries appearing in the CLARI training split are removed from ranking evaluation. Reproducibility is strengthened by full hyperparameter tables, algorithmic architecture pseudocode, and a project page, but the provided text does not state a public code, data, or weight release URL. Methodological concerns: (1) CLARI checkpoints are re-evaluated under a protocol the authors adapted (OXtal collision detection and reference selection), so the headline generation comparison is not directly the baseline's native evaluation; (2) model selection uses validation SolC on the same distribution family it is evaluated against, and ablation models are selected at k=30 candidates (acknowledged); (3) ranking relies on the UMA MLIP energy proxy rather than DFT; (4) the small target counts in CSP5/6/7 (6/5/8) make those comparisons statistically fragile despite bootstrap resampling. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained generative model run on concrete CSP benchmarks, plus a downstream ranking workflow). Practical: Trained and sampled on eight NVIDIA H200s in bf16; inference is a standard flow sampler, so it runs on commercially available multi-GPU hardware, though per-target generation of 1,000 candidates is non-trivial. Efficient: The cached pair representation cuts 200-step sampling time by 20.1× relative to the uncached design (at 21.3→28.0 GiB peak memory), and Packora-L (187M) matches or beats a 354M baseline; downstream relaxation is 30–47% faster in wall-clock than CLARI-H candidates. Effective: Evidence covers generator coverage on six benchmarks and end-to-end recovery under one relaxation/ranking pipeline, but 'solves CSP' is only measured against experimental forms with an MLIP ranker — not a full DFT-grade polymorph prediction. Scalable: Not stress-tested: training tops out at 512-atom cells; larger crystals, disorder, hydrates/solvates at scale, and the scaling trajectory beyond 187M parameters are untested — only a 6-configuration width study supports the scaling claim. The paper delivers a trained model family (88M and 187M) and an evaluation protocol; no code/weights URL is stated in the provided text. Strengths: (1) The cacheable post-entry pair-refinement design is a genuine and well-motivated architectural contribution — condition-only Pairmixer caching yields a 20.1× sampling-speedup while sacrificing only 0.005 validation SolC. (2) The two-track evaluation separating generator coverage from end-to-end ranking under a fixed relaxation/ranking pipeline is a methodological improvement over prior incomparable protocols, directly following blind-test practice. (3) The design-space study converts folklore into evidence — e.g., L1 vs L2 (0.486 vs 0.407), Muon vs AdamW (0.486 vs 0.447), and the balanced-scaling Pareto result — useful to anyone building flow-based structure models. (4) Honest handling of conditioning: template dropout p=0.5 gives the best mean SolC across five inference settings (0.487 vs 0.483 and 0.264 for p=0 and 1) and even improves unconditioned performance (0.459 vs 0.442). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that one-at-a-time ablations do not capture interactions among architecture, training, conditioning, inference, and scaling choices, so the recipe is not guaranteed globally optimal; and that model selection used k=30 candidates, whereas the optimal checkpoint may depend on the generation budget, given their own evidence of a small-budget-success vs large-budget-coverage trade-off. These are stated directly and matter — a credibility positive. They do not, in the provided text, acknowledge the MLIP-only ranking pipeline, the re-evaluated CLARI protocol, or the lack of a DFT-grade end-to-end demonstration. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The ranking track's energy evaluator is UMA-S-1.2, a machine-learned potential; the classical CSP standard is dispersion-corrected DFT ranking, and polymorph energy orderings are notoriously sensitive to method — the headline ranking improvements (e.g., mean rank 102.17→47.11) are unvalidated against DFT or experiment beyond COMPACK matching. (2) CLARI baselines are re-scored under an adapted evaluator; publishing both protocols' numbers for all systems would strengthen the comparison, and OXtal results at 30 candidates are imported from its original paper rather than re-run (with a re-evaluated protocol noted as the reason, but the asymmetry remains). (3) Several ablation decisions (e.g., 10:1 loss ratio, two-stage curriculum) were tuned on validation data drawn from the same CSD distribution as the test benchmarks; generalization to genuinely novel chemotypes (large flexible molecules, salts/hydrates at scale) is not directly measured. (4) No release of code or weights is stated in the provided text, limiting reproduction of the 912k-structure training run. (5) The claim of supporting organometallics is made via training-data scope (425,795 organometallic training entries), but no benchmark isolates organometallic performance specifically — the six test sets are organic-dominated. Bottom Line: For anyone building or deploying generative CSP systems, this is the current strongest published generator with the most useful ablation evidence in the area and is worth reading closely; a physicist needing a certified polymorph ranking should still pair it with DFT-level reranking, but there is no stronger generative baseline covering the same ground.

Verb-ICL: Rethinking In-Context Learning for Structured Prediction

F Bai, H Miao, SS Batra, H Hassanzadeh, A Saeedi… · openreview.net · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VERB-ICL, a two-stage pipeline for few-shot structured prediction that selects which examples to annotate via token-level coverage maximization and then augments those annotations with LLM-generated natural-language error feedback attached to each demonstration. - Why it's important: Annotation for structured prediction (entity spans, logical forms) is expensive and task-specific, so getting more value out of a fixed labeling budget directly reduces the cost of deploying LLMs on information extraction and semantic parsing. - How it does it: It treats the unlabeled pool as one aggregate "test instance" and greedily maximizes BERTScore-Recall-style token coverage over it (reusing SET-BSR), then runs leave-one-out ICL on the selected examples and, for errors, prompts a stronger LLM to produce gold-grounded feedback delivered inline as "Notes" next to the demonstration that produced it. - The good: The evidence is layered and unusually thorough for this area — average gains of +3.9 to +4.3 points over seven baselines across six datasets and two LLMs, a four-dimension ablation of the feedback design, an error-type analysis showing both components cut structural violations (ATIS 400 vs. 491 for Random), and a contamination check using feedback models with knowledge cutoffs predating the PHEE dataset. - The missing: The scaling analysis (16→512 examples) and budget-sweep claims are run on only two of the six datasets (NCBI and ATIS), and the method assumes access to a stronger generator model (GPT-4.1) than the inference model, a dependency whose cost/benefit trade-off is only partially characterized. - Read it or not: Read it if you build few-shot IE or semantic parsing systems or work on selective annotation/active learning for ICL; skip it if you need fine-tuning-time data selection or non-structured-prediction tasks, where it is only touched in an appendix.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying LLMs on structured prediction tasks face two compounding costs: outputs are compositional at the sub-sentence level, and tasks carry human-defined conventions (entity boundary rules, logical-form syntax) that pretraining cannot supply. Under few-shot in-context learning with a fixed annotation budget, the practitioner must decide which examples to label. Prior selective-annotation methods (vote-k, IDEAL, CoverICL) build graphs over sentence-level embeddings, which capture global semantics but miss the token-level local patterns these tasks actually predict over, and they treat the LLM as a black-box predictor rather than exploiting its ability to consume natural-language guidance. The paper targets the gap: no prior work asks both which examples to annotate and what the annotation should contain. Key Idea: Reframe the annotation budget along two axes: spend it on examples that collectively maximize token-level coverage of the unlabeled pool (adapting demonstration-selection coverage to annotation selection by treating the whole pool as one aggregate test instance), and enrich each gold-labeled example with verbalized error feedback — a leave-one-out prediction error, diagnosed by an LLM against the gold label, distilled into a reusable instruction that travels with the demonstration and surfaces in future prompts exactly when that demonstration is retrieved. Methodology: Stage 1 (selection): compute contextual token embeddings for the unlabeled pool, build a global coverage matrix C ∈ R^{u×(Σd_i)} (with a top-K column heuristic, K=10, to bound memory), and run greedy submodular maximization (Nemhauser et al. constant-factor guarantee) to select M examples; annotation is simulated by revealing gold labels of selected examples. Stage 2 (feedback): for each selected example, retrieve demonstrations from the other selected examples via SET-BSR, run ICL, and for incorrect predictions prompt GPT-4.1 to emit structured-JSON feedback (error type, description, actionable rule); at test time, prompts use an "Input–Notes–Output" format with feedback inline. Inference is standard ICL with 8 retrieved demonstrations, temperature 0. Critical design decisions, each ablated: gold-grounding beats label-free self-critique (the most consistent factor: −5.0 EM on ATIS if removed); inline positioning beats a global notes block on NCBI (+3.6 F1) but is within noise on ATIS; retrieval-selected rather than all-notes delivery is cheaper and task-dependent in benefit; using all feedback unfiltered beats a strict "did it fix the original error" verification filter in 10 of 12 settings. The selection component is SET-BSR (Gupta et al., 2023) repurposed — not a new algorithm — and the feedback design is positioned against LEAP, Self-Refine, and prompt optimization along four named dimensions. Key Results: With GPT-4o-mini across six datasets (NCBI, TweetNER7, PHEE for IE; GeoQuery, ATIS, MTOP for semantic parsing) at a 64-example budget, VERB-ICL averages 56.0 versus 51.7 for the best baseline (K-Means) and 50.7 for Random; at 16 examples it averages 46.6 versus 42.8 (IDDS). Per-dataset at 64 examples: NCBI 71.3 F1, ATIS 53.0 EM, GeoQuery 56.5 EM, MTOP 36.5 EM. Selection alone (VERB-ICL w/o EF) already beats all baselines. Gains persist with Qwen2.5-7B (50.1 vs. 46.3 best baseline at 64) and GPT-5.4-mini on two datasets. Scaling to 512 examples on NCBI approaches the 5k-example full-training-set result (75.1 vs. 77.7 F1). Feedback generated by GPT-4.1 outperforms GPT-4o-mini-generated feedback on ATIS (53.0 vs. 49.7), while pre-2024-cutoff models still improve PHEE (released 2024), an anti-contamination argument. Cost: $0.033–$0.162 per run versus $0.395–$0.611 for LLM-based selection baselines on NCBI. Manual audit: 87–100% of feedback judged useful (e.g., NCBI: 74% general + 13% concrete useful, 11% misdiagnosis). Structural violations dominate errors (81–86% under Random on ATIS/MTOP) and both components reduce them. Baselines are current (CoverICL EMNLP 2024, IDEAL ICLR 2024, LDCAL 2024) and were strengthened by re-pairing them with SET-BSR retrieval. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (weakly) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel move is the reframing — attaching per-demonstration, gold-grounded verbalized error feedback generated at annotation time, which no prior selective-annotation or prompt-optimization method does in this configuration (LEAP uses zero-shot errors, global notes, no demonstrations; prompt optimizers need held-out validation sets). The selection component is a direct reuse of SET-BSR applied to a new problem (annotation rather than demonstration selection); the pipeline is a competent composition of existing pieces, and the paper's own four-dimension ablation is what substantiates that the specific configuration, not the generic idea of learning from errors, drives the gains. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Ablations isolate each feedback-design dimension with adjacent-pair comparisons; simpler-selection controls (BoW-coverage, Longest-n) rule out token-granularity-alone and length-bias explanations; three random seeds with standard deviations are reported for main tables (some appendix analyses, e.g., Tables 13–15, are single-seed, acknowledged); embedding-model choice is itself ablated over four models. Code is released at https://github.com/bflashcp3f/Verb-ICL. Concerns: annotation is simulated from fully labeled source datasets rather than real annotator workflows; MTOP test is subsampled to 1,000 instances; the manual feedback-quality audit is small for some datasets (n=38 for NCBI); and feedback generation uses GPT-4.1, a model different from and stronger than the inference model, which slightly muddies attributions. No Goodhart-style train-on-test issue is apparent, and the contamination check is a genuinely good-faith design. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL / SYSTEMS):** - Practical: Yes — runs via OpenAI API or a 7B open model plus a DeBERTa encoder; no training infrastructure required. - Efficient: Cheaper than LLM-based selection baselines ($0.033–$0.162 vs. $0.395–$0.611 on NCBI) because feedback is generated only for selected examples, not the whole pool. - Effective: Evidence supports the claim for IE and semantic parsing under ICL at ≤512-example budgets; effectiveness for real human annotation workflows is asserted by analogy, not measured. - Scalable: Only claimed and tested to 512 examples on two of six datasets; behavior at 10× budgets or on larger schemas is untested, though the token-coverage matrix is the likely memory bottleneck (mitigated by the top-K heuristic). The deliverable is a released code artifact plus a reusable design-space characterization (four feedback dimensions) for future work. Strengths: - The two-axis framing (which examples × what annotations contain) is a real conceptual contribution to selective annotation, and the paper's ablation discipline (four feedback dimensions, adjacent-pair isolation) is above the bar for this subfield. - The error-type analysis (structural vs. value violations) gives a mechanistic explanation for why the method works — both components target the dominant error class — rather than just reporting aggregate scores. - The contamination control (feedback models with pre-dataset-release cutoffs still helping on PHEE) and the verified-vs.-all-feedback finding (strict per-instance verification is counterproductive) are independently useful empirical results. - Honest negative-adjacent results are reported: feedback positioning is within noise on ATIS, feedback-selection preference is task-dependent, and misdiagnosis rates are published per dataset. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors note that verification filtering underperforms using all feedback (offering no principled filtering criterion, "better criteria may exist"), that feedback-selection and positioning choices are task-dependent rather than universally optimal, and that the structural/value error analysis is only applicable to schema-defined tasks (semantic parsing), not entity spans in IE. They do not include a dedicated limitations section; limitations emerge mainly through the ablations, which they confront directly rather than minimize — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The budget-scaling claim rests on two datasets only (NCBI, ATIS); the other four are evaluated at 16/64 examples, so "continues to gain as the budget increases" is extrapolated beyond the measured evidence for most tasks. - The gold-grounding requirement means feedback quality depends on gold labels of selected examples — fine within the annotation budget, but the paper does not test sensitivity to noisy or disagreement-prone gold labels, which is the realistic annotation regime. - All structural-error analysis and the two contamination/scale narratives use GPT-4o-mini/GPT-4.1 from one vendor; no open-weight generator above 7B is tested for feedback generation, so the finding that stronger generators help more (ATIS gap of 3.3 points) may partly reflect proprietary-model idiosyncrasies. - The fine-tuning result (Table 11) is limited to BERT-base on CoNLL03 against a single baseline, too thin to support the data-selection-for-fine-tuning extension. - Feedback usefulness is audited by the authors themselves; no inter-annotator agreement or independent raters are reported. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing few-shot IE or semantic parsing with LLMs gains concrete, well-ablated, cheap-to-adopt techniques here — inline gold-grounded error notes and token-coverage annotation selection are both individually usable — making this the strongest current reference for annotation-budget-constrained ICL on structured prediction, ahead of vote-k/IDEAL/CoverICL.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a controlled experimental framework that manipulates the base model distribution, prompt distribution, and reward granularity to empirically explain why RL post-training of LLMs succeeds or fails, resolving contradictions in the RLVR literature. - Why it's important: Recent findings (e.g., 'spurious rewards' improving math scores, claims that RL merely selects rather than creates capabilities) have confused practitioners about when to use RL post-training, which is a costly and central part of modern LLM pipelines. - How it does it: The authors artificially inject (SFT+) or suppress (SFT-) the probability of a target behavior in base models, then cross this manipulated prior against sparse binary rewards versus dense shaped rewards (Levenshtein distance, a hand-built Process Reward Model) and narrow versus broad prompt distributions with random rewards. - The good: The dense-reward result is the strongest evidence: a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model with only 3.9% prior success on AIME Problem 4 reaches 92.2% exact-match under a milestone-based PRM reward, while flat-lining at 10.2% under sparse rewards — directly refuting the 'RL can only upweight pass@k' claim in the tested setting. - The missing: All headline reasoning conclusions rest on a single AIME problem, and the dense PRM reward is an oracle built from the known ground-truth solution (five hand-specified milestones), so the practical claim that dense rewards 'unlock new behaviors' is untested where a good dense reward is not already available. - Read it or not: Worth reading for RL practitioners and researchers reasoning about RLVR mechanics who want clean causal evidence on coverage, reward density, and prompt-distribution effects; skip it if you want production-scale training results or a new algorithm.

Impact (62) is capped since the practical prescription requires exactly the oracle-quality reward the paper cannot demonstrate at scale. Problem & Motivation: Researchers and practitioners applying RL post-training to LLMs face contradictory evidence: some report that random or 'spurious' rewards improve math benchmark scores (apparently only for Qwen-family models), while others argue RLVR cannot exceed the base model's pass@k capability. Both literatures lack causal explanations because full-scale post-training conflates base model prior, prompt distribution, and reward design. The paper addresses the community of NLP researchers and engineers who must decide whether, with what reward, and on what data to run RL post-training, closing the gap between correlational reports and a mechanistic account of when RL succeeds. Key Idea: Treat the base model's prior probability of the target behavior as an experimental independent variable — by SFT-inflating (SFT+) or SFT-suppressing (SFT-) that prior — so that the 'coverage' hypothesis (RL with sparse rewards only reinforces behaviors with sufficient initial probability mass) can be tested causally rather than observationally, and so the moderating roles of reward density and prompt-distribution breadth can be separated. Methodology: The paper formulates RLVR as a finite-horizon MDP that reduces to a contextual bandit (sequence-level verifiable reward) with a KL-constrained objective U(π) = E[1/c · r(x,y) − D_KL(π‖π_ref)]. Phase 1 uses two tasks: (a) generating a fixed target movie quote from the Cornell Movie-Dialogs Corpus, and (b) solving AIME 2025 Problem 4 (answer 117). Base models (OLMo 3, Qwen2-7B, Qwen3-1.7B/8B, Qwen2-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) are manipulated into Base / SFT+ (prior inflated, e.g., quote produced 42.8% for Qwen3-8B) / SFT- (prior driven to 0.00%) variants, then trained with either a sparse binary verifier (with anti-rambling length penalty) or dense rewards: Levenshtein edit distance for the string task, and a 5-milestone LLM-as-a-judge PRM (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) with exponentially increasing milestone weights [0.05, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25], a 0.6 near-miss override, loop penalty (−0.3), and formatting penalty (−0.5). Phase 2 trains Qwen2.5-Math-7B and OLMo 3 (Base/SFT/DPO checkpoints) with uniformly random rewards from [0,1] on either a narrow prompt distribution (100 math prompts from DeepScaleR) or a broad one (10k prompts from WildChat / OLMo 3 RLVR mix, run across three 8×H100 nodes, 8 samples per prompt), tracking per-token entropy and log-likelihood on fixed in-distribution and held-out prompts every 50 steps, plus GSM8K, MMLU, IFEval. Critical design decisions: (1) SFT± as the prior-manipulation instrument — well-justified and clean; (2) the exponential PRM reward curve to avoid local minima from linear partial credit — reasonable but oracle-designed; (3) excluding RL algorithmic variation from scope by fixing one algorithm — justified by citing existing algorithm-comparison work, but it leaves hyperparameter sensitivity unexamined. Key Results: Under sparse rewards, post-RL success tracks the pre-RL prior almost perfectly: Qwen3-8B SFT+ (42.8% prior) reaches 100.0% on the quote task while its Base and SFT- variants (0.00% prior) stay at 0.00%; Qwen2-7B Base (3.52% prior) converges to 99.9% only after a ~40-step exploration plateau; Qwen3-1.7B Base (0.48% prior) reaches only 10.0%. On AIME Problem 4 (128-sample eval), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Base goes from 3.92% to 10.2% under sparse reward but 92.2% under the dense PRM reward, slightly exceeding the SFT+ model's 85.9%; the SFT- model reaches 0% exact match but its dense average reward climbs to ~0.6, showing partial milestone learning. For spurious rewards, narrow-D training on Qwen replicates the improvement from Shao et al. (2025), whereas broad-D training spikes entropy and degrades benchmarks; on OLMo 3, narrow-D training with random rewards collapses GSM8K from 86% to ~32% by step 400 while MMLU (~65%→62%) and IFEval (~79%→77%) are preserved — domain-targeted corruption, not global unlearning — whereas broad-D causes global entropy increase and simultaneous collapse of all three benchmarks. Baselines are the same base models under differing conditions rather than competing methods; scale is standard (1.5B–8B models, single-problem reasoning), and the dense-reward result (dense beating sparse exactly where the prior is low) is the counter-intuitive headline finding. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with elements of a controlled diagnostic methodology (new experimental formulation). The genuinely novel contribution is the causal manipulation of base-model coverage (SFT+/SFT-) combined with reward-density and prompt-distribution controls, which reconciles the 'spurious rewards' and 'pass@k ceiling' findings into one framework. The individual mechanisms — KL-constrained RLVR, coverage intuition, reward shaping, entropy tracking — are all standard classical-RL and recent-LLM ideas applied to a new diagnostic setting; the PRM design and Levenshtein reward are competent engineering, not conceptual advances. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are effectively the core design — every factor (prior, reward type, prompt breadth) is systematically varied, which is stronger than post-hoc ablation. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; evaluations use 10,000 samples (quote task) and 128 samples (AIME), where 128 samples on a single problem gives coarse resolution (~±3% binomial noise). Code (github.com/sankarh-1/demystifying-rl-finetuning) and a project website are released, and full hardware/algorithm details are in appendices, aiding reproduction. Methodological concerns: (1) the dense PRM is an oracle constructed from the known solution's milestones — it evaluates whether a good dense reward suffices, not whether such rewards can be obtained in practice (the PRM literature cited shows mixed real-world results); (2) all reasoning conclusions derive from one AIME problem, risking overfitting the narrative to a single instance; (3) 'LLMs were used in development of the code base' is disclosed; (4) evaluation on the authors' own manipulated setups is appropriate here since the goal is mechanism isolation, not benchmark SOTA. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (controlled diagnostic experiments, no deployed system). Practical: Yes — experiments run on single A100 80GB or L40s 48GB GPUs (plus 3×8×H100 nodes for the OLMo prompt-distribution experiments), within reach of academic labs. Efficient: The sparse-reward and string experiments are cheap; the PRM requires a 32B judge model and the broad-D runs use 24 H100s, so dense-reward RLVR at scale inherits the known cost of LLM-judge scoring. Effective: The evidence shows the mechanisms operate as claimed in the sandbox and on one math problem, but the practical prescription — 'get a dense and correct reward' — is exactly the hard part in real domains, so effectiveness on the actual practitioner problem is only a proxy. Scalable: Not tested — all models are ≤8B (plus a 32B judge) and the reasoning task is a single problem; the authors claim relevance to full-scale post-training but present no 10×–100× evidence. Deliverable: paper plus released code and evaluation pipeline; no trained models or benchmark dataset released as artifacts. Strengths: - The SFT+/SFT- prior-manipulation design converts the coverage hypothesis from an unfalsifiable narrative into a causal experiment with exact probability measurements (10,000-sample evals), which no prior RLVR analysis does directly. - The dense-versus-sparse crossover result (dense reward on Base at 92.2% vs. sparse at 10.2%, with SFT+ at 85.9%) is a clean, quantitative refutation of the 'RL only selects pass@k behaviors' claim within the tested setting, and the qualitative finding that the Base model composed novel solution paths supports a genuine capability-formation reading. - The prompt-distribution experiments cleanly decompose the spurious-rewards phenomenon: narrow-D sharpens the prior (improving Qwen, corrupting OLMo's math domain), broad-D causes global entropy-driven unlearning — a useful unification backed by entropy/likelihood trajectories rather than benchmark scores alone. - Honest scoping: the paper explicitly excludes RL algorithmic variation and flags that some conclusions 'may seem obvious' to RL experts, positioning itself correctly as a controlled primer. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge the simplified toy setting ('Although simplified, this setup enables precise analysis...'), that conclusions may be obvious to RL-literate readers, that PRMs have shown mixed results in prior literature (their single-problem setup is 'idealized'), and that spurious-reward gains hold only in 'a restricted setting that does not apply to most of RL post-training.' They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive — though they do not quantify how far the sandbox results transfer to production-scale RLHF/RLVR. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-instance reasoning evaluation: every reasoning conclusion rests on one AIME problem; coverage, threshold effects (e.g., Qwen2-7B's 3.5% prior succeeding after 40 steps), and the dense-reward crossover should be validated across a problem suite before generalizing to 'RLVR' broadly. - The oracle PRM conflates two claims: 'dense rewards can unlock new behaviors' and 'we can build accurate dense rewards.' The paper shows only the first; the second is the practical bottleneck and is assumed. - No seeds, error bars, or sensitivity analysis for the RL hyperparameters (the paper deliberately fixes one algorithm, but prior vs. reward interactions could be KL-coefficient-dependent, and the KL term appears in the objective without reporting the chosen c). - The spurious-rewards experiments use different model families for different roles (Qwen for replication, OLMo for the base/SFT/DPO progression) rather than crossing both factors fully, leaving the model-family × prompt-distribution grid incomplete. - The 128-sample AIME evaluation makes the Base-vs-SFT+ dense comparison (92.2% vs 85.9%) statistically fragile, yet the paper reads it as dense 'slightly outperforming' sparse-trained SFT+. Bottom Line: A rigorous, unusually well-controlled diagnostic study that every RLVR researcher should read for its causal evidence on coverage, reward density, and prompt-distribution effects — but practitioners should treat its dense-reward prescription as conditional on being able to construct an oracle-quality reward, which the paper does not and cannot yet demonstrate at scale.

EDGE: Experience-Distillation for Guided Exploration in Agentic Reinforcement Learning

C Xie, Y Zhou, W Yang, S Song, Y Deng, S Ren… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EDGE, a GRPO-based agentic RL framework that treats retrieved experience as a temporary training-time scaffold — estimating each experience's marginal gain from paired rollouts, distilling only beneficial scaffold behavior into the policy via gated reverse-KL, and co-evolving the experience bank — so the deployed agent needs no retrieval at inference time. - Why it's important: Experience-augmented agents either carry a persistent retrieval dependency and token overhead at deployment, or suffer negative transfer when unfiltered experience is injected; naive memory augmentation (EvolveR, GRPO+Mem0) actually degrades below vanilla GRPO, so the training-vs-deployment tradeoff of experience reuse is a real, costly problem. - How it does it: Each GRPO rollout group is split G/2 experience-conditioned (teacher context) vs G/2 experience-free (student context); the success-rate gap Δe gates a reverse-KL distillation loss computed on the student's own trajectories, and an EMA utility score drives experience pruning while a reflector LLM synthesizes new experiences from failed/successful trajectory contrasts. - The good: Ablations on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B show the gain gate is the load-bearing component — removing it drops success to 72.3%, 9.8 points below vanilla GRPO — directly demonstrating that unvalidated experience injection is actively harmful, and retention without scaffolds reaches 96.0% vs 82.9% (SkillRL) and 92.3% (EMPO2). - The missing: The core marginal-gain estimate uses only K=4 rollouts per condition (group size 8), so gating decisions rest on a high-variance binary-reward difference whose reliability under this noise is analyzed theoretically (Hoeffding bound) but never validated empirically; ablations are also confined to a single environment and model scale. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building experience/memory-augmented LLM agents or working on agentic RL exploration — the scaffold-to-parameter framing and the gating ablation are genuinely instructive — but skip if you only need another RL benchmark increment.
