#36 — Innovative (73)

Learning from the Test : Self-Referential Differential Testing for Deep RL Agents

J He, J Shi, Z Yang, M Cheng, D Lo · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Delta, a two-phase testing framework that detects both safety-critical failures and policy-optimality bugs in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents by training a "challenger" agent with offline RL on the trajectories logged during safety fuzzing and using it as a differential oracle. - Why it's important: Existing DRL testing detects crashes but not suboptimal decisions, which cause economic loss and can escalate into safety hazards, and optimality has no ground-truth oracle in complex environments — this is the first automated approach to that oracle problem. - How it does it: The core trick is self-referential differential testing: the AUT's own fuzzing logs (diverse edge cases plus successes and failures) are reused as an offline RL dataset to train a challenger that can be beaten only by improving on the AUT, so any initial state where the challenger earns higher cumulative reward is a concrete optimality bug. - The good: Across five environments, Delta's BCQ-based challengers found an average of 2,517.9 optimality bugs per environment — 50.2% more than the best of three strong safety-testing baselines adapted to the same oracle — with the largest gaps in distinct bugs (e.g., 467.4 vs. 93.2 in Acrobot, +401.5%), and the found bugs translated into measurable AUT repair (+12% reward on Walker2D, up to 100% safety-failure reduction). - The missing: Evaluation is confined to low-dimensional Gymnasium/MuJoCo control tasks with one well-trained AUT per environment and a deterministic-oracle assumption; bug counts at initial-state granularity run into the thousands in two hours, so the practical severity and non-redundancy of these "bugs" remain unvalidated by developers or downstream users. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on testing or quality assurance of RL-based software — it is the first concrete, replicated treatment of the optimality-oracle problem and ships a replication package; skip it if you need evidence beyond standard control benchmarks, since the authors themselves defer autonomous-driving-scale validation to future work.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is the strength — the self-referential oracle reframing of the optimality-oracle problem is a genuinely new problem-plus-method contribution, and reusing safety-fuzzing logs as offline-RL data is non-obvious (Non-Obviousness 78). Rigor (74) is solid for the genre (75 challengers, CIs, Mann-Whitney U, ablations, public replication package) but is pulled down by adapted baselines that conflate oracle with search, unvalidated bug severity at δ=0, and no false-positive audit. Completeness (76) benefits from unusually candid limitation acknowledgment; Resilience (68) drops for extrapolation to high-dimensional MDPs with states ≤17 dims tested. Impact (60) reflects a Figshare replication package rather than a packaged tool. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*74 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*76 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*60 = 73.
empirical Novelty 78 Rigor 74 Non-Obv 78 Completeness 76 Resilience 68 Impact 60
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: DRL agents are increasingly deployed in healthcare, autonomous driving, and robotics, but the testing literature focuses almost entirely on safety-critical failures (crashes, constraint violations). Suboptimal policies — e.g., a robot arm wasting energy or a delivery robot picking congested routes — reduce efficiency and trust, and can escalate into safety hazards. Detecting suboptimality faces a testing-oracle problem: in complex MDPs the true optimal policy (maximum cumulative reward) is unknown or intractable, and manual expert assessment cannot scale across the vast initial-state space. Re-training multiple candidate agents for differential comparison is also prohibitive because training high-performing DRL policies can take weeks and billions of environment interactions. The affected community is software-engineering and ML-testing researchers plus practitioners deploying DRL systems; no prior work directly targets automated optimality testing without domain-specific metamorphic relations (e.g., Decictor requires known optimal paths). Key Idea: Reuse the safety-fuzzing logs of the agent under test (AUT) as a free, high-quality offline RL dataset: because the AUT is (by assumption) a well-trained policy and fuzzing deliberately drives it through rare edge cases, behavior cloning or conservative offline RL on those trajectories yields a "challenger" agent that is competent but not identical to the AUT. The challenger then serves as a self-referential oracle: if from the same initial state it achieves higher cumulative reward than the AUT, that state is a demonstrable optimality bug — no ground-truth optimum needed. A challenger that never wins the differential is evidence the AUT is near-optimal, so the oracle is informative in both outcomes. Methodology: Delta has two phases. (1) Safety testing adopts CureFuzz (black-box fuzzing with a Random-Network-Distillation curiosity mechanism and multi-objective seed selection) — the authors explicitly do not propose a new safety method; every trajectory (s,a,r,s′ tuples) executed during fuzzing is logged into a static dataset D. (2) Optimality testing trains challenger agents on D with one of three offline RL algorithms — BC (behavior cloning), BCQ (batch-constrained Q-learning), or CQL (conservative Q-learning) — then runs differential fuzzing: seeds are initial states sampled uniformly, mutated by small perturbations; a seed's "energy" E(σ)=α·Diversity+β·Regret+λ·(1−Inconsistency) prioritizes mutation, where Diversity is the RND prediction error ‖T(s)−P(s)‖² averaged over the trajectory, Regret is A(σ)=exp(R_challenger−R_AUT) (flagging a bug when A>1, i.e., R_ca > R_AUT + δ with δ=0 in all experiments), and Inconsistency is LSH-based trajectory overlap between the two agents. Seeds are admitted to the corpus via dynamic thresholds (above-average diversity, regret>1, or below-average inconsistency), and the loop runs on a two-hour budget. The framework assumes black-box access, deterministic AUT policies, and deterministic environment dynamics (a Mann-Whitney-U-based statistical oracle over N=5 rollouts is added as an extension for stochastic environments). Key design decisions: reusing safety-testing data rather than collecting a dedicated dataset (justified on cost grounds), the exponential regret shaping to prefer clear challenger wins over uniformly hard scenarios, and dynamic rather than fixed thresholds — the first two are argued persuasively, the energy weights α, β, λ are not individually ablated. Key Results: Tested on CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot (discrete, DDQN AUTs) and Hopper, Walker2D (continuous, SAC AUTs), all near-saturated (e.g., CartPole 495.7±6.8, 97% success rate). RQ1: BCQ challengers detected the most optimality bugs in every environment (e.g., 3,752.0±649.9 in MountainCar vs. 1,243.2 for BC and 2,144.0 for CQL), averaging 2,517.9 bugs/environment; challengers trained offline in minutes versus hours-to-days for the AUTs; notably CQL challengers with the highest rewards were not the best bug finders. RQ2: Against MDPFuzz, CureFuzz, and GMT (all given the same BCQ challenger and 2-hour budget, 5 runs each), Delta found on average 50.2% more total bugs and the most distinct bugs everywhere — 467.4 vs. 93.2 in Acrobot (+401.5%) and 1,648.8 vs. 769.2 in Hopper (+114.4%) — with Mann-Whitney U significance and Cohen's d effect sizes; it lost the Distance (bug-spread) metric only in CartPole (0.071 vs. GMT's 0.084). RQ3 ablations: removing Regret causes the largest drop in total bugs (5,450.0→2,238.4 in Acrobot, −59%); removing Diversity halves distinct bugs in CartPole (81.0→39.4). RQ4: fine-tuning the AUT on challenger-superior trajectories with CQL raised mean reward in all five environments (Walker2D 3,925.5→4,399.3, +12%; CartPole hit the 500 maximum) and reduced known safety failures by 74.1–100%; an independent CureFuzz re-campaign confirmed robustness gains (e.g., CartPole 0 failures; Acrobot 1,183.6→265). Stochastic extension (Hopper-Noise with wind): Delta 87.8 bugs vs. 32.4 for the best baseline (+171%). Scale is standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale; baselines are current state-of-the-art DRL testers from 2022–2024. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM + NEW METHOD (with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component). The genuinely novel move is the self-referential oracle — converting safety-fuzzing logs into an offline-RL challenger that operationalizes differential testing for the optimality-oracle problem, which no prior DRL-testing work addresses. The surrounding machinery is a competent recombination of established components: CureFuzz (the authors' own prior work) for phase 1, standard offline RL (BC/BCQ/CQL), RND-based novelty, LSH overlap, and energy-guided fuzzing in the style of prior fuzzers; the claimed insight that safety-testing data doubles as offline-RL training data is the non-obvious part, and the observation that highest-reward challengers are not the best bug finders is a genuine empirical finding. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for the genre. Five independent runs per configuration (75 challengers total), 95% confidence intervals throughout, Mann-Whitney U tests with Cohen's d for the main comparison, an ablation isolating each energy term (though not the weights α, β, λ), a utility study (RQ4) showing the bugs are actionable, a behavioral-clustering analysis complementing initial-state bug counts, and a stochastic-environment extension. A replication package (source code, datasets, results) is released at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29196884.v1. Concerns: baselines were given Delta's oracle and challenger rather than compared in their native settings, so the delta may conflate the oracle with the energy-guided search; bug counting at initial-state granularity (5-interval grids, 100 for MountainCar) inflates counts into thousands and is only partially mitigated by the distinct-bug and clustering analyses; the authors evaluate on their own framework's metrics, and there is no false-positive audit of flagged bugs (e.g., wins attributable to challenger luck under δ=0). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a testing pipeline run by the authors, producing a tool). Practical: Yes — implemented in Python 3.9 on a single server with an AMD EPYC 7643 and RTX A5000 GPUs, using open-source d3rlpy/Gymnasium/MuJoCo. Efficient: Challenger training is markedly cheaper than AUT training (e.g., minutes vs. tens-to-hundreds of minutes per Figure 4), and the dataset collection is a zero-cost byproduct of mandatory safety testing, though the paper's efficiency accounting excludes that collection time. Effective: The evidence shows the oracle detects reproducible suboptimal initial states and that fixing them raises reward and robustness on the same benchmarks — effectiveness at real-world optimality assurance is still a proxy, since no deployed system or human validation is involved. Scalable: Untested beyond two-hour campaigns on low-dimensional environments; the authors claim applicability to more complex domains but present no experiment there, and challenger quality is explicitly bounded by safety-testing coverage. Deliverable: a public replication package (code, datasets, results) on Figshare; not a packaged library or trained-model release. Strengths: - The self-referential oracle cleanly sidesteps the optimality-oracle problem with a mechanism that yields information in both outcomes (challenger wins ⇒ bug; challenger loses ⇒ evidence of near-optimality) — a genuinely new framing in DRL testing. - Turning the otherwise-discarded safety-fuzzing logs into offline-RL training data is a clever, zero-marginal-cost reuse that also makes Delta composable with any safety tester, not just CureFuzz. - The evaluation closes the loop: bugs are not just counted but consumed (CQL fine-tuning on challenger-superior trajectories) to show +12% reward on Walker2D and 74–100% safety-failure reductions, independently re-verified by a fresh CureFuzz campaign. - Honest construct-validity discussion: the authors explicitly frame reported bug counts as a "sound-but-not-complete lower bound" and add behavioral clustering to compensate for the granularity of initial-state counting. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations unusually directly: (1) the challenger can only be as good as the safety-testing dataset — under-exploration causes false negatives, so bug counts are a lower bound, and Delta presumes already-thorough safety testing (§6.3, §7); (2) the oracle depends on the reward function as the reference objective, with reward design declared orthogonal; (3) the main results assume deterministic policies and dynamics, addressed only via the Hopper-Noise statistical extension; (4) evaluation is limited to benchmark control tasks, with real-world domains (autonomous driving) deferred to future work; (5) initial-state bug counting may not reflect behavioral diversity (mitigated by clustering); (6) efficiency figures exclude data-collection time, justified as a byproduct of mandatory safety testing. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Bug severity and deduplication are unvalidated: thousands of "bugs" in a two-hour campaign on near-saturated agents suggests many flagged states differ only marginally in reward (δ=0), and no human study or cost model establishes which of these matter economically — the motivating pain point (energy waste, economic loss) is never measured directly. - The baseline comparison gives MDPFuzz/CureFuzz/GMT Delta's challenger-oracle but keeps their own seed-selection heuristics, so the reported +50.2% conflates the new oracle with Delta's regret/inconsistency-guided search; an oracle-controlled ablation pairing each baseline's search with a random oracle is absent. - Only one AUT per environment (DDQN or SAC), trained to near-saturation; the framework's behavior on weak, mid-training, or diverse-policy AUTs — where differential outcomes would differ most — is unexplored, as is sensitivity to the unfixed energy weights α, β, λ. - There is no false-positive analysis of the differential oracle itself: with δ=0 and single rollouts in the deterministic setting, small numerical or initialization asymmetries between AUT and challenger evaluations could contribute wins; the statistical oracle is only exercised in one noisy environment. - All five environments have state dimensions ≤ 17; the claim of applicability to high-dimensional, image-based, or real-world MDPs (where LSH on raw states and RND novelty behave differently) is extrapolation beyond the evidence. Bottom Line: For researchers and practitioners building DRL testing infrastructure, this is the first substantive and honestly evaluated attack on the optimality-oracle problem and is worth reading for the self-referential-oracle idea alone, but its benchmark-scale evidence and unvalidated bug severity mean it complements rather than replaces deeper domain-specific evaluation.

Super Library Agent: Joint Generation and Maintenance of Multiple Applications Beyond the Single Codebase (24 ▲ )

Daegyu Sung, Yukyeong Lee, Geon Park, Yumin Choi, Sung Ju Hwang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 1 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Super Library Agent (SLA) problem — an LLM agent that sequentially generates a portfolio of related applications while maintaining a shared library of reusable components — and builds SLA-FULL, a scaffold with index-based candidate extraction and call-graph-conditioned migration that reduces portfolio LOC by 5–9% and verbosity by up to 38% without hurting functionality. - Why it's important: LLM coding agents deployed organizationally generate portfolios of near-duplicate applications whose shared logic drifts apart, and agentic maintenance accumulates verbosity, dead code, and structural erosion; a cross-application shared library directly targets this duplication and makes cross-application policy changes cheaper (patch size 256 vs. 936 added LOC vs. zero-shot). - How it does it: The core move is to summarize every AST-delimited code chunk in one-line natural language, have an LLM selector propose explicit cross-application extraction/migration candidates over these summaries, then hand each migration agent a structured extraction trace plus a caller/callee call-graph neighborhood so dependency edits propagate correctly. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough for an agent paper — three trials per suite, per-suite breakdowns, paired t-tests with bootstrap CIs, an ablation of every major component, a second backbone (minimax-m3), a low-reuse stress suite, and a maintenance-round experiment — and the maintainability gains (e.g., Verbosity 0.1603→0.0994 on WebGen-Bench) are statistically significant. - The missing: The inference cost is severe — 8.3× zero-shot LLM spend on WebGen-Bench (3.1× on PaperBench) — and the paper's functionality gains are never statistically significant, so the method buys maintainability at a large compute premium on benchmarks adapted (not designed) for this setting. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building multi-repo or long-horizon coding agents, since the problem formulation and failure analysis (extraction recall, migration correctness) are genuinely new; practitioners seeking cheap maintainability wins can skip it given the 3–8× cost overhead.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is driven up by Novelty (78, a genuinely new problem formulation — online cross-application library learning — plus the valuable negative result that naive extraction worsens erosion) and Completeness (76, with direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure and released code), but pulled down by Rigor (72, reduced for the preprint status, LLM-judge/backbone model overlap, an unexplained null on the inherited MDL metric, and benchmarks adapted rather than built for the setting) and Impact (58, since 3–8× inference overhead on synthetic portfolios limits near-term adoption despite the MIT-licensed artifact). Resilience (73) is solid — claims are well-bounded and the functionality null is honestly reported. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*76 + 0.15*73 + 0.10*58 ≈ 73.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations maintain portfolios of related, independently deployable applications that share domain logic, UI patterns, and operational conventions. When LLM coding agents generate each application independently, shared logic is duplicated, and prolonged agentic maintenance accumulates "slop" — functionally correct but verbose, structurally eroded code (as documented by SlopCodeBench). Prior library-learning work (DreamCoder, Stitch, LILO, Librarian) operates post-hoc on a single codebase or fixed corpus; Librarian's authors explicitly leave multi-repo library creation as open. The gap is an online setting: applications arrive sequentially, the shared library is consumed during generation, and updated abstractions must be migrated back into previously generated codebases. Key Idea: Match code by what it does, not how it is written — replace implicit, surface-similarity-based reuse discovery with LLM candidate selection over natural-language chunk summaries, and make migration safe by passing extraction traces (which symbol came from where, why it generalizes, how to replace it) plus explicit call-graph caller/callee context to a dedicated migration agent. This decomposes one fragile joint task into extraction and migration with an explicit structured hand-off. Methodology: The setting is formalized as: given requests x1..xN and empty library L0, at step t the agent produces a new codebase, an updated library, and patched previous codebases, optimizing a Pareto trade-off between functionality and joint maintainability; the ideal library contains every component used by ≥2 applications. SLA-FULL runs per round: (1) a coding agent generates codebases reusing the current library; (2) an indexer builds NL-summary entries for AST chunks (cocoindex-code, gpt-5.4-nano summaries); (3) intra-codebase consolidation removes local duplication before cross-app extraction; (4) a library-extraction agent (deepseek-v4-flash) selects cross-app candidates from summaries and extracts parameterized components; (5) per-application dependency-migration agents receive extraction traces and an "also-refactor" list of import/caller/callee files and rewrite code to consume the library. No explicit loss function; MDL (negative log-probability under Qwen-2.5-7B, dependency-aware variant) is used as an evaluation metric, not an objective. Critical design decisions: NL-summary-based candidate selection (justified by ablation — beats Ward clustering and no-candidates on 4/5 maintainability metrics, though it initially drops accuracy from 76.95 to 72.95, which call-graph conditioning recovers); splitting extraction and migration into separate agents (justified by the naive single-agent baseline's erosion increase, e.g., 0.1567 vs. 0.0987); and prompt-only enforcement of the constraint that the library never imports from applications (asserted, not verified with static checks). Key Results: On WebGen-Bench (3 disjoint 8-task suites × 3 trials) SLA-FULL achieves accuracy 77.21 vs. 76.04 zero-shot (not significant), LOC 8552 vs. 9393 (−9.0%), tokens 65633 vs. 70364 (−6.7%), Erosion 0.0987 vs. 0.1032, and Verbosity 0.0994 vs. 0.1603 (−38%); on PaperBench (5 suites of 4 papers × 3 trials), Code-Dev Score 0.4809 vs. 0.4687 with lowest values on all five maintainability metrics. Against LIBRARIAN (post-hoc library construction, K=8), SLA-FULL significantly reduces Erosion and Verbosity on WebGen and tokens/Verbosity on PaperBench; naive SLA variants increase Erosion (up to 0.1567), showing unguided extraction concentrates complexity. Maintenance under shared policy updates: SLA-FULL needs 256 added LOC vs. 936 for zero-shot. Library utilization: 13.3 exported components vs. 4.2 (LIBRARIAN), with more behavioral hooks and domain-level abstractions. Backbone transfer with minimax-m3 holds. Cost: 8.3× zero-shot spend on WebGen, reducible to 4.9× with fewer migration rounds at a quality cost (accuracy −2.8 points, Verbosity +11%); session reuse saves 11.7% cost only with prompt caching. In the low-reuse N=16 stress suite, SLA-FULL still has the best size metrics but accuracy falls below zero-shot (65.88 vs. 69.02). Baselines are current and reasonably strong (LIBRARIAN, OpenHands, Claude Code as scaffolds), though all use the same deepseek-v4-flash backbone. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (online, cross-application library learning during sequential portfolio generation) plus NEW METHOD (candidate-guided extraction over NL chunk summaries and trace/call-graph-conditioned migration). The individual techniques — LLM summarization, retrieval-style candidate selection, call-graph analysis (Ryder 1979), MDL-based evaluation — are standard; the novelty lies in the problem formulation, the decomposition into extraction/migration agents with a structured trace hand-off, and the empirical demonstration that naive library construction actively worsens structural erosion. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (candidate selection method, pre-extraction consolidation, call-graph conditioning each isolated, with each component shown to matter). Three trials per suite with mean ± std, paired t-tests with bootstrap 95% CIs over task-level pairings (n=24 WebGen, n=20 PaperBench), and honest reporting that functionality differences are never significant. Code, prompts, per-run export inventories, and generated portfolios are released (https://github.com/sbigstar0310/super-library-agent, MIT). Concerns: (1) heavy reliance on LLM-judge metrics (Appearance score, PaperBench Code-Dev Score) with the judge (deepseek-v4-flash) being the same model family as the backbone; (2) the MDL metric barely improves and is sometimes worse than zero-shot for the authors' own method (34195 vs. 34875, not significant), which the authors attribute to the reference model's training data rather than investigating further; (3) benchmarks were adapted into suites rather than designed for this setting — the authors acknowledge this. Note this is a preprint (arXiv, 2026 dating) with future-dated model/citation names; results should be treated as unreviewed. Deployability: (EMPIRICAL profile):** - Practical: Runs on hosted LLM APIs (deepseek-v4-flash, gpt-5-mini, Claude) plus standard agent harnesses — no exotic hardware required. - Efficient: Poor — 8.3× zero-shot LLM spend on WebGen-Bench and 3.1× on PaperBench; the paper's own cost-reduction strategies only partially mitigate this (4.9× at best, with quality loss). - Effective: Effective on maintainability proxies (LOC, tokens, Verbosity, Erosion, patch size) at preserved functionality, but the headline goal — sustainably maintainable codebases — is only proxied by one maintenance round on synthetic benchmark applications. - Scalable: Untested beyond N=8 (one stress test at N=16); the authors only claim, and the cost model suggests, that migration overhead grows with portfolio size, so 10–100× portfolios are extrapolation. Delivers a software artifact: released code, prompts, evaluation files, and generated portfolios under MIT license; no trained model. Strengths: - Genuinely new problem formulation: online, cross-application library construction with migration back into prior codebases, with a precise formal definition and a failure-mode analysis (extraction recall, migration correctness) that predicts the observed erosion increase in naive baselines. - The negative result for naive library construction is valuable: unguided extraction raises Erosion (0.1567 vs. 0.1032 zero-shot), demonstrating that a shared library alone is insufficient — an insight competitors would likely miss. - Exceptional evaluation hygiene for an agentic systems paper: per-suite breakdowns, significance testing with CIs, component-level ablations, backbone transfer, scaffold comparisons (OpenHands, Claude Code), a deliberately low-reuse stress suite, and transparent cost accounting including the prompt-caching dependency of their own cost saving. - The maintenance experiment (shared policy patch across the portfolio, 256 vs. 936 added LOC) directly measures the benefit that motivates the formulation rather than only static code metrics. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: no SLA-native benchmarks exist (suites were adapted from single-task benchmarks); applications are benchmark artifacts with no users, commit history, or production constraints, so patch-size reductions are untested on real software; only one maintenance round is measured, so error compounding and library degradation under requirement drift are unobserved; maintainability metrics are proxies that do not measure whether code is actually easier to modify; and the ethical section candidly notes that a faulty library edit propagates to every dependent application at once. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No static verification of migration correctness: the paper reports accuracy/test outcomes but never checks for dangling references, unused exports, or import consistency programmatically, despite these being the stated failure modes; exports with 0% reuse appear in their own inventories (e.g., loadSubmissions, removeFromStorage), indicating dead library code the metrics partially miss. - The library-imports-nothing constraint is prompt-enforced only; no analysis of what happens when an LLM violates it. - Functionality deltas across all methods are statistically indistinguishable, so the paper effectively demonstrates a maintainability-only contribution; the abstract's framing of "preserving functionality" slightly overstates a null result. - MDL — the metric inherited from the closest prior work (Librarian) — shows no significant improvement for SLA-FULL, and the explanation (reference-model training data quality) is speculative and unexamined. - Erosion results on WebGen Suite 3 (0.2185 for SLA-FULL vs. 0.2167 zero-shot) suggest the Erosion improvement is driven by one or two suites; per-suite variance is large relative to the aggregate effect. - Judge-model overlap: the PaperBench evaluator and the backbone are both deepseek-v4-flash, a potential self-evaluation bias not discussed. - Cost analysis stops at LLM spend; wall-clock time, latency, and human review burden for the automated rewrites of deployed-adjacent code are unaddressed. Bottom Line: A rigorous and honestly reported paper that convincingly establishes a new problem — online cross-codebase library learning for coding agents — and shows real maintainability gains, but its 3–8× inference cost and synthetic-benchmark evaluation mean practitioners should read it for the formulation and failure analysis rather than adopt the scaffold today; researchers working on long-horizon or multi-repo agentic software engineering should read it now.

RecurSE: Bounded Recursive Self-Evaluation for LLM Rubric Judges

K Liu, Z Zhuang, R Weng, J Ye · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RECURSE, an RL training regime in which an LLM rubric judge generates its own scalar training reward—a synchronized copy of the policy audits the judge's reasoning against meta-rubrics—with no gold labels or teacher models in the RL reward, plus a theoretically motivated early-stopping monitor (PAV). - Why it's important: Improving LLM judges normally requires expensive human annotations, external reward models, or distillation from stronger teachers; removing these from the training reward could make judge improvement cheap, private, and self-sustaining, which matters because judges steer post-training for open-ended generation at scale. - How it does it: The core moves are (1) interface decoupling—judge emits per-rule YES/NO verdicts while the checker emits a free-standing 0–4 scalar, severing a degenerate token-copying shortcut that inflates self-assigned rewards—and (2) PAV, a holdout composite of judge rule accuracy and checker ranking fidelity (weight 2 on fidelity, from a triangle-inequality bound on pairwise score-difference error) used to stop before validation deception. - The good: The most credible evidence is the diagnostic convergence: checker fidelity peaks near step 130 on the SV-HARD monitor and independently peaks at the same checkpoint on held-out HealthBench (accuracy 82.5%→85.9%→82.9%), and PAV achieves mean oracle regret of 1.20 points (Qwen-9B) vs 5.41 for accuracy-only stopping, without ever seeing transfer benchmarks. - The missing: The loop is not supervision-free—PAV requires a compact but real human-verified holdout (SV-HARD, 100 prompts), and the checker itself is noisy at its best (exact-match rate 48.2%, MAE 1.03), so the paper does not establish how accurate the self-produced reward must be for the loop to work, nor is there a release of code/weights stated in the main text. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone working on LLM-as-judge training, reward-hacking, or self-improvement loops—the surface-coupling shortcut analysis and PAV stopping monitor are genuinely reusable ideas—but skip it if you only want judge benchmarks, since absolute gains on transfer suites are modest (e.g., CheckEval Pearson ρ 0.422→0.441).

Novelty (80) and Non-Obviousness (82) are the drivers: the surface-coupling shortcut diagnosis and the PAV stopping monitor are genuinely new formulations, backed by controlled experiments and bootstrap CIs. Completeness (75) benefits from direct, non-minimizing limitation acknowledgment. Impact (55) suffers from no stated artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*55 = 72.

Problem & Motivation: LLM-as-judge systems evaluate open-ended text and steer post-training, but improving the judge itself typically depends on costly human annotation, learned reward models, or distillation from stronger teachers. The authors observe that rubric-based judging and auditing of evaluative reasoning instantiate the same underlying verification capability, so a model could in principle supervise its own improvement in a closed loop. The central obstacle is circularity: self-produced rewards invite shortcuts where the optimizer inflates reward without improving evaluation quality, and without external anchors there is no signal for when to stop training. Two coupled questions govern the design: when can self-improvement occur, and when must it stop? Key Idea: The key insight is that naive self-evaluation fails through a shared readout surface: when judge and synchronized checker both emit YES/NO verdicts from identical weights, gradient updates that boost YES tokens on judge outputs simultaneously inflate the checker's reward (formalized as S = aU + bB + ε, where B is surface token bias and synchronization makes b > 0). Structurally decoupling the output interfaces (verdicts vs. scalar score) closes this channel while preserving capability transfer via per-step weight synchronization, and a bound-derived composite monitor (PAV) tells the practitioner when the unanchored loop has exhausted its reliable reward regime. This is a genuine, non-obvious formulation—not merely applying existing RLHF machinery, though the RL substrate (group-relative advantages à la GRPO/DeepSeekMath, sequence-level loss à la GSPO) is standard. Methodology: Three components. (1) Judge–checker recurrence: given a rubric instance x = (h, y, r1:K), the trainable judge πθ samples n=8 rollouts emitting reasoning plus indexed per-rule YES/NO verdicts (Pass 1, sole gradient path); a frozen snapshot C̄θ synchronized to θ each step audits the reasoning against meta-rubrics and emits a 0–4 scalar as the sole reward (Pass 2, inference only). Rewards are normalized within prompt groups (group-relative advantages, invariant to affine reward transforms) and optimized with a clipped sequence-level policy loss (εclip = 0.005, lr 3×10⁻⁶, no KL for 9B). (2) Interface decoupling: shared evidence-block input layout but disjoint output formats (indexed verdicts vs. free-standing scalar in reserved delimiter tags); a format gate masks malformed rollouts and blocks prompt-injection of fake checker scores. (3) PAV monitor: on a 100-prompt human-verified holdout (SV-HARD, labels never in RL reward), compute V = Â + 2(1−ê_C)/3, where the weight 2 follows from the triangle inequality |(δi − δj)|/4 ≤ (|δi| + |δj|)/4 bounding pairwise ranking error by 2e_C; the estimator is unbiased at fixed checkpoints, with 10,000-iteration cluster bootstrap CIs and three-fold stability checks. Critical design decisions: per-step synchronization (justified by the frozen-checker ablation, which plateaus at 62.7% vs 73.7% SV-HARD), the scalar-vs-verdict readout (justified by RQ2 experiments), and the fixed a priori weight 2 (shown empirically robust for λ ∈ [1.59, 11.03]). Key Results: Tested on Qwen3.5-9B (main), Gemma-4-E4B-it (cross-architecture), and Qwen3.6-27B, trained on RubricHub cluster splits with responses synthesized from a 16-model three-tier pool, evaluated on four held-out suites (HealthBench 1,459 prompts, RubricBench 2,294 pairs, CheckEval-Summ 1,600 summaries, ProfBench 120 queries with ≈29 rules each). SV-HARD rule accuracy rises 60.8%→73.7% (+12.9, Qwen-9B), 55.9%→61.1% (+5.2, Gemma), 73.1%→77.0% (+3.9, Qwen-27B); all four transfer suites improve at PAV-selected checkpoints (e.g., Qwen-9B HealthBench 82.5%→85.9%, RubricBench 76.0%→79.1%, CheckEval ρ 0.422→0.441, p=0.0032; ProfBench 73.1%→74.7%, p=0.008). Final checkpoints degrade on transfer (SV-FULL 95.3%→89.7%), confirming boundedness. Ablations: frozen checker 62.7%, external 27B checker 73.1% SV-HARD but worse suite-wide (HealthBench 79.8% vs 85.9%), self-consistency collapses to 56.5%, teacher SFT reaches only 64.2% (6.4k traces) and 70.2% (17k traces) on SV-HARD. Downstream: DPO on Qwen-27B with RECURSE-judge preference labels yields GPQA 81.46 vs 80.87 base (vs 79.02 with base-judge labels), GuideBench +1.63, SOP-Maze +2.37. Notably, the external 27B checker beats the main run on CheckEval (0.471 vs 0.441), and the external checker arm is competitive on SV-HARD—co-evolution wins suite-wide but not universally. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (closed-loop judge–checker recurrence with interface decoupling and no external anchors in the RL reward) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the surface-coupling shortcut and the validation-deception dynamics where judge accuracy and checker fidelity diverge). The PAV monitor is a NEW FORMULATION of a stopping criterion with a simple supporting bound. Standard components reused: GRPO-style group-relative advantages, GSPO sequence loss, verl/FSDP/vLLM infrastructure, DPO for downstream transfer. The novelty claim relative to Self-Taught Evaluators, Meta-Rewarding, SELF-JUDGE, and Grad2Reward—specifically, removing all external anchors from the RL reward rather than retaining synthetic pairs or frozen meta-judges—is well supported by the taxonomy table in Appendix R, though the delta over Meta-Rewarding is incremental in mechanism (both use a judge auditing judgments; the difference is synchronization and decoupling rather than a frozen external meta-judge). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a preprint. Ablations isolate each component (frozen vs. synchronized checker, coupled vs. decoupled readout, self-consistency, two SFT scales); error quantification includes 10,000-iteration prompt-cluster bootstrap CIs (e.g., PAV 0.742, CI [0.685, 0.797]), three-fold validation-split stability, paired t-tests and cluster-bootstrap significance on transfer gains, and an offline selector comparison with mean oracle regret. The 100-prompt holdout sample-size concern is addressed directly (400 judge–checker trajectories per checkpoint; SV-FULL corroboration). Concerns: no code, data, or weight release is mentioned anywhere in the provided text; the PAV monitor and transfer evaluation share the same judging style family (RubricHub-derived SV-HARD vs. distinct public suites—partially mitigated by cluster isolation and cross-domain corroboration); multiple-testing across sequential checkpoints is acknowledged but not formally resolved; no confidence intervals on headline Table 2 numbers beyond the significance tests in Appendix N. Preprint (arXiv, marked "Preprint"), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (RL-trained systems with measured transfer). Practical: Runs on standard multi-GPU RL infrastructure (verl, FSDP, vLLM, TP=4 for 27B) with no external API dependency. Efficient: The checker doubles rollout-generation compute but is inference-only; parameter synchronization costs ≈1.2s/step (<2.5% of ≈45–60s iteration time at 27B), and it avoids recurring API fees and RM training data collection. Effective: Evidence shows improved judge accuracy and downstream DPO gains, but the improvement is real only within the PAV window—unstopped training degrades transfer—so effectiveness is conditional on the monitor working as claimed. Scalable: Tested up to 27B and 200 steps; the authors claim the recipe extends to holistic/multilingual/multimodal judging but provide no experiments beyond 27B, and checker degradation dynamics (score inflation, verbosity drift past 32k tokens) suggest the useful window may shrink with scale—only claimed, not tested. Delivers a method and training recipe in paper form; no released artifact is stated. Strengths: (1) The surface-coupling shortcut is a sharp, well-diagnosed failure mode specific to weight-synchronized self-evaluation (distinct from classical reward hacking against a static RM), backed by both a structural causal model and a controlled experiment showing reward inflation (0.465→0.698) with flat accuracy (0.729→0.730) under coupled readouts versus concordant growth under decoupling. (2) PAV is derived from an explicit pairwise error bound with the weight fixed a priori, and its practical value is demonstrated by oracle-regret comparison (1.20 vs 5.41 for accuracy-only selection) rather than assertion. (3) The dual-variable difficulty-coupling analysis explains, with data, why scaled static teacher SFT (17k traces, four frontier teachers) fails for judge training while on-policy rollouts succeed—an insight that transfers beyond this specific system. (4) Honest treatment of the human-verified holdout: the paper does not claim zero human involvement, only zero gold labels in the RL reward. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: scope limited to English rubric benchmarks and three models up to 27B; the 100-prompt human-verified holdout is a real upfront cost (gold kept out of RL reward, not out of the pipeline); sequential monitoring across checkpoints lacks formal family-wise error control; the process checker could theoretically assign high scores to flawed rationales if it develops systematic biases; and bounded RSI here fixes the task, optimizer, and checking protocol, so conclusions do not extend to open-ended recursive self-modification. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment—a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No code, data, or checkpoint release is mentioned, which materially limits reproducibility given the method's sensitivity to prompt templates, format gates, and stopping windows. (2) The checker's own ceiling is low—best exact-match 48.2%, MAE 1.03 on a 0–4 scale—yet the paper never characterizes how reward-model accuracy degrades as a function of checker quality; a sensitivity study on weaker/stronger initial judges is missing. (3) A natural baseline is absent: GRPO with a small number of human labels (comparable to the SV-HARD verification budget) injected directly as ground-truth reward on a subset of training prompts would test whether the elaborate self-checking loop beats simply spending the same human effort on sparse verifiable rewards. (4) The external-27B-checker arm beats the main run on CheckEval (0.471 vs 0.441), which the narrative of co-evolution superiority does not fully reconcile. (5) Transfer gains on the two hardest suites are small in absolute terms (CheckEval +0.019 ρ; ProfBench +1.6pp on 120 queries) and could be sensitive to checkpoint selection variance despite the reported significance. (6) PAV is validated on one primary and one replication trajectory; whether the λ=2 weighting and the stability interval hold for other training regimes (different LR, batch size, or horizon) is untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or improving LLM judges should read this for the interface-decoupling diagnosis and the PAV stopping monitor—both immediately reusable and better-validated than most self-improvement proposals—but should not adopt the full closed-loop recipe without first running the missing sparse-human-label baseline, since the paper's own evidence leaves open whether self-produced rewards beat simply spending the holdout budget on direct supervision.

Knowing When Not to Reuse: Conditional Experience Transfer in Autonomous LLM Post-Training (145 ▲ )

Tingyun Li, Wenfeng Feng, Weiqing Li, Abudukelimu Wuerkaixi, Guohua Liu, Yuewei Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BCIT (Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer), a reject–validate–train authorization policy that decides, before any weight-changing training, whether a past update's source-context evidence justifies spending full-training compute on a candidate from the current parent model. - Why it's important: Autonomous LLM post-training systems accumulate a history of past updates and naively reusing them after the parent model has changed wastes training compute and can corrupt the sequential training trajectory through harmful promotions. - How it does it: Each historical candidate is scored as Qi = Si × Ai (source-strength × current-context compatibility) with a non-compensable hard-conflict veto; candidates either go to full training (only with grade-A replicated evidence and Qi ≥ 0.70), a budget-capped ~20% validation trial from the current parent, or rejection, and every fully trained child faces a shared promote-or-rollback rule. - The good: The evaluation is unusually disciplined — outcome-blind authorization audits, prespecified baseline amendments, six paired equal-budget seeds with exact sign-flip tests, and a claim-to-evidence map; BCIT beats its strongest additive-score ablation by +0.90 points (95% CI [0.27, 1.52]) in final cross-task mean under a 36-GPU-hour cap. - The missing: Everything is tested on exactly one model (Qwen3-4B), three capabilities, and one retention benchmark; the headline authorization result (25% vs 62.5% harmful authorization) is not statistically significant (McNemar p = .25), and no code or artifact release is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building agent-driven or automated post-training/ AutoML pipelines who needs a principled controller for reusing past training runs; skippable for researchers focused on scaling or model-merging, since the method is untested beyond a 4B model and three tasks.

Problem & Motivation Autonomous post-training systems (e.g., LaMDAgent, TREX, EvoTrainer) automate the loop of proposing fine-tuning updates, training candidates, and evaluating outcomes, and in doing so accumulate a library of past updates with observed effects. The paper identifies a decision these systems do not currently handle: an update's effect is bound to the parent model, data mixture, training stage, and evaluation contract under which it was observed, so treating a past success as context-free permission to retrain from a changed parent both wastes compute and, if the resulting child is promoted, permanently shifts the parent checkpoint for all later decisions. The authors call this candidate-level decision problem "conditional experience transfer" and argue prior transferability estimators (LEEP, LogME, Taskonomy), case-based reasoning, and partial-budget methods (Hyperband-style) all operate at the task/model level or after integration — none decide whether one weight-changing candidate's source-context effect warrants validation or full-training budget from the current parent. Key Idea The core move is non-compensability: bind every observed effect to its source context and require that source evidence (Si) and current-context compatibility (Ai) both be high, via a multiplicative score Qi = Si·Ai, so strong source evidence cannot buy authorization under a mismatched context; additionally, a small set of named hard conflicts (e.g., incompatible output schema, dialect/backend mismatch) acts as an absolute veto, and weak or missing evidence is resolved only by buying current-state evidence through a short, budget-capped training trial from the current parent — never by fabricating or generalizing a label. Authorization and adoption are also cleanly separated: validation checkpoints are never promoted, and a frozen promotion rule shared across all compared policies is the only path to changing the parent. Methodology BCIT operates between candidate generation and full training. Each historical candidate is a state-bound record (update, source context xs, source evidence Es, applicability conditions Bi, provenance ρi). Source strength is Si = d(ei)·clip(δsrc/κi, 0, 1), where δsrc is the frozen signed source metric change, ei is an evidence grade with discounts d(A/B/C) = 1/.75/.5, and κi = 0.02; only grade A (replicated matched-control evidence) may bypass validation (χi). Compatibility Ai averages five pre-specifiable fields (capability family, data identity, runtime, parent stage, evaluator/protocol) scored 0/.5/1. Authorization: Reject if Hi = 1 or Qi < τl = 0.30; Train if Qi ≥ τh = 0.70 and χi = 1; otherwise Validate if a faithful short run exists (prefix or restart), else Reject. Validation runs the candidate from the current parent at ≤20% nominal budget and yields Pass/Fail/Inconclusive; Pass routes to full training, Fail rejects, Inconclusive routes to full training only under a pre-reserved fallback lease. New proposals (≤3 per episode, quota-bounded) have no source score and must validate. Memory is split into a frozen per-episode library and an online history of observed events, consolidated with provenance checks between episodes. Four design choices stand out: (1) the multiplicative (rather than additive) positive-score combination — directly ablated against Additive+Veto; (2) the hard-conflict veto as non-compensable rather than a feature — ablated; (3) outcome-blind freezing of decisions and thresholds before target outcomes open — methodologically strong; (4) human-specified (not learned) boundaries — acknowledged as a limitation but justified here for auditability. Key Results All experiments use one Qwen3-4B base model, transferring experience from FinQA/Spider/xLAM to TAT-QA/BIRD/BFCL with IFEval as a −2-point retention guardrail, under 36-GPU-hour equal-budget episodes (six paired seeds for primary comparisons). (RQ1) Across 24 matched candidate–context pairs, 13/24 candidates fail to improve their target and only 3/11 target-improving updates also preserve both retention metrics; a standard SQL SFT gains +2.25 points on BIRD but loses 22.74/18.71 points on IFEval prompt/instruction accuracy. (RQ2) In the outcome-blind Audit-24, BCIT authorizes 2/8 harmful candidates (25.0%) versus 5/8 (62.5%) for Flat-Additive while keeping 9/10 beneficial candidates (90.0% vs 80.0%); the McNemar test gives p = .25, so this is directional, not significant. (RQ3) At a 20% validation budget, short-run and full-run target directions agree for 20/24 candidates (83.3%, Spearman ρ = .72), and a Pass predicts Beneficial full outcomes with 80.0% precision and 80.0% recall at a median 17% of full cost; four sign reversals and two false Passes remain. (RQ4) BCIT reaches a 47.0 cross-task mean versus 44.4 (Flat-Additive, +2.63, 95% CI [2.10, 3.16], exact sign-flip p = .03125), 45.5 (Validate-All, +1.50), 46.1 (Additive+Veto, +0.90), 45.7 (BCIT-Retrieve, unpaired, three seeds), and 42.5 (base model); BCIT promotion yield is 74.2% (46/62) versus 44.4% (28/63) for Flat-Additive. The AUC advantage over Additive+Veto (+0.47, CI [−0.003, 0.935]) includes zero. Single-task specialists beat BCIT on their own task (e.g., SQL specialist 49.3 vs 44.3 on BIRD) but each consumes a full budget and produce no shared multi-capability model. The baselines are well-constructed ablation-style comparators sharing candidates, evidence, adoption rule, and budget — but they are author-constructed policies, not published autonomous post-training systems. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM + NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel contribution is the problem formulation: candidate-level authorization of experience reuse as a distinct control point before weight-changing training, with the observation that promotions change the parent and hence the relevance of all later evidence. The method itself is a transparent, deliberately non-learned combination of simple components (evidence discounting, compatibility averaging, a product score with thresholds, a hard veto, capped validation, shared adoption); the paper correctly presents this as a prespecified protocol rather than a learned optimizer. Prior transferability and AutoML work supplies the ingredients; the composition and the decision point are new. Rigor & Reproducibility Rigor is above the bar for this venue class. Ablations isolate each component: removing candidate-specific applicability raises harmful authorization from 25.0% to 75.0%, adding a veto to the additive score lowers it from 62.5% to 37.5%, and removing BCIT's veto raises it to 50.0% (though the additive-vs-product comparison alone is confounded with the veto in Flat-Additive — Additive+Veto addresses this). Primary comparisons use six paired seeds with paired t intervals and exact sign-flip tests; the smallest attainable p = .03125 is honestly reported. The protocol amendment adding Validate-All and Additive+Veto was prespecified before those baselines' outcomes were opened. The audit is outcome-blind with thresholds calibrated on disjoint units; final test outcomes are sealed. The authors retain a null 24-GPU-hour pilot in the supplement — a credibility positive. Concerns: the Audit-24 cohort (n = 24, eight per capability) yields wide exact-binomial intervals (e.g., BCIT harmful rate CI [3.2, 65.1]) and non-significant paired discordance; the four studies share candidates and are not independent replications; component ablations use only three descriptive seeds; and the validation-fidelity study shares full outcomes with the audit. No code, data, or model release is mentioned anywhere — the supplement references CSV files but no public repository. Human-specified boundaries (grades, discounts, thresholds, five applicability fields, κ values) are frozen but their specification cost and sensitivity are unexamined. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs the full decision pipeline, though it also ships as a protocol/system design). - Practical: Runs on a 4B model with bf16, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, and an effective batch of 32 on four GPUs — entirely within commercially available hardware. - Efficient: Validation consumes a median 17% of full-training cost per candidate; BCIT finishes episodes using 0.74 fewer GPU-hours than Validate-All on average, and the fixed 36-GPU-hour cap with charged failures makes accounting explicit. - Effective: The evidence shows it improves equal-budget final-model quality and reduces harmful authorization on the tested 4B/three-capability setup; whether it solves the broader sequential-adaptation problem at other scales is a claim, not a measurement. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 4B, three tasks, and one retention benchmark; the authors explicitly state that validation fidelity and compute trade-offs "may vary with model scale" and leave longer trajectories to future work. The work delivers no software artifact — no library, CLI, checkpoint, or dataset release is stated; it stops at paper form with a reusable protocol. Strengths - The problem formulation is the real contribution: isolating the pre-full-training authorization decision and showing formally and empirically why source-context evidence is not permission (13/24 candidates fail on target; 8/11 target-gains violate retention on at least one metric). - The evaluation discipline is genuinely unusual: outcome-blind decision freezing, prespecified baseline amendments, paired equal-budget seeds with exact tests, a claim-to-evidence map, and retention of a null pilot result. - The hard-veto/multiplicative-score design is validated by its ablation pattern — each component's removal moves harmful authorization in the predicted direction (25% → 50% without veto; → 75% without applicability conditions). - The short-to-full validation fidelity study evaluates every compiled pair, not just passed trials, and honestly reports four sign reversals and two false Passes rather than filtering. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that evidence covers one 4B model, three target capabilities, one retention benchmark, and human-specified boundaries; that the four studies share candidates and are complementary rather than independent replications; that only complete-policy comparisons have six paired seeds while component ablations are descriptive; that validation fidelity and compute trade-offs may vary with scale, data, and schedule; and that learned boundaries, broader domains, and longer trajectories remain future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No comparison against any published autonomous post-training system (LaMDAgent, TREX, EvoTrainer are cited but not run); all baselines are author-constructed score variants, so the reported margins establish BCIT's internal design choices, not superiority over the systems practitioners would actually deploy. - The RQ2 headline (25% vs 62.5% harmful authorization) is statistically non-significant (p = .25) and rests on n = 24 units sharing capability/recipe structure; the paper flags this but the abstract and conclusion do not carry the caveat forward with equal weight. - The human specification burden is unquantified: who writes the five applicability fields, the named conflicts, the evidence grades, and κ scales for a new domain, and how brittle is authorization to specification error? Nothing measures inter-annotator reliability or misspecification sensitivity. - Validation fidelity (RQ3) is measured on the same 24 candidates whose full outcomes feed the audit, so authorization and fidelity results are not independent — the authors note study sharing but not this specific coupling risk. - Exploration is essentially untested: the ≤3-proposal quota and proposal-generation agent are specified but no results isolate whether new proposals ever contribute (the 62 fully trained candidates' provenance split is not reported). - A thresholds-on-a-knife-edge risk: with τl = 0.30 and τh = 0.70 fixed by hand on a score built from hand-set discounts, the sensitivity of the 47.0-vs-46.1 margin (BCIT vs Additive+Veto) to threshold perturbation is unknown. Bottom Line For anyone engineering autonomous post-training or repeated-fine-tuning pipelines, this paper names and operationalizes a real decision point that existing systems silently get wrong, with evaluation rigor well above the norm — read it for the formulation and protocol, while discounting the magnitude of the gains, which are proven only on one 4B model, three tasks, author-built baselines, and margins (0.9–2.6 points) that would not survive much noise.

CEDAR: Automata as Verifiable Interfaces for Language-Guided Embodied Action

L Chen, A Velasquez, A Trivedi · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CEDAR, an embodied-agent framework that grounds natural-language goals and constraints as deterministic finite automata (DFAs) over environment event traces, so skills and specifications become composable, verifiable finite-state objects rather than free-form LLM-generated code. - Why it's important: Code-generating LLM agents (VOYAGER, CODEACT) treat constraints as prompt context or one-time subgoals, so persistent instructions like "sleep at night" are silently violated by long-running or reused skills; CEDAR makes constraints enforceable by construction. - How it does it: An LLM answers membership queries as a noisy semantic teacher over a retrieved task alphabet, active DFA learning (CAPAL) builds hypothesis automata, execution and human feedback supply counterexamples, and constraints are enforced by exact DFA product intersection with skill automata. - The good: Under matched simulator/API observations in Minecraft, CEDAR achieves 5/5 joint task-and-constraint success on the sleep-at-night task while all four code-baseline conditions (including assertion-augmented VOYAGER and CODEACT) achieve 0/5, and cumulative LLM queries drop from 75 (VOYAGER) to 37 (CEDAR) at the final "Find a Diamond" milestone via skill-DFA reuse. - The missing: The headline constraint results rest on n=5 trials with very wide Clopper–Pearson intervals, and there is no comparison against natural-language-to-temporal-logic translation systems or shield-based safe-RL baselines despite those being the closest prior approaches. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in LLM agents, formal methods for agents, and neuro-symbolic control who want a concrete architecture for verified, composable learned constraints; skip it if you need continuous-state, vision-based, or safety-critical results, which the authors explicitly do not claim.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The core move — grounding both skills and constraints as regular languages so closure properties give exact composition — is a genuine NEW FORMULATION, driving Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78). Completeness (82) is a standout: a dedicated expressiveness section and failure-mode appendix confront limitations directly, and baseline discipline (assertion-augmented variants, matched observations) is above average. Rigor (62) is pulled down by n=5 headline trials, no NL-to-LTL baseline for the closest prior approach, self-referential alphabet evaluation, and no code release; Resilience (72) holds because claims are explicitly caveated. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Users tasking embodied agents with natural language rarely give only terminal goals; they impose temporal, spatial, and safety constraints ("collect diamonds but sleep at night", "stay in this biome") that must persist as the world changes. LLM code-generation agents produce plausible programs but their skills are free-form code with no stable object to verify, no algebraic composition (e.g., intersecting a skill with a newly stated constraint), and no precise object to repair from a failing trace. The gap is architectural: there is no representation shared between learned skills and learned constraints that supports formal operations. The work targets researchers and practitioners building long-lived LLM-driven agents in symbol-rich simulators such as Minecraft and iTHOR. Key Idea: Treat the LLM as a noisy semantic teacher, not a policy: ground both natural-language goals and constraints as regular languages over traces of executable symbols, learn them via counterexample-guided active DFA learning, and exploit closure properties of regular languages — product intersection for constraint enforcement, concatenation for skill chaining, and template substitution over a noun-specific alphabet for skill reuse. The persistence of a constraint then follows from it living inside the composed controller's state, rather than from repeated prompting. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) Alphabet construction — a RAG-style retriever selects from a 1,429-symbol global inventory (16 action primitives, 9 event predicates, 1,404 objects) symbols with implemented environment bindings, which an LLM prunes into a task-specific alphabet; the LLM cannot invent sensors. (2) Active DFA learning — CAPAL (Chen et al., ICLR 2026, the authors' prior noise-tolerant active-learning algorithm) issues membership queries answered by the LLM, maintains a persistent query cache with gold-override counterexample labels, uses a statistical class-query test with noise bound η̄ and Rivest–Schapire counterexample analysis, and builds hypothesis DFAs via an observation table and discrimination tree. (3) Execution-backed equivalence — the learned DFA is executed by shortest-path-to-accepting; mismatched outcomes are returned as counterexamples that trigger refinement, and missing-predicate detections trigger alphabet expansion with learner restart. (4) Storage and composition — skills are stored as ⟨A, v, n, E, D⟩ tuples with labeled evidence; exact noun-match reuse, noun-substitution template adaptation, or fresh learning is chosen; specification DFAs are composed with skill DFAs by product intersection (equation L(Ag) ∩ L(Ac)). Critical design decisions: separating semantic grounding from control structure (justified by the persistence argument); restricting the LLM to selecting among implemented predicates (well-justified against an observation-advantage objection); and accepting the regular-language expressiveness restriction, which the authors analyze honestly in a dedicated section (tasks with finite milestone predicates and bounded horizon H yield regular success languages). Human counterexamples are used only for the three specification demonstrations. Key Results: All comparative claims come from Minecraft with the same simulator/API observations given to baselines. Sleep-at-night (n=5 trials/condition): CEDAR achieves 5/5 diamond found, 5/5 constraint-compliant, 5/5 joint success, mean terminal health 18.4±2.61; VOYAGER with assertions gets 4/5, 2/5, 0/5 (health 8.4±4.56); CODEACT with assertions 0/5, 3/5, 0/5; no code baseline achieves joint success. The authors correctly note the 95% binomial intervals are wide and interpret this descriptively. Mine-minerals-only-at-night (24,000-tick budget, 5 trials): CEDAR 137±12 mining actions, 387±13 objects vs VOYAGER 106±4.6 and 229±14. Biome constraint: heatmaps show CEDAR stays in the windswept forest while VOYAGER crosses boundaries. Goal completion (25 trials/task): CEDAR with skill library reaches 23/25 on Diamond Pickaxe vs VOYAGER's 17/25, 25/25 on Lava Bucket and Compass; CEDAR without a library is worse on Compass (9/25) due to learning overhead. Amortization: 37 vs 75 cumulative LLM queries at the diamond milestone; total wall-clock 33.1s vs 62.4s. Grounding reliability: alphabet retrieval accuracy 0.9372±0.10 and overlap 0.9208±0.10 against 44 validated target alphabets; perturbation-based counterexample discovery accuracy 0.9358 (though Emerald Ore drops to 0.4909). iTHOR feasibility: 5 tasks, 4 succeed in one pass, COOK POTATO repaired via one counterexample with no extra LLM calls (2 LLM calls per task). Baselines are current and reasonably strengthened with assertion-and-repair variants. Notably, CEDAR without a skill library underperforms on some tasks — the paper reports this rather than hiding it. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW FORMULATION component. The genuinely novel move is using regular languages as a shared executable representation for both learned skills and learned natural-language constraints within one embodied-agent architecture, enabling intersection, concatenation, reuse, and counterexample-guided relearning that free-form code skills cannot support. The authors are appropriately explicit that the DFA-learning algorithm (CAPAL, Angluin-style MAT learning with LLM oracles), LLM-as-semantic-teacher, and counterexample-guided automaton refinement are inherited from prior work (including the authors' own); the contribution is the architectural integration, not the learning theory. This is a competent composition of known automata-learning techniques into a new setting, elevated by the constraint-persistence argument. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist in meaningful forms: baselines with and without runtime assertions, CEDAR with and without a skill library, expert-constructed DFA upper-bound diagnostics (10/10 on most tasks), and separate analyses of alphabet retrieval and counterexample discovery as isolated dependencies. Clopper–Pearson confidence intervals are reported for all binary success rates, and the authors repeatedly and correctly caveat that n=5 comparisons are descriptive only. Conditional prompting-iteration means are flagged as conditioning on success. Wall-clock measurements are separate from task statistics. Methodological concerns: (1) the three specification-DFA demonstrations rely on human counterexamples supplied by a single author-annotator, so inter-annotator sensitivity is unmeasured; (2) no code, data, or model release URL is mentioned in the provided text; (3) the alphabet-retrieval evaluation uses target alphabets derived from the authors' own 44 validated DFAs — a self-referential evaluation; (4) no comparison against NL-to-LTL translators or shield-based safe RL, which the authors acknowledge. The preprint is candid about failure modes (silent alphabet omissions, rare long-horizon counterexamples, shared semantic misunderstanding) in a dedicated appendix. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system run in two simulators). Practical: Yes — it runs on standard LLM APIs (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini, text-embedding-3-large) plus the Minecraft/iTHOR simulators, requiring structured simulator APIs but no special hardware. Efficient: Front-loaded cost (18.5±14.3s DFA construction) is amortized: fewer cumulative LLM queries (37 vs 75) and lower total execution time (33.1s vs 62.4s) than VOYAGER by the final milestone, and near-zero skill-addition cost (0.021s vs 2.653s). Effective: Evidence supports persistent constraint enforcement in the evaluated discrete, symbol-rich settings; the exact-intersection guarantee is only relative to the learned automata, not to the user's intended semantics, and the authors say so. Scalable: Untested beyond small automata — product state growth is worst-case multiplicative, retrieval was evaluated only on the fixed 1,429-symbol inventory, and the authors state small compositions do not guarantee scalability. The work stops at paper form in the provided text; no artifact release is mentioned. Strengths: (1) The core insight — that constraint persistence is a representational problem, and that DFA closure properties give an exact composition operation that code skills structurally lack — is genuinely clarifying and well-argued. (2) The experimental fairness discipline is above average: baselines receive the same simulator state, assertion-augmented baseline variants are added specifically to close the obvious loophole, and CEDAR's event predicates are shown to be recodings of API variables the baselines can access. (3) The paper is unusually honest: a dedicated "When Do Regular Languages Suffice?" section bounds its own expressiveness, the Limitations section enumerates silent-alphabet-omission and incorrect-human-feedback failure modes, and small-sample results are explicitly flagged as descriptive. (4) The decomposed evaluation of grounding reliability (retrieval accuracy, counterexample discovery accuracy) separates mechanism quality from end-to-end task success. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront: evidence limited to Minecraft (iTHOR tests only grounding and repair, not constraints or reuse); CAPAL's dependence on structured API observations, not raw vision; the regular-language ceiling (no unbounded counting, recursion, or unbounded memory); silent omission of missing or unretrieved predicates that can cause over-acceptance; incorrect human counterexamples steering learning, with single-annotator feedback and no inter-annotator analysis; worst-case multiplicative product-automaton growth; retrieval evaluated only on the fixed inventory; and learned specification DFAs being uncertified safety specifications unsuitable for safety-critical deployment. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The absence of any NL-to-LTL translation baseline (e.g., NL2LTL, Lang2LTL-2) is the most significant omission — the acknowledged closest approach for grounding language constraints is discussed but never run, so the claim that active learning beats direct formula translation for this interface is unsupported. (2) The headline sleep-at-night result (5/5 vs 0/5 joint success) uses five trials per condition; the paper's own confidence intervals ([0.478, 1.000] vs [0.000, 0.522]) overlap is avoided only marginally, and a 20–30-trial version would substantially strengthen the central claim. (3) The human counterexamples for the three specifications come from one author, so the specification-learning pipeline has never been tested with realistic annotator noise or disagreement — precisely the setting where learned (vs. hand-coded) constraints matter. (4) The three constraint demonstrations and three skill-composition examples are hand-picked; there is no evidence of how often natural-language constraints in the wild fall inside the expressible regular fragment or require implemented predicates that happen to exist. (5) No comparison against a shielding system given an independently validated formal specification, which would isolate the value of learning the specification rather than receiving it. (6) No code release is stated, which limits reproducibility of a system paper whose pipeline has many implementation-level choices. Bottom Line: A practitioner building verifiable or long-lived LLM agents should read this for the architectural insight that learned constraints must be first-class composable objects — the Minecraft evidence is thin (n=5 on the headline result, no LTL baseline) but the formulation is sound, honestly bounded, and likely to seed stronger follow-up work.

XREPOTEST: Benchmarking Multilingual Repository-Level Unit Test Generation for Large Language Models

DL Quang, DC Van, NL Hai, LN Van, AMT Bui… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces XREPOTEST, a repository-level unit test generation benchmark of 3,642 focal functions across 30 real-world repositories in five understudied languages (Rust, Go, Julia, PHP, Ruby), plus a containerized evaluation framework and a new Invocation Rate (IR) metric, evaluated over 14 LLMs under five context-augmentation settings. - Why it's important: Existing test-generation benchmarks are mostly standalone, Python/Java-centric, and inflate estimates of deployment readiness — Figure 1 shows pass rates and coverage collapse when moving from McEval standalone tasks to real repositories, so the field currently over-credits models on exactly the task they will be used for. - How it does it: The benchmark extracts non-trivial focal functions via tree-sitter ASTs from star-filtered repositories, executes generated tests inside Docker containers using each language's native runner (cargo test, go test, Test.jl, PHPUnit, RSpec), and scores pass rate (TPR), compilation success, line coverage, mutation score, and a static AST check that a generated test directly calls the focal function (IR). - The good: The IR metric exposes a real blind spot with concrete evidence: 9.7% of all TPR-passing suites never directly invoke the focal function (28.3% in Rust), and the headless Claude Code agent raises PHP pass rate by 11.5% while cutting IR from 98.9% to 27.6% — a failure pass-rate-only evaluation would score as success. - The missing: There are no non-LLM baselines (no search-based generators like the ones the paper cites for comparison) and no fine-tuned test-generation specialists, so it is impossible to tell whether the frontier-model numbers (best ~27% TPR standard-setting) are an LLM ceiling or a prompting ceiling; the contamination analysis is a weak perplexity proxy on a different artifact (repo test code, not focal functions). - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or evaluating LLM test-generation systems — the IR-vs-TPR divergence and the context-vs-reliability trade-off are actionable findings — but skippable for readers who only need confirmation that repo-level testing is hard in non-Python/Java languages.
