Problem & Motivation: Automated unit testing consumes roughly 15% of developer time, and LLMs are increasingly proposed to do it. Two evaluation gaps motivate the work: (1) most benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, McEval, TestEval) isolate functions from their repositories, so models never have to satisfy build systems, dependency graphs, or framework conventions — leading to inflated readiness estimates; and (2) the repo-level benchmarks that do exist (Defects4J, TestPilot, TestGenEval) are concentrated on Java, Python, and JavaScript, leaving Rust, Go, Julia, PHP, and Ruby — languages with distinct mechanics like Rust's borrow checker and Ruby's metaprogramming — essentially unmeasured at repository level. The audience is LLM researchers, evaluation builders, and teams deciding whether generated tests are deployable in production software estates. Key Idea: The core move is behavioral-target checking: alongside standard pass/coverage metrics, statically verify (via tree-sitter AST call-identifier extraction) that each generated test suite contains a direct call to the focal function, yielding the Invocation Rate. This single cheap check separates "the test compiles and passes" from "the test tests the assigned function," exposing indirect-invocation and mocked-API artifacts that inflate TPR and coverage. The second supporting idea is a controlled context axis — focal-only, file-level, LSP-resolved symbols, BM25, and dense (UniXCoder) retrieval — run over the same tasks in identical containers, so context-strategy effects are attributable. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Benchmark construction: for each language, 6–10 repositories with ≥500 GitHub stars and standard build manifests are selected across ≥2 domains; tree-sitter parses sources into ASTs and extracts top-level functions filtered by ≥10 body lines, an explicit return, non-test status, and syntactic validity, producing 3,642 focal functions (Julia 684, Rust 931, Go 706, PHP 646, Ruby 675). (2) Prompt construction: each focal function is paired with the focal/class-signature "standard" context plus optional static (full file, LSP-resolved argument types/callee signatures/control-flow references) or dynamic context (BM25 with k1=1.5, b=0.75, or UniXCoder cosine retrieval over 50-line windows with stride 5, top-k=10). (3) Containerized evaluation: tests are extracted from fenced code blocks, integrated per language convention, and run in Docker with the native runner; metrics are all-or-nothing TPR, macro-averaged focal-function line coverage, CSR, mutation score (Go/Rust/Ruby only), and IR (normalized by all N samples, so unparsable output counts as a miss). All 14 models run with greedy decoding and a fixed prompt template. Design decisions mostly justified: the all-or-nothing TPR and per-sample macro-coverage definitions prevent inflation; retrieval hyperparameters are ablated (Appendix G shows ≤1.0–3.3% coverage variation across window/top-k settings). The IR check itself is deliberately shallow (presence of a call identifier), which the Julia multiple-dispatch case study shows is a real residual weakness (a test can call the right name but dispatch to the wrong overload — IR=100%, coverage=0%). Key Results: Standard-setting (focal context only), even frontier models top out near 27% TPR: Claude 4.5 Sonnet leads Rust (12.78% TPR, 11.56% coverage), Julia (19.88% TPR), and PHP (26.93% TPR, 41.76% coverage); GPT-5.2 leads Go (25.78% TPR) and Ruby (25.78% TPR but only 7.80% coverage). Small models are dramatically worse (Qwen3-8B: 0.00–0.88% TPR on Ruby/Julia). Mean CSR is 57.4%; mean mutation score is 3.2% (GPT-5.2 best: Go 19.62%, Rust 4.14%, Ruby 6.29% lower-bound). File-level context is the most consistent augmentation (Claude on Go: 23.65→34.14% TPR; confirmed significant, McNemar χ²=17.65, p=1.5e-05), but on Ruby it collapses IR from 85.63% to 53.19% across all three frontier models — a systematic effectiveness-vs-reliability trade-off. Failure-mode analysis (per-sample normalized) identifies API hallucination as the dominant failure (48.05% of Rust samples standard-setting; 47.90% Julia; 42.17% Ruby), and context redistributes rather than eliminates it (Rust: 48.05→36.09% but Logic & Assertion rises 26.42→30.79%). Agentic evaluation (headless Claude Code, stratified ≤10 functions/repo) improves TPR 1.2–2.6× on all five languages but drops PHP coverage by 33.3% and IR by 71.3%. One-round execution-feedback repair (GPT-OSS-120B) lifts TPR by 9–26% with IR unchanged. The paper contrasts these numbers with the McEval standalone gap (Figure 1) to argue standalone evaluation overestimates readiness. Baselines are current frontier models (GPT-5.2, Claude 4.5, DeepSeek V4-pro), so the model comparison is against a strong field, though no non-LLM generators are run. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the first repository-level, execution-based unit-test benchmark covering five non-Java/Python languages with per-language containerized toolchains and mutation testing in three of them, and (b) the IR metric and its evidence that pass-rate-only evaluation systematically mis-scores both passive and agentic generation. The context-augmentation machinery (BM25, UniXCoder, LSP, file context) is a standard combination of existing repo-level code-generation techniques applied to a new setting; the pipeline engineering is competent execution rather than a methodological contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: retrieval hyperparameter sweep (Table A.8), failure-mode distributions per model/language (Tables A.12–A.13), hallucination sub-taxonomy, bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples) and Holm-Bonferroni-corrected McNemar tests across 90 pairwise comparisons (62% significant). Multiple models (n=14) and explicit tier separations (e.g., Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 21.16% vs GPT-OSS-120B at 8.06% on Rust/file-context, χ²=89.63) are reported. Dataset and code are stated to be publicly available (the abstract references a repository; no URL is printed in the provided text beyond "§ XREPOTEST"). Methodological concerns: (i) the benchmark is built and evaluated by the same authors with no external replication yet, though contamination is addressed via a perplexity analysis (Ruby 26.94–32.74 vs 3.52–6.11 elsewhere) that is indirect — it measures perplexity of repository test code under two small code models, not the focal functions under the evaluated frontier models; (ii) low absolute TPRs make small model differences statistically fragile, which the authors themselves flag; (iii) the agentic comparison uses a small stratified subset and a different scaffold (full repo access) than the passive baseline, so the 1.2–2.6× TPR gains conflate scaffolding with model capability; (iv) greedy decoding, single seed per configuration, no variance across decoding runs. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and measurement study with executed experiments; no new generator is proposed). - Practical: Runs on commodity hardware — Docker containers with native toolchains; frontier models are API-based and open-weight models are ≤120B, all servable on a single multi-GPU node. - Efficient: Evaluation cost is dominated by containerized per-sample builds and runs; the agentic mode was cost-limited to ~10 functions per repository, indicating the full-benchmark agentic protocol is expensive. - Effective: Evidence is strong for the diagnostic claim (the benchmark separates models and exposes pass-rate blind spots) but the benchmark itself does not solve test generation — the measured ceilings (~27% TPR, 3.2% mean mutation score) show the underlying task is far from solved. - Scalable: The authors claim the framework extends to new languages with only a test runner and build config, and the design supports this, but only 5 languages and ~30 repositories are actually tested; behavior at 10× repository count or in monorepos with heavy dependency trees is untested. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (containerized evaluation framework, dataset with metadata, prompting templates) rather than stopping at paper form, contingent on the promised public release. Strengths: - The IR metric is a small, cheap, and well-validated idea: the 9.7% overall IR-failure-among-passing-suites rate (28.3% Rust), the PHP agentic case (TPR +11.5%, IR −71.3%), and the Julia dispatch-mismatch study (7 of 16 focal functions at zero coverage despite 100% IR) together demonstrate that pass rate and coverage alone mislead — this is the paper's most transferable contribution. - Real engineering across five heterogeneous ecosystems: per-language containers, native runners, focal-function-scoped coverage instrumentation (llvm-cov, go coverprofile, Coverage.jl, PHPUnit, SimpleCov), and mutation testing in three languages where tooling is immature — a scope no prior benchmark attempts. - Statistical discipline unusual for benchmark papers: bootstrap CIs, paired McNemar tests with multiple-comparison correction, and explicit acknowledgment of which rankings are indistinguishable. - Actionable negative results: file-level context beats LSP-based and retrieval-based context on average, and richer context can hurt reliability (Ruby IR collapse) — a counter-intuitive finding with per-language failure-mode evidence behind it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: fixed prompt and greedy decoding may under-serve particular models; retrieval results are not from a tuned pipeline; the five-language, curated-repository scope may not generalize to other languages, domains, or frameworks. They also flag (in the SWE-bench correlation section) that the 12-model correlation is underpowered and presented as observational. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No non-LLM baselines: search-based or symbolic generators are cited as motivation but never run, so the benchmark cannot position LLM performance against classical techniques, and the claim that LLMs are the promising alternative rests on prior literature rather than this paper's measurements. - IR is a name-presence check: it credits a test that calls the focal function name with wrong arguments, on the wrong overload (their own Julia case study), or through a stub — the metric catches indirect invocation but not shallow or non-behavioral direct invocation; a dispatch-aware or execution-trace-based IR would be strictly stronger and the paper does not discuss this ceiling. - The contamination analysis evaluates the wrong objects: perplexity is computed on repository test code under two 9B/22B models, not on the focal functions or contexts under the frontier models actually evaluated, so the "low leakage risk" conclusion is only weakly supported — though the very low absolute scores provide indirect corroboration. - Prompting is a single fixed template per language with no sensitivity analysis, despite the acknowledged possibility that prompt design drives large absolute differences; "standard setting" numbers may partly measure template fit per model. - Repository selection skews toward popular, well-structured libraries (≥500 stars, standard build files, testing-friendly domains like DSA — where models do best), so difficulty for messy production codebases is likely underestimated. - The agentic comparison changes two variables at once (model scaffold and subset), and the reported TPR gains (up to 98.4% on Go) are not directly comparable to the main-table numbers. Bottom Line: This is currently the best available instrument for measuring repository-level unit test generation outside Java/Python, and its IR metric should be adopted by any evaluation harness in this area — but read it as a diagnostic tool with real blind spots, not as a settled ranking of model capability.

LatentPress: Context Compression Beyond Text and Vision (101 ▲ )

Zhengze Zhou, Hejian Sang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LatentPress, a soft-token context-compression interface in which a small reader-matched writer (~0.1% of decoder parameters) maps conversational histories and long documents into continuous vectors that a frozen LLM reads directly through its input-embedding interface, with no text reconstruction at inference. - Why it's important: Long-running agents and long-document QA pipelines currently pay a heavy latency and token cost to re-read or re-encode raw text (or to reconstruct text from images), so a machine-facing representation that cuts both write and read cost 4-16x without touching the decoder is directly deployable. - How it does it: A writer reuses two frozen decoder layers plus a tiny identity-initialized linear adapter to pool token embeddings into soft tokens, using a hand-specified rate schedule (user turns lossless, assistant turns pooled 8-32x for conversations; uniform 4-16x for documents), trained with reconstruction plus forward-KL distillation from the full-context decoder. - The good: On LongMemEval oracle-evidence QA, LatentPress reaches 0.504 accuracy at 7.70x compression versus 0.490 for uncompressed evidence and 0.426 at best for DeepSeek-OCR, and it writes in 43 ms per conversation (roughly 20x faster than the OCR route) and reads 5-9x faster than raw context. - The missing: The strongest result depends on a role-based schedule hand-tuned to preserve user turns verbatim, and the paper's own ablation shows accuracy collapses to 0.087 when roles are swapped — the evaluation never tests whether this schedule transfers to a setting where answer-bearing facts are not concentrated in user turns. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on context compression, KV/input-space prompting, or agent memory interfaces; skippable if you only need a production summarization or retrieval solution today, since the oracle-retrieval setting and in-domain training requirements limit immediate applicability.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down by Resilience (68) and Non-Obviousness (70): the headline role-based schedule is hand-specified and the paper's own role-swap ablation (0.087) shows it is benchmark-aligned rather than a general compression ability, and the oracle-evidence setting means the multi-hundred-K-token haystacks motivating the work are never tested. Novelty (75) is solid — a frozen decoder consuming directly-written soft tokens at 7.7x with a 0.1% adapter is a genuinely new combination — and Rigor (72) benefits from 5-seed error bars, mechanism-isolating ablations, and released code, but is held back by missing Gist/xRAG/AutoCompressor comparisons and single-run wall-clock numbers. Completeness (72) is a credibility positive given the direct limitations section. Impact (70) reflects the released adapters and large latency wins, discounted for per-reader writers and no retrieval integration. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*70 = 72.

Problem & Motivation: Assistants and agents accumulate conversation histories and documents that later decisions depend on, but the default machine-facing interface for stored context is discrete text: systems retrieve, summarize, prune, or (in the visual-compression line) render-then-OCR text before a language model consumes it. Text is human-readable and interoperable but pays decode/reconstruct costs even when the only consumer is a model. The gap addressed is representational: can compressed context cross into a frozen decoder directly as continuous vectors, at meaningful compression ratios, without training the decoder and without a reconstruction stage? The authors explicitly scope to the WRITE/READ boundary — not retrieval, memory updates, or conflict resolution. Key Idea: The core insight is that a frozen decoder's input-embedding interface is a sufficient and cheap injection point for compressed context: a reader-matched writer (borrowed bottom-2 frozen decoder layers + a small trained adapter) can emit soft tokens in the reader's own embedding space, and for structured conversational input, preserving the role that carries the answer-bearing facts losslessly (user turns, k=1) while pooling the rest (assistant turns, k=8-32) captures most of the value at 4-8x compression. The second enabling choice is a two-term objective: teacher-forced reconstruction plus forward-KL distillation of the frozen decoder's full-context next-token distribution into its compressed-context behavior (lambda=1.0). Methodology: Pipeline: (1) WRITE — segment context (turns or chunks), apply a rate rule pi (role-based: k_user=1, k_assistant in {8,16,32}; uniform for documents), fuse literal embeddings with contextual features via a lightweight H, mean-pool neighboring positions into soft tokens; (2) READ — concatenate soft tokens with the embedded question and generate greedily from the frozen decoder via inputs_embeds. The loss is L = L_rec + lambda*L_fkl, where L_rec is teacher-forced cross-entropy on target tokens and L_fkl is per-token forward KL between the decoder's full-context and compressed-context distributions. Training uses 2,000 UltraChat conversations (LongMemEval setting, zero-shot transfer) or QA splits (LongBench cross-domain/in-domain), 1,000 steps, batch 1 with grad accumulation 8, AdamW lr 1e-4, bf16 decoder / fp32 head. Critical design decisions: (a) freezing the borrowed encoder layers — well-justified by the ablation showing frozen beats fine-tuned at every rate (+0.018 to +0.066); (b) the role-based rate schedule — justified by the role-allocation ablation, but it exploits known input structure and is acknowledged as hand-specified; (c) reader-matched per-model writers rather than a universal compressor — necessary because soft tokens are tied to a reader, but it means the artifact does not transfer across decoders. Key Results: LongMemEval (500 oracle-evidence questions, Llama-3.1-70B judge, 5 seeds): LatentPress scores 0.476/0.478/0.504 at 4.62/6.27/7.70x compression vs 0.490 uncompressed, 0.452/0.318/0.174 for ICAE at 4.12/8.96/17.28x, 0.426/0.390/0.312 for DeepSeek-OCR at 2.33/5.97/9.34x, and 0.184 for text summary at 12.06x; uniform soft-token pooling collapses to 0.06-0.12. The frontier holds on Qwen3-8B (0.514 at 6.10x) and Qwen3-1.7B (0.434 at 4.56x vs OCR 0.264), spanning a 4.7x scale range. LongBench-QA (six English subsets, F1): raw baselines are 43.80 (Qwen2.5-7B), 47.93 (Qwen2.5-14B), 30.80 (Qwen3-8B); in-domain LatentPress at 4x reaches 49.06/57.99/39.62 respectively, but 16x falls below raw on all readers (37.78/40.30/26.12). Cross-domain transfer is only partly successful (best at 4x, e.g. 45.13 vs raw 43.80 on Qwen2.5-7B). Efficiency: write cost 43 ms/conversation vs ~934 ms OCR and 350-700 ms ICAE on one H100; read latency 0.43-0.49 s/example vs 2.44-4.14 s raw and 2.71-4.34 s cached OCR (5.0-9.2x and 5.5-9.4x); end-to-end cold-cache job time 6.0-13.7x faster than OCR. Surprising findings: uncompressed oracle evidence (0.490) is not the accuracy ceiling, and in-domain compression at 4x can exceed full-context reading (57.99 vs 47.93), consistent with compression acting as regularization or noise filtering. Baselines (ICAE, DeepSeek-OCR, LLM summaries) are current and relevant, though Gist, AutoCompressor, and xRAG are only positioned in a table, not run. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL component and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel is the combination — a fully frozen decoder, direct input-embedding consumption without reconstruction, small (~0.1%) trainable footprint, and variable role-based rates within one interface — which the positioning table shows no prior method (Gist, AutoCompressor, ICAE, xRAG, DeepSeek-OCR) achieves jointly. The individual ingredients (soft tokens, KL distillation, mean pooling, borrowed encoder layers) are standard; the empirical finding that a frozen reader can match its own uncompressed oracle-evidence accuracy at 7.7x with a 0.1% adapter is the non-obvious part. The role-based schedule itself is a heuristic observation, not a learned mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: role-allocation ablation (learned vs pooled writer: 0.476 vs 0.325; role-swapped: 0.087), encoder-training ablation (frozen wins at all rates), judge-free token-F1 confirming the accuracy ranking, per-category breakdowns, and a taxonomy of six failure modes at high compression. Error bars are reported (mean±std over 5 seeds for all learned methods; deterministic baselines noted as such); greedy decoding removes sampling variance. Code is released at https://github.com/HJSang/LatentPress. Methodological concerns: (1) the primary LongMemEval setting uses oracle evidence sessions, idealizing retrieval — the authors state this explicitly and isolate it as scope, but it means no result covers the full haystack setting; (2) the role-based schedule's core prior (preserve user turns) is well-matched to LongMemEval's user-fact-heavy question distribution, and the authors show the schedule is load-bearing (role-swap drops to 0.087) without testing the schedule on a corpus where facts live elsewhere; (3) wall-clock efficiency numbers are single-run with no variance estimates (acknowledged); (4) the strongest LongBench result requires in-domain training on the target benchmark's training splits, which is a fair but less impressive claim than the zero-shot story. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact). - Practical: Runs on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB with bf16 decoders and only a small adapter to train; no exotic hardware required. - Efficient: Trainable footprint is 4.2M-26.2M parameters (~0.1% of decoder); writing is one forward pass (43 ms/conversation) and reading is 5-9x faster than raw context, clearly beating the OCR reconstruction route on every measured axis. - Effective: Evidence supports the reading/compression claim in oracle-evidence and in-domain settings, but does not yet show it solves the end-to-end memory problem (no retrieval integration), and 16x compression degrades below raw. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 7B-14B readers and 2,000-conversation training; the paper claims future learned rate policies could push higher, but scale behavior on much longer histories or larger readers is only extrapolated. The work delivers a code artifact and trained adapters; no pretrained universal writer or model weights beyond the repo are mentioned. Strengths: (1) The interface-level framing — separating WRITE from READ and asking what representation should cross the boundary — is a clean, useful abstraction, and the honest positioning table against Gist/ICAE/xRAG/DeepSeek-OCR makes the contribution boundary easy to verify. (2) The zero-shot transfer design (UltraChat-trained writer, unseen LongMemEval labels, three readers across two families) credibly rules out benchmark memorization for the headline result. (3) The ablation suite actually isolates mechanisms: freezing vs fine-tuning the borrowed encoder, learned writer vs pooled embeddings, role allocation vs role swap, and two independent metrics (LLM-judge accuracy and token-F1) agreeing on the ranking. (4) The efficiency evaluation is unusually careful, separating write cost, warm-read cost, cold-cache and amortized-cache OCR accounting, with a failure-mode analysis (repetition loops, leaks, JSON envelopes) that anticipates reviewer objections about Qwen3-8B's high-rate degradation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: oracle-evidence evaluation isolates compression/reading and leaves retrieval, memory updates, and conflict resolution to future work; the compression schedule (role-based and uniform) is hand-specified and dynamic/learned rate allocation is future work; learned token-wise fusion H is left unimplemented; the in-domain LongBench result trades off the zero-shot property; and 16x compression loses verbatim detail and falls below raw. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them — the Limitations section is specific and the schedule is described as a deliberate heuristic for testing the interface, not oversold as a contribution. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The headline role-based result leans on a prior that happens to align with the benchmark: LongMemEval's answer-bearing facts concentrate in user turns, and the paper's own role-swap ablation (0.087) shows the schedule, not general compression ability, drives much of the gain; no experiment tests a domain where assistant or document content carries the answer-bearing detail (LongBench uses uniform rates precisely because roles are absent, so the two evaluations never stress the same mechanism). (2) xRAG, AutoCompressor, and Gist — cited as the closest methods — are positioned but not empirically compared, leaving ICAE and DeepSeek-OCR as the only head-to-head baselines. (3) LongMemEval evaluation is 500 questions with an LLM judge; per-question-type samples are small and no significance tests are reported, though 5-seed stds partially mitigate this. (4) The claim that soft tokens are a practical "machine-facing interface" rests on two benchmarks with short-to-medium histories (chunk length 2,048 tokens in training); behavior on the multi-hundred-K-token haystacks that motivate the motivation section is untested. (5) Per-reader writers mean soft tokens are not portable across decoders — a real deployment constraint for the "stored context" framing that is mentioned but not analyzed (e.g., cost of maintaining N writers). Bottom Line: This is the strongest current evidence that a near-frozen decoder can consume directly-written soft-token context competitively at 4-8x compression with ~0.1% trainable parameters and large latency wins, but a practitioner should read it as a promising interface demonstration with a benchmark-aligned schedule, not yet as a drop-in replacement for retrieval or summarization pipelines.

TRACER: Per-Tool Context Retention for LLM Agents via Consequence-Attributed Reinforcement Learning

Z Lin, Y Wu, M Yang, X Liu, Y Liu, Q Ke, Q Guo · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TRACER, a REINFORCE-trained policy that assigns a continuous retention ratio to each individual tool output during agent context compression, priced against downstream tool re-invocation cost via a learned counterfactual outcome model. - Why it's important: Enterprise data agents accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens per session from SQL and search outputs, and naive compression that deletes needed content triggers compensatory re-invocations (a single SQL call can cost 10K+ tokens), so compression-time savings are routinely erased or inverted. - How it does it: Compression is cast as a sequential per-tool decision problem; a Beta-distribution MLP policy emits per-output retention ratios, and a two-channel credit scheme fuses a uniform re-invocation penalty floor with a learned Transformer outcome model that predicts the cost delta of fully retaining each tool versus the chosen ratio. - The good: On 40 held-out production queries across three compressor backends, TRACER cuts total token consumption 29–46% versus keep-all at comparable-or-higher task success, beats a tuned static tool-type policy by 15–18% additional savings, and the outcome model is validated against real single-tool intervention rollouts (Spearman ρ=0.66, 84% sign accuracy) — an unusually direct test of a learned credit signal. - The missing: No comparison against the learned context-management baselines the paper itself cites (SUPO, AdaCoT, ACON, LLM-DCP) — all baselines are fixed heuristics — and the primary testbed is only 120 proprietary queries (40 held-out) from one production agent. - Read it or not: Worth reading for engineers building long-horizon tool agents who must allocate context budgets, and for RL researchers interested in tool-output-granularity credit assignment; skippable if you only want public-benchmark results, since the headline numbers come from an internal deployment.

Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (80) is the standout: demonstrating that standard compression heuristics can be net-costly once re-invocations are priced reframes how agent compression should be evaluated, and the compression–consequence formulation (Novelty 78) is a genuine NEW FORMULATION rather than a method combination. Rigor (70) is strong on statistics (5 seeds, Wilcoxon p=0.008, bootstrap CIs) and unusually strong on interventional validation of the outcome model (ρ=0.66, 84% sign accuracy), but is reduced for the arXiv preprint status, the 120-query proprietary testbed, and the absence of any learned baseline (SUPO, ACON, LLM-DCP) despite the paper citing them as closest competitors. Problem & Motivation Enterprise data agents answer business queries by chaining 5–10 tool calls (SQL execution, knowledge search, permission checks), each appending outputs to a monotonically growing context that routinely reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens. Existing compression — token-level pruning (LLMLingua family), turn-level summarization, step-level dropping — applies uniform strategies across heterogeneous content and, more fundamentally, evaluates compression in isolation: when a removed detail is later needed, the agent re-invokes the tool, and these recovery costs compound across repeated compression events. The authors name this the compression–consequence gap and support it empirically: several fixed baselines increase total token consumption by 3–24% relative to keeping everything. The stakeholders are operators of production agentic systems facing cost budgets and context-window limits; the gap closed is that no prior method prices downstream re-invocation consequences into per-tool retention decisions. Key Idea The core insight is that compression quality must be measured by its downstream causal consequence, not compression-time token savings: each tool output should receive a retention ratio conditioned on the query, learned by RL with a reward that explicitly penalizes post-compression tool re-invocations, and credit for the single episode-level reward should be densified by a learned outcome model performing single-tool counterfactuals (predicted cost under the chosen ratio versus r_i:=1) — COMA-style counterfactual credit assignment instantiated at tool-output granularity while the agent's action policy stays frozen. Methodology TRACER is a three-stage pipeline. (1) Phase 0 runs the agent five times per training query with full retention to establish token baselines T_base and reference tool-call timelines. (2) During online training, at each compression event a 174→128→64→16 MLP (102K total trainable parameters) maps per-tool features (size, relevance, recency, redundancy, context pressure) to per-slot Beta-distribution means over retention ratios on [0.05, 1.0]; a fixed compressor (truncation, Self-Info clause ranking, or LLM summarization) applies the ratios and the agent continues. The objective J(θ) combines a terminal reward R_base = success − λ_tok·clamp(T/T_base, 0.2, 2) with an event-local penalty P_recall,t = λ_recall·clamp((N_post−N_pre)/N_pre, 0, 2), where N_pre comes from replaying compression-trigger boundaries over the keep-all reference timelines. (3) Post-episode credit assignment uses two channels: a uniform floor distributing P_recall over active tools, and a learned 2-layer 4-head Transformer outcome model predicting per-tool re-invocation counts, log token totals, and success probability, whose counterfactual difference Ĉ(s,a) − Ĉ(s,a; r_i:=1) yields bidirectional per-tool credit. Updates are REINFORCE with a per-query EMA baseline; the Beta parameterization is shown (via the log-moment identity) to make action-independent baselines unbiased. Critical design decisions: per-output-instance slots rather than per-tool-type (justified by the query-conditioned gains over the tool-type baseline); the two-channel fusion with a 20-episode warmup and β annealing to 1 (justified by the ablation); and treating the recall penalty via time-window matching against reference timelines (acknowledged as noisy — a provenance-based upgrade is specified in Appendix E but not used in reported results, a partially justified compromise). The authors candidly note in Appendix D that the shaped surrogate gradient is not an unbiased estimator of ∇J for the stated objective. Key Results On 40 held-out production queries with a Claude Sonnet 4.6 agent: TRACER achieves token ratios of 0.694 (truncation), 0.541 (summarization), and 0.706 (Self-Info) versus keep-all — 31%, 46%, and 29% savings — while matching or exceeding baseline success (e.g., 0.77 vs. 0.73 for uniform truncation; 0.81 vs. 0.80 for summarization), with re-invocation rates held at ≤0.025. Fixed baselines often backfire: recency under summarization consumes 19% more tokens than keep-all. The tuned tool-type-conditional static policy saves 11–28%; TRACER adds 15–18% beyond it. Attribution ablation (5 seeds, pooled Wilcoxon p=0.008): the outcome model raises success by 2.2–4.8 pp and cuts iso-success token ratio by 3.4–4.7% versus RL-only with uniform credit. Interventional validation: predicted versus measured single-tool consequences give Spearman ρ=0.61–0.73 across backends, 80–86% top-3 consequence-tool overlap, 80–88% sign accuracy. Zero-shot cross-backbone transfer to GPT-5.5 and Qwen-3.7-Max retains 18–40% savings (GPT-5.5 preserves 78–87% of training-backbone gains). On a held-out AGORA-style step-level compressor, a truncation-trained policy transfers zero-shot at 31% savings; in-place training reaches 34%. On LOCA-bench (public, 5 held-out environments × 5 seeds × 3 context windows of 96K–256K), TRACER reaches 0.38–0.48 success versus keep-all's 0.37 and 18–25% token savings over heuristic baselines. Baselines are reasonable within the fixed-strategy class but no learned compression baseline is compared. Test scale is modest: 120 proprietary queries plus LOCA-bench; no stress-scale testing. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION (compression–consequence gap as a sequential per-tool retention-ratio decision with re-invocation-priced reward) plus NEW METHOD (two-channel counterfactual credit assignment at tool-output granularity with a frozen agent policy). The building blocks — REINFORCE, Beta policy heads, COMA-style counterfactual crediting, learned outcome models — are standard; the genuine novelty is the decision granularity (per-tool-output continuous ratios), the reward that prices recovery calls against keep-all reference timelines, and the empirical demonstration that fixed compression on agentic loops can be net-negative. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are present and targeted (attribution on/off with shared architecture, reward, and schedule), with 5 seeds, paired Wilcoxon tests (p=0.008 pooled), interquartile means with stratified bootstrap 95% CIs, and training curves with ±1 std bands. The iso-success token-ratio conditioning in the ablation is a thoughtful guard against savings-via-failure confounds. The interventional rollout validation of the outcome model (3 paired seeds per intervention on held-out states) is a methodological strength rarely seen for learned credit models. A code supplement exists (policy, outcome model, training loop, statistical utilities, anonymized query schema), but Appendix M is explicit that the supplement cannot support exact end-to-end replay: no production agent, no checkpoints, no raw trajectories, and some query targets deliberately redacted. Methodological concerns: evaluation is primarily on the authors' own 120-query production corpus; the recall penalty's time-window matching is noisy (provenance upgrade deferred); no learned context-management baselines; the deployment cost/benefit analysis (3–6 week break-even at $2,800 training cost, 1000 sessions/day) is a self-computed scenario, with input-token pricing only and no summarizer-model cost counted — the authors flag these exclusions themselves. Note: this is an arXiv preprint (2608.29363), not peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method trained and evaluated on a live production agent and a public benchmark). Practical: Yes — the policy and outcome model total ~102K parameters and run on CPU; the only heavy components are the existing agent and compressor calls. Efficient: Training is 25–42 hours per 100-episode five-seed compressor run (~400 compute-hours and $2,800 total campaign); inference overhead is negligible, and savings of 29–46% on total session tokens translate to a claimed 3–6 week break-even at production traffic. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on held-out production queries and LOCA-bench (success preserved or improved while tokens drop 18–46%), though LOCA-bench absolute success rates are low (0.37–0.48), so gains are partly on hard tasks where all methods struggle. Scalable: Only claimed — the 16-slot design rejects events with >16 eligible outputs, and nothing tests larger tool counts, longer horizons, or higher session volumes beyond the 1000/day deployment estimate. The work delivers a source-inspectable code supplement and trained-policy training recipe; it stops short of a deployable artifact for anyone without a compatible production backend. Strengths - The consequence-aware reframing is substantive: the paper does not merely propose a policy, it empirically demonstrates that several standard compression heuristics increase total token cost once re-invocations are counted (e.g., recency under summarization: +19%), which reframes how the community should evaluate compression for agents. - The interventional validation of the learned outcome model against real single-tool counterfactual rollouts (Table 3: ρ=0.66, 84% sign accuracy) converts a plausible modeling assumption into measured evidence — this is the paper's most credible piece of support. - Engineering prudence in the credit design: the uniform penalty floor guarantees a correct-if-coarse signal even if the outcome model degrades, and the Beta score-function derivation (Appendix A) makes the baseline choice provably unbiased rather than incidental. - Exceptional candor in the appendix: explicit boundaries on what the code supplement can and cannot reproduce, acknowledgment that the shaped gradient is not an unbiased estimator of the true objective, and a cost-benefit calculation that lists its own exclusions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors directly confront several limitations, a credibility positive: the time-window recall proxy conflates natural call-count variation (with a provenance upgrade specified but not used in reported numbers); the shaped surrogate is not an unbiased gradient estimator; transfer results are labeled "initial evidence"; the break-even analysis excludes summarizer compute, output-token pricing, latency, and maintenance, and "should not be read as net profit"; the released query file has redacted targets and is "not a drop-in replacement" for the private evaluation set; events with more than 16 eligible outputs are rejected rather than handled; and cross-backbone transfer degrades substantially for Qwen-3.7-Max (62–76% of gains retained vs. 78–87% for GPT-5.5). Analyst-Identified Gaps - No comparison against learned context-management baselines (SUPO, AdaCoM, ACON, LLM-DCP, AGORA's own retention mechanism) that the related-work section itself identifies as the closest competitors; the tool-type-conditional heuristic is the strongest baseline actually run, so the margin over the true state of practice is unmeasured. - The headline numbers rest on 40 held-out queries from a single proprietary agent and tool suite; LOCA-bench partially mitigates this, but its results show only 1–11 pp success gains over keep-all at modest savings, and the production evidence cannot be independently replayed. - The recall penalty's reference N_pre,t assumes keep-all call counts are the correct counterfactual baseline; if the compressed agent legitimately needs fewer calls (e.g., by reasoning from retained context differently), the penalty could discourage genuinely efficient behavior — this assumption is never tested. - Phase 0 requires five keep-all rollouts per training query plus reference timeline replay, a per-environment data-collection cost that is quantified for this campaign but whose burden at other scales or on other benchmarks is not analyzed. - The 16-slot capacity cap and the rejection (rather than merging) of larger events is a real scalability boundary mentioned only in the appendix feature specification, not in the main-text claims. - Cross-backbone transfer is evaluated only zero-shot against a policy trained on one backbone; whether a small amount of target-backbone fine-tuning closes the gap is unexplored (the AGORA compressor experiment shows in-domain training helps, but the analogous backbone experiment is absent). Bottom Line A practitioner deploying long-horizon tool agents gains real, well-validated insight from this work — both the negative result that fixed compression can be net-costly and the reusable consequence-attributed credit design — but anyone expecting a head-to-head comparison against modern learned context managers will need to look elsewhere, since TRACER's measured edge is only over hand-tuned heuristics on an internal testbed.

Problem & Motivation: Visual document retrieval (indexing PDF page screenshots for Visual RAG) is currently done by repurposing generative VLM architectures: either dual-tower CLIP-style encoders or causal VLMs (ColPali, ColQwen2.5, DSE) that bolt a pretrained vision tower onto a causal language model. This inherits parameter count, causal-attention overhead, and a two-model lifecycle for what is fundamentally an encoding task. Text-side evidence (Ettin) suggests native masked bidirectional encoders beat decoder-to-encoder adaptations on retrieval, but no multimodal equivalent existed: prior shared-backbone multimodal encoders (ViLT, OneR, M3AE) either start from pretrained ViTs or target generation. The gap is a native, from-scratch, bidirectional, vision-tower-free multimodal encoder sized and priced for document retrieval. Key Idea: Train one bidirectional Transformer from random initialization on raw image patches and text, using a single masked discrete-diffusion text-denoising objective where image patches remain visible and condition text recovery — the model learns to read images solely as a means of predicting masked text, with no image-side loss at all. The higher minimum corruption rate on multimodal segments (U(0.30,1) vs. U(0,1) for text-only) is the specific trick that suppresses text-only shortcuts and forces reliance on visual evidence. Retrieval heads (late-interaction + dense) are then trained jointly on top so one forward pass yields both representation types. Methodology: Three phases. (1) Tokenizer: whitespace-unconstrained byte-level BPE, 131,072 vocab, trained on FineWeb-Edu/FineWeb2-HQ/FineMath/StarCoderData plus image transcripts. (2) Pretraining: 524B packed tokens (55% text-only, 45% multimodal: FineVision, PDFA/LightOnOCR, DocAtlas, PixelProse); inputs are text tokens via ALBERT-style factorized embeddings and 32×32 patches via LayerNorm+2-layer MLP; 2D RoPE (diagonal coordinates for text, row/column for images); interleaved sliding-window (±256/±1024) and global attention; GQA with QK-RMSNorm; zero-initialized residual branches; NorMuon + MasterAdamW optimizers; WSD schedule; bfloat16 on 16–32 H100s. The loss is inverse-rate-weighted cross-entropy on masked positions (weight capped at 20). A cross-modal ablation probe measures image gain (accuracy with patches minus accuracy with zero tensors). (3) Retrieval fine-tuning: 20K steps, GradCache large-batch contrastive training, L_late (InfoNCE, τ=0.02, MeanMaxSim) plus Matryoshka dense loss at 4–5 widths; self-mined visual hard negatives in two stages; ~192K synthetic queries generated by Qwen3.5-9B and filtered by Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B; LIK fused MaxSim kernels reduce training memory. Critical design decisions: 32px patches (~¼ the tokens of 16px), no image-side loss, and dual-head joint training — the first two are motivated but not ablated, the third is ablated (joint training helps late-interaction +1.38 nDCG points on ViDoRe v3, p=10⁻⁴, but slightly hurts dense on BEIR-15, −1.85 points). Key Results: On ViDoRe v3 (8 public tasks, nDCG@10): NeoMME-260M 0.523, NeoMME-800M 0.556, vs. ColModernVBERT-250M 0.261, ColSmol-256M 0.207, ColSmol-500M 0.340, Vultron Flash-850M 0.565, ColQwen2.5-3.75B 0.524. On ViDoRe v1/v2 the 260M model reaches 0.860/0.522 nDCG@5-scale aggregates, beating sub-300M peers by 5.4 and 11.5 points. Text retrieval (BEIR-15): 800M late-interaction 0.5126 and dense 0.3686, behind dedicated models (LateOn 0.5722, GTE-ModernBERT 0.5519) despite being 5× larger. Efficiency: 51.3 pages/s at 2048×2048 on L40S (ColModernVBERT: 26.0); query latency 21.0 ms on L40S; hierarchical token pooling factor 8 + int8 queries/binary documents compresses embeddings from ~1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255×) retaining 95.19% nDCG@10; image gain reaches 38.4/40.5 percentage points at 90% text masking. Baselines are current (2025–2026 models) but many scores are taken from MTEB rather than rerun under one harness. Scale is modest but standard for encoders (524B tokens vs. ModernBERT's ~2T text tokens). A notable negative result: frozen natural-image 16-shot probes average only 13.2% accuracy, consistent with the absence of any image-side objective. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (arguably NEW FORMULATION for multimodal pretraining) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is the specific combination: a from-scratch, vision-tower-free, single bidirectional Transformer over raw patches, pretrained with image-conditioned masked text diffusion (no image loss), then adapted to dual dense/late-interaction document retrieval — the paper's own related-work survey correctly notes no prior system combines these. Each component (shared patch-text encoders à la ViLT, masked diffusion à la MDLM/LLaDA, late-interaction retrieval à la ColPali, token pooling, asymmetric quantization) is established; the deployment analysis (255× compression frontier, cross-hardware throughput grid) is competent engineering of known techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: Moderate-to-good. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensive and direct — a credibility positive. Problem & Motivation: Vision-language models fail at image change detection — missing differences, hallucinating changes, or describing them vaguely — even when prior work suggests the visual information is present in the encoder (the "perception–expression gap" per Rahmanzadehgervi et al. 2024, Orgad et al. 2025). Existing selective-verification methods require resources beyond the output text: token logits (REVERSE), attention maps (VERA), extra models (ReCoVERR), or multiple API calls (paraphrase consistency). Anyone deploying frozen, API-only VLMs on visual comparison tasks has no cheap, transparent way to decide when a response deserves a second look. SAVER targets exactly this gap: a zero-cost check on the already-produced response text. Key Idea: Correct VLM change descriptions contain checkable verbal evidence tied to the change type (a removal claim needs absence language, a color claim needs a transition phrase), while expression failures omit exactly this evidence — so the presence/absence of evidence in the output text alone is a cheap, transparent trigger for selective reprompting. The gate never judges correctness, only whether the response commits to a specific, checkable claim. Methodology: SAVER has three stages. (1) Evidence extraction: case-insensitive keyword/pattern matching (with a 20-character proximity window for change-verb-near-property patterns) maps the free-text response to a binary evidence vector e(r) ∈ {0,1}^K (e.g., K=4 for CLEVR-Change: absence, presence, color_change, material_change) plus a predicted change type from predefined type-indicating phrases, defaulting to "unclear." (2) Gate decision: trigger if the type is unclear, required evidence for the predicted type is absent, or conflicting evidence is present; otherwise accept (Eq. 2, with per-dataset required/conflict mappings in Table 1). (3) Selective reprompting: triggers route to a structured enumerate-Image-1 → enumerate-Image-2 → compare → answer prompt (chain-of-thought style); expected cost is 1 + trigger-rate API calls. Pattern sets can be generated in a single LLM call (Claude Sonnet 4.5, given the task description, taxonomy, and 16 example responses) with an optional single self-critique pass that flags over-broad patterns. Critical design decisions: (a) rule-based rather than learned gating — well justified by the transparency requirement and ablations; (b) conflict checks as a core gate structure — well justified by the Appendix F degradation study showing silent under-triggering without them; (c) hand-tuned keyword lists per dataset — acknowledged as a limitation, partially mitigated by the LLM-generation result. Key Results: On CLEVR-Change (N=632), SAVER improves accuracy over the direct-prompt baseline for all four models (all p<0.001, McNemar with Bonferroni): GPT-4o 72.8→86.2 (+13.4), Gemini 81.5→93.0, Qwen2.5-VL-7B 56.5→82.3 (+25.8, the headline gain), LLaMA-4-Scout 82.3→88.9. On MagicBrush (N=340), gains are smaller (GPT-4o +5.3, Qwen +17.6; Gemini's +0.9 is not significant), and B1 (always-structured) outperforms SAVER on all models — errors there are perceptual. On Spot-the-Diff (N=197), no significant improvement for any model (all p>0.05). SAVER beats self-consistency (SC-5: 77.4% at 5.0 calls vs. 86.2% at 1.39 calls for GPT-4o on CLEVR). Fix:Broke ratios run 2.5:1 to 74:1, and B1 breaks 3–9.5× more correct baselines than SAVER. LLM-generated patterns fully replace the manual gate on CLEVR-Change (no significant difference), fail on MagicBrush due to over-broad patterns, and a single self-critique pass restores manual-gate accuracy for two of four models. Baselines are current (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, LLaMA-4-Scout), and evaluation is at standard benchmark scale (197–632 samples per dataset), not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (inference-time, rule-based evidence gating for selective reprompting on frozen VLMs) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (expression failures are detectable from output text alone, and gate precision above a random-gate baseline predicts when selective reprompting will help, r_s=0.68–0.74). The constituent techniques — keyword matching, gate rules, chain-of-thought-style structured reprompting, self-consistency comparison — are all standard; the novelty is the combination and the diagnostic framing of verbal evidence as a zero-cost trigger signal, which is genuinely new relative to logit-, attention-, or extra-model-based verification, though the scope (change detection with a structured output taxonomy) is narrow. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough and genuinely load-bearing: random (C1), length (C2), inverted (C3), and generic-reprompt (C4) gates, plus three further gate variants (C5–C7) and a parameterized pattern-degradation study distinguishing graceful over-triggering from silent under-triggering. Statistics are reported properly: bootstrap 95% CIs (1,000 resamples), McNemar's tests with Bonferroni correction across 12 cells, seed 42, and full hyperparameters (temperature 0, max tokens, retry policy) in Appendix M. Evaluation is keyword matching manually verified at 98% agreement on 50 CLEVR samples; the authors directly confront the potential circularity between gate keywords and evaluation keywords (zero overlap on CLEVR; the inverted-gate ablation tests it). Caveats: no code, data, or logs release is mentioned; two models (Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) were retired mid-study, making one reported cell an explicit lower bound; the MagicBrush sample contains zero replace instances; and results are per-benchmark splits of 197–632 samples, so per-cell CIs are wide (e.g., LLaMA CLEVR +6.6 [3.8, 9.3]). The Claude 3.5 Sonnet result is an exploratory 200-sample subset. No evidence of Goodhart-style development-on-eval, since the gate keywords were set once and the gate/evaluation vocabularies are disjoint. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (inference-time method evaluated via API experiments on frozen models). Practical: Yes — the gate is keyword matching on already-produced text, and everything runs through commercial APIs (OpenAI, OpenRouter). Efficient: Zero overhead when the gate accepts (majority of samples; 1.11–1.49 calls/sample average), beating SC-5's 5.0 calls by 3.6× for a larger gain, though B1 is cheaper (1.0 call) and more accurate on MagicBrush. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the expression-failure problem on synthetic/edited-image benchmarks, but explicitly only a proxy for general change reasoning — perception failures pass the gate unchecked (27–46% of accepted Spot-the-Diff responses are wrong). Scalable: Not tested beyond these benchmark sizes; the authors claim extensibility to domains like manufacturing inspection and document comparison but provide no experiments there. The work delivers no software artifact — no library, CLI, or released gate configurations; it stops at paper form, though the prompts and keyword lists are printed in full and pattern generation costs ~$0.02–0.05 per dataset. Strengths: (1) The ablation design is unusually strong for a lightweight prompting paper — the inverted-gate (C3) and generic-reprompt (C4) controls cleanly separate gate logic from keyword presence and second-chance effects, which is exactly the analysis most reprompting papers omit. (2) The Fix/Broke analysis reframes the comparison with always-structured prompting around collateral damage (B1 breaks 76 vs. SAVER's 8 correct GPT-4o baselines on CLEVR), which is the practically relevant metric in high-stakes deployment. (3) The gate-precision-vs-random-gate diagnostic (Appendix E) plus the 0.68–0.74 Spearman correlation gives practitioners a cheap, pre-deployment test for whether the method will help — a rare and valuable form of scope honesty. (4) Reporting the Spot-the-Diff null result as a first-class finding, with a case study showing why (evidence-rich, perceptually wrong outputs), strengthens rather than weakens the paper's credibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that keyword vocabularies and the fixed proximity window were not tuned per dataset and that new domains require new patterns (language-dependence included); they flag and empirically rebut the gate/evaluation keyword-circularity concern; they explicitly warn against safety-critical deployment without domain-specific validation; they state that SAVER only addresses expression failures, so perceptual errors pass unchecked (Spot-the-Diff null); and they disclose that one self-critique pass fails for Qwen on MagicBrush and that the Qwen Spot-the-Diff LLM-gen cell is a lower bound due to model retirement. This is a directly and thoroughly confronted limitations section — a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Dataset scale is small — 197–632 samples per benchmark — and three benchmarks with a single task family (change captioning) is thin evidence for the general "any structured-taxonomy domain" claim; the manufacturing/medical/document extensions in Appendix K are untested speculation. (2) Evaluation by keyword matching, even at 98% verified agreement, was only validated on CLEVR-Change; the MagicBrush and Spot-the-Diff scoring was not human-verified, and recall-based Spot-the-Diff scoring interacts differently with keyword matching. (3) All main models are closed-weight APIs, so no experiment probes whether the evidence-expression gap holds for open models at other scales beyond the single 7B point. (4) The gate's required/conflict mappings embed dataset-specific assumptions about what evidence each change type needs; nothing shows these mappings transfer or how sensitive results are to a different hand-designer's choices (the ablations vary trigger selection and pattern breadth, not the underlying mapping design). (5) No code release is mentioned despite the method being trivially releasable, which limits reproducibility of the exact pattern sets. (6) The self-critique repair is evaluated on the same failure it was observed on (the bare "changed"/"different" patterns were visible in the authors' own analysis), so the critique experiment is not a fully independent test of self-repair. Bottom Line: A practitioner adding a verification layer to frozen VLMs for structured visual comparison tasks gains a genuinely useful, cheap, and transparent trigger plus a practical go/no-go diagnostic, and should read this; researchers seeking a general solution to VLM change reasoning will find the scope narrow and the strongest alternative (always-structured prompting where perception dominates) is already covered by the paper's own comparisons.

Revisiting Local Context for Long-Horizon Streaming 3D Reconstruction (28 ▲ )

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ABot-Recon, a ~1B-parameter streaming 3D reconstruction model that predicts only local quantities (a point map in the current camera frame and an adjacent-frame relative pose) within a fixed 12-frame KV-cache window, and recovers global trajectory and geometry by sequential composition — demonstrating that persistent learned long-range memory is not required for ultra-long streaming reconstruction. - Why it's important: Streaming reconstruction models that carry persistent or hierarchical long-range state degrade or become expensive as sequences grow; this work removes that machinery entirely while keeping per-frame cost and memory constant, which matters for robotics, autonomous driving, and embodied agents processing hours-long video. - How it does it: The core move is reformulating prediction targets to be reference-frame-equivariant and temporally local — adjacent-frame relative pose plus a current-frame point map — stabilized by a lightweight (4.75M-parameter) motion–visual rotation refiner and a composition-aware pose loss that supervises multi-gap composed transformations weighted by temporal gap. - The good: On Oxford Spires the model achieves 4.35 m ATE and 0.12° RPE-R, cutting both errors ~40% versus the best streaming baselines (LingBot-Map: 7.32 m; HorizonStream: 8.81 m), while running at 24.45 FPS with 6.71 GB GPU memory — faster and leaner than both. - The missing: On VBR without loop closure its ATE (30.14 m) is not better than HorizonStream (29.02 m) or LingBot-Map (29.45 m), and classical optimization-based methods with intrinsics (DPVO: 1.56 m) still dominate on Oxford Spires — the paper does not stress-test the length-generalization claim quantitatively beyond ~19k frames. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building streaming geometry, odometry, or SLAM-adjacent learned systems, because it makes a credible, well-ablated counter-argument to the prevailing trend of ever-more-elaborate temporal memory; skippable if you only care about reconstruction accuracy on bounded scenes where persistent context wins.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. This is the strongest paper in the cluster: Novelty (75) rests on a falsifiable formulation-level claim — length-invariant local targets can replace persistent long-range memory — argued against purpose-built long-horizon baselines rather than strawmen, with Non-Obviousness (75) from the counter-intuitive thesis and a well-ablated composition-aware loss that directly targets error accumulation. Rigor (70) is solid (released code, component-wise ablations, candid dataset-defect documentation) but held down by the arXiv-preprint status, absent variance reporting, ~7.7% internal training data, and the π³-initialization confound. Impact (72) is the highest here thanks to the released model and best-in-class throughput/memory, while Resilience (68) is dented by the VBR-without-loop-closure loss and the >20k-frame length-generalization claim resting on qualitative evidence. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*72 = 72.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Streaming 3D reconstruction from unbounded video requires causal inference with bounded memory and computation. First-generation streaming models (Spann3R, CUT3R, StreamVGGT) use recurrent states or finite buffers but drift over long sequences; the most recent systems (LingBot-Map, HorizonStream) extend past 10,000 frames by architecting persistent or multi-level long-range memory, making history management a central design burden. The authors observe a distinct failure mode: when pose and geometry targets are defined relative to a temporally distant reference (an anchor or first frame), the regression range grows with sequence length, making the per-step prediction problem progressively harder. The open question is whether long-horizon capability can come from the parameterization of predictions rather than from memory architecture. Key Idea: Keep the learned temporal context strictly local (windowed causal attention over K=12 frames, discarding everything older) and formulate targets whose estimation range never grows: a point map in the current camera coordinate frame and an adjacent-frame relative transformation, which are equivariant under reference-frame changes. Global trajectory and geometry are then pure composition of local measurements, and drift is fought not with memory but with a temporal rotation refiner (a gated TCN over recent motion–visual evidence that predicts an SO(3) residual) and a composition-aware loss that supervises chained poses over multiple temporal gaps with gap-weighted normalization — directly penalizing accumulated error rather than per-pair error. Methodology: The model initializes from π³'s publicly released weights and replaces absolute pose prediction with adjacent-frame relative pose. A shared encoder produces dense frame tokens and learnable camera tokens; windowed causal attention (frame i attends only to cached KV of the preceding 11 frames) yields per-frame point map Pᵢ, confidence Sᵢ, and camera tokens. Relative pose is regressed from a pairwise descriptor of adjacent camera tokens ([zᵢ₋₁, zᵢ, zᵢ−zᵢ₋₁, zᵢ⊙zᵢ₋₁]). The rotation refiner fuses motion evidence (from the pairwise descriptor) with visual evidence (coarse-to-fine cross-attention over dense tokens), aggregates a K-frame causal window via a gated TCN, and applies a residual rotation via exponential map; translation is left unrefined (justified as translation being more stable than rotation, but not ablated against refining translation). Training uses 30 datasets (62.05% synthetic / 37.95% real, including ~7.7% internal data), extensive per-dataset filtering of annotation errors (documented in appendix), and three stages: 32-frame clips (32K iters, 48×H20), 128-frame clips with the refiner enabled and differential learning rates (38K iters, 32×AMD MI308), and a 4K-iteration confidence-only calibration. The loss combines composition-aware pose loss (all pairs within gap K−1, weight αᵢⱼ ∝ (j−i)^γ), residual smoothing, point-map, normal, and confidence terms. Loop closure at inference is training-independent: FAISS retrieval over DINOv2-SALAD descriptors feeds a sparse pose-graph optimization. Inference uses FlashInfer paged KV-cache for constant-memory streaming. Key Results: Camera pose: Oxford Spires ATE 4.35 m / RPE-R 0.12° (vs. LingBot-Map 7.32 m / 2.29° and HorizonStream 8.81 m / 0.20°); loop closure lowers ATE to 4.02 m. KITTI average ATE 18.25 m (13.49 m with LC), best RPE-R (0.10°) and RPE-t (0.10 m) among streaming methods. VBR ATE 30.14 m without LC — statistically comparable to HorizonStream (29.02 m) and LingBot-Map (29.45 m) — improving to 9.99 m with LC, the best reported. On Oxford Spires, DPV-SLAM (2.95 m) and DPVO (1.56 m) achieve lower ATE but require camera intrinsics, which ABot-Recon does not. Reconstruction: best on Oxford Spires (CD 1.37 m, F1 91.81% vs. LingBot-Map 1.68/90.58) but only competitive indoors (TUM-Dynamic CD 0.11 vs. TTT3R's 0.06; 7Scenes CD 0.06 vs. LingBot-Map's 0.05). Efficiency on KITTI-02 (4,661 frames, H100): 24.45 FPS, 6.71 GB, versus LingBot-Map at 19.74 FPS/18.87 GB and HorizonStream at 8.02 FPS/13.04 GB. Ablations on KITTI/Oxford/VBR show each component matters: composition loss cuts KITTI ATE from 56.60 to 27.66 m, 128-frame training to 22.31 m, and the 0.48%-parameter refiner to 18.25 m. Baselines are current (2025–2026 systems), all reproduced under a unified protocol except SLAMFormer-∞ (quoted from its paper). Maximum quantitatively evaluated length is 18,846 frames (VBR); qualitative results reach 48,656 frames and 8.6 km with loop closure. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel element is the claim — backed by experiments — that long-horizon streaming reconstruction needs no persistent learned long-range state if prediction targets are kept local and composition is directly supervised; the components (windowed causal attention from StreamVGGT/STream3R, relative-pose ideas from R3, TCN refinement, SLAM loop closure) are known techniques, but their combination under a length-invariant target parameterization, plus the composition-aware multi-gap loss, is a real conceptual contribution rather than an engineering tweak. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-structured (baseline → +composition loss → +long-sequence training → +refiner), isolating each component's contribution across three benchmarks; the running-RPE and multi-gap-RPE analyses (Figure 6) specifically probe the drift mechanism, which is the right diagnostic for the claim. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, and single-sequence ATE variability is large (e.g., VBR Campus-0: 11.06 m vs. Colosseo-0: 48.12 m for the same method). Code is released (github.com/amap-cvlab/ABot-Recon) with a project page. Methodological concerns: training uses ~7.7% unquantified internal Alibaba data; the backbone is initialized from π³, so the result is a reformulation plus fine-tuning, not from-scratch validation of the formulation; some baseline results are quoted from papers (SLAMFormer-∞); and all trajectories use Sim(3) alignment, which partially absorbs scale drift — standard but favorable to all methods equally. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2608.27529), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system evaluated on benchmarks, with code released). - Practical: Runs frame-by-frame on a single NVIDIA H100 at 24.45 FPS and 6.71 GB peak memory; no intrinsics required at test time. - Efficient: Uses less memory and higher throughput than the strongest baselines (LingBot-Map, HorizonStream); CUT3R/TTT3R are slightly faster but drift far more. - Effective: Strong evidence for the stated long-sequence tracking problem on 4–19k-frame benchmarks; the intrinsics-free constraint is a real deployment advantage over DPVO/Droid-W, though it concedes absolute accuracy to them where intrinsics are available. - Scalable: Compute is O(NK) and memory O(K) by construction, and qualitative results reach 48k frames, but no quantitative evaluation beyond ~19k frames — the 10–100× scaling claim rests on architecture and qualitative evidence, not measurement. Delivers a software artifact: released code, model, and project page; the loop-closure backend is described as training-independent and pluggable. Strengths: - A clean, falsifiable thesis — length-invariant local targets beat persistent long-range memory — argued against baselines specifically designed for the long-horizon setting, not strawmen. - The composition-aware pose loss is a well-motivated and ablated contribution: supervising chained transformations with gap-weighted emphasis directly targets the error-accumulation mechanism, cutting KITTI ATE from 56.60 to 27.66 m on its own. - Exceptional efficiency result: best-in-class tracking accuracy at lower memory (6.71 GB) and higher throughput (24.45 FPS) than the direct competitors it beats. - The 4.75M-parameter refiner delivering 18–27% ATE reductions is a strong accuracy-per-parameter result, and the appendix's candid documentation of dataset-annotation defects (BlendedMVS flips, TartanAir sky depth, OmniWorld intrinsics) is a useful contribution in itself. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that gains are less pronounced on compact indoor benchmarks (7Scenes, TUM-Dynamic) because persistent geometric context remains useful in spatially confined scenes with frequent revisits, and that their reconstruction results are "not uniformly the best." They acknowledge that loop closure helps only when revisits exist, and list future needs: dynamic-scene handling, external memory, larger pretraining, and selective long-range constraints where local continuity is ambiguous. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline "superior long-horizon performance" claim is uneven: on VBR without loop closure, ABot-Recon's ATE (30.14 m) is marginally worse than both HorizonStream (29.02 m) and LingBot-Map (29.45 m); the decisive win there comes only from the bolt-on loop-closure backend, which is standard SLAM machinery rather than part of the learned formulation. - No ablation of the choice to refine rotation but not translation — the stated justification is asserted, not tested. - Single-run results with no variance reporting across a heterogeneous 30-dataset mixture make the ~1–3 m margins over LingBot-Map on Oxford Spires hard to assess statistically. - The length-generalization claim (fixed prediction range ⇒ sequence-length invariance) is quantitatively validated only to 18,846 frames; the 48k-frame results carry no ground truth, so the strongest version of the claim is untested. - Reliance on π³ initialization leaves open whether the local formulation or the inherited prior carries the performance; a from-scratch or alternative-backbone ablation is absent. - Internal (non-public) training data and the closed internal Synthetic/Real splits limit exact reproducibility of the reported numbers even with released code. Bottom Line: A practitioner building streaming perception systems should read this: it delivers a credible, efficient, well-ablated demonstration that local prediction plus reliable composition can match memory-heavy architectures on long sequences — though the evidence is strongest for odometry-style tracking, weakest on the generalization claim beyond 20k frames, and the field's memory-based alternatives remain competitive on several benchmarks.

#47 — Innovative (71)

Benchmarking the Robustness of Agentic Systems to Adversarially-Induced Harmful Behaviors

J Nöther, A Singla, G Radanovic · openreview.net · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BAD-ACTS, a benchmark with a 16-category taxonomy of harms, five multi-agent environments, and a curated dataset of 937 harmful actions (238 manually edited core + 699 extended) for measuring how easily LLM-based multi-agent systems can be manipulated into executing harmful actions. - Why it's important: Agentic systems can execute real-world actions (purchases, messages, file operations, code execution), so a single corrupted or adversarial agent turning peers into harm-executors is a live deployment risk, not a hypothetical. - How it does it: The benchmark corrupts one agent in an emulated multi-agent environment with a target action from the dataset and scores success via rule-based (keyword/tool-log) detection of the harmful tool execution, avoiding unreliable LLM judges. - The good: Attack success rates of 40%–90% across eight models, replicated over three seeds with standard errors, plus the counter-intuitive finding that more capable models (Llama-70b, GPT-4.1) are systematically more vulnerable, with per-category breakdowns showing agent-specific harms (unauthorized transactions, file deletion, resource stealing) succeed far more often than text-generation harms (toxicity, impersonation). - The missing: The proposed Guardian Agent defense reduces attack success rate by only 27%–63% relative, and the benchmark's environments and harmful actions were generated with LLMs the authors themselves curated — the defense is evaluated on the same benchmark it was designed on, and no external validation exists. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate multi-agent LLM systems and need a concrete safety testbed with a reusable taxonomy; skip it if you only care about single-agent jailbreaking, which AgentHarm and InjecAgent already cover.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is solid — the adversary-as-peer threat model for tool-using multi-agent systems is genuinely new relative to InjecAgent/AgentHarm, and the keyword-vs-LLM-judge validity study is a real methodological contribution. Non-Obviousness (72) is lifted by the capability-robustness inversion and the agent-specific-vs-text-harm guardrail dissociation, both empirically confirmed across categories. Rigor (70) is above area norms (three seeds with standard errors, released code, disclosed costs) but is pulled down by Goodhart circularity — the Guardian Agent defense is developed and evaluated on the same benchmark — plus fully emulated tools with an always-passing code executor and self-validated human agreement. Completeness (70) and Resilience (70) are respectable given the authors' candid limitations section, but the missing defense baselines, fixed zero-shot adversary, and homogeneous model populations leave the defense claims and threat-magnitude claims vulnerable.
