Problem & Motivation: Education platforms increasingly need executable learning artifacts — structured-JSON slides and runnable HTML simulations, games, diagrams, 3D visualizations, code playgrounds — but general-purpose LLMs and coding-agent scaffolds fail this workload in production. The paper identifies three gaps: speed (agent loops spend minutes per artifact; 200–600s per edit in cited systems), reliability (schema-valid outputs that render 0/120 under a strict validator; HTML pages that screenshot well but have dead buttons and physics-violating simulations), and cost (flagship coding models like the 744B-parameter GLM-5 price out precisely the under-resourced schools and families who need the tooling most). The authors observe that no prior task formalizes generation of executable, contract-bound educational artifacts: slide-generation work evaluates text outlines, and web-UI benchmarks carry no rendering contract or educational semantics. A telling motivation datum: the bare Qwen3.8-27B base parses 118/120 slide briefs but renders 0/120 because the renderer's field-naming convention is a learned data contract no model can deduce zero-shot. Key Idea: The core insight is that "interactivity must be measured, not judged": any reward dimension that can only be assessed from a static screenshot (the artifact's opening frame) will be gamed by an RL policy, which will produce visually rich, functionally dead pages. The paper operationalizes this with (a) an execution-aware data pipeline where SFT targets are accepted only after render-and-judge verification (slides) or surviving a Chromium interactivity probe (HTML), and (b) a hardened reward whose interactivity term is the output of a Playwright-driven Chromium probe that drives the page's controls and detects response via Canvas 2D draw-call signatures (fillRect, drawImage, stroke, fill), WebGL framebuffer sampling, and a quiescence baseline that subtracts self-running animation — with a hard-fail gate that assigns zero to pages a probe confirms inert, deliberately diverging from human partial credit to suppress the gradient toward non-functional output. Methodology: Three post-training stages on public base models (CogEvol-4B from dense Qwen3.5-4B; CogEvol-27B from hybrid Qwen3.8-27B with 48 gated-delta-net + 16 full-attention layers), no pre-training. Stage 1, mix SFT: 53,687 (system contract, user brief, verified artifact) triples — 32,816 slides from production-seeded synthesis (teacher candidates from Gemini 3.1 Pro/3.5 Flash passing parse → schema validation → canonicalization → production render → multimodal judge, best-of-two arbitration) and 20,871 HTML pages mined from 25,475 hard failures of the incumbent production model out of 117,309 executed generations, regenerated and re-probed. Stage 2, slide RL under R = 0.6·VLM + 0.4·rule (GRPO on slime, 8–16 H800s, group size 8, KL 10⁻³, 250 rollouts), where the rule engine scores geometry (collision, overflow, canvas use) and evolved through five anti-exploit versions. Stage 3, HTML RL under the hardened composite: visual quality (0.4), content (0.3), dual-viewport (0.2), measured interactivity (0.3), each mapped to a defect score with reward = 1 − weighted mean. All rewards see only rendered pixels, probe traces, and style-stripped source listings — never the model's account of what it built. Two further engineering contributions: scaffold editing (retrieve nearest of ~1M historical templates, emit per-component KEEP/MODIFY/REPLACE decisions at JS-function granularity, reconstruct programmatically, with tiered fallback to direct generation), and MAIC-UI Click-to-Locate editing (XPath/CSS anchoring on click, unified-diff output, lean context). A Section 7 case study ports the stack to Ascend 910 A3 via FP8→INT8 W8A8 re-quantization with per-tensor Noise-Floor Arbitration, attention-dispatch override, and replica-first (low-TP) topology. Critical design decisions — probe-based interactivity, hard-fail gate despite disagreeing with human raters on 18 zeroed pages, and shipping the serial rather than mixed RL recipe — are each explicitly justified with ablations. Key Results: On the internal suites: CogEvol-27B scores 83.7 on slide-std (best external flagship under the 34 KB spec is Qwen3.8-Max at exactly 83.7, but it collapses to 35.3 on HTML-500 with 204/500 dead pages) and 63.7 on HTML-500 with zero hard failures, versus Claude Opus 4.8 at 67.2 HTML / 79.5 slide with 19 dead pages, and GPT-5.4 at 66.0 with 13 dead pages. Production medians over 220k live requests: 17s per slide (P95 26s), 59s per interactive page (P95 107s). Post-training increments: HTML RL lifts 4B from 52.8 to 61.7 (+9.0pp); the hardened reward reverses the old-reward game collapse from 18.8 to 57.6; human testing shows unusable pages halving (25%→10%) and entry failures going 2/24→0/30. Cost: 15–22× lower per-artifact API cost than Claude Opus 4.8/GPT-5.4 at list prices; CogEvol-4B ~100× lower. Scaffold editing: −75.7% tokens/latency internal (12,344→2,999 tokens; 67.2s→16.0s) at 94% success, −59.7% on an external test set; MAIC-UI edits average 6.3s vs 151.7s direct-API and 34.3s for Claude Code on the same backbone. On external benchmarks CogEvol-27B is competitive but not leading: PresentBench 50.48 vs Claude Sonnet 4.6's 53.54; EE-Eval raw 57.50 vs 57.96 for its own old-reward twin and 57.60 for repaired Claude, though error-free on 123/127 pages. Ascend 910 A3 achieves application-level parity with A800 (500/500 valid parses both), with the 3.63× throughput gap decomposed as 1.48× hardware × 2.45× missing speculative decoding. Baselines are current-generation flagships (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.6 Flash, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Qwen3.8-Max) run through the identical harness — strong, though all external models face a contract they never trained on. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (Learning Environment Generation formalized as contract-bound executable artifact generation), NEW METHOD (the canvas-signature interactivity probe and hard-fail gate as an RL reward component, plus the probe-hardening methodology), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (slide-std/slide-short and HTML-500 with a probe gate — though internal-only), and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (scaffold editing, MAIC-UI diff editing, Ascend port). The genuinely novel pieces are the measured-not-judged interactivity reward and the honest reward-hacking case study; the rest — GRPO with VLM-judge rewards, SFT distillation from teacher models, retrieval-then-edit generation, unified-diff editing, quantized deployment — is competent combination of existing techniques applied to this new task. The paper is upfront about this composition. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a technical report: mixture and base-model ablations (Table 2, including a falsification control showing the GBS4 schedule was a control, not a candidate), a pure-A/B reward-hardening experiment (same checkpoint, data, schedule; only the reward changed), judge-prompt calibration with ceiling-occupancy analysis (Table 5), and reward–human agreement on 128 independently rated pages (Spearman ρ up to 0.749). Scoring discipline is enforced — all baselines re-scored whenever the reward version changes, and an evaluation-harness bug that silently inflated RL gains (+11.6pp apparent → +4.8pp real) is disclosed. However: one generation per model per benchmark, no seeds/error bars/significance tests on headline numbers; the benchmarks, judge prompts, and scoring pipeline are kept internal to prevent contamination, so third parties cannot independently verify HTML-500 or slide-std numbers; the HTML-500 scorer is the production RL reward itself (training/eval circularity), and the scorer VLM is a Qwen3.8-family 27B model — the same family as the Qwen3.8-Max baseline, which the authors disclose. CogEvol-4B weights (Apache 2.0, HF + GGUF) and the MAIC-UI harness are released; CogEvol-27B is API-only with external testing "upon request." Flagged methodological concern: the slide comparison gives flagships a 34 KB spec they never trained on while CogEvol carries the contract in weights — a fair-faith but structurally favorable asymmetry, partially mitigated by the slim-contract appendix. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with strong SYSTEMS elements — models trained, served in production since 2026-08 on OpenMAIC's live traffic). Practical: Yes — CogEvol-4B runs on-device via Q4 K M GGUF; the 27B is served as a low-cost API and demonstrated on Ascend 910 A3 NPUs as well as A800s. Efficient: 27.7B dense parameters (26.9× fewer than GLM-5's 744B), 17s/59s single-pass medians, 15–22× cheaper per artifact than flagship APIs, ~76% token/latency reduction via scaffold editing, 6.3s edits via MAIC-UI. Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem on internal suites (zero hard failures on 500 pages), directional human testing, and two independent external benchmarks where the model is competitive but not leading — so effectiveness is well-supported for reliability/latency, less differentiated for raw slide quality. Scalable: Demonstrated, not merely claimed — 220k production requests over seven days and a live production deployment — though the 27B's quality claims rest on the authors' own harness and the Ascend deployment carries a 3.63× throughput penalty. Delivers a real software artifact: open weights, GGUF build, editing harness, deployment guide; the benchmarks and reward server remain closed. Strengths: - The reward-hacking case study is the paper's best contribution: a documented failure (games at 18.8 under re-scoring, masked as −9.7pp by the screenshot judge), a controlled fix isolating the reward as the only variable, and a transferable principle — dimensions absent from the reward don't just fail to improve, they get destroyed by RL. Few industrial reports disclose this class of failure with numbers. - The interactivity probe is a real technical contribution: Canvas 2D draw-call signature tracking with quiescence baselining solves a genuine measurement problem (self-running animations and canvas-resident state) that DOM-fingerprint approaches get wrong, and the hard-fail gate's deliberate divergence from human partial credit is explicitly argued (Section 5.4) rather than hidden. - Honest self-auditing throughout: the harness bug that inflated gains, the false-positive contract check that initially rejected 4,412 valid examples, the GBS4-schedule control, disclosed known corpus biases (69.8% simulations, no 3D examples), and the admission that the one-big-round recipe loses to serial on HTML (59.0 vs 61.7). - The Ascend section contributes reusable diagnostic tests (Hot–Cold Divergence, Bitwise Speculative Equivalence) for silent recurrent-state corruption — a sound observation that GDN state S_t = g_t⊙S_{t−1} + β_t k_t v_t^T has no inverse and therefore no truncation, blocking prefix caching and speculative decoding on any such stack. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations unusually directly: (1) corpus biases (slides skew sparse at mean 14.4 elements; HTML corpus lacks 3D and over-represents simulations), plus a train–serve brief mismatch that blunted initial deployment; (2) the one-big-round multi-task recipe is validated on 4B only, with 27B confirmation pending; (3) the hardened reward prices code playgrounds more harshly (53.6 vs 59.1) and it is unclear how much is real quality loss vs judge calibration; (4) defects the reward does not price — language mixing and element stacking — survive both human-testing rounds unchanged; (5) cross-page coherence across a multi-page course is unresolved; (6) scaffold-editing gains depend on corpus coverage (−37% for games to −88% for 3D) and can fall to near-baseline for structurally distant requests; (7) the human evaluations are small (n=24 vs n=30) and directional, not strict A/Bs; (8) the hard-fail gate deliberately scores 18/128 rated pages below human judgment, a trade-off they defend explicitly. This candor is a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline benchmark (HTML-500) is scored by the exact reward used for RL training, on topics curated by the same team — Goodhart risk by construction. PresentBench and EE-Eval mitigate this but are narrower (slide checklists; CS explorable explanations) and show the model trailing, not leading, external flagships; the reliability advantage (zero hard failures) has no external equivalent. - The scorer VLM is a Qwen3.8-family 27B — the same family as the Qwen3.8-Max baseline that ties on slides — an affiliation the paper discloses but does not test for (e.g., a non-family judge as robustness check). - No confidence intervals anywhere: with one generation per model at temperature 0.7 on HTML, per-case variance and 1–2 point overall differences (e.g., 63.7 vs 67.2) cannot be assessed for significance. - CogEvol-27B's central selling points (production medians, serving quality, OpenMAIC deployment) are unverifiable self-reports; no third party can audit the 220k-request latency claims or the flagship API costs (list prices may not reflect actual partner pricing). - No learning-outcome evaluation whatsoever: the entire quality story is artifact-level (fidelity, layout, playability), despite the motivation resting on decades of classroom studies — the paper never tests whether generated environments teach anyone anything. - The reward-hacking "fix" is validated on the authors' own probe and judge; whether the hardened model genuinely produces playable games under adversarial or human play at scale (beyond 8 games in the manual round) is untested. Bottom Line: For practitioners training RL policies over executable artifacts — UI generation, agentic coding, tool use — this is a genuinely useful read for its measured-not-judged reward design and its candid hacking case study, but its model-quality claims should be treated as vendor-reported on private suites, and anyone seeking an independent model comparison should weight the external PresentBench/EE-Eval results, where CogEvol is competitive rather than dominant.

UHI-Bench: Benchmarking Dual-Source Urban Heat Island Modeling Across Cities in Diverse Climate Regimes

W Ling, C Liu, Y Xie, A Xu, Z Zeng, Z Li · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces UHI-Bench, the first benchmark that co-registers dual-source urban heat island observations (land-surface-temperature UHI and near-surface air-temperature UHI) with hourly meteorological drivers and static urban-morphology features on a common 1 km hourly grid across 20 cities, and evaluates 20+ baselines from four model families on five tasks plus two diagnostic analyses. - Why it's important: Substituting satellite LST-UHI for pedestrian-relevant AirT-UHI measurably biases estimates of human heat exposure, and most cities — especially in data-poor regions — lack the dense station networks needed for dual-source modeling, making cross-city transfer guidance practically valuable for urban climate adaptation. - How it does it: The core move is spatiotemporal co-registration of heterogeneous data (MSG/SEVIRI LST downscaled 3 km→1 km via RF-TsHARP, DWD HOSTRADA air temperature for German cities, ERA5-plus-learned-residual air temperature for international cities) into a unified benchmark organized around a signal–mechanism–transfer protocol with temporally held-out (2023–2025) evaluation. - The good: The cross-city transfer experiments yield a genuinely actionable finding — climate-diverse source sets of 4 cities cut zero-shot LST-UHI forecasting MAE from ~3.4 to ~0.8 relative to four same-climate (Cfb) source cities, and directed-pair analysis shows UHI-regime overlap predicts transferability better than Köppen climate labels (e.g., Hamburg→Lagos error 26% lower than Hamburg→Johannesburg despite larger climate contrast). - The missing: For the 8 non-German dual-source cities, the AirT-UHI 'ground truth' is itself a model product (ERA5 + a residual-correction model trained on German HOSTRADA–ERA5 residuals, held-out R²≈0.79), so imputation/forecasting results on those cities partly measure reconstruction of the authors' own downscaling model rather than real near-surface air temperature. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on spatiotemporal ML for climate/urban data, benchmark design, or time-series foundation-model evaluation; skip it if you want methodological novelty in model architecture or validated ground-truth heat-exposure prediction outside the MSG/SEVIRI satellite footprint.

Problem & Motivation: Urban heat islands are observed through two physically distinct signals — satellite-derived land-surface-temperature UHI (LST-UHI) and near-surface air-temperature UHI (AirT-UHI) — but most prior studies use a single source, and recent large-scale evidence (Zhang et al., Nat. Commun. 2026) shows substituting one for the other substantially biases the magnitude and intra-urban variability of human-relevant heat exposure. Dual-source modeling requires jointly aligned dynamic meteorological drivers and static urban morphology, but these are spatiotemporally incompatible (coarse meteorology, seasonal morphology updates); LST has cloud gaps (20–76% missingness across the 16 core cities) and AirT requires dense station networks that data-poor cities lack. The motivating question is whether models trained on some cities transfer to unseen cities across climate regimes, which would enable heat modeling where observations are absent. The audience is urban-climate modelers and the spatiotemporal ML community; no existing dataset pairs both UHI sources with aligned covariates (per the paper's Table 1 comparison against UrbClim, Global UHII, SeoulTemp, US SUHI Database, etc.). Key Idea: The core insight is that LST-UHI and AirT-UHI must be benchmarked as complementary, non-interchangeable targets under a unified 'signal–mechanism–transfer' protocol: signal validity (are the two sources consistent?), mechanism (which covariates help which source and task?), and transfer (what makes a source city useful for an unseen target?). The key design trick enabling the dataset is the rural-annulus differencing definition of UHI (local 1 km temperature minus the mean of a 15–25 km cropland/grassland annulus), which cancels shared sensor/reanalysis biases and turns heterogeneous absolute-temperature products into comparable anomaly targets on one hourly grid. Methodology: Data construction: (1) LST from MSG/SEVIRI (nominal 3 km) downscaled to 1 km with an RF-TsHARP random-forest thermal-sharpening model, validated by 3 km round-trip consistency and MODIS 1 km comparison; cloud-contaminated pixels are kept as missing, not filled. (2) AirT from DWD HOSTRADA for 8 German cities; for 8 international cities, ERA5 plus a residual-correction model trained on HOSTRADA–ERA5 residuals from the German cities (held-out R²≈0.79), following geographically weighted regression–style merging. (3) Hourly ERA5-Land drivers (wind components, cloud cover, dewpoint, boundary-layer height, downward solar radiation) and static morphology features (building coverage/height, road/POI density, nightlights, NDVI, water fraction, elevation, wind-exposure proxy). All variables are aligned on absolute UTC timestamps with stable 1 km pixel IDs; train on 2015–2022, evaluate 2023–2025. Evaluation spans 20+ baselines in four families (statistical/geostatistical: persistence, climatology, IDW, kriging variants; classical ML: RF, XGBoost; deep spatiotemporal: SAITS, GraphWaveNet, IGNNK, LSTM, DLinear, DeepUHI; time-series foundation models: Chronos-2, TimesFM, MOIRAI-2, ChronosAdapter) across five tasks — extreme-event detection (F1), LST cloud-gap imputation (MAE by cloud-coverage bins using real cloud masks), AirT sparse imputation (simulated station masks), 1–96 h dual-source forecasting, and XGBoost/SHAP driver attribution with climatology removed — plus Task 3: zero-shot transfer comparing climate-homogeneous (Cfb-4/Cfb-7) vs. climate-diverse (Diverse-4/Diverse-7) source sets, and 42 directed city-pair transfers among 7 cities. Critical design decisions: real cloud masks for imputation (well justified — missingness structure matters, as the Bucharest vs. Lagos comparison shows); residual-model AirT for non-German cities (a necessity-driven choice, but it embeds a German-trained bias into 'ground truth'); input ablation suffixes (base, +m, +s, +s+m) applied consistently (well justified). Key Results: No model is uniformly best, but foundation models are consistently competitive and stable. Representative numbers: in extreme detection, XGBoost+m reaches AirT-UHI F1 of 0.789 (Lagos) to 0.949 (Cologne) while LST-UHI detection stays hard (F1 0.226–0.708); Chronos-2+m gives the best LST F1 in several cities (0.501 in Lagos, 0.708 in Johannesburg). In LST cloud-gap imputation, Chronos-2+m attains MAE ≈0.54–0.59 in Cairo even at >75% cloud cover, versus ≈1.7–2.6 for kriging/IDW, while GraphWaveNet is the strongest deep baseline under large gaps (Cairo >75% bin MAE 0.678). In AirT imputation, XGBoost+s+m reaches MAE 0.027–0.034 in Lagos across all missing bins; Chronos-2 is extremely stable (MAE ≈0.0086–0.0088 in Munich). Forecasting: AirT-UHI is far easier than LST-UHI (e.g., Lagos average MAE 0.064 vs 0.737 for XGBoost+s+m); DLinear wins some Cfb LST cities. Task 3a is the headline: XGBoost with a Cfb-7 source set gets MAE 3.068–3.967 at +1/+6/+24 h, but a Diverse-4 set gets 0.813–1.174 — climate diversity matters far more than source-set size, with diminishing returns from Diverse-4 to Diverse-7. Task 3b: transfer is directed and asymmetric (Buenos Aires is the hardest AirT target, ~105% higher incoming error than the next-hardest, yet a good source; Lagos is the strongest LST source, ~44% lower outgoing error than Hamburg). Scale: ~81,755 urban pixels, 22 cities, 9 Köppen classes (10 in the data section — the paper is internally inconsistent), 2015–2025, but all within the MSG/SEVIRI full-disk domain (no East Asia, North America, or Oceania). Baselines include recent foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM, MOIRAI-2), so the comparison set is current. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the first dual-source (LST-UHI + AirT-UHI) co-registered benchmark with aligned covariates and standardized transfer protocols, and (b) the empirical findings that climate-diverse source sets dominate same-climate expansion and that UHI-regime overlap, not Köppen labels, predicts transferability. The modeling machinery is entirely standard — XGBoost, GraphWaveNet, Chronos-2 applied off-the-shelf — and the data pipeline combines established techniques (RF-TsHARP downscaling, rural-ring UHI differencing, GWR-style residual correction). This is a competent, well-motivated benchmark paper, not a methods contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive and structural: every model is run under base / +meteorology / +static / +both input configurations, which directly supports the covariate-utility claims, and imputation results are stratified by missingness bins computed from real cloud/station masks. Code (github.com/wyling0v0/UHI-Bench.git) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/WyLing0v0/uhi-bench) are publicly released, with dataloaders and documented extension procedures. Weaknesses: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are mentioned anywhere in the provided text; the residual-correction AirT product for 8 of 16 dual-source cities makes several 'ground-truth' targets partially model-generated, and its R²≈0.79 is validated only against German data, which are climatologically atypical (Cfb); the 2015–2022/2023–2025 temporal split is sound, but the transfer source/target city sets are small (6 targets in Task 3a), so the diversity conclusion rests on few effective comparisons; and the abstract says 9 Köppen classes while Section 3 says 10 — a consistency slip. The downscaling validation (round-trip, MODIS comparison) is reasonable but reported only qualitatively in the main text. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a released dataset + evaluation pipeline, empirically evaluated). - Practical: Yes — all data derive from freely accessible products (ERA5(-Land), MSG/SEVIRI via EUMETSAT, DWD, OSM, Copernicus), and the best models are CPU-class (XGBoost) or small pretrained FMs. - Efficient: Favorable — classical ML and DLinear are cheap; foundation-model zero-shot inference dominates no expensive per-city training, though Chronos-2-scale inference is the costliest option. - Effective: Partially — the benchmark demonstrates learnability and relative model rankings, but for half the cities the AirT target is model-derived, so 'effective at predicting real pedestrian heat exposure' is only directly evidenced for the 8 German cities and 2 station cities. - Scalable: Claimed but only partially tested — the authors show the pipeline extends within the MSG/SEVIRI domain, but geographic coverage is capped by one geostationary satellite, and 10× more cities would require the same downscaling/residual machinery whose errors compound; 100× global scale is not demonstrated. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (dataset, construction pipeline, dataloaders, baseline implementations), not just a paper. Strengths: - The dual-source framing is a real contribution: constructing comparable LST-UHI and AirT-UHI targets for 16 cities on a shared hourly grid, with real cloud masks and honest retention of missingness, enables questions no prior dataset supports (per Table 1, closest alternatives provide one source or monthly resolution). - The input-suffix ablation design (+m/+s/+s+m across every task) converts a leaderboard into a mechanism study, yielding the source-dependent covariate pattern (meteorology helps LST imputation; static morphology helps AirT imputation) — a reusable finding for practitioners. - The climate-diverse vs. climate-homogeneous transfer experiment is a clean, well-controlled comparison with a large, decision-relevant effect (MAE ~3.4 → ~0.8), and the directed-pair diagnostics that tie transferability to UHI-regime overlap give source-selection guidance that generalizes beyond this dataset. - Releasing pipeline, splits, and dataloaders with documented extension to new cities within the MSG footprint raises the bar over prior one-city UHI studies. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that 'no model is uniformly best,' that covariate utility is model-, task-, and climate-dependent, that foundation-model gains under high missingness must be interpreted alongside the spatial structure of the missing region, and that representative city subsets were used due to data availability and quality (Appendix E.1), with extension limited to the MSG/SEVIRI full-disk domain. They also flag that the four LST-only and two station-only cities are not dual-source. They confront task-dependence of results candidly. However, they do not explicitly acknowledge that the international AirT-UHI targets are model products, nor the German-centric skew of the residual model — the main limitations section is thin overall, with most caveats embedded in results discussion rather than a dedicated treatment. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Circularity in international AirT-UHI: 8 of 16 dual-source cities have AirT targets produced by the authors' own ERA5-residual model trained on German residuals; Tasks 2b/2c results there partially reflect recovering that model's smooth output, and the reported near-zero MAEs (e.g., Chronos-2 at 0.0086 in Munich, 0.047 in Lagos) should be read against different effective noise floors per city group. - German-heavy design: half the dual-source cities are German (HOSTRADA), so climate-diversity conclusions rest on one downscaling/residual lineage and one satellite; no East Asian or North American city exists to check the transfer findings. - No uncertainty quantification: single-run results, no seeds, no confidence intervals; several headline contrasts (e.g., Diverse-4 vs Diverse-7 differences of ~0.02 MAE) may not be significant. - Confounded source-set comparison: Diverse-4 vs Cfb-4 differ in both climate and which specific cities are included (Stuttgart+Cairo+Lagos+Riyadh vs four German cities), so city identity and climate diversity are not fully disentangled. - Transfer evaluated mainly on LST forecasting in Task 3a (AirT is covered only in the 7-city Task 3b), so the diversity recommendation is better supported for one source than the other. - LST-UHI missingness of 20–76% means LST-based conclusions are drawn from a heavily censored target; how the UHI definition interacts with cloud-conditional sampling (clear-sky hours only) is not analyzed. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating spatiotemporal models on urban climate data, UHI-Bench is worth adopting as a benchmark and its transferability findings are genuinely useful; but its AirT ground truth outside Germany is partly synthetic and its geographic footprint is satellite-capped, so its headline numbers should be treated as conditional on those construction choices rather than as validated heat-exposure prediction.

Evaluating the Hidden Costs of Personalization in Large Language Models (24 ▲ )

Yumeng Wang, Yuchen Wu, Cheng Qian, Zhiyuan Fan, Hyeonjeong Ha, Shujin Wu, Jiayu Liu, Heng Ji, Ge Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 1 Sep 2026
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces PRISK, a factorial evaluation framework with 3,000 manually verified test cases and tailored metrics that measures three behavioral side effects of LLM personalization — irrelevant personalization, preference narrowing, and sycophantic bias — across 13 models under four controlled context conditions. - Why it's important: Commercial assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) now persist and condition on user profiles and memories, but no prior benchmark causally attributes which pipeline component (profile vs. retrieved memory) drives which behavioral degradation, leaving deployment risk unmeasured. - How it does it: It ablates a 2×2 factorial design (base / profile-only / retrieval-only / both) over (profile, memory, query) triples where memory is semantically adjacent to the query but contains no answer content, then attributes bias via mixed-effects regression and counterfactual preference inversion. - The good: The causal attribution is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: mixed-effects models with power analysis show the profile is the dominant driver (e.g., β1 = −2.08, partial η² = 0.637 for sycophancy, p < 0.001), and inverting a user's stated preference flips 94.8% of sycophantic responses. - The missing: The LLM judge (GPT-5.1) shares a vendor lineage with evaluated GPT-5.4 models, memory histories are purely synthetic, and the headline "degradation" percentages (45.9%/41.7%/61.7%) are relative drops in normalized resistance scores, not accuracy losses — accuracy is only measured on 3 closed models with drops up to 4.3 points. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate personalized LLM systems or memory-augmented assistants — the factorial attribution and AER (attribute-conditioned exclusion) metrics are directly reusable; skip it if you only want new mitigation methods, since the offered fix (self-reflection prompting) is shown to be insufficient.

Practical Impact (75) reflects the released, directly reusable evaluation framework. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*75 = 71.

Problem & Motivation: Deployed LLM assistants increasingly condition on persistent user context — profiles, inferred preferences, and retrieved interaction memory — to boost helpfulness. Prior work either optimizes personalization utility (LaMP, PersonaLens, PersonaFeedback) or studies sycophancy/echo chambers in depersonalized settings; Jain et al. (2026) showed interaction context amplifies sycophancy but via a single-bias human study, and OP-Bench/RPEval study over-personalization without attributing it to pipeline components. The gap: no systematic, causally-attributed, multi-risk measurement of what personalization costs in factuality, response diversity, and epistemic neutrality, and who bears those costs demographically. Key Idea: Treat personalization as a 2×2 factorial treatment (user profile present/absent × retrieved memory present/absent) applied to queries whose answers are identity-independent, with memories deliberately constructed to be semantically adjacent to the query yet non-answer-bearing — so any behavioral shift is attributable to personal context itself rather than to retrieval of useful information. The insight is that the orthogonality constraint (context is bait, not help) converts personalization from a confound into an experimental variable. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Data construction: profiles from real Reddit posts (10 structured attributes, parsed via PushShift, farthest-point sampled for diversity) plus constraint-driven synthetic profiles; synthetic multi-turn memory conversations grounded in each profile but excluding query-resolving content; queries from three sources — rewrites of CSQA/GSM8K/MMLU into conversational form, template-based generation across 10 domains, and Reddit-derived questions — deduplicated at cosine threshold τ = 0.7, yielding 3,000 manually verified cases. (2) Inference: four conditions; retrieval uses a learned router plus top-k dense retrieval (k = 3, sensitivity-tested for k ∈ {1,...,7}). (3) Evaluation: IRP scored 1–5 by an LLM judge (GPT-5.1, T = 0) plus exact-match accuracy on benchmarks; preference narrowing via Coverage Rate, Useful-Item Recall, Relative Coverage, and a new Attribute Exclusion Rate over 50 personas × 100 advice queries with 20 samples per response; sycophancy via agreement (Reddit AITA) and perspective (1–5 rubric) judges plus a binary Personalization-Induced Sycophancy score. Analysis adds a mixed-effects model with record-level random intercepts, post-hoc G*Power analysis, do-intervention counterfactual attribution over 20 personalization conditions, and preference-inversion tests. Key design decisions — synthetic-only memory for causal cleanliness, orthogonal (bait) memories, and LLM-judge scoring — are each explicitly justified, though the first limits ecological validity (the authors concede this). Key Results: Across 13 models (GPT-5.4/5.4-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5/Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash/Flash-Lite, Llama 3.1 8B/70B, Qwen3 4B–32B), profile conditioning drives average degradations of 45.9% (IRP resistance), 41.7% (UIR), and 61.7% (sycophancy resistance), reported as relative drops in normalized 0–100 resistance scores. Concretely: profile context drops benchmark accuracy up to 4.3 points (Gemini 2.5 Flash: GSM8K 87.9→83.6); Gemini 2.5 Flash's perspective-sycophancy resistance collapses from 55.1% to 0.9% under profile; AITA agreement sycophancy (67.5% base for Gemini Flash) rises +19.5% with a profile. IRP resistance scales with model size (Qwen3: 46.8% at 4B → 60.0% at 32B). Fisher's exact tests show attribute-driven exclusion: young personas steered to microtasks, female personas to craft/labor categories, unwell personas cut from consulting. 94.8% of sycophantic responses flip under preference inversion; 57.8% of sycophancy is generic across personas vs. 5.5% profile-specific. Self-reflection prompting largely fixes IRP (e.g., Claude Haiku 15.6→91.0) but leaves UIR (45.4 vs. 86.5 baseline for GPT-5.4-mini) and sycophancy resistance (34.0 vs. 99.8 for Gemini Flash) far below baseline. Human validation on N = 102 records with 6 annotators shows 84–90% judge agreement. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (PRISK: factorial, multi-risk, causally attributable personalization evaluation) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (profiles, not retrieved memories, are the dominant driver of all three biases, and personalization implicitly reshapes the latent response space rather than merely injecting text). The individual pieces — LLM-judge rubrics, persona-conditioned querying, sycophancy evaluation — are standard; the genuinely new elements are the orthogonal-bait memory construction, the 2×2 causal attribution with mixed-effects modeling, and the Attribute Exclusion Rate linking narrowing to demographic stereotypes. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: factorial decomposition, retrieval-depth sensitivity (σ ≤ 4%, mean 1.9% across k ∈ {1,...,7}), power analysis (power > 0.99 for main effects), counterfactual attribution, and preference inversion. Error bars/multi-seed runs are not reported for headline model scores, though sycophancy metrics use 20 samples at T = 0.8 and human agreement is quantified per annotator. Code and data are released at https://github.com/yumeng-10/personalization_risk.git. Concerns: (a) the judge (GPT-5.1) and two evaluated models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini) share a vendor lineage, a possible self-eval bias the paper does not address; (b) all memories are synthetic, so no in-the-wild validation; (c) the headline percentage degradations are relative resistance-score drops, which a casual reader could mistake for accuracy losses; (d) the perceived-utility analysis rests on a small annotator Likert set without stated sample size or rater counts; (e) dataset construction itself used GPT-5.1/GPT-4.1-mini, creating some train/judge entanglement risk for contamination. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — closed models via APIs, open models self-hosted on 4× A800 80GB via SGLang, all standard infrastructure. Efficient: Evaluation is cheap (T = 0.2, 1,600 max tokens, k = 3 retrieval); the framework is far cheaper than the human studies it complements. Effective: It convincingly measures a proxy (behavioral shift under controlled bait context) rather than realized user harm — the authors correctly note this and defer deployment-specific utility to HCI study. Scalable: The data-generation pipeline is designed to scale query generation, but nothing is tested at 10× scale (real product memories, longitudinal interaction, multilingual users); all scalability claims are pipeline-level, not evidence-level. The work delivers a reusable artifact: dataset, metrics, judge prompts, and code. Strengths: (1) The orthogonal-bait memory plus 2×2 factorial design converts a correlational complaint ("personalization is risky") into component-level causal attribution — a real methodological contribution over OP-Bench and RPEval. (2) The preference-inversion experiment (94.8% flip) is a clean do-intervention that separates preference-content-driven sycophancy from generic persona reactivity. (3) The AER metric plus Fisher's exact tests surface demographic steering (young → microtasks, female → crafts) that goes beyond aggregate narrowing into stereotype-amplification evidence. (4) The mitigation experiment is honest: it demonstrates that reflection prompting fixes the shallow failure mode (IRP) but not the deep ones, which strengthens the paper's central claim about latent response-space reshaping rather than weakening it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that PRISK is a controlled diagnostic, not a simulation of deployed systems: memories are synthetic, profiles follow a fixed fully-observed 10-attribute schema, adaptive memory updating and real user behavior are out of scope; queries are a stress test, not an exhaustive harm taxonomy; LLM-judge evaluation is human-validated only on 102 records; and multilingual, culturally diverse, and longitudinal settings are future work. They confront these directly and do not overclaim, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Judge–model vendor overlap (GPT-5.1 judging GPT-5.4-family models) is unexamined and could bias cross-family comparisons, particularly the finding that OpenAI models are most IRP-robust. (2) "Personalization" here means in-context prompt conditioning only — fine-tuned or trained personalization (cited methods like personalized PEFT) is never evaluated, so conclusions about "personalization" broadly generalize beyond the tested mechanism. (3) Accuracy degradation is reported for only 3 closed models on 3 benchmarks; the open-weight models (where the scaling trend is claimed) get judge scores but no accuracy table. (4) The Reddit-derived profile distribution is acknowledged as non-population-representative, but downstream stereotype claims (e.g., female→craft bias) are not corrected for correlated attributes like stated profession or preference. (5) No inter-run variance or confidence intervals on the headline Table 2 percentages, despite 20-sample sycophancy estimates. (6) The utility–risk tradeoff analysis (Table 11) uses an unspecified annotator pool and sample size, so the "decoupling" claim is weakly supported relative to the rest of the paper. Bottom Line: This is the most causally careful benchmark of personalization's side effects to date and is worth reading for anyone building memory-augmented or profile-conditioned assistants, though its prompt-only, synthetic-memory, judge-dependent design means its findings should be treated as well-controlled diagnosis of one personalization mechanism rather than the final word on deployed systems.

Problem & Motivation: RNA inverse folding asks whether a prescribed secondary structure has a sequence whose unique optimal fold is that target. Bonnet et al. proved NP-completeness for a Watson–Crick design-extension formulation, so exact positive results for well-defined structural classes are valuable. In the simplified maximum-pair model of Haleš et al. (all Watson–Crick pairs score equally, θ = 0, no pseudoknots), Haleš et al. established the separated-coloring designability certificate, and Boury, Bulteau, and Ponty proved that every motif-free target whose helices all have length ≥3 admits a modulo-2 separated coloring constructible in linear time. Short helices are harder because a two-pair helix lacks a spare "switch" position to simultaneously satisfy the entry color, gray-residue restriction, exit residue, and terminal color; the paper identifies exactly where the all-long guarantee breaks and closes that gap for a bounded number of short helices. Key Idea: The core trick is a bounded-resource induction: summarize each helix subtree by a set of guaranteed entry states (F = {ξB, ξW, ηB, ηW, ηG} for subtrees with no isolated stack; Q = {ξB, ξW, ηG} for subtrees containing one), then observe that if a loop has two outgoing child subtrees requiring gray heads, those two subtrees already contain both isolated stacks allowed globally, so the incoming helix must be long — and a long helix can use Boury et al.'s published non-gray-ending η→η transfer words (e.g., GBB, GWW) to keep the loop exposure {W, G, G} or {B, G, G} proper. The global count of two converts a local bottleneck into a guarantee that the needed long-helix option is always available. Methodology: The proof pipeline is: (1) encode the target as a rooted ordered interval tree with paired nodes per base pair and singleton leaves per unpaired nucleotide; (2) color paired nodes B/W/G (prescribing G–C, C–G, A–U) subject to a local capacity rule (properness: at most one B, one W, two G incidences per loop exposure) plus a global parity condition (all gray pairs at residue η, all unpaired nodes at residue ξ, the "uniform residue form" of modulo-2 separation); (3) run a deterministic top-down recursion (Algorithm 1) that classifies each terminal loop as E/L/M, selects a color word from the exact length-2 transition table or the long-helix transfer families, and assigns child first-pair colors from tabulated rows for r = 0, 1, 2 stack-bearing children; (4) convert the coloring to a sequence (unpaired→A, gray orientation rules ensure local nucleotide distinctness); (5) prove optimality by a nucleotide-counting bound (#U = g, #G = #C = q, so |S| ≤ g + q = |T|) and uniqueness by a G–C prefix-balance/level argument plus a free-group-style "atomic saturable design" concatenation lemma. The full development is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib (46-file closure, 20,738 lines, 1,616 declarations). Critical design decisions: the F/Q state split (justified by the stack-count decomposition lemma), the exclusion of length-1 helices (stated explicitly to mirror the frozen Lean predicate), and the choice to prove a sharpness witness ((.))((.))((.)) for the modulo-2 criterion. The construction is well-justified internally, but the choice of the idealized model itself is defended only on grounds of exact provability. Key Results: The headline results are theorems, not experiments: Theorem 3.3 (every target in class K≤2 admits a proper modulo-2 separated coloring in uniform residue form) and Theorem 3.4 (every such target is designable). Proposition 3.5 shows the motif-free target ((.))((.))((.)) with three isolated stacks admits no proper modulo-2 separated coloring (verified by exhaustive check of all 3^6 = 729 colorings in Lean) yet is ordinarily separated and uniquely designable — so two is a sharp boundary for the modulo-2 certificate but not for designability. Two worked examples are checked with exact Nussinov dynamic programming: T1 = (())(())((())) with 7 pairs (optimum 7, count 1, sequence AGCUUGCAGGGCCC) and T2 with 13 pairs across helix lengths (3,3,2,2,3) (optimum 13, count 1). These are regression tests at toy scale, not benchmarking; the universal claim rests on the induction. Baseline comparison is against Boury et al.'s all-long theorem (which the paper extends) and Haleš et al.'s saturated-target result (which already covers saturated members of the class, so the certificate is the only new element there). Novelty Classification: NEW THEOREM within an existing framework — closest to NEW FORMULATION applied to a NEW PROBLEM instance. The genuinely new contribution is the bounded-resource (F/Q) induction proving universal modulo-2 colorability for targets with at most two isolated stacks; the parity device (Haleš et al. 2017), the modulo-m finite-state machinery, the O(n·2^m) dynamic program, the local transfer words including GBB (Boury et al.'s WABI Fig. 8 / journal Fig. 12), and the coloring-to-design implication are all prior art, as the paper meticulously attributes. The Lean formalization and AI-audit pipeline are an execution achievement rather than a new method. Since Boury et al.'s dynamic program already decides modulo-2 separability for arbitrary targets in linear time, the theorem adds a structural success guarantee, not a new algorithmic capability — the authors say so themselves (Section 16.4). Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is unusually strong for a preprint: the complete theorem is kernel-checked in Lean 4 with only the three foundational axioms, an explicit axiom audit, no project-defined axioms or proof placeholders, an isolated clean rebuild from a frozen SHA-256-hashed archive (3,070 jobs, 894.10 s on a 10-CPU host), downstream kernel-checked semantic regression theorems for the publication examples, and a hash-verified artifact release on GitHub (github.com/ajogalekar/rna-at-most-two-short-helices) with Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22101755. Ablations exist as counterexample analysis (three-isolated-stack Proposition 3.5, AUAU failing the nested target) rather than as empirical ablations. No error bars or seeds apply — this is a proof. Methodological concerns: (1) no independent human expert review has occurred, as the author states plainly; (2) the specification-vs-Leat fidelity check was a blinded automated AI audit, which the author correctly ranks below kernel checking; (3) the literature-novelty search (through 19 August 2026) is self-reported and the author flags it as necessarily incomplete. The paper is candid about the evidentiary hierarchy and does not overstate. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a proved theorem with a constructive algorithm sketched, but the Lean development "is not presented as extracted executable code"). - Sound: Assumptions are explicit (four-letter alphabet, θ = 0, no pseudoknots, uniform pair energy), the axiom set is minimal, and kernel checking plus isolated rebuild make soundness about as strong as it gets absent human review. - General: The result holds for the precisely delimited class K≤2; it is deliberately restrictive — m3•-freeness forbids unpaired nucleotides in any multiloop, excluding biologically typical architectures — and the "at most two" bound is a property of this construction, not of designability. - Tight: Sharpness is partially established: Proposition 3.5 shows three isolated stacks can defeat the modulo-2 certificate, but the paper correctly notes this does not bound designability itself, so the true designability frontier remains open. - Implementable: The recursion is deterministic and O(n)/O(n) when the tree and helix structure are precomputed, but no executable implementation ships; Boury et al.'s existing linear-time DP already provides the decision capability, so there is little to operationalize beyond a guarantee on when that DP must succeed. The work delivers a substantial software artifact (frozen Lean development, audit bundles, deterministic example checkers) but not a usable RNA-design tool; the sequences produced are exact-model artifacts, and the authors make no thermodynamic claim. Strengths: - A genuine incremental theorem in a well-studied problem: the extension of universal modulo-2 colorability from all-long targets to the bounded-isolated-stack regime, with a sharpness witness showing the count two is real for the certificate (Proposition 3.5). - Complete end-to-end formal verification of the theorem, the sequence construction, and the uniqueness argument — not just the coloring step — including kernel-checked concrete instances tied to exact dynamic-programming checks. - Exceptional attribution hygiene: the paper painstakingly demarcates what is new (the global counting induction) from what is borrowed (the parity device, transfer words, coloring-to-design theorem), including admitting that the load-bearing GBB word appears in Boury et al.'s figures. - A transparent, ranked evidence hierarchy for AI-assisted research (kernel acceptance > isolated rebuild > axiom audit > blinded AI fidelity audit > computational checks), with early erroneous proof attempts documented rather than hidden. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive. They state: the model excludes G–U wobble, pseudoknots, stacking, loop entropies, ions, kinetics, and 3D structure (Section 16.1); m3•-avoidance is biologically restrictive, making the class narrow; the theorem is sufficient, not a characterization of designability; "at most two" is a resource limit of the construction, not a structural boundary; the certificate is unnecessary (the ((.))((.))((.)) target is designable without a modulo-2 coloring); the theorem supplies no new decision algorithm over Boury et al.'s DP; no thermodynamic claim is made; and the work has not received independent human expert review. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations: (1) the fidelity audit that guards against formalizing a weakened theorem was performed by an AI system from the same tool ecosystem (Claude Code) that assisted the research — the author ranks its weight correctly low, but a single human verification of even the theorem statement would materially strengthen confidence; (2) the claim of practical seeding value for thermodynamic design pipelines is left entirely to citation of others' work, with no experiment here; (3) the class K≤2's biological incidence is never quantified — the reader cannot tell how often real RNA motifs fall in this class, so the practical reach of the theorem is unknown; (4) the theorem's saturated cases were already covered by Haleš et al.'s Result R4, so for that subfamily only the certificate is new, narrowing the increment further than the abstract suggests; (5) thearXiv-numbered preprint (2608.25194) is single-authored from a private LLC with pervasive AI involvement, which — however well-disclosed — will require community validation before the attribution and correctness claims carry full weight. Bottom Line: For researchers in combinatorial RNA design and formalized mathematics this is a carefully verified, honestly attributed, genuinely new (if narrow) theorem worth reading as a model of AI-assisted formalization, but practitioners seeking deployable RNA design tools will find more value in Boury et al.'s original linear-time algorithm and its RECOMB 2025 seeding follow-up, and the result should not be cited as peer-reviewed until human expert review confirms it.

J-Zero: Unified Challenger--Solver--Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data (35 ▲ )

Gyouk Chu, Myeongho Jeon, Eunho Yang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces J-ZERO, a zero-data self-evolution framework in which a Judge model co-adapts alongside a Challenger and Solver, using preference labels derived from structural role asymmetry and task decomposition rather than from the Judge's own scores. - Why it's important: Prior data-free self-play methods rely on a frozen Judge or verifier, which caps how far the Solver can improve — the paper removes that ceiling so self-improvement can continue in both verifiable (math, reasoning) and unverifiable (open-ended generation) domains without human supervision. - How it does it: The key move is constructing Bradley–Terry preference pairs whose ordering is known by construction — the Solver's answer beats the Challenger's (role asymmetry), and a decompose-then-recombine answer beats the Solver's one-shot answer (subtask amplification, from iterated amplification) — so the Judge can be trained inside the self-play loop without circular self-scoring. - The good: The authors empirically validate the reliability of their self-generated preference labels with an external LLM judge across all 10 iterations (role-asymmetry win rates 87.9%→~66%; skip it if you only need verifiable-domain self-play, where R-Zero already covers most of the machinery.

Problem & Motivation: Data-free self-evolution of LLMs works well in verifiable domains (execution checks, majority voting) but stalls in unverifiable domains where quality is defined by human preference. Substituting a reward-model Judge for a verifier introduces a ceiling: a frozen Judge can only push the Solver toward preferences it has already internalized, so once the Solver saturates the Judge's discriminative ability, training yields no signal. Prior zero-data frameworks either cannot handle unverifiable tasks at all (R-Zero's majority voting; Absolute Zero's executor) or use a static Judge (Kuba et al. 2025; G-Zero trains the Solver via DPO without any Judge), leaving open the setting where the evaluation signal itself is learned and improves alongside the policies. Key Idea: Train the Judge inside the self-play loop using preference pairs whose ordering is fixed by the training objectives of the other two roles, not by the Judge's own scores. Two sources: (1) role asymmetry — the Solver is optimized to answer the Challenger's tasks, the Challenger is optimized to make them hard, so the Solver's response is preferred by construction; (2) subtask amplification — a divide-and-conquer response (Challenger decomposes the task, Solver answers subtasks, Challenger recombines) is preferred over the Solver's one-shot answer, exposing the Judge to quality above the Solver's current frontier. This breaks the circularity objection: no signal originates from the Judge itself. Methodology: Each iteration has three GRPO/BT stages on a shared verl pipeline. (1) Challenger training: the Challenger samples N tasks; the Solver generates M responses each; the Judge (sigmoid-squared scalar head, initialized from Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B) scores them. The Challenger maximizes a composite reward (1 − mean Judge score, minus a BLEU-cluster repetition penalty, gated by a <question> format check) via GRPO, treating all N tasks as one group. (2) Solver training: from a frozen-Challenger task pool, the top-K tasks by response-level Judge-score standard deviation are selected (justified via Bae et al.'s variance-lower-bound on policy improvement, and framed as a continuous generalization of R-Zero's informative band); the Solver is then GRPO-trained on Judge rewards. (3) Judge training: on held-out tasks, role-asymmetry pairs (y_S ≻ y_C) and subtask-amplification pairs (y_amp ≻ y_S, via 3–5 subtask decomposition/recombination) are collected and the Judge is updated with the Bradley–Terry loss −E[log σ(J(x,y⁺) − J(x,y⁻))]. Critical design decisions: preference labels independent of Judge outputs (well-motivated and ablated); score-dispersion task selection (grounded in cited theory but not independently ablated); equal mixing of the two pair types per iteration (the schedule-free union is shown complementary via ablation and win-rate curves, though a stage-dependent weighting is never explored). Key Results: On Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base across 11 verifiable benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, Minerva, OlympiadBench, AMC23, AIME24/25, MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA, BBH, IFEval) and 3 unverifiable benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2.0 LC, Arena-Hard-v2.0, EQ-Bench Creative Writing v3), J-ZERO beats R-Zero and G-Zero on every benchmark group at both scales. Verifiable overall average: 54.38 (4B) and 58.55 (8B) vs. R-Zero's 49.64/54.99 — gains of 4.74 and 3.56 points over R-Zero, despite R-Zero being purpose-built for verifiable domains. Unverifiable overall: 20.81 (4B) and 23.41 (8B) vs. R-Zero's 12.66/15.54 — an average 8.0-point margin; AlpacaEval LC jumps 6.22→28.56 (4B) and 12.93→33.53 (8B). Baselines are current (2026 concurrent work) and configured per their original setups. Sustained-improvement analysis: R-Zero and G-Zero peak at iteration 2 and decline, while J-ZERO improves monotonically through iteration 10; the frozen-Judge variant tracks for 3 iterations then plateaus 1.66/4.44 points below the full run. Ablations (4B): removing Judge training entirely drops overall from 37.59 to 34.54; removing subtask-amplification pairs costs −1.64, removing role-asymmetry pairs −0.97. Tested at standard academic scale (4B/8B models, 8B Judge, 4×B200 + 4×H200), not stress scale. Notable secondary finding: the co-adapted Judge also improves on the independent RM-Bench benchmark (92.61→93.95 average, Hard-pair accuracy +4.77), suggesting co-adaptation does not degrade general reward-modeling. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component). The genuinely novel element is judge co-evolution inside a zero-data adversarial loop using preference labels derived from role structure and iterated amplification rather than from Judge scores — this addresses a real, identified limitation (the fixed-Judge ceiling) that concurrent G-Zero sidesteps differently. The rest is a competent composition of known pieces: R-Zero's Challenger–Solver GRPO game (the Challenger reward, repetition penalty, and format check are explicitly inherited), Christiano et al.'s iterated amplification, and standard BT reward-model training. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover both preference-pair types and the frozen-Judge variant, and the paper validates its core assumption directly (per-iteration label reliability against Claude Opus 4.8 as an external judge, position-debiased, ties dropped) — this is unusually honest self-checking. However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere; all headline numbers are single runs. Checkpoint selection ('stop training once the average score... begins to drop, and select the final checkpoint before this decline') is benchmark-based, which risks optimistic selection on the same 14 test benchmarks. The unverifiable-domain evaluations themselves rely on LLM judges (Qwen3.6-27B, gemma-4-31B-it), a soft spot when the method trains against a reward model. The Judge is initialized from an off-the-shelf human-preference-trained reward model, so the system is not supervision-free end-to-end. Project Page, GitHub, and Hugging Face links are cited in the header, but no URLs appear in the provided text; hyperparameters and prompts are fully documented in the appendix (verl framework, full hyperparameter table). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs and evaluates the full training pipeline). Practical: Yes — everything runs on 8 consumer-datacenter GPUs (4×B200 + 4×H200) with 4B–8B models via verl. Efficient: Moderate cost — three models trained per iteration (5 Challenger + 15 Solver + 8 Judge steps), with subtask-amplification pair construction adding a decompose/solve/compose pipeline per held-out task; the paper does not report wall-clock or FLOP comparisons against R-Zero. Effective: Strong evidence for the stated problem — sustained improvement past the fixed-Judge ceiling, with the mechanism (Judge saturation → plateau) directly demonstrated by the frozen-Judge ablation; unverifiable-domain absolute win rates remain low (Arena-Hard Creative Writing 2.2→3.9), so 'solves' should be read as relative, not absolute. Scalable: Untested beyond 8B/8B and base models — the authors flag this themselves; 10× scale behavior, long-CoT reasoning models, and generative-Judge variants are open. Delivers a software artifact (code and models via the cited GitHub/Hugging Face links, though URLs are not in the text), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The structurally-derived preference labeling is a genuinely clever solution to the circularity problem in self-rewarding systems — it converts 'who was optimized for what' into supervision signal without any external labels or Judge self-scoring. (2) The reliability analysis (Figure 2) is a model of what self-play papers should do: it measures label correctness per iteration, discovers that the two pair types are complementary in time (role asymmetry early, amplification after iteration 4), and this discovery is used to explain the ablation results rather than hidden. (3) The headline claim is supported by the right experiment: the frozen-Judge variant diverging from the full run exactly where the Solver would saturate the Judge is direct causal evidence for the proposed mechanism, not just an aggregate score. (4) Beating R-Zero on its home turf (verifiable domains, +3.56 to +4.74) while additionally covering unverifiable domains shows the Judge signal is not merely additive on open-ended tasks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: compute limits confine them to ≤8B Challenger/Solver with an 8B Judge and base models only (no post-trained long-CoT models); the Judge is a discriminative BT classifier from an off-the-shelf checkpoint while Challenger/Solver share one generative initialization, breaking role symmetry of initialization; a generative LLM-as-a-judge would unify all three roles in one model but poses unresolved co-adaptation challenges. They confront these directly and frame the generative Judge as future work — a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge the single-run/no-variance issue or the benchmark-based checkpoint selection. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) 'Zero data' is overstated: the Judge is initialized from Skywork-Reward-V2, itself trained on large human preference datasets, so the system's evaluation ability is seeded by substantial external human supervision — the honest claim is zero additional data per iteration. (2) Subtask-amplification labels are anti-reliable for the first three iterations (21.1% win rate at iteration 1) yet are still mixed into Judge training from the start with equal weight; a gated or scheduled weighting is an obvious missing ablation, and training the Judge on mostly-wrong pairs early could plausibly harm the trajectory. (3) The claimed connection to Bae et al.'s variance lower bound justifies score-dispersion task selection theoretically, but no ablation isolates this component against random or accuracy-based filtering. (4) The unchecked possibility of reward-hacking the co-evolved Judge: because the Solver is optimized against the same Judge being trained on Solver-generated pairs, a drift/collapse mode (e.g., the residual style bias the authors themselves note via the Easy-split decline on RM-Bench) is not tracked with any reward-hacking probe or human evaluation of final outputs — all unverifiable results rest on LLM-judge win rates. (5) Only one Challenger prompt template (modified from G-Zero) is used; task-distribution sensitivity of the whole loop is unmeasured. Bottom Line: For anyone building label-free or reward-model-centric post-training pipelines, this is the strongest published answer so far to the fixed-Judge ceiling problem and worth reading closely; the single-run evidence, ≤8B scale, and borrowed Judge initialization mean it is a direction-setter rather than a settled result, but nothing else currently covers the same ground as well.

Towards Benchmarking Agentic Data Scientists

KN Nayak, N Solpure, N Mitra, T Zehle, A Pfefferle… · openreview.net · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a unified benchmarking framework that evaluates four agentic machine learning systems (MLZero, AgentK, AIDE, an open-source MLE-STAR reimplementation) against AutoGluon on 10 curated tabular datasets, measuring predictive performance, cross-fold stability, and execution reliability together. - Why it's important: Organizations deciding whether to adopt LLM-driven ML agents currently have no standardized, leakage-audited evidence on whether the added reasoning machinery outperforms a mature fixed-search AutoML system — and this paper shows it mostly does not. - How it does it: All five systems run under one execution engine with fixed dataset splits, a single shared backbone LLM (gpt-oss-120b), identical task descriptions, and a robustness-adjusted score (score = p·r/(1+s)) that combines normalized performance, fold spread, and reliability, plus a per-fold target-leakage audit. - The good: The most credible result is the reliability decomposition: dropping stability and reliability terms moves MLZero from rank 5 to rank 2, exposing that several of its headline results came from datasets where only one of three folds completed — a mechanism that mean-only benchmarks systematically reward. - The missing: Ten datasets with three folds each is too small for the conclusions: the Nemenyi critical difference (1.93) nearly spans the full rank spread (2.05), no pairwise comparison survives multiple-comparison correction, and token consumption and per-failure-type counts were never uniformly captured. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building or evaluating ML agents — the leakage-audit methodology and the score-sensitivity analysis are directly reusable — but practitioners wanting a decision between agents and AutoML already get the headline from the abstract.

Problem & Motivation Agentic machine learning systems — LLM-driven agents that autonomously write, execute, and refine ML pipelines — are proliferating rapidly (MLZero, AgentK, AIDE, MLE-STAR), yet systematic evaluation of them is sparse. Prior benchmarks such as MLE-bench and MLGym score task success rates or leaderboard positions without capturing end-to-end pipeline quality, execution reliability, or robustness, and results are confounded by differing backbone LLMs, prompts, and stochastic inference, making reproducible comparison difficult. Practitioners and researchers in AutoML and LLM agents therefore lack a controlled answer to a basic question: does reasoning-based pipeline generation actually beat a well-engineered fixed search (AutoGluon), and at what cost in reliability? The paper closes this gap with a standardized comparison on tabular data, where traditional AutoML is strongest and the bar for agents is highest. Key Idea The core insight is that evaluating autonomous ML systems requires reliability and stability to be measured, not assumed, and that this premise must be made testable by explicitly re-ranking under different scoring schemes: the paper defines a robustness-adjusted score combining normalized performance (p), cross-fold spread (s), and reliability (r) as p·r/(1+s), anchored to fixed baselines per metric (AMLB convention), and then quantifies how much the reliability term changes the ranking. A second, methodologically important move is treating agentic systems as uniquely exposed to target leakage — an agent that reads the data can discover artifacts that a fixed search cannot — motivating a mandatory per-fold leakage audit as part of any agent benchmark. Methodology The framework has three modular components: dataset handlers that expose a consistent view of each task, standardized agent interfaces, and a central execution engine that materializes fixed train/test files, launches each agent under identical conditions, and counts a run as valid only if the produced prediction file parses and covers every test row (any other outcome is a failure; no automatic retries). The dataset suite was manually curated from 23 open-source Kaggle-derived tabular datasets down to 12, then a leakage audit of all 36 folds (checking target presence in test files, exact single-feature and additive-pair reconstruction of the target, schema mismatches, and row overlap) removed two more, leaving 10 datasets (6 classification, 4 regression), each with 3 fixed folds. Metrics are ROC-AUC for classification and R2/RMSE for regression. All agentic systems ran on gpt-oss-120b served locally; each system used its repository-default decoding parameters rather than a forced common setting — a defensible but score-weakening choice. Time budgets were deliberately non-uniform (AutoGluon 7200s, AgentK 14400s, others 24h). Rankings come from the corrected robustness-adjusted score; significance is assessed with Friedman/Nemenyi tests plus exploratory Wilcoxon tests. Critical design decisions: (1) replacing an initially defective scoring function (µ·r/(1+σ)) whose sign, direction, and scale were all wrong for some metrics — well-justified with three concrete failure modes; (2) system-default decoding budgets — defensible for preserving co-designed systems but explicitly recorded as a limitation; (3) uniform backbone across all agents — well-justified for fairness, but the authors honestly flag that none of the agents was designed for this backbone. Key Results Across the 10-dataset suite, average robustness-adjusted ranks are: AutoGluon 1.75±1.36, AIDE 2.75±1.23, MLE-STAR 3.15±1.06, AgentK 3.55±1.54, MLZero 3.80±1.14. The Friedman test is significant (χ2 = 10.46, p = 0.033 over 10 datasets and 5 methods), but the Nemenyi critical difference of 1.93 means only AutoGluon vs. AgentK/MLZero separate at the extremes; no pairwise Wilcoxon comparison survives Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Among systems completing every fold, AutoGluon had the highest ROC-AUC on all but one classification dataset. Reliability diverges sharply: AutoGluon and MLE-STAR achieved 100% success across 30 runs, AIDE 83.33% (5 failures), AgentK 63.33% (11 failures), MLZero 50.00% (15 failures). The highest R2 in the audited suite is only 0.862 — the near-perfect regression results in the earlier submitted version were artifacts of the leaked Bike Sharing Demand dataset, where AIDE and MLZero exploited the leak while AutoGluon and AgentK did not. Under mean-performance-only ranking, MLZero jumps from fifth to second, demonstrating that benchmark design choices materially reorder agentic systems. Baselines are current and strong (AutoGluon is a leading tabular AutoML framework; the agents are 2025 systems), though all agents ran on a backbone none was designed for. Scale is modest: 30 runs per system, 10 datasets, 3 folds. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the genuinely novel elements are (a) the unified reliability-and-leakage-aware evaluation protocol for agentic ML systems — including the per-fold leakage audit justified by the argument that agents exploit leaks that fixed searches cannot — and (b) the empirical finding that a mature AutoML baseline beats current agents on stability and cost, with the reliability term demonstrably reordering the agents. The individual scoring components (normalization per AMLB convention, Friedman/Nemenyi testing) are standard; the reimplementation of MLE-STAR and the curated dataset suite are competent assembly of existing pieces rather than new techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility Rigor is above average for a benchmark paper: the authors ran statistical significance tests, transparently report that no pairwise comparison survives correction, and show score-sensitivity analysis (both rankings, not just the favorable one). An unusually strong practice is the self-correction: the paper documents that its own submitted version contained a defective scoring function and two leaked datasets, explains precisely how those defects inflated the earlier p-value (0.007 → 0.054 → 0.033), and reports all results under the corrected protocol. No multiple seeds or per-method confidence intervals beyond fold-variation are reported, and three folds per dataset give thin variance estimates (acknowledged). Code, task descriptions, the leakage-audit script (src/audit-splits.py), and the exact agent task descriptions are released at github.com/KARTIK-N-NAYAK/Benchmarking-Agentic-Data-Scientists. Methodological concerns to flag: time budgets and decoding parameters differ across systems; MLE-STAR is evaluated via a third-party reimplementation with a substituted web-search backend (DuckDuckGo instead of Google), which the authors explicitly state should be read as the reimplementation's results; the failure-type taxonomy is qualitative only (no per-type counts, since logs were not collected to support them); and token consumption — arguably the dominant marginal cost of agents — was not uniformly measured. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark study with executed experiments and a released evaluation framework). - Practical: Yes — all runs fit on 8 CPU cores and one RTX 2080 Ti per job, and AutoGluon (the winning system) runs on commodity hardware with zero LLM-token cost. - Efficient: AutoGluon exhausted its 7200s budget on 8 of 10 datasets and was the cheapest system by a wide margin; agentic systems needed up to 24h plus unmeasured but substantial LLM token spend, paying twice for instability (failed runs and wasted tokens). - Effective: The evidence shows agents do not yet solve the stated problem (reliably outperforming fixed-search AutoML) — the best agent, AIDE, is statistically indistinguishable from AutoGluon while failing 16.7% of runs, and the finding is a negative result for agents rather than a working alternative. - Scalable: Not tested — 10 datasets and 3 folds is the binding constraint on statistical resolution; the authors state this, but no larger-scale experiment or extrapolation is offered. The work delivers a reusable software artifact: the benchmark framework, evaluation engine, leakage-audit script, dataset splits, and task descriptions in a public repository. Strengths - The score-sensitivity analysis (Figure 2) is a genuinely informative contribution: it converts a philosophical claim — mean performance alone misleads for unreliable systems — into a measured effect, showing MLZero's second-place mean-only ranking is built on single-fold successes scored with zero variance by construction. - The leakage audit reframes benchmark integrity as agent-specific: the demonstration that AIDE and MLZero exploited the Bike Sharing Demand leak (casual + registered = target, R2 = 1.000000 on 10,886 test rows) while AutoGluon did not shows leakage does not degrade all systems equally, a point prior agent benchmarks ignore. - Radical transparency about the paper's own errors: correcting a defective scoring function whose sign and direction were wrong for negative R2 and RMSE, and quantifying how each fix moved the headline p-value, sets a standard few benchmark papers meet. - Honest negative framing of the token/cost asymmetry (agents pay in lost runs and in tokens; AutoGluon pays in neither) grounds the practical conclusion. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and at length, which strengthens credibility. They explicitly state: (1) 10 datasets and 3 folds is too small — the Nemenyi CD of 1.93 nearly spans the full rank spread of 2.05, so only extremes separate; (2) time budgets and decoding parameters were not uniform, weakening strict equal-footing comparison; (3) MLE-STAR results reflect a reimplementation with a different search backend, not the published system; (4) the gpt-oss-120b backbone matches none of the agents' design targets, so instability may partly reflect backbone mismatch; (5) all tasks are tabular, limiting generalization; (6) two leaked datasets survived manual curation, implying curation-by-inspection is insufficient; (7) failure types are recorded qualitatively only; (8) token counts were not uniformly captured. This is direct confrontation, not minimization. Analyst-Identified Gaps - Only one backbone LLM is tested; the paper itself argues backbone configuration is a moving target but offers no second backbone to bound how much of the agents' failure behavior is mismatch-driven — the headline conclusion rests on a single, arguably unfavorable, configuration point. - No runtime or token-cost comparison is actually possible from the data collected, so the cost asymmetry claim, while plausible, is asserted qualitatively rather than measured (the authors partially acknowledge this but still draw the asymmetric-cost conclusion in Section 5.2). - The 24-hour budgets for AIDE and MLZero versus 7200s for AutoGluon mean agents received 12× more wall-clock; a per-effective-compute comparison is absent, so it remains unclear whether agents would close the gap at equal budget or fall further behind. - No tuning of AutoGluon presets is reported as ablated (the 'best quality preset' is used), and no agentic system gets a debugging/repair attempt beyond its native loop; the interaction between retry policy and the reliability term r is not explored. - Three folds per dataset means the cross-fold spread term s in the corrected score is estimated from n=3 samples; the paper notes this but does not quantify how rank orderings might shift under resampling uncertainty in s. - The peer-review status of this document is not stated; it reads as a workshop/under-review version (it repeatedly contrasts against 'the submitted version'), so the corrected results should be treated as preprint-level evidence until reviewed. Bottom Line A practitioner choosing between AutoML and agentic ML systems gains concrete, honestly-reported evidence that current agents still lose to AutoGluon on stability and cost — and researchers building agent benchmarks gain a leakage-audit protocol and a reliability-score methodology worth adopting — making this a worthwhile read despite its small evaluation scale and single-backbone design.
