Rigor (68) reflects unusually careful gold-set construction (four annotators including a math-education researcher, per-class kappa honestly reported) but is reduced by the single-seed, single-1.7B-model training experiment, the explicitly unvalidated semantic-space tracking, the 48-trajectory validation base, and a possible annotator-contamination surface with MATH-Perturb. Completeness (70) is a credibility positive — the authors openly label the training 'preliminary' and admit space tracking lacks a gold standard — though the length confound on the focus finding goes unaddressed. Resilience (60) is the weak dimension: the HA-Plan-GRPO margin is vulnerable to prompt-engineering-noise and privileged-information objections with no isolating ablation, and the correctness-prediction gain (0.664 vs 0.618 AUROC on 100 problems) is modest. Impact (65) reflects a released code artifact and reusable taxonomy, but no model weights and a diagnostic (not yet deployable training) contribution. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*65 = 70.
empirical Novelty 78 Rigor 68 Non-Obv 75 Completeness 70 Resilience 60 Impact 65
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLMs score well on math benchmarks, but accuracy says nothing about how a solution is organized — whether the model commits to an algebraic interpretation, abandons it for enumeration, and returns. Existing CoT analyses capture surface properties (length, "wait/aha" markers, generic episode labels like Plan/Verify, graph structure) but never track the mathematical interpretation under which each local action is taken. Mathematics education has studied exactly this question for decades via semantic spaces and heuristics, but those methods rely on manual think-aloud coding and have not been applied to or scaled for LLM traces. The paper targets researchers who want process-level diagnostics of LLM math reasoning and a principled handle on whether post-training broadens or narrows strategic behavior. Key Idea: Treat a CoT trajectory as an observable problem-solving record and encode it as two aligned annotation layers — a sequence of semantic spaces (inferred interpretations) and multi-label heuristic tags per content unit — then summarize reasoning quality by how heuristic effort is distributed across spaces (entropy-based effective number of spaces and of contiguous space-segments). The core technical move is operationalizing Favier & Dorier's education framework as a prompted LLM annotation state machine: representation-changing heuristics (H1, H2, H3, H5, H8, H11) trigger a NEW/RETURN/MAINTAIN decision against a memory buffer of prior space definitions. Methodology: Three pipeline stages: (1) content-unit segmentation of the CoT into heuristic-bearing spans via prompting; (2) multi-label heuristic tagging against a consolidated 11-family taxonomy (plus N1–N4 non-heuristic labels); (3) semantic-space tracking, where only units containing space-changing heuristics invoke a tracking model that decides NEW (open space), RETURN (resume a buffered space ID), or MAINTAIN. From the resulting space sequence S and heuristic sequence H, the paper defines the space distribution q(i), the segment distribution p(k) over maximal contiguous runs, and computes effective numbers N_eff_space = exp(−Σ q log q) and N_eff_trans (same over segments, per their Eq. 2), plus a transition ratio ρ = N_eff_trans/N_eff_space and a heuristic frequency vector u(h). The annotator model was selected against a gold set of 48 MATH-Perturb trajectories (1,598 units from 8,334 sentences) coded by four authors including a math-education graduate researcher under consensus adjudication; Qwen3.5-27B (weighted F1 70.44, macro F1 61.36) was chosen over Grok-4.1-Fast (76.98/65.04) for cost/reproducibility. Downstream analyses use logistic regression for correctness prediction, Jensen–Shannon divergence of heuristic distributions under problem perturbation, Density/Coverage (k-NN, cosine, k=3) in heuristic-frequency space for base vs. post-trained comparisons, and finally GRPO training (2×B200, 200 steps, verl) comparing Plan-GRPO vs. HA-Plan-GRPO, which appends an 11-heuristic menu to the rollout prompt. Critical design decisions: consensus human coding is well justified by education tradition; using LLM annotators validated on 48 trajectories is a pragmatic but thin foundation; the space-tracking stage is deliberately NOT validated against labels (authors state no objective gold standard exists) and is instead prompt-calibrated manually — the weakest-justified component. Key Results: (1) Correctness prediction on the 100-problem Omni-MATH subset (15 models, 5-fold stratified CV): CoT length AUROC 0.504±0.03, self-revision markers 0.618±0.03, ThinkARM episode features 0.618±0.02, SHAPE heuristic frequencies 0.653 (H) / 0.664±0.02 (H+N). (2) Across 15 models, reasoning models show higher space coverage (N_eff_space 1.81–2.53, ρ 0.40–0.51) than instruction-tuned models (1.37–1.71, 0.19–0.32); incorrect trajectories consistently show higher N_eff_space, N_eff_trans, and ρ than correct ones — the focused-exploration finding. (3) On MATH-Perturb hard perturbations (four post-trained models), Pass@1 drops (e.g., Qwen3-8B .96→.84, Qwen3-32B .92→.76), yet heuristic distributions diverge early (D_JS 0.19–0.21 within the first 5 units, hard > simple at p<.05 by paired Wilcoxon) and models open more spaces while revisiting more (Δρ up to +.11) — adaptive but non-converging restructuring. (4) Base→post-trained pairs show Density >1 (1.032–1.250) with Coverage <1 (0.531–0.871), vs. cross-model baseline 0.520/0.437, supporting heuristic-level mode-seeking under RLVR. (5) HA-Plan-GRPO on Qwen3-1.7B-Base: Avg@64 36.80 vs. 30.00 (Plan-GRPO) vs. 23.54 (base) on original problems, 17.72 vs. 14.52 vs. 11.84 on hard. Baselines are current and directly relevant (ThinkARM, MATH-Perturb, published base/post-trained pairs). Scale is modest: 48 gold trajectories, 100 problems for prediction, 115 problems for perturbation analysis, 1.7B model for training. The perturbation finding (adaptation without convergence) is the most interesting counter-intuitive result. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a domain-grounded, scalable annotation framework importing semantic-space/heuristic constructs from mathematics education into CoT analysis — a genuinely new transfer of theory, not just new labels) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDINGS (heuristic-level mode-seeking under RLVR; correct trajectories concentrate effort in few semantic spaces) and a modest NEW METHOD contribution in training (heuristic-augmented rollout prompting in GRPO). The Density/Coverage metrics, entropy-based effective counts, logistic-regression evaluation, and GRPO with planning are standard tools; the training result in particular is a competent combination of existing ideas (planning-based RLVR + prompt augmentation) applied in the new lens. Rigor & Reproducibility: Partial ablations exist: annotator-model selection is done properly against gold data with weighted/macro F1 and Cohen's kappa per class (Table 9 shows weak classes, e.g., H2 F1 0.432); Plan-GRPO vs. HA-Plan-GRPO isolates the heuristic-prompt effect by holding reward, optimizer, and prompt structure fixed; the Density/Coverage analysis includes a sensible cross-model negative control; early-divergence analysis (5/10 unit prefixes) rules out a late-stage artifact. Error bars are reported for AUROC (5-fold CV) and significance tests (paired Wilcoxon, p<.05) for perturbation results, but not for the training experiment, which appears single-seed with no variance estimates. Code is released at github.com/holi-lab/SHAPE-of-CoT. Methodological concerns: (a) the same 48 MATH-Perturb trajectories ground the annotator, and MATH-Perturb is also the main evaluation set — small but real contamination surface; (b) all SHAPE features for large-scale analyses are LLM-generated annotations whose reliability rests on 48 hand-coded trajectories from 6 seed problems; (c) semantic-space tracking is explicitly unvalidated (authors acknowledge no gold standard exists); (d) the correctness-prediction comparison uses only 100 problems, so the 0.046 AUROC margin over ThinkARM is modest and possibly not robust; (e) proprietary hidden-trace models (GPT-o3-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash) are analyzed on unverifiable reasoning traces — a faithfulness confound the paper cites in related work but does not address for its own annotations. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (analysis framework + small training experiment). - Practical: Yes — annotation runs via prompted LLMs (open-weight Qwen3.5-27B), and GRPO training fits on 2×B200 in ~3–3.5 hours. - Efficient: Annotation cost is non-trivial ($100 for 445 trajectories with Grok-4.1-Fast, motivating the open-weight annotator); training is cheap by post-training standards. - Effective: Diagnostic value is well evidenced (beats baselines on correctness prediction, reveals mechanism behind known RLVR pathologies); the training fix is only demonstrated on one 1.7B model at 200 steps against 23.54% baseline accuracy — evidence of promise, not of a solved problem. - Scalable: Untested; all analyses are ≤115-problem benchmarks and ≤8B models for analysis, 1.7B for training; scaling annotation quality control beyond 48 gold trajectories is unaddressed. The work delivers a released code artifact with prompts/guidebooks and a reusable taxonomy, but no trained model weights are mentioned. Strengths: - Genuinely imports a mature theoretical framework (Pólya, Koichu, Favier & Dorier) rather than inventing ad-hoc CoT labels, and takes the operationalization seriously: content-unit segmentation, consensus coding, and interpretive adjudication are lifted from the education literature rather than improvised. - The gold-standard construction is unusually careful for LLM-annotation papers: four human annotators, one a math-education researcher, 1,598 units, documented borderline-case adjudication, and per-class kappa honestly reported including weak classes. - The three empirical findings form a coherent arc — heuristic features predict correctness, correct trajectories are space-focused, RLVR narrows heuristic distributions — and the mode-seeking result provides a strategic-level (not surface-form) counterpart to prior diversity-collapse work, with an appropriate negative control. - The perturbation analysis (adaptation without convergence, divergence within the first 5 content units) is a well-controlled insight that accuracy-only evaluation structurally cannot produce. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states SHAPE analyzes only observable CoT traces (implicitly conceding the faithfulness problem the related-work section documents — verbalized reasoning may be post-hoc) and that validation is limited to mathematical benchmarks, with other domains left to future work. The paper also openly labels the training results "preliminary" and openly admits semantic-space tracking lacks an objective gold standard and was only prompt-calibrated. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No error bars, seeds, or variance for the HA-Plan-GRPO results; a 6.8-point Avg@64 margin from a rollout-prompt change on one 1.7B model at one seed could be prompt-engineering noise, and the paper's own framing (planning already gives +6.5) leaves little headroom for the heuristic increment. - Possible circularity in the correctness-prediction experiment: SHAPE features are produced by an LLM annotator whose quality is only validated on 48 trajectories from 6 seed problems of the same benchmark family; annotator bias correlated with problem difficulty could inflate AUROC on the 100-problem set. - The heuristic-augmented training prompt tells the model which heuristics exist, so the gain may reflect privileged output-format information rather than the SHAPE diagnosis; no ablation with an equal-length non-heuristic planning prompt isolates this. - Correct trajectories' lower N_eff could partially be a mechanical consequence of shorter correct traces (fewer opportunities to open spaces); no length-controlled analysis of the focus finding is reported. - Models with hidden proprietary traces are annotated as if their CoT reflects computation, a concern the paper itself surveys but does not mitigate. - The RETURN decision depends on a memory-buffer state machine whose per-step accuracy is never measured against anything, so all N_eff_space/N_eff_trans numbers inherit unquantified tracking error. Bottom Line: A thoughtful and unusually well-grounded diagnostic framework that gives LLM-math-reasoning researchers a real, education-theoretic lens on CoT structure and credible evidence that RLVR narrows strategic behavior, but the training contribution is a small preliminary demonstration — read it for the analysis lens and findings, not for a method you should adopt for post-training yet.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VideoHarness-RSI, a controlled framework that recursively searches executable context-construction code around a frozen VLM (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) for long-video QA, selecting harnesses via strict development-set frontier promotion and evaluating them on held-out and cross-benchmark data. - Why it's important: Long-video performance depends heavily on how evidence is packed into a limited context, but prior systems conflate model changes with context-construction changes, so nobody knows how much gain the harness program alone contributes; Problem & Motivation: Long-video understanding is bottlenecked by context construction: relevant evidence is sparse in hours of video, and a VLM cannot consume everything. Prior systems (VideoAgent, Deep Video Discovery, WorldMM, Homer, VideoSEAL, LongVu) change evidence representation, retrieval, tools, workflow, and sometimes the model simultaneously, making it impossible to attribute gains to the context-construction program itself. Practitioners building long-video QA systems cannot currently tell whether investing in a better harness, a better model, or more frames pays off. The paper closes the gap of studying the executable context constructor as an isolated, independently optimizable layer around a fixed model and fixed answer interface. Key Idea: Treat the harness — the executable program mapping (video, question) to a bounded multimodal context — as the sole mutable object, and run an LLM-proposer-driven search over such programs with a deliberately strict retain-only-on-strict-improvement rule, freezing everything else. The analytical Write–Read–Pack decomposition (construct addressable representation; retrieve question-conditioned evidence; pack bounded context) defines the search space without mandating any component. The core trick is the contract: model, decoding, metric, and per-call visual capacity (K=40) are fixed, so any accuracy change is attributable to the program. Methodology: The framework formalizes optimization as H* = argmax over executable constructors of development accuracy of a frozen VLM M answering from H(V, q; K). The outer loop is a propose–execute–evaluate–retain cycle: the proposer (Claude Opus 4.6 via Claude Code) inspects the frontier and an archive of prior code, scores, and traces; candidates are smoke-tested and evaluated end-to-end on the 350-question LVBench development split; the frontier updates only on strict point-estimate improvement. Two initialization regimes are studied: weak seeding from Uniform-40 and strong seeding from AKS (adaptive keyframe sampling, Tang et al. 2025). Controls include Uniform-40, CLIP-KNN, Caption-KNN, AKS, re-implementations of WorldMM/Homer/VideoSEAL patterns under the same interface, and proprietary-VLM rows (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash). A post-hoc AKS-90 control tests whether cumulative token consumption alone explains gains. Mechanism analysis uses LVBench's annotated evidence intervals only after inference (evidence-visibility, conditional accuracy). Critical design decisions: (1) strict deterministic promotion without statistical testing — defensible for leak-prevention but admits selection noise; (2) per-call K=40 cap with cumulative cost reported separately — a well-motivated and honest choice, since the winner exploits multi-call execution; (3) held-out and cross-benchmark data never entering promotion — well-justified and enforced with released verification scripts. Key Results: On the 882-question LVBench held-out split with frozen Qwen3-VL-8B: Uniform-40 36.3%, CLIP-KNN 41.7%, AKS 46.6%, uniform-seeded StatedTimeAddressDecode 49.0%, AKS-seeded CardinalityLedger 54.8% (483/882). Development: AKS 49.7 → CardinalityLedger 58.3 over four strict promotions in 10 iterations (StatedInterval 53.7, SurveyCommit 55.7, PointerLadder 57.4, CardinalityLedger 58.3). Matched-cost control: AKS-90 (90 frames, ~19,583 visual tokens) reaches 49.2% held-out versus CardinalityLedger's 54.8% at 19,210 tokens — the gap persists at matched cumulative visual-token budget (Δ+5.6 pp, CI [2.4, 8.7]). Cross-benchmark direct reuse: MLVU 75.0 vs AKS 72.0 vs uniform 63.2; Video-MME 67.5 vs 66.9 vs 59.9. Proprietary comparison: uniform sampling with GPT-5 reaches 46.5%, below the searched 8B-model harness. Baselines are current (AKS is a 2025 method; WorldMM/Homer/VideoSEAL are 2025–2026 works re-implemented under a common interface). Statistical support is strong for the main comparison (McNemar p=3.39e-7; paired bootstrap, 20,000 resamples). Traces show the discovered program is query-adaptive: 14.3% of dev questions take an interval-bypass path, 77.7% take a two-stage coarse-to-fine ladder, 6.3% add a counting ledger. Notably, the exploratory high-capacity caption-retrieval study in Appendix D fails to beat uniform on test (43.31 vs 42.83, p=0.72), an honestly reported negative result. Scale is standard (LVBench/MLVU/Video-MME), not stress-scale; search cost (proposer tokens, wall-clock) is not reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the search mechanism itself is a standard combination. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the controlled formulation of long-video context construction as the sole mutable optimization object with a fixed frozen-VLM interface and auditable lineage, and (b) the empirical findings that search advances a strong hand-crafted frontier and that gains survive matched-token and cross-benchmark controls. The propose–evaluate–retain loop is inherited from ADAS/AFlow/Meta-Harness, and the authors say so explicitly; the contribution is the disciplined instantiation and evaluation protocol, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above average for this subfield. Ablations that matter are present: the AKS-90 matched-token control directly tests the compute-confound; literature-inspired re-implementations control for design-pattern alternatives; evidence-visibility analysis links accuracy to mechanism; an oracle sweep (Table 7) quantifies remaining context-selection headroom (8.9–21.1 pp depending on K). Significance testing is real: exact two-sided McNemar and paired bootstrap CIs for the key comparisons. Code, the seed-42 split, per-question predictions, complete trajectories with code/parentage/traces, and context sidecars are released (github.com/Tencent/VideoHarness-RSI), with verification scripts for the headline statistics. Concerns: (1) promotion uses deterministic point estimates on 350 questions, so noise-driven promotion is possible (the authors concede this); (2) the LVBench subset lost 20 of 103 videos to availability issues, so absolute numbers are not comparable to published LVBench results; (3) the split is question-level, so the same video can appear in both development and held-out — video-level leakage is possible and unaddressed; (4) a proprietary proposer (Claude Opus 4.6) may carry benchmark-level prior knowledge of LVBench, which the authors acknowledge but cannot rule out; (5) one seed, one model, one proposer — no error bars over search itself. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework with executed experiments; the artifact is a searched harness plus evaluation infrastructure). - Practical: Yes — the answering stack is an 8B open-weight VLM plus CLIP ViT-B/32 on commodity hardware; the only proprietary component is the offline proposer. - Efficient: Mixed — the winner costs ~2.2× the AKS parent in cumulative input tokens (19,210 vs 8,788) and ~2× frames, and the accuracy-per-token argument is only established against one matched control (AKS-90); end-to-end latency and monetary cost are explicitly not measured. - Effective: Yes for the stated problem — held-out and two cross-benchmark results with paired statistics show the harness, not just extra tokens, drives gains; but effectiveness is shown only on multiple-choice QA benchmarks with letter-only scoring. - Scalable: Not tested — no evidence on longer videos, larger VLMs, more search iterations, or more trajectories; claims of generality are limited to direct cross-benchmark reuse and are correspondingly modest. Delivers a software artifact: released harness code, search archive with full lineage, evaluation dumps, and verification scripts. Strengths: - The AKS-90 matched-cumulative-token control is the paper's best move: it preempts the obvious confound (multi-call harnesses just buy more pixels) and shows the searched program still wins by +5.6 pp at equal visual-token budget. - Strict separation of search evidence from evaluation evidence — held-out and cross-benchmark data never touch promotion — combined with released complete trajectories, per-question dumps, and scripts that re-verify the McNemar/bootstrap numbers, sets a high auditability bar for harness-search work. - The two-regime design (weak Uniform seed vs strong AKS seed) is a genuinely informative experimental structure: it shows both structure discovery from scratch (36.3 → 49.0 held-out) and frontier advancement beyond a strong hand-crafted baseline (46.6 → 54.8). - Honest negative and mechanism reporting: a non-promoting high-capacity retrieval study, a trajectory where later candidates fail or tie, and trace-level analysis of query-adaptive execution depth (interval bypass vs L0→L1 ladder vs counting ledger) make the claims interpretable as program behavior, not just scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: one frozen VLM, one data seed, limited search trajectories (no cross-model or search-variance evidence); the LVBench subset with unavailable videos and a question-level rather than video-disjoint split; possible benchmark-level prior knowledge in the proprietary proposer; equal per-call budgets not implying equal cumulative cost; per-video rather than cross-question memory; and that "recursive self-improvement" means iterative harness-code improvement, not model self-amplification. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Video-level leakage: the question-level split means development and held-out questions can come from the same video, so some of the held-out gain may reflect video-specific context patterns; a video-disjoint split ablation is absent. - Benchmark-format exploitation: the discovered programs are heavily specialized to LVBench's question idioms (StatedTimeAddressDecode targets literal timestamp questions; CardinalityLedger targets counting questions). The MLVU/Video-MME transfer gaps shrink (MLVU +3.0, Video-MME +0.6 over AKS), consistent with part of the LVBench gain being format-specific; no analysis decomposes gains by question type on the transfer benchmarks. - No comparison against applying an existing harness-search method (ADAS, AFlow, Meta-Harness) to the same setting, so the claimed benefit of the controlled contract over off-the-shelf search is untested. - Search cost (proposer tokens, candidate evaluation compute, wall-clock) is never reported, so the expense of reaching the improved harness is unknown. - Single proposer and single promotion seed: with 350-question dev splits, several reported candidate scores differ by margins within plausible noise; no repeated searches from the same seed test whether CardinalityLedger is typical or lucky. - The Video-MME advantage over AKS (+0.6 pp) is within any plausible noise band but is presented in a table without significance testing, inviting over-reading of transfer. Bottom Line: A practitioner in harness search or long-video systems should read this for its unusually disciplined controls — especially the matched-token experiment and full search-lineage release — while treating the headline LVBench numbers as partly benchmark-format-specific and awaiting multi-seed, multi-model replication before concluding the searched harnesses generalize broadly.

EarlyEval: Cheaper Agent Evaluation via Early Outcome Prediction (110 ▲ )

Yuling Shi, Zhensu Sun, Junsen Dong, Chengcheng Wan, David Lo, Xiaodong Gu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 3 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EarlyEval, a framework that halves an LLM agent's benchmark rollout by training LightGBM success and failure classifiers on historical, outcome-labeled agent trajectories and halting a new agent's run the moment either classifier crosses a calibrated confidence threshold, predicting the final outcome from the partial trajectory. - Why it's important: A single evaluation pass of a frontier agent over an agentic benchmark costs $300–$2,270 (per the OpenHands Index figures cited), paid repeatedly across development cycles, and prior efficiency work only shrinks the task list rather than the per-task rollout cost. - How it does it: Historical trajectories are expanded into step-wise labeled prefixes, converted to a ~400-dimensional feature vector (behavioral counters/patterns, TF-IDF+SVD text embeddings, optional gold-patch overlap features), and two separately trained gradient-boosted ensembles with Platt-calibrated probabilities fire a dual-threshold halting rule. - The good: The leave-one-agent-out evaluation is genuinely rigorous — it separately withholds both the same model and the same scaffold for TerminalBench — and shows 26.0% step reduction on SWE-bench Verified at 95.0% accuracy with only 1.1pp mean resolve-rate distortion and leaderboard rank correlation ρ=0.991. - The missing: All headline operating points are selected post hoc on the same evaluation data (choosing the lowest threshold keeping Δ|Pass@1| under ~2pp), there are no error bars or multiple seeds (single seed 42), and the success predictor collapses on two of three benchmarks, so the dual mechanism is really failure-only there. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building agent benchmarks or paying for repeated agent evaluations, since it defines and validates a new efficiency axis (per-task early stopping) complementary to benchmark distillation; skippable if you only consume leaderboard numbers once.

Problem & Motivation Teams developing LLM agents re-run agentic benchmarks dozens of times per development cycle, and each pass is expensive because multi-step rollouts compound model calls and context-window growth: the paper cites $715–$935 per pass on SWE-bench Verified and up to $2,270 on SWE-bench Multimodal for a single agent configuration. Prior efficiency work (Anchor Points, tinyBenchmarks, adaptive testing) reduces the number of tasks evaluated but leaves the cost of executing each retained task unchanged. The gap the paper targets is the orthogonal axis: within a single task's rollout, the final outcome is often inferable from intermediate behavior long before completion — e.g., an agent that applies the correct one-line fix, or one that repeatedly retries the same edit against an unchanged error message — so the remaining steps (including running test suites) are wasted spend. Key Idea The core insight is that an agent's final benchmark outcome is statistically predictable from its partial trajectory prefix, and that the needed supervision already exists for free: public leaderboards and benchmark releases accumulate thousands of complete, outcome-labeled trajectories from other agents on the same benchmark, from which agent-agnostic prefix classifiers can be trained. The trick that makes it cheap and deployable is representing each prefix as a fixed-length hand-crafted feature vector (rather than raw text) so a LightGBM ensemble can re-score every step in sub-millisecond CPU time, avoiding an LLM judge whose per-step inference cost would cancel the savings. Methodology The pipeline has two stages. (1) Offline: historical trajectories (each with binary outcome y) are expanded into prefixes τ:k for every step k, each prefix mapped to a fixed-length feature vector with three families — behavioral features (115 features: activity counts, last-step properties, event timing, working patterns like stalling/repeated-action indicators, error and test status), textual features (320 dims: TF-IDF word n-grams over independently vectorized blocks — task prompt, action history, recent action, all feedback, recent feedback — compressed to 64–128 dims via Truncated SVD), and reference-solution features (82 dims: gold-patch descriptors plus Jaccard/hit overlap between files, API symbols, and tests the agent touched and those in the gold patch; disabled on benchmarks without gold patches). (2) Online: at each step of a new agent's run, two calibrated LightGBM ensembles score the prefix — a success predictor trained to target y=1 and a failure predictor targeting y=0 — and Platt scaling (1D logistic regression fit on a held-out validation fold) recalibrates probabilities; the run halts at the first step where p+ ≥ s or p− ≥ f, otherwise continues. Critical design decisions: (a) two separate classifiers rather than one joint classifier, justified as capturing asymmetric success/failure evidence and creating an explicit abstention region — supported by the finding that the two predictors almost never fire on the same trajectory (step savings are exactly additive); (b) prefix weighting by 1/(T+1) to equalize per-trajectory loss mass, reasonable but unvalidated; (c) a shared fixed LightGBM hyperparameter configuration across all benchmarks, convenient but the paper does not show sensitivity to it. Key Results Experiments span three benchmarks with 21,678 outcome-labeled trajectories total: SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks, 16 agents via mini-SWE-agent, 7,805 trajectories), TerminalBench (89 tasks, 37 scaffold+LLM configurations, 6,757 trajectories), and Toolathlon (108 tasks, 22 LLMs, 7,116 trajectories), all evaluated under leave-one-agent-out cross-validation. Headline results: on SWE-bench Verified at threshold 0.95, the dual mechanism halts 34.8% of runs at 95.0% accuracy, cutting 26.0% of steps, 32.7% of input tokens, and 28.7% of output tokens with Δ|Pass@1| = 1.1pp and ρ = 0.991 (81% of agents keep exact rank). Toolathlon at 0.90: 23.0% step savings at 96.6% failure-predictor precision, Δ|Pass@1| = 0.9pp, ρ = 0.994. TerminalBench: 24.6% step savings (no-same-model split) at ρ = 0.959, and 12.7% (no-same-scaffold) at ρ = 0.994. Lowering thresholds to 0.75 on SWE-bench raises step savings to 63.4% but inflates Δ|Pass@1| to 4.1pp, demonstrating a monotone tunable trade-off. Notable findings: the success predictor is reliable only on SWE-bench (precision 88.3–93.9%) and collapses on the others (coverage near zero on Toolathlon; precision 61.4–69.0% on the no-same-scaffold TerminalBench split), while the failure predictor is robust everywhere (89.4–99.4% precision); unseen scaffolds hurt prediction far more than unseen base models. Ablations show behavioral features are the main driver (removing them drops step savings from 26.0% to 16.4%), reference features are dispensable, and LightGBM dominates an MLP (87.9% accuracy, 20.0% savings), two logistic regressions, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen-0.5B judge (90.7% accuracy, 17.9% savings, plus per-step LLM inference cost). Baselines are reasonable but the comparison set is small and only tested on SWE-bench Verified; the study is run at standard benchmark scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM framing plus NEW METHOD: the paper defines early outcome prediction for benchmark evaluation — halting an agent rollout once its judged outcome is predictable — which is distinct from deployment-time agent early-exit work (which tries to preserve the agent's own success) and from benchmark distillation (which reduces task count). The method itself is a competent, well-engineered combination of standard components (gradient-boosted trees over hand-crafted trajectory features, prefix expansion, Platt calibration, dual-threshold abstention); the novelty lies in the problem framing, the use of public leaderboard trajectories as free supervision, and the empirical demonstration that this is feasible with strict agent-level leakage control, not in any individual technique. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are present and informative: per-family and per-group feature ablations (RQ3, Table V) show redundancy across and within families, and backbone ablations (RQ4, Table VI) compare against an MLP, two linear baselines, and an LLM judge under the identical protocol. The leakage controls are unusually careful: trajectory-level task-partitioned splits, leave-one-agent-out rotation, and two additional TerminalBench settings removing all trajectories sharing the held-out agent's model or scaffold. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported — everything uses fixed seed 42 — and the "recommended operating point" for each benchmark is chosen as the lowest threshold keeping Δ|Pass@1| within ~2pp on the same data being reported, a mild Goodhart risk since threshold selection and fidelity claims share the evaluation set. Prediction accuracy is computed only over trajectories actually halted (a selected subpopulation), though per-predictor precision is helpfully reported alongside. Code and experimental data are released at https://github.com/inphotoo/earlyeval. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2609.02783); no peer-review status is stated. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small SYSTEMS component via the released code). - Practical: Yes — the predictor is a LightGBM ensemble scoring a few-hundred-dimensional feature vector in sub-millisecond CPU time per step, runnable on any commodity machine alongside the evaluation harness. - Efficient: Per-step overhead is negligible by design, and the method nets 13–26% step savings and up to 44.1% input-token savings; the cost of assembling the training pool is amortized since it reuses publicly available labeled trajectories. - Effective: The evidence shows it preserves both absolute scores (within ~1–2pp) and rankings (ρ ≥ 0.959) on held-out agents, which is the stated goal for iterative development — though the authors themselves scope it away from producing canonical citable leaderboard numbers. - Scalable: Not directly tested beyond these three benchmarks and 37 agents; the authors claim predictors can be refreshed cheaply as benchmarks accumulate runs, but behavior under distribution shift (new scaffolds fundamentally changing trajectory structure — their own TerminalBench result hints at this) is untested at 10× scale or over time. Deliverable: a released software artifact with experimental data, plus a reusable recipe (feature schema, halting rule) for other benchmarks. Strengths - Genuinely new efficiency axis for agent evaluation with a clear, defensible problem statement that cleanly separates it from benchmark distillation and deployment-time early exit, backed by a well-differentiated related-work section. - The leave-one-agent-out protocol with scaffold-level and model-level withholding is a credibility standout; most evaluation-methodology papers would not have controlled for residual scaffold leakage, and the finding that unseen scaffolds degrade prediction more than unseen models is a real, non-obvious empirical contribution. - Honest reporting of asymmetric predictor performance: the paper explicitly shows its success predictor fails on two of three benchmarks and recommends practitioners validate predictors per benchmark, rather than hiding the weakness. - The feature-redundancy ablation (RQ3) substantiates the design claim that reference-free operation is viable, directly explaining why the method transfers to benchmarks without gold patches — a concrete mechanism, not just a robustness number. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility. In Discussion they state: (1) the method requires a pool of completed outcome-labeled trajectories on the target benchmark, so it cannot help with first-ever evaluations of brand-new benchmarks; (2) early stopping introduces a systematic ~1–2pp deviation in measured resolve rates, so they explicitly recommend it for iterative relative comparison only, not for canonical citable leaderboard scores; (3) the threats-to-validity section addresses internal (leakage, mitigated), external (generalization to unseen agents/benchmarks), and construct validity (whether token/step proxies capture real savings). They do not, however, dwell on the success-predictor collapse outside SWE-bench or the scaffold-sensitivity finding as limitations per se, though both are visible in their own results. Analyst-Identified Gaps - Operating-point selection and fidelity reporting share the same evaluation data (the ~2pp Δ|Pass@1| constraint is enforced on the reported numbers), so the headline operating points are mildly optimistic; a nested validation split for threshold selection would close this. - The success predictor's near-zero coverage on Toolathlon and TerminalBench means the "dual" mechanism is effectively failure-only there, and the paper's abstract and conclusion do not surface this asymmetry — a reader could over-credit the symmetric design. - No statistical uncertainty: single seed, no confidence intervals on ρ or Δ|Pass@1|; with 16–37 agents, rank-correlation estimates are fragile, and the TerminalBench no-same-model split's ρ = 0.959 with 59% exact ranks may not be distinguishable from alternatives. - Time-based distribution shift is unaddressed: predictors trained on yesterday's leaderboard trajectories may silently degrade as scaffolds and models evolve — precisely the regime the method targets — and no longitudinal experiment or drift monitoring is proposed. - Only the halting decision is learned; the counterfactual cost of trajectories the predictor declines to halt (the 65–87% that run to completion) bounds total savings well below the 50%-level reductions the motivating examples suggest, and the paper does not analyze what fraction of theoretical savings the abstention region forfeits. - The LLM-judge baseline is a single 0.5B LoRA model; a stronger off-the-shelf judge (or a cheaper prompting-based predictor) is not tested, so the "LightGBM is the right backbone" conclusion rests on a narrow comparison. Bottom Line This is a solid, honestly-reported systems-empirical paper that opens a genuinely new and practical axis of agent-evaluation cost reduction — read it if you run or maintain agentic benchmarks, but treat its savings as the modest 13–26% of steps it actually delivers rather than the halving its motivating examples imply, and expect to re-tune predictors as your benchmark's agent population drifts.

Learning Simple Test-Time Environments for LLM Web Agents

J Li, Z Liu, Z Huang, P Li, Y Liu, M Yan, Y Liu · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TTED, a label-free test-time learning framework in which an LLM web agent decomposes a complex web observation into sub-goal/sub-observation pairs ("trial steps"), gathers self-assessed experience in these simplified sub-environments, and adapts its policy via in-context learning or reinforcement learning before executing the full task. - Why it's important: LLM web agents collapse on cluttered real-world interfaces (Qwen3-8B success rate falls from 85% to 19% as CompWoB+ components grow from 3 to 8), and label-free test-time adaptation fails there because both exploration and self-assessment degrade; this work directly targets that compositional generalization failure without ground-truth rewards. - How it does it: The agent performs explicit environment decomposition (predict a localized sub-goal, extract the task-relevant sub-observation from the accessibility tree), scores the decomposition and action with an LLM-as-judge reward (r_goal, r_obs in [0,5]; r_action in {0,1}), and trains decomposition and action policies jointly with off-policy REINFORCE using rollout importance sampling and cross-environment advantage normalization. - The good: TTED-RL reaches 21.0% success on a 561-task WebArena subset versus 12.1% for the base model, 14.8% for ground-truth-supervised RL, and 12.5-13.5% for monolithic TTT/TTRL, with statistical significance (p < 10^-4 vs. two baselines) and 0.85 human-agreement reward labeling versus 0.68-0.71 for baselines. - The missing: The headline "beats ground-truth RL" claim rests on a transductive setup — the policy is trained via RL on trajectories drawn from the same WebArena distribution it is evaluated on — while the ground-truth RL baseline is not given the same test-distribution exposure, and the method is only trained on 8B/14B open models with a self-judged reward loop. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on LLM agent training and test-time adaptation, because the decomposition-as-learning-unit idea and the reward-quality analysis (Table 2) are genuinely instructive; practitioners seeking deployed web automation should note the absolute success rates (21.0%) remain far below proprietary frontier agents (GPT-5.5: 67.3%).

Problem & Motivation LLM web agents perform well in curated, low-clutter environments but fail on realistic websites where a single observation mixes search panels, forms, content containers, and modal widgets. The paper argues this is a compositional generalization gap: each sub-structure is manageable in isolation, but their joint presence breaks both action generation and self-assessment, so test-time methods (prompting, reflection, test-time training) that rely on exploration success and self-judged rewards become ineffective precisely when complexity rises. The problem affects anyone building label-free, inference-time-adaptable web agents, since reliable ground-truth rewards for post-training are scarce in real deployments. Prior test-time methods (TTRL's self-consistency rewards, TTT) either cannot supervise free-form decomposition or operate on the full cluttered environment, leaving the coupled exploration/self-assessment failure unaddressed. Key Idea Decompose the test-time environment itself, not just the plan: instead of optimizing the policy against the full complex environment (or decomposing only the goal, as planning does), TTED rewrites each state into localized sub-environments E^(i) = (S^(i), A, T, R^(i)) — aligned sub-goal plus extracted sub-observation with the original action space — so that exploration succeeds more often and the LLM self-assessor produces far more accurate reward labels in the simplified context. Local gains from these cheap, reliable learning units are then composed (via ICL demonstrations or RL parameter updates) to solve the full task. The supporting empirical insight is that self-assessment accuracy is context-dependent: reward labeling agreement with humans jumps from 0.68-0.71 (monolithic) to 0.85 inside decomposed sub-environments. Methodology TTED is a two-stage framework formalized on an MDP E = (S, A, T, R). Stage 1 (trial steps) has four steps run by the same LLM at high temperature over unfolded accessibility trees: (1) decomposition — predict sub-goal g_t^(i) = pi_goal(g, o_t, H_{t-1}) and extract sub-observation o_t^(i) = pi_obs(o_t, g_t^(i)); (2) action generation pi_action(g_t^(i), o_t^(i), H_{t-1}); (3) self-assessment as a generative reward model producing (r_goal, r_obs in [0,5], r_action in {0,1}); steps pass only if decomposition scores exceed a threshold and r_action = 1, otherwise retry up to a limit; (4) summary appended to history; rejected trials execute no environment action. Stage 2 adapts the policy: for single-turn static pages (CompWoB+), ICL conditions final action generation on curated passing demonstrations, with reliability boosted by executing actions in Selenium simulations of the sub-observation HTML plus LLM-generated JavaScript verification; for multi-turn realistic sites (WebArena), RL updates all parameters (decomposition + action policies) with undiscounted REINFORCE using an off-policy scheme: rollout importance sampling ratio rho_t = pi_theta(a|s)/pi_theta_old,inf(a|s), rewards linearly mapped to [-1,1], and advantages standardized across the training mini-batch across different sub-environments (REINFORCE++-style normalization) under a GSPO loss. Critical design decisions: (a) joint optimization of decomposition and action heads — justified by the ablation showing sub-goal decomposition alone is the largest contributor; (2) learning from rejected trials (r_action = 0 does not imply bad decomposition) — justified qualitatively for data efficiency; (3) cross-environment advantage normalization rather than per-group GRPO estimation — supported by the scaling ablation (21.0% vs. 17.6-17.8% for REINFORCE/GRPO variants), though the justification is empirical rather than theoretical. Key Results On CompWoB+ (600 self-generated composite tasks, 100 per size from 3-8 components), unadapted Qwen3-8B falls from 85% to 19% success as components grow 3 to 8, and GPT-4o-mini from 97% to 46%; TTED-ICL raises the 8-component rates to 61% (Qwen3-8B) and 88% (GPT-4o-mini); Qwen3-14B reaches 78% at 8 components. On a 561-task WebArena subset (Reddit tasks excluded for network failures), Qwen3-8B: base 12.1%, SFT w/ GT 14.1%, RL w/ GT 14.8%, TTT (RL) 12.5%, TTRL 13.5%, TTED (SFT) 17.6%, TTED (RL) 21.0% at 3200 sub-environments (19.4% at only 800). Out-of-distribution on WorkArena without further training: 22.7% vs. 18.2% base. Qwen3-14B: 19.3% to 22.5% on WebArena. Reward-labeling human agreement (normalized AD, 82 WebArena tasks, annotators at 0.85 Cohen's kappa): TTED 0.85 vs. TTRL 0.68 and TTT 0.71. Ablations: removing sub-goal decomposition drops WebArena SR to 12.4%, removing sub-observation extraction to 15.0%, removing both (= TTT) 12.5%. Significance: three repeated runs with <0.5% absolute variation; TTED 21.0% with 95% Wilson CI [17.9, 24.6], one-sided tests p < 10^-4 vs. base and TTT, p = 0.0032 vs. RL w/ GT — but the Qwen3-14B gains are not significant (p = 0.061-0.153). Efficiency: TTED increases interaction steps (8.29 vs. 4.72) yet cuts average prompt tokens (3948 vs. 6339); training costs 14.8-21.3 GPU-hours on 8x A100-80GB, comparable to TTT. Baselines are recent and relevant (TTRL NeurIPS'25, TTT ICML'25, AgentOccam, Plan-and-Act), though the TTT baseline is the authors' own monolithic re-implementation. Scale is standard research scale (8B-14B models, hundreds of tasks), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (test-time environment decomposition as a label-free adaptation unit, covering both ICL and RL instantiations), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (CompWoB+, an automated synthesis engine extending CompWoB from ~50 to 600 tasks with 3-8 components), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (label-free test-time RL via decomposition surpassing ground-truth-supervised RL on WebArena). The core trick — splitting observations into goal-aligned sub-views — builds on established ideas (observation pruning like AgentOccam/FocusAgent, LLM-as-judge rewards, TTRL-style test-time RL, REINFORCE++ normalization); the genuine novelty is treating localized decomposed environments as learning signal units rather than mere context reduction, and the demonstration that this specifically repairs self-assessment quality under compositional complexity. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are present and informative: component ablation (Table 4), reward-labeling quality against human labels (Table 2), advantage-estimation and budget-scaling ablations (Table 3), model-scale replication (Qwen3-14B), and three-run significance testing with Wilson intervals. Code and data are released at https://github.com/THUNLP-MT/TTED, and prompts, hyperparameters, GPU-hours, and retry limits are documented in appendices. Methodological concerns: (1) the primary WebArena result is developed and evaluated on the same benchmark distribution by design (transductive test-time adaptation), which inflates the comparison against non-transductive ground-truth RL baselines; (2) the TTT baseline is implemented by the authors rather than taken from an external reference implementation; (3) CompWoB+ is the authors' own benchmark, mitigated partly by inheriting CompWoB's reward rules; (4) reward signals come from the same backbone model being trained (self-reinforcement risk the authors partially acknowledge); (5) the GPT-5.5 comparison (67.3%) is on full WebArena-Verified with different verifiers, so cross-benchmark numbers are context only. Statistical rigor on the main 8B result is solid; the 14B result is honestly reported as not significant. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods run and measured on real benchmarks, with a released system). - Practical: Runs on 8x NVIDIA A100-80GB with open Qwen3-8B/14B and vLLM/VeRL — commercially available hardware. - Efficient: Test-time RL costs 14.8-21.3 GPU-hours per adaptation run and adds exploration steps (8.29 vs. 4.72 steps/task), but reduces per-action prompt tokens by ~38%, a favorable trade given six-figure-token web pages. - Effective: Evidence shows it improves success rate and OOD transfer on WebArena/WorkArena, but the mechanism is validated against a proxy self-assessed reward whose fidelity (0.85 human agreement) is measured only on 82 tasks with two annotators; absolute performance (21.0%) remains far from production-grade. - Scalable: Test-time compute scaling is tested from 800 to 3200 sub-environments with consistent gains (19.4% to 21.0%), but 10x-100x scale, larger backbones, and genuinely open-web deployment are untested. Delivers a software artifact: released code, CompWoB+ dataset generation engine, and trained checkpoints implied by the repository. Strengths - The core reframing — decomposition of the environment as a unit of test-time learning rather than a context-shortening heuristic — is a real conceptual contribution, cleanly distinguished from planning (Appendix A.1 gives an explicit formal contrast: planning optimizes the full-environment reward, TTED optimizes summed sub-environment rewards). - The measurement that self-assessment accuracy is the bottleneck and improves specifically under decomposition (0.68-0.71 to 0.85 human agreement) is the paper's most convincing piece of evidence and links mechanism to outcome. - The RL engineering is competent and honestly ablated: rollout importance sampling for inference-engine rollouts, bounded [-1,1] reward mapping, and cross-environment advantage normalization each demonstrably matter (normalization alone: 17.6% to 21.0%). - Honest statistics where it counts: three repeats, Wilson CIs, p-values, and transparent reporting that the 14B gains are not significant, plus efficiency numbers showing TTED is not cost-free. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state (Appendix A.2): (1) decomposition quality is capped by the backbone model's capability — poor decomposition propagates errors, especially where real-world boundaries are implicit; (2) self-assessment inherits bias and noise from the same backbone, with no external verifier in the multi-turn RL setting. They also acknowledge in case studies that residual failures stem from action-space misalignment and overthinking rather than decomposition errors, and in the ethical statement that TTED is a prototype, not a production system. This is direct, non-minimizing engagement with limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The "outperforms RL with ground-truth rewards" headline compares a transductive method (RL on test-distribution trajectories) against a non-transductive one; a fairer framing would report GT-RL with equivalent test-distribution exposure or evaluate on a held-out split. - No comparison against strong prompting/reflection/planning test-time baselines actually run under the same budget (Plan-and-Act, reflection-style methods are discussed as orthogonal but not combined or measured), so the marginal value of decomposition over well-tuned inference-time reasoning is unquantified. - The CompWoB+ ICL path uses Selenium simulation and JavaScript verification — a strong deterministic reward only available for static pages; the realistic path falls back to pure LLM judgment, and the paper does not test how much of the WebArena gain would survive without the GRM's hand-written scoring principles, a potential Goodhart surface where the judge prompt encodes substantial task knowledge. - WebArena evaluation uses a 561-task subset with all Reddit tasks removed and a swapped fuzzy-matching judge (GPT-5-mini instead of GPT-4o-Turbo); absolute numbers are therefore not directly comparable to published WebArena results from other papers. - Human reward-agreement evaluation covers only 82 tasks and 2 annotators; self-assessment drift during training (the reward model and policy co-evolve) is not tracked over training steps. - Only Qwen3 backbones are trained; whether the decomposition skill is learnable in weaker models — the very regime where the authors admit decomposition quality collapses — is untested. Bottom Line A researcher in LLM agent training gains concrete, transferable insight here — especially that decomposition is the lever that makes label-free test-time RL viable on cluttered web environments, backed by a careful reward-quality analysis — making this worth reading despite the transductive evaluation framing and absolute performance levels that remain far from frontier proprietary agents.

KTPO: K-Step Test-Time Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Discovery

D Li, F Zhao, S Cao, H Zhang, JE Gonzalez, I Stoica · openreview.net · Ion Stoica - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces KTPO, a test-time RL method that trains 4B–9B open-weight LLMs on short k-step program-refinement trajectories initialized from a pool of previously discovered programs, achieving or approaching human/AI records on seven mathematical and systems-optimization tasks. - Why it's important: Existing LLM-driven discovery systems (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve) keep the model frozen and rely on frontier or proprietary models over hundreds of refinement steps; KTPO shows the policy itself can be trained cheaply (8×H100, one node) to close that gap. - How it does it: It sidesteps the long-horizon RL problem by optimizing only k=4–8-step refinement segments seeded from a curated pool, with a +1/0/−0.5 improvement-based GRPO reward and pool eviction driven by the model's measured improvement rate over its parents. - The good: Under matched compute and identical backbone (Qwen3-4B), KTPO beats ThetaEvolve (2.632±0.002 vs 2.559±0.045 on Circle Packing) and all four evolutionary baselines (OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, GEPA, AdaEvolve) on both Circle Packing and Cloudcast, isolating the method as the source of the gains. - The missing: Qwen3.5-9B headline results (including the record-setting EPLB, Cloudcast, and Circle Packing numbers) are single-seed best scores with no variance reported, and ablations are run on only one task (Circle Packing). - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-driven program search or test-time training — it is the first credible demonstration that test-time RL on small open models rivals frontier-model evolutionary systems; skip it if you only need the mechanism, which is a straightforward GRPO-over-refinement-segments recipe fully summarized in Section 3.

Problem & Motivation: Open-ended discovery problems — circle packing, the Erdős minimum overlap problem, SQL column ordering, multicast cost minimization, MoE load balancing — are attacked by LLM-guided program search (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, OpenEvolve, ThetaEvolve). These systems keep the LLM frozen and run evolutionary search over hundreds of refinement steps. Applying RL to the model over full search trajectories is impractical at that horizon, and the one existing test-time-training approach (ThetaEvolve) learns only single-step refinement, forfeiting multi-step exploration strategies. The open problem: how to train the policy itself for discovery tasks whose natural horizon (hundreds of steps) exceeds what current RL infrastructure and credit-assignment methods handle. Key Idea: Train on short k-step refinement segments, but initialize each segment from a previously discovered program near the model's current capability frontier — so the model never needs credit assignment over hundreds of steps, yet search still compounds across hundreds of steps because each trained segment starts where prior search left off. The frontier is estimated cheaply and automatically by each parent's improvement rate (fraction of children that beat it); mastered programs define an eviction threshold that prunes the pool. Methodology: Each iteration runs three phases (Algorithm 1). (1) Refine: sample B=16 parents uniformly from pool P; for each, generate N=16 children, each via k=8 steps of sequential revision conditioned on evaluator score and diagnostic feedback (error tracebacks, constraint violations). Add all valid children with positive score to P. (2) Train: per-child reward is +1 if the best score across the k steps beats the parent, 0 if valid but non-improving, −0.5 if invalid (max rather than mean over steps so intermediate missteps aren't penalized); the whole k-step rollout shares one trajectory-level reward; GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO-style asymmetric clipping [0.2, 0.28], truncated importance sampling, lr 10⁻⁶. (3) Update pool: compute each parent's improvement rate βᵢ; parents with βᵢ ≥ τₜ (decaying linearly 0.3→0.0) are declared mastered; the rolling mean of recent mastered-parent scores becomes the eviction threshold. Three design decisions stand out: (a) replacing islands/MAP-Elites with a flat pool + improvement-rate eviction — justified by ablation (fixed top-10 pool 2.414±0.215 vs KTPO pool 2.523±0.021, a 10× variance reduction); (b) trajectory-level max-over-steps reward — motivated but not ablated against mean; (c) eviction-threshold decay schedule — ablated in Appendix B (2.523 vs 2.501 without decay), a modest gain. Key Results: Circle Packing (n=26): Qwen3.5-9B ties the best known 2.63598 (ThetaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve); Qwen3-4B reaches 2.6353±0.0004 over 3 seeds (best 2.63579), above the human 2.634. Erdős minimum overlap: 0.380938 (4B) within 1.1×10⁻⁵ of the human bound 0.380927; TTT-Discover (gpt-oss-120B) remains best at 0.380876. ADRS systems tasks (baselines from Cemri et al. 2026 using GPT-5 / Gemini-3-Pro): LLM-SQL best .738 (4B) vs human .692 but below AdaEvolve-GPT-5 .775; Cloudcast $626.9 (9B) vs human $626.2 and prior AI record $637.1; EPLB .14638 (9B) — new best vs prior .1453; Prism 26.256 vs AdaEvolve's 26.37; TXN 4149 vs 4348. Matched-compute comparisons are the strongest evidence: KTPO 2.632±0.002 vs ThetaEvolve 2.559±0.045 at ~51k evals (3 seeds), and KTPO 2.617 / $698.1 vs four evolutionary baselines (2.422–2.522 / $798.8–911.2) at 20k programs with the same Qwen3-4B backbone. Ablations (Circle Packing, 4B): no pool −0.011, no eviction −0.019 (pool grows to 60k+ programs, average output flat at ~1.0), k=1 −0.022, and training vs inference-only lifts average output from ~0.5 to ~2.2. Wall-clock cost is 40.8h vs 21.9h for inference-only (1.86×), of which the GRPO update itself is only 14%. Baselines are current (2025–2026 systems including GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro), and all headline models are 4B–9B open-weight. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) replacing the evolutionary-search database (islands, MAP-Elites, elite archives) with a flat program pool plus improvement-rate-driven eviction as the substrate for test-time RL, and (b) showing multi-step (k>1) trajectory-level RL beats single-step training for discovery. GRPO, curriculum-via-difficulty filtering (DAPO, Polaris), evaluator-feedback refinement, and pool-based search are each standard; the contribution is their specific recombination — and the matched-compute evidence that the recombination, not model scale, produces the records. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and directly target the three structural components (pool, eviction, k), plus a training-vs-inference-only control on both Qwen3-4B and a 1.5B model — this is the paper's methodological strength. Qwen3-4B results report mean±std over 3 seeds; however, Qwen3.5-9B results are single-seed and reported as best score across all seeds and rollouts, which invites selection bias on the record-setting numbers. Code is released (https://github.com/DachengLi1/KTPO); initial programs are the standard benchmark seeds, explicitly untuned. Concerns: (1) Circle Packing uses a "tolerant evaluator" following prior work — a known source of score inflation in this literature, unexamined here; (2) some baseline numbers (ADRS rows) are imported from Cemri et al. rather than re-run, though the matched-compute re-runs partially compensate; (3) the improvement-rate reward and pool eviction are developed and ablated on the same benchmarks used for headline claims (7 tasks is reasonably broad, but ablation coverage is one task); (4) no significance testing beyond seed std. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — a single 8×H100 node with optimizer states offloaded to CPU, using the open-source Slime framework. Efficient: 1.14×–1.86× the wall-clock of inference-only search at matched evaluation budget, with the RL update itself costing only 14% of total time; the extra cost comes from longer, more valid generations. Effective: Evidence covers seven real tasks with matched-compute controls, so the core claim is well supported — though 9B records rest on single-seed best scores, and the ADRS tasks are benchmarks rather than production systems. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — results top out at ~102k LLM evaluations; the paper shows k=4 saturates relative to k=8 (diminishing returns), but the behavior of improvement-rate eviction and pool dynamics at 10× the horizon or on much larger models is unexplored, and the method requires per-task test-time training (no cross-task transfer shown). Delivers a software artifact: released code; no model weights or dataset release mentioned. Strengths: - The matched-compute, matched-backbone comparisons (vs ThetaEvolve at 51k evals and vs four evolutionary baselines at 20k programs) are unusually clean experimental design for this subfield — they actually isolate the method variable, which most AlphaEvolve-style papers do not do. - Replacing islands/MAP-Elites/elite archives with a flat pool plus a self-measured improvement-rate eviction signal is a real simplification with quantified payoff (pool held at ~1,300 vs 60,000+; average output score 1.0→2.0; 10× variance reduction vs fixed top-K), not just parsimony for its own sake. - The training-vs-inference-only control on two model scales (4B and 1.5B) convincingly shows RL training improves average solution quality, not merely best-of-N luck — a distinction most search papers ignore. - Honest wall-clock accounting, including the non-obvious indirect cost that a better policy generates longer, more expensive programs. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper states that Qwen3.5-9B results are single-seed, best-score-only, and that 4B results additionally report best-across-seeds alongside mean±std — the reporting asymmetry is disclosed rather than hidden. It notes diminishing returns beyond k=4 and that Prism/TXN still trail AdaEvolve's best. It does not include a dedicated limitations section; the disclosure style is to flag reporting conditions inline, which is direct on measurement issues but leaves scope limitations (per-task training, evaluator sensitivity, transfer) unaddressed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 9B headline records (EPLB .14638, Cloudcast $626.9, Circle Packing 2.63598) are single-seed best scores; the 4B multi-seed results on the same tasks are consistently worse, suggesting seed-level luck contributes to the records. - The "tolerant evaluator" on Circle Packing is adopted from prior work without sensitivity analysis — the 2.63598 tie could be evaluator-dependent, a known pitfall in this benchmark. - No held-out-task evaluation: the method, prompts, and reward shaping are all developed on the same seven tasks used for the headline table; generalization of the KTPO recipe to a genuinely new domain is untested. - The trajectory-level reward is assigned uniformly to all tokens across k steps — no credit assignment across the k refinement steps is explored, and the max-vs-mean reward choice is asserted ("so that the model can explore") but not ablated. - No evaluation of what test-time training does to the model's general capabilities or to performance on other tasks (cross-task interference is a standard concern with per-task RL that goes unmentioned). - Table 1's framing of LLM-SQL as "outperforming human record" (.738 vs .692) is technically true but the same table shows AdaEvolve-GPT-5 at .775; the 4B result closes the gap but does not win that task. Bottom Line: For anyone building LLM-driven discovery or test-time-training systems, this is essential reading — it is the first demonstration that a 4B–9B open model with test-time RL matches frontier-model evolutionary search under matched compute, and the matched-compute protocol alone sets a standard the rest of this subfield should adopt; its main caveats are single-seed headline records and untested scaling beyond ~100k evaluations.

#69 — Innovative (69)

DARE: Diffusion Large Language Models Alignment and Reinforcement Executor

Y JingYi, Y Jiang, X Hu, S Cheng, B Qi, J Shao · openreview.net · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DARE, an open-source framework that unifies post-training (SFT, PEFT, preference optimization, and eight dLLM-specific RL algorithms) and evaluation for masked and block diffusion language models on a single execution stack built on verl and OpenCompass. - Why it's important: The open-source dLLM ecosystem fragments every RL algorithm into paper-specific codebases with their own forks, rollout engines, and evaluation scripts, making fair algorithm comparison unreliable and reproduction costly — a bottleneck that LLM (autoregressive) RL frameworks cannot fix because dLLMs need diffusion-aware forward/reverse processes and ELBO-style likelihood surrogates. - How it does it: The core move is architectural separation: a shared PPO-style workflow (rollout → reward → log-prob recomputation → advantage estimation → actor update) with small model- and algorithm-specific hooks at the plug-in points (corruption process, trajectory construction, likelihood bound, policy loss), plus decoupled attention backends for rollout (Fast-dLLM + FlashAttention KV-cache) versus actor updates (flash_attn_varlen) and serving-stack rollout for block diffusion models. - The good: Matched-setting runtime measurements show concrete wins — rollout drops from 1839.6 s (d1 codebase) and 107.59 s (BGPO codebase) to 70.97 s under DARE — and unified runs of seven RL algorithms across two backbones expose a genuinely useful empirical finding: no algorithm dominates across tasks, and rankings flip between LLaDA and Dream. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, the Dream-7B sanity checks show large unexplained discrepancies against reference numbers (up to ±21.6 points on ARC-C and HumanEval), and several DARE-vs-original reproductions diverge by 4–6 points (e.g., BGPO MATH 40.0 vs 45.7), so measurement reliability inside the unified stack is not fully established. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build or evaluate post-training pipelines for diffusion LLMs — it is the most complete open substrate for the area — but skip it if you want a new algorithm, since the paper contributes no new objective and says so explicitly.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Impact (85) is the strongest dimension: a released open-source framework that is now the sensible default substrate for dLLM post-training, plus the reusable finding that no RL algorithm dominates across tasks and backbones — knowledge only obtainable under matched execution. Rigor (60) is mixed: matched-setting runtime measurements and backend ablations are real, and the sanity-check deltas (including the authors' own −10-point Dream failure) are unusually candid, but Dream discrepancies of ±20 points go unexplained, reproduced algorithm results diverge 4–6 points from originals, and there is no variance reporting for ranking claims. Completeness (72) is high thanks to direct, non-minimizing limitation acknowledgment; Novelty (55) and Non-Obviousness (55) are moderate (hook factorization is a good insight but the components are all existing). Resilience (68) is solid — the paper explicitly bounds its claims as infrastructure, not method. Weighted composite: 0.15*55 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*55 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*68 + 0.30*85 = 69.
