Problem & Motivation: Since 2025, masked diffusion LLMs (LLaDA, Dream) and block/semi-autoregressive diffusion LLMs (SDAR, LLaDA2.x) have matured, but their post-training infrastructure has not: each RL paper (d1, VRPO, MDPO, CJ-GRPO, SPG, BGPO, EBPO, Coupled-GRPO) ships its own repository with distinct model forks, rollout implementations, reward interfaces, and evaluation scripts. This causes three concrete harms the authors name: slow research iteration (each integration re-implements infrastructure), unreliable cross-paper comparison (algorithmic differences entangled with execution differences), and high engineering barriers for newcomers. The gap cannot be closed by autoregressive RL frameworks (verl-style systems for LLMs) because dLLMs require denoising-trajectory likelihood surrogates, bidirectional attention, and model-family-specific rollout backends rather than exact single-trajectory sequence log-probabilities. The intended users are researchers developing and comparing dLLM post-training methods. Key Idea: The central insight is that dLLM post-training algorithms that look like distinct methods in distinct codebases actually share one execution skeleton, and differ only in a few well-defined hooks — the forward corruption process, trajectory construction rule, likelihood estimator/bound (sequence-level vs block-level ELBO approximations, one- or two-step Monte Carlo surrogates, trajectory-level optimization), and policy loss. Factorizing the framework into a shared workflow plus these hooks (workers / dataflow / workflow abstractions) is what makes matched-protocol algorithm comparison possible. A secondary systems insight is that the optimal attention backend differs by phase: rollout for masked dLLMs benefits from KV-cache reuse (Fast-dLLM + flash_attn with cache) while actor updates on packed variable-length sequences need flash_attn_varlen, so the two backends should be decoupled. Methodology: DARE is an execution layer built on verl (distributed training) and OpenCompass (evaluation), adding dLLM-specific actor, rollout, reward, and model wrappers. The unified executor follows a PPO-style loop: (i) rollout generation via the diffusion reverse process, (ii) reward computation/verification, (iii) old-policy and optional reference-policy log-probability recomputation, (iv) advantage/return estimation, (v) actor update. Algorithm plug-in points are the hooks listed above; SFT/PEFT/VRPO use simplified variants of the same executor. Model coverage spans MDLMs (LLaDA, Dream, LLaDA-MoE) and BDLMs (SDAR, LLaDA2.0, LLaDA2.1). Systems design: MDLM training uses flash_attn_varlen plus sequence parallelism; MDLM rollout uses Fast-dLLM with FlashAttention backends; BDLM rollout uses LMDeploy/SGLang with FlexAttention and fused kernels (e.g., SDAR's logits-free fused linear cross-entropy) for training; LoRA is supported. RL experiments use unified hyperparameters (rollout group size 8, block length 32, KL off, 16 MC samples where needed), training on GSM8K+MATH, 16K DeepCoder-filtered problems, and Countdown/Sudoku. Critical design decisions: (1) hook-based factorization — well justified by Table 1 showing eight algorithms previously scattered across five codebases; (2) decoupled rollout/update backends — justified by the Figure 2 latency measurements; (3) integrating evaluation into the same stack — motivated but the dLLM-aware extensions to OpenCompass are described only at a high level. The paper explicitly states it introduces no new alignment objective. Key Results: The headline empirical finding is algorithm non-dominance: on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, CJ-GRPO is best on GSM8K (85.6 vs baseline 76.5), Coupled-GRPO best on MATH (41.0) and Countdown (77.9 vs baseline 16.8), VRPO best on HumanEval (52.4) and MBPP (42.8), and BGPO best on Sudoku (42.6); on Dream-7B-Instruct the ranking shifts again (CJ-GRPO best on GSM8K/MATH at 85.7/50.7, Coupled-GRPO best on code). SPG is markedly unstable on Dream (25.2 on MATH, 17.7 on HumanEval), showing algorithm robustness varies across backbones. Evaluation sanity checks: LLaDA-8B-Instruct within 1.62 points and SDAR-8B-Chat within 1.37 points of reference values across nine and five benchmarks respectively; Dream-7B-Instruct diverges badly (−10.07 HellaSwag, +21.56 ARC-C, +20.15 HumanEval), attributed to comparison against a blog figure rather than a specified artifact. Runtime under matched settings: DARE rollout 70.97 s / 923.5 tok/s versus BGPO's 107.59 s / 609.1 tok/s and d1's 1839.6 s / 35.6 tok/s; training step 188.73 s versus 297.94 s (BGPO) and 2051.8 s (d1). Backend ablations: SFT latency 22.1 → 10.8 s (~2.0×) with flash_attn_varlen; MDLM rollout 161.6 → 73.4–73.5 s (~2.2×) with Fast-dLLM; claimed ~4× end-to-end MDLM RL speedup and >14× BDLM RL acceleration (the latter attributed to repository documentation, not a table in the paper). Baseline models are current-generation open dLLMs; the RL baselines are the original algorithm papers' own numbers, which is appropriate but not strictly controlled. Scale is standard (7–8B dense models; SDAR-30B-A3B only for evaluation), tested on math, code, and planning tasks. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (no uniformly dominant RL algorithm across tasks and backbones, made visible only under matched execution). The genuinely novel part is the unified hook-factored executor spanning MDLMs and BDLMs with decoupled phase-specific attention backends; the individual algorithms, the PPO-style loop, verl, OpenCompass, Fast-dLLM, FlashAttention, LMDeploy, and SGLang are all existing components competently combined. The paper is honest about this positioning — it self-describes as a "reusable research substrate," not a method contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations of the systems components exist (Figure 2 backend comparisons; Table 6a matched-runtime measurements), but there are no ablations isolating which framework abstractions matter for result quality, and no seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere. Code is released at https://github.com/yjyddq/DARE. Reproducibility is handled unusually well for a systems paper: the authors publish sanity-check deltas against official repositories (Table 5), including their own failures on Dream, and side-by-side DARE-vs-original-paper numbers for five algorithms (Table 6b), explicitly framing agreement as approximate because benchmark variants and decoding configurations differ. Methodological concerns: (1) the Dream sanity-check discrepancies (±10–21 points) undermine confidence in evaluation equivalence for that model family and are only partially explained; (2) several reproduced results deviate meaningfully from originals (e.g., BGPO MATH 40.0 vs 45.7; SPG MBPP 41.9 vs 50.6), which the authors attribute to protocol differences but do not resolve; (3) the >14× BDLM speedup is a repository-reported figure, not a peer-reviewed measurement in the paper; (4) evaluation of the framework's own models uses hyperparameters tuned per model per benchmark, which complicates strict comparison. Code and data are public; no model weights are trained or released by this paper itself. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built framework, evaluated by measurements and integrated experiments). - Practical: Yes — it runs on standard verl-compatible training infrastructure with public model checkpoints, though specific GPU counts/hardware are not stated in the paper. - Efficient: Measurably better than the fragmented alternatives it replaces (rollout 70.97 s vs 107.59 s and 1839.6 s under matched settings; ~2.0–2.2× backend-level speedups), which is the paper's strongest systems evidence. - Effective: Evidence supports the unification claim — eight algorithms run in one stack with sane reproduction of trends — but effectiveness of the dLLM-aware evaluation extensions is only partially validated (Dream discrepancies). - Scalable: Untested beyond 7–8B training scale (evaluation-only at 30B MoE); the >100B LLaDA2.0 support is claimed via model integration but no training experiments at that scale are reported. The deliverable is a real software artifact (open-source framework) plus reusable benchmark baselines; the paper's empirical finding (no universal RL winner) is itself reusable knowledge. Strengths: - Genuine systems novelty: this is the first open framework to host masked and block diffusion LLM post-training under one hook-factored executor, converting eight previously scattered algorithm codebases into comparable configurations (Table 1's provenance column documents the fragmentation concretely). - Unusually candid reproducibility reporting: publishing sanity-check deltas including a −10.07-point Dream HellaSwag miss and per-algorithm DARE-vs-original divergences is more honest than typical framework papers. - The matched-infrastructure comparison yields a real finding practitioners cannot get from individual papers: RL algorithm rankings flip between backbones and tasks (e.g., SPG drops from 40.6 to 25.2 on MATH when moving from LLaDA to Dream), and ELBO-based methods show Monte-Carlo-noise-sensitive training curves versus the stability of d1/Coupled-GRPO/CJ-GRPO. - Concrete, measured systems wins (2.0× training, 2.2× rollout, ~4× end-to-end MDLM RL) with the specific design rationale (decoupled rollout/update attention backends) that others can reuse independently of the framework. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that DARE introduces no new alignment objective (it is infrastructure, not a method); that Dream comparisons rest on a blog figure rather than a specified evaluation artifact and should be read as approximate; that exact numerical agreement with original papers is not expected due to differing benchmark variants, decoding configurations, and protocols; that MDLMs suffer fixed-length exploration limits pending variable-length denoising integration; and in future work they name missing vision-language/omni-model support, the need for more comprehensive efficiency ablations, and deployment-oriented evaluation backends. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: single-run results for all algorithm comparisons make it impossible to distinguish small ranking differences (e.g., 83.5 vs 83.7 GSM8K) from noise, which matters because the paper's headline claim is precisely about rankings. - The cause of Dream's evaluation discrepancies is not investigated — ±20-point swings on ARC-C and HumanEval suggest either different prompting/sampling or a genuine evaluation-layer difference, and leaving this unresolved weakens the "reproducible evaluation" claim for one of three supported MDLM families. - The BDLM path (SDAR, LLaDA2.x) has no post-training algorithm-comparison experiments — all RL comparisons use MDLM backbones — so the framework's BDLM RL capability is asserted rather than demonstrated. - The >14× BDLM acceleration and ~4× MDLM end-to-end speedup lack in-paper experimental setup detail (hardware, cluster configuration), limiting verification. - Training data is restricted to math/code/planning with verifiable rewards; no preference-optimization results tables are shown despite DPO/VRPO being advertised integrations (VRPO appears in the tables, plain DPO does not). - Potential self-coverage concern: several authors are affiliated with SDAR/LLaDA2.x-lineage work, and those models receive favorable coverage; no adverse-result ablation exists for the BDLM stack (dogs-not-barking). Bottom Line: For anyone doing RL or preference optimization on diffusion LLMs, DARE is now the sensible default substrate and its matched-comparison finding — that no RL algorithm wins across tasks and backbones, with Coupled-GRPO and CJ-GRPO the strongest overall compromises — is worth the read on its own; researchers outside the dLLM niche will find little beyond a competent verl extension.

HALO: A Heterogeneity-Aware Language-Aligned IMU Foundation Model for Open-Set Human Activity Recognition

Z Ding, L Zhang, X Ouyang · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HALO, a ~35M-parameter IMU foundation model trained on 10 public HAR datasets that handles variable sampling rates (20–100 Hz), variable channel counts (3–45), and sensor placements, and performs open-vocabulary activity recognition via cosine-similarity retrieval against a text label bank with no per-dataset classifier. - Why it's important: Wearable HAR models today are bound to a fixed sensor configuration and a closed set of class labels, so every new device, placement, or activity taxonomy requires retraining — a domain-specific foundation model with a language-based label interface removes that per-deployment engineering cost. - How it does it: A two-stage recipe: (1) self-supervised pretraining of a channel-independent, seconds-based patch tokenizer encoder that injects natural-language sensor-placement descriptions into each channel embedding, then (2) CLIP-style contrastive alignment to a frozen Sentence-BERT encoder using soft targets derived from text–text similarity so synonymous labels ("walking"/"strolling") reinforce rather than contradict each other. - The good: HALO leads all 8 aggregate metrics across 4 evaluation settings on 5 held-out datasets (e.g., 42.0% vs. 28.3% zero-shot open-set accuracy over 87 labels, +13.7 pp over MOMENT) with 10× fewer trainable parameters, and the gain survives a fairness control where HALO itself is given baseline-matched 20 Hz inputs and generic channel descriptions. - The missing: All models — including HALO — collapse to near-zero zero-shot accuracy on two severe out-of-domain datasets (HARTH, VTT-ConIoT), exposing that the cross-dataset transfer gains are confined to moderate shift; ablations use a single seed and 100-epoch budgets, and code/weights are promised only "upon publication." - Read it or not: Worth reading for ubiquitous-computing and time-series-foundation-model researchers who need a concrete template for heterogeneity-robust sensor pretraining plus language alignment; practitioners seeking robust zero-shot HAR under real distribution shift can skip the zero-shot claims and focus on the 1–10% few-shot results and deployment profiling.
Why this rank

Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (68) rest on the sensor-conditioning and soft-contrastive-target insights (−19.6 pp ablation delta), a real contribution atop otherwise standard components. Problem & Motivation: IMU-based human activity recognition is deployed on smartwatches and phones for health monitoring, rehabilitation, and sports analytics, but no unified model generalizes across subjects, devices, and activities. Two barriers: (i) sensing heterogeneity — datasets span 20–100 Hz sampling rates, 3–45 channels across accelerometers/gyroscopes/magnetometers at different body placements, so a fixed-width input layer or timestep-indexed positional encoding breaks across deployments; (ii) label shift and closed-world classifiers — ten training datasets yield 87 inconsistently named activity labels, so a model trained on one vocabulary cannot emit labels from another, and synonym mismatches ("jogging" vs. "running") count as errors even when semantically correct. The authors argue prior work solves these axes in isolation: self-supervised HAR models (LIMU-BERT, CrossHAR) transfer representations but require per-dataset classifiers; general time-series foundation models (MOMENT, 341.2M parameters) lack HAR inductive biases; text-aligned models (LanHAR) decouple the label interface but lack sensor pretraining. Key Idea: Convert heterogeneity from an obstacle into a representational signal: tokenize IMU sessions in physical seconds (adaptive pooling absorbs variable patch length), process every channel with shared weights while injecting a natural-language description of each channel's sensor type and body placement ("Accelerometer X-axis, waist-mounted smartphone") via a frozen Sentence-BERT embedding — and then align IMU embeddings to text with soft contrastive targets computed from text–text similarities, so label synonyms share target mass instead of acting as contradictory negatives. Open-set recognition then falls out as cosine retrieval over any runtime-swappable label bank. Methodology: Stage 1 pretrains an 8-layer dual-branch Transformer encoder (~19M params) on 10 datasets with masked autoencoding (50% patch mask ratio, MSE on normalized signal) plus patch-level InfoNCE contrastive learning (temperature 0.2, jitter/scale/time-warp augmentations), equal weights. Critical design decisions: (a) seconds-based patching (0.75–2.0 s train range, fixed 1.0 s at eval) with a spectral-temporal tokenizer (multi-scale 1-D CNN + FFT-MLP, both adaptively pooled) — justified by a sensitivity analysis showing the fixed 1.0 s choice is within 1.3 pp of per-dataset optima; (b) channel-independent processing with alternating temporal and cross-channel attention plus zero-padding masks for variable channel counts — standard PatchTST-style channel independence extended with cross-channel fusion via learnable queries; (c) sensor conditioning H' = H0 + γe_c with a learnable scale initialized at 0.1 — well justified, as its removal costs 19.6 pp zero-shot open-set accuracy, the largest ablation effect. Stage 2 aligns the encoder to a frozen all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (22.7M) via bidirectional CLIP-style loss with FIFO queues (Q=256), learnable temperature, and adaptive soft targets: the in-batch text–text similarity matrix is z-score-normalized, sharpened (τ_s=0.5), and softmaxed so "walking"/"strolling" share ~0.4 target mass while unrelated pairs share <0.01. Synonym-aware label augmentation (WordNet-derived maps, ~2.3 synonyms/label, 80% replacement probability with template wrapping) reduces residual conflict. Inference is argmax cosine similarity over any candidate label set with per-patch majority voting for zero-shot; supervised transfer fine-tunes end-to-end on 1% or 10% of test-dataset labels. Key Results: On five held-out test datasets (MotionSense, RealWorld, MobiAct, Shoaib, Opportunity) under four settings, HALO leads all 8 aggregate metrics against five baselines (LiMU-BERT, MOMENT, CrossHAR, LanHAR, LLaSA): zero-shot open-set 42.0% accuracy / 21.0 macro-F1 (MOMENT 28.3/7.2), zero-shot closed-set 53.1/37.2, 1% supervised 76.5/70.0, 10% supervised 85.7/81.7. The fairness control shows HALO with 20 Hz resampled inputs and generic channel descriptions still beats MOMENT on 3 of 4 settings (30.6 vs. 28.3 ZS-O). On two severe-OOD datasets all embedding models collapse zero-shot (<3% on HARTH, <9% on VTT-ConIoT); with 10% supervision HALO leads on HARTH (78.3%) but MOMENT leads on VTT-ConIoT (34.8%). Ablations: sensor conditioning removal costs −19.6 pp ZS-O; text augmentation −7.0 pp at 1%; signal augmentation closes a 9.5 pp generalization gap. Scaling study (6M/35M/63M) finds 35M is the sweet spot — the 63M model overfits and regresses 8.2 pp ZS-O. On-device profiling on an iPhone 16 Pro shows 7.16 ms average latency (5.26× faster than MOMENT's 37.69 ms, slower than CrossHAR's 0.29 ms), 32.81 MB peak memory. A real-world iOS case study (3 body placements, 6 SFT classes, 2 unseen labels) reports 97.5% accuracy over 40 windows with 30.35 ms end-to-end pipeline latency. Baselines are current (2024–2025) and the authors deviate from baseline protocols in the baselines' favor, though input conditions are not identical across models (HALO at native rates with rich descriptions vs. 20 Hz for most baselines) — partially but not fully neutralized by the Table 7 control. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the specific integration) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the systematic cross-dataset benchmark with open-set evaluation over 87 labels and the finding that sensor conditioning dominates zero-shot transfer). The genuinely novel elements are contextualized sensor conditioning via natural-language placement descriptions and synonym-aware soft contrastive targets; the remaining components — seconds-based patching, channel-independent PatchTST-style tokenization, masked autoencoding, InfoNCE, CLIP-style alignment to Sentence-BERT, FIFO queues — are standard techniques competently combined. UniMTS and LanHAR respectively cover parts of this ground (heterogeneous motion pretraining; CLIP-style HAR alignment), so the integration, not any single ingredient, is the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations isolate the three main components and a dedicated fairness control (Table 7) evaluates HALO under baseline-equivalent inputs — a credibility positive. Methodological concerns: (i) ablation runs use 100 Stage-2 epochs vs. 200 for the final model with a single seed (footnote 2), and no multi-seed runs, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere; (ii) code and pretrained weights are only promised "upon publication" — no repository exists in this preprint; (iii) input asymmetries persist in headline numbers (HALO at native rates with rich descriptions vs. baselines at 20 Hz; MOMENT padded to 512 timesteps), only partially addressed by the fairness control; (iv) synonym-group scoring is given to classifier baselines but text-aligned models use exact string match, a defensible but consequential protocol choice; (v) LLaSA's training data overlaps two test sets, a confound the authors disclose. Evaluation on 17 public datasets is broad and mostly external to the authors, mitigating Goodhart concerns on the main benchmark. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — an iOS deployment and on-device profiling). Practical: Yes — trained on a single A100 80 GB, runs on an iPhone 16 Pro at 7.16 ms/window via Core ML. Efficient: ~35M trainable parameters (~58M at inference including frozen MiniLM) vs. MOMENT's 341.2M; 32.81 MB peak memory; text and label embeddings precomputed offline; slower than tiny baselines (CrossHAR 0.29 ms) but within real-time budgets. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem under moderate shift (wins all 8 aggregate metrics, and the case study validates mid-session placement changes), but zero-shot effectiveness evaporates under severe sensor shift (HARTH <3%), so the "zero-shot" claim is only valid in a benign regime. Scalable: Not tested beyond ~13K sessions and 87 labels; the authors themselves show the recipe overfits at 63M parameters, so scaling claims would be speculative. Deliverable: a trained model checkpoint and codebase promised at publication, plus an iOS demo application described (video linked); as of this preprint, no public artifact. Strengths: - The fairness control (Table 7) is genuinely rigorous: re-evaluating the proposed model under the baselines' degraded input regime (20 Hz, generic descriptions) and still winning 3 of 4 settings preempts the most obvious objection to the headline numbers. - Sensor conditioning via natural-language placement descriptions is a real, well-supported design insight — converting metadata heterogeneity into semantic signal, backed by the largest ablation delta (−19.6 pp ZS-O) and the observed +24.5/+19.7 pp zero-shot gains on placement-sensitive datasets. - Soft contrastive targets derived from text–text similarity is a clean, general solution to the label-synonym-conflict problem that plagues any multi-dataset supervised training, transferable beyond HAR. - Honest negative results: reporting total zero-shot collapse on HARTH and VTT-ConIoT, the Medium-model overfitting regression, and MOMENT winning at 1% on two datasets — the paper does not bury its failure modes. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (1) zero-shot collapse under severe distribution shift on HARTH and VTT-ConIoT, framed as an open challenge; (2) dataset-level (rather than per-sample) channel–text conditioning, evidenced by the −9.9 pp RealWorld zero-shot drop with richer global descriptions; (3) the 87-label vocabulary and 384-dim embedding space as coverage ceilings; (4) LLaSA's training-data overlap with two test sets; (5) the ~13K-session corpus as a capacity ceiling that larger corpora could shift. They confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility. This is a March 2026 preprint (arXiv:2608.27233) with a revised version in preparation, so numbers and framing may change; results are not peer-reviewed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No multi-seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests on any headline number; with 5-dataset averages and margins as small as +2.3 pp (fairness-control ZS-O), seed noise could matter. - The case study's 97.5% accuracy covers only 40 windows, 6+2 classes, and one user setup — far too small to substantiate real-world robustness claims, and it is self-reported by the system's authors. - Zero-shot evaluation against classifier baselines is structurally awkward: classifier models predict only from the 87 training labels while HALO retrieves over text embeddings; the synonym-group scoring concession narrows but does not eliminate the interface asymmetry, and an obvious missing baseline is UniMTS, which the related work discusses but does not compare against. - Synonym maps are hand-curated per dataset (2.3 synonyms/label average) — the method's synonym robustness is partly baked in by the evaluators' own curation, and no experiment tests sensitivity to synonym-map quality. - The "zero-shot open-set" setting tests retrieval over 87 seen labels; truly novel-label recognition is only exercised in the tiny case study (2 unseen labels), not on a held-out dataset with systematically novel vocabulary at scale. - Severe-OOD failure is diagnosed but not addressed — no adaptation technique (e.g., test-time normalization, sensor-aware augmentation targeted at gravity contamination) is attempted on HARTH, leaving the headline capability silent exactly where deployment risk is highest. Bottom Line: A practitioner building cross-device HAR systems should read this — the sensor-conditioning and soft-contrastive-alignment tricks are concretely useful and the fairness-conscious evaluation is a model for the subfield — but anyone expecting genuine zero-shot robustness beyond mild distribution shift should treat the collapse on HARTH/VTT-ConIoT as the operative finding, and UniMTS plus the forthcoming revised version deserve comparison before adopting HALO itself.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ExTS, a Monte Carlo tree-search policy for LLM agentic search that jointly redesigns node selection and expansion decisions, and shows it is competitive with or beats task-specific tree-search baselines (+5.5% average relative gain) across four domains under a single fixed configuration. - Why it's important: Agentic LLM systems burn tens to hundreds of expensive model calls per search, and standard UCT allocates that budget poorly, so better budget allocation directly cuts cost and improves final candidate quality in prompt optimization, code generation, and workflow search. - How it does it: The core move is treating expansion itself as a value-of-information decision: a stochastic "virtual child" sampled from the parent's reward pool competes with real children during selection, while temperature-shaped rewards and quality-gated (score-thresholded) progressive widening control where budget flows. - The good: The strongest evidence is the fixed-configuration transfer — one hyperparameter set (PUCT, C=1.0, T=0.3, α=√2, M0=3) plugs into four distinct frameworks (GEPA, TreeQuest, K-MSE, AFlow) and matches or beats each framework's own tuned baseline, e.g., 64.89% vs 58.55% on HotpotQA and 19.1% vs 17.1% pass@1 on LiveCodeBench-hard. - The missing: Code is promised but not yet released ("until then, please contact us"), several headline gains are small or within noise (HoVeR +0.2%, K-MSE +1.3% with overlapping standard deviations), and the GPU kernel generalization result is a single run with no error bars. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building inference-time search or agentic optimization loops who needs to understand why UCT fails at low budgets and what a reward-aware tree policy looks like; skippable for readers far from inference-time compute allocation.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building LLM agentic search systems (prompt optimizers, code-refinement loops, workflow generators, molecular structure solvers) face a regime the authors call budget-constrained agentic search: validation is expensive, generation requires multiple LLM calls, and total budget is tens to hundreds of evaluations. Prior work innovates on the "harness" (value functions, action spaces, reflection) while retaining vanilla UCT or linear search, and algorithm-side alternatives (AB-MCTS, GEPA, AFlow) each target a single task type. The specific gap is that no cross-task tree policy conditions expansion on node quality or shapes rewards for the narrow score distributions typical of validation-heavy domains. Key Idea: Make expansion a first-class, value-of-information decision rather than an obligation. Concretely, three coupled mechanisms: (1) temperature-based discriminative reward shaping φ(r) = (e^(r̂/T)−1)/(e^(1/T)−1) that convexifies narrow score distributions so the exploitation term differentiates candidates; (2) a virtual child whose score is estimated by sampling k scores from the parent's reward pool at a "fair-share" visit count, so uncertain/unproven branches get high-variance estimates that naturally compete with deepening; (3) quality-conditioned branching — an expansion gate at the τ-quantile of observed scores plus progressive widening M(v) = M0 + ⌊log_b(n_v/n0)⌋ gated on the γ-quantile (γ=0.75, τ=0.25 defaults). A success-rate weight (n⁺/n)^α discounts nodes whose subtrees produce invalid outputs. Methodology: The system formalizes validation-heavy search as (S, A, f, B): a stochastic LLM refinement operator A, a validator f returning a score or ⊥, and budget B. The search loop is standard select–expand–validate–backpropagate, but selection uses ExUCT(v) = (n⁺_v/n_v)^α · φ̄(r_i) + explore(n_par, n_v) with either UCT (log decay) or PUCT-style (linear decay, default, no learned prior) exploration. At each internal node, a virtual child score is computed by estimating fair-share visits n_fair, sampling k = max(1, ⌊n_fair·n⁺_v/n_v⌋) rewards from R_v ∪ {s_v}, and comparing against the best real child; expansion wins if the virtual score exceeds it. Quality gates block expansion of below-τ-quantile nodes and cap width at M0 for below-γ-quantile nodes. Critical design decisions: (a) nonparametric bootstrap for the virtual child instead of AB-MCTS's parametric Bayesian posteriors — justified by arguing conjugate/MCMC posteriors are unreliable at small budgets, and supported by the FPU ablation; (b) global normalization with drift-handling diagnostics — acknowledged as a weakness under high score drift (HoVeR); (c) PUCT decay without a policy prior for simplicity — justified by wanting task-agnostic defaults, though the ablation shows the PUCT/UCT choice is task-dependent (+6.45 pp for PUCT on HotpotQA, +0.88 pp for UCT on HoVeR). Key Results: All experiments run 3 seeds (seeds 0/42/1024) except GPU kernels. Prompt optimization (Qwen3-8B, 300 test examples): HotpotQA 64.89±0.83 vs GEPA Pareto 58.55±5.32 (+10.8%, 6.4× lower variance); HoVeR 50.45±2.18 vs 50.33±2.45 (within noise). Code generation (Claude Sonnet 4, LiveCodeBench v6, budget 128): hard split 19.1% pass@1 vs AB-MCTS-A 17.1% and StandardMCTS 18.1%; easy/medium splits saturate at 100%/85.8% for all methods. Molecular elucidation (Claude Sonnet 4.6, 216 molecules, 16 rollouts): 91.0±0.6% exact-match vs K-MSE's MCTSr 89.8±0.4%. Workflow optimization (DROP, AFlow framework, 20 rounds): 90.96±0.93 F1 vs CoT 89.28±1.78 and AFlow 87.89±2.29, at $15.26 vs CoT's $36.70. A fifth domain (GPU kernel optimization, 40 tasks, single run) improves geometric-mean speedup from 4.15× to 4.36× over an optimized MCTS baseline. Baselines are current and strong (GEPA, AB-MCTS, AFlow, MCTSr are the published best for each task, each fully tuned). Ablations show every component contributes: removing failure penalty costs −7.78 pp on HotpotQA, virtual child −3.22 pp, gated widening −2.34 pp. Sweeping the exploration constant C from 1.0–2.0 in standard MCTS (44.3–45.6%) cannot close the gap to 46.2%, ruling out the trivial explanation. Tree-shape analysis shows the mechanism: ExTS produces shallower leaves (3.73 vs 4.43) but finds best nodes deeper (1.09 vs 1.03) on non-trivial molecules, +2.9 pp there. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING contribution. The genuinely novel pieces are the virtual child as a nonparametric, prior-free VOI estimate competing at fair-share visit counts, and score-gated progressive widening; the diagnostic framework (refinement variance, score spread, drift, failure rate) linking landscape structure to hyperparameter sensitivity is a useful empirical contribution. The building blocks are recognizable redesigns of classical MCTS ideas (FPU, progressive widening, PUCT), and the paper is explicit about this lineage — this is a well-motivated adaptation of known primitives to a new regime, not a fundamentally new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: leave-one-out on HotpotQA, component swaps against classical mechanisms (fixed FPU=0.5/0.8 and score-agnostic widening both lose), PUCT-vs-UCT per task, and LiveCodeBench ablations (gated widening −1.3 pp overall; root-exclusion removal −1.0 pp). Multiple seeds and mean±std are reported nearly everywhere; no significance tests. Code is announced for github.com/amazon-science/ExTS but not yet available at publication. Methodological concerns: (a) several effects are small relative to seed variance (K-MSE +1.3% with ±0.6 vs ±0.4 std; HoVeR +0.2%); (b) ExTS* configurations are tuned on the same test tasks they are reported on, which the authors defend as fair given baseline tuning, but the diagnostic-to-hyperparameter mappings are effectively derived from these same runs (post-hoc rationalization risk); (c) the pilot-run diagnostics are computed from the baseline's own search tree, coupling them to the baseline method; (d) the GPU kernel result is a single run, self-corrected from a validation flaw in the original baseline's methodology (transparently disclosed); (e) BAVT, the closest budget-aware method, is not compared due to lack of open source. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (algorithm evaluated via experiments across four harnesses). - Practical: Yes — it is a plug-in tree policy on top of existing open frameworks (GEPA, TreeQuest, AFlow, K-MSE) using commercial LLM APIs; no special hardware beyond the GPU kernel domain's A100. - Efficient: It reduces cost where conditioning depth matters (DROP at $15.26 vs $36.70 for CoT), and converts a fixed budget into more performance, though it trails at very small budgets (B<8 on LiveCodeBench) due to calibration overhead. - Effective: Evidence supports solving the stated problem (better budget allocation) with matched budgets across four domains, but two of the four headline wins are marginal or within noise, so effectiveness is concentrated in high-failure-rate and hard-instance regimes. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested at large scale — budgets max at 128 evaluations; behavior at 10–100× budget or on much larger search spaces is untested, and the paper's own premise (UCT's asymptotic regime is irrelevant) suggests ExTS's advantage could shrink at scale. Delivers a method paper with a promised (not yet released) software artifact; no trained models or datasets contributed. Strengths: - The fixed-configuration cross-domain result is the paper's real contribution: one hyperparameter set beating four separately tuned task-specific baselines is a credible transfer claim that most LLM-search papers do not attempt. - The virtual child is a genuinely neat mechanism — a node-specific, data-dependent FPU replacement whose stochasticity encodes finite-sample uncertainty, demonstrated convincingly against fixed FPU constants and against the C-sweep objection (Section 5.1). - The worked example (Appendix I) reconstructing a real decision from a live run, including the exact probabilities of the virtual-vs-real comparison, is unusually transparent for this literature. - The pilot-run diagnostic framework (failure rate, score spread, drift, refinement variance) gives the field a vocabulary for why no single search configuration dominates, with concrete mappings to hyperparameter choices. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: single model per domain due to API cost; no study of how model scale alters the landscape; diagnostics are conditioned on model/scorer/budget and so describe the landscape as seen by that configuration rather than intrinsic domain properties, with cross-model transferability untested; the pilot tree consumes budget not spent on the final search. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The ExTS* "pilot-adapted" results are tuned per task on the evaluation tasks themselves; the diagnostic guide (Table 13) is derived from the same runs it then explains, so its predictive value on genuinely new tasks is unverified — the authors partially flag this but do not test it on a held-out task. - No theoretical grounding: no regret, convergence, or consistency analysis for ExUCT; the PUCT-style exploration without a prior has no guarantee that low-score gated nodes are ever revisited enough to escape false negatives under the adaptive quantile threshold. - Global min-max normalization with temperature shaping is brittle to outlier scores (one extreme candidate reshapes the entire φ landscape), and the score-drift diagnostic exists precisely because this is a problem, yet the default config still uses global normalization. - Several positive results rest on narrow margins with overlapping confidence intervals; a significance-aware treatment would likely survive for HotpotQA and LiveCodeBench-hard but not obviously for K-MSE or HoVeR. - Easy/medium LiveCodeBench splits saturating at identical rates means two-thirds of the benchmark provides no discriminative signal; the effective evaluation is 82 hard problems. - The AI-assisted writing disclosure and the single-run GPU kernel experiment both warrant mild caution about result robustness in the appendix domain. Bottom Line: For practitioners building or tuning LLM agentic search loops, this is one of the more credible and useful tree-policy papers in the budget-constrained regime — the fixed-configuration transfer and the virtual-child mechanism justify reading it even with the unreleased code and the modest margins on half the benchmarks.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ProofEvolve, an inference-time neuro-symbolic framework that evolves AND-OR proof DAGs in Lean 4, ranks partial proofs by a kernel-grounded "verified closure" fitness, and reuses kernel-checked sub-proofs across problems through a persistent, typed theorem-schema library. - Why it's important: Current neural provers discard verified partial progress — either baking experience into weights via costly retraining or confining it to the current problem — so each new theorem is proved from scratch despite formal proofs being the one setting where intermediate results are machine-checkable and therefore perfectly reusable. - How it does it: An LLM proposes decompositions, repairs, and schema recombinations; Problem & Motivation: Neural and agentic theorem provers fail to preserve verified progress across time. Training-based systems (AlphaProof, Goedel-Prover-V2, DeepSeek-Prover-V2) store experience only in weights, so new results affect later problems only after another expensive training cycle; agentic systems (Hilbert, LEAP, COPRA) reuse intermediate lemmas only within the current proof. Meanwhile a one-character edit can invalidate a complete proof text even when most verified sub-arguments survive (Nagashima 2019). The authors argue this breaks the recursive structure that formal verification uniquely enables: Lean's kernel certifies every step, so partial and completed proofs should accumulate as reusable symbolic knowledge. The beneficiaries are anyone using automated theorem proving for competition mathematics or, ultimately, recursive self-improvement in scientific discovery. Closest prior work is DreamProver (wake-sleep lemma libraries) and LEGO-Prover (growing libraries, where storage was shown not to guarantee reuse — Berlot-Attwell et al. 2025), which this paper directly engages. Key Idea: Convert Lean's binary kernel verdict into a graded, monotone fitness over partial proofs — "verified closure" ρ, computed by reverse-topological recursion over the AND-OR proof DAG (max over alternative edges, weighted sum over conjunctive children) — and prove ρ(D)=1 ⟺ root closed and ρ monotone under DAG extension; then let closed sub-DAGs be extracted as prenex theorem schemas (∀x, A₁→…→Aₘ→C) that later proofs instantiate as a single kernel-checked hyperedge, with any unprovable premise becoming an explicit child subgoal. This pair (graded kernel-grounded selection + typed cross-target recombination) is the reconstructable trick. Methodology: Four stages. (1) Neural proposal: a frozen LLM policy proposes one of three edits to a frontier state — decomposition (closing term or constructor with typed obligations), schema recombination (select an applicable library schema from a retrieval-shortlisted candidate set), or repair (re-propose after a Lean error, only at previously rejected states); every edit passes through a step_K operator that requires a kernel-checked, acyclic extension. (2) Selection: a MAP-Elites archive keyed by descriptor (binned depth, dominant tactic family, schema-index region) keeps one DAG per niche, incumbents win ties; parents are sampled by softmax over ρ with temperature τ; frontier scheduling prioritizes the state whose counterfactual closure (Eq. 13) yields the largest ρ gain. (3) Extraction: newly closed states are abstracted in dependency order over their free constants/hypotheses; failed generalization yields no schema. (4) Library growth across targets is monotone (L_t ⊆ L_{t+1}). A soundness theorem (Theorem 1, proved by induction in Appendix B) shows every accepted edge, closed node, and library entry stays kernel-verified, so returned proofs type-check by construction. Critical design decisions: uniform edge weights in ρ (asserted, not ablated); the schema library acts as a retrieval corpus only, never entering the Lean environment or axiom footprint (well-justified, keeps proofs axiom-clean); rejection of native_decide proofs (well-justified, avoids out-of-kernel code paths). The framework is positioned as Neuro[Symbolic] in Kautz's taxonomy. Key Results: Using Claude Opus 4.8 as the base model under matched per-target budgets (pass@16 for the no-search baseline), ProofEvolve averages 57.8% across three competition benchmarks vs 50.5% for LEAP and 45.9% for Hilbert (the strongest reproduced agentic baselines, same base LLM): PutnamBench 71.2% (vs 64.7% LEAP), IMO-LeanProofBench 53.3% (vs 36.7% LEAP, 60 problems), CombiBench 49.0% (vs 50.0% LEAP — a one-point deficit). Inference-only Opus 4.8 scores 0.0% on Putnam and IMO. Ablations (60 IMO problems, 5 seeds) show all three operators matter, with larger effects on the Advanced split (full: 32/60; −repair: 9; −decomposition: 11; −recombination: 14). Test-time budget scaling over 8 open-weight configurations (Qwen3.5-397B, Qwen3.6-35B, Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, gpt-oss-120b) shows 7/8 configs increase kernel-verified transitions with budget and distinct targets solved rises from 2 to 10 across 485 targets — small absolute numbers. The controlled synthetic study shows a growing library solves 19.8% vs 7.3% (2.7×) when reset per target. The Lean Workbook study: library built from 5,546 of the prover's own kernel-checked proofs over 9,968 source theorems; on 744 screened held-out theorems, K=8 retrieval lifts solve rate 49.5%→53.4% (+3.9pp, ±0.7 run SD over 3 runs), random retrieval 49.6%, K=64 gives +5.3pp; only 351→322 copy analysis supports genuine transfer. Baselines are current and matched (2025–2026 systems, same base model); the open-weight cross-method comparison is honestly declared inconclusive. Scale is standard for the field (hundreds of targets), not stress-scale; compute reaches 224 B200 GPUs for serving and "a few thousand B200-GPU-hours" for the library study. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (verified closure as a kernel-grounded fitness functional with proven monotonicity, and typed schema recombination that exposes residual premises as subgoals) plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (self-built verified libraries transfer to unseen theorems at ~4pp where random retrieval transfers nothing). The scaffolding is a competent combination of known ingredients — MAP-Elites archives (Mouret & Clune 2015), LLM-proposed variation with symbolic verification (FunSearch/AlphaEvolve), AND-OR proof DAGs (LEAP), and lemma libraries (LEGO-Prover, DreamProver) — applied to the cross-target inheritance setting; the authors are transparent that DreamProver is the closest system. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for the three variation operators (5 seeds, error bars in Fig. 3); main Table 1 reports means over three independent runs but without reported variance; the Workbook study reports run-to-run SDs and paired contrasts. Verification discipline is above the norm: independent re-verification of every solve with restricted #print axioms (400+ re-verifications, 0 false positives), exclusion of native_decide, no unresolved metavariables, and a 5-judge LLM leakage screen that removed 25.6% of the evaluation split with bimodal agreement honestly disclosed. The appendix flags its own parser-coverage bias in the scaling study (missing outcomes skew means upward at larger budgets) and refuses cross-method conclusions from the weak open-weight subset — unusual candor. However: no public code, data, or library release is mentioned anywhere; the mechanism-level ablation covers operators but not the archive, scheduling (Eq. 13), or temperature; the soundness theorem is near-trivial given the kernel (it largely restates Lean's guarantees); and the 5 leakage judges are all Claude-family models, so their correlated biases are unquantified. Evaluation of the full system is on the same style of competition benchmarks used to tune design decisions, though no benchmark-specific development is disclosed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a search framework run and measured, not a deployed tool). - Practical: Runs on a vendor API plus a local Lean kernel, or on self-hosted open-weight models on B200 nodes via vLLM/SGLang — all commercially available; Lean 4.29.1 with a pinned Mathlib commit is the only special substrate. - Efficient: Matched per-target budgets make it cost-comparable to LEAP/Hilbert at equal solve quality; library construction (~5 fleet-hours for 5,546 proofs) is cheap relative to any RL training run, but per-target wall-clock (up to 3,600 s at 2×) is substantial. - Effective: Evidence supports the claim on Putnam and IMO-style problems, but CombiBench shows no gain over LEAP and the cross-problem reuse benefit is measured only with search disabled (in-context exemplars), so the full loop's reuse benefit on real benchmarks is unproven. - Scalable: Tested to 2× budget and to a 5,546-entry library with monotone gains, but only 11 distinct targets were solved across all open-weight runs — the 10×–100× story (a library of millions of schemas, retrieval quality at scale) is extrapolation. Deliverable: paper form only; no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model artifact is released. Strengths: (1) Verified closure is a genuinely new selection signal: it converts kernel-accepted partial structure into a graded, provably monotone fitness, solving the well-documented fragility of selection over binary-verified candidates. (2) The library-isolation experiment design — relevant vs random retrieval from an identical self-built library, paired contrasts, copy-rate analysis, and a pre-registered-style leakage screen — is a model for attributing gains to mechanism rather than prompt stuffing, and directly answers the LEGO-Prover reuse critique (Berlot-Attwell et al.). (3) The soundness invariants (Theorem 1, Corollary 1) formalize the claim that the evolving trusted state never admits unverified objects, making the "recursive self-improvement without soundness decay" argument precise. (4) Honest self-auditing: the parser-coverage bias, the refusal to draw cross-method conclusions from weak open-weight results, and the disclosure that the Workbook study exercises only the in-context mode are credibility positives. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the Lean Workbook study isolates one mechanism (retrieved schemas act as in-context exemplars, not typed realizer compositions; archive, decomposition, repair, and ρ are switched off); that the composite budget scaling does not isolate any single resource; that parser coverage may bias scaling means upward; that per-model monotone scaling is not established and open-weight solve counts are too small for cross-method claims; and that growing-library gains are demonstrated in a controlled synthetic setting plus one real-data study. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a notable strength. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The central narrative is recursive self-improvement through typed schema recombination, yet no experiment measures the full system's performance as a function of its own accumulated library during the main benchmark runs — the 2.7× controlled gain and the +3.9pp real-data gain are both outside the end-to-end pipeline. (2) No code or artifact release is mentioned, which for a framework paper with many hyperparameters (τ, archive descriptors, weight scheme, retriever) limits reproduction. (3) The IMO-Lean margin (53.3% vs 36.7%) rests on 60 problems (~10 solves of difference), and no confidence intervals are given for Table 1; CombiBench, the largest-diversity benchmark, favors LEAP. (4) Uniform edge weights in ρ and the frontier-scheduling rule are never ablated, so the contribution of the specific fitness design vs any graded progress signal is unclear. (5) DreamProver, identified as the closest system, is discussed but not empirically compared. (6) The 158-lemma ProofLib environment extension used in open-weight runs (one reported solve depends on it) blurs the "library is retrieval-only" claim for those runs. (7) The 5.6pp CombiBench-side conclusion that "the strongest systems are within one point" is presented without variance, and three runs cannot distinguish a 1pp gap. Bottom Line: For researchers building agentic or library-based formal provers, this is worth reading for the verified-closure fitness and the exemplary library-attribution methodology, even though the headline self-improvement claim is validated only in a weakened in-context form and stronger-evidenced alternatives (LEAP; DreamProver, untested here) cover adjacent ground.

Aspire: Can Models Self-Evolve from Vague Goals?

Problem & Motivation: Humans who improve at open-ended skills ("become a better physicist") must themselves decide what to learn, how to learn it, and how to verify progress. Existing LLM self-evolution work—PostTrainBench, LaMDAgent, SEAL, MLE-bench, RE-Bench—starts only after a human has converted a broad capability request ("improve math reasoning") into a fixed task, dataset, metric, and success criterion, reducing self-evolution to searching over how to optimize. The paper targets the missing axis: given only a vague capability direction, can an agent diagnose its own gaps, decompose sub-goals, construct training and validation signals, and achieve genuine, retained capability gain? The authors ground this in forward-deployed-engineer work in industry, where turning a vague deployment need into a working system is exactly the human-dominated labor that benchmarks presuppose away. Key Idea: The core insight is that vague-goal self-evolution can be measured only if evaluation stays an external, agent-invisible instrument: the agent gets a natural-language capability goal plus a typed tool interface (data actions, train actions, loop actions) executed by a controller, while a hidden, versioned, expert-authored evaluation set returns at most bounded aggregate scores—never items, answers, rubrics, or per-item feedback. This decouples "what to optimize" (agent's job) from "how to measure it" (controller-side instrumentation), and retention is enforced by rollback: a candidate replaces the base only if it beats the base score under a predeclared selection rule, so retained improvement is a selection outcome, not a training outcome. Methodology: Aspire defines a campaign Γ = (G, E_G, J, A, B, Σ): a vague goal G, a versioned hidden evaluator E_G with judge J, a typed action contract, a budget, and a predeclared terminal selection rule. Two evolution surfaces are supported: weight evolution (mutable model M with fixed harness and decision model) and harness evolution (mutable harness H with fixed weights). The agent-facing tool composes data operations (search, download, import, synthesize), training launches (SFT, GRPO, LoRA), status queries, self-evaluation on agent-owned validation data, and branch/stop actions; the controller maps these to managed backends, enforces budget, checks dataset registration against the hidden set for contamination, verifies checkpoint lineage/provenance, and handles rollback (retain k only when Δraw(k) > 0, guaranteeing Δret ≥ 0 by construction). The hidden evaluation set contains 520 expert-authored items across six goals (science reasoning 75, humanities/social science 110, health/medicine 100, mathematics 126, composite logic/reliability/instruction-following 89, writing 20 task bundles), authored from scratch with GPQA/MMLU-Pro/MedQA only as difficulty references, screened by blind multi-model difficulty calibration (Seed-2.0, GPT-5.2, Gemini-3, L0–L3), deduplication, overlap audits, scorer binding, and SHA-256 version freezing. Two RQ2 protocols are run: final-only (24 runs, 40 GPU-hours each, one terminal checkpoint evaluated, Avg@2 over two runs per model–goal pair) and adaptive-feedback (30 configuration–goal cells, one run each, bounded repeated aggregate queries on the same fixed slice). Critical design decisions: (1) hiding the evaluator entirely vs. exposing it is well-justified as the only way to test operationalization rather than proxy-fitting; (2) rollback-based retention is well-justified and honestly framed as making Δret ≥ 0 tautological; (3) the adaptive-feedback protocol's reuse of the same 520-item slice for repeated selection is acknowledged as feedback-guided selection rather than independent replication—a known weakness. Key Results: - RQ1 (vague vs. explicit task): Under PostTrainBench's evaluators, vague-goal prompting scores 27.07 for Claude Opus 4.8 vs. the 32.90 official explicit-task reference, and 29.58 for GPT-5.6 vs. 36.23. In 48 matched Claude Opus 4.8 run pairs, vague-goal trajectories spend 2,109 more seconds of decision-model thinking and 0.61 more GPU-idle hours per pair, while active training/evaluation time drops 1.27 hours; LoRA use rises from 24.1% to 89.8% of runs; evaluation-feedback density is 0.57 evaluations per training start vs. 2.63 for official GPT-5.6 (4.6×). - RQ2 (weight evolution, Qwen3.5-4B/9B base): Final-only protocol: 0/6 of Qwen3.5-4B and 1/6 of Qwen3.5-9B model–goal pairs exceed base (science: 45.33→48.00, +2.67, the sole positive pair); 3/24 individual runs beat base. Adaptive-feedback: 28/30 cells produce an evaluated checkpoint, 21 eligible, only 1 retained above-base improvement (GPT-5.6 Terra on math, 17.86→20.10); of 62 within-lineage transitions 28 rise, 13 tie, 21 fall. A striking failure mode: five checkpoints trained with numeric-label MMLU SFT (21,000 single-digit targets) produce all-single-digit outputs and score 0, 0, 0, 6.141, 0; three blind-continuation runs burn 26.6–32.3 GPU-hours on 16–20 training jobs and submit final checkpoints scoring 0.159, 2.540, and 0. - RQ3 (harness evolution, Qwen3.5-4B runtime, 20-item writing evaluation): The original Qwen-Agent reference scores 28.64 task-macro / 27.65 example-micro; the best of three GPT-5.6-created successor harnesses (Sol) reaches 27.22/25.97, still 1.42 task-macro points below reference; Luna's template-editing harness scores 19.32/18.33 after overfitting to an 8-item self-checklist. All numbers are means over three frozen-harness executions; per-execution dispersion is not reported. - Scale is standard-to-small: single 4B/9B base models, ≤40 GPU-hours per run, 322.6 training GPU-hours total for adaptive-feedback and 149.2 for final-only. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (formalizing vague-goal-driven self-evolution and "target operationalization" as a distinct axis from how-to-optimize search) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (sealed 520-item expert-authored hidden evaluation plus a controller-environment with rollback-based retention and dual evolution surfaces). The individual mechanisms—LoRA/GRPO training backends, benchmark hiding, agent harnesses—are standard; the genuinely new elements are the problem formulation, the information-boundary protocol, and the retained-vs-best-checkpoint outcome accounting, which is applied to a new setting rather than derived from new algorithmic ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style decomposition is present in a useful form: the paper separates best-evaluated, eligible, and retained checkpoints and separately reports baseline, best, and rollback outcomes, so the reader can see that closing the loop ≠ improving capability. However, there are no error bars, no multi-seed runs (the authors state plainly that adaptive-feedback is "a complete 5×6 design but not a multi-seed estimate"), and RQ1's comparison mixes released official PostTrainBench scores with the authors' own runs under possibly differing metadata—explicitly flagged as not a prompt-only causal effect. RQ3 reports only three executions per frozen harness measuring runtime variation, not creation replication. No code, dataset release, or model weights URL is stated beyond a project page (https://self-developing-agents.github.io/); the portable adaptive-feedback artifact deliberately excludes content-bearing traces, which are available only under controlled access. Methodological concerns: the adaptive protocol repeatedly queries the same fixed 520-item slice for checkpoint selection (the authors themselves note the sole retained gain is "evidence of feedback-guided selection rather than an independently replicated capability gain"); the hidden-set judge (gemini-3.5-flash with an 8,192-token budget and 10% fail-closed threshold) is not validated against human agreement; and the writing goal for RQ3 has only 20 items. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper builds and runs a benchmark environment and experiments; it is also, in effect, a systems artifact, but the evidence reported is experimental). - Practical: Yes in principle—the environment abstracts distributed training behind typed actions—but deployment requires the controller infrastructure, hidden evaluation set, and managed GPU backends that are not shown to be released. - Efficient: Runs are capped at 40 GPU-hours and 10 hours wall time per cell; total RQ2 compute is ~472 training GPU-hours, modest for the questions asked. - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark successfully exposes a real gap—agents complete training loops but rarely retain goal-aligned gains—rather than showing that any method solves vague-goal self-evolution; the negative result is the product. - Scalable: Not tested: decision-model scale is confounded in final-only (model, base, and base score change together), no recursive handoff beyond round 1 is evaluated, and the paper explicitly defers refreshed evaluation versions and drift control to future work. The work delivers a benchmark artifact (hidden evaluation set, environment, protocol contracts); no public code/data release is confirmed in the text. Strengths: - Genuinely new problem axis: it is the first benchmark, to the authors' demonstrated knowledge, that severs goal operationalization from optimization search, and the formalization (what-to-learn vs. how-to-learn as coupled decisions) is crisp and reconstructible. - Honest outcome accounting: the explicit separation of best-evaluated vs. eligible vs. retained checkpoints, and the admission that Δret ≥ 0 is a selection artifact, preempts the most common self-deception in self-improvement evaluation (and anticipates the RSIBench-Data retention failure finding). - High-quality contamination control: items authored from scratch with tracked provenance, blind multi-model difficulty screening, semantic/exact dedup, overlap audits against reference benchmarks, a second registration-time overlap gate on agent training data, and SHA-256 version freezing—more rigorous than most agent-benchmark releases. - Actionable negative findings with mechanism: the numeric-label MMLU SFT format-collapse (21,000 single-digit targets → all-single-digit outputs, scores 0–6.14) and Luna's proxy-overfitting case (8/8 on its own checklist, 19.32 on hidden items) are concrete, diagnosed failure modes, not just low aggregate numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length: they state RQ1 comparisons are "descriptive rather than a prompt-only causal effect"; that the adaptive-feedback retained gain is selection-on-the-test-slice evidence, not independent replication; that goals are limited to six; that one run per configuration–goal cell is not a multi-seed estimate; that RQ2 evaluations do not measure preservation of unrelated capabilities; that the composite logic/reliability goal is not three separately identifiable targets; that trace-level causal claims require controlled access; and the conclusion explicitly bounds claims by evaluation-set coverage and scoring quality, naming repeated runs, refreshed versions, and recursive evolution with drift control as future work. This candor is a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The rubric-based judge for open-ended items is never validated for human agreement or inter-judge stability, yet all writing and many reasoning scores depend on it; a 10% fail-closed threshold is stated but not characterized. - RQ2 measures only the target goal, so catastrophic forgetting of general capability—which the authors cite as motivation for instruction-tuned starting points—is itself unmeasured; the claim that updates "should preserve useful behavior" is never tested beyond the goal slices. - The 20-item writing evaluation makes RQ3 (differences of 1.42–9.32 task-macro points) statistically fragile with no dispersion reporting, so the ranking of successor harnesses is descriptive at best. - The adaptive-feedback protocol has an inherent Goodhart risk beyond what the authors note: even with items hidden, bounded aggregate queries on a fixed 520-item slice let the decision model perform black-box selection on the test set; a held-out confirmation slice was available by construction (items are versioned) but not used. - The sole retained gain (Terra math 17.86→20.10, +2.24 points on one run) is well within plausible run-to-run variance given the final-only run-to-run swings visible in Appendix C.3 (e.g., 4B math runs at 16.746 and 0.159), yet it is the headline positive result. - No comparison against any baseline strategy for vague-goal operationalization (e.g., a fixed prompt-decomposition heuristic, or a human-written curriculum), so the reader cannot tell how much of the failure is the task and how much is the agent stack. Bottom Line: For anyone building self-improving agents or AI-for-AI benchmarks, this paper is worth reading for its problem formulation, sealed-evaluation protocol, and unusually honest negative results showing that loop-closing is not capability-closing—while noting that its headline numbers rest on single runs and an unvalidated judge, so it should be treated as a rigorous first characterization of a new problem, not a definitive measurement.

Xincheng Wei, Yifan Ding, Yoshua Li, Dongsheng Ma, Rongxiang Weng, Xunliang Cai, Wenjian Ding, Yao Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 2 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DiagEvo, a self-play framework in which a lightweight diagnostician LLM extracts recurring error causes from the solver's failed trajectories into a hierarchical Active/Mastered memory, and the challenger uses that memory to generate cause-targeted questions plus a double-confidence filter to remove high-conflict pseudo-labels. - Why it's important: Label-free self-play methods (R-Zero, Absolute Zero) plateau because questions drift in surface complexity without targeting what the solver actually fails at, while guided methods (DARC, SPICE, R-Few) depend on external resources like human examples, corpora, or difficulty labels; this closes that gap using only information generated inside the self-play loop. - How it does it: The core trick is comparative diagnosis — for each failed trajectory, an LLM locates the earliest reasoning divergence from a pseudo-label-agreeing trajectory and names a transferable 10–20-word error cause — with promotion to Mastered governed by solver self-consistency and a frequency schedule (ε = F1/(F1 + Ft/k)) that rebalances targeted vs. free generation. - The good: With a 4B diagnostician it beats all five baselines on all three solvers across nine benchmarks (72.3% math average on Qwen3-8B, +4.5 over R-Zero; 57.4% overall, +1.1 over DARC), with 3-run standard deviations, a component ablation, oracle-agreement analysis, and only 5.7% wall-clock overhead from diagnosis/memory. - The missing: Overall margins over the strongest baseline (DARC) are ~1 point — comparable to or smaller than the per-benchmark standard deviations — with no significance testing against baselines, and some DARC baseline scores are transcribed from another paper rather than re-run. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on self-improving LLMs or curriculum generation and want a concrete, cheaply instrumented way to turn solver failures into a next-round curriculum; skip it if you need cross-domain results or statistically robust comparisons, since training and evaluation are math-only with narrow margins.

Problem & Motivation: In multi-round self-play, a challenger LLM generates questions and a solver LLM trains on them, and sustained improvement requires questions to stay near the solver's evolving competence boundary. Label-free methods steer generation with difficulty/learnability/diversity signals estimated from solver responses, but these say how hard a question is, not why the solver fails — so the same error cause recurs across superficially different questions, question length inflates (45.6 → 168.9 words without memory in the paper's own measurement), and performance plateaus. Guided methods fix this by importing external task resources (human-annotated examples in R-Few, document corpora in SPICE, difficulty labels and a privileged teacher in DARC), which breaks the closed-loop self-evolution setting. The unresolved question is whether a curriculum signal sufficient to target unresolved weaknesses can be derived purely from artifacts the self-play loop already produces. Key Idea: The solver's own failure history is a sufficient curriculum signal: compare a failed trajectory with one that agrees with the majority pseudo-label, have a frozen diagnostician LLM name the earliest transferable reasoning divergence as an error cause, organize causes under skill nodes in a two-level memory, and let per-cause Active/Mastered states and episode frequencies both parameterize the generation mixture and gate promotion — turning diagnosis memory into an online curriculum scheduler. Methodology: Each round alternates four stages using GRPO (following R-Zero's setup: LR 1e-6, KL 1e-2, batch 256, group size 8; 8× H200, BF16, FlashAttention-2). (1) The challenger updates via GRPO on an uncertainty reward (maximized at 50% solver self-consistency) with BLEU-cluster repetition penalty, then generates curriculum candidates as a mixture: with probability ε the challenger explores freely; otherwise it samples an Active cause proportional to active-episode frequency f(e) and generates a targeted question, optionally 'cross-state stitching' an Active cause with a Mastered sibling from the same skill node. The odds of targeting vs. exploration follow Ft/(kF1) where Ft is total active-episode failures. (2) For each candidate, the solver samples N=12 construction responses; the majority answer becomes the pseudo-label, and double-confidence filtering retains questions with p1 ∈ [0.25, 0.75] (absolute, intermediate difficulty) and p1 ≥ 1.6·p2 (relative, the new constraint against unstable two-way splits); GRPO then trains the solver on retained pairs with ±1 agreement rewards using a separate set of optimization responses. (3) Memory maintenance is a hybrid code+LLM pipeline: comparative extraction (one LLM call also routes failures to known causes), embedding-based deduplication screening with LLM confirmation, skill-node assignment or creation, and end-of-round node consolidation; causes are promoted from Active to Mastered when mean self-consistency on targeted questions reaches θup = 0.70, which resets episode frequency and shifts probability back toward exploration. Critical design decisions: (a) diagnosis uses only failed trajectories from questions retained by the filter — justified by cost control but means diagnosis sees a filtered slice; (b) promotion is measured by self-consistency against pseudo-labels, not ground truth, which the authors acknowledge; (c) single-pass, no-recheck node assignment — efficiency-motivated but acknowledged as a single point of failure in the authors' own prompts. Key Results: Tested on Qwen3-4B-Base, Qwen3-8B-Base, and OctoThinker-8B-Hybrid-Base across five math benchmarks (AMC, Minerva Math, MATH-500, GSM8K, OlympiadBench; GPT-4o judge per simple-evals) and four general benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA, GPQA-Diamond, BBEH; exact match). With the default 4B diagnostician, Qwen3-8B reaches 72.3% math average (R-Zero 67.8, DARC 71.1) and 38.8% general average (R-Zero 36.2, DARC 37.8), for 57.4% overall (+1.1 over DARC); on Qwen3-4B and OctoThinker-8B it reaches 53.5% and 41.9% overall, +1.3 over DARC each. Baselines are current and strong (R-Zero, Absolute Zero, SPICE, R-Few, DARC), but Absolute Zero/SPICE/R-Few/DARC scores are transcribed from the DARC paper while base models and R-Zero were re-run (reproduction matches within 0.1–0.5 points). Diagnostician scale (4B → 30B-A3B → 235B-A22B) adds only ~1 point to math and ~0.2–0.5 to general. Ablations on Qwen3-8B show each component matters but modestly: frozen challenger −3.8 math points, no filtering −2.9, absolute-only filtering −1.4, no state updates −2.2, no stitching −1.5, random-pair stitching −1.0. Oracle agreement (GPT-5 relabeling) rises from 65% to 72% with the memory and to 75% with relative confidence. Performance peaks at round 5 (72.3%) then declines to 71.4% by round 7; the memory grows from 151 to 244 causes with ~36 skill nodes stabilizing after round 3. Math-only training transfers to general benchmarks (e.g., OctoThinker general average 10.7 → 28.4). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING claim. Genuinely novel: closing the diagnostic feedback loop inside self-play — deriving the curriculum from the solver's failure history rather than external resources — and the Active/Mastered state machine with frequency-driven exploration scheduling. The ingredients are each standard: agent memory (Reflexion, ReasoningBank), difficulty filtering (R-Zero, online difficulty filtering), majority-vote pseudo-labeling, GRPO, and LLM-based trajectory analysis; the relative-confidence constraint (p1 ≥ τ·p2) is a simple variant of vote-share thresholding. The contribution is a specific, well-motivated composition rather than a new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover the three main components (generation policy, memory state updates/stitching, filtering), and hyperparameter sensitivity is reported for k (72.3% at k=0.5, range 71.3–72.3 across k∈{0.2, 0.5, 1, 2}) and τ (peak at 1.6). DiagEvo results are mean ± std over three runs (per-benchmark stds mostly 0.2–1.3 points); baselines are apparently single-run and no significance tests are reported, so the 1.0–1.3-point margins over DARC are within roughly one standard deviation of the authors' own measurements. Four baseline rows are taken from DARC's paper rather than re-run — mitigated by a careful reproduction check (base and R-Zero deviations <1.0 per-benchmark) but still a cross-paper comparability caveat. A GPT-5 oracle validates pseudo-label quality, with human inspection of 50 questions/round. Notably, the ablation table's 'pure free exploration' peak (69.5%) matches the round-by-round plateau analysis, an honest internal consistency check. Extensive appendices give full prompts, transition rules, hyperparameters, and a runtime breakdown (diagnosis + memory = 5.7% wall-clock). No code, data, or model release is mentioned. The framework is developed and evaluated on the same math-generation/evaluation ecosystem as R-Zero and DARC, so benchmark alignment with the design iteration is a live concern. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor from the memory pipeline). Practical: Runs on a single node of 8 H200 GPUs with off-the-shelf frozen open models (Qwen3-Instruct-2507 diagnostician, text-embedding-v4), so within reach of well-resourced labs but not commodity hardware. Efficient: Adds only 5.7% wall-clock over the R-Zero base loop (94.2% of time is generation, pseudo-labeling, and GRPO updates that R-Zero already requires); the diagnostician can be a 4B model with negligible quality loss. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated problem (sustained improvement without external resources, beating R-Zero by 4.5 math points and even externally guided DARC by ~1 point overall) via a real proxy — but oracle agreement of 75% means roughly a quarter of training pseudo-labels are likely wrong. Scalable: Tested only to 7 rounds and 8B-scale solvers; performance declines after round 5, so longer horizons are untested, and scaling the memory (244 causes at 5 rounds) to many more rounds or domains is claimed, not shown. Delivers no released artifact — paper form only, with enough appendix detail (prompts, all hyperparameters) that reproduction is plausible. Strengths: (1) The problem framing is genuinely well-chosen: the paper cleanly separates label-free self-play's difficulty-aware but diagnosis-blind guidance from externally guided methods, and its solution strictly occupies the unoccupied quadrant. (2) The Active/Mastered state machine with frequency reset on promotion is a thoughtful mechanism — it automatically rebalances toward exploration as causes are resolved, and the round-by-round memory analysis (188 → 117 Active, 127 Mastered) shows the intended dynamics actually occur. (3) Honest diagnostic work: the paper measures oracle agreement per variant to separate the memory's effect (+7 points) from the filtering constraint's effect (+3) on pseudo-label quality, and quantifies the question-length pathology of unguided self-play (45.6 → 168.9 words) that motivates the whole approach. (4) The cost story is strong and specific: a 4B frozen diagnostician, 5.7% overhead, and a measured insensitivity to diagnostician scale (only ~1 point from 4B to 235B-A22B) make the method practical, not just a demo. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three. (1) Pseudo-label confidence: both filter constraints measure solver agreement, not correctness, so a shared systematic error passes the filter — they name this directly and propose future verification signals. (2) Training horizon: the number of rounds is fixed in advance (5 in main experiments) while performance peaks there and declines by round 7; they propose round-stopping criteria. (3) Evaluation scope: training is math-only, so cross-domain gains are transfer observations, not evidence the diagnosis loop works in open-ended or multi-turn settings. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge the thin statistical margins over DARC or the reliance on transcribed baseline scores in the main limitations discussion. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical strength: the headline 'beats every baseline' claim rests on overall margins of 1.0–1.3 points over DARC, while DiagEvo's own per-benchmark standard deviations reach ±0.7–1.3 and no paired significance test is run — a reviewer cannot rule out that DARC at equal tuning is equivalent. (2) The ablation deltas for the memory components (state updates −2.2, stitching −1.5, random-pair −1.0) are small and single-seeded, so the hierarchical machinery's cost-benefit is not firmly established even though the oracle-agreement analysis helps. (3) Diagnosis is trained on a filtered, majority-vote-label world: since failed trajectories are only compared against the pseudo-label, the diagnostician learns 'why the solver disagreed with the majority,' and systematic solver-wide biases become invisible curriculum blind spots — a deeper version of the acknowledged shared-error problem that the paper does not probe. (4) The round-5 peak invites selection-concern: the checkpoint was chosen after observing the 7-round curve, and only round-5 results are reported in the main table. (5) Evaluation uses GPT-4o as judge for math (inheritable judge bias) and a GPT-5 oracle whose agreement with pseudo-labels is taken as a quality proxy — circular if GPT-5 shares the solver's systematic failure modes on generated questions, though human inspection of 50 questions/round partially mitigates this. (6) No code release is stated despite full reproducibility detail. Bottom Line: For researchers building self-improving LLM pipelines, this is worth reading — it is the first credible demonstration that a closed-loop, externally-resource-free curriculum can be mined from solver failure trajectories at trivial overhead, beating both label-free and externally guided baselines — but the sub-1.5-point margins over DARC, math-only scope, and missing code mean it is a strong directional result rather than a settled advance.

H Tian, M Li, Y Mi, S Zhu, Z Yang, Y Wang, H Zhu, Q Hu · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a construction-and-validation protocol for LLM-agent tasks whose difficulty is gated by a small hand-authored knowledge artefact (private conventions, reference tables, utility operators) that is deliberately withheld or provided as a controlled, audited experimental variable, with deterministic executable verifiers and a configuration-relative calibration screen for task retention. - Why it's important: Synthetic agent tasks are either solvable from the generator's existing knowledge (adding little signal) or under-specified and unverifiable;
