Jianlyu Chen, Yuyang Hu, Hongjin Qian, Jiawei Liu, Wenqing Wei, Xiaolong Chen, Defu Lian, Zhicheng Dou, Chaozhuo Li, Qiwei Ye, Zheng Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 3 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DisCo, an agent framework that automatically distills declarative sources (GitHub repositories, papers) into verified, structured "skills" (SKILL.md + references/ + scripts/ graphs), yielding the AREX-Skill Library of 5,353 skills from 1,000 ML repositories, and shows a skill-equipped Codex agent beats its skill-free twin on four research-agent benchmarks. - Why it's important: Autonomous ML-research agents waste task budget rediscovering package behavior and method know-how through trial and error; a reusable, pre-verified operational-knowledge layer could convert that wasted budget into performance without changing the model or harness. - How it does it: A four-stage distillation pipeline — scope capabilities, ground evidence, construct a skill graph, verify-and-repair — run either offline per source (task-agnostic) or on demand per task (task-oriented), with skills consumed via progressive disclosure and a taxonomy router. - The good: The headline controlled comparison is striking and broad: the same GPT-5.5 Codex agent rises from 31.11% to 72.89% Any-Medal on the full 75-task MLE-bench (+134.3% relative), improving across all difficulty tiers and beating the strongest public baseline (64.44%). - The missing: For MLE-bench, skills are built per-task using up to 24 GPU-hours of diagnostic trial-and-error on the very task being scored, with that construction budget excluded from the matched-budget comparison — the largest reported gain therefore confounds distilled knowledge with per-task exploration the baseline never receives. - Read it or not: Read it if you build agent harnesses or knowledge layers for autonomous ML agents — the skill-graph design and controlled ablations are directly reusable — but treat the MLE-bench number as an upper bound inflated by the per-task construction phase.

Problem & Motivation: Autonomous ML-research agents are conventionally described as a model backbone plus a harness (orchestration, memory, verification). Both components lack the domain expertise — which method to pick, which package API to call, which configuration is sane, which pitfalls invalidate a run — that separates knowing a method from making it work. The authors call this missing layer "operational knowledge"; it exists abundantly in repositories and papers but in forms written for humans and too large to load at task time. Practitioners building research agents currently fill this gap by hand, at a labor cost that scales with domain and release cadence. The paper's problem is to produce this knowledge automatically and at scale from declarative sources, so that discoveries amortize across tasks rather than being re-derived in every run. Key Idea: Package operational knowledge as three-layer skill graphs (a SKILL.md knowledge interface, a references/ knowledge substrate, and a scripts/ execution interface), and produce them with a verified four-stage distillation — z →scope Q →ground X →construct G̃ →verify (G, R) — where the choice of anchor (a source for task-agnostic distillation, a task for task-oriented distillation) determines source selection and the verification signal, and no skill is admitted without checks, with surviving gaps recorded in a construction record R. The separation of distillation from summarization via mandatory verification is the load-bearing move; the skill format itself follows Anthropic's existing Agent Skills spec. Methodology: DisCo is one agent with two modes over a fixed backbone and harness. Creator mode runs the four-stage pipeline: (1) scoping — for a repository anchor, source understanding plus capability identification; for a task anchor, task decomposition plus capability-gap analysis; (2) grounding — knowledge extraction from the source, or active source discovery via web search for a task anchor, with explicit evidence include/exclude boundaries (excluding generated files, vendored deps, caches; for MLE-bench, blocking the competition webpage and competition-specific content); (3) construction — assembling a repository-level entry skill routing to component skills for workflows (data prep, training, inference, evaluation, serving, troubleshooting), each self-contained with provenance (source commit, version); (4) verification — assertion-backed usability cases, safe native examples/tests/CLI checks/smoke scripts, static gates (link integrity, self-containment, local-path leakage), with localized repair and rerun on failure. The library is organized by an LLM-induced two-level taxonomy (20 areas, 178 families) built before final assignment via a locator/judge/aggregator loop over 100 stable batches, with router pages enabling progressive disclosure at run time. Task-oriented variants differ: MLE-bench builds one descriptive (non-executable) graph per competition from up to 24 GPU-hours of diagnostic trials; PaperBench distills up to 10 related-work papers per target into 3–5 module skills each, verified by isolated tests plus a recovery experiment that excludes the original implementation; FrontierCS builds a single frozen 9-node/42-link recovery-router graph refined via paired trials; PassNet refines its graph on a 4k-instance training split via screening-and-dispatch over paired trajectories. Evaluation attaches skills as operating context K to a fixed GPT-5.5 Codex harness, holding backbone, harness, and run-time budget constant; the design decisions to make skills descriptive-only (no runnable solution scripts) and to exclude target artifacts are well-justified anti-leakage measures, though the MLE-bench exploration phase itself remains the weak link. Key Results: With GPT-5.5 backbone and Codex harness held fixed: MLE-bench (full 75 competitions, mean±SEM over 3 runs) rises from 31.11% to 72.89% Any-Medal (+41.78 points, +134.3% relative; High tier 13.33%→62.22%, +366.8%), also beating the strongest public baseline (Famou-Agent 2.0 at 64.44% with Gemini-3-Pro-Preview). PaperBench (20 papers, official grader) rises from 29.45% to 39.59% (+10.14 points), improving 18 of 20 tasks with regressions on 2 (sample-specific-masks −5.07, stay-on-topic −4.52), attributed to retrieval-precision failure. FrontierCS (188 Agent Track tasks, 5-hour budget) rises from 70.63 to 77.14 (+9.22%), with a paired bootstrap 95% CI of [3.41, 9.83]; the skill-equipped Codex Pareto-dominates Claude Code entries on score/tokens (4.47M vs 13.85–14.72M)/steps/tool calls. PassNet (200 samples, A100) AS Score rises from 1.343 to 1.5313 (+14.0%), correctness 81.35%→90.76%, failed samples 14→5, exceeding TorchInductor's 1.419. Construction costs ~$40 per repository plus per-task budgets (e.g., ≤24 GPU-hours exploration per MLE-bench task) that are NOT counted in the run-time comparison. Public MLE-bench baselines are current and strong (2025–2026 leaderboard entries); skills help most on low-baseline and high-difficulty tasks. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (operational knowledge as an explicit third agent component K alongside model and harness) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the AREX-Skill Library and DisCo distillation pipeline) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (large controlled gains from adding distilled skills under matched backbone/harness/budget). The skill format is Anthropic's existing Agent Skills specification, progressive disclosure is prior art the authors cite, and knowledge distillation from experience (Voyager, Agent Workflow Memory, ExpeL) is established; what is genuinely new is distilling from static declarative artifacts at ecosystem scale with mandatory verification and provenance records, rather than from interaction traces. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and analyses are present and often careful: paired per-task analyses on FrontierCS (per-task gains vs. token usage, Spearman ρ ≈ 0.006–0.015, ruling out extra-compute explanation; a skills-vs-previous-graph comparison isolating each revision), paired trajectory verification on PassNet construction with an instructive error analysis (an overly absolute vendor-operator rule blocking a conv3d rewrite), pass/fail taxonomy of native checks, and 3-run SEM on MLE-bench. Code is released at https://github.com/VectorSpaceLab/AREX-Skill, and the library snapshot is public. Methodological concerns: (1) the MLE-bench with-skills condition implicitly benefits from a 24 GPU-hour exploration phase on the scored task that the no-skill condition and all public baselines lack, and the construction budget is explicitly excluded from the matched-budget comparison — the headline +134.3% should be read with this asymmetry in mind; (2) MLE-bench results are the authors' own runs reported against leaderboard numbers rather than a fully controlled cross-system comparison; (3) benchmark skills for FrontierCS and PassNet were refined using paired trials on development/training tasks, a legitimate but adjacent optimization loop; (4) PaperBench has only 20 tasks, so per-paper variance is high; (5) this is a preprint with vendor-adjacent self-reported runs on unreleased frontier models (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6-sol), which limits independent verification. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built library and agent evaluated by benchmark deployment). Practical: Yes — skills are plain files consumable by any Agent Skills-compatible harness (Claude Code, Codex); construction requires frontier-model API access (~$40/repo). Efficient: Run-time cost is favorable (4.47M tokens/task on FrontierCS vs 13.85–14.72M for Claude Code entries, with higher score), but one-time construction is substantial (~$40k+ for the 1,000-repo collection plus 24 GPU-hours per MLE-bench task). Effective: Evidence shows large improvements on all four benchmarks under matched run-time conditions, but the effectiveness claim is partially proxy for the MLE-bench case due to the uncounted construction phase. Scalable: The 1,000-repo / 5,353-skill snapshot is itself a scale test of construction, and the progressive-disclosure router keeps context load bounded; untested is whether retrieval quality degrades at 10× library size — the two PaperBench regressions already hint at routing precision limits. Deliverable: a public software artifact (skill library + distillation pipeline), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The controlled single-variable experimental design — same backbone, harness, and run-time budget, with skills frozen before execution — is the right way to isolate a knowledge layer, and the consistency of gains across four heterogeneous benchmarks (Kaggle-style engineering, paper replication, algorithm optimization, compiler passes) is persuasive. (2) Mandatory verification with construction records R, evidence boundaries, and provenance metadata (commit, version) meaningfully distinguishes this from prior trace-derived memory work where skill quality is unverifiable. (3) The anti-leakage discipline is unusually explicit: descriptive-only skills, exclusion of target papers/artifacts/competition pages, and recovery experiments that cannot read the original implementation. (4) The FrontierCS usage analysis (gain uncorrelated with extra tokens) directly addresses the most obvious confound. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront the two PaperBench regressions directly, diagnosing a retrieval-precision failure mode where retrieved skills distract from idiosyncratic task strategies, and proposing better routing or fallback-to-unguided reasoning. They note the one-time construction budget is separate and not counted in run-time comparisons (stated transparently, though not treated as a limitation of the headline claim), that the library is a curated rather than exhaustive snapshot, and that skills can become stale as sources drift (motivating refresh workflows). This is a credibility-positive level of candor on failure modes. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The MLE-bench construction phase runs diagnostic trials on the exact task being evaluated — even with the competition webpage blocked and skills restricted to descriptive form, the distilled graph encodes task-specific exploration experience the baseline lacks, so +134.3% conflates distillation with per-task search; a skills-from-a-different-task control (cross-task transfer only) would disentangle this. (2) No experiment evaluates the public 1,000-repo library's contribution on any benchmark — the repository snapshot (the paper's title contribution) is never the skills being measured; all four evaluations use paper-derived or task-oriented graphs. (3) No comparison against cheaper alternatives to operational knowledge, e.g., simply giving Codex the raw README/docs of relevant repositories, retrieval over the source repos, or few-shot examples — the skills-vs-nothing gap may substantially overstate skills-vs-alternatives. (4) Only one backbone and one harness are tested, so generality of the gain across models/harnesses is unverified despite portability being a stated selling point. (5) No human evaluation of skill quality on the 5,353-skill library (e.g., sampling verification-passing skills for correctness), so library-level quality rests on the pipeline's own checks. Bottom Line: A practitioner building autonomous ML agents should read this for the verified skill-distillation pipeline and the cleanest controlled demonstration to date that an externalized knowledge layer pays off, while discounting the MLE-bench headline (constructed on-task, budget uncounted) and noting that the flagship 1,000-repo library is never actually evaluated on the benchmarks.

Problem & Motivation: Astrophysical MHD/GRMHD codes (here H-AMR) discretize PDEs on block-structured AMR grids distributed across GPU clusters. Two trends create a load-balancing gap: (1) floating-point performance has grown much faster than interconnect bandwidth, making ghost-cell communication the bottleneck at scale — some production runs cannot scale past ~100 GPUs and take months to evolve; and (2) new physics modules (implicit radiation source terms whose Newton-Raphson iteration counts vary by up to an order of magnitude, future Monte Carlo photon packets and test particles) create up to ~4× cost variation between mesh blocks, while local adaptive timestepping (LAT) with up to 5 time levels means different blocks are updated 2^t times more often. Space-filling curves (SFCs) — the standard in most contemporary MHD codes — assume quasi-uniform cost density and balance only aggregate workload, which is provably insufficient under lock-step execution: the paper gives a two-GPU example where aggregate-balanced partitioning incurs 12 effective block updates versus 8 optimal. Practitioners running petascale-to-exascale simulations on Frontier and Aurora face this problem directly. Key Idea: The core insight is that under lock-step, multi-timelevel execution, runtime is determined by the per-substep critical path — max over GPUs of the cumulative cost (and block count) at each time-level prefix — not by aggregate workload. CRUX therefore defines a lock-step objective IC = Σ_t 2^max(T−t−2,0) · max_g C_t^(g) over time-level prefix sums, and balances both cost and block counts per level (the block count also keeps pre-/post-electric-field-synchronization work uniform and implicitly controls communication volume, which the cost benchmark does not measure). A second key move is the three-stage decomposition: Stage 0 builds a per-time-level split Morton-curve baseline (establishing an empirical lower bound on achievable imbalance since the true minimum is unknown a priori); Stage 1 minimizes per-level imbalance via greedy 1-opt migrations and same-level 2-opt swaps; Stage 2 minimizes the topology-weighted communication objective J_comm under hard constraints that max_g C_t^(g) and max_g N_t^(g) never increase — so communication optimization provably cannot degrade computational balance. Methodology: The pipeline is: (Stage 0) for each time level t, traverse an independent Morton ordering of that level's blocks, assigning contiguous segments to GPUs to hit target cost C_t,target = (1/G)Σ C_t, with a post-processing pass that reassigns blocks to GPUs left empty; (Stage 1) greedy local search over 1-opt moves and 2-opt swaps, first on the pairwise block-count objective J_t(g,h) = max(N_t^(g), N_t^(h)) until local optimality, then on the cost objective H_t(g,h) = max(C_t^(g), C_t^(h)) constrained to preserve the achieved block-count envelope; candidate targets are restricted to GPUs hosting neighbors of the block (up to six, plus one uniformly random GPU for exploration); (Stage 2) greedy minimization of J_comm = Σ_n Σ_b Σ_ℓ G_{b,ℓ} w(n,m) with the Dragonfly topology weight hierarchy (0/1/2/4/8/16 for same-MCM/same-GPU/same-node/same-switch/same-group/different-group), admissible only if all per-level maxima do not increase. The framework is a constrained local-search/graph-partitioning heuristic, not a formal optimization method (no optimality guarantees beyond local optimality under the move set). Critical design decisions: (1) balancing block counts in addition to cost — justified by GPU parallelism across blocks, the mid-timestep electric-field synchronization split, and unmeasured communication cost, though this is argued rather than ablated; (2) the fixed load-envelope constraint in Stage 2 — well-justified, and the provable non-degradation property is a genuine strength; (3) restricting candidate moves to neighbor-hosting GPUs — justified by observed performance but the authors note the global-search alternative showed no benefit and was dropped without systematic study. Per-block costs are measured by a synthetic benchmark run before each rebalance (~every 10 minutes in production); heterogeneous hardware is handled via per-process performance factors (validated only on a single A100 + RTX 3090 pair). Stages 1–2 are OpenMP-parallel on CPU with buffered, revalidated commits and a STRIDE tuning parameter; single-sweep complexity is O(|B|). Key Results: Benchmarked on four production GRMHD configurations (Table 1): 96–96,236 meshblocks of 48×48×64–56×32×48 cells, 1–5 LAT time levels, max/min block cost 1.0–4.2, on 96–5,400 GPUs (Frontier MI250X, Aurora Intel Max), with effective resolutions of ~10^8–10^11 cells. Against the SFC-SPLIT baseline (Table 2, Figure 2): MHD_LARGE_NOLAT throughput 0.292→0.300 ×10^8 zcps/GPU (~3% gain); MHD_LARGE_LAT 1.28→1.41 ×10^8 (~10%); RAD_MID_LAT 4.35→4.63 ×10^6 (~7%, with memory Smax 5.09→4.13 GB and imbalance metric I 449→407); RAD_LARGE_LAT 3.80→4.96 ×10^6 (~31% throughput gain, I 351→214, a ~39% reduction), though in that case inter-group communication rose from fCluster 0.26 to 0.74 — the authors attribute this to trading communication locality for a much lower critical path. Memory-usage variation drops by up to ~3× versus SFC. LAT itself yields ~4.5× effective throughput for MHD_LARGE versus the single-timestep run. The algorithm partitions ~10^5 meshblocks across ~10^4 GPUs in ~10 seconds on a 32-core CPU. Baselines are the code's own SFC and split-SFC variants; no external partitioner baselines. A single heterogeneous-GPU test (A100 + RTX 3090) showed ~5% speedup over A100-only. The paper is a preprint (arXiv:2608.30080, astro-ph.IM); no error bars, seed variation, or significance testing are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel element is recasting load balancing for lock-step multi-timelevel AMR as per-time-level-prefix critical-path minimization (with a joint block-count objective), plus the load-envelope-constrained communication refinement — existing tools (Zoltan, ParMETIS, SFCs) assume a single scalar weight and aggregate balancing. Problem & Motivation: Time series classification (TSC) in healthcare, sensing, and industrial monitoring increasingly involves multivariate signals where discriminative evidence lives in specific channels, temporal intervals, or cross-channel relationships (delays, phase, correlation). Existing time series foundation models handle this via representation transfer: a frozen encoder produces features and a task-specific classifier is fitted on every target dataset, which requires target-task optimization and is sensitive to readout and classifier choices. Existing in-context classification methods (TIC-FM, TiCT, TimEE) avoid target fitting but are developed and evaluated primarily for univariate series and do not model aligned temporal and cross-channel interactions while accommodating variable channel counts. The gap is a single pretrained model that performs support-conditioned classification for both univariate and multivariate inputs with heterogeneous channel configurations and no target-specific parameters. Key Idea: The core trick is episode-consistent channel-to-slot randomization: randomly assign a task's channels (with reuse when C < Ns) to a fixed G×S group-slot grid, encode each group with shared dual-axis attention, then concatenate slots in fixed order — yielding a representation whose width is independent of the channel count while channel-axis attention within each group still captures joint cross-channel interactions. This is paired with a matching pretraining prior: synthetic episodes where all classes share one temporal background and differ only through sparse rules (motifs, position/order, informative-channel selection, phase/delay, correlation), with instance-level nuisance transforms and episode-wise label permutation so the model must infer label semantics from the context rather than memorize pattern→index mappings. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Signal-level encoding: RSSC samples an episode-wide channel-to-slot assignment (coverage sampling: without replacement if C ≥ Ns, permuted reuse otherwise); each selected channel is resampled to L0=512, patchified into M=32 tokens (normalized values, first differences, local mean/std via shared conv encoders), processed by 3 dual-axis Transformer layers (temporal attention within slots, channel attention across the S=4 slots per group), then a summary-token readout and fixed-order concatenation with learnable group/slot embeddings produce h_t ∈ R^dh (dh = GS·ds = 512). (2) Task-level calibration: Column Distribution Modeling builds, per feature axis, a context-only induced-attention bank (queries cannot modify it), and decodes per-cell affine parameters (W_j, B_j) that calibrate task-specific feature scales; a row-wise Transformer then mixes axes within each sample (no cross-sample flow). (3) Leakage-protected ICL: label embeddings are added only to context tokens, and an additive attention mask makes context the only keys/values, so query-to-query information flow is impossible; queries are predicted in parallel under query cross-entropy on synthetic episodes. Deployment uses ensembling over 8 cyclic label permutations and 4 RSSC draws (32 members, temperature 0.9) and a hierarchical tree extension for K > 10 classes. Critical design decisions: episode-consistent (rather than per-sample) slot assignment, justified as giving slots task-local semantics; context-only calibration banks, justified by leakage protection; and purely synthetic pretraining (20% univariate / 80% multivariate episodes, 6000 steps, 4×V100), justified by the zero real-data claim and validation on 64 synthetic episodes. All three are reasonably well justified, though the G=4, S=4 grouping is not ablated. Key Results: UEA-30 (full official train split as context, test as query): ChorusTIC 72.27% avg. accuracy, avg. rank 3.57, vs. MantisV2+LR 70.50% (rank 4.02), UniShape+RF 69.72%, TabICLv2 67.96%, TabICL 65.33%; relative gains of ~2.51% over the best frozen baseline and ~6.34–10.62% over generic ICL baselines. UCR-128: 81.16% (rank 4.43) vs. TIC-FM 80.01%, MantisV2+LR 80.03%, TiCT 79.17%. Low-label UEA: 5-shot 62.88% (vs. UniShape+RF 62.19%, ~1.11% relative) and 10-shot 68.47% (vs. MantisV2+LR 65.80%, ~4.06% relative), averaged over 5 support sets on 28/24 eligible datasets. Context scaling: monotonic improvement from 64.81% (20% of train split) to 69.13% (60%), ranked first at every fraction. Ablations on UEA-30: removing task-conditioned calibration −1.61 pp, removing cross-channel rules from the prior −1.20 pp, removing label-permutation ensembling −0.89 pp, removing channel-axis attention −0.58 pp. Statistical testing: Wilcoxon signed-rank with Holm correction — on UCR-128 differences vs. 6 baselines remain significant (e.g., Mantis+RF 93/4/31, adjusted p=5.2e-6); on UEA-30, only MOMENT+SVM and NuTime+RF survive correction; the win/tie/loss vs. MantisV2+LR is 18/3/9. Baselines use authors' official checkpoints and default protocols (current, not outdated, though no end-to-end fine-tuned TSFM or classical TSC baselines like HIVE-COTE/InceptionTime are included). Scale is standard (public archives), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (RSSC fixed-width channel-agnostic encoding + context-only column calibration + leakage-protected ICL) combined with a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK contribution in the labeled multivariate episodic prior, and an EMPIRICAL FINDING that a fully synthetic-prior model matches or beats fitted-classifier TSFMs across complete archives. The in-context classification objective, dual-axis attention, and induced-attention calibration are each recognizable from existing work (TiCT, TabICL, Perceiver-style bottlenecks); the genuine novelty is the joint design of a channel-count-invariant episode representation with a pretraining prior whose discriminative rules exercise exactly the cross-channel structure the architecture models — a coherent co-design rather than an isolated algorithmic breakthrough. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and each ablated variant is pretrained from scratch under an identical schedule and seed, which is stronger than checkpoint-only ablations; the inference ablation correctly reuses the full checkpoint. Fixed-shot results average over 5 shared support sets (seeds 0–4), and win/tie/loss counts plus Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests are reported — unusually thorough for this area. However: no error bars or per-seed variance are given for the headline full-context averages; the evaluation seed is fixed at 0 despite stochastic RSSC sampling; only 4 ablation factors are tested (group/slot counts G, S and pretraining mixture ratios are not ablated); hyperparameters were selected on synthetic validation, which is clean but unverified against real-data sensitivity. Code is stated to be available at https://github.com/fangjuntao/ChorusTIC (the repository itself was not verified from the paper). Methodological concerns: the ~2 pp margin over MantisV2+LR on UEA-30 does not survive multiple-comparison correction, so the headline multivariate claim rests on average rank as much as on significance; and all 32 ensemble members make latency comparisons to single-pass baselines unevaluated. This is a preprint (arXiv, with several cited works also preprints), so numbers warrant moderate confidence pending peer review. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — released code and a pretrained checkpoint). Practical: Pretraining used 4× V100 32GB and inference is a frozen forward pass, so it runs on commodity hardware. Efficient: Inference requires 32 ensemble evaluations (8 label permutations × 4 RSSC draws) plus per-task context encoding; relative cost vs. single-pass baselines like TIC-FM or MantisV2+LR is not reported — this is the main unstated cost. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the no-target-fitting classification problem at archive scale with the best average rank on both UEA-30 and UCR-128, though per-dataset variation is large (e.g., 0.46 on FingerMovements, 0.26 on AtrialFibrillation) and margins over the best baseline are within noise on UEA. Scalability beyond tested regime is claimed, not tested: pretraining used C ≤ 10 channels and K ≤ 10 native classes (a hierarchical extension exists for larger K but is evaluated only in an appendix); behavior at 100+ channels or very long contexts is untested. Deliverable: code repository plus a released checkpoint (step-6000), i.e., a usable software artifact, not just paper form. Strengths: (1) The episodic synthetic prior is the paper's real intellectual contribution — classes sharing a background while differing through sparse, controlled temporal and cross-channel rules, with episode-wise label permutation — directly aligning pretraining with the in-context deployment protocol and eliminating any risk of benchmark contamination (no real series used in training). (2) RSSC is a clean solution to a real problem (variable channel counts → fixed-width representations) that preserves within-group cross-channel attention rather than the channel-independent encoding common in TSFMs. (3) The leakage protection is engineered end-to-end and verified structurally: context-only calibration banks, context-only keys/values, and query-query masking are each explicitly enforced, not merely asserted. (4) Evaluation discipline is above the field's norm: full archives (not subsets), matched support sets across methods, official baseline checkpoints, ablations retrained from scratch, and Holm-corrected significance testing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that UCR and UEA 'do not encompass the full range of deployment conditions' and name missing channels, asynchronous sampling, and domain shift as uncovered, promising a broader benchmark. They also implicitly acknowledge label-index sensitivity (via permutation ensembling) and stochastic-slot variance (via RSSC ensembling). This is a direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment of scope, though the compute cost of the mitigating ensembles is not surfaced as a limitation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical significance undermines the headline: after Holm correction on UEA-30, the improvement over MantisV2+LR (the strongest baseline) is not significant, and the text's 'notable' comparison against fitted classifiers is weaker than the abstract implies — the authors do not acknowledge this. (2) Missing baselines: no end-to-end fine-tuned TSFM (which would bound the target-fit cost side of the trade-off), no classical strong TSC methods (HIVE-COTE, InceptionTime, ROCKET variants — RocketPFN is discussed as concurrent but not compared), so 'training-free wins' is shown only against a curated baseline pool. (3) The 32-member ensemble inflates inference compute ~8–32× over baselines with no latency/throughput accounting, and the label-permutation ensemble's −0.89 pp ablation gain partly reflects test-time ensembling rather than model quality — a potentially unfavorable apples-to-apples comparison never addressed. (4) The architecture (G=4, S=4, dual-axis depth) and pretraining mixture (0.2/0.8 univariate/multivariate) are not ablated, so the claim that the cross-channel machinery (rather than sheer capacity or the calibration module) drives multivariate gains rests on a single prior-ablation row (−1.20 pp). (5) Pretraining uses 6000 steps with a batch of 36 episodes on 4 V100s — a small budget relative to typical foundation models; whether performance is undertrained or saturated is unknown, and no training-scale sensitivity is reported. Bottom Line: For researchers working on in-context or foundation-model time series classification, this is worth reading for its synthetic episodic prior and channel-agnostic slot mechanism — both reusable ideas — but a practitioner should treat the multivariate advantage as modest and unproven against fine-tuned or classical baselines, and weigh the 32-pass inference cost before adopting it over MantisV2+LR or TIC-FM.

Neuro- Formal Verification : Agentic Language-Agnostic Formal Program Reasoning

SK Lahiri · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces neuro-formal verification (NFV), a pipeline where an LLM agent translates a Python program, its specification, and its environment into Dafny (or C for CBMC), drives agentic proof search, and returns a machine-checked proof of correctness or a machine-checked proof of a bug — or abstains. - Why it's important: Formal verification is confined to experts in verification-aware languages, while the growing volume of AI-generated mainstream code ships with only tests and review for assurance; NFV aims to give mainstream developers proof-backed verdicts without formal-methods expertise. - How it does it: The core move is a staged, goal-blind discipline — library theories and preconditions are synthesized and frozen before the specification is visible, translations carry provenance tags and are audited against mechanical checks, so the LLM can search for proofs freely but cannot silently rewrite the program or the goal to make verification succeed. - The good: The framework emits a verdict with a machine-checked artifact on 57.3% of a 206-entry dataset at 92.2% precision, and the error analysis traces all 11 wrong verdicts to concrete causes (mostly preconditions the docstring never stated), which is unusually honest diagnostics. - The missing: Evaluation is restricted to tiny HumanEval-derived programs (median 7 LOC), and most precision is earned by abstention — the pipeline answers only 128 of 206 entries, so 43% of the workload gets no verdict and nothing is shown about real-world-scale code. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on agentic program verification, specification synthesis, or LLM+verifier architectures — the staged/frozen discipline and the failure taxonomy are directly reusable; skip it if you want evidence on industrial-scale code, where the paper offers none.

Problem & Motivation: Mainstream-language developers have no path to formal assurance: verification-aware languages (Dafny, F, Verus, Lean) require expertise and green-field co-development of code and proof, while per-language verifiers for mainstream languages (VCC, Frama-C, CBMC) are fragmented, slow to build, and demand environment modeling that historically took teams like SLAM/SDV decades. Meanwhile, a growing share of code is AI-generated ("vibe-coded"), raising demand for assurance exactly where formal methods are least available. The paper targets a developer in a mainstream language L who poses a property informally (a docstring assertion) and wants a push-button answer with a checkable proof artifact — explicitly framed as empirical accuracy* rather than soundness, since the intent formalization step cannot be sound by construction. Key Idea: The key insight is that LLMs are now good enough at writing Dafny proofs to serve as the front end and proof search engine for mature verifiers, provided the pipeline enforces goal-blindness and artifact integrity: environment theories and preconditions are synthesized before the specification is seen and then frozen, translated source lines carry `src:`/`synth:` provenance tags that are re-checked on every repair round, translation repair loops see only syntax/resolution errors (never verifier goals), and refutation is cast as proving a negated goal under a witness precondition — so every issued verdict is a machine-checked positive claim, and failure to verify becomes an abstention rather than a (unsound) bug report. Without this discipline, the paper shows the LLM+verifier baseline simply rewrites the code or strengthens preconditions until any program verifies (50% precision, with 57% of its "proofs" of rewritten code). Methodology: The framework defines five stages: (1) intent formalization — synthesize the environment theory EF (library contracts, e.g., a recursive definition of Python's `sum` from its docstring) and the formal specification SL from the informal assertion; (2) program translation PL→PF (here, Python→Dafny, purely neural); (3) specification translation SL→SF; (4) agentic proof search — an LLM proposes invariants, lemmas (e.g., `ShiftedSum`, `DivDistrib`), and intermediate asserts, with the verifier checking each, plus a repair loop over verifier failures; (5) proof mapping back to the source language (sketched, not evaluated). Two backend instantiations are studied: a Dafny deductive pipeline (verification and refutation arms, with refutation reusing stages 1–2 byte-identically, negating SF, and installing the LLM-proposed witness as a precondition, subject to reachability and goal-shape checks) and a CBMC bounded-model-checking pipeline (C translation with undefined-behavior checks, refutation only, witness traces rather than proofs). Budget parameters: 5 attempts × 10 repair rounds. The dataset is 206 (program, spec) pairs — 103 correct HumanEval references plus 103 independently-written mutants — curated from the nl2postcond benchmark (FSE 2024) with two filtering steps, stratified into library tiers L0–L3 by the Python surface that must be axiomatized. Key Results: With gpt-5.6-sol and the Dafny backend: verification proves 72/103 correct programs (70% recall, 93.5% precision); refutation refutes 47/103 mutants (46% recall, 88.7% precision); the combined refute-then-verify pipeline issues 118 correct verdicts on 128 issued, i.e., 57.3% recall at 92.2% precision, F1 0.71. CBMC refutes 65/103 mutants (63% recall) at 90% precision — the best bug-finding configuration. Baselines: LLM-as-a-judge answers all 206 entries at 72% precision (58 wrong, including rejecting 56 of 103 correct programs); an undisciplined LLM+Dafny loop "proves" 98% of everything at 50% precision due to artifact corruption; Nagini (symbolic Python verifier) proves 0–2% for want of environment formalization and proof automation. Weaker models degrade sharply: gpt-5-mini reaches 54%/33% with 60%/67% precision, claude-haiku-4.5 proves 11% and refutes 7%. All 11 wrong verdicts were individually traced: 6 spurious refutations from preconditions the docstring never stated (e.g., missing `|a| = |b|`, no-NaN, `p > 0`), 4 spurious proofs from stronger preconditions or incorrect type signatures (e.g., `seq<int>` excluding float inputs that kill the mutant), and 1 library formalization that transcribed the mutant's own bug. Tier analysis shows L3 (module imports) is the weakest (33% verify, 11% refute) and string handling drives L2a failures. Programs are small: median 7 LOC, max 29, 55% with loops. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the goal-blind staged discipline with provenance tags, frozen artifacts, and mechanical audits as the mechanism that separates NFV's 92% precision from the 50% precision of naive LLM+verifier, and (b) the empirical demonstration that frontier models cross the threshold where this architecture yields high-precision verdicts at all. The components — translation to an IVL, SMT-backed verification, LLM invariant synthesis, intent formalization — are each established; the contribution is the integration discipline and its measurement, plus the reframing of verification for mainstream code as an empirical-accuracy (precision/recall/abstention) problem rather than a soundness guarantee. The refutation-as-proved-negated-goal-under-witness construction is a clean but arguably standard trick. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-grade analysis is strong in one direction and thin in another: every wrong verdict is attributed to a cause (Table 5), a tier breakdown isolates where the approach struggles, and a model-capability ablation holds prompts, checks, backend, and budget fixed across four LLMs. There are no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no significance tests; the claude-sonnet-4.6 row was stopped before finishing (203/206 entries). A key confound: dataset curation used claude-sonnet-4.5 for the filtering step, and the flagship eval model (gpt-5.6-sol) is from the same lab's competitor set — no cross-contamination is discussed for the eval model itself, but the corpus was filtered with an LLM, a step the authors acknowledge is non-deterministic and provide identifiers to reconstruct. The dataset is derived from public prior work (nl2postcond, HumanEval, EvalPlus), with all 206 entries and postconditions listed in Appendix A. The authors state the dataset, pipeline, and table-generating scripts "will be released shortly as open source" — no URL is given, so reproducibility is promised, not demonstrated. A methodological concern: the "reference implementations are correct" ground truth is assumed from tests, and the paper itself finds one label wrong (HumanEval 116), suggesting label noise; also, the LLM-as-judge baseline is a weak strawman (no abstention, single prompt) rather than the strongest neural baseline. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system/pipeline run and measured, not deployed). - Practical: Yes — it needs only an LLM API plus the open-source Dafny and CBMC toolchains, all freely available. - Efficient: Not stated in cost terms; the budget of 5 attempts × 10 repair rounds of frontier-model calls per entry is likely substantial per verdict, and 62% of entries yield no verdict at all, so cost per useful verdict is high. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves a proxy — verifying tiny HumanEval programs against mostly-synthetic postconditions — not the stated problem of assuring real production or AI-generated code; within the proxy, precision is credible because verdicts carry machine-checked artifacts. - Scalable: Untested and arguably doubtful for the CBMC arm (bounded verification deteriorates with call depth, as the authors note); the Dafny arm's modularity is claimed to scale, but nothing over 29 LOC is evaluated, and the 43% abstention rate would likely worsen on larger code. Deliverable: a promised open-source release (dataset, pipeline, scripts) — not yet available at publication; no trained model, no CLI/tool product, and stage 5 (proof sketches in the developer's language) exists only as design. Strengths: - The goal-blind/frozen-artifact discipline is a real, transferable contribution: the LLM+verifier ablation (98% "proof" rate at 50% precision, 57% rewritten code) demonstrates quantitatively that artifact integrity checks — not better proof search — are what make the architecture trustworthy. - Refutation as a proved negated goal under a witness precondition is a well-chosen formulation: it converts the ambiguous "verifier failed, so maybe a bug" into a checkable positive claim, and the paper clearly articulates why proof-failure-as-bug-report is unsound. - The failure taxonomy (Table 5: every wrong verdict traced to a missing precondition, a stronger precondition, or a corrupted library formalization) is the kind of diagnostic honesty rarely seen, and it correctly localizes the dominant error source to intent formalization — which is also where the most headroom lies. - The library-tier stratification (L0–L3) usefully separates the two failure modes of environment modeling (recall loss) from intent formalization (precision loss), showing they have different causes. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are direct: the workflow is not sound formal verification (intent formalization cannot be, and they name the result "formal program reasoning"); they start at an already-synthesized specification and do not attest EF against tests; they stop at verdicts in Dafny rather than proof sketches over Python (deferred to a user study); the dataset contains only tiny programs ("no result here is evidence about scale"); the remaining 43% abstention is called out; and they note the majority of wrong verdicts stem from precondition synthesis and that component rankings may differ on other workloads. This is a credibility positive — the limitations section and the per-verdict error analysis confront weaknesses rather than minimize them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison against the strongest plausible neural baseline: an LLM agent that runs the Python program on LLM-proposed inputs (test-based refutation) would likely match CBMC's refutation rate cheaply, and the paper's own footnote ("we assume we cannot simply run P") concedes the assumption without testing where it breaks. - Ground truth is test-derived and partially LLM-curated; the paper finds one label wrong, so the reported 92% precision carries unquantified label noise in both directions. - The LLM-as-judge baseline is a single unprompted-commit strawman; a judge with self-consistency, test execution, or abstention would narrow the gap, and no neural baseline for verification (as opposed to refutation) is given. - Single run per configuration for the main tables (Table 4 explicitly "one run each") with stochastic LLM calls and no seed variance; the precision estimates carry unreported uncertainty. - All artifacts are verified in Dafny's semantics, but correctness claims are about Python; the translation-equivalence risk (e.g., Python's arbitrary-precision ints vs. Dafny's `int`, float vs. `real` — which the paper itself shows matters in HumanEval 20 and 133) is acknowledged anecdotally in the error analysis but never systematically measured, even though the dataset was chosen partly to avoid it. - The claimed language-agnosticism is asserted, not shown: everything is Python→Dafny or Python→C; no second source language is evaluated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic verification or code-assurance tools gains a concrete, well-diagnosed architecture — the goal-blind staged pipeline and its failure taxonomy are worth copying — but anyone expecting evidence that this works on real codebases will have to wait for the promised larger datasets and user studies.

Problem & Motivation: Formal verification has been economically prohibitive for sixty years: expert teams spend years on landmarks like CompCert, seL4, and CakeML, and requirements changes force re-verification. Generative AI has collapsed the cost of producing candidate proofs and designs but not the cost of trusting them — hallucinated proofs are indistinguishable from real ones to a non-expert reviewer. The paper addresses the resulting governance question (framed via 2026-era AI formalization artifacts: a 986k-line LLM-generated Lean economics corpus, an AI-produced zeta-function bound): at AI speed, who can afford machine verification, and how is its reliability governed? The intended audience is researchers and practitioners directing AI development at scale. Key Idea: The core move is making the proof kernel the sole arbiter of truth in the multi-agent workflow itself, not just a post-hoc checker: mathematical claims pass between agents only as kernel-checked artifacts, human review is eliminated for proofs entirely (replaced by kernel-checked "certificates" that imply the proved statement and let a human review a weaker-but-readable restatement), and everything the kernel cannot check is checked by structured opposition (adversarial refuter passes, independent witnessing, pre-registered instruments, append-only error ledgers). Human attention is treated as the scarcest resource and is confined to two ends of the pipeline: stating what is wanted and reading certificates. Methodology: The Salt method is stated as six required invariants (five artifacts per task — implementation, specification, kernel-checked proof, adversarial tests, certificate; no claim without a checker; append-only ledger with errors as first-class results; immutable statements; human-reserved irreversible acts; declared conditional hypotheses) plus six advisory articles (single orchestrator, priced executors, hard attempt budgets, explore-then-refute phases, scheduled daily councils, independent witness per landing). The reference configuration is five long-running agent seats (coordinator, mathematics, compiler, silicon, evidence) on Claude-family models under consumer subscriptions, sharing a repository and append-only message bus. The verification chain is deliberately non-uniform and disclosed link-by-link: Lean 4 kernel (with axiom audits, no native_decide) for spec-to-artifact emission; Yosys SAT equivalence checks for Verilog correspondence and netlist equivalence, because no general Verilog-to-Lean importer exists; a synthesis miter for link 3. Three checkers were built by three different agents and disagreed twice. Measurements (token meter, human-time rubric, silence-window autonomy) were pre-registered instruments with published extractors. Key design decisions — certificate-mediated review, statement immutability (R4), and human-reserved irreversible acts (R5) — are each motivated by a specific recorded failure in the ledger, which is the paper's justification style throughout. Key Results: The headline is an existence proof with measurements, not a benchmark comparison. In 37 days (2026-07-06 to 2026-08-11): 2,087 mathematics commits (zero silent days; mean 56.4/day, peak 178) producing 320,000+ Lean lines under the strict extractor (658,103 raw; 29.3% of mathlib by identical extractor) including kernel-checked proofs of Siegel–Walfisz, the large sieve, Bombieri–Vinogradov, Chen's theorem, VMVT, and the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums — stated at "surveyed strength" after the fleet's own priority survey retracted two claimed firsts; 1,379 systems commits over 7 days; and a RISC-V/Batcher–Banyan design (902 flip-flops in the 2026-08-10 submission, 288 kernel-emitted at the die, 31.9%) submitted to Tiny Tapeout shuttle run 32284710003. Metered 4.86-day window: 28.07M output tokens, 36,844 requests, 376 tokens per inserted line (explicitly not extrapolable). Human engagement floor: 37h 21m of 116h 40m wall clock. Autonomy: 43.0% of math commits inside ≥1h silence windows, longest 20h 56m carrying 26 commits and 12,310 lines. Zero incorrect proofs reached the record (structurally impossible under the kernel). There are no baselines — no comparison team, no unverified-AI condition, no cost-per-theorem derivable from subscription pricing. As the authors concede, the hardware is a submission, not a measured chip. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the Salt governance configuration for kernel-grounded multi-agent development) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the economic inversion of verification cost in the fast-generation regime, with instrumented evidence) and a modest NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the fleet protocol and verification chain). The genuinely novel elements are the certificate layer (kernel-checked implications making statement review tractable), the kernel-proof of the method's own reach (formal barrier results: no Maynard-class weight crosses the twin gate; least k with M_k > 2 is five), and the governed-accounting discipline. The formalization techniques, Lean 4, Yosys equivalence checking, and agent orchestration patterns are standard existing ideas applied to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually strong for measurement governance: the token meter and human-time rubric are pre-registered, extraction records are published, the error ledger is append-only with a same-day retraction standing in it, and both Lean repositories are public since 2026-08-16 (github.com/jyh/salt, github.com/jyh/saltworks) with one-command replay of every theorem. The paper scrupulously distinguishes measured from stated (e.g., it declines to state a die-level provenance ratio for the shipped revision because the structural join was not re-run). Weaknesses: no ablations on the method itself (which of the twelve articles actually matter is untested), no error bars on the headline counts, no independent audit of the human-time or silence-window instruments (the extractors are published but self-run), no generated-vs-authored split of the corpus, and Goodhart exposure — the metrics (commits, silence windows, engagement floors) are defined by the authors and self-scored. The economic claim rests on a 4.86-day window the authors themselves flag as the study's largest measurement gap. This is a non-peer-reviewed preprint, sole-authored, with the AI vendor's models as the subject's instrument. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a systems case study with measurements; the artifact chain exists as code and a submitted design). Practical: Yes — consumer AI subscriptions and open tools (Lean 4, Yosys, LibreLane, Tiny Tapeout); no special hardware required. Efficient: Verification adds no dollar-metered cost the records can derive, and the paper's thesis is that it saves human time; but the only measured window is 4.86 days and the method consumed ~37h/week of a formal-methods expert. Effective: The evidence shows trustworthy artifact production at measured pace, not fabrication (no chip) and no new mathematics (theorems are formalizations of known results); effectiveness against the real pain point — allowing non-experts to direct AI work — is claimed but the single subject is an expert. Scalable: Untested beyond one person; the authors explicitly disclaim generalizability. Delivers software artifacts (two public repositories, error ledger, instruments, protocol documents, shuttle design files) plus a reusable method specification; not a packaged library or tool. Strengths: - The certificate construct — kernel-checked implications from a proved statement to readable restatements, so a human can only ever read something weaker than what was proved — is a genuine and transferable contribution to human-in-the-loop verification at AI scale. - Measurement integrity that goes against self-interest: retracting a favorable verification-cost ratio when a re-run contradicted it, correcting the author's own time figure downward by 11h 50m via machine-proof of keystroke provenance, and stating the provenance census at both RTL and die scope with the scope sentence traveling with the number. - The reflexive result — kernel-proofs delimiting the method's own mathematical reach (the twin-gate barrier) — converts a failure into a formal object, which the authors correctly note is without precedent in a formalization campaign. - The non-uniform verification chain is disclosed as a finding: it maps precisely where the verified-hardware boundary sits for a small team in 2026. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive): no new headline mathematics; SAT-only links in the hardware chain; one expert subject with no generalization or labor-market claims; priority claims dated against a fast-moving field; no generated-vs-authored corpus split; the economics instrument covers only the final window; and no physical chip exists — delivery estimated 2027-05-12, with no result resting on measured silicon. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No control condition of any kind: the central economic claim (verification becomes essential at AI speed) is asserted from one self-directed run with no comparison against unverified AI development, single-agent development, or a non-expert director — the inversion is plausible but unmeasured as a comparative claim. - The method's twelve articles are presented as case-law-derived, but no ablation shows which invariants carry the result; a reader cannot tell whether R1–R6 or A1–A6 are load-bearing or ceremonial. - All instruments are authored, run, and interpreted by the sole beneficiary of the results; pre-registration mitigates but does not eliminate self-scoring, and the "zero incorrect proofs" figure is true by construction (the kernel definition), which should not be read as a quality signal about statements — the paper admits this but the abstract's framing invites the stronger reading. - The die-level provenance headline (31.9% kernel-emitted) is for the earlier submission, not the shipped revision, and 12.9% of die cells are kernel-emitted once tool-inserted cells are counted — the abstract-level framing risks overstatement. - The claims of formalizing Siegel–Walfisz, Chen's theorem, etc., rest on the authors' own priority survey; no external verification of the corpus's mathematical significance or correctness of statements (as opposed to proofs) is reported. - Physical correctness is entirely unvalidated: no silicon measurements exist, so the "to silicon" endpoint is a tapeout submission, not a working verified chip. Bottom Line: A rigorously self-audited and genuinely novel existence proof that kernel-grounded agent fleets can operate at research pace under one person's part-time direction — read it for its governance instruments and honest accounting, not for mathematics or hardware, and treat its economic thesis as a well-instrumented single case rather than a demonstrated general result.

Grounded Checklist Partial Credit for Agent Skill Trajectories

S Qin, L Yin, X Wang · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GCPC, a human-governed, LLM-instantiated pipeline that scores agent execution trajectories with verifier-grounded checklists, yielding partial credit that reveals progress hidden by binary PASS/FAIL outcomes. - Why it's important: Binary task-level evaluation compresses long-horizon agent executions into one bit, making it impossible to see whether procedural skills improve or degrade execution when the final outcome is unchanged — a gap that matters for anyone diagnosing or comparing agent skills. - How it does it: Humans define reusable item-contract, provenance, and validation rules once; an LLM instantiates a frozen, task-specific checklist from the instruction and official verifier; a judge labels each item Yes/No/Abstain from execution-log evidence alone; and a deterministic scripted step applies the official outcome afterward. - The good: On 4,455 deduplicated SkillsBench trajectories, GCPC's AUC against official outcomes (0.689) beats holistic judging by the same model (0.619), with a large ablation program, reliability checks (Krippendorff's α = 0.905–0.937), evidence-replacement falsification tests, and zero-adaptation transfer to Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench. - The missing: The headline paired result is statistically fragile — ΔAUC +0.056 with a 95% CI of [−0.002, 0.118] that includes zero — and the human-validity study covers only 96 trajectories from 12 tasks with a moderate correlation (ρ = 0.382). - Read it or not: Read it if you build agent-evaluation harnesses or benchmarks and need a defensible fine-grained scoring design; skip it if you want a validated reward signal or a statistically airtight improvement over checklist baselines — it is neither.
Why this rank
Scored with the Empirical profile. Completeness (80) is a standout — the limitations section confronts the SWE-bench failure mode and the Goodhart/reward-signal risk directly — and Rigor (70) reflects an unusually thorough ablation and falsification program. But Rigor is capped by the headline ΔAUC 95% CI crossing zero, the small human-validity subset, and the absence of any released code, prompts, or checklists, which is a real gap for a paper whose selling point is auditability; this drags Practical Impact down to 48. empirical Novelty 64 Rigor 70 Non-Obv 60 Completeness 80 Resilience 66 Impact 48
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM agents running long-horizon tool-use tasks (software engineering, CLI, web, scientific simulation) are evaluated almost exclusively by binary verifier outcomes, which erases partial progress and is especially blind to procedural skills — interventions designed to change how an agent works even when the final PASS/FAIL does not change. Practitioners who author or evaluate agent skills (the SkillsBench community) therefore cannot tell whether a skill helped when the binary outcome stays FAIL→FAIL. Fine-grained alternatives exist, but face a scalability–trustworthiness dilemma: human rubrics are costly to author per task, while LLM-generated checklists suffer from missing requirements, inconsistent granularity, and judges that reward plausible-looking logs over actual artifact state. The paper targets the retrospective setting where instructions, executable verifiers, and trajectory corpora already exist. Key Idea: Separate the human and the model: humans govern how checklist items are written, grounded, and validated (reusable rules), while an LLM instantiates which items per task — with every item required to carry a verbatim quote from the task instruction, an assigned verification route (assertion / generated / judge), mechanical provenance validation, and a frozen checklist that never sees any trajectory — plus an abstention option so missing log evidence is not scored as failure, and a deterministic post-hoc step that injects the official verifier outcome only after log-based scoring is complete. Methodology: Two stages. (1) Checklist synthesis, run once per task: a generator model (Claude Sonnet 4.6) applies fixed human rules to (instruction, verifier) to produce 4–15 grounded items per task; a deterministic validator rejects items whose quotes do not appear verbatim, whose assertion references do not resolve to real verifier tests, or which merely restate test code. Across 87 SkillsBench tasks, 713 items were produced (82.3% assertion / 14.9% generated / 2.8% judge routes), all passing the gates. (2) Trajectory scoring: a judge from a different model family (GPT-5.4-mini) labels each item Yes/No/Abstain using only displayed tool outputs and file contents in the execution log; agent claims do not count as evidence. A scripted step then applies the official outcome: on PASS, assertion-route items are overwritten to Yes (PASS propagation) and one virtual endpoint item is appended (Yes on PASS, No on FAIL), ensuring a failed trajectory cannot score perfectly. The GCPC score is |Yes| / |decided|, with Abstain excluded from the denominator; companion metrics are Perfect (no item judged No) and evidence coverage (|decided| / |items|). Critical design decisions: freezing checklists before any trajectory is seen (prevents trajectory-specific adaptation, well-justified), abstention instead of forced verdicts (explicitly stress-tested — recoding Abstain as No raises PASS–FAIL separation from 0.338 to 0.445 but only by treating missing evidence as failure, a well-argued choice), and cross-family generator/judge separation (reduces shared-model bias, though the effect is not isolated). The formal machinery is deliberately thin — a ratio of satisfied decidable items; the contribution is the auditable pipeline, not a new aggregation formula. Key Results: On a deduplicated n = 4,455 SkillsBench v1.1 population (87 tasks, 713 items, binary-outcome trajectories), plain GCPC achieves AUC 0.689 against official outcomes versus 0.619 for a holistic judge on identical trajectories (paired ΔAUC +0.056, task-clustered 95% CI [−0.002, 0.118], positive in 97.1% of 2,000 bootstrap draws — note the CI includes zero). Descriptive comparisons: Generic fixed checklist 0.613, TICK as published 0.598, adapted TICK 0.610. Against human judgments (96 trajectories, 12 tasks, 5 annotators), GCPC reaches 0.730 pairwise preference agreement and ρ = 0.382 with mean progress ratings, versus 0.613 and 0.218 for the holistic judge; annotators' holistic inter-rater reliability was only α = 0.466. The headline application: across 1,946 matched with/without-skill pairs, the 879 FAIL→FAIL pairs (invisible under pass@1) split into 20.9% improving by more than 0.10 GCPC and 18.7% regressing by the same margin. Sanity directions hold: FAIL→PASS pairs have median Δ = +0.227, PASS→FAIL median Δ = −0.222. Ablations decompose the official-outcome step (endpoint item +0.194, PASS propagation +0.034 in PASS–FAIL separation), show criterion judgments flip when decisive evidence is replaced (73.5% to No), and falsify the audit schema (coverage 99.4% real vs. 0.0% irrelevant definitions). Reliability: three-pass scoring gives Krippendorff's α = 0.905 (116 trajectories) and 0.937 on an independent 60-task set. Zero-adaptation transfer works at the synthesis level (Terminal-Bench 2.0: 585 items, 98.8% validity; SWE-bench Verified: 336 items, 94.9%), but on SWE-bench log-only GCPC ties 58 of 74 resolved/unresolved pairs with 42.1% of criteria abstaining — an honest boundary case. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (TICK is a 2024 published checklist method; the holistic judge is a standard comparator). This is a preprint and appears to be single-institution work with self-collected human annotations. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (as an evaluation pipeline) with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION character. The genuinely new elements are the verifier-linkage provenance contract, the frozen-before-trajectories discipline, item-level abstention, and the deterministic official-outcome postprocessing step — none of which, per the paper's own Table 1, co-occur in prior systems (TICK, CheckEval, AgentBoard, Odysseys, Mind2Web 2). The core ingredients — LLM-generated checklists, LLM-as-judge, partial credit, rubric grounding — are all established; the novelty is their disciplined composition for the retrospective skill-evaluation setting, and the paper explicitly frames its contribution as an auditable pipeline rather than a new metric. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for this area: checklist-construction arms isolate task-specificity, Panel B decomposes the two official-outcome operations, forced-verdict and evidence-replacement stress tests probe the abstention rule and evidence sensitivity, and a schema-falsification check validates the audit layer. Uncertainty is handled with 2,000 task-clustered bootstrap resamples at fixed seeds; test–retest noise floor (0.037), thresholds, and matching rules were preregistered as fixed before analysis. No code, data, or checklist artifacts are stated as publicly released — no URL appears in the text, which is a real gap for a pipeline paper whose value is its auditability. Methodological concerns: (1) the headline paired ΔAUC confidence interval includes zero, so the primary discrimination claim is suggestive, not established; (2) the human-validity subset is small (96 trajectories, 12 tasks; criterion-level α = 1.00 rests on 12 doubly-rated criteria); (3) the checklist synthesis was developed on SkillsBench tasks and much of the analysis is on the same benchmark, though the 20-unseen-task coverage check and zero-adaptation transfer partially mitigate Goodhart risk; (4) the judge and generator are specific commercial models (GPT-5.4-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6), and a judge swap (Claude Haiku 4.5) drops GCPC Spearman ρ to 0.615, showing meaningful judge dependence. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (an evaluation pipeline run on large existing trajectory corpora; no new agent system is built). Practical: Yes — it needs only API access to a generator and a judge model plus the target benchmark's trajectories and verifier; no special hardware. Efficient: Checklist synthesis is once per task (713 items across 87 tasks), and scoring is per-trajectory item judgment, so cost is a few LLM calls per trajectory — cheaper than human rubric authoring, though the paper itself notes it does not reduce model-inference cost. Effective: It demonstrably solves the diagnostic problem on SkillsBench (hidden skill effects exposed) and partially on Terminal-Bench (passing trajectory preferred in 40/69 decidable pairs, p < 10⁻⁹), but on SWE-bench log-only scoring is largely uninformative (58/74 ties) — effectiveness is bounded by what execution logs expose. Scalable: The synthesis rules transferred without modification across three benchmarks and to unseen tasks, which is the right kind of evidence; the paper does not test scaling to orders-of-magnitude more tasks, but nothing in the design suggests a bottleneck beyond API cost. Deliverable: a described pipeline and protocol; no software artifact, library, or released dataset is stated. Strengths: - The trustworthiness architecture is the real contribution: verbatim-quote provenance, mechanical validation gates (all 713 production items pass), frozen checklists, cross-family judge separation, and the clean separation of log evidence from verifier information are individually simple but jointly address documented failure modes of auto-generated rubrics (RubricBench-style gaps, judge positive bias) more concretely than prior checklist work. - The skill-effect analysis (1,946 matched pairs; 879 FAIL→FAIL pairs with 20.9% improving and 18.7% regressing by >0.10) delivers a concrete, quantified finding that binary evaluation structurally cannot produce — this is the paper's most useful empirical result. - The falsification program (evidence replacement flipping 73.5% of judgments, irrelevant-schema coverage collapsing to 0.0%, idle-agent floor scoring 0) is the kind of adversarial self-testing rarely seen in evaluation-methodology papers. - Honest negative reporting: the SWE-bench boundary case (58/74 tied pairs, 42.1% abstention) and the refusal to treat outcome-inclusive agreement as independent validity evidence show disciplined claim-evidence separation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that GCPC is limited by what the instruction, verifier, and log make observable (explicitly citing the 58/74 tied SWE-bench pairs); that criterion judgments vary across judge models; that GCPC with official outcome inherits verifier errors and therefore its PASS/FAIL agreement is not independent validity evidence; that their scalability claim covers authoring labor, not inference cost; and — notably in the Ethical Considerations — that GCPC's granularity makes it an attractive but unvalidated RL reward signal vulnerable to Goodhart-style gaming, so they release it as an audit instrument only. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations treatment and a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline paired comparison is not statistically significant at 95% (CI [−0.002, 0.118]); the paper presents the 97.1%-positive bootstrap share prominently but a strict reviewer will note the CI crosses zero, and no multiple-comparison correction discussion accompanies the many reported contrasts. - No released code, prompts, checklists, or annotations are mentioned — for a paper whose selling point is auditability, the absence of an auditable artifact is ironic and limits independent verification. - The generator and judge are single fixed commercial models; the judge-swap test exists but there is no generator-swap ablation, no open-weight-model condition, and no cost accounting of the pipeline. - The human-validity study is small and its blinding is imperfect (the authors note some logs revealed the harness used), and holistic inter-annotator agreement of α = 0.466 makes the human target itself noisy — the ρ = 0.382 ceiling may partly reflect annotation noise rather than scoring method quality. - Checklists were developed and largely validated on SkillsBench tasks; only a 20-task unseen-coverage check guards against overfitting the synthesis rules to that benchmark, and no baseline ablation isolates how much the verbatim-quote/provenance gates (vs. simply using a checklist) drive the AUC gain over TICK. - The paper does not evaluate GCPC against any process-level judging baseline (e.g., AgentProcessBench-style step scoring), so the claim that requirement-level items beat process-level judgment is positioned, not tested. Bottom Line: For anyone building or auditing agent-evaluation harnesses, this is worth reading for its unusually disciplined pipeline design and the quantified demonstration that skills change execution in ways pass@1 cannot see; for everyone else, the modest and statistically fragile gains over checklist baselines and the absence of released artifacts mean the ideas can be absorbed from this summary without a deeper read.

Jie Wu, Zhenru Zhang, Beichen Zhang, Xuwu Wang, Yuhui Su, Mouxiang Chen, Peng Wang, Zhihai Wang, Que Shen, Hao Zhou, An Yang, Fei Huang, Yujiu Yang, Dayiheng Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Terminal-Universe, a pipeline that converts recorded terminal-agent trajectories into reusable, executable environments (via deterministic replay of file operations plus an agentic completion stage) and re-queries them to synthesize 37.3k verifier-filtered training tasks, including cross-workspace and multi-round variants. - Why it's important: Terminal-agent post-training needs orders of magnitude more realistic, verifiable environments than manual curation or repository-history mining can supply, and the vast stock of existing agent trajectories is currently a frozen, low-value artifact rather than a renewable source of supervision. - How it does it: It exploits trajectory–environment duality: replaying read/write/edit operations in chronological order recovers each file's pre-agent state, and an LLM completion agent fills in missing files and dependencies without solving the task, after which four re-querying modes (Intent Recovery, Single-WS, Cross-WS breadth, Multi-Round depth) generate tasks paired with agent-authored pytest verifiers and pass-filtered teacher rollouts. - The good: The cleanest evidence is the ablation showing that re-solving recovered tasks (Intent Recovery, 52.1 avg on Terminal-Bench 2.1) beats SFT on the original trajectories (36.7) at identical data volume — a 15.4-point gap that directly validates the core thesis that environments dominate trajectories as a training resource. - The missing: All tasks, solutions, and verifiers are generated and judged by a single teacher model (Qwen3.7-Max), so verifier blind spots, task-coverage limits, and possible solution–verifier collusion are never independently audited, and no code or data artifact is reported as released. - Read it or not: Practitioners building terminal/coding-agent training corpora should read it for the reconstruction recipe and the environment-expansion ablations; researchers outside agentic data synthesis can skip it, since the gains are competent SFT distillation on top of a strong proprietary teacher.
