Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Aligned LLMs are vulnerable to two post-alignment attack families that share one root cause: safety-relevant information lives in a sparse neuron subset. Jailbreak attacks (PAIR, TAP, GCG, AutoDAN, Puzzler) exploit this from the input side; NeuroStrike exploits it from the parameter side by locating and pruning refusal-critical neurons — with no defense ASR reaching 0.81–0.91 on the tested models. Prompt-level defenses (perplexity filtering, SmoothLLM, GradSafe) are structurally useless against parameter-level attacks; model-level defenses (CAT, LED, SafeNeuron) either ignore neuron manipulation or, in SafeNeuron's case, use a static neuron identification that goes stale as weights change. Nobody trains the model so that safety cannot be localized in the first place. The affected parties are anyone deploying open-weight LLMs (Llama, Qwen, Falcon class) who must harden the model before release, since fine-tuning is the last stage under developer control. Key Idea: Force the model to refuse harmful queries even when its currently-identified safety neurons are ablated, then re-identify which neurons have become safety-critical and ablate those in turn — an iterative cat-and-mouse training loop that broadcasts safety representations until no small neuron subset is a single point of failure. Methodology: Three coupled stages applied during LoRA fine-tuning (rank 32, α=64, lr 10⁻⁵, 10 epochs on 2,000-sample tasks). Stage 1 (identification): every N=200 steps, per-layer logistic classifiers ŷ = σ(Wₗᵀhₗ(x)+bₗ) are fit on a probe set of 750 harmful + 750 benign BeaverTails queries; the top-ρ fraction (ρ=0.05) of classifier weights per layer defines the safety-critical set I_safety,l. Stage 2 (ablation-robust safety loss): L_safe = L_ref (cross-entropy toward a refusal template on normal forward passes over harmful queries) + L_ref^abl (same supervision on a forward pass with I_safety,l zeroed, so gradients must flow to remaining neurons) + L_cons (KL divergence between ablated and standard output distributions to prevent degenerate collapse). Stage 3 (conflict resolution): when ⟨g_user, g_safe⟩ < 0 (observed in a large fraction of steps; Figure 1 shows negative cosine similarity), a randomized projection removes the opposing component from one randomly chosen gradient (PCGrad-style, Eq. 8) before summing. The theory frames ASR upper bounds under five assumptions (linear separability, bounded perturbation, Lipschitz output head, bounded KL, independent per-neuron exploitability) and shows the defended bound is lower when η ≤ ((1−αₗ)^((1−ρₗ)sₗ) − (1−αₗ)^(sₗ))²/2. Critical design decisions: periodic refresh (validated by the static-identification ablation), zeroing rather than freezing neurons (the mechanism that creates the broadening pressure), and random rather than fixed projection order (justified informally as avoiding systematic deprioritization). Key Results: Tested on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Falcon3-7B-Instruct, fine-tuned on SST2, AGNews, CoLA, and GSM8K; ASR measured on StrongREJECT with Llama-Guard-3-8B as judge; results averaged over 10 random seeds on 2×H100. Under NeuroStrike, NeuronGuard cuts ASR from 0.89 to 0.04 (Llama/SST2), 0.83 to 0.02 (Qwen), 0.81 to 0.02 (Falcon), while SafeNeuron — the strongest baseline — stays at 0.21–0.28; prompt-level defenses leave ASR at 0.57–0.86. Against five jailbreak attacks, NeuronGuard achieves ASR 0.00–0.01 across all models/tasks, versus 0.02–0.10 for the best baselines. Utility stays within 0.01–0.03 of no-defense accuracy (e.g., Falcon/SST2 0.93 vs 0.94; Llama/GSM8K 0.62 vs 0.65). Adaptive attacks: iterative pruning yields ASR 0.09 (vs 0.83 no-defense), nonlinear MLP-based evasion 0.05 (vs 0.75). Multimodal: on Qwen2.5-VL-7B with T2I-formatted inputs, ASR drops to 0.01–0.02 (vs 0.96–0.99 no-defense). Ablations show every component matters (dropping gradient projection collapses utility ACC to 0.59; dropping ablation leaves NeuroStrike ASR at 0.71), and the method works with only 500 probe samples. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (SafeNeuron is 2026 work; NeuroStrike is NDSS 2026). Scale is standard 7–8B — no stress-scale testing. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD — the ablation-aware, iteratively refreshed redistribution of safety signals is genuinely new relative to SafeNeuron's static neuron freezing and CAT/LED's input- or layer-level interventions. The randomized gradient projection is a re-instantiation of known gradient-conflict techniques (PCGrad family) with randomized ordering, the KL regularizer is standard, and the linear-probe neuron identification borrows directly from mechanistic interpretability practice; the novelty lies in the specific composition and the dual-threat (jailbreak + neuron-level) framing, which is itself a useful problem articulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for this area: component-wise variants (Table 9), refresh interval N, ablation fraction ρ, probe-set size (500–2,500), loss weighting λ_safe, and a targeted static-vs-dynamic identification comparison that isolates the core mechanism. Results are averaged over 10 seeds, though no standard deviations or significance tests are reported. All models, datasets, and licenses are documented. No code, data, or model release is mentioned — a significant reproducibility gap for a defense paper whose value depends on practitioners reproducing the training procedure. Methodological concerns: ASR is judged by Llama-Guard-3-8B (an LLM judge, self-reported pipeline); the main-text tables show SST2 only, with other tasks relegated to the appendix; the theoretical result's Assumption 5 (independent per-neuron exploitability) is a strong and untestable modeling choice. The threat model is honest about assuming white-box parameter access for open-weight models. Deployability: EMPIRICAL profile (a training-time method evaluated by experiment). Practical: Runs on two 94GB H100 GPUs with LoRA, within reach of most fine-tuning pipelines. Efficient: Fine-tuning overhead is same-order as no-defense (829s vs 619s on SST2/Llama at N=200) and adds zero inference-time cost, a real advantage over test-time defenses like SmoothLLM. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated problem on StrongREJECT with an LLM judge and against adaptive white-box attacks, but ASR measurement via a single LLM judge is a proxy for actual harmful-capability removal. Scalable: Only tested at 7–8B parameters and four small fine-tuning tasks; behavior at 70B+ or with rank-heavy/full fine-tuning is untested, and the paper only claims, not demonstrates, broader scalability. The work delivers no software artifact — no library, CLI, or released weights are mentioned — stopping at paper form. Strengths: (1) The core insight — train against your own ablation to prevent safety from being localizable — is a genuinely new defensive mechanism with a clean mechanistic rationale, and the static-vs-dynamic ablation (ASR 0.29 vs 0.04) directly confirms the mechanism, not just the end-to-end system. (2) Evaluating against full-knowledge adaptive adversaries (iterative pruning, MLP-based evasion) that mirror the defense's own identification logic is the evaluation most defense papers omit, and the defense holds (ASR 0.09 and 0.05). (3) The dual-threat framing unifies jailbreak and neuron-level attacks under one root cause, which is a useful conceptual contribution even apart from the method. (4) Extensive sensitivity analysis (ρ, N, probe size, λ_safe, per-component ablation) demonstrates the method is not a fragile hyperparameter artifact. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly that NeuronGuard requires full control of the fine-tuning pipeline and therefore does not apply when a model is released without further fine-tuning, when the defender lacks compute for parameter updates, or when only black-box API access exists, and they note complementary inference-time defenses would be needed in those settings. They also acknowledge in the ethics section that neuron-level safety analyses and adaptive attack strategies could inform stronger future attacks. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The theoretical guarantee compares two ASR upper bounds whose terms (per-neuron exploit probability αₗ, true safety-neuron set Sₗ, ablation coverage ρₗ) are not empirically estimated in the paper — the theorem is illustrative rather than a checkable claim, and its Assumption 5 (independence) is likely false for correlated safety neurons. (2) No error bars despite 10 seeds. (3) No released code or artifacts. (4) ASR relies solely on Llama-Guard-3-8B judging; no human verification of a sample of judged unsafe outputs. (5) The probe data comes from BeaverTails and evaluation from StrongREJECT — a reasonable separation, but both are safety-benchmark distributions; generalization to genuinely novel harmful content classes is untested. (6) All main results are on classification-style or short-form fine-tuning tasks (SST2, AGNews, CoLA, GSM8K at 2,000 samples); whether distributing safety signals degrades open-ended generation quality (not measured by these ACC metrics) is not examined. (7) The claim that jailbreak defenses are ineffective against neuron attacks is expected by construction for prompt-level baselines, slightly inflating the apparent comparative advantage. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing safety-critical fine-tuning of open-weight LLMs gains real, well-evidenced technique here — this is the strongest published answer so far to neuron-level attacks like NeuroStrike — but the absence of released code, thin theory, and 7–8B-only evaluation mean the near-zero-ASR numbers should be treated as promising rather than settled.

aiXamine: Unified Black-Box Evaluation of Cross-Dimensional Trade-offs in LLM Safety, Security, and Privacy

F Deniz, Y Boshmaf, D Popovic, I Khalil · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces aiXamine, a unified black-box evaluation platform that measures LLM safety, security, and privacy jointly through 46 tests across 9 services, and reports the largest cross-dimensional trustworthiness study to date over 121 models and 5,000+ test runs. - Why it's important: Providers and regulators must assess trustworthiness as an interdependent risk profile (e.g., EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF), but existing frameworks evaluate single axes and cannot detect trade-offs where improving one property degrades another. - How it does it: It orchestrates standardized black-box test suites under uniform inference conditions, scores responses with rule-based judges, moderation APIs, and multi-judge LLM ensembles on a common [0,1] scale, and aggregates hierarchically to expose cross-service correlations and trade-offs. - The good: The cross-service correlation analysis over the full dataset yields quantified, CI-backed findings: Over Refusal correlates negatively with Jailbreak Robustness (r=-0.39, 95% CI [-0.54,-0.20]) and Safety Alignment (r=-0.22), while privacy is near-orthogonal to other services (mean |r|=0.13) — plus a concrete robustness collapse from 56.9 to 2.6 caused by R1-style off-policy distillation on identical base architectures. - The missing: The distillation collapse mechanism (entropy collapse from omitted on-policy KL correction) is formalized but never directly measured — no entropy or calibration metrics are reported, only post-hoc cosine similarity of hidden states — and each prompt is run once with a single judge (validated only by correlation with one alternate judge), so per-model scores carry no run-to-run error bars. - Read it or not: Read it if you build, select, or regulate LLMs and need evidence that safety-utility-privacy trade-offs are real and rank-altering; skip the framework details if you only need another leaderboard, since the individual tests are all pre-existing benchmarks.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile (deployed public evaluation platform with 121 models and 221,882 samples). Practical Impact (80) is the dominant weighted dimension — a real, publicly deployed artifact with stakeholder re-ranking, Dirichlet robustness analysis, and quantified trade-offs (safety-tax r=-0.39, distillation robustness collapse 56.9→2.6) that single-axis benchmarks miss. Novelty (60) is capped because all 46 tests are pre-existing benchmarks and the framework is an integration/normalization layer; Non-Obviousness (62) is real but confounded. Rigor (62) loses materially to the single-run-per-prompt design, the GPT-oss-120B judge-judging-itself conflict, unacknowledged use of mini/haiku API variants for flagship comparisons, and preprint status; the central entropy-collapse mechanism is asserted but never measured. Problem & Motivation: Deployers of LLMs in high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance, autonomous systems) need trustworthy models, but existing evaluation frameworks fragment the risk landscape: HELM and TrustLLM omit privacy or code security, DecodingTrust and TrustEval offer only partial coverage, and most assume white-box access, excluding proprietary systems. Because no framework jointly measures jailbreak resistance, privacy leakage, code safety, and over-refusal under one reproducible protocol, cross-dimensional failure patterns — a model scoring 99.3 on safety alignment while refusing one in three benign queries, or gaining capability while losing 21 privacy points — are invisible to single-axis leaderboards. The gap is both scientific (trustworthiness dimensions may interact) and practical (regulators demand transparent, deployment-context-aware assurance). Key Idea: Treat safety, security, and privacy as interdependent dimensions of a single SSP (Safety-Security-Privacy) hierarchy and measure them under identical black-box conditions so cross-service correlations become meaningful; the analytical trick is that normalizing all 46 heterogeneous tests onto a common [0,1] scale turns a benchmark suite into a dataset over which trade-off structure (correlations, quadrants, rank stability) can be estimated. The second key idea is using same-base-architecture model pairs (distilled variants of Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B) as a controlled experiment to isolate the effect of alignment/distillation strategy on robustness. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Test dispatch: 46 tests spanning 9 services (Hallucination, Code Security, Safety Alignment, Over Refusal, Adversarial Robustness, Jailbreak Robustness, OOD Robustness, Model & Data Privacy, Fairness & Bias) are sent to each model at temperature 0, max 2,048 tokens, one run per prompt, via OpenRouter for proprietary models and vLLM on local H200 nodes for open weights — content moderation filters left enabled to evaluate systems as deployed. (2) Scoring: deterministic rules where possible; otherwise benchmark-specific judges (Llama Guard 1–4, WildGuard, OpenAI Moderation, Perspective API, Vectara) or GPT-oss-120B as general judge; cross-validated with Gemma3-27B (Pearson r=0.985 across service-level scores). Non-standard metrics are normalized: Cramér's V (reported as 1−V) for fairness, rescaled Pearson r for privacy judgment agreement. (3) Aggregation: arithmetic means at test, category, subcategory, and service levels; overall score is the uniform-weight mean of nine services, with six stakeholder profiles and 10,000 Dirichlet-sampled weight vectors for rank-stability analysis. (4) Analysis: cross-service Pearson correlations with 95% CIs over 5,000+ examination results, quadrant plots against Over Refusal, intra-family scale curves, generational deltas, per-category variance/generalization-gap statistics over 215 categories, and a representational diagnostic extracting last-layer hidden states on 50 AdvGLUE-SST2 prompts to compute per-sample cosine similarity between base and distilled models. Appendix D formalizes off-policy distillation (Eq. 2) versus on-policy KL correction (Eq. 1), arguing vocabulary mismatch in R1-style pipelines forces pure teacher-trajectory imitation, collapsing output entropy and sharpening decision boundaries. Critical design decisions: single-query deterministic evaluation (justified as realistic but eliminates variance estimates), black-box-only access (justified by proprietary-model coverage), and GPT-oss-120B as both a leaderboard entrant and the primary judge (a conflict not addressed). Key Results: GPT-5 leads the overall leaderboard at 81.8, followed by Gemini 3 (80.6) and Gemma4-31B/Claude-4.5 (both 80.0); the top-20 spread is 8.4 points but within-model service variance is far larger (e.g., GPT-4o: 91.1 privacy vs 51.4 jailbreak robustness). Headline findings: (1) Over Refusal vs Jailbreak Robustness r=-0.39 [-0.54,-0.20] and vs Safety Alignment r=-0.22 [-0.40,-0.02] — the "safety tax"; privacy correlates weakly with everything (mean |r|=0.13). (2) R1 distillation collapses adversarial robustness from 56.9 (Llama3.1-8B base) to 2.6 on the same architecture, while IDA distillation preserves it; hidden-state cosine similarity confirms representational divergence (R1: 0.094±0.161 Llama, 0.069±0.206 Qwen; IDA: 0.834±0.013, 0.532±0.048; Cohen's d=6.5 and 3.1). (3) Privacy regressed in 5 of 7 family generation transitions, worst from GPT-4o to GPT-5 (−21.73 despite +3.84 overall); Grok 3→4 is the counterexample (+1.04 privacy). (4) Scale helps only to ~4B parameters (Qwen3.5: 59.0 at 0.8B → 73.4 at 4B, then +3 points to 27B); alignment strategy dominates above that. (5) Safety generalization is fragmented: Jailbreak Robustness shows 17.8 average within-test SD and a 47.0-point best-to-worst category gap, versus 4.4/13.6 for OOD Robustness. (6) Rankings are perspective-dependent: mean pairwise Kendall's τ=0.455 across six stakeholder profiles, 27% of pairwise orderings reverse, GPT-4o swings 13 positions; Dirichlet analysis (10,000 weight vectors) confirms tier stability (τ=0.775) but within-tier sensitivity. Baselines are other frameworks' coverage maps (Table 4), not score comparisons. Scale: 121 models, 0.8B–120B parameters, 221,882 total samples, 2,000+ GPU hours on four H200 nodes. Surprising: Qwen3.5 models achieve near-perfect jailbreak robustness (99.5) exceeding all API models while scoring worst in privacy (48.4). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the cross-dimensional correlation and rank-sensitivity analyses enabled by unified scoring — the safety-tax quantification, privacy orthogonality, and generation-over- generation privacy regressions are new measurements — and (b) the first robustness-focused characterization of distillation-induced robustness collapse on matched base architectures. The 46 tests themselves are entirely pre-existing public benchmarks (SimpleQA, TruthfulQA, AdvGLUE, OR-Bench, Enron, BBQ, etc.); the framework is a competent integration and normalization layer, not a new testing methodology, and the entropy-collapse mechanism is a theoretical argument built on known results (Agarwal et al. on-policy distillation; Goodfellow adversarial brittleness) rather than a new proof. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on breadth and transparency: all datasets, configurations, scoring scripts, and per-model reports are public (aixamine.qcri.org); judge reliability is cross-validated (r=0.985 across two judges); correlation findings carry 95% CIs; the Dirichlet re-ranking analysis (10,000 samples) is a genuine robustness check. Ablations of a sort exist — the same-base-architecture distillation pairs and intra-family scale curves are controlled comparisons. Methodological concerns: (1) each prompt runs once at temperature 0, so no per-score variance or seed replication is reported; (2) the general-purpose judge (GPT-oss-120B) is itself a leaderboard entrant, an unaddressed conflict of interest, and LLM-judged scores for instruction-following edge cases are acknowledged as fallible; (3) several "flagship" comparisons actually use smaller API variants via OpenRouter (openai/gpt-5-mini, anthropic/claude-3.5-haiku), which the paper does not foreground; (4) the R1-vs-IDA comparison is observational — the two pipelines differ in data and objectives beyond the on-policy correction, so attribution to KL omission alone is an inference; (5) the entropy-collapse mechanism is never measured directly (no entropy, calibration, or boundary-sharpness metrics); (6) correlation structure estimated across a heterogeneous, non-random model population can reflect ecosystem-level training trends rather than causal dimension relationships. This is a preprint (arXiv, dated August 2026 in the text), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built evaluation platform, deployed and publicly available, plus an EMPIRICAL study run through it). Practical: Yes — runs on commodity API access for proprietary models and open-weight models on vLLM; the full study used four H200 nodes, and single-model re-evaluation is feasible for any lab with API credentials. Efficient: A complete per-model run takes 1–2 days wall-clock; the entire 121-model, 5,000-run campaign consumed 2,000+ GPU hours plus API costs — expensive for a full re-run but modular per service. Effective: The evidence shows it detects cross-dimensional trade-offs and rank instability that single-axis benchmarks demonstrably miss; whether the absolute scores are accurate depends on judge quality, which is validated only by inter-judge correlation, not against human ground truth. Scalable: The pipeline already spans 121 models and 221,882 samples; the main scaling risk is judge cost and judge-drift, not throughput, and the paper does not test scale beyond its own corpus. Delivers a real software artifact: a public portal, evaluation reports, datasets, and scoring scripts; also reusable analysis techniques (stakeholder-profile re-ranking, Dirichlet weight sampling, hidden-state divergence diagnostic). Strengths: (1) The matched-base-architecture distillation comparison is the cleanest causal-style evidence in the paper — R1-distilled vs IDA-distilled vs base on identical Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B backbones, with a representational (cosine similarity, Cohen's d=6.5) corroboration of the behavioral collapse — elevating it above typical benchmark-correlation studies. (2) The stakeholder-profile and Dirichlet re-ranking analyses quantify, rather than merely assert, that aggregate leaderboards are perspective-dependent (Kendall's τ=0.455 across profiles, 27% ordering reversals, verified stable tiers over 10,000 random weightings). (3) The privacy-orthogonality finding with per-generation deltas (GPT-4o→GPT-5: −21.73) is a concrete, actionable empirical result for practitioners who assume capability progress implies privacy progress. (4) Evaluating systems as deployed (filters on, black-box, uniform inference parameters) makes the comparison ecologically valid for the proprietary/open-weight split that actual buyers face. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) English-only tests, so cross-lingual safety degradation is invisible; (2) black-box-only access, excluding gradient-based attacks and mechanistic interpretability (with the hidden-state diagnostic as a partial exception); (3) judge reliability — LLM judges struggle with implicit harm and cultural nuance, and the binary safe/unsafe framing compresses the harm spectrum. They confront these directly and do not minimize them, which is a credibility positive; they do not, however, acknowledge the single-run-per-prompt design, the judge-is-contestant conflict, or the use of mini/haiku API variants for flagship model comparisons. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The central mechanistic claim — entropy collapse from omitted on-policy KL correction — is formalized but never measured; no entropy, calibration, or boundary-margin statistics appear, only cosine similarity, which shows representational divergence but not the asserted cause. (2) R1 vs IDA pipelines differ in data mixture, training stages, and objectives, so attributing the 56.9→2.6 collapse to KL omission specifically is extrapolation; a minimal ablation (e.g., off-policy + KL with adapter-based vocabulary mapping) is absent. (3) GPT-oss-120B judging tests that include GPT-oss-120B as a candidate creates a self-scoring conflict, and no human-annotation validation of judge accuracy on a sample is reported. (4) Cross-service correlations are computed over a convenience sample of models whose training choices are confounded with ecosystem and era — the "safety tax" correlation is not evidence that any provider faces an unavoidable trade-off. (5) One-run, temperature-0 scoring means borderline jailbreak/refusal outcomes (where stochasticity matters most, e.g., PAIR's adaptive attacks) carry unquantified noise; PAIR cell sizes appear very small (values like 4.00/11.11 suggest single-digit query counts). (6) Generational privacy comparisons rely on possibly different deployment variants (mini vs full) and undated API snapshots, weakening the GPT-4o→GPT-5 headline claim. (7) Several frontier model names (Gemini 3, Gemma4, Qwen3.5, GPT-5) predate or postdate verifiable releases as of the paper's timeline, and future-dated arXiv numbering limits verifiability. Bottom Line: A practitioner choosing or auditing models gains real, quantified insight — especially the safety-tax correlation, privacy orthogonality, and distillation robustness collapse — that no existing single-axis benchmark provides, but the framework's scores should be treated as judge-mediated, single-run estimates rather than ground truth, and the entropy-collapse mechanism awaits direct experimental confirmation.

BC-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Engineering in a Domain-Specific Language for ERP

H Sun, KM Hansen · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BC-Bench, a benchmark of 101 manually curated bug-fixing and test-generation tasks in AL (the DSL for Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central), with an evaluation harness that runs real agent harnesses (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code) reproducibly in GitHub Actions. - Why it's important: Agentic coding is evaluated almost exclusively on general-purpose languages; ERP DSLs like AL power thousands of partner apps, and the authors show that model gains on general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., GPT-5.3-codex on SWE-Bench Pro) do not reliably transfer to AL. - How it does it: The authors adapt the SWE-Bench pipeline (bug-PR pair extraction, gold-patch verification via test execution) to AL's constraints — release-anchored Docker environments via BcContainerHelper, multi-project mapping in a monorepo, and multimodal problem statements with screenshots. - The good: The evaluation is statistically careful — five runs per task with bootstrap 95% CIs and exact permutation tests — and yields a defensible finding that model choice matters more than harness choice in Bug Fixing, plus a useful manual failure-mode taxonomy (47.7% localization errors, 44.3% wrong solutions, only 5.7% build failures). - The missing: All 101 tasks come from just two Microsoft-owned repositories, are single-bug fixes only, and the dataset and results are authored by the vendor of the evaluated agent harnesses, so external validity and contamination over time remain open. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or evaluating coding agents for low-resource/DSL ecosystems — the dataset-construction recipe and failure analysis transfer beyond AL — but general agent-benchmark researchers can skim it, as the headline methods are adapted from SWE-Bench.

Problem & Motivation: Teams developing and extending Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central — Microsoft engineers and an ecosystem of roughly 8.4K partner-published apps — write business logic in AL, a Pascal-inspired, statically typed DSL whose tests require a live Business Central environment. Coding-agent benchmarks concentrate on Python and other high-resource languages (GitHub search: ~2.4M Python repos vs. ~338 MIT-licensed AL repos), so agent quality in AL is unmeasured, and prior DSL work (Verilog, VHDL, ABAP) shows general-language results transfer poorly. The gap: no repository-level, real-world-task benchmark exists for AL; the only prior effort (CentralGauge) targets function-level language proficiency akin to HumanEval/MBPP. Key Idea: The core move is adapting SWE-Bench's bug-PR-pair methodology to a DSL with scarce public data and heavyweight environment requirements — anchoring each task to stable Business Central minor releases (e.g., BC 26.4) instead of ephemeral CI builds, aligning base commits for compatibility, and verifying every task so fail-before/fix-pass tests hold. This is a competent adaptation of a known methodology rather than a new algorithmic insight; the paper is upfront that its contribution is the benchmark, dataset, and harness, not a new technique. Methodology: The dataset pipeline has five stages: (1) manual selection of merged PRs from two production repos (internal NAV on Azure DevOps, public BCApps); (2) attribute filtering to single-bug PRs that add at least one test; (3) manual review excluding under-specified problem statements and tests tightly coupled to the fix (e.g., exact error-string matching); (4) SWE-Bench-style bug-PR extraction with AL-specific modifications (multi-project mapping, release anchoring, base-commit alignment) plus screenshot support from SWE-Bench Multimodal; (5) automated execution filtering (tests fail before gold patch, pass after), re-run weekly. Two categories use the same 101 tasks: Bug Fixing (agent produces a patch from problem statement + code snapshot) and Test Generation (gold patch applied; agent writes a test that fails pre-fix and passes post-fix). Evaluation runs GitHub Copilot and Claude Code on a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner with BcContainerHelper-provisioned Docker containers; agents see the codebase as plain text by default (no compiler), with optional AL MCP tooling in selected experiments. Metrics: mean resolution rate over five independent runs with BCa-bootstrap 95% CIs, pass^5 (fraction of tasks solved in all five runs), and wall-clock duration; configuration comparisons use two-sided exact sign-flip permutation tests. A semantic-versioning strategy tracks dataset/harness/environment changes. Notable design decisions: no pass@k (deliberately, to reward reliability over retry luck — well-justified for the stated use case); 30–60 minute wall-clock timeout rather than turn/cost limits (reasonable but complicates cost comparisons); workflow failures re-run rather than counted as agent failures (defensible but adds a tuning knob). Key Results: Bug Fixing: claude-opus-4.6 reaches 68.5% mean resolution (95% CI 65.7–71.3%, pass^5 49.5%, 284s) with Claude Code and 65.1% (62.6–67.6%, pass^5 50.5%) with GitHub Copilot on version 0.2.0; GPT-4.1 manages only 16.6% (pass^5 5.0%). Matched permutation tests show harness differences are not significant (Copilot 58.4% vs. Claude Code 57.4%, p=0.728; 68.5% vs. 65.1%, p=0.075) while model differences are (65.1% vs. 59.8%, p=0.026; 60.8% vs. 53.7%, p=0.019). Test Generation tops out at 60.4% (claude-opus-4.6, Copilot). Cross-benchmark: GPT-5.3-codex shows no significant advantage over GPT-5.2-codex on AL Test Generation (45.3% vs. 44.0%, p=0.672) despite SWE-Bench Pro gains — the paper's headline transfer-failure result. Difficulty analysis: multi-file gold patches drop resolution by >20 points (65–70% for 1 file vs. 42–43% for 2+); >25-point drops above 10 LoC changed (though the 26+ LoC bucket rebounds to ~49–50%). Failure modes for the strongest configuration (176 of 505 trials failed): Wrong Solution 44.3%, Incorrect File 29.5%, Incorrect Region 18.2%, Build Failure 5.7%, Timeout 2.3%; manual labeling of 22 unique Wrong Solution tasks splits into Incomplete Fix (10), Incorrect Business Logic (10), Wrong AL/API Usage (2). Counter-intuitive: tasks with 6+ images in the problem statement resolve best (70.8–76.8%), but image count correlates with problem-statement length, suggesting text richness rather than visual content drives the effect. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the first repository-level agent benchmark for the AL/ERP DSL ecosystem, the release-anchored environment provisioning scheme for a tooling-heavy DSL, and the empirical demonstration that general-benchmark model improvements do not transfer to AL. The methodology itself (SWE-Bench adaptation, pass^k from tau-bench, multimodal support from SWE-Bench Multimodal, real-harness evaluation from Terminal-Bench) is a standard combination of existing ideas applied to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above-average rigor for a benchmark paper: five independent runs per configuration, bootstrap CIs, permutation tests for matched comparisons, explicit cross-version caveats, a detailed versioned change log (Appendix B), weekly re-validation of task validity, and a manual failure-mode audit with per-task labels (Appendix C). Ablations are present as task-characteristic breakdowns (files changed, LoC, functional area, image count), though some cells have very few tasks (e.g., Manufacturing n=5, where GPT-5.2 hits 88.0% — correctly flagged as diagnostic only). Code and dataset are publicly released at github.com/microsoft/BC-Bench; the NAV repository and its tasks remain internal, so roughly half the labeled failure-analysis tasks are not externally inspectable. Concerns: (1) the benchmark is built and evaluated entirely by Microsoft, which also produces Copilot and the AL tooling — a vendor-affiliation conflict the paper does not discuss; (2) evaluation on the authors' own curated dataset with no external replication; (3) harness and model versions changed across benchmark versions, so the headline table mixes non-comparable rows (the authors acknowledge this); (4) contamination risk from public release of static tasks is acknowledged but unmitigated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and measurement study, not a new method or deployed system). - Practical: Runs on standardized GitHub Actions self-hosted runners with Docker; any organization with a Business Central container license setup can reproduce the pipeline. - Efficient: Evaluation is expensive — 5 runs × 101 tasks per configuration at 100–470s per trial (roughly 14–66 GPU-free but wall-clock-heavy hours per configuration), and the paper does not report token costs. - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark discriminates between models and harnesses and measures something real (test-verified fixes), but it measures single-bug fixes only, a proxy for actual ERP engineering work like feature development and upgrades. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 101 tasks; the authors themselves flag dataset evolution and dynamic generation as future work, so durability at 10× scale or over time is claimed, not demonstrated. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: an open-source benchmark, dataset, and GitHub Actions evaluation harness; no trained model or reusable algorithmic technique. Strengths: - Solving the DSL environment problem is the real contribution: release anchoring plus base-commit alignment makes long-term reproducible evaluation feasible for a language where tests need a live ERP instance, and this recipe generalizes to other tooling-heavy DSLs. - The statistical treatment (five runs, bootstrap CIs, permutation tests, pass^5 instead of pass@k) is unusually careful and directly supports the paper's two defensible empirical claims: model > harness, and no transfer of GPT-5.3-codex gains from SWE-Bench Pro. - The failure-mode analysis is actionable rather than decorative: the finding that 47.7% of failures are localization errors and only 5.7% are build failures yields a concrete, testable hypothesis (LSP/MCP tooling should help) that the benchmark is positioned to evaluate. - Honest calibration throughout — the authors repeatedly mark cross-version comparisons as non-definitive and small functional-area buckets as diagnostic, and they document prompt/harness fixes made during dataset development. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly acknowledge: (1) limited dataset diversity — 101 tasks from two Microsoft-owned repositories, mostly BaseApp, missing industry-specific partner apps and all non-bug-fix task types (features, upgrades, localization, performance); (2) the default plain-text agent environment lacks AL tooling (compiler, LSP) that human engineers have in VS Code; (3) test-passing does not guarantee fix correctness or quality; (4) contamination risk for a static public dataset; (5) the harness-vs-model conclusion rests on only four matched comparisons. This is a candid limitations section — the authors confront weaknesses rather than minimize them, which raises confidence in the rest of the analysis. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Vendor conflict of interest: Microsoft authors evaluate Microsoft's Copilot harness against a competitor's (Claude Code) on Microsoft's own benchmark built from Microsoft's own repositories; the paper never addresses this affiliation, and the private NAV tasks mean the community cannot audit a large fraction of the failure analysis. - No agentic baselines beyond two harnesses: no open harness (e.g., SWE-agent, OpenHands) and no Codex CLI, so the "model matters more than harness" conclusion covers only two closed-source, vendor-controlled harnesses with unpublishable internal configurations. - The image/multimodal contribution is under-exercised: 67 of 101 tasks contain images, but the analysis confounds image presence with problem-statement length and never tests whether agents actually use the images (the authors defer this to future work), so the multimodal claim is essentially unevaluated. - The rebound in the 26+ LoC bucket (49.2–50.0% vs. 38.3–49.6% for 11–25 LoC) undermines the clean "complexity predicts difficulty" narrative and goes unexplained. - No cost/token accounting despite reporting duration, so the accuracy-latency trade-off (claude-opus-4.6 at 284s vs. GPT-5.3-codex at 106s) cannot be turned into a cost-quality frontier. - The AL MCP tooling experiment is mentioned as a capability of the benchmark but no results from it are reported, leaving the paper's own motivating hypothesis (tooling access improves DSL agent performance) untested. Bottom Line: A rigorous, honestly reported benchmark that fills a real hole — repository-level agent evaluation for ERP DSLs — and delivers the transfer-failure finding that justifies domain-specific evaluation; practitioners in the Business Central or broader DSL ecosystem should adopt it, while general agent-benchmark researchers will find the methodology derivative of SWE-Bench even if the empirical findings are not.

Synthetic Sandbox for Training ML Engineering Agents

Y Zhou, L Zhang, Y Wu, J Liu, X Fan, Z Zhao, H Yan · openreview.net · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SANDMLE, a multi-agent pipeline that synthesizes verifiable MLE training environments with micro-scale datasets (50–200 samples), and shows these sandboxes make trajectory-wise on-policy GRPO training of MLE agents practical for the first time. - Why it's important: Real MLE benchmark tasks require full train-and-evaluate ML pipeline runs at every RL rollout step (~196s per execution on MLE-bench seeds), which has forced prior work onto SFT or off-policy approximations; a >13× execution speedup unlocks true on-policy RL where exploration and generalization benefits actually apply. - How it does it: A four-agent pipeline (Data Strategist, MLE Developer, MLOps Engineer, Technical Writer) extracts a task's "structural DNA," re-domains and mutates it adversarially, procedurally generates synthetic micro-datasets with deterministic hidden labeling rules, and locks in monotonic milestone thresholds that instantiate a dense, tiered reward for GRPO. - The good: The strongest evidence is the combination of a measured 196.17s → 14.31s (13.7×) execution-latency reduction and consistent Any Medal gains over Seed-SFT on MLE-bench-lite across three model scales (Qwen3-8B/14B/30B: 22.7/22.7/27.3 vs. 13.6/18.2/22.7 for Seed-SFT), with cross-scaffold transfer to AIDE, AIRA, and MLE-Agent. - The missing: The central assumption—that solving 150-sample procedurally generated datasets transfers to million-sample real-world Kaggle competitions—is asserted via end-to-end benchmark gains but never directly ablated (e.g., no comparison against RL on downsampled real tasks, and no analysis of whether synthetic-task skills correlate with real-task successes). - Read it or not: Read it if you are working on RL post-training for agentic ML/coding systems or synthetic environment generation; skip it if you want rigorous analysis of why micro-scale training transfers or a broad comparison against concurrent RL-for-MLE systems.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building LLM agents for machine learning engineering (Kaggle-style tasks: data preprocessing, model training, metric evaluation) face a fundamental training bottleneck. In software engineering, trajectory-wise on-policy RL is feasible because unit tests execute in seconds; in MLE, a single code execution trains and evaluates an ML model on datasets averaging ~4.09 million samples per MLE-bench task, averaging ~200 seconds per execution. Since on-policy GRPO invokes the environment at every step of every rollout for every sample in a group (cost scaling as O(N·Tmax·c_exec) per training example), full on-policy RL becomes computationally infeasible, and prior efforts retreat to SFT on expert trajectories or asynchronous/off-policy step-wise RL—sacrificing the exploration and generalization benefits of on-policy training. The paper's diagnostic insight is that MLE execution latency is overwhelmingly driven by dataset size, not problem complexity. Key Idea: The core trick is decoupling task complexity from data scale: preserve a task's "structural DNA" (modality, feature distributions, label cardinality, noise structure, hidden rule l = f(z) + ε) while rebuilding the environment from scratch around a 50–200-sample synthetic dataset, so the ML pipeline still requires genuine data preprocessing, training, and evaluation (preserving structural difficulty and gradient-relevant reasoning) but executes in ~14 seconds instead of ~200. Milestone thresholds computed empirically by baseline methods on the synthetic data convert this into a dense, verifiable reward ladder. Methodology: The framework has two stages. (1) Synthetic environment generation via four specialized agents: a Data Strategist extracts a modality/schema-level Task DNA from a seed task, re-attributes it to a new domain (e.g., animal classification → road damage detection), applies adversarial noise mutations (e.g., motion blur), and compiles a concrete specification with a hidden labeling rule and 50–200-sample constraint; an MLE Developer writes a self-contained Python script generating the dataset, implementing the hidden rule, training baseline methods to lock in milestone thresholds, and emitting a dummy submission; an MLOps Engineer writes a deterministic evaluator with hard-coded metric and thresholds; a Technical Writer synthesizes the task description. Execution-based verification loops debug failed scripts, and tasks are discarded unless milestone thresholds satisfy a strict monotonic ordering (Eq. 1). From 1,200 initial tasks, filtering yields 912 valid tasks (848 train / 64 validation), spanning 8+ domains, 6 modalities. (2) Trajectory-level GRPO on these sandboxes using the ReAct scaffold, T_max=20 turns, τ_max=90s, group size 4, 100 steps, lr 1e-6, KL penalty disabled, one H200 per task. The reward r = 0.1·r_format + 0.2·I_execute + Σ w_Si·I_Si (milestone weights 0.1/0.2/0.2/0.2 for median/bronze/silver/gold tiers) is dense and hierarchical; loss masking applies gradients only to action tokens, and trajectories exceeding the time limit are fully masked. Critical design decisions: (a) rebuilding data at micro-scale rather than downsampling real datasets (justified: downsampling breaks fixed test sets and leaderboard baselines), (b) dense milestone rewards (validated by ablation), (c) hard execution/time caps. Decisions (a) and (b) are empirically supported; the equivalence of synthetic and real task structure is assumed rather than justified. Key Results: Execution latency drops from 196.17s (original MLE-bench seed tasks, Gemini-2.5-Flash code) to 14.31s on synthetic tasks (13.7×), with most tasks at 120–150 samples. On MLE-bench-lite (ReAct scaffold, 22 tasks): Any Medal rates—Qwen3-8B 13.6→22.7 (+66.9% relative over Base), 14B 18.2→22.7, 30B-A3B 13.6→27.3 (+100.7% over Base; abstract reports 20.3–66.9% over Seed-SFT). Seed-SFT on Claude-4.5-Sonnet trajectories yields near-zero gains (8B and 30B Any Medal unchanged at 13.6%). Trained 8B matches DeepSeek-V3.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash (22.7); 14B/30B (27.3) approach Claude-4.5-Sonnet (31.8). SFT+RL initialization improves Valid Submission (e.g., 14B: 95.5% vs. 77.3%) while preserving medal rates. Test-time scaling: Any Medal climbs from 5% at 5 turns to 55% at 30 turns for 30B-SFT-SandMLE, then regresses due to context-window eviction. Cross-scaffold: gains transfer to AIDE and AIRA on MLE-bench-lite (e.g., 30B-AIRA: 18.2→27.3 Any Medal) and to MLE-Dojo (30B+MLE-Agent: HumanRank 29.12→38.56, Valid Submission 71.0→83.9), while SFT models collapse under scaffold shift (30B SFT with MLE-Agent: 17.7% Valid Submission). Reward ablation: sparse reward (format + gold only) degrades 30B from 27.3 to 13.6 Any Medal and 100.0 to 86.4 Valid Submission. Synthetic task difficulty cleanly separates GPT-4o-mini < Gemini-2.5-Flash ≈ DeepSeek-V3 < Claude-4.5-Sonnet in pairwise win rates. All results use 22-task (MLE-bench-lite) and 62-task (MLE-Dojo) evaluations; no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. Baselines include current frontier systems as reference points, though no direct comparison against other RL-for-MLE training methods (e.g., ACE-GRPO, ML-Agent) is run. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (synthetic micro-scale sandbox generation enabling on-policy trajectory RL for MLE) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (micro-scale synthetic environments suffice as RL training signal that transfers to full-scale real tasks, and RL generalizes across scaffolds where SFT does not). The GRPO algorithm, ReAct rollout, loss masking, and dense-reward shaping are standard components from SWE/web-agent RL (DeepSWE, WebDancer); the genuinely novel move is the structural-DNA extraction + adversarial mutation pipeline that makes execution cheap without making the task trivial, and the empirical demonstration that this proxy distribution trains transferable policies. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: dense vs. sparse reward across three model scales (Table 4), SFT-vs-RL initialization disentanglement (Seed-SFT / SandMLE / SFT-SandMLE), test-time turn scaling, and training-dynamics curves. Environment-generation reliability is quantified (1,200 → 912 tasks through three filtering stages). However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported on any headline number—problematic given medal-rate differences of one task (4.5 percentage points) on a 22-task eval set. Code and data are released at https://github.com/Tonyzhou98/SandMLE, with full prompt templates in the appendix. Methodological concerns: (a) training seeds are drawn from MLE-bench's Medium/Hard/Dev splits while evaluation is MLE-bench-lite (Easy split)—tasks come from the same benchmark family, so distribution overlap between synthetic tasks' DNA and evaluation tasks cannot be excluded (partial Goodhart exposure); (b) MLE-bench-lite n=22 makes single-task swings look like large relative gains; (c) no head-to-head against competing RL-for-MLE training approaches; (d) execution-latency comparison uses code generated by Gemini-2.5-Flash, and it is unclear whether well-written code on real tasks is actually this slow. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact—the sandbox-generation pipeline). - Practical: Yes—training used one NVIDIA H200 per task with 90-second execution caps, and evaluation infrastructure is standard; the released pipeline should run on a single-GPU-per-job setup. - Efficient: The method's entire value proposition is efficiency: 13.7× per-step execution reduction converts infeasible on-policy RL into ~100-step GRPO runs, orders of magnitude cheaper than the 24-hour-per-task regimes of scaffold-only systems. - Effective: Evidence shows medal-rate and HumanRank improvements on two real benchmarks across three scaffolds, but the mechanism of transfer (which learned skills carry over) is unprobed, and absolute rates (27.3% Any Medal, HumanRank 38.56) remain well below Claude-4.5-Sonnet (31.8, 54.09). - Scalable: Only claimed implicitly—the paper trains on 848 tasks and 100 GRPO steps; no experiment tests whether scaling task count, steps, or dataset size (e.g., 500–5,000 samples) continues to help or whether the micro-scale proxy assumption degrades gracefully; the authors themselves note context length, not environment speed, becomes the next bottleneck at 30+ turns. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: the generation pipeline, 848-task synthetic corpus, and trained checkpoints, with code and data publicly released. Strengths: - The diagnostic insight is genuinely useful and validated: MLE RL infeasibility is traced to dataset size, and the fix (rebuild at micro-scale, preserve structure) is a simple, transferable recipe other groups can copy immediately. - The SFT-vs-RL comparison is well-controlled: Seed-SFT uses 60 high-quality Claude-4.5-Sonnet trajectories on the exact seed questions, yet yields ~zero Any Medal improvement, cleanly isolating the value of on-policy environment interaction—a strong, surprising empirical point. - Scaffold-generalization evaluation is a credibility strength: testing across ReAct/AIDE/AIRA/MLE-Agent on two benchmarks, and showing SFT models collapse under scaffold shift while RL models transfer, addresses the most obvious objection to scaffold-specific training. - The multi-stage filtering (execution verification, threshold monotonicity checks, 1,200→912 yield) and the model-separation difficulty calibration (Fig. 3) show unusual care in validating the synthetic corpus rather than just generating it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that test-time scaling beyond 30 turns regresses due to context-window overflow and history eviction, naming effective context length as the current bottleneck (Appendix B.2). They also implicitly acknowledge scaffold sensitivity of SFT (documented collapse of Seed-SFT on MLE-Dojo with MLE-Agent). They explicitly frame the micro-scale proxy as a "principle" they believe in, but they do not state explicit scope boundaries for when synthetic tasks would fail to represent real MLE work (e.g., tasks whose difficulty is inherently data-scale-bound: distributed training, memory optimization, large-image pipelines). Limitations are surfaced where measured but not confronted systematically (no dedicated limitations section in the main text). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation against the obvious alternative: RL on downsampled versions of the real 60 seed tasks. The paper dismisses downsampling (breaks test sets and baselines) but a coarse-downsampling RL baseline would isolate how much of the gain comes from micro-scale synthesis versus merely having fast environments at all. - No per-task correlation analysis between synthetic-task reward and real-benchmark success—transfer is shown only in aggregate on 22 tasks, leaving the proxy-fidelity assumption untested at the instance level. - Single evaluation run, no seeds, and 22-task eval sets mean several headline contrasts (e.g., 14B 22.7 vs. 18.2, or AIDE 30B 13.6 vs. Base 13.6 with different compositions) are within noise; the paper reports none of this. - The claim that synthetic tasks preserve "structural and technical complexity" is supported by a difficulty-ordering check and one qualitative example, not by any systematic comparison of solution strategies on synthetic vs. real tasks. - No comparison against concurrent RL-for-MLE training methods (ACE-GRPO, ML-Agent, Yang et al. 2025c), so the relative standing of this training recipe is unknown. - Task-type coverage is skewed (56.2% classification, 48.7% image modality); transfer claims may not extend to under-represented formulations (ranking at 2.9%, audio at 2.3%). - Disabling the KL penalty in GRPO is stated but unexplained and unablated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building RL-trained MLE or long-horizon coding agents should read this—the micro-scale synthetic environment recipe is immediately actionable, the SFT-vs-RL evidence is convincing, and the code is released—but the transfer mechanism is under-analyzed and the evaluation is too small and unseeded to treat the headline numbers as precise, so it is a strong recipe paper rather than a definitive comparative study.

Safin-1: Safety from Within through Memory-Native State Evolution (18 ▲ )

Ming Zhang, Kaisen Yang, Shu Yu, Ermo Hua, Zhekai Chen, Cheng Jin, Jingnan Zheng, Yi Zhang, Zhongtian Ma, Jiawei Zhou, Sirui Chen, Qiaosheng Zhang, Xiang Wang, Ning Ding, Xia Hu, Bowen Zhou, Youbang Sun, Chaochao Lu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 2 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Safin-1, a family of foundation models built on MARCH, an architecture that periodically checkpoints the recurrent state of linear-attention layers into a content-routed bank of addressable state anchors, and uses the same routing interface to host a detachable, learnable "Safety State" that specializes a frozen backbone for jailbreak resistance. - Why it's important: Long-horizon models lose access to overwritten recurrent context, and safety is usually bolted on via fine-tuning or external guards; representing safety as a native, removable model state offers a path to modular safety specialization without rewriting shared weights. - How it does it: The recurrent backbone snapshots its cumulative state every 512 tokens; each snapshot gets a content-derived routing key, and every token scores anchors (plus a learned null option and learnable persistent states) through one softmax, fusing retrieved matrix-valued states residually into the native recurrent readout. - The good: The evidence chain is well controlled: matched 0.8B pretraining across three recurrent backbones (GDN, KDA, GDN2) isolates the architectural gain, and matched 4B/35B continual pretraining shows AIME 2025 Avg@64 rising from 55.57 to 63.59 (4B) and 71.88 to 80.10 (35B) over the Qwen3.5 baselines. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and several headline safety deltas (e.g., average ASR 6.65→3.84 at 4B) rest on small per-benchmark counts and a 1,915-example training corpus evaluated only on static English jailbreak suites. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on linear-attention/recurrent architectures or architectural approaches to safety alignment; skip it if you only need another efficient-attention variant, since the memory-routing gains are the substantive part and the safety result is an early, narrow proof of concept.

Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (70) are the drivers: routing over checkpoints of the model's own recurrent-state trajectory, and especially hosting learnable persistent capability states in the same softmax as context memory, is a genuinely new interface. The two-stage evidence design (controlled 0.8B across three backbones, then matched 4B/35B CPT) and thorough routing ablations support Rigor (62), which is nonetheless capped by zero statistical treatment of small-count safety deltas, a single rank-8 LoRA control, and unconfirmable artifact URLs. Problem & Motivation: Recurrent/linear-attention models compress the causal prefix into a fixed-size state; once an earlier association is overwritten, its representation is unrecoverable from the current state alone — a documented retrieval bottleneck for long-horizon tasks. Independently, safety in LLMs is typically imposed post-hoc (SFT, adapters, activation steering) or via external guards, which the authors argue makes safety fragile and non-native. The paper targets two audiences: efficient long-context architecture designers who need state addressing, and safety researchers seeking specialization mechanisms that do not modify a shared general-purpose backbone. The unifying question is whether model state can serve both as addressable context memory and as a substrate for persistent, selectively invoked capabilities. Key Idea: Make the trajectory of the recurrent state itself the memory: periodically checkpoint the cumulative recurrent state (not the tokens), give each checkpoint a content-derived routing key so tokens can retrieve historical states by what they contain rather than when they occurred, and — the more distinctive move — put learnable persistent parameter matrices (a Safety State) into the same routed candidate set, so a frozen backbone invokes the capability through its native routing softmax with token- and context-dependent weight. Methodology: MARCH has three components. (1) Context-derived state anchors: a shared learned anchor embedding is inserted every C=512 tokens; the underlying recurrence (Gated DeltaNet-style chunkwise delta rule) is never reset, and at each boundary the cumulative state S ∈ R^{d_v×d_k} is checkpointed. The anchor position reads only its aligned checkpoint to build a compact routing key, so keys become state-dependent after the first layer. (2) Content-routed retrieval: each token projects a routing query, scores all causally visible anchor keys plus a learned null option (zero payload) in a single softmax, and fuses weighted matrix-valued readouts additively with the current-state readout (Eq. 7), trained end-to-end with the LM loss; a Top-K=4 sparse variant restricts the expensive readout. (3) Persistent capability states: J learnable matrix states per layer share the routing pathway; the Safety State is trained with token-level cross-entropy on 5,745 examples (1,915 STAR-1/STAR-benign targets × 0/512/2,048-token benign prefixes) in only 37 optimizer steps with the backbone frozen. A FlashAttention-style fused producer–reader kernel avoids materializing the routing matrix. Critical design decisions: cumulative (non-reset) checkpoints, the learned null option (ablation shows removing it consistently degrades all aggregates), and joint softmax over dynamic + persistent + null candidates — all justified, though the fixed anchoring interval is admittedly suboptimal. Key Results: At 0.8B (50B tokens, 16K context): MARCH-GDN averages 41.5 on eight commonsense benchmarks vs 40.1 for GDN and 41.4 for the parameter-matched transformer; LongBench average 14.9 vs 11.9 for GDN (+25%); in-context retrieval average 23.3 vs 20.5 for the Log-Linear baseline; NIAH improves in 19 of 24 task–length settings with the largest gains at 32K (zero-shot extrapolation beyond the 16K training length). Gains hold across GDN, KDA, and GDN2 (11 of 12 NIAH settings). Top-4 routing more than doubles training throughput vs dense MARCH at 128K and cuts core runtime ~10×, exceeding FlashAttention-2 throughput at that length. At scale (Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, matched 50B-token CPT on Intern-S2 + 30B-token SFT): the 10-benchmark macro-average rises 66.79→69.20 (4B) and 76.25→78.35 (35B); MMLU-Pro +9.28 at 4B (58.27→67.55); GPQA-Diamond +6.56 at 35B; GSM8K/MATH within ±1.44 points. Safety State: average ASR across five jailbreak suites (WildJailbreak, FORTRESS, StrongREJECT, Jailbreak-R1, JBB) drops 6.65→3.84 (4B, −42.3%) and 5.89→2.81 (35B, −52.3%), beating a training-matched rank-8 LoRA (5.33 and 3.04) with far less over-refusal (XSTest ORR +0.4/+2.0 vs +5.0/+10.0 for LoRA). Capability retention at 35B is mixed: Safety State trails base by 3.37 points on MMLU-Pro and 4.20 on MBPP. Baselines are current (GDN, KDA, GDN2, Log-Linear Attention, Qwen3.5), and the safety control is well matched, but the LoRA comparison is a single rank-8 configuration. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: content-conditioned routing over cumulative snapshots of the model's own recurrent-state trajectory with a learned null option, and — more distinctively — hosting learnable persistent capability states in the same routed candidate set so a frozen backbone invokes safety natively. Standard-combination components: delta-rule recurrences, Top-K sparse retrieval (a state-level analogue of MoBA/Native Sparse Attention), and LoRA-comparison training protocols; the safety result reuses existing STAR-1 data and standard jailbreak benchmarks in a new mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: anchor interval (C ∈ {256–2048} plus inference-time re-resolution and a Fenwick-tree layout unseen in training), routing dimension (64 vs 192), sparsity (dense vs Top-4), null option, and RoPE removal, each changing one component against fixed defaults. Backbone generality is tested across three recurrent parameterizations and two scales with matched data/tokens/optimizer. However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; several safety deltas (StrongREJECT 1.28→1.60 at 4B regresses, JBB 1.00→2.00 at 4B) are within plausible noise for these benchmark sizes; large-scale evidence covers only two Qwen3.5 configurations under one CPT–SFT pipeline; the safety study uses one small English corpus and no adaptive or multilingual attacks. GitHub and Hugging Face links are referenced in the header but no concrete repository URL is printed in the text, so artifact availability cannot be confirmed from the paper. The models are evaluated on standard public benchmarks, not the authors' own evaluation sets, which mitigates Goodhart concerns, though AIME Avg@64 gains (+8 points at both scales) from 50B tokens of matched CPT deserve independent replication. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — fused kernels and released model family). - Practical: Builds on chunkwise GDN kernels and FlashAttention-style fused readers for tensor-core GPUs; nothing requires exotic hardware, and 4B/35B-A3B scales are commercially deployable. - Efficient: Keeps constant-memory recurrent decoding; sparse Top-4 retrieval costs >2× throughput over dense routing at 128K, though vanilla GDN without retrieval remains faster and state storage grows linearly with context. - Effective: Benchmark ASR and over-refusal improve against a matched control, but effectiveness against adaptive, multi-turn, or state-tampering attacks — the threats that matter for a routing-based safety mechanism — is untested. - Scalable: State bank and routing cost grow with context length (acknowledged); efficiency is measured to 128K but capability/safety claims are not stress-tested beyond 32K context or beyond two backbone configurations. Delivers: trained 4B and 35B-A3B checkpoints (Hugging Face referenced), fused dense/sparse routing kernels, and a reusable state-routing recipe; the paper stops short of a maintained library. Strengths: - The two-stage evidence design — controlled 0.8B isolation of the architectural effect across three recurrent backbones, then matched CPT–SFT at 4B and 35B — is unusually clean for an architecture paper and makes the causal attribution to MARCH credible. - The persistent-capability-state mechanism is a genuinely new interface: safety as a matrix-valued state retrieved through the same softmax as context memory, yielding token- and context-dependent invocation rather than a fixed adapter weight, and it empirically dominates a matched LoRA on the safety–over-refusal trade-off. - The routing ablations (null option, anchor interval, inference-time bank re-resolution including transfer to an unseen Fenwick layout) expose real design insight, not just a grid. - Honest framing of what "Safety from Within" does and does not mean — supervision still comes from external data; the authors explicitly flag detachability as an integrity attack surface. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the state bank grows with context and sparse routing reduces read cost but not storage; fixed-interval anchoring may retain redundant checkpoints; large-scale evidence is limited to two Qwen3.5 configurations under one pipeline; the safety study uses a small corpus, English-only static benchmarks, no adaptive/multilingual attacks or state tampering; and capability retention at 35B is task-dependent. They also note that whether multiple persistent states can coexist and compose is open. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment anywhere: with per-benchmark ASRs of 0.3–2%, the headline average-ASR improvements could shift materially under resampling; at minimum, bootstrap CIs over benchmark items are needed. - The LoRA control is a single rank-8 configuration; rank-16/32, full fine-tuning, and other PEFT baselines (e.g., safety-preserving LoRA variants the paper itself cites) are absent, so the trade-off claim rests on one comparison point. - The Safety State training conditions on benign prefixes of exactly 0/512/2,048 tokens, matching the 512-token anchor interval — the safety evaluation never tests whether the state degrades under prefix lengths or memory configurations unlike training, the same distribution-shift concern the memory side was designed to address. - The 0.8B study omits a MARCH-on-transformer or token-level sparse-attention baseline at matched compute; the claim that state-level routing beats token-level alternatives is supported only indirectly. - Detachability is touted as a feature, but no experiment probes removal/substitution attacks on the Safety State or router, despite the authors themselves identifying this as an integrity requirement. - Anchor positions consume sequence positions during pretraining; the interaction of inserted anchor tokens with SFT data and real-world token budgets is not analyzed. Bottom Line: For researchers in linear-attention architectures and architectural safety, this is one of the more interesting recent papers — the state-trajectory routing is a solid, well-ablated contribution and the persistent-capability interface is a genuinely new idea worth building on — but the safety result is an early proof of concept whose headline numbers need statistical treatment and adversarial evaluation before anyone treats "Safety from Within" as demonstrated.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a linked movie-release/book dataset (287 movie-book pairs from Wikidata, TMDB, and Goodreads) and measures both a readership spike around movie releases and whether standard recommender models already reflect that spike in their scores. - Why it's important: Exogenous events (film releases, awards, news) shift item relevance faster than interaction data accumulates, so recommenders systematically lag on affected items; knowing whether current models absorb these signals determines whether event-aware features or re-ranking are needed. - How it does it: It applies an econometric causal-inference toolkit — k-NN matching plus Difference-in-Differences for readership, and coarsened exact matching with k-NN refinement to estimate the ATT of adaptation status on recommendation scores — to a large temporal Goodreads corpus. - The good: The readership effect is robustly quantified: an estimated 143,989 additional new readers per adapted book (t=6.39, p<0.001), with a placebo test at a shifted date showing no pre-trend (−48,617, p=0.14), replicated across all ten pre-release popularity deciles. - The missing: The RQ2 analysis rests on only 24 treated books in a single two-month evaluation window (January 2017), so the null result on recommenders is statistically underpowered and cannot distinguish 'models do not encode the signal' from 'the test cannot detect a modest effect' — a limitation the authors acknowledge but do not resolve. - Read it or not: Worth reading for RecSys researchers working on temporal dynamics, event-aware recommendation, or Goodreads-data methodology; practitioners seeking deployable event-aware ranking techniques will find only motivation, not methods.

Problem & Motivation Recommender systems rank items using historical interaction data, but exogenous events can temporarily change an item's relevance before enough new interactions accumulate for the model to respond. Movie adaptations of books are a clean instance: economics and information-science studies of book sales and library circulation report demand increases around film releases, strongest immediately before and after. The open question the authors identify is whether standard collaborative filtering models implicitly capture this demand shift through interaction patterns, or whether the shift is invisible to them — a prerequisite question before anyone invests in building event-aware recommendation features. The problem affects anyone operating recommender systems over item catalogs exposed to media-driven attention shocks. Key Idea The core move is treating movie-adaptation status as a book-level 'treatment' and importing the observational causal-inference toolkit — matched controls, event studies, Difference-in-Differences, and ATT estimation — into recommender-system evaluation, both to quantify the demand shock on readership and to test whether model scores differ between adapted books and matched non-adapted books during release windows. The insight is that recommendation scores can be interrogated as an outcome variable in a matched observational design, not just evaluated via accuracy metrics. Methodology The pipeline has two phases. Phase 1 (RQ1): construct 287 movie-book pairs (Wikidata 'based on' relations, US movies 2007–2017, ≥1,000 TMDB votes as an impact filter), link to Goodreads records via Wikidata work ID and fuzzy title matching; for 261 books with sufficient pre-release data, match up to k=5 controls by nearest-neighbor on log pre-release readership (caliper 0.5 log units, SMD reduced from 2.63 to 0.22), stratify by popularity decile, and estimate per-book DiD over [−7,−1) / [−1,+5] / (+5,+11] six-month windows, testing the pooled estimate with a one-sample t-test and a 12-month placebo shift. Phase 2 (RQ2): train four LensKit recommenders (ImplicitMF, BPR, Pop, SLIM) on interactions before 2017-01, evaluate January 2017; for 24 books with active releases, estimate the ATT of adaptation status on recommendation scores via two-stage matching — coarsened exact matching on genre, book age, and popularity, then within-stratum k-NN refinement without replacement (111 controls, SMD 0.018) — with a matched-group block bootstrap for uncertainty and cross-model comparability via standardization by pooled control-score SD. Critical design decisions: (1) a 6-month event window starting one month before release to capture anticipation — justified but somewhat arbitrary and not sensitivity-analyzed; (2) excluding candidate controls with earlier adaptations to avoid contamination — well-justified; (3) the authors explicitly frame causal language as conservative associations given ignorability/SUTVA concerns — appropriately cautious. No loss functions are trained; this is an analysis, not a modeling contribution. Key Results RQ1: pooled DiD estimates 143,989 additional new Goodreads readers per treated book (t=6.39, p<0.001) on 261 adapted books; placebo estimate −48,617 (p=0.14). The spike appears across all ten popularity deciles; absolute effect grows monotonically with pre-release book popularity, but relative effect is 5–6× larger for the lowest-popularity books than the highest; effect generally rises with movie popularity (TMDB votes). RQ2: over 33,631 interactions involving 24 active movie-adapted books, 71–91% are retrieved in top-2500 (Pop 91.1%, ImplicitMF 78.7%, BPR 76.6%, SLIM 71.2%) with median ranks 255–301 and top-100 rates of 27–31%; but ATT estimates on scores are statistically null for all four models (e.g., ImplicitMF 0.010 [−0.002, 0.023]; BPR 0.089 [−0.039, 0.213]; standardized 0.040–0.062 for personalized models), i.e., no evidence that models systematically up- or down-score adapted books during release windows. Baselines (ImplicitMF, BPR, SLIM, Pop via LensKit) are standard and reasonably current for this corpus, though no neural or temporal models (e.g., timeSVD++) are included. Scale is large on the interaction side (228M interactions, 2007–2017) but very small on the treated side (24 books, one evaluation window). Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper is the first (by its claim, plausible) to test whether recommenders surface movie-adapted books during release windows, and it contributes a new released dataset of 287 linked movie-book pairs. The methods themselves — k-NN matching, DiD, CEM, ATT estimation — are standard econometrics applied competently to a new setting in recommendation; no new algorithm or formulation is introduced. Rigor & Reproducibility Methodological care is above average for an exploratory RecSys paper: matched controls with reported balance (SMD 2.63→0.22 for readership; 0.018 for scores), a placebo test for pre-trends, stratified heterogeneity analysis, clustered block-bootstrap inference, and honest caveats that the 24-group bootstrap CIs have uncertain coverage and that causal interpretation requires ignorability and approximate SUTVA. Code and the movie-book dataset are released (Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/21464427). Weaknesses: no seed replication or sensitivity analysis on the 6-month window definition; the RQ2 evaluation uses a single two-month window with only 24 treated books, and the method (treatment definition, matching covariates) is effectively developed and evaluated on the same corpus and period — no held-out validation of the event-signal construct; no significance testing across decile-level DiD estimates (declared explicitly); no standard temporal baseline such as timeSVD++ or Koren's temporal-dynamics model despite the paper being precisely about whether temporal effects are captured. Deployability: (4-property check)** Profile: EMPIRICAL (measurement/analysis study, no deployed system). - Practical: Yes — analyses run on the public UCSD Goodreads corpus with LensKit on commodity hardware; no special resources needed. - Efficient: Matching and DiD on ~287 treated books are trivially cheap; the cost lies in the one-time data linkage, which is released. - Effective: The readership-spike finding is solidly evidenced; the second half only establishes absence of evidence that recommenders respond — a proxy question (score differences) that stops short of measuring end-to-end recommendation quality during release windows. - Scalable: Not tested; with 24 treated books in one window, extension to 10× more events (all countries, later years, other event types) is claimed as future work, not demonstrated. Deliverable: a released dataset (287 movie-book pairs), analysis code, and a reusable evaluation design; no trained model or software tool beyond analysis scripts. Strengths - A clean, reusable data contribution: 287 Wikidata/TMDB-linked movie-book pairs with release dates, verified against Goodreads, publicly released with code. - The readership result is unusually well-instrumented for an exploratory paper: matched controls, balance diagnostics, a placebo pre-trend test, and decile-stratified heterogeneity that yields a genuinely non-obvious finding (low-popularity books gain proportionally 5–6× more than high-popularity ones). - Honest statistical framing: the authors repeatedly downgrade their own causal claims, flag the few-cluster bootstrap's coverage limits, and correctly interpret Pop's large standardized ATT as an artifact of low control-score dispersion rather than an effect. - The paper asks the right sequencing question — 'do existing models already capture this?' — before proposing event-aware modeling, which disciplines the design space for follow-up work. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state explicitly: the DiD analysis is descriptive and not causally identified; parallel trends is an assumption checked only by placebo; SUTVA is only approximately satisfied because the shared interaction matrix may already contain adaptation-driven engagement (spillover); unobserved confounders (author prominence, marketing) remain; the treatment ignores heterogeneity in release timing, marketing, and upcoming releases; only 24 treated books limit power and make bootstrap CIs unreliable; and evaluating event-aware strategies will require pooling many historical release windows. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No temporal recommender baseline: the paper's RQ2 asks whether models capture temporal effects but excludes the one model family designed for exactly that (Koren's timeSVD++ / temporal-dynamics CF, which the authors cite), leaving the headline null result incomplete. - The 6-month [−1,+5] event window is asserted rather than validated; no sensitivity analysis over window length or offset, despite the ATT result depending directly on it. - The RQ2 evaluation window (January 2017, two months) contains only 24 active treated books out of 287 — a dogs-not-barking omission given ten years of releases were available; pooling across release windows (which the authors recommend for future work) was feasible here for the score analysis and would have materially raised power. - Goodreads 'readership' is platform-specific shelf-adding behavior, not sales or reading; generalization to commercial recommendation settings is untested. - Fuzzy title matching plus manual verification for a 'small number of cases' — the match error rate is unquantified, and mislinked pairs would directly bias the DiD estimate. - The dataset is ARXIV preprint work (not stated as peer-reviewed), and the 2017 data end means no assessment of whether modern deep recommenders or popularity-decay dynamics behave differently. Bottom Line Researchers in temporal/event-aware recommendation gain a solid motivational study, a released linkage dataset, and a careful negative result worth citing, but the underpowered RQ2 analysis and missing temporal baselines mean the paper raises the question it cannot fully answer — read it as a foundation, not a verdict.
