ZJ Cheng, ZY Jia, Z Zhou, YF Li, LZ Guo · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SymboLLM-FE, a two-stage automated feature engineering pipeline in which genetic-programming symbolic regression generates mathematically grounded candidate formulas over Spearman-sorted feature subsets, and an LLM then converts those formulas into interpretable pandas feature code with a closed-loop validation against a downstream predictor. - Why it's important: LLM-based AutoFE methods typically need dozens of iterative generate-and-validate rounds (e.g., OcTree ~50 rounds) and risk hallucinated features, while traditional AutoFE produces opaque formula features; a method that achieves competitive accuracy with only 2–5 LLM calls and traceable features addresses both cost and trustworthiness in tabular ML pipelines used in finance and healthcare. - How it does it: The core move is inverting the usual LLM role — symbolic regression (gplearn GP with parsimony penalty over expanding-sliding windows of Spearman-ranked feature subsets, reducing subset count from O(2^n) to O(n^2)) does the statistical heavy lifting, and the LLM is confined to a refinement/semantic-annotation role anchored to the validated formulas rather than open-ended generation. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough for this subfield: 7 AutoFE baselines × 4 downstream models × 6 datasets × 3 metrics × 3 seeds, with Wilcoxon significance tests showing significant gains on 4 of 6 datasets (e.g., Academic p<0.001), plus an ablation confirming each component contributes (77.16 full vs. 76.07 w/o Spearman sorting, 75.92 w/o window, 76.84 w/o LLM). - The missing: Effect sizes are small (typically <1 point accuracy, often within one standard deviation of CAAFE/FEBP), two datasets fail significance, and the bold claims of 100% hallucination elimination and interpretability are validated qualitatively on a Titanic case study rather than a rigorous benchmark; scalability to high-dimensional data is asserted but never tested beyond 36 raw features. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build LLM-based AutoFE systems and want a concrete, well-benchmarked template for grounding LLMs in statistically validated candidates; skip it if you want strong evidence that interpretability or hallucination guarantees actually hold, or if you need methods for wide/high-dimensional tables.

Problem & Motivation Practitioners building predictive models on tabular data (credit scoring, medical diagnosis, Kaggle-style competitions) face a trade-off in automated feature engineering. Traditional AutoFE (AutoFeat, OpenFE) blindly stacks mathematical operators on raw columns, producing features that win accuracy but have no semantic meaning — problematic in regulated domains like quantitative finance where feature provenance matters. LLM-based AutoFE (CAAFE, OcTree, FEBP, LLM-FE) generates semantically named features but needs many costly generate-validate iterations and can hallucinate. The paper's own Table 1 illustrates this: OcTree needs 50 API calls for 79.52 accuracy, FEBP 29 calls for 79.36, while traditional methods hit ~79.5 with uninterpretable features. The gap is a framework delivering both performance and interpretable features at low LLM cost. Key Idea Demote the LLM from generator to refiner: let cheap symbolic regression discover which mathematical combinations of features actually correlate with the target, then have the LLM translate those statistically validated formulas into semantically named, executable features — anchoring the LLM's generative space to a finite set of grounded formulas so hallucination is bounded by construction. The expanding-sliding-window enumeration over Spearman-ranked features is the second, supporting trick that keeps the SR workload polynomial. Methodology Stage 1 (Formula Construction): compute Spearman correlation of each feature with the target, sort ascending, then enumerate feature subsets via an expanding window (size k from ⌊n/2⌋ to n) and sliding window within each k, yielding ~O(n²) subsets per Eq. 2 (e.g., 66 subsets for Credit-g's 20 features, 171 for Ailerons' 33). Each subset trains a gplearn SymbolicRegressor/SymbolicClassifier (population 20,000, ≤120 generations, parsimony coefficient Ω grid-searched over {0.005–0.05}, 14 protected operators, MSE + Ω·size fitness). Output is a repository of (subset, performance, formula) triples. Stage 2 (Feature Generation via LLM): each formula plus its MAE is rendered in natural language and combined with a structured code-generation prompt; the LLM (GPT-4/o1/DeepSeek-R1) emits pandas code adding/dropping columns via chain-of-thought; a downstream predictor (TabPFN/CatBoost/XGBoost/MLP) validates on a held-out validation split; predictor scores are fed back for refinement until convergence (2–5 calls total). Design decisions: (1) Spearman over Pearson/SHAP/MI — justified empirically by highest Kendall's τ consistency (0.65) with other importance metrics (Appendix D); (2) LLM restricted to refinement — well-motivated and supported by the ablation (w/o LLM drops 0.32 points); (3) window adjacency assumes synergistic features rank adjacently — the authors themselves flag this as a failure mode. Strict train/validation/test separation is claimed to prevent leakage. Key Results On six datasets (Credit-g, Spaceship, Cmc, Academic, Ailerons, Tesla) with TabPFN downstream, SymboLLM-FE reaches 77.00/81.27/57.97/77.89 accuracy and 5.02/2.16 RMSE vs. a no-FE baseline of 77.03/80.79/57.85/77.33/5.10/2.39 — beating the best of seven AutoFE baselines on Spaceship, Cmc, Academic, Ailerons, and Tesla, but losing to CAAFE on Credit-g (78.00 vs. 77.00). Wilcoxon tests confirm significance on 4/6 datasets; Credit-g (p=0.2248) and Ailerons (p=0.95) are not significant. Gains over traditional AutoFE average 1.23% and ~1% over LLM-based AutoFE. Efficiency: 2–5 LLM API calls (1,147–3,587 tokens/call), SR time 0.89–30.24 minutes, versus OcTree's 50 calls and FEBP's reported 43.71 minutes. On four Kaggle competitions, SymboLLM-FE+TabPFN beats vanilla TabPFN and OpenFE+TabPFN by an average 2.5pp. Full sweeps over CatBoost, XGBoost, MLP, TabPFN (Appendix E) show mostly top-2 results, though some MLP rows show high variance (e.g., Spaceship 76.43±13.90). GP-only baselines (Shapley-GP, LAS-GP, SAM-GP, Modular-MTGP) are matched or beaten on 5/6 datasets. Baselines are current and appropriate (2023–2025 methods). Testing scale is standard small-tabular (1,000–12,250 samples, 8–36 features) — not stress-scale. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component). The genuinely new element is the pipeline direction: using symbolic regression output as a grounding substrate for LLM refinement in AutoFE, distinct from LLM-SR work (Shojaee et al. 2025) that uses LLMs to aid equation discovery. The components themselves — GP-based symbolic regression, Spearman presorting, sliding windows, LLM code generation with feedback loops — are all standard; the contribution is their composition and the role inversion, which is a sensible but incremental synthesis rather than a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations exist and are informative: removing Spearman presorting, the window mechanism, or LLM refinement each degrades accuracy (77.16 → 76.07/75.92/76.84) with paired t-tests (p<0.001 for three variants, p=0.0142 for w/o LLM) and confidence intervals. Three random seeds with mean±std are reported throughout; Wilcoxon significance versus best baselines is provided. Code is released at github.com/LAMDA-NeSy/SymboLLM-FE; prompts and hyperparameters are documented. Concerns: (1) the interpretability/hallucination audit (Appendix H) is qualitative, self-defined, and run on the Titanic dataset, which is not in the main benchmark — a self-graded evaluation; (2) main-table margins are small and often within one standard deviation; (3) a copy-paste artifact appears in Table 11 (FEBP's Academic F1 value 67.04±11.96 duplicated from the SymboLLM-FE row), suggesting imperfect table verification; (4) the ablation mean (77.16) does not match the main-table SymboLLM-FE result (77.00) on what appears to be the same dataset. This is an arXiv preprint (2608.28408, August 2026), apparently under review; results should be treated as not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Yes — gplearn (CPU), one NVIDIA 4090 for MLP, and a few commercial LLM API calls; nothing exotic. - Efficient: Favorable relative to LLM-based AutoFE — 2–5 API calls and ≤30 minutes of SR versus 29–50 iterative rounds for OcTree/FEBP/LLM-FE — but SR time grows with dataset size and the authors concede it becomes prohibitive on high-dimensional data. - Effective: Partially — it beats strong baselines on most datasets with statistical support, but wins are <1 point in several cases and the interpretability benefit, the headline motivation, is demonstrated only through annotated case studies, not a measured downstream benefit (e.g., expert acceptance or regulatory validation). - Scalable: Not demonstrated beyond 36 raw features; the O(n²) subset bound is proven, but SR runtime per subset is not bounded, and the authors explicitly state high-dimensional data incurs prohibitive time overhead. The work delivers a software artifact (open-source code with SR configurations and prompt templates); no trained models or datasets are released. Strengths - The role inversion (SR discovers, LLM annotates) is a genuinely useful architectural pattern that converts the LLM's hallucination weakness into a bounded-refinement strength, and the ablation (w/o LLM: 76.84 vs. 77.16) empirically shows the LLM stage adds real value beyond raw SR formulas. - Evaluation breadth is a clear execution strength: 7 baselines spanning both paradigms, 4 downstream models, 3 metrics, 3 seeds, significance testing, plus a separate GP-variant comparison (Appendix J) that most LLM-AutoFE papers omit. - The cost analysis is concrete and falsifiable: formula counts match the derived arithmetic bounds (Table 4), token cost is decoupled from sample size, and the 4-call regime is verified per dataset rather than merely claimed. - The efficiency framing reframes LLM-AutoFE's main pain point (iteration count) into a measurable, competitive number — a useful framing for future comparisons. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state two limitations directly and honestly: (1) despite the O(n²) reduction, symbolic regression incurs prohibitive time overhead on high-dimensional datasets, limiting feasibility in resource-constrained or real-time settings; (2) the sorted-sliding-window construction can miss synergistic effects between features that are not adjacent in the Spearman ranking, so joint predictive contributions of non-consecutive variables may be overlooked. This is a credible, non-minimizing limitations section. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central interpretability and hallucination-elimination claims rest on self-authored qualitative audits on one dataset (Titanic) not present in the main benchmark; phrases like "zero deviation into ungrounded transformations" and "immune to stochastic hallucinations" are architecturally asserted, not measured against a defined metric or independent audit. - The case-study interpretations are occasionally strained (e.g., reading tan(age) as the "women and children first rescue doctrine"), which weakens the claim that LLM annotations carry genuine domain meaning rather than post-hoc rationalization. - No evaluation on wide or high-dimensional tabular data despite scalability being a headline motivation; the largest raw feature count tested is 36. - The Kaggle comparison (Figure 3) includes only OpenFE as a baseline and reports average 2.5pp improvement from a figure whose exact scores are not tabulated, making it hard to verify. - Gains on Credit-g and Ailerons are not significant and CAAFE beats the method on Credit-g; the abstract's framing of general superiority papers over this. - The data-leakage/hallucination-free architectural claims (Appendix L) are stated categorically without an adversarial test (e.g., injecting biased or contaminated features to see whether the pipeline propagates them). Bottom Line A practitioner working on LLM-assisted tabular feature engineering gains a concrete, well-benchmarked design pattern — ground the LLM in symbolic-regression output and cap it at a refinement role — that is worth adopting or at least benchmarking against, but the interpretability and hallucination guarantees that motivate the paper remain asserted rather than demonstrated, so treat those claims as hypotheses to test in your own domain.

When Privacy Hurts Mergeability: Geometry-Aware Model Merging under Differential Privacy

J Liu, J Liu, N Xi, Y Miao, D Wei, K Cheng, J Ma · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DP-Merging, a differentially private fine-tuning framework that modifies the training of task models so that the released private models remain mergeable in parameter space, and identifies the two geometric properties (local sharpness and reference drift) that DP degrades. - Why it's important: Model merging lets parties combine task models without sharing private data, but naive DP fine-tuning destroys merge compatibility — on ViT-B/32 at ε=4, weight averaging drops from 79.7% (individual DP models) to 46.0% merged accuracy — so anyone deploying privacy-preserving multi-task merging currently faces a ~30-point penalty. - How it does it: It applies two interventions during DP fine-tuning — a sharpness-aware objective built from clipped noisy gradients (two privatized gradient evaluations per iteration, jointly RDP-accounted) and an L2 anchor to the public pretrained initialization (privacy-free as post-processing of public quantities) — targeting the curvature and displacement terms of a second-order merge-gap bound. - The good: The gains are consistent across six merging operators, three ViT backbones, RoBERTa-Base/Large on GLUE, and four privacy budgets, and are largest exactly where the theory predicts — under the tightest privacy (e.g., +6.1 points at ε=1 vs. +4.6 at ε=4 on ViT-B/32 with TIES-Merging). - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; there is no evidence that DP-Merging preserves (rather than trades away) individual model utility before merging; and a direct comparison to non-private merge-aware fine-tuning (e.g., sharpness-aware merging of Lee et al. 2025, cited as [20]) is absent. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on model merging, DP fine-tuning, or their intersection — the geometric diagnosis is the real contribution — but skip it if you want large-scale (LLM-scale) validation or deployment-ready tooling; it is a preprint with no released code.
Why this rank

Novelty (72) is genuinely decent (NEW PROBLEM framing of mergeability under DP with a sound paired-Gaussian privacy accounting), and the geometric diagnosis earns Non-Obviousness (75). Impact (50) is low: a recipe in paper form with 2× training cost unquantified and no released artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*50 = 65.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations fine-tuning foundation models on private task data want to combine task models via parameter-space merging without centralizing data. Even though merging is data-free, released task weights leak information about fine-tuning data, so each task model must be trained under differential privacy before release. The paper shows empirically that DP fine-tuning (gradient clipping + Gaussian noise) degrades not just individual model accuracy but specifically the geometric compatibility needed for merging: private task models sit in sharper loss basins (local sharpness) and drift farther from the shared pretrained initialization (reference drift), so interpolation or averaging across tasks incurs large loss increases. Prior merging work assumes non-private models; prior DP fine-tuning work optimizes only for single-model utility. The gap is that nobody had characterized or repaired mergeability under privacy constraints. Key Idea: The core insight is that the merge gap — the loss increase when replacing a task model with the merged model — decomposes (via second-order expansion) into a curvature term (local sharpness around each task solution) times a displacement-squared term, and both terms are specifically inflated by DP. Therefore, the fix belongs in the private fine-tuning stage, not in a new merging operator: make each private solution flatter (robust to displacement) and keep task vectors short (small displacement), while the merging step itself stays a privacy post-processing operation. Methodology: Each task runs DP-SAM-style fine-tuning from the shared pretrained model w0. Per iteration: (1) compute the clipped noisy gradient g̃ on a Poisson-sampled minibatch; (2) construct an ascent perturbation ε = ρ·g̃/‖g̃‖ along that gradient; (3) compute a second clipped noisy gradient h̃ at w+ε; (4) update with w ← w − η(h̃ + 2λ(w − w0)), where the anchor term depends only on public w0 and is privacy-free. The two gradient queries are composed as a paired Gaussian mechanism (sensitivity √2·C) under Rényi DP with Poisson subsampling; perturbation construction, anchoring, and final weight averaging are post-processing. Theoretically, Theorem 5.2 bounds the average merge gap by εt‖Δt‖ + (βt/2)‖Δt‖² + (Mt/6)‖Δt‖³, and the anchor yields ‖wt − w0‖ ≤ (Gt+ζt)/(2λ), coupling the two interventions to the bound. Critical design decisions: (a) performing sharpness-aware training on already-noised gradients (justified by the paired-mechanism privacy analysis, though it doubles the per-iteration private gradient cost); (b) anchoring to w0 rather than to a task centroid (justified because it needs no cross-task communication); (c) fixing ρ=0.05, λ=0.05 uniformly across all tasks and backbones — justified only by the sensitivity tables, which show flat optima near these values but no per-task tuning study. Key Results: On the 8-task vision benchmark (SUN397, Cars, RESISC45, EuroSAT, SVHN, GTSRB, MNIST, DTD) at ε=4 with ViT-B/32, DP-Merging improves merged average accuracy for every operator: TIES-Merging 57.5%→62.1%, WUDI 56.5%→60.8%, Task Arithmetic 54.2%→58.1%, Weight Averaging 46.0%→49.7%. With ViT-L/14 the gains grow (TIES 58.1%→62.7%; weight averaging 51.6%→57.3%). On GLUE with RoBERTa-Large at ε=4, averages range 73.9–77.0 for DP-Merging vs. 71.6–74.7 for naive DP across operators (e.g., WUDI 74.7→77.0). Across budgets ε∈{1,2,4,8} with TIES-Merging, gains shrink as ε loosens (visual: +6.1 at ε=1, +4.7 at ε=8; language: +3.8 at ε=1, +1.5 at ε=8), matching the diagnosis that DP distortion is the target. Ablations (Table 5) show both components contribute (e.g., TIES: 57.5 naive → 60.7 w/o alignment → 59.8 w/o flatness → 62.1 full). Merged models still trail the DP individual reference (62.1% vs. 79.7% for the best configuration), so merging recovers only part of the multi-task gap. Baselines are current (WUDI-Merging, PCB 2024; TIES 2023) and all are given identical DP budgets and merging hyperparameters — a fair protocol. All results are at standard benchmark scale (ViT up to L/14, RoBERTa-Large), not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (characterizing mergeability degradation under DP) plus NEW METHOD (a merge-aware private fine-tuning framework) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (DP inflates sharpness and reference drift, with gains inversely proportional to ε). The genuinely novel part is the problem framing and the coupling of DP accounting with sharpness-aware training for mergeability; the components themselves are standard — SAM-style sharpness-aware training (including a DP-SAM variant, Park et al. 2023, cited as [27]) and L2-anchoring familiar from lp-ft-style regularization — applied to a new setting, with the merge-gap bound being a competent Taylor-expansion argument rather than a deep theoretical result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations isolate each component, hyperparameter sensitivity is reported for ρ and λ, robustness across six merging operators and four privacy budgets is demonstrated, and the privacy accounting (paired subsampled Gaussian, RDP composition) is worked out in the appendix. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; all headline numbers appear to be single-run. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. The merge-gap diagnostic (interpolation loss landscapes, sharpness, drift measurements) is measured only on the authors' own selected tasks. One methodological concern: the method and its hyperparameters are developed and evaluated on the same 8-task vision benchmark used throughout, and the loose upper-bound theorem is presented as an explanation without any quantitative fit of the bound to observed gaps. The main empirical claim that DP-Merging does not sacrifice individual-model utility is not directly tested — the "DP + Individual" row is for naive DP fine-tuning, not for DP-Merged-style fine-tuned models evaluated individually. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent training recipe but no released artifact). - Practical: Yes — implemented with Opacus on NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs with models up to ViT-L/14 and RoBERTa-Large, all commercially accessible hardware. - Efficient: Roughly 2× training compute versus standard DP fine-tuning because each iteration performs two privatized gradient evaluations (plus one extra forward pass at the perturbed point), a cost the paper never quantifies in wall-clock terms. - Effective: The evidence shows it substantially narrows — but does not close — the merged-vs-individual gap (best merged 62.1% vs. 79.7% individual on ViT-B/32), so it solves the relative mergeability problem, not the absolute multi-task utility problem. - Scalable: Untested beyond ~350M-parameter encoders; claims about larger models or heterogeneous architectures are explicitly deferred to future work, and the 2× private-gradient cost could compound badly at LLM scale. The work delivers a recipe (Algorithm 1) and analysis in paper form only; no library, code, or trained weights are released. Strengths: - The geometric diagnosis is the real contribution: decomposing the merge gap into curvature × displacement, then measuring both quantities (Figure 3) as functions of the privacy budget, turns a vague "DP hurts merging" observation into a testable, actionable mechanism. - The intervention placement is well argued: by modifying only the private fine-tuning stage and keeping merging as post-processing, the method composes with any data-free merging operator and provably inherits the underlying DP guarantee — validated empirically across six operators rather than one cherry-picked rule. - The privacy analysis is non-trivial and done correctly: the two adaptive gradient queries per iteration are jointly accounted as a paired subsampled Gaussian mechanism (√2·C sensitivity), including the reverse-direction bound — a step many applied DP papers would hand-wave. - The empirical trend that gains grow as ε tightens (+6.1 at ε=1 vs. +4.6 at ε=4) is a falsifiable prediction of the mechanism, not just an aggregate improvement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The appendix (Section D) states: (1) performance on highly heterogeneous tasks or substantially different architectures is unexplored; (2) experiments cover only standard benchmarks and mid-to-large models (ViT-L/14, RoBERTa-Large), leaving larger models and real-world datasets untested; (3) per-task results vary, with some tasks showing marginal or slightly negative changes. The authors confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. They do not acknowledge the doubled training cost, the absence of variance reporting, or the untested effect on individual model utility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The most important unstated assumption: DP-Merging's sharpness-aware and anchored objectives plausibly reduce individual task-model accuracy (both are known to trade off standalone fit), yet the paper never reports DP-Merging-trained models evaluated individually — so the +2 to +6 point merging gains could partially reflect a utility-for-mergeability trade hidden from the reader. The dogs-not-barking signal: Figure 3 shows DP-Merging reduces sharpness and drift, but no table shows standalone DP-Merging accuracy against "DP + Individual." - No comparison against non-private merge-aware fine-tuning baselines — Lee et al. 2025 (sharpness-aware merging, cited as [20]) is the obvious direct competitor for the flatness component, and applying it under DP is the natural baseline the paper omits. - Single-run results with no seeds or confidence intervals: several reported gains (e.g., +1.3 for weight averaging on RoBERTa-Large) are within plausible seed noise for GLUE tasks. - The uniform hyperparameters (ρ=0.05, λ=0.05) across all tasks and backbones are convenient for fair comparison but the sensitivity tables show the optimum shifts with backbone (e.g., λ=0.05 vs. 0.01 across tables), suggesting hidden tuning variance. - The merge-gap bound is loose and post-hoc: no experiment fits the bound's terms to measured gaps, so the theory explains direction, not magnitude. - Only full fine-tuning of encoders is tested; the interaction with LoRA/PEFT-based DP fine-tuning (the practical default for large models) is unexamined, despite the authors' own prior work on private LoRA. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on privacy-preserving multi-task model deployment gains a genuinely useful diagnosis (sharpness and drift as the levers of DP-induced mergeability loss) and a simple, privacy-sound recipe that reliably buys 2–6 points of merged accuracy, but should read it as a well-executed combination of SAM and L2-anchoring in a new setting — verify the individual-utility trade-off and training-cost overhead themselves before adopting it, since the paper does not.

POLYFLOW: A Neuro- Symbolic Framework for Static Cross-Language Information Flow Analysis

H Yang, Z Zhong, J Guo, H Cai · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces POLYFLOW, a neuro-symbolic static information flow analyzer for Python–C and Java–C systems that inverts the usual LLM-agent pattern — a Joern-based static analyzer acts as controller and invokes an LLM "expert panel" only for the 19 hard language features (decorators, function pointers, reflection, macros, etc.) that break conventional analysis — and delivers xFlowBench, the first cross-language micro-benchmark with ground-truth flow facts. - Why it's important: Multilingual software (PyTorch, Android, JNI systems) harbors cross-language vulnerabilities rooted in semantic mismatches and implicit flows that language-siloed static analyzers, coverage-limited dynamic tools, and generalizing learning-based detectors all miss, leaving real systems exposed. - How it does it: It builds a cross-language interprocedural CFG (CICFG), augments it via fixed-point iterative feature handling where LLMs inject missing nodes/edges, then uses control-flow-reachability taint approximation followed by function-by-function LLM refinement with two cheap non-reasoning models cross-validated and a reasoning model arbitrating disagreements, with static facts used to check LLM outputs. - The good: It found 17 previously unknown cross-language vulnerabilities across 9 real projects (one assigned CVE-2025-55562, one fixed upstream), none found by any baseline, with 91.8% F1 on the micro-bench and 76.8% precision on real systems. - The missing: The quantitative comparison includes only one learning-based baseline (xLoc, which detected zero paths); strong static cross-language baselines (MultiQL, AXA, JNIFER) are discussed only qualitatively, and the evaluation contains internal inconsistencies (ablation text cites 272 true positives where Table 6 reports 454; one ablation precision of 160%). - Read it or not: Worth reading for program-analysis and LLM-assisted-analysis researchers — the analyzer-as-controller pattern is a genuinely useful inversion of current agentic designs — but practitioners seeking a deployable cross-language scanner should note the ~12.9-hour average runtime per project.

Problem & Motivation Modern systems increasingly couple a host language (Python, Java) with native C via FFIs, and the language boundary creates cross-language vulnerabilities: tainted data sourced in one language reaches a sink in another, often through implicit flows induced by features like Python decorators/reflection, Java virtual dispatch, or C function pointers/macros. Existing defenses each fail differently: language-specific static analyzers operate in silos and choke on hard features (breaking intra-language flow segments, hence the cross-language path); static cross-language frameworks (MultiQL, AXA, JNIFER, CSS) need per-language mature infrastructure and handcrafted interop rules; dynamic tools (PolyCruise, PolyFuzz) only find bugs exercised by tests, which are scarce in multilingual projects; learning-based detectors (xLoc) fail to generalize beyond training bug patterns. The authors' motivating study of open-source projects and tooling (Joern, CodeQL, Infer, SonarQube, Clang) identified 19 features across Python, Java, and C that cause missing nodes or edges in control-flow representations, and their prevalence study shows these features are routine, not edge cases (e.g., first-class functions in 10/14 Python-C projects, reflection in 87% of Java-C projects, conditional compilation in 80%). Key Idea The core insight is an inversion of the prevailing neuro-symbolic architecture: instead of an LLM-centric agent calling symbolic tools, a traditional static analyzer is the controller that (1) builds an approximate cross-language CFG from explicit flows only, (2) invokes LLMs in minimal, statically-determined scopes (a function or feature-presence unit) exactly where hard features defeat symbolic reasoning, and (3) re-integrates LLM outputs as graph facts (new CICFG edges/nodes, expanded taint sets) subject to static fact-checking and multi-LLM negotiated agreement. A secondary mechanism is the two-phase precision ladder: cheap control-flow reachability from sources to sinks over-approximates candidate paths, so expensive per-function LLM taint reasoning is spent only on structurally feasible source–sink pairs. Methodology Phase 1 (Augmented Control Flow): Joern produces per-function CFGs, which are stitched into per-language call graphs and merged with FFI-mediated inter-language edges to form a CICFG. A fixed-point worklist algorithm (Algorithm 1) runs 18 dedicated feature handlers (the 19th, recursion, is native to Joern); each handler follows a detect → identify missing nodes/edges → augment pattern, with a feature-dependency mapping triggering re-runs of related handlers until convergence (e.g., resolving a function pointer target may expose new macro expansions). Phase 2 (Feature-Oriented Data Flow): for each user-specified (or LLM-extracted) source–sink pair, the CICFG is sliced to control-flow-reachable subgraphs (directed taint approximation), then functions along each path are traversed one at a time with an accumulated taint set; feature handlers and the expert panel (prompted with the function snippet and current taint set, few-shot templates per feature) extend the taint set with aliases and implicit flows until the sink is reached or the path dies (Algorithm 2). The expert panel runs two non-reasoning LLMs and escalates disagreements to a reasoning LLM as arbiter (temperature 0). Objective is not a loss function but a detection task: report source-to-sink taint paths. Critical design decisions: (1) LLM scoping to single functions/FPUs — justified by token limits and hallucination reduction, though it sacrifices interprocedural semantic context the authors acknowledge is delegated to the static controller; (2) fixed-point feature iteration — justified by transitive feature interactions; (3) control-flow-only approximation before refinement — justified for scalability, a standard over-approximation/refinement trade-off. Key Results On xFlowBench (104 micro-benchmarks, 198 data points covering 19 features), the expert panel achieved 97.9% precision, 87.3% recall, 91.8% F1 for implicit flow identification. On 29 real projects (1.5K–1,363K LOC; 14 Python-C, 15 Java-C), POLYFLOW reported 591 paths with 454 true positives at 76.8% overall precision (100% on five projects), with source identification precision averaging 80% (Python-C) / 83% (Java-C) and sink precision 95% / 93%. The sole quantitative baseline, learning-based xLoc, detected zero vulnerability paths on all projects. Ablations: disabling feature-oriented data flow drops precision to 31.8%; disabling CICFG augmentation drops true positives to 348 (−23%); disabling the expert panel yields 375 TPs at 73.8% precision. Efficiency: 12.86 hours and 482.5 MB peak memory per project on average (worst outlier ~2 GB for pyo), 2.81M tokens average, per-query latency 2.5–2.7 s; runtime is dominated by the LLM-driven steps. Bug discovery: 17 previously unknown vulnerabilities across 9 projects (bounter, pygit2, aubio, ultrajson, Japronto, bitarray, Cvxopt, LWJGL, Jep) — types include heap OOB read, format string, unchecked allocation/DoS, arbitrary memory write — one assigned CVE-2025-55562, one fixed upstream; MultiQL, PolyCruise, PolyFuzz, and xLoc found none of them. Test scale is genuinely real-world (subjects up to 1.36M LOC). Note: reported numbers contain inconsistencies (Section 6.3 states full POLYFLOW found 272 TPs where Table 6 reports 454; ablation Table 10 shows a 160% precision for simplejson; Table 13 lists 18 bugs against the claimed 17; Java-C Phase 2 Step 1 timing duplicates Phase 1 Step 2 values in Table 11). Novelty Classification NEW METHOD + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK: the genuinely novel elements are the analyzer-controlled (rather than LLM-controlled) neuro-symbolic architecture with scoped, fact-checked LLM augmentation of a cross-language CFG, the systematic catalog of 19 flow-breaking features with dedicated handlers, and xFlowBench as the first ground-truth cross-language information-flow micro-benchmark. The individual ingredients — Joern ICFGs, worklist fixpoints, few-shot LLM prompting, multi-LLM voting, taint slicing — are standard; the contribution is their integration and the inversion of control, which is more than a straightforward combination but built from known parts. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are present and isolate all three components (ACF, FDF, EP) with per-project results. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, though temperature 0 partially stabilizes LLM behavior; LLM nondeterminism across API versions is unaddressed. The paper claims an open-source implementation and artifact package, but no URL or repository identifier appears in the provided text. Methodological concerns: (1) the micro-benchmark evaluation is on the authors' own xFlowBench, developed alongside the tool — feature handlers were designed against the same feature taxonomy the benchmark tests, a Goodhart risk; (2) the only quantitative baseline is xLoc, a learning-based method that predictably fails, while the strongest static competitors (MultiQL, AXA, JNIFER, CSS) receive only qualitative discussion; (3) recall on real-world projects is never measured (no ground truth), so only precision is reported there; (4) the numeric inconsistencies listed under Key Results (272 vs. 454 TPs, 160% precision, duplicated timing rows) suggest rushed assembly that a camera-ready must fix; (5) 16 of 18 reported bugs are "pending" — exploitability was confirmed for only a minority. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built, evaluated analysis tool). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single workstation (Threadripper 3970X, one RTX 3090, 256 GB RAM) with commodity LLM APIs; no special infrastructure. - Efficient: Costly relative to conventional analyzers — ~12.9 h and ~2.8M tokens per project, dominated by LLM steps — acceptable for offline audit, prohibitive for CI/CD. - Effective: Yes for the stated problem: 76.8% precision on real code and 17 novel vulnerabilities with a CVE constitute direct evidence, not merely proxy metrics, though 20–30% reported paths are false positives requiring triage. - Scalable: Tested up to 1.36M LOC with stable per-query latency and precision across project sizes, but the paper claims rather than demonstrates behavior beyond that; LLM costs grow with codebase size (15M tokens for pytables) and could become a bottleneck at 10× scale. The work delivers a software artifact (an open-source tool with pluggable LLM interface, modular feature handlers, and the xFlowBench dataset), not just a paper. Strengths - The control inversion — static analyzer as controller, LLMs as scoped, on-demand oracles whose outputs are re-integrated into a symbolic representation and fact-checked — is a substantive and transferable architectural idea, contrasting with LLM-agent-first designs like IRIS or LLift. - The 19-feature taxonomy (Table 1/2) with per-feature detection cues and augmentation patterns is a reusable empirical contribution grounded in a motivating study of real projects and tool behavior, and the prevalence study (RQ1) demonstrates these features are routine in real multilingual code. - End-to-end validation on 29 real repositories with security-community-facing outcomes (a CVE assignment, an upstream fix, 17 novel bugs invisible to four different baseline families) — evidence that survives contact with practice rather than only micro-benchmarks. - xFlowBench fills a real evaluation void: no prior cross-language static-analysis benchmark with ground-truth flow facts existed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and at reasonable length (Sections 4.2 and 7.2): dependence on LLM accuracy and hallucination risk despite the expert panel; sensitivity to source/sink definition quality; support restricted to Python–C and Java–C via FFI only (non-FFI interfacing uncaptured); inherited Joern parsing limitations; computational cost with long runtimes on very large systems as a deliberate rigor–speed trade-off; reports requiring manual exploitability validation; and non-trivial per-language-pair engineering to extend. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The expert-panel ablation (375 TPs at 73.8% without EP vs. the full system) suggests the panel's marginal contribution is smaller than the narrative implies; per-component attribution is muddied by the 272-vs-454 TP inconsistency. - No comparison of LLM-driven feature handling against handcrafted rule-based handling of the same 19 features — a cheap ablation that would show whether LLMs are actually necessary or whether deterministic handlers (e.g., CHA, which the polymorphism handler already falls back to) suffice. - Soundness is never quantified on real code: the 87.3% recall comes only from the authors' own micro-bench; nothing measures what fraction of real flows the LLM augmentation misses. - The static baseline gap is a dogs-not-barking omission: MultiQL, AXA, and JNIFER are analyzed only through anecdote, leaving the claim of superiority over "various kinds of SOTA baselines" quantitatively supported only against the weakest baseline class. - LLM nondeterminism, model identity/version, and cost sensitivity to model choice are unreported; it is unclear whether results hold across model generations. - Ground truth for the 591 real-project paths appears to be the authors' own manual validation, i.e., self-adjudicated precision. Bottom Line A practitioner or researcher working on multilingual program analysis or LLM-assisted static analysis gains real value here — a credible inverted neuro-symbolic design, a usable benchmark, and CVE-backed evidence that it finds bugs current tools miss — but the weak static baselines, own-benchmark micro-evaluation, and internal numeric inconsistencies mean the headline comparisons should be read as directional rather than definitive.

Problem & Motivation Practitioners training LLM agents with RL face two coupled bottlenecks on open-ended tasks like deep research and travel planning: (1) a data–evaluation bottleneck — expert rubric annotation is expensive, and existing open-ended benchmarks are static post-hoc testbeds with no training data; (2) an optimization bottleneck — long-horizon, multi-turn tool-use tasks yield brittle rewards, causing advantage collapse where rollout groups provide weak contrast and policy learning stalls at local refinement. Off-policy distillation from a fixed teacher compounds distribution mismatch across tool-use turns (a failure mode the authors cite from OPCD), and blind imitation can ingest wrong tool choices or missed constraints. The target audience is teams training open-ended agents without large human-labeled corpora. Key Idea Use a self-generated rubric as the interface between task construction and policy optimization, made trustworthy by two mechanisms: (a) tool-grounded rubric construction — the Generator must observe real tool outputs before writing tool-dependent criteria (binary gate R_tool), preventing hallucinated supervision; and (b) reward-gated self-distillation — a teacher built from the same policy conditioned on coach memory is trusted only when its rollouts empirically beat standard rollouts (Δr > τ), then internalized via reverse KL on on-policy trajectories. The triangle-shaped difficulty reward (maximal at ~50% Solver success) supplies an automatic curriculum. The gating insight is the most non-obvious element: nearly one-third of coach memories are neutral or harmful (8.3% negative, 19.6% ambiguous), so unconditional self-distillation amplifies noise. Methodology Three stages. (1) Global co-evolution: the Generator samples a query q and rubric set ρ under strict JSON format prompts, rewarded R_G = R_tool·R_fmt·(1+R_diff), where R_diff = 2·max(0, 1 − |c − K/2|/(K/2)) with c = number of successful Solver rollouts out of K=8 (γ=0.9 threshold). The Solver is optimized with group-based RL (G=16 rollouts, up to 40 tool rounds) on r_S = 0.8·s_i + 0.2·I[s_i=1], where s_i is the LLM-judged rubric satisfaction rate. (2) RG-SED: a coach LLM summarizes group feedback into role-specific memory m_a; the same policy conditioned on p_a ⊕ m_a acts as a transient teacher; if Δr = R̄_m − R̄_s > τ (τ=0.05, λ_0=0.5 with warm-up/decay schedules), token-level reverse KL is applied on on-policy standard trajectories with stop-gradient through the teacher distribution; final loss L_a = L_RL + λ_t·L_SED per role. (3) Training runs three co-evolution cycles with pool refresh every 120 steps, 500 deduplicated queries per refresh, and in-context negatives to combat query homogenization. Critical design decisions: the triangle difficulty reward (justified by the argument that boundary tasks maximize group reward variance); gate-before-distill (justified by the w/o-reward-gating ablation and the 8.3% harmful-memory statistic); and same-policy teacher to bound student–teacher divergence (empirically supported: RG-SED's D_KL stays ≈0.2–0.35 vs GKD's ≈0.4–0.55). Judge consistency with 3-human majority vote is 82.3% (ECR-DeepResearch) and 77.9% (ECR-Travel). Key Results On Qwen3.5-9B, ARISE-RL reaches avg 0.569 across four benchmarks (ResearchRubrics 0.479, ECR-DeepResearch 0.781, VitaBench 0.417, ECR-Travel 0.599), exceeding Claude-4.6-Sonnet (0.495), Gemini3-Pro (0.494), GPT-5.2 (0.442), and Qwen3.5-397B (0.508); gains hold on Qwen3-8B (0.267 → 0.358). Same-backbone self-evolution baselines trail: Dr. Zero 0.531, Absolute Zero 0.508 (re-implemented under identical judge/tool stacks — current, fair comparisons). Against on-policy distillation baselines OPCD and GKD (teacher = Qwen3.5-397B), RG-SED wins on all eleven benchmark axes. Ablations on Qwen3.5-9B: removing RG-SED costs 0.057–0.081 avg points (largest component), removing the gate costs ~0.05, tool-grounded rubric and difficulty-shaped reward each ~0.02–0.05. Automated Synthesis of Cloud Emulators

A Bhatnagar, Z Yang, S McClure, Y Qiu, S Ratnasamy… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces CLOUDEMU, a neurosymbolic pipeline that automatically synthesizes cloud emulators from provider documentation and aligns them against the live cloud as an oracle, producing working emulators for AWS EC2 (88k lines of generated code, 90 resource types) and GCP Compute Engine (65k lines, 91 resource types). - Why it's important: Manual emulator construction cannot keep pace with the cloud's API surface — the leading emulator LocalStack covers only ~35% of APIs across four popular AWS services after 10+ years and 800+ contributors — forcing DevOps teams into costly, risky testing against real clouds. - How it does it: It compiles documentation into a symbolic resource index, constrains LLM code generation within a pre-built state-machine scaffolding (so the LLM only fills semantic "holes" in a typed template), then runs differential testing between emulator and real cloud and applies symbolic-then-LLM repair to close behavioral gaps. - The good: The ablation is convincing and quantified: on 267 CLI cases, accuracy climbs from 76%/42%/36% (direct-to-code) to 98%/94%/93% (error class/response/state consistency) as each component is added, and the Terraform gains are even larger (state consistency 4% → 80-100%). - The missing: Evaluation is confined to one service per provider (EC2, GCE) with modest test suites (50 CLI + 50 Terraform vs. AWS; 45 Terraform cases vs. GCP), no error bars or repeated runs, and no evidence the approach works on the other ~235 AWS services or non-state-machine-style APIs. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-assisted systems synthesis, DevOps tooling, or specification-driven code generation — it is the clearest published demonstration that structured symbolic scaffolds plus oracle alignment beat both hand-built emulators and naive LLM generation; skip it if you only need cloud testing results at large scale, which it does not deliver.

Problem & Motivation: DevOps engineers manage cloud infrastructure through CLI/SDK scripts and IaC frameworks (Terraform, etc.) that invoke cloud APIs; testing these programs against the real cloud is metered, slow, and risky, while emulators that mock APIs locally are incomplete and drift out of date. The pain point is well-quantified: AWS has 240+ services with EC2 alone exposing 756 APIs (Table 1), AWS ships ~3,000 API changes per year, and LocalStack emulates only ~35% of APIs across four sampled services. Low coverage is combinatorially punishing (one missing API breaks a whole DevOps program), and low accuracy is dangerous — e.g., LocalStack wrongly succeeds at DeleteVpc with an attached Internet Gateway where real AWS returns "DependencyViolation". Multi-cloud deployments multiply the manual effort per provider. The gap this closes is a construction method whose cost scales with documentation, not engineering headcount, and which tracks the moving target via re-synthesis. Key Idea: Cloud resources are naturally modeled as a hierarchy of interacting state machines, and cloud documentation is correspondingly structured and paginated along resource/API boundaries — so the emulator-building task decomposes into (1) symbolic parsing of documentation into a resource dependency index, (2) LLM code generation confined to filling typed holes in a pre-written state-machine template, and (3) treating the real cloud as an oracle for differential testing and repair. The core move is restricting the LLM to per-resource semantic inference inside a symbolic scaffold, suppressing hallucination by construction, with alignment closing residual gaps from ambiguous or incomplete prose. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Documentation wrangling: a symbolic parser (1.2k LOC) decomposes documentation at service/resource/API boundaries into a resource index whose nodes are attribute maps (canonical keys like AWS:EC2:VPC, mixing symbolic API signatures with textual descriptions) and whose edges are strict/optional cross-resource dependencies derived from API parameter analysis. (2) Code synthesis (~7k LOC framework): a provider-agnostic state-machine template (states + transitions) is instantiated per node via an index traversal, parents before children; explicit state variables and API I/O schemas are compiled symbolically, while transition bodies are generated by an LLM inside a "check-and-fix" loop that iterates until symbolic invariants hold (correct I/O types, dependency-empty-before-delete constraints, naming conventions). (3) Automated alignment: test cases are generated by combining per-API symbolic execution (path constraints as coverage targets) with LLM-authored CLI/Terraform programs; traces from emulator and cloud are aligned by matching API calls on logical resources to suppress noise (generated IDs, timestamps, latency reordering); discrepancies are classified into MISSING_FIELD / EXTRA_FIELD / VALUE_MISMATCH / STATUS_MISMATCH, patched first by symbolic passes (response seeding, format repair) then by LLM repair with re-localization, with stalling cases escalated to the OpenHands coding agent. Coverage-guided test selection via greedy set-cover over branch targets is evaluated as an alternative to scraped cases. There is no explicit global objective function; correctness is operationalized as three fidelity levels (L0 error-class parity, L1 response-field fidelity, L2 state consistency) measured on held-out test traces. Key Results: Versus real AWS on 50 CLI + 50 Terraform cases: CLOUDEMU achieves 100% API coverage on the sampled cases versus ~70% case coverage for LocalStack, and beats LocalStack on all three fidelity levels for both CLI and Terraform (LocalStack matches error-class parity on simple CLI cases but the gap widens on Terraform, where LocalStack accepts dependency violations). The 267-case CLI ablation shows D2C → Index → SM → Full scores of 76→87→91→98 (error class), 42→57→58→94 (response fidelity), 36→54→57→93 (state consistency); on 63 Terraform cases, 78→79→95→97, 0→0→84→100, and 4→0→82→80. The state-machine scaffold alone fixes response-format errors completely and cuts VPC API signature mismatches from 29.9% to 9%. Alignment against LocalStack-guided targets costs 21 s/case (3.4k tokens) versus 126 s/case (4.1k tokens) against real AWS; synthesis costs 52 s and 478k tokens per resource (~1.3 h total for EC2); half of patches touch <84 lines and finish in <30 s, with a long tail (top 10% >246 lines, >180 s). Coverage-guided test generation exercises 88% more unique APIs and finds 2.5× the discrepancy yield of scraped cases at a 50-case budget. On GCP Compute (45 Terraform cases, 18 resource types), alignment lifts accuracy from 0.644/0.571/0.545 to 0.956/0.857/0.734 across the three levels. Weaker LLMs (GPT 5.1, 5.2-mini) show no visible accuracy drop versus larger models, which the authors attribute to the symbolic scaffold. Baselines are the de-facto standard emulator (LocalStack/Moto) and a direct-LLM-prompting ablation; no other synthesis baselines (e.g., Floci) are quantitatively compared, only cited as suffering fidelity problems. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a credible NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING that symbolic scaffolding lets even small LLMs synthesize large stateful systems. The genuinely novel elements are the documentation-to-resource-index compilation and the closed loop of cloud-as-oracle differential testing driving LLM repair of a synthesized emulator; the ingredients (spec mining, active automata learning à la Hermes, neurosymbolic constrained decoding, program repair) are existing ideas, but the paper's claim to be the first end-to-end LLM translation of API documentation into an executable hierarchical state-machine emulator for cloud services is plausible. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and each component demonstrably matters (the Index and SM steps carry most of the gain), and the main AWS comparison uses held-out test cases separate from the alignment set — a design choice the authors state explicitly. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; the 330-case ablation uses LocalStack — a system built from the same documentation — as the alignment oracle (a partial Goodhart risk, though the headline AWS comparison avoids it); test suites are small (50+50 AWS, 45 GCP) and partly scraped rather than systematically sampled; the "100% API coverage" claim is scoped to randomly chosen cases rather than a full API audit. No code, data, or emulator artifact release is mentioned in the paper. The implementation is described in enough detail (12.4k LOC breakdown, per-resource LLM call counts, model names) that reproduction is plausible if an artifact is released, but none is verifiable from the text. A minor internal inconsistency (EC2 described as exposing "up to 200 APIs" in §1 but 756 in Table 1 and "upward of 500" in §2.1) slightly undermines the quantitative framing. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built pipeline producing a deployed tool, evaluated empirically). Practical: Yes — the emulator runs as a local Flask-gated instance consumable by standard CLI/Terraform workflows, and needs only commercial LLM API access. Efficient: Synthesis is cheap (~1.3 h, ~478k tokens/resource); AWS-guided alignment is the expensive part at 126 s/case plus real-cloud invocation and cleanup costs. Effective: Within the tested scope (EC2/GCE, three fidelity levels on hundreds of cases) it clearly outperforms the incumbent, but evidence covers a proxy subset of the cloud, not the full service catalog where its coverage claim matters most. Scalable: Not tested beyond two services; scaling to all 240 AWS services is claimed via the index-traversal design but never demonstrated, and cross-service state interactions (the paper's own GCP network-peering failure case suggests the per-resource scaffold may not compose everywhere) remain unvalidated at scale. The deliverable is a system + generated emulators described in the paper; no public artifact release is stated. Strengths: - The core intellectual contribution — using a resource-agnostic state-machine scaffold so the LLM only infers semantics for small, local text fragments while symbolic code handles interfaces, schemas, and dependency invariants — is well-motivated and directly validated by the ablation (e.g., Terraform response fidelity jumping from 0% to 84% when the scaffold is added). - The cloud-as-oracle alignment loop is a genuinely closed feedback design: it detects divergence from noisy traces, localizes the root-cause API, classifies the mismatch, and applies symbolic-before-neural repair, with error-class breakdowns (Table 3) showing the two oracles expose complementary fault classes. - The generalization result is earned, not asserted: the same pipeline transfers to GCP with only template-layer changes (Operation objects, string IDs, JSON errors), and the GCP failures are diagnosed at the level of specific mechanism gaps. - Honest framing of what emulators cannot do (latency, rate limits, concurrency semantics), which sharpens the contribution's scope rather than blurring it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the emulator ignores performance characteristics (latency, rate limits, network behavior) and failure injection, ruling out chaos engineering and performance testing; that concurrency and consistency properties are not simulated; and that emulators are third-party efforts because providers prioritize real features. They also note the GCP network-peering failure requiring bidirectional state updates outside the per-resource scaffold. These are confronted directly in §5, which is a credibility positive; the limitations of the evaluation scale (single service per provider, small test suites) are, by contrast, not explicitly confronted. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The headline "outperforms LocalStack, built by a large team over a decade" comparison covers one AWS service; LocalStack's documented weak spot is other services, so the breadth claim is inferred, not measured. (2) The ablation's oracle (LocalStack) is itself derived from the same documentation the system consumes, so ablation fidelity numbers partially measure agreement between two documentation readers — the authors partially acknowledge this via the error-class breakdown but not the circularity itself. (3) No comparison against one-shot LLM synthesis with a coding agent (Floci is dismissed with a citation, no numbers). (4) The claim that weaker models suffice rests on one experiment with three frontier models of unspecified variance; a single-seed comparison cannot support a robust conclusion. (5) Whether the approach handles non-CRUD-style APIs (streaming, asynchronous workflows, services without clean state-machine structure) is untested and unacknowledged. (6) Test suites mix scraped and authored cases with unclear sampling frames, making the fidelity percentages hard to extrapolate. (7) No released artifact is mentioned, which for a systems paper substantially limits verification and uptake. Bottom Line: A practitioner building developer tooling or working on LLM-driven program synthesis should read this — the scaffold-constrained-generation-plus-oracle-alignment recipe is transferable and the ablation evidence is real — but anyone needing a production emulator beyond EC2/GCE, or a reproducible artifact, will find the current paper stops well short of its own coverage ambitions.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Agent-G2, a hint-based RL framework that draws the expert-trajectory guidance depth per task from a Gaussian whose center and spread are estimated online from rollouts already collected for GRPO, requiring no probe rollouts or learned depth predictor. - Why it's important: Reward sparsity in long-horizon agent tasks makes exploration from the initial state fail, and existing hint-depth schedulers either share one depth across heterogeneous tasks (misallocating >60% of assignments) or pay 3–5× extra rollout cost for per-sample probing. - How it does it: The core move is replacing the point estimate of guidance depth with a per-cluster Gaussian — a global EMA baseline shifted by cluster success toward a 0.5 target sets the mean, and within-cluster success variance sets the spread — refreshed by the same rollouts that update the policy. - The good: A controlled diagnostic shows the informative-depth band is well fit by a Gaussian (σ=0.22, R²=0.92), and ablations cleanly attribute the gains (removing stochastic sampling drops ALFWorld success from 95.3% to 89.8%; removing GRPO drops it to 26.6%). - The missing: The headline 1.5-point margin over the strongest hint-based baseline at 1.5B is smaller than the reported seed-to-seed standard deviation (±2.3), and no significance tests are reported; evaluation is also limited to two text-based benchmarks where ALFWorld is near saturation (98.4% at 7B). - Read it or not: Worth reading if you train LLM agents with RL and use expert demonstrations, since the band-not-point insight and zero-overhead scheduling transfer directly; skip if you work outside hint-based agent RL, where the observation is less relevant.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners training LLM agents with RL on long-horizon tasks (household control, web navigation) face terminal-only binary rewards: on-policy rollouts from the initial state rarely succeed, so GRPO-style group advantages collapse. Hint-based RL mitigates this by executing a prefix of an expert trajectory before each rollout, but performance is critically sensitive to the guidance depth — too shallow yields no successes, too deep saturates rewards and eliminates advantage contrast. Prior methods treat depth as a deterministic scalar: schedule-based methods (linear/cosine/step decay, target-accuracy) share one depth across all tasks in a batch, ignoring heterogeneity (e.g., a 2-step vs. 20-step ALFWorld task); per-sample probing (binary search, enumeration) resolves this only by spending O(log n) extra rollouts per sample — the paper measures 4.83× the per-step wall-clock cost for enumeration. Prior hint-depth work was developed almost exclusively on math reasoning, where task difficulty is uniform; agentic batches mix widely varying difficulty. Key Idea: Useful guidance depths do not concentrate at a single optimum but occupy a band whose training-signal profile (Bernoulli variance of rollout success) is unimodal, approximately symmetric, and Gaussian around the band center — so the right object to estimate is a depth distribution, not a depth point. The trick that makes this practical: the two Gaussian moments map onto statistics that GRPO rollouts already produce (per-cluster mean success drives the center; within-cluster success variance drives the spread), so per-task depth diversity is obtained for free inside the existing training loop. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) offline clustering — tasks are partitioned into K=3 clusters by expert-trajectory length as a difficulty proxy; (2) adaptive Gaussian schedule — a global baseline µ_global is nudged by a fixed step Δ=0.1 toward the direction that drives batch accuracy to the target p_target=0.5, per-cluster EMA statistics A_k (cluster success) and V_k (within-cluster success variance) are updated from each batch, and each task receives µ_i = clip(µ_global + λ(p_target − A_k), 0, 1), σ_i = max(γV_k, σ_min); (3) sampling and rollout — one ratio d_i ~ N(µ_i, σ_i²) is drawn per task, converted to a prefix length, expert actions executed in the environment, and R=8 policy rollouts run from the post-prefix state; (4) training — the objective is L_GRPO + η·L_aux with η=0.5, where L_aux is teacher-forced SFT on the sampled expert prefixes; (5) closed-loop schedule update from the same terminal rewards. The framework is a heuristic moment-matching controller (EMAs, clipping, fixed step sizes), not an optimization over an explicit objective — the target-0.5 centering follows the Florensa et al. (2018) curriculum principle. Critical design decisions: stochastic (rather than deterministic-mean) sampling is well justified by the band observation and ablation; length-based offline clustering is the weakest justification — effective empirically but acknowledged as non-adaptive; the Bernoulli-variance proxy for "training informativeness" is plausible but never validated against an actual gradient-signal measure. Key Results: On ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Agent-G2 reaches 95.3% overall success (98.4% at 7B), improving over the strongest hint-based baseline (Enumeration, 78.1%/96.1%) by +1.5/+2.3 points, over RLVMR (strongest Aux-RL) by +7.4/+6.6, and over the strongest hint-free baseline (BEACON, 75.6%/79.7%) by +3.9 points at both scales. On WebShop it scores 92.3 reward at both scales with 78.9%/84.4% purchase success — the strongest non-probing method, though Enumeration beats it at 7B (89.8 reward). Per-step cost is 88s vs. 57–80s for scheduled baselines (0.65–0.91×) and 285–425s for probe-based baselines (3.24–4.83×); Agent-G2 reaches scheduled baselines' final accuracy in roughly half the gradient steps. Ablations on ALFWorld/1.5B: no sampling 89.8%, uniform sampling 88.3%, no adaptive center 91.4%, no adaptive spread 93.8%, K=1 89.1%, no L_aux 86.7%, no L_GRPO 26.6%. Clustering ablation: length-quantile K=5 gives 96.5±1.9, random clustering 89.4, K=10 drops to 86.2. The 1.5B model surpasses all 7B non-probing baselines on ALFWorld. Baselines are current (2024–2026 methods including GiGPO and BEACON) and share Agent-G2's GRPO backbone, isolating depth allocation as the variable. Notably, gains over the closest hint-based competitors are small relative to seed noise, while gains over hint-free and Aux-RL families are large. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (informative depths form a Gaussian-like band, not a point) plus NEW METHOD (zero-overhead online Gaussian depth scheduler with global-local decomposition). The genuinely novel element is the reframing of guidance depth as a distribution to cover rather than a scalar to find; the scheduler itself is a competent combination of standard components (EMA statistics, target-accuracy centering, GRPO, prefix SFT) applied to the new framing, and the transfer of hint-based RL from math reasoning to agentic benchmarks is a new setting rather than a new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough and target the right components (sampling form, both adaptive moments, clustering, loss terms), including a clustering-design appendix study with a random-assignment control that rules out "partitioning per se" as the source of gains. Results are averaged over 5 seeds; standard deviations appear only in the appendix clustering table (e.g., ±2.3 for the headline 95.3%), and no significance tests are reported — the +1.5-point margin over the strongest 1.5B hint-based baseline is inside this seed noise, a concern the paper does not address. The diagnostic Gaussian fit is verified across three training windows (R² 0.89–0.94), not just one checkpoint. Code and training scripts are promised under MIT license "upon publication" (links in the abstract exist but release is not confirmed in the text); the build is on the public GiGPO/verl stack and uses the same expert pool as ETO/RLVMR, which is a fair-comparison positive. No Goodhart concern arises since the diagnostic is run on a separate sweep protocol, but the entire diagnostic is conducted on one model/benchmark pair (Qwen2.5-1.5B / ALFWorld), and the generality of the Gaussian-shape observation to other settings is asserted rather than measured. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — runs on a single 8×H800 node in the verl framework (a 1.5B ALFWorld run takes ~10 hours), well within commercial reach. Efficient: Adds ~25–55% per-step wall-clock over scheduled baselines (88s vs. 57–80s) but is 3.2–4.8× cheaper than probe-based alternatives, and converges in roughly half the steps; overall the best cost-accuracy point in the paper's own measurements. Effective: Strong evidence it solves the benchmark problem at the tested scale, but it requires one expert trajectory per training task plus an environment capable of executing expert-action prefixes — a substantive deployment prerequisite the effectiveness claim depends on. Scalable: Tested only at 1.5B–7B parameters, 150–200 gradient steps, batch size 16, and two benchmarks; the paper claims cross-scale robustness from 1.5B→7B but nothing beyond, and near-saturation ALFWorld scores leave little headroom to detect differences at 7B. Deliverable: a software artifact (code/training scripts, MIT license, pending release) built on verl/GiGPO; no pretrained model weights are stated. Strengths: - The diagnostic (Section 2) is the paper's real intellectual contribution: it quantifies the structural failure of shared-depth schedulers (15–23% in-range across five checkpoints) and the cost-precision trade-off of probing, then shows the band structure with a fit checked across training windows — turning a tuning heuristic into a falsifiable observation. - The zero-extra-rollout property is achieved by construction, not just claimed: the schedule is refreshed from GRPO's own terminal rewards, and the paper verifies this with an explicit wall-clock cost table rather than rollout-count arguments alone. - Ablation "Sampled-Prefix SFT" (26.6% vs. Agent-G2's 95.3%) cleanly isolates that the gain comes from RL on sampled post-prefix states rather than imitation of expert tokens — a well-designed control many hint-based papers omit. - Honest baseline engineering: all schedule/search baselines share the same GRPO backbone, and the expert-trajectory pool is identical to ETO/RLVMR's, isolating the algorithmic variable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) the method requires one expert trajectory per training task and does not extend to suboptimal demonstrations or language hints without further work; (2) the Gaussian family is motivated by two-benchmark fits and may miss multimodal or skewed depth profiles (mitigated partially by the uniform-sampling ablation); (3) difficulty clusters are defined offline by trajectory length and do not adapt as the policy improves. These are confronted directly and honestly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical rigor on the headline claim: the +1.5/+2.3-point margins over the strongest hint-based baselines are not shown to be significant, and the only reported seed standard deviation (±2.3) is as large as the margin; the strongest claims are really about hint-free/Aux-RL baselines. - Evaluation breadth: only two text-based benchmarks, one of which (ALFWorld at 7B, 98.4% with 100% on four of six task types) is effectively saturated, leaving no room to measure differences where they matter; no GUI, code-agent, or higher-branching environment tests whether the band observation holds elsewhere. - The Bernoulli variance p(1−p) is a proxy for "training informativeness"; the paper never connects the in-range band to an actual gradient-norm or advantage-variance measurement, so the central mechanistic claim rests on an unvalidated proxy — and the peak at Δd=0 is true by construction of d*_i, leaving only symmetry and decay as non-trivial fit content. - The environment must support executing expert action prefixes to reach post-prefix states; the paper does not discuss what happens in environments with irreversible actions, partial observability mismatch, or expert trajectories that fail under the current environment dynamics. - WebShop at 7B shows Enumeration (a probe-based method) beating Agent-G2 by 5.4 reward points (89.8 vs. 84.4); the "strongest non-probing" framing is accurate but softens that probing remains competitive when budget allows. Bottom Line: For anyone doing hint-based or curriculum RL on LLM agents, this paper is worth reading for the band-not-point diagnostic and a genuinely free per-task scheduler, but the headline superiority over the best tuned baselines rests on margins within seed noise on two near-saturated benchmarks — treat it as a strong engineering insight with a sharp observation, not a settled winner.
