Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Operators of enterprise and critical-infrastructure networks need automated defenses that respond to advanced persistent threats and zero-day exploits faster than signature updates allow. DRL-based autonomous defense (e.g., in the CybORG/CAGE challenge line) learns response policies, but its action space is fixed by the environment designer, so when a new vulnerability or attacker technique appears — the paper's motivating example is CVE-2019-0787 — the policy can only scan, remove known malware, or restore hosts, and fails. Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) in STIX format contains exactly the needed knowledge (CVEs, malicious IPs, courses of action), but prior LLM/knowledge-assisted defenses (e.g., Loevenich et al.) use CTI as descriptive context without specifying how it becomes selectable, PPO-compatible actions. The gap the paper closes is the CTI-to-policy grounding problem: converting semantic threat knowledge into an executable decision interface compatible with standard PPO training. Key Idea: The core trick is configuration-level action-space augmentation: treat CTI not as context for the policy network but as a pre-execution expansion of the action set. For each CTI configuration c, the executable interface is A_c = A_base ∪ Act_c, where A_base is the five-action OpenC2 baseline (monitor, analyze, decoy, remove, restore) and Act_c is a set of LLM-generated, schema-validated OpenC2-compatible options (e.g., "patch CVE-X on server Y", "block IP 119.188.248.40"). Because the interface is constructed before training or evaluation — never online — the actor remains a standard PPO distribution over discrete options, and LLM latency (41.8 s mean per grounding) is amortized out of the millisecond decision loop. This is a genuinely useful formulation of the CTI-operationalization problem, though the individual ingredients (LLM structured extraction, cosine-similarity relevance filtering, PPO, hierarchical MARL) are all standard. Methodology: The pipeline has two stages. (1) Configuration-level CTI grounding (Algorithm 1): extract vulnerability/IOC/COA fields from STIX JSON, score relevance against system/asset information using a cosine-similarity 'CTI matching coefficient', build a constrained prompt (allowed action/target catalogs, temperature 0.0, GPT-5.5 via OpenAI API), parse ⟨Action, Target, Arguments⟩ tuples, and validate them against the OpenC2 schema, an action whitelist, and scenario target constraints, with fallback to A_base on failure. (2) Multi-agent PPO defense (Algorithm 2): a control policy π_φ picks defense mode z_t ∈ {B, M} (agent specialized against the topology-aware Bline attacker vs. the exploratory Meander attacker), and the selected agent's PPO actor samples from A_c. Rewards are negative penalties (Eq. 3): -0.1 per compromised user/operational host, -1 per compromised server, -1 per Restore action, -10 for service-disruption impact on the operational server; the objective is the standard discounted PPO return with actor-critic advantage estimation. Training uses RLlib PPO on PyTorch (lr 0.001, γ=0.99, clip 0.3, train batch 4000, hidden layers [256,256], 5M timesteps, seed 42) on an NVIDIA A100; evaluation uses 100 episodes at 30/50/100 (and 200/300/500-step prolonged) horizons in a CybORG topology of three subnets and ten hosts. Critical design decisions: asynchronous grounding to keep LLMs out of the decision loop (well justified, with measured latencies), validation/whitelisting of LLM output with fallback (well justified, addresses hallucination), and a lightweight fixed hierarchy rather than learned communication (acknowledged as a simplification but reasonable for PPO compatibility). Key Results: On the 30/50/100-step scenarios, AD-CTIDRL(1) achieves a total reward of -47.184, improving on TL-Embedding (-118.096), Ensemble (-90.322), TL-PPO (-84.420), HIPPO (-66.114), and CardiffUni (-54.570) by 60.05%, 47.76%, 44.11%, 28.63%, and 13.53% respectively; results for Tang et al. and Loevenich et al. are taken from published figures rather than re-run. CTI coverage scaling yields AD-CTIDRL(2) -33.270 and AD-CTIDRL(3) -25.042, with AD-CTIDRL(4) (-25.158) showing diminishing returns beyond attacker-reachable hosts. In prolonged 200–500-step scenarios, AD-CTIDRL(4) reaches -100.166 versus HIPPO's -363.255 (a 72.43% penalty reduction). Ablations attribute the gain to CTI grounding, not just multi-agent structure: OpenC2-only multi-agent scores -72.004 (ABR 0.949, availability impact 0.146) versus full AD-CTIDRL -25.100 (ABR 0.982, CSCR 0.000, AI 0.023). In an emerging-attack two-stage experiment, CTI-equipped agents hold rewards near -15.0 (Bline) and -33.8 (Meander) after step 100 while CTI-free baselines drop sharply. Online latency is 1.586 ms mean (P95 3.337 ms) per decision; LLM grounding costs 42.17 s mean (P95 75.25 s) per configuration. Against SleepAgents, all methods score 0 — no spurious defensive actions. Baselines span 2021–2025 work including CAGE-2's official CardiffUni entry, so they are reasonably current, though several are compiled from prior publications rather than re-executed under identical conditions. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component: the genuinely novel element is the CTI-to-policy grounding formulation — semantic STIX intelligence converted into a validated, OpenC2-compatible, PPO-consumable action interface per CTI configuration — plus the asynchronous design that keeps LLM inference off the decision path. The rest (PPO, hierarchical control with two specialist agents, cosine-similarity retrieval, LLM structured-output prompting with schema validation) is a competent combination of existing techniques applied to the CybORG setting; no new dataset, algorithm, or theory is introduced. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is above average on ablation design: a two-level protocol explicitly separates multi-agent control from CTI grounding, plus four CTI-coverage sensitivity variants, a hidden-layer-size sweep, a no-attacker control condition, and a latency decomposition — this is more careful than most CybORG-based papers. However, weaknesses are material: a single random seed (42) with no error bars or significance tests (box plots in Fig. 4 show spread but no statistical treatment); code and data are only 'available from the corresponding author on reasonable request', not publicly released; the LLM component uses a closed commercial API (GPT-5.5), making exact reproduction impossible; and several baselines (Tang et al., Loevenich et al.) are compared using numbers extracted from their papers rather than re-run. There is also an internal inconsistency: Table 4's headline total of -47.184 (AD-CTIDRL(1)) does not match the ablation table's 'Full AD-CTIDRL' -25.100, and the main-text abstract claims are computed against the weaker variant. The emerging-attack evaluation uses CTI configurations constructed for the very attacks being tested, so the adaptability result partially reflects Goodhart-style alignment between grounding inputs and test scenarios. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation-based system with experiments actually run). Practical: Yes in simulation — a single A100 trains it and online inference is millisecond-level CPU-scale, but real deployment requires an OpenC2-executable infrastructure and a paid LLM API the paper does not demonstrate. Efficient: The online loop (1.586 ms mean) is cheaper per step than any LLM-in-the-loop alternative; the 42–75 s per-configuration grounding cost is acceptable if CTI updates are infrequent. Effective: Within CybORG it demonstrably solves the stated proxy (reward, blocking rate, zero critical-server compromise), but effectiveness against real emerging attacks is only inferred, not measured. Scalable: Untested beyond a 10-host topology and two attacker types; the authors claim scalability in the conclusion without evidence at 10–100× network size, and per-host CTI coverage experiments hint that grounding cost grows with protected-asset count. The work stops at paper form — no library, tool, or trained model artifact is released. Strengths: (1) The CTI-to-policy grounding formulation is a clear, well-motivated reframing — treating CTI as an action-interface generator rather than policy input is a specific, transferable idea. (2) The asynchronous grounding/online-decision separation is backed by an unusually honest latency table (41.8 s LLM generation vs. 1.586 ms online decision) that anticipates the obvious objection to LLM-in-the-loop defense. (3) The validation layer (OpenC2 schema check, action whitelist, target constraints, rejection of hallucinated fields, fallback to baseline actions) is a concrete answer to LLM unreliability in a safety-relevant setting, with prompts and rules printed in the appendix. (4) The ablation study actually isolates the claimed contribution: CTI grounding contributes roughly a 2.9× reward improvement over the same multi-agent framework without it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge that performance is constrained by CTI timeliness and quality, that DRL policies have limited explainability, and that all evaluation is simulation-based; the discussion also concedes the coordination mechanism is a lightweight fixed hierarchy that does not learn communication or network topology, and that deployment reliability depends on LLM output consistency and validation, with future work on provenance checks, adversarial testing, and monitoring. This is a fairly direct confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive — though the conclusion's claim of 'scalability' sits uneasily beside the acknowledged simulation-only scope. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged issues, a reviewer would flag: (1) single-seed training with 5M timesteps and no variance across seeds — PPO in CybORG is known to be seed-sensitive, so the headline margins (e.g., 13.53% over CardiffUni) may not be robust; (2) the internal inconsistency between Table 4 totals (-47.184) and the ablation's 'Full AD-CTIDRL' (-25.100) with different per-step values, which is never reconciled; (3) the emerging-attack experiment constructs the CTI interface from the same STIX knowledge that defines the new attack, so the system is never tested on CTI it did not help author; (4) no ablation of the cosine-similarity relevance filter or of the LLM itself (e.g., a rule-based STIX-to-OpenC2 mapper could plausibly achieve much of the gain without an LLM, which would deflate the novelty claim); (5) no report of LLM grounding failure/invalidation rates, so the robustness of the validation layer is unmeasured; (6) comparison to Loevenich et al. — the closest LLM+DRL prior — uses copied literature numbers over intervals rather than a controlled re-run. Bottom Line: A practitioner in autonomous cyber defense gains a concrete, well-ablated design pattern for operationalizing CTI as PPO action interfaces — worth reading for the grounding-plus-validation architecture — but the simulation-only, single-seed evidence and untested LLM dependency mean the field likely needs the promised real-network and cross-CTI generalization studies before this displaces simpler retrieval-augmented or rule-grounded defenses.

QisMC: A Model Checker for QISKIT Program Debugging

A Dai, M Ying · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds QisMC, the first model checker that accepts Qiskit programs directly, verifies them against temporal properties in a new quantum computation tree logic (qCTL), and returns source-level counterexample traces when properties fail. - Why it's important: Modern Qiskit programs use mid-circuit measurement, classical feedforward, and while-loops (dynamic circuits), but existing Qiskit debugging tools (assertions, property-based testing, static analysis) cannot specify or exhaustively check how properties must hold across execution paths, nor explain violations. - How it does it: The core move is reducing qCTL model checking to classical CTL model checking: subspace-based quantum propositions are resolved at each program location by bidirectional strongest-postcondition/weakest-precondition fixed-point iterations over subspaces (implemented symbolically with CFLOBDD decision diagrams), after which the remaining problem is handed to NuSMV. - The good: The scalability evaluation is convincing and honestly reported — QisMC verifies GHZ-state programs up to 300 qubits in 1.6 s and linear-structured Grover instances up to 300 qubits in 38 s, while baseline QPMC fails above 4 qubits and QTC-Maude needs 229 s for 17-qubit Grover; it also finds a previously unpublished bug in a published VQSS protocol configuration. - The missing: There is no statement that QisMC's code is publicly released, and the evaluation's automated protocol (inject a random Pauli error, check the derived property) is artificial rather than a study of real debugging workloads; the tool also silently exceeds timeouts on 11 of 40 Benchpress circuits. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on quantum software verification or want to model-check dynamic quantum circuits — it is the first working tool of its kind — but skip it if you need probabilistic quantitative properties (explicitly out of scope) or a production-ready released artifact.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Novelty (78) is the driver — the first model checker for Qiskit dynamic circuits via an elegant qCTL-to-CTL reduction with proven soundness/completeness — and Non-Obviousness (75) reflects the genuinely insightful sp/wp subspace-bounding move that reuses the classical CTL stack. Rigor (65) is supported by theory proofs, Stim cross-validation, and unusually honest negative results, but single-run timings and the absence of a stated public release hold it back; Impact (55) is limited by the missing artifact and a synthetic error-injection benchmark protocol. Problem & Motivation: Developers of dynamic quantum programs in Qiskit — repeat-until-success circuits, quantum error correction loops, distributed quantum computing protocols — need to specify properties over execution paths (does the loop terminate? is the state always in a code subspace?) and, when a property fails, need a concrete execution explaining where and how it fails. Existing techniques address only slices of this: runtime assertions and property-based testing check particular program points or bounded runs, static analysis flags specific bug classes, and prior quantum model checkers (QMC, QPMC, QTC-Maude) either restrict to stabilizer states, cannot express quantum-state properties as atomic propositions, or lack counterexample generation and loop support. No prior tool simultaneously offers native Qiskit input, temporal specification combining classical and quantum propositions, exhaustive verification, and diagnostic counterexamples. Key Idea: Treat quantum-state satisfaction as a locality-level Boolean question: although runtime quantum states form an uncountable set, satisfaction of a Birkhoff-von Neumann subspace proposition at a program location is decidable by computing two subspace bounds per location — the strongest postcondition sp(l) and weakest precondition wp(l) — via bidirectional fixed-point iteration over the control flow graph; once every quantum proposition in a qCTL formula is resolved to true/false at each location, the whole qCTL model checking problem collapses to an ordinary CTL problem solvable by NuSMV. This sidesteps the infinite-state-space problem without abstracting away the quantum states themselves. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Model construction: a Qiskit QuantumCircuit (or OpenQASM 2 file) is parsed into a control flow graph and translated into a quantum-classical transition system — a 7-tuple with finite locations, Hilbert space H, super-operator-labeled transitions, and dual labeling functions f (classical propositions) and f-tilde (Hilbert subspaces). (2) Quantum reasoning: a BFS-style backward fixed-point iteration (Algorithm 1) computes wp per location, initialized from annotations, refined by pre-images under transitions (unitary inverse, projector pre-image, or the 0/identity collapse for initializations), with a dual forward pass for sp; complexity is O(n·d⁴) worst-case with d = dim(H), rarely hit in practice due to CFLOBDD compression. (3) Reduction: each quantum proposition ψ in the qCTL formula is replaced by a fresh classical proposition ω_ψ, labeled true at location l iff sp(l) ⊆ ⟦ψ⟧ ⊆ wp(l) (Theorem 5.2, proved sound and complete by structural induction in Appendix B.2). (4) Checking and debugging: the resulting CTL problem is submitted to NuSMV; counterexample traces are mapped back through a location-to-statement table into Qiskit source-level diagnostic paths. Critical design decisions: the hierarchical three-layer qCTL syntax (restricting quantum connectives to the quantum layer, justified by the failure of excluded middle for subspace satisfaction), the sp/wp consistency mechanism for annotations at multiple locations (justified via Tarski fixed points), and CFLOBDD over explicit matrices (justified empirically, with the paper itself exposing its structural sensitivity). Key Results: On Grover and Bernstein–Vazirani benchmarks from VeriQBench, QisMC verifies programs up to 100 qubits within seconds (all 49 Grover and 99 BV instances); QTC-Maude needs 229 s (>4.7M rewrites) for 17-qubit Grover and 1515 s for 11-qubit BV, and QPMC fails with runtime exceptions beyond 4 qubits. Against quantum abstract interpretation (Yu & Palsberg, PLDI 2021), QisMC is 2–3 orders of magnitude faster: grover-8 in 0.342 s vs 101 s, grover-16 in 3.112 s vs 800 s, ghz-100 in 1.079 s vs 318 s, and it completes ghz-300 in 1.603 s and grover-150-linear (300 qubits) in 38.056 s. On 40 Benchpress-medium circuits (10–30 qubits), 29 verify quickly (e.g., 0.024–35.4 s) while 11 time out at 600 s (bwt with >100k gates, parameterized-gate circuits like ising/knn/wstate, qft_n18). In the Bernoulli factory case study, an injected fault yields a 46-location counterexample trace. Notable findings: 7/49 Grover and 28/99 BV error-injected instances are correctly verified as still satisfying the property (independently confirmed for Clifford cases via the Stim simulator), showing the tool does not flag every perturbation; and QisMC discovers that a published ⟦5,1,3⟧-code VQSS configuration destroys the secret state, a real bug in the literature. Baselines are the only two open-source quantum model checkers (reasonable, since QMC has no public implementation), but they are dated tools, and qCTL itself drops QPMC's probabilistic specifications. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (qCTL with hierarchical quantum/classical layers and sp/wp semantics) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (first model checker for Qiskit programs with statement-level counterexamples). The genuinely novel elements are the reduction of quantum-subspace temporal checking to classical CTL and the first use of decision-diagram symbolic representations (CFLOBDDs) inside quantum model checking; the supporting machinery — CTL semantics, Tarski fixed-point computation, Gram–Schmidt subspace intersection, and the Birkhoff-von Neumann logic itself — is a competent combination of established ideas assembled into a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The theory includes proofs for the fixed-point algorithm's termination, soundness, and completeness (Prop. 5.1), the qCTL-to-CTL reduction (Thm 5.2), and the subspace intersection algorithm (Prop. 6.2). Ablation-style insight comes from the topology experiment (tree- vs. linear-structured Grover oracles), which isolates when the CFLOBDD backend degenerates, and from Clifford-case cross-validation with Stim. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported — runtimes are single runs on one 128-thread, 503 GiB server. Code release for QisMC is not stated anywhere in the paper (baseline tool URLs are given, but no repository for QisMC itself), which limits reproducibility. A methodological soft spot: the automated Benchpress/VeriQBench evaluation injects random Pauli errors rather than studying realistic bug distributions, so the headline benchmark numbers measure a synthetic protocol; the honest negatives (timeouts, numerical failures at 256+ qubits) are, however, reported in full. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated on benchmarks). Practical: Runs on a commodity Linux server (2× Xeon 8358P, 503 GiB RAM) with Python/C++ (pybind11) plus NuSMV — no exotic hardware. Efficient: Seconds for most 10–30 qubit circuits and up to 300 qubits on favorable structures, orders of magnitude faster than QPMC, QTC-Maude, and matrix-based abstract interpretation, but with a worst-case O(n·d⁴) bound and exponential blowups on QFT-like or tree-structured circuits. Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem on benchmarks and one real found bug, but the synthetic error-injection protocol and absence of user studies mean real-world debugging effectiveness is only proxied. Scalable: Tested up to 300 qubits on favorable families; the paper itself demonstrates that 10–100× growth fails on unfavorable topologies (tree Grover ≥63 qubits), floating-point-parameterized circuits, and >250-qubit programs with accumulated numerical error — so scalability is conditional, not general. Delivered artifact: a described tool (Python/C++ with NuSMV and CFLOBDD backends), but no public repository is mentioned in the paper. Strengths: (1) The qCTL-to-CTL reduction is the intellectual core: by showing subspace-proposition satisfaction is Boolean per location once sp/wp bounds are fixed, the authors reuse the entire mature classical model-checking stack (including counterexample generation) instead of building a quantum solver from scratch. (2) The evaluation is unusually honest for a tool paper — it reports the timeout cases, the CFLOBDD topology sensitivity, and the floating-point failures at 256+ qubits alongside the wins. (3) Finding a genuine bug in a published VQSS protocol configuration (not an injected fault) is the strongest evidence that the workflow has practical diagnostic value. (4) The hierarchical qCTL design, with an explicit argument (Remark after Def. 4.3) for why quantum connectives cannot be naively mixed with path quantifiers, shows real care about the non-Boolean semantics of quantum propositions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that qCTL cannot express probabilistic properties (QPMC's advantage), that the CFLOBDD backend is highly sensitive to circuit topology (tree-structured Grover ≥63 qubits) and to floating-point gate parameters, that numerical error accumulation breaks verification on programs above ~250 qubits with no exact symbolic fix currently available, and that QFT-style circuits exhibit exponential decision-diagram growth. They confront these directly and concretely (with root-cause analysis per timeout class in Table 5), which is a credibility positive; the proposed future direction (exact algebraic representations for Clifford+T) is plausible but unproven. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No statement that QisMC is publicly released — for a tool paper this is a significant omission that prevents independent reproduction. (2) The automated benchmark protocol (random Pauli injection against derived output properties) has no demonstrated connection to how developers actually specify and debug properties; a study of specification effort and false-alarm rates on realistic bugs is absent. (3) No comparison against non-model-checking verifiers beyond the one abstract-interpretation tool — e.g., symbolic execution (Fang & Ying) or automata-based methods (Chen et al., PLDI 2023) — so the claimed end-to-end advantage over the broader verification landscape is not measured. (4) The claim that the framework generalizes beyond Qiskit is asserted, not tested on any second language. (5) The wp/sp semantics assume the restricted condition form x = c; the paper notes workarounds but never quantifies the specification burden this imposes on realistic programs. Bottom Line: This is the first credible, working model checker for Qiskit's dynamic programs and a genuine advance for quantum software verification — practitioners building tools or verifying control-flow-heavy quantum circuits should read and try it — but until the artifact is released and its synthetic benchmark protocol is complemented by real-world debugging evidence, its practical impact rests on promising demonstrations rather than proven deployment.

Agentic Artifact Creation: Systems, Evaluation, Principles, and Opportunities (52 ▲ )

Tianfu Wang, Zhezheng Hao, Xilin Xia, Lixin Liu, Mengkang Hu, Hongzhang Liu, Xi Chen, Ziyan Liu, Xiankun Lin, Weijia Zhang, Nicholas Jing Yuan, Hui Xiong · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This survey introduces a formal paradigm of "agentic artifact creation" — stateful construction in which an AI system materially builds or revises a deliverable and intermediate observations redirect later work — and organizes 259 works (230 systems, 29 benchmarks, retrieved through August 20, 2026) under this definition. - Why it's important: Success of generative AI increasingly depends on producing complete, dependable deliverables (posters, videos, CAD models, repositories) whose interacting requirements make failure propagation, weak failure localization, and broad regeneration the dominant pain points — a dimension prior surveys organized around models, agents, or modalities rather than the delivered artifact. - How it does it: It decomposes every construction episode into three functional roles — an Operational Representation (intermediate form + edit interface), a Construction Policy (decision control + agent topology), and Runtime Verification (observation source + feedback function) — and uses this vocabulary to compare six artifact families, application contexts, and evaluation practice. - The good: The functional decomposition plus the qualitative difficulty lens (decision interdependence, failure observability, repairability) yields genuinely transferable insights across modalities — e.g., decomposition reduces local complexity but increases coordination/reassembly costs, and learned judges add little independent evidence when they share the generator's blind spots. - The missing: The four synthesized design principles and the six research challenges are qualitative hypotheses never validated by any experiment, measurement, or case study; the survey also concedes that per-source query exports and pre-reconciliation labels were not retained, limiting auditability of the corpus construction. - Read it or not: Worth a full read for researchers building artifact-generating agent systems or benchmarks who need a shared vocabulary and a map of 259 works across text, visual, audio, video, spatial, and behavioral artifacts; practitioners seeking concrete architecture recipes or quantitative comparisons will find a taxonomy, not numbers.

Novelty (70) is genuine — the delivered-artifact-as-unit-of-analysis formulation with the three-role functional architecture is a real NEW FORMULATION — but the four principles and six challenges are unvalidated hypotheses, which caps Resilience (60) and Impact (55). Completeness (75) is a credibility positive: honest boundary work on hard cases and non-minimizing limitation reporting. Problem & Motivation: Generative models produce drafts and components cheaply, but real workflows require complete deliverables whose parts must jointly satisfy interacting acceptance criteria — a poster must preserve source content, fit a page, and communicate; a repository must satisfy tests and dependencies. In such settings, failures visible in the final output are hard to trace, and one-way generation pipelines cannot redirect later actions based on intermediate observations. Existing surveys organize the field around model families, agent architectures, creative workflows, software agents, tool trajectories, human collaboration, or evaluation methods (the paper's Table 1), leaving the delivered artifact — its acceptance criteria, editable state, observations, and repair scope — without a unifying analytical treatment. The survey addresses researchers and system builders who currently lack a common vocabulary for why construction is harder in some modalities than others. Key Idea: The core organizing insight is to make the delivered artifact the unit of analysis and define the field by a control-loop property rather than an architecture: an episode counts as agentic artifact creation iff the system materially constructs/revises the artifact, carries artifact or process state across decisions, and uses at least one intermediate observation to redirect subsequent work. Once this boundary is fixed, cross-family comparison reduces to three questions: does the intermediate form expose targets the edit interface can modify, do observations reveal relevant consequences in time, and does feedback support a feasible policy response? Misalignment among these — e.g., a precise diagnosis with only whole-artifact regeneration available — neutralizes otherwise capable components. This is a formulation insight, not an algorithmic one. Methodology: The paper is a systematic survey with a formal framework layered on top. Corpus construction: searches of arXiv, Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, ACM DL, and IEEE Xplore from January 2023 to August 20, 2026, using agentic-process terms crossed with artifact-family terms, supplemented by citation tracing and venue audits; after deduplication and screening against the stateful-construction definition, 230 systems and 29 benchmarks were retained and coded by corpus role, family, subtype, cross-cutting facets, and provenance. The analytical framework specifies the construction loop as R_{t+1} = U(R_t, a_t), a_t = π(T, R_t, f_t), f_{t+1} = V(T, R_{t+1}, o_{t+1}), with delivery A = D(R_τ) upon acceptance. Critical design decisions: (1) the screening rule excludes direct generators, observation-independent workflows, and artifact-consuming/evaluation-only systems — well-justified and consistently applied; (2) the six-family taxonomy (textual, 2D visual, audio, video, spatial, behavioral) with 16 sub-profiles — mostly justified, though assignment of boundary cases (e.g., simulators vs. games, agentic world modeling) requires case-by-case argument the authors handle explicitly; (3) the four principles (Externalize Commitments, Define Control Boundaries, Make Feedback Actionable, Revalidate Affected State) are synthesized qualitatively from the corpus rather than derived or validated, which the authors acknowledge. Key Results: As a survey, its "results" are syntheses rather than measurements: a coded corpus of 259 works (with 120 published/accepted records traced to venues — 19 at ICLR, 18 at ICML, 14 at NeurIPS, 11 at ACM MM, etc.); family coverage of 251 family-assigned records (behavioral 73, 2D visual 61, textual 34, video 37, spatial 35, audio 11, with 13 video records cross-profile and no strict spoken-audio record). Recurring findings: construction difficulty tracks decision coupling and failure-observability timing, not modality alone; benchmark maturity is uneven (strongest for 2D visual and behavioral artifacts; audio/video/spatial often rely on protocols released with system papers); only three of the reviewed protocols evaluate a system property beyond task capability (each covering exactly one property — reliability or controllability); a Design Arena leaderboard snapshot (Aug 19, 2026) is used to argue that aggregate Elo ranks conceal task-specific standings (e.g., one frontier model at the 87.5th percentile on slides but 34.2nd on native Android). One cited quantitative anchor: the Mr. Dre benchmark reports 16–27% regression in previously covered content or citation quality during repeated revision. No accuracy/F1/speedup comparisons are performed by the survey itself. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW PROBLEM framing, plus a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK-adjacent contribution (a coded, released corpus of 259 works under a strict definition). The genuinely novel element is the delivered-artifact-as-unit-of-analysis lens with the three-role functional architecture, which no adjacent survey uses as its primary axis (per the paper's own Table 1 comparison). The underlying mechanisms surveyed — ReAct, Reflexion, MetaGPT-style role decomposition, SWE-agent-style execution feedback — are all established; the contribution is the cross-family synthesis, the evaluation-target taxonomy (artifact vs. trajectory vs. system properties), and the four principles, not any new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The inclusion rule is operational and explicit, and the screening is reproducible in principle from the released coding files at github.com/GeminiLight/awesome-agentic-artifact-creation. Weaknesses the authors self-report: database-specific query exports, per-source yields, and pre-reconciliation labels were not retained, so the retrieval stage cannot be fully audited. There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests — appropriate for a survey, but also no quantitative meta-analysis (e.g., aggregating reported success rates across the 230 systems), so all cross-family comparisons remain qualitative. Benchmark selection in Table 4 prioritizes "influence and publication record, then complementary target and evidence coverage" — a defensible but subjective sampling rule with three rows per family. The principles chapter explicitly labels itself qualitative and hypothesis-generating. No Goodhart-style contamination arises since the survey develops no technique evaluated on a benchmark, though its leaderboard evidence is a self-reported vendor-adjacent snapshot. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: the paper is neither EMPIRICAL, THEORETICAL, nor SYSTEMS in the primary sense — it is a survey/position paper; applying the EMPIRICAL check to its corpus-curation component as the closest match: Practical: the coded corpus and GitHub list are plain artifacts usable by anyone; Efficient: not applicable (no compute claims); Effective: the taxonomy and principles demonstrably organize 259 heterogeneous works, but their predictive value for system design is untested; Scalable: the framework is defined abstractly and should extend to new families, but the corpus cut-off (Aug 20, 2026) and rapid field growth mean immediate staleness pressure. Deliverable: a curated, coded paper corpus and taxonomy (repository at agentic-creation.github.io / awesome-agentic-artifact-creation); no software tool, trained model, or reusable proof technique. Strengths: - A crisp, operational definition (stateful construction with observation-driven redirection) that does real exclusion work — it cleanly separates agentic artifact creation from direct generation, generic problem-solving agents, and evaluation-only systems, which is rare among survey taxonomies. - The three-role functional architecture (Operational Representation / Construction Policy / Runtime Verification) with sub-taxonomies (intermediate form, edit interface, decision control, agent topology, observation source, feedback function) is genuinely reusable as a system-design checklist and as a paper-coding scheme; Table 3 instantiates it for ~30 representative systems, exposing gaps (e.g., ATVG reports almost no functional details). - The alignment argument — that a component is only as useful as its fit with the others (a bitmap supports perceptual review but not object-level repair; a precise diagnosis is worthless when only whole-artifact regeneration is available) — is the survey's most transferable non-obvious insight. - Honest boundary work: explicit treatment of hard cases (simulators vs. games, world models vs. delivered scenes, cross-output dependency patterns) rather than hand-waving them into a family. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that database-specific query exports, per-source yields, and pre-reconciliation labels were not retained, and they document coding limitations in the released files. They explicitly frame the difficulty lens as "qualitative conditions rather than independent causal factors or a universal ranking," the four principles as non-sequential relations rather than a maturity ladder, and the six challenge directions as "hypotheses." They acknowledge that spoken audio has no strict construction record in the corpus, that some application-workflow systems are omitted from family views, and that cross-family evidence for a versioned dependency/evidence graph (Section 7.4) is "too sparse to establish one mechanism." This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The four principles and six opportunities are never instantiated in even one worked case study or validated against held-out systems; a skeptical reader cannot tell whether a system violating a principle fails predictably. - No quantitative synthesis of the corpus: the 230 systems' reported success rates, costs, and failure modes are never aggregated, so cross-family difficulty claims rest on narrative reading rather than measurement. - The evaluation chapter's strongest empirical exhibit is a leaderboard snapshot of models that could not be independently verified (and whose vendor-style Elo numbers carry the self-report caveats the survey itself preaches against). - Inter-rater reliability of the corpus coding (how many coders, agreement statistics on family/profile assignment) is not reported; with boundary cases this intricate, coding consistency is a material question. - The survey's own advice on budget-matched comparison is not applied to its corpus: it cannot say whether agentic construction outperforms direct generation plus regeneration at matched cost in any family — the one comparison its thesis most needs. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous available map of artifact-building agent systems and a genuinely useful vocabulary for anyone designing or benchmarking them, but its principles remain unvalidated hypotheses — read it as a well-executed survey that frames the field, not as evidence that any particular control structure works.

LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes (195 ▲ )

Chuyan Chen, Haoxing Chen, Kun Chen, Zhenglin Cheng, Long Cui, Ruishan Fang, Zhangxuan Gu, Zhicheng Huang, Zhenzhong Lan, Yuanting Lei, Haoquan Li, Jianguo Li, Rongchuan Li, Sidu Li, Tao Lin, Deyuan Liu, Jiacheng Liu, Lin Liu, Yuxuan Lou, Zhisheng Lu, Yuxin Ma, Shuheng Shen, Peng Sun, Chaoyang Wang, Hongjun Wang, Xiaomei Wang, Yongxin Wang, Chengzhang Wu, Hongru Wu, Jun Xie · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LLaDA-Image, a 6B-parameter Diffusion Transformer trained from scratch under a fully open recipe that performs unified text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing, plus a TwinFlow-distilled 2–4-step variant (LLaDA-Image Turbo), with weights, code, and training recipes publicly released. - Why it's important: Proprietary image generators publish no data, training, or recipe details, and prevailing training paradigms require expensive paired image–text data during the most compute-intensive stages; an inspectable, reusable recipe lowers the entry barrier for training competitive generators on a moderate data budget. - How it does it: The core move is decoupling visual-prior learning from language alignment — pre-training and mid-training use only unlabeled images, where a frozen dLLM-based VLM derives the conditioning signal from the same image region the DiT learns to generate (masked self-conditioning), followed by staged text alignment, joint generation–editing training, and DMD2-style few-step distillation on a shared backbone with signed-time roles. - The good: LLaDA-Image scores 53.53 (EN) and 53.38 (CN) on Qwen-Image-Bench, exceeding the next-best open model (Z-Image Turbo, 51.66/52.71) on both tracks, and the entire stack — four checkpoints, training code, and detailed recipes — is released. - The missing: No ablation isolates the benefit of the image-only pre-training/mid-training curriculum against a conventional paired-data baseline at equal compute, and no error bars, seeds, or human evaluation back the headline benchmark numbers, which mix self-reported and third-party scores. - Read it or not: Practitioners building or training open image generators should read it for the concrete stage-by-stage recipe (resolutions, batch sizes, data ratios, optimizer settings); anyone seeking novel generative-modeling theory or ablated evidence for the paper's data-efficiency claims can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training open image-generation systems face three linked bottlenecks: paired image–text data is expensive and lossy (captions describe whole images whose details vanish under downsampling to low training resolutions), unified generation-and-editing models must preserve reference-image evidence without task-specific backbones, and deployment requires compressing long diffusion trajectories cheaply. The authors target the question of what it takes to train a strong generator from scratch with a fully open, inspectable recipe, for the community currently dependent on closed systems (GPT-Image, Nano-Banana, Seedream) or on open models whose recipes are only partially disclosed. Key Idea: Images alone contain the semantics needed to supervise their own generation: a frozen VLM can extract a conditioning signal from the same crop the DiT must reconstruct, with image-token masking preventing a trivial identity mapping. This converts the most compute-heavy training stages from paired-supervision to sparse-to-dense prediction on unlabeled images, and a resolution-aware cropping strategy keeps condition and target faithful (only mild downsampling of informative crops to 256²) — removing the caption-mismatch problem that plagues paired training at low resolution. Everything else (flow matching, AR-bucket training, DMD2-style distillation, checkpoint averaging) is a competent assembly of known techniques around this curriculum. Methodology: The pipeline has five sequential stages. (1) CoT supervised fine-tuning of the understanding backbone: block-diffusion masked training (block size 32) on ~2.6M packed 16,384-token sequences at 9:9:2 generation:understanding:text ratio, with complementary-mask pairs consumed as two optimizer steps; only this stage updates the VLM, which is frozen thereafter. (2) Image-only pre-training at 256²: SigLIP-VQ features of the target crop are token-masked (keep probability 1−ρimg), appended to a fixed auxiliary prompt, passed through a Residual Query Adapter into the frozen VLM, projected by a shallow Transformer connector, and used to condition a single-stream 6B DiT trained with the flow-matching objective L = E‖F_θ(x_t, t, h_cond) − (z − x)‖². (3) Image-only mid-training at 512² with aspect-ratio-bucketed variable resolution. (4) SFT: 512² text alignment → 1024² buckets → refinement on text-rich/portrait data → joint T2I:I2I editing training at 1:1 ratio; editing conditions the DiT via a dual pathway (SigLIP-VQ semantic reference tokens plus clean FLUX.2 VAE latents concatenated with the noised target latent), while the reference image bypasses the VLM entirely; logit-normal timestep sampling (P_mean=0.8, P_std=0.8) biases supervision toward high-noise states; checkpoint merging averages converged nearby checkpoints. (5) TwinFlow distillation: DMD2 reverse-KL distribution matching with real and fake score roles sharing one DiT backbone via signed times (+t generator / −t fake score) and dual output heads, 1:2 generator-to-fake-score update schedule, 4-step backward simulation, followed by TBSM-based reinforcement tuning. Throughout the DiT, parameter-free RMSNorm replaces all normalization layers and the Muon optimizer replaces AdamW for generation stages. Critical design decisions: freezing the VLM with only RQA/connector trainable (justified by cost and preserved understanding, ablated only for the CoT SFT stage on 18 understanding benchmarks); the 1:1 T2I:I2I mixing as capability replay (asserted, not ablated); reference bypassing the VLM (argued qualitatively, not ablated). Key Results: On Qwen-Image-Bench (1,000 stratified prompts, five aspects), LLaDA-Image scores 53.53 EN / 53.38 CN overall — first among open models, ahead of Z-Image Turbo (51.66/52.71) and Boogu-Image 0.1 Turbo (51.61/51.53), but clearly behind closed GPT-Image 2 (65.23/64.69) and Nano-Banana 2.0 (59.59/59.82). On LongText-Bench it reaches 0.923 (EN) / 0.913 (ZH), below Qwen-Image 2512 (0.956/0.965). On CVTG-2K it achieves 0.875 average word accuracy (second overall), 0.945 NED, 0.818 CLIPScore, degrading only from 0.892 (2 regions) to 0.857 (5 regions). On GenEval it scores 0.85 overall with a notably weak counting score of 0.53 (vs 0.91 for Seedream 3.0); on DPG-Bench 87.48. On GEdit-Bench editing, it reaches GO 7.336 (EN) / 7.294 (CN) — below all leading specialized editors (FireRed-Image-Edit 7.943, Qwen-Image-Edit 2511 7.877), with the authors flagging perceptual quality (GPQ 7.182 EN) as the weak component. Turbo runs at 2–4 sampling steps with a modest benchmark drop (~0.3–1.5 points). Baselines span current 2025–2026 open and closed systems, but baseline scores are raw self-reports from the corresponding models rather than a unified evaluation harness, and all benchmark testing is at standard scale (≤1024² generation). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely reusable contribution is the fully documented, open, real-data-dominant progressive curriculum demonstrating that >90% image-only training (220M samples, 98% real) suffices for a competitive 6B unified generator — an empirical system claim rather than a new algorithm. The image-only self-conditioning comes from prior IOMM work, TwinFlow/DuMo/TBSM distillation components are the authors' own prior papers, and Muon, parameter-free RMSNorm, logit-normal timestep sampling, flow matching, AR buckets, and checkpoint averaging are all existing techniques; the unified editing pathway (semantic + pixel reference streams bypassing the VLM) is a sensible configuration of known conditioning ideas rather than a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thin: the only controlled before/after evaluation is CoT SFT on 18 understanding benchmarks (Table 11, e.g., MMBench-EN 81.5→86.1, VL-RewardBench 47.8→55.7, but SimpleVQA 44.0→42.1 and MathVision 26.7→24.3); the central claims — image-only pre-training sufficing, real-dominant data yielding better long-run realism, T2I:I2I replay preventing forgetting, reference-bypass editing — are stated as Recipes/observations without controlled experiments. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere. Reproducibility is a genuine strength: weights (Base, Turbo, and FP8 variants), training/inference code, bucket configurations, and even captioning/filtering prompts are released on GitHub and Hugging Face. Methodological concerns: headline Qwen-Image-Bench scores mix self-reported baseline numbers with the authors' own evaluations; the benchmark itself originates from an ecosystem adjacent to the compared baselines; the qualitative "Real or Generated?" reader challenge is explicitly disclosed as non-controlled; and GenEval/DPG are dismissed as unreliable when convenient while still reported, a selective-evidence pattern a reviewer should note. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a trained system with released artifacts and benchmark evaluation. - Practical: Yes — a 6B model with FP8-quantized checkpoints and a 2–4-step Turbo variant targets commodity deployment; exact hardware requirements are not stated. - Efficient: Turbo reduces inference to 2–4 steps (vs 50 in some baselines' pipelines), and the distillation head adds no inference-time overhead; training compute totals are not reported. - Effective: Strong evidence for bilingual T2I (open-source leading on Qwen-Image-Bench, both tracks), but editing effectiveness is only partial — GEdit-Bench scores trail dedicated editors by 0.5–0.6 GO points, and the realism/ceiling claims for real-data training are supported only by qualitative examples. - Scalable: Untested beyond the 1024² training budget; native 2K generation is explicitly future work, and no evidence exists on how the recipe behaves at 10× data or model scale. The work delivers a substantial software artifact: four released checkpoints, training and inference code, and reusable recipe documentation (github.com/inclusionAI/LLaDA-Image; Hugging Face collection inclusionAI/llada-image). Strengths: - The decoupled curriculum is the paper's real intellectual contribution: >90% of the 220M-sample generation pipeline runs image-only, and the resolution-aware cropping argument (captions describe whole images, so paired training forces destructive downsampling while image-derived conditions do not) is a concrete, well-articulated insight. - The unified editing design avoids a separate editing backbone by feeding the reference image directly to the DiT through two complementary streams (SigLIP-VQ semantics + clean VAE latents), and one checkpoint serves both tasks — validated on GEdit-Bench in both languages while retaining T2I capability. - End-to-end reproducibility is unusually thorough: hyperparameters per stage (Table 2), exact AR-bucket tables, dual captioning prompts, and filtering logic are all published, making the recipe genuinely reusable rather than aspirational. - Honest benchmark handling in places: the report discloses that GenEval/DPG rankings diverge from human preference, reports the model's own counting weakness (0.53) prominently, and admits editing perceptual quality lags specialists. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that GenEval and DPG-Bench do not reliably track modern capability; that the real-data recipe converges more slowly on early benchmarks than synthetic-heavy alternatives; that editing perceptual quality (GPQ) trails specialized editing models; that text rendering degrades with region count, length, and layout complexity; that world-knowledge coverage of specialized or culturally specific subjects is limited; and that 2K generation is unaudited future work. They also explicitly scope the report as documenting trade-offs rather than claiming universal optimality of every component. This is a credibility positive — limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, though the biggest evidentiary gaps (no ablation of the core curriculum claims) are not framed as limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No controlled comparison of image-only pre-training/mid-training against a conventional paired-data pipeline at matched compute and data budget — the paper's central efficiency claim rests on assertion and prior IOMM results, not on this model. - The claims that real-dominant data yields a "higher long-horizon capability ceiling" and that 1:1 T2I:I2I mixing prevents forgetting are supported by no ablation, learning-curve evidence, or forgetting measurement. - Baseline numbers are self-reported by competing vendors/labs under potentially different protocols rather than re-evaluated in one harness; no human preference study backs the Qwen-Image-Bench headline claims. - The frozen VLM is fine-tuned only via CoT SFT and RQA, but the paper does not test whether a stronger or unfrozen understanding backbone would improve generation — the understanding-generation coupling is assumed, not measured. - Training compute (GPU-hours, energy) is absent, so the "moderate data budget" claim cannot be converted into a cost comparison. - Counting failure (0.53 on GenEval) is reported but unexplained and unaddressed. Bottom Line: For anyone training or fine-tuning open image generators, this is one of the most complete and reusable public recipes available and worth reading in full; as a research contribution it is primarily a strong engineering report whose data-efficiency and real-data-ceiling claims deserve, but do not receive, controlled experimental support.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ZimaBlue, a 5B-parameter World Action Model trained through a three-stage curriculum (causal embodied video pre-training on 120,000+ hours of human/robot egocentric video, multi-embodiment video-action mid-training on 6K hours of robot trajectories, and target-robot post-training) plus a Slow-Fast dual-system inference architecture for real-time robot control. - Why it's important: Action-labeled robot trajectories are expensive and scarce, so the paper targets the central scaling bottleneck in generalist robotics: converting abundant but action-free egocentric video into transferable control competence, with measured zero-shot success rising from 36.1% to 77.8% as video scale grows. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a jointly denoised video-action flow-matching objective over a unified 100-dimensional cross-embodiment state-action interface, plus an asynchronous dual-system where a 0.5B Fast DiT cross-attends to cached layer-wise video K/V features from the frozen 5B Slow DiT, with DMD distillation (8→2 steps) and Torch compile cutting closed-loop latency from 450 ms to 33 ms on an RTX 4090. - The missing: The real-robot evidence rests on 12 tasks × 10 rollouts on a single Franka platform with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, and the 120K-hour corpus includes an unstated volume of proprietary egocentric video that cannot be reproduced by others. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on VLA/world-model policies or robot data strategy — the scaling curve and unified action interface are directly relevant — but skip it if you want statistically robust comparisons or non-preprint rigor, since this is a company-style technical report with modest per-task sample sizes.

Problem & Motivation: General-purpose robots must follow open-ended language instructions and generalize across scenes, viewpoints, and embodiments, but VLA models are bounded by action-labeled robot data, which is expensive to collect even with teleoperation/UMI systems, while simulation suffers sim-to-real gaps. The paper argues that the scalable embodied data source is first-person human video (rich in affordances, contact events, tool use, and failure recovery), but such video lacks action labels and contains non-physical content (animation, edits), and generic video diffusion backbones (like Wan2.2, ZimaBlue's initialization) are optimized for descriptive video synthesis, not instruction-conditioned, causally grounded, sequential control. The gap addressed: how to convert action-free video at scale into causal physical priors usable for closed-loop manipulation, rather than merely retrofitting a video generator. Key Idea: Treat video scaling as the primary axis for World Action Models via a data-pyramid curriculum that assigns each data source its natural role — video-only causal pre-training for world knowledge, cross-embodiment video-action mid-training for action grounding through a unified 100D semantic state-action space with chunk-relative (anchor-frame-relative) action geometry, and target-embodiment post-training for precise control — combined with a Slow-Fast decomposition in which the Fast action branch conditions on the Slow world model's intermediate layer-wise video K/V caches rather than explicit generated future video, decoupling long-horizon predictive reasoning (Slow, low frequency) from 30 Hz reactive control (Fast). Methodology: Stage I re-purposes Wan2.2-TI2V-5B into a causal video dynamics model using a block-causal, teacher-forced flow-matching objective over video latents, with a three-row vertical multi-view canvas and view-validity masks so single-view egocentric and multi-view robot data share one representation; two phases move from a broad mixture (EPIC-KITCHENS, Egocentric-100K, EgoDex, DROID, AgiBot, Galaxea, etc.) to a curated manipulation-centric subset. Stage II adds four embodiment families (DROID, AgiBot, Galaxea, RoboMIND2-Franka) projected into the unified 100D interface (validity-masked, zero-filled inactive slots; 6D rotation; chunk-anchor-relative translations and joint deltas, normalized to [−1,1]); the Slow DiT jointly denoises future video latents and 24-step action chunks with coupled noise levels, L_sup = λ_vid·L_vid + λ_act·L_act, where noisy future video and action tokens mutually attend. Stage III specializes Slow to the target domain (60K steps on DROID for real-robot; interface-level encoders/decoders for unseen sim benchmarks), then trains the 0.5B Fast branch (initialized from Slow's first 12 layers, channel-interpolated) with Slow frozen, using an action-only flow-matching loss that samples time offsets to simulate asynchronous Real-Time Chunking (RTC). Deployment uses asynchronous dual-stream inference plus two-stage Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD, with two-time-scale fake-score updates and truncated two-step UniPC rollouts) compressing each branch from 8 to 2 DiT evaluations, then Torch compile. Critical design decisions: (1) unified 100D slot layout — reasonable and clearly specified; (2) auxiliary action supervision on Slow only for alignment, not deployment — justified by ablation of Slow-only vs. dual-system; (3) introducing Fast only at post-training on frozen Slow features — an efficiency choice that is plausible but not ablated against joint optimization. Key Results: Real-robot zero-shot on 12 held-out Franka tasks (10 rollouts/task; Toys scored per-object): overall success rises monotonically 36.1% (baseline, Wan2.2 init + DROID post-training) → 46.1% (+6K h multi-embodiment) → 66.9% (+60K h video) → 77.8% (+120K h video); Standard suite 87.9%, Perturbed suite 57.5%, beating official DROID-post-trained checkpoints of π0.5 (54.4% overall; 65.4 Standard / 32.5 Perturbed) and 14B DreamZero (53.6% overall). Standouts: microwave closing 0/10→9/10 and air-fryer 6/10→9/10 from cross-embodiment data; 60K→120K video adds only +5.0 on Standard but +22.5 on Perturbed. Dual-system vs. Slow-only: 77.8% vs. 63.9% overall, with the larger gain on Perturbed (57.5% vs. 30.0%). Latency: 449.6 ms (Slow) → 145.6 ms (async dual-system) → 33.0 ms (DMD + compile), a 13.6× total speedup, at a 2.8-point success cost (75.0%). Benchmarks: LIBERO-Plus 86.7% zero-shot (best, +0.9 over InternVLA-A1.5) and 92.0% with SFT (+1.9 over CAC-VLA), with camera viewpoint the weakest category (58.1% zero-shot); RoboTwin 2.0 94.5% average (best, +0.4 over ABot-M0.5), Clean–Randomized gap only 0.4 pp; RoboCasa365 49.5% overall and 16.5% Composite-Unseen — more than double ABot-M0.6's 7.9% — though second to Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (57.4%), which uses 100K hours of real-robot data. Baselines are recent (2025–2026) and generally strong. The counter-intuitive-ish finding is that video scale helps robustness-to-shift far more than in-distribution execution. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a controlled scaling curve showing egocentric video hours causally improve zero-shot manipulation, especially under visual shift) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the integrated Slow-Fast WAM with K/V-cache coupling, unified action interface, and 33 ms closed loop) + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (DMD + async inference + compile). The individual ingredients — video-action flow matching, RTC-style chunking, dual-system policies, DMD distillation, cross-embodiment token layouts — are established (DreamZero, LingBot-VA 2.0, AHA-WAM, RTC, π0.5 all close relatives); the genuine novelty is the demonstrated video-scaling result and the specific K/V-cache injection mechanism, not any single algorithmic component. Rigor & Reproducibility: The headline scaling ablation is well-controlled: all four configurations share identical DROID post-training data, schedules (Slow 60K / Fast 160K steps), and 8-step inference, isolating pre-training data. Ablations exist for dual-system vs. Slow-only and for acceleration stages. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; 10 rollouts per real task (the authors themselves note per-task sampling noise and lean on suite-level macro averages); the full real-robot evaluation is confined to one Franka platform and one post-training dataset; the corpus includes a "substantial volume of human egocentric proprietary video" that is not released, so the 120K-hour configuration is not reproducible even though code is posted (github.com/ZimaBlue-WAM/ZimaBlue; project page zimablue-wam.github.io); no model weights are stated as released. Some benchmark evaluations mix training and evaluation regimes (RoboCasa365 uses the pre-training Human300 split; RoboTwin post-trains on the benchmark's own demonstration mixture), so benchmark numbers partly measure in-distribution fine-tuning, and the zero-shot real-robot "scaling" ladder is cumulative rather than a factorial design (video-only and mid-training-only arms are not fully crossed). This is a preprint/technical report, not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact). - Practical: Yes — the full dual-system runs closed-loop on a single consumer NVIDIA RTX 4090 at 33 ms, which is unusually concrete for this literature. - Efficient: Strong — 13.6× latency reduction over naive Slow inference; training cost for 120K hours of video pre-training is not stated. - Effective: The evidence supports the generalization claim on 12 real tasks and three sim benchmarks, but real-robot gains rest on small sample sizes and one embodiment; Perturbed tasks remain at only 5–7/10. - Scalable: Only claimed beyond 120K hours — the monotonic trend supports continued scaling, but there is no evidence at 10–100× data or on non-Franka deployment embodiments. Deliverables: public code repository and project page; trained weights and the proprietary video portion are not stated as released, so the artifact is partially reusable. Strengths: - The controlled data-scaling ladder (identical post-training, cumulative pre-training) is the cleanest evidence yet published, to this reviewer's knowledge, that action-free egocentric video hours translate into zero-shot manipulation success, with the gain concentrated exactly where a world-model hypothesis predicts (perturbed/unseen distributions: +22.5 pp on Perturbed from 60K→120K hours; Composite-Unseen more than doubled on RoboCasa365). - The Fast-branch mechanism — cross-attending to frozen layer-wise video K/V caches rather than requiring explicit future-video generation on the control path — is a concrete, well-motivated solution to the WAM latency problem, validated by the dual-system ablation (+13.9 pp overall, +27.5 pp on Perturbed). - The unified 100D semantic slot layout with chunk-anchor-relative action geometry and validity masking is a careful, fully specified cross-embodiment interface that others could adopt independently. - Honest failure analysis: the authors report the distilled model's 2.8 pp regression, the camera-viewpoint weakness on LIBERO-Plus (58.1% zero-shot, +37.3 after SFT), and characterize remaining failure modes rather than hiding them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: per-task sampling noise from limited rollouts (advocating suite-level averages); remaining failures on Perturbed tasks (5/10–7/10 even for the full model), attributed to lack of progress-aware replanning and corrective control; camera-viewpoint generalization as a pre-training-diversity bottleneck; the need for broader, multi-embodiment evaluation benchmarks; and future needs for reasoning modules and in-context skill acquisition. These are confronted directly, which strengthens credibility, though the proprietary-data and single-embodiment constraints are not framed as limitations of the evaluation's external validity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical fragility: with 10 rollouts/task, a 2.8 pp difference (75.0% vs. 77.8%) is within noise; no variance or significance reporting undermines fine-grained comparisons, including several 0.1–0.9 pp benchmark margins touted as wins. - The baseline (36.1%) is far below π0.5 (54.4%) under the same DROID post-training, raising the possibility that part of the "video pre-training" gain compensates for a weak reactive-policy baseline rather than pure world-model benefit; a VLA head trained on the same mid-trained backbone would disentangle this. - The 120K-hour corpus mixes public datasets with undisclosed proprietary egocentric video, so the headline configuration cannot be independently reproduced, and the video-vs-robot data ratio (the paper's own Figure 7 argument) partly rests on unreleasable data. - The cumulative ladder never tests video pre-training without multi-embodiment mid-training or vice versa at fixed post-training, and all real-robot results are on the same embodiment (Franka/DROID) used in mid-training — cross-embodiment transfer to a truly unseen real robot is never measured. - Sim benchmark numbers partly involve fine-tuning on benchmark-derived data (RoboTwin mixtures, RoboCasa365 Human300), so "best on leaderboard" claims conflate pre-training value with task-specific adaptation; Goodhart risk on leaderboard-style comparisons is not discussed. - Pre-training compute cost, carbon, and wall-clock for 120K hours of video are unreported, preventing a data-vs-compute efficiency assessment. Bottom Line: A practitioner in robot learning or VLA/world-model research gains real, actionable evidence — particularly the video-scaling curve and the K/V-cache dual-system recipe — that justifies reading this report, despite the small-N evaluation, proprietary data caveats, and the likelihood that the same ground will be covered more rigorously by follow-up peer-reviewed work from DreamZero, LingBot-VA, and π-lineage teams.

CIVA: Critic-Induced Value-Subspace Attacks on Visual World-Model Agents

J Wang, M Zhu, T Zhang, J Ruan, W Wang, S Liang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CIVA, a two-stage white-box attack that extracts a low-rank perturbation subspace from a frozen DreamerV3 agent's critic gradients via SVD and, at test time, optimizes only subspace coefficients with EMA smoothing to degrade the agent's episodic return. - Why it's important: Visual world-model agents are candidates for safety-critical deployment, but existing frame-wise pixel-space RL attacks are diluted by recurrent latent dynamics and are computationally heavy per frame, so defenders lack an accurate picture of the realistic attack surface. - How it does it: The core move is to run critic-guided PGD offline on clean rollouts, stack the resulting perturbations into a matrix, take its top-r right singular vectors (r=32 of D=12,288 pixels), and then do causal online PGD only in this victim-aware coefficient space with a temporal EMA on the coefficients. - The good: The ablations cleanly isolate the key claim: swapping the critic-induced basis for a random basis of identical rank collapses reward drop from 26.07% to 6.90% on DMC walker walk, showing the gains come from critic alignment, not low rank per se. - The missing: All evidence comes from a single victim backbone (DreamerV3), three tasks, and 5 seeds with one episode each; no black-box, transfer, or adaptive-defense evaluation is reported, and the suboptimality bound in Appendix A.4 relies on informal assumptions. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on adversarial robustness of world-model or model-based RL agents — the critic-subspace observation is genuinely useful; skip it if you need black-box threat models or multi-architecture evidence.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (58) and Impact (50) pull the composite down: only 5 evaluation episodes per cell with no variance reporting, a single DreamerV3 backbone, no defended or black-box victims, a heuristic suboptimality bound, and code only promised with no repository — the attack surface characterization is preliminary. Novelty (70) is solid — the critic-induced subspace with decisive random-basis and reward-head controls is a real structural finding — and Non-Obviousness (70) benefits from the KL/reward-drop decoupling observation, but the narrow white-box threat model (Resilience 60) limits how far the claims travel.
empirical Novelty 70 Rigor 58 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 65 Resilience 60 Impact 50
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Dreamer-style visual RL agents act through a recurrent latent state accumulated over many frames rather than through a single observation. Prior observation-space attacks on deep RL (MAD, UAP-RL, PA-AD, Illusory, DAPGD) mostly optimize perturbations independently per frame in full pixel space, which the authors argue is mismatched with world-model agents in three ways: recurrent latent dynamics dilute isolated high-frequency noise (C1), full-pixel per-frame PGD is expensive under a per-frame compute budget (C2), and a tight ℓ∞ budget forces a trade-off between return suppression, temporal coherence, and visual stealth (C3). The motivating question is what a strong, causally constrained online attack on a frozen DreamerV3 agent looks like, as a prerequisite for defending such agents. Key Idea: Effective attack directions against a world-model agent concentrate in a low-dimensional subspace induced by the victim's own critic — perturbations obtained by descending the critic's categorical value surrogate lie, up to first order, in the pull-back of the encoder Jacobian applied to latent-space critic gradients, whose rank is bounded by the latent dimension d_s (≈32) rather than the pixel dimension D (12,288). Extracting this basis once via SVD and confining online optimization to it makes the attack cheap, temporally coherent (EMA on coefficients filters jitter without leaving critic-effective directions), and effective. Methodology: CIVA has two stages. Stage A (offline): after a 200-step warm-up, run L=8 steps of ℓ∞ PGD (ε=24/255, step size ε/4 with RMS-normalized gradients) per frame for M=600 frames on a clean rollout, minimizing the expected bin index v(o)=Σ k·softmax(ℓ_k(o)) of DreamerV3's categorical critic — a monotone surrogate of predicted return; stack the flattened perturbations into Δ∈R^{600×12288} and take the top r=32 right singular vectors as basis V_r. Stage B (online, causal): per frame, warm-start from the previous post-EMA coefficient, run 8 PGD steps on α_t∈R^32 against L_val(δ_t)=v(o_t+δ_t) using pixel gradients projected via g_α=V_r^T g_δ, smooth with α_t=0.75·α_{t-1}+0.25·α*_t, lift to δ_t=V_r α_t, and project onto the ℓ∞ ball and pixel range (residual <10^-3). This is constrained first-order optimization over a learned low-rank parameterization; no RL-style training of the attacker. Critical design decisions: (a) using the critic rather than the reward head as the attack signal — justified by the V4 ablation (reward-head subspace drops effectiveness to 4.84%); (b) EMA in coefficient space rather than pixel space — argued via a frequency-domain analysis that pixel-space EMA would smooth the perturbation off critic-effective directions; (c) a two-step lift-project-reproject approximation of the non-axis-aligned constrained projection — justified empirically by the small residual, though the accompanying suboptimality bound (Appendix A.4.iii) mixes a smoothness argument with an Eckart–Young tail bound informally and is not a rigorous theorem. Key Results: All results are on a frozen DreamerV3 victim at 64×64×3 resolution with ε=24/255, 5 seeds × 1 episode each, on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU. On DMC walker walk (natural reward 952.25), CIVA achieves 703.97 (26.07% drop) vs. UAP-RL 23.25%, DAPGD 18.79%, PA-AD 17.38%, Illusory 16.50%, MAD 1.84%; TempAbs is 0.646 vs. 10–20 for per-frame baselines, and SSIM is 0.710. On Atari Pong (natural 21.0), CIVA reaches 3.0 (85.71% drop) vs. MAD's 66.67% and under 25% for all other baselines, with TempAbs 0.394. On Crafter (natural 10.10), CIVA ties UAP-RL at 29.70% drop with the best SSIM (0.970) and near-best TempAbs (0.27). The paper also reports ~10× lower per-frame attack latency than full-pixel PGD (measured against its own V2 ablation, not a published timing baseline). Baselines span 2020–2025 and are reasonably current; 5 episodes is a small evaluation sample, and no variance or significance statistics are reported. A notable secondary finding: large Action-KL does not imply strong attack (PA-AD attains KL 1.35 on DMC with only 17.38% drop; DAPGD attains 1.960 on Crafter with 9.90% drop). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an embedded NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING). The genuinely novel element is the provenance of the attack subspace: it is extracted from the victim critic's own attack gradients rather than from input statistics (PCA), hand-crafted bases (DCT), or random projections as in prior subspace attacks, and it is deployed causally with coefficient-space EMA. The remaining machinery — PGD, truncated SVD, EMA smoothing, ℓ∞ projection — is a standard combination of existing techniques applied to a new victim class (recurrent world-model agents). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-targeted, isolating the critic-induced basis (V1: random basis, 6.90% drop vs. 26.07%), the subspace constraint itself (V2: full-pixel PGD, 12.61%), the EMA (V3: +0.77 pp reward drop but ~3× TempAbs), and the signal source (V4: reward head, 4.84%). No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; each cell averages only 5 episodes. Appendix A.1 gives substantial reproducibility detail (training steps, train ratios, metric definitions, per-baseline algorithms in A.4), and the paper states code will be released, but no URL or repository is given in the provided text. Concerns: evaluation is restricted to the authors' own chosen tasks and a single backbone; the theoretical justifications in A.4(ii)–(iii) are heuristic rather than proven; and the ~10× latency claim is self-referenced against the paper's own full-pixel variant rather than an external implementation. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (attacks actually run against a trained victim, plus a small built toolchain). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on a single 96 GB consumer/prosumer GPU (RTX PRO 6000) with JAX/Flax, and the online stage only optimizes 32 scalars per frame. - Efficient: Online cost is ~r/D of full-pixel PGD (32 vs. 12,288 parameters) with an order-of-magnitude latency reduction claimed; Stage A requires one offline SVD over a 600×12,288 matrix plus 600 PGD probes, which is cheap. - Effective: The evidence shows large return suppression on all three tasks under a matched budget and protocol, but only against undefended DreamerV3 victims — no evidence it degrades robustly-trained or defended agents. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 64×64 observations and 1,000-step episodes; the authors themselves note the subspace may need refreshing under distribution shift, and scaling to higher resolutions or other architectures is unclaimed beyond a rank-selection recipe. The work delivers a method plus promised code; no released artifact URL is provided in the text. Strengths: - The core empirical observation — that critic-guided perturbations concentrate in a subspace whose rank tracks the latent dimension, with the top 32 singular values explaining >95% of spectral energy — is a concrete, checkable structural finding about world-model agents, not just a trick that happens to work. - The ablation design is unusually decisive for an attack paper: the random-basis control (V1) directly rules out the "any low-rank basis works" explanation, and the reward-head control (V4) rules out "any victim gradient works." - The evaluation respects a causal, per-frame compute budget applied uniformly to all baselines, and reports stealth metrics (TempAbs, SSIM) alongside effectiveness, exposing the trilemma that prior work usually ignores. - The observation that Action-KL is a misleading proxy for attack strength (KL and reward drop decouple on both DMC and Crafter) is a useful negative result for the subfield. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that CIVA assumes white-box access to the victim critic and its gradients, does not apply to strict black-box settings, requires clean rollouts from the target agent offline, may need subspace refresh under environment shift, and was evaluated on a single backbone (DreamerV3) across three tasks. The limitations section is direct and does not minimize; the broader-impact statement honestly notes potential misuse against deployed visual policies while arguing white-box requirements limit realistic risk. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Only 5 evaluation episodes per cell with no variance reporting; on sparse-reward Crafter in particular (integer achievement counts), 5 episodes may not support the tie with UAP-RL at 29.70%. - No evaluation against any robust or adversarially-trained victim, so the paper measures only the undefended attack surface — the most relevant question for its stated defense motivation is untested. - No black-box, transfer, or query-based variant, even a weak one; the practical threat of a white-box attacker with critic gradient access is narrow. - The theoretical material in Appendix A.4 (low-rank argument, O(L_v σ²_{r+1}) suboptimality bound, EMA transfer-function analysis) is presented as justification but is heuristic; the bound's assumptions (stationarity of the inner problem, proximity of test frames to the probed distribution) are not verified. - Subspace is extracted from a single clean rollout of the victim's own policy; robustness of the basis to policy distribution shift during the attacked episode (where the agent's behavior diverges from the rollout) is asserted via the bound rather than measured. - Per-frame latency comparison lacks absolute wall-clock numbers and external baseline timings. Bottom Line: A practitioner in adversarial RL or world-model robustness should read this — the critic-induced subspace observation and the clean ablations are a real contribution to understanding the temporal adversarial surface of Dreamer-style agents — but the single-backbone, undefended-victim, 5-episode evidence base means it is a strong attack proposal, not yet a characterization of the threat that defenders must actually plan for.
