Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the question of when AI assistance to AI R&D crosses from ordinary acceleration into a self-amplifying feedback regime — I. J. Good's intelligence-explosion hypothesis restated as a measurable stability question. The affected community includes AI-forecasting researchers, AI-policy analysts, and economists modeling growth with AI inside the R&D production function. Existing work supplies ingredients (economic growth models with AI as a research input, benchmarks like RE-Bench, MLE-bench, PaperBench that measure components of the research loop, expert-elicitation surveys for AGI timing) but does not identify the dynamical condition under which the feedback loop becomes unstable, nor how feedback delay, hardening research frontiers, multi-actor transfer, and physical compute constraints jointly shape that transition. The specific gap closed is the absence of a local-stability criterion separating recursive amplification from fast-but-subcritical progress. Key Idea: The core insight is an epidemiological transplant: define a reproduction number for AI research capability, R_AI = g/σ = χa/σ, where a is the recursive gain of AI research capability on future R&D productivity, χ ∈ [0,1] is the fraction of that gain surviving the full development pipeline ("operational closure"), and σ is the local rate at which the research frontier hardens. R_AI > 1 means a capability perturbation reproduces itself faster than the frontier dampens it — a stability boundary, not a capability threshold. Because baseline throughput v scales both the damping term and the feedback term in the linearized dynamics, compute and spending shift the pace of progress without moving the criticality boundary; feedback delay τ instead limits how fast amplification becomes visible (λ* → ln R_AI/τ as vστ → ∞). A second key move treats the ecosystem, not the agent: with cross-actor transfer, criticality is governed by the spectral radius ρ(K) of a reproduction matrix, so the network can be supercritical while every actor is individually subcritical. Methodology: The framework has three layers. (1) Measurement scaffolding: capability x(t) is defined via Eq. (1) as resource-price-adjusted log cost improvement over a fixed weighted task panel — explicitly a local coordinate, not a universal intelligence scalar. (2) A delayed nonlinear dynamics, Eq. (3): ẋ(t) = r(t) f[x(t)] e^{Φ(x[t−τ(t)],t)}, with ∂Φ/∂x = g = χa and σ(x) = −d ln f/dx; linearizing around a reference trajectory with speed v gives the scalar positive-delay system ξ̇ = −vσ ξ(t) + vg ξ(t−τ), whose characteristic equation λ + vσ = vg e^{−λτ} yields Proposition 1 (all roots stable iff R_AI < 1). Proposition 2 shows that with a finite frontier f(x) = (1 − x/X)^β, σ = β/(X − x) diverges, so any bounded-gain system returns to subcriticality — supercritical episodes are transient within a paradigm. Proposition 3 extends this to n coupled actors via the reproduction matrix K_ij = g_ij/σ_i, with stability governed by ρ(K) in the zero-delay case. (3) Numerical scenarios (deterministic ODE/DDE integration; code released at github.com/burtsev/recursive-criticality-ai): normalization x0 = 0, X = 1, β = 2, logistic closure χ(x) with k = 10, τ = 0.5 yr, r_ref = 1/24 yr⁻¹ calibrated to expert-survey AGI medians (2047–2050), AGI/ASI thresholds at x = 0.50/0.80. Critical design decisions: (a) scalar one-dimensional capability — mathematically convenient but a strong simplification, acknowledged as local; (b) closure modeled as logistic in capability, asserted rather than justified from pipeline data; (c) scenario parameters a ∈ {0.5, 3, 6, 15} chosen to span dynamical regimes, explicitly not empirically constrained — a decision the authors flag honestly. Key Results: These are analytical propositions plus conditional numerical demonstrations, not measurements. Analytically: the criticality threshold R_AI = 1 exists and is independent of baseline throughput; the dominant root near criticality is λ ≈ vσ(R_AI − 1)/(1 + vσ R_AI τ); at high throughput λ saturates at ln R_AI/τ; finite frontiers force R_AI → 0 as x → X. Numerically (Table 1, four scenarios vs. a no-RSI baseline with T_AGI = 24 yr, T_ASI = 96 yr, Δ = 72 yr): subcritical feedback (a = 0.5) still advances AGI by ~2.7 yr and ASI by ~22 yr; weak supercriticality (a = 3) gives Δ ≈ 11.8 yr; transient takeoff (a = 6) gives Δ ≈ 2.7 yr; rapid transition (a = 15) compresses the AGI-to-ASI interval from 72 years to 0.45 years. Strategic-network scenarios (Table 2): an open ecosystem of individually subcritical actors (max K_ii = 0.65, ρ(K) = 1.55) produces the shortest transition (~2.8 yr), beating closed labs (ρ(K) = 1.01) and a globally competitive blocs configuration (ρ(K) ≈ 1.15, τ = 1 yr) despite lower research effort (m_r = 0.8). Hardware scenarios show physical headroom F_soft_AGI ∈ {8, 2, 0.75} with Q = 100 and g_phys = 0.25 yr⁻¹ can delay both thresholds or only the AGI-to-ASI interval. The most counter-intuitive finding: subcritical systems can still gain substantially from recursive feedback, and supercriticality can begin and end invisibly. There are no baselines in the empirical sense — baselines are alternative parameterizations of the authors' own model. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (recursive criticality as a local stability transition with a reproduction-number criterion, plus the multi-actor spectral-radius extension) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in a weak sense (structural theorems about regime separation, not data findings). The delay-differential machinery is a scalar instance of standard positive-delay-systems stability theory (the authors cite Briat 2018), and the authors candidly note Cunningham et al. (2026) independently derive a closely related elasticity-threshold condition; the genuinely novel elements are the operational-closure concept, the throughput-invariance of the critical boundary, the transient-supercriticality result, and the reproduction-matrix treatment of research ecosystems — the rest is competent application of known stability theory to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Propositions 1–3 are stated with explicit assumptions and are elementary for anyone familiar with delayed linear stability; no proofs are shown in the text beyond the characteristic equation, but the results follow directly. No ablations in the ML sense, but the scenario design holds (β, k, τ, r_ref) fixed while varying only a — a deliberate single-parameter ablation isolating the central mechanism. Error bars and seeds are not applicable (deterministic dynamics); instead the authors repeatedly disclaim that scenarios are "conditional demonstrations and not probabilistic forecasts." Code and a computational notebook are released at https://github.com/burtsev/recursive-criticality-ai. Methodological concerns: (a) the key parameters are not identified from any data — the model is developed and exercised entirely in a hypothetical parameter space (Goodhart risk is absent, but empirical validity is entirely untested); (b) r_ref is calibrated to expert surveys whose definitional consistency the authors themselves question; (c) Proposition 3 is proven only for the zero-delay case while all strategic scenarios use τ = 0.3–1.0 yr, leaving a gap between the proved result and the illustrated regime; (d) the capability coordinate Eq. (1) is defined but never operationalized on real cost panels. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL (with illustrative deterministic numerical scenarios; no primary experimental claim on real systems). - Sound: Assumptions are stated and the linearized propositions are correct for the scalar positive-delay case, but Proposition 3 excludes delay and all results are local (valid for slow coefficient variation and small perturbations) — global dynamics of the nonlinear system are only explored numerically. - General: The framework requires a scalar capability coordinate, a slowly varying coefficient regime, a monotone frontier-hardening function, and (for Prop 3) zero delay — restrictive conditions relative to real multi-paradigm, multi-scale R&D, though the authors scope the finite-frontier result to a single paradigm. - Tight: These are stability thresholds, not approximation bounds; there is no tightness question in the bound sense, though the dominant-root approximation near criticality is only first-order. - Implementable: The framework directly suggests a measurement protocol (estimate recursive gain, closure, cycle duration, frontier hardening, cross-actor transfer across successive development cycles), but no follow-up work has operationalized any of these estimates, and the paper itself runs none. The work delivers a software artifact of limited reuse value (a reproduction notebook for scenario figures) and reusable conceptual machinery (the R_AI criterion and reproduction-matrix formalism); it stops at paper form — no dataset, model weights, or measurement tool. Strengths: - The R_AI criterion is a genuinely useful analytic device: it collapses the takeoff question into a measurable balance between recursive gain and frontier hardening, and its throughput-invariance yields the paper's sharpest and most defensible claim — fast progress and recursive amplification are distinct phenomena that require different evidence to diagnose. - The multi-actor extension is the most original result: showing that an ecosystem of individually subcritical actors can be collectively supercritical (ρ(K) > 1) reframes governance questions from "is any lab self-improving?" to "what is the network's reproduction number?" — a non-obvious structural insight. - Intellectual honesty as an execution strength: the paper consistently separates claims from evidence, labels all numerical outputs conditional on stated parameterizations, acknowledges the independent Cunningham et al. derivation, and specifies exactly which quantities would need to be measured to make the framework predictive. - The decomposition of interventions (effort multipliers change pace; closure/gain/delay changes change the regime; physical compute constrains deployability without changing criticality) gives the governance community a clean taxonomy that prior verbal treatments lacked. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state explicitly that: numerical scenarios are conditional demonstrations, not forecasts; β, a, k, and χ are "not presently constrained by direct empirical estimates"; r_ref and τ are illustrative calibrations to uncertain expert surveys; R_AI > 1 is a local condition that does not imply indefinite growth; the finite-frontier result is paradigm-local and breakthroughs can reset X; AGI/ASI thresholds at x = 0.50/0.80 are illustrative; bounded parallelizability may bind before the delay-limited regime. This is direct, repeated confrontation of limitations rather than minimization — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No identification strategy: the paper proposes measuring g, χ, σ, τ, and transfer, but offers no design for how to estimate them causally (its own related-work section notes benchmarks "do not yet identify how an improvement causally affects subsequent productivity"), so the framework's falsifiability is currently nominal. - The scalar capability coordinate is a stronger assumption than acknowledged: real R&D feedback is multidimensional (code, experiments, theory, evaluation infrastructure), and a single x with a single σ can misattribute which margin is hardening. - Proposition 3 is zero-delay but every strategic scenario has τ ∈ [0.3, 1.0] yr; the proved network result and the illustrated network dynamics are in different regimes, and no delay-robustness analysis of ρ(K) is given. - Closure χ is modeled as increasing in capability alone, yet the paper itself notes bottlenecks (human review, experimental capacity, secure execution) bind as throughput rises — χ(x, t) depending on scale is mentioned but never modeled, so the throughput-invariance of R_AI may fail in exactly the high-throughput cases of interest. - Sensitivity of the headline numbers (e.g., the 0.45-yr AGI-to-ASI compression) to the threshold placements x_AGI = 0.50 and x_ASI = 0.80, which are arbitrary, is not reported; the asymmetry result (larger effects on later thresholds) plausibly depends strongly on this choice. - No comparison against alternative takeoff formalisms (e.g., Davidson's compute-centric takeoff model or Aghion–Jones–Jones) on the same scenarios, so the reader cannot judge whether R_AI adds predictive or merely descriptive power relative to existing economic models. Bottom Line: A practitioner in AI forecasting, AI governance, or the economics of AI-driven R&D gains a genuinely clarifying analytical vocabulary (the R_AI criterion, operational closure, and the network reproduction matrix) that is worth adopting, but should treat every number in the paper as un calibrated illustration — there is currently no stronger alternative that separates recursive amplification from ordinary acceleration this cleanly, and the field would benefit most if the authors' proposed measurement program were executed next.

S3Gym: Can LLMs Turn Self- Testing and Self-Judging into Self-Improvement?

J Shi, S Tao, Y Wu, Z Wang, J Zhang, J Liu, X Lei… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces S3Gym, an interactive benchmark of seven text-based games with executable environment verifiers that evaluates whether LLM agents can convert their own exploration experience into improved future behavior, testing three experience-incorporation pathways (History ICL, Summary Memory, parameter Training) under a unified protocol that separates permissive exploration from strict held-out evaluation. - Why it's important: Existing agent benchmarks evaluate LLMs as fixed policies and never test whether agents can actively test their own behavior, judge the resulting experience, and use it to improve—a capability gap that currently requires human forward-deployed engineers to close in production. - How it does it: Withholds verifier-computed rewards from the agent during exploration, forces the agent to self-score each action, then compares those self-judgments against ground-truth rewards and measures whether the resulting experience (retained as raw history, compressed into summaries, or internalized via SFT) transfers to stricter held-out game configurations. - The good: Across 98 runs and 116,117 transitions, the paper shows that self-judging reliability is nearly uncorrelated with subsequent improvement (overall ρ(A,g) = −0.010), revealing that accurate local scoring alone is insufficient—a finding that redirects attention from judgment calibration to experience transformation. - The missing: Only 3 evaluation episodes per checkpoint and no confidence intervals or significance tests, making many reported gains—especially on sparse-reward games like Chess—statistically fragile; the training pathway is tested on a single 8B model (Qwen3-8B) and the negative transfer on PvZ (score drops from 23 to 6) is observed but not diagnosed. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building self-improving agents or designing the next generation of adaptive-agent benchmarks, because the judgment–improvement decoupling finding and the task-structure-dependent summary-vs-history result are actionable; skip if you only need another static agent leaderboard.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents deployed in interactive environments accumulate behavioral experience, but existing benchmarks (AgentBench, AgentBoard, KORGym, TextWorld, ALFWorld) treat the evaluated model as a fixed policy—they measure static capability at evaluation time without testing whether the agent can use its own past interactions to improve future decisions. The paper frames this gap using the forward-deployed engineer (FDE) analogy: in industry, human engineers supply the feedback signal layer (tests, judges, validation mechanisms) that turns a capable model into a working system, and no existing benchmark isolates whether agents can construct and act on that feedback signal themselves. The specific gap closed is the absence of a unified protocol that (a) separates model-generated self-judgments from environment-verifiable outcomes, (b) compares multiple experience-incorporation mechanisms under identical conditions, and (c) tests transfer to stricter held-out configurations rather than the same configuration used during exploration. Key Idea: Withhold environment verifier rewards during exploration, require the agent to produce both an action and a self-judged score at every step, then measure (1) whether those self-judgments agree with the verifier's actual rewards and (2) whether judged experience—incorporated via raw history in context, compressed natural-language summaries, or supervised fine-tuning on high-scoring actions—produces measurable improvement on held-out configurations. The core insight the paper delivers is that self-judgment reliability and self-improvement are nearly decoupled: agents can score their actions accurately yet fail to convert that signal into transferable behavioral change. Methodology: Each self-improvement cycle follows: Explore → Judge → Consolidate → Update → Evaluate. During exploration (30 episodes per cycle, permissive configurations like 9×9 Minesweeper with extra lives), the agent receives observations, within-episode history, and pathway-specific experience state; it outputs (action, self-judged score) jointly. The environment returns the next observation, visible feedback, and a hidden verifier reward retained benchmark-side. Experience is consolidated into one of three forms: (1) History ICL—score-annotated trajectories serialized into context (100k-token limit); (2) Summary Memory—model-compressed strategies with retain/avoid/next-direction structure, cached per session; (3) Training—supervised fine-tuning on high-scoring actions from exploration trajectories (only tested on Qwen3-8B, 20 checkpoints). Evaluation occurs every 3 exploration episodes using 3 strict-mode episodes on held-out configurations (e.g., first-mine-terminates Minesweeper, uniform opponent sampling in Trust Evolution). Metrics: average score across checkpoints, maximum score, and AUC+ (positive area above initial-score baseline via trapezoidal integration). Critical design decisions: (a) verifier rewards hidden from the agent during exploration—justified as isolating self-judgment from ground-truth guidance; (b) separate exploration and evaluation distributions—justified as testing transfer rather than memorization; (c) SFT treated as auxiliary rather than primary pathway—justified by optimization-variable confounds, though this limits depth of training analysis. Key Results: - Context-level pathways (7 proprietary models, 7 games): Under Summary Memory, GPT-5.5 achieves highest average scores on Minesweeper (0.742), Nullify (0.576), and Snake (10.697); Gemini-3.5-Flash leads on Chess (0.547), PvZ (44.697), and Trust Evolution (17.242) under History ICL. Summary Memory produces dramatic gains for some pairs: Gemini-2.5-Flash Minesweeper AUC+ rises from 0.000 (ICL) to 7.794, and PvZ from 24.402 to 238.501. But it produces severe losses for others: GPT-5.5 PvZ AUC+ drops from 548.499 to 33.219, and Gemini-3.5-Flash Trust Evolution drops from 200.000 to 55.095. - Self-judging reliability (116,117 transitions): Event agreement ranges from 0.496 (Chess, near chance) to 0.881 (PvZ); NMAE ranges from 0.041 (Tetris) to 0.882 (PvZ). Judgment–improvement coupling is near zero across the full benchmark: ρ(A, g) = −0.010 and ρ(−E, g) = −0.018, with tertile gaps also negligible. Run-level correlation between agreement and NABA is r = −0.23. - Parameter Training (Qwen3-8B): Trust Evolution score rises from 0 to a maximum of 30 (AUC+ = 163.5); Snake reaches 1 at three intermediate epochs but returns to zero; Minesweeper, Nullify, and Tetris remain at zero throughout; PvZ shows severe negative transfer (23 → 6 at every updated checkpoint). - Baselines: No external method baselines are compared; the comparison is internal across the three pathways and seven models. Tested at standard scale (30 exploration episodes per game per model), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The benchmark environment set builds on KORGym's game framework, but the evaluation protocol—withheld verifier rewards, mandatory self-judging, and paired exploration/evaluation configurations—is a genuinely new formulation. The most novel empirical contribution is the near-zero coupling between self-judgment quality and subsequent improvement, which contradicts the implicit assumption in Reflexion-style methods that better judgment leads to better improvement. The three pathways (History ICL, Summary Memory, SFT) are standard techniques; the contribution is the controlled comparison under a unified protocol, not the mechanisms themselves. Rigor & Reproducibility: - Ablations: The paper compares pathways within the same models and games, which serves as an implicit ablation of experience representation. No component-level ablations (e.g., varying summary length, judgment format, or training data filtering thresholds) are reported. - Error bars / significance: None reported. 3 evaluation episodes per checkpoint is small; for sparse-reward games like Chess (binary 0-1), single-episode variance likely dominates reported Avg and AUC+ values. No multiple seeds or confidence intervals. - Code/data: A project page is listed (https://self-developing-agents.github.io/), but the paper text does not explicitly confirm a public code or data release. - Methodological concerns: The training pathway is evaluated on a single open 8B model, limiting generality of training-level conclusions. The judgment–improvement coupling analysis pools all models and games per game, which may mask model-specific effects. AUC+ is scale-dependent across games (acknowledged by authors), preventing cross-game aggregation. Models with incomplete results are excluded, introducing potential selection bias toward stronger or more stable models. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: SYSTEMS (a benchmark and evaluation framework). - Practical: Runs on API-accessible proprietary models plus one open 8B model; the games are text-based with lightweight programmatic verifiers, so no special hardware is needed. - Efficient: 30 exploration episodes + 11 evaluation checkpoints × 3 episodes = ~63 episodes per model–game–pathway combination; total compute cost is moderate but not reported explicitly. - Effective: The benchmark measures the stated diagnostic capability (can agents self-improve from experience?) rather than a proxy, though the 3-episode evaluation sample weakens the reliability of per-checkpoint scores. - Scalable: Adding more games or models is architecturally straightforward; the paper has not tested whether findings hold with more evaluation episodes, longer exploration budgets, or larger open models for the training pathway. Delivers a benchmark framework and evaluation protocol; project page exists but code availability is not confirmed in the paper text. Strengths: - The separation of model-generated self-judgments from verifier-computed outcomes is a clean and genuinely new diagnostic design that enables the judgment–improvement decoupling finding—a result with direct implications for Reflexion-style and ReasoningBank-style methods that assume judgment quality drives improvement. - The paired exploration/evaluation configurations across seven games test transfer rather than same-configuration memorization, which most prior self-improvement benchmarks (SEAGym, PAST-Bench) do not enforce. - Honest reporting of negative results: the paper explicitly shows that Summary Memory degrades performance on several model–game pairs, that parameter training produces negative transfer on PvZ, and that judgment–improvement correlation is near zero—rather than selectively highlighting successes. - The trajectory-level case analysis (successful vs. failed summaries with concrete ∆NABA values) provides mechanistic insight into when summaries work (compact causal abstractions like "plan backward for exact cancellation") and when they fail (state-contingent details like lane timing in PvZ or exact mine positions in Minesweeper). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - The paper states that "self-improvement is neither automatic nor uniform" and that parameter training "remains unstable in the current implementation." - The authors note that verifying why training fails on Minesweeper, Nullify, and Tetris "requires trajectory-level analysis," implicitly acknowledging they did not perform this diagnosis. - The authors acknowledge that AUC+ values cannot be compared across games due to different score scales. - The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - 3 evaluation episodes per checkpoint is statistically underpowered for games with binary or near-binary scores (Chess, Nullify); a single lucky episode can dominate Max and AUC+ without representing reliable capability gain. No variance estimates are provided to assess whether reported differences between pathways exceed noise. - No comparison against an oracle-judgment condition (where verifier rewards are provided during exploration) to quantify how much self-improvement is lost due to imperfect self-judging versus inherent difficulty of experience incorporation. - The training pathway is tested only on Qwen3-8B with a simple SFT objective; no RL-based methods (GRPO, PPO), no larger open models, and no comparison to external preference-optimization techniques. The negative transfer finding on PvZ may be an artifact of the SFT setup rather than a fundamental limitation of parameter-based self-improvement. - The judgment–improvement coupling analysis pools across models and games within each game, potentially masking strong model-specific coupling that averages to zero. - No ablation of the summary prompt format, summary length budget, or judgment score granularity—all of which could substantially affect Summary Memory performance. - The exploration configurations are uniformly easier than evaluation configurations; the paper does not test whether closing the difficulty gap (or reversing it) changes the relative effectiveness of pathways. Bottom Line: A researcher designing self-improving agents or the next adaptive-agent benchmark gains a genuinely useful diagnostic framework and a counter-intuitive empirical finding (judgment quality ≠ improvement) from reading this paper, though the small evaluation samples and single-model training results mean specific numerical claims should be treated as directional rather than definitive.

IAPO: Influence-Aware Policy Optimization for Credit Assignment in Multi-Turn Service Agents

B Ren, Y Mao, Y Yang, W Que · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces IAPO, a GRPO variant that redistributes the trajectory-level advantage across per-action tokens by routing it through a typed influence-dependency graph (support-use and failed-use edges) extracted from each completed rollout by a frozen LLM annotator. - Why it's important: Multi-turn service agents get only a terminal outcome reward, and existing fine-grained credit methods need resettable environments, recurring states across rollouts, or an auxiliary critic/scorer — none of which fit free-form user dialogue where a live user cannot be reset or branched. - How it does it: A frozen annotator (Qwen3-32B, temperature 0) labels directed support-use and failed-use edges among the agent's own actions within a single transcript; edge counts become log-features, standardized into bounded multiplicative weights (clipped at c, length-normalized to mean one) that multiply the GRPO advantage, with sign-conditioned branches (support-weighted with error discounting for positive advantage, error-evidence-only routing for negative advantage). - The good: A controlled comparison where IAPO differs from GRPO only in the trajectory-to-token advantage map, evaluated over three seeds with standard deviations, plus hyperparameter and annotator-swap ablations (e.g., Gemma4-31B annotator yields 40.90% vs. 42.18% on τ2-Bench at 8B), showing the routing is not flat (86.5% of steps move >10% from uniform credit). - The missing: The dependency edges that define the entire credit signal come from an LLM annotator with no human-verified ground truth — cross-annotator agreement (mean edge F1 0.87) shows the annotators agree with each other, not that the labels are correct — and no code or data release is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you train LLM agents with outcome-only rewards in non-resettable multi-turn settings (dialogue, customer service), since it demonstrates a credible within-rollout alternative to critics and counterfactual resampling; skip if you only care about single-turn RLHF or already use privileged-environment credit methods like GiGPO.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (70) are solid — sourcing per-action credit from within-rollout support-use/failed-use dependency structure is a genuinely different credit mechanism with provable safety properties, and the controlled GRPO comparison makes the +12.57 pp gain attributable. Problem & Motivation: In multi-turn service interactions (after-sales, banking, telecom), task information unfolds over time: users clarify or revise goals mid-episode and tool responses expose state that determines which later actions are valid. A terminal reward therefore cannot indicate which early actions contributed — the contribution of a clarifying turn becomes identifiable only after a later turn reveals how its information was used, a setting the authors name "evolving-state credit assignment." Group-based RL (GRPO and variants) broadcasts one group-relative advantage to every token, giving no per-action signal. Existing fixes need cross-rollout comparability (GiGPO needs recurring environment states; tree/reset methods need forkable environments — both absent in free-form dialogue with live users) or an external scoring channel (masked-context scoring, teacher models, learned critics on privileged information) that can drift from the outcome. The gap: no method redistributes outcome credit using only dependency structure already realized inside a single completed interaction. Key Idea: A completed rollout already records how information flows between the agent's own actions — a later action either consumes information an earlier action elicited or supplied (support-use), or repeats/uses an observable error from an earlier action (failed-use) — so these typed within-rollout dependencies, with user turns and tool returns resolved to the actions that elicited or produced them, suffice to route the unchanged trajectory-level advantage to individual actions. The routing is provably conservative: weights are positive, bounded, and length-normalized so total advantage mass, sign, and the GRPO optimization interface are preserved. Methodology: IAPO keeps GRPO's sampling (G rollouts per task) and group-normalized advantage Â_τ = (R_τ − μ_G)/(σ_G + ε) untouched. Pipeline: (A) sample and score rollouts as in GRPO; (B) a frozen annotator LLM extracts a typed influence-dependency graph G_τ over assistant actions, accepting an edge i→j only when three conditions hold jointly — necessity (removing the referenced information unit leaves a_j unsupported), explicit binding (the unit is bound to a concrete argument, branch, or recovery action), and source priority (most comprehensive source, earliest on ties). User turns and tool returns are evidence only, resolved to eliciting/calling actions; an error indicator e_i marks observable tool/schema/rule failures or explicit rejections; (C) edge counts d+_i, d−_i, d_in_i feed log-features φ+_i = log(1 + d+_i + d_in_i) and φ−_i = log(1 + e_i(1 + d−_i + d_in_i)), standardized by length-weighted mean/deviation, exp-clipped at c, and renormalized into weights m± with length-weighted mean one. Sign-conditioned routing: for positive advantage, w+_i(β+) is the closed-form solution of a length-mean-constrained routing problem that discounts steps by above-average error evidence; for negative advantage, w−_i = m−_i (error-evidence only, deliberately conservative). Token advantage is A_{i,ℓ} = Â_τ w_i, passed to the standard clipped PPO-style loss. Three critical design decisions: (1) multiplicative bounded weights rather than additive corrections — well justified, since additive corrections could flip sign or total, and Prop. 1–3 prove mass conservation, uniform fallback, and sign preservation; (2) sign-conditioned asymmetric branches — justified by ablation showing positive and negative branches respond differently to the β+ sweep, ruling out a pure degree-based explanation; (3) an LLM annotator as the dependency oracle — the least-justified decision, validated only by cross-model agreement, not against gold labels. Key Results: Tested on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B (thinking disabled) trained on the 178-task τ2-Bench training split, 8× NVIDIA H20 GPUs, verl/FSDP, N=16 samples/prompt, max 30 turns; evaluated against matched GRPO, GiGPO, and InfoPO, plus the released MUA-RL-8B checkpoint, over three seeds with standard deviations. Headline at 8B: τ2-Bench domain-macro pass1 rises from 29.61% ± 3.56 (GRPO) to 42.18% ± 2.55 (+12.57 pp), with the largest split gain on telecom (+18.19 pp, 21.74→39.93), the domain requiring delayed state use; UserBench +4.61 pp, AgentChangeBench +4.41 pp; BFCL-v4 Multi-Turn stays flat (39.36 vs. 39.04), indicating no loss of out-of-distribution function-calling ability. IAPO at 4B averages 31.31% vs. GRPO's 27.81%. At 8B it edges GiGPO (31.96) and InfoPO (30.82) on the 4-benchmark average (34.11). Tool-call redundancy drops from 46.00 to 29.74 at 4B. Ablations: β+=0 alone yields 32.50 on τ2 (vs. 42.18 at the default 0.05); c=0.5 keeps τ2 at 42.29 but collapses transfer (UserBench 17.78); the projected negative-branch alternatives are consistently lower. Cross-annotator audit over 2,349 action nodes: mean edge-typed F1 0.87, Cohen's κ 0.83, routing-weight Spearman ρ 0.73–0.77 (m+) and 0.96–1.00 (m−). Reported external numbers (Fission-GRPO-8B 41.27 on τ2) come from prior work trained on 630 tasks with a different data recipe, so they are context, not a controlled comparison. Baselines are current (2025–2026 methods), though GiGPO and InfoPO were used with authors' defaults without tuning. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (within-rollout dependency-routed advantage redistribution) with a NEW PROBLEM framing ("evolving-state credit assignment" for non-resettable user-dialogue agents). The genuinely novel move is sourcing per-action credit exclusively from support-use/failed-use structure realized inside one completed rollout, with user/tool observations as provenance but zero gradient credit — no competitor does this. The supporting machinery is a competent combination of standard ingredients: LLM-as-annotator for graph construction, softmax-style standardized features, length-weighted normalization, and a GRPO backbone; the four propositions are straightforward consequences of positive, mean-one multiplicative weights rather than deep theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Reasonably strong for an RL paper: three seeds with standard deviations on all main comparisons; a controlled baseline (GRPO) differing only in the advantage map; ablations isolating β+, c, the negative branch, and the annotator model; a cross-annotator consistency audit with quantified agreement statistics; and a behavioral case study. However, most ablation cells (Table 3) report single numbers without seed variance, so the β+ sweep differences (e.g., 0.05 at 42.18 vs. 0.1 at 33.96) cannot be assessed for noise; the annotator-swap ablation uses one seed's worth of numbers as well. No significance tests are reported. The central methodological concern is circularity of the credit signal: dependency labels are produced by an LLM (Qwen3-32B) with no human-verified gold standard — agreement across annotator models measures consensus, not correctness, and the paper acknowledges disagreement modes (boilerplate attribution, attribution breadth on failed steps) but reports no audit of whether edges are semantically right. No code, data, or checkpoint release is mentioned anywhere in the paper. Evaluation relies on the τ2-Bench protocol with a GPT-5.2 user simulator, so results are simulator-mediated; the τ2 in-domain gain is on a held-out test split, which mitigates but does not eliminate training-eval coupling since all training is on τ2 tasks. Hyperparameters (β+=0.05, c=0.25) appear tuned on the same benchmarks used for reporting, per the ablation table. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trains and evaluates models, but ships no system). - Practical: Runs on 8× NVIDIA H20 GPUs with an open verl/FSDP GRPO stack and Qwen3-4B/8B models, but requires an additional Qwen3-32B annotator call per rollout whose cost is not quantified. - Efficient: Adds the annotator's per-rollout inference cost on top of GRPO with no reported overhead figure, so the training-time cost relative to GRPO is unknown; inference cost is identical to GRPO (same policy). - Effective: The evidence shows improved success rates on simulated-user benchmarks versus matched GRPO and two credit-assignment baselines, with flat OOD retention — it solves the proxy (simulator-scored task success), not deployment with real users. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B models and a 178-task training split; the authors claim the approach generalizes but present no evidence at larger model or task scale, and annotator reliability on longer, more complex transcripts is unexamined. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, dataset, or trained weights are stated as released. Strengths: - A genuinely different credit source: within-rollout realized dependency structure, which sidesteps the two structural blockers (no recurring states, no forkable environment) that make GiGPO-style and tree/reset-style methods inapplicable to live user dialogue — a real gap, not a re-argument of existing work. - Disciplined conservativeness: the method provably cannot invent reward (mass conservation, sign preservation, uniform fallback), so it degrades to GRPO when the graph is uninformative; this is the right safety property for a heuristic routing layer. - The controlled comparison is clean — GRPO and IAPO share everything except the trajectory-to-token map — so the +12.57 pp τ2 gain at 8B is attributable, and the flat BFCL-MT result is the right check against reward-hacking-style overfitting. - Honest analysis of routing non-flatness (w+ std 0.222, span 0.637–1.505, 86.5% of steps moved >10%) and disagreement forensics on low-agreement annotator nodes, which preempts the "it's secretly uniform" and "it's annotator noise" objections with data. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper has no explicit limitations section. Limitations are addressed implicitly and partially: the annotator-dependence is confronted directly via the cross-model swap and consistency audit (a credibility positive), and the caption discloses that reported Fission-GRPO/ToolACE/BitAgent numbers come from different, larger training corpora, i.e., are not comparable. The LLM-annotation correctness question, annotator compute cost, single-domain training, and simulator-based evaluation are not explicitly flagged as limitations by the authors. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ground truth for the core signal: every claim about credit quality rests on inter-annotator LLM agreement; a small human-labeled subset of dependency graphs is the obvious missing validation, and systematic annotator biases (e.g., consistently mis-attributing elicitation) would be invisible in agreement statistics. - Single-seed ablations: the hyperparameter sweep (Table 3) drives the choice of β+=0.05 and c=0.25 on the evaluation benchmarks with no error bars, raising a Goodhart risk that the reported gains are partly hyperparameter selection on test. - Annotator cost opacity: IAPO's selling point is requiring no extra critic or resampling, but a 32B LLM call per rollout is itself a nontrivial recurring cost; without a throughput/cost figure, the "cheaper than alternatives" framing is unevaluated. - Attribution errors propagate uncorrected: if the annotator misses a support edge, the corresponding action silently reverts toward uniform credit; there is no analysis of how routing degrades under edge omission or hallucination. - Simulator dependence: both training (implicit user simulator) and evaluation (GPT-5.2 simulators) are simulator-mediated; no human-in-the-loop or real-user evaluation is attempted or discussed. - Scale untested: 4B/8B models and 178 training tasks are modest; nothing shows the annotation quality or the routing benefit survives at 70B+ or on transcripts far longer than τ2's typical episodes. Bottom Line: A practitioner training outcome-reward agents in non-resettable multi-turn settings gains a concrete, provably-safe alternative to critics and counterfactual resampling with credible controlled evidence behind it, but should wait for a code release and human-validated annotation before adopting it, since the entire method stands or falls on an unaudited LLM annotator.

CAI-DLLM: Convergence Aware Inference for Diffusion Language Models

F Amin, S Afroz, DS Nikolopoulos · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CAI-DLLM, a training-free inference method for masked diffusion language models that uses first-step denoising confidence as a free token-difficulty signal to assign per-token step budgets, block-adaptive commit thresholds, and early-exit detection, delivering up to 44.8× wall-clock speedup on LLaDA-8B and up to 95.3% energy reduction. - Why it's important: Diffusion LLM inference is expensive because every denoising step runs a full transformer forward pass over all tokens, including already-stabilized ones, and existing caching methods (Fast-dLLM/DualCache, ES-dLLM, dLLM-Cache) apply a uniform denoising budget regardless of token convergence speed — so compute is wasted on easy tokens while hard tokens get no extra refinement. - How it does it: The method harvests the max token probability from the mandatory step-zero forward pass (c(0)_i), uses it to bucket tokens into 8/32/64-step budgets, relaxes a cosine commit-threshold schedule across output blocks (end threshold 0.70→0.40), applies position-aware commit multipliers within blocks, and force-commits/exits when fewer than 1.5% of tokens are newly committed for 4 consecutive steps — all with no retraining, extra predictor, or weight change. - The good: A motivation analysis over 1,319 GSM8K prompts empirically establishes the core claim (first-step confidence >0.50 implies stabilization in ~5 steps; <0.25 implies 30–50 steps), and the ablations cleanly attribute the bulk of the speedup to adaptive parallel decoding (e.g., LLaDA HumanEval: 139.8→424.3 TPS from APD alone) rather than the added heuristics. - The missing: Baseline coverage excludes several concurrent diffusion-LLM accelerators (FlashDLM, Sparse dLLM, D2F, Spiffy) for lack of compatible implementations, and the headline 44.8× speedup on LLaDA BBH buys a 4.42-point accuracy drop (56.75→52.33), so the method's best-case numbers conflate the largest gain with the largest quality cost. - Read it or not: Read it if you are deploying or building inference systems for masked diffusion LLMs (LLaDA/Dream family) and can tolerate 1–4 point accuracy loss for order-of-magnitude latency/energy wins; skip it if you need lossless acceleration or work only with autoregressive models.

Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (58) and Novelty (62) jointly constrain the composite. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Masked diffusion language models (LLaDA, Dream) generate many tokens in parallel but still require repeated denoising steps, each a full transformer forward pass over the sequence. Practitioners deploying these models pay this cost even when most tokens stabilize after a few steps. Prior accelerators reduce per-step cost via KV caching (dKV-Cache, dLLM-Cache, Fast-dLLM) or early-layer token skipping (ES-dLLM), but all apply the same denoising budget to every token and every output block. The paper's motivation analysis on LLaDA-8B-Instruct/GSM8K (1,319 test prompts) shows the waste is real: relative L2 hidden-state drift is 2–3% in early layers (L0–L8) versus 6–14% in deep layers (L17–L31), later output blocks converge faster than earlier ones, and token difficulty separates cleanly by first-step confidence (c(0) > 0.50 stabilizes in ~5 steps; c(0) < 0.25 takes 30–50 steps). The specific gap closed: no existing method varies denoising computation per token. Key Idea The core insight is that the confidence from the first denoising step — already computed in every standard decoding run, so free — is a reliable one-shot predictor of token convergence difficulty, and it can drive an entire inference controller (per-token budgets, block-level threshold schedules, position-aware commit rules, and a grinding-phase early exit) without any re-evaluation, retraining, or extra forward passes. Methodology The method is a training-free decoding controller layered on standard block-wise masked diffusion decoding (built on the ES-dLLM codebase with its KV-cache backend). Pipeline per output block: (1) the step-zero forward pass yields per-token confidences s_i = c(0)_i, which assign each token a maximum budget B_i ∈ {8, 32, 64} based on confidence and within-block position (s_i > 0.50 & p < 32 → 8; s_i < 0.25 or p ≥ 48 → 64; else 32); (2) a cosine commit-threshold schedule starts strict at θ_s = 0.90 and relaxes to a block-specific end threshold θ_e^(b) = 0.70 − 0.10(b−1), i.e., 0.70/0.60/0.50/0.40 for blocks 1–4, justified by measured faster convergence in later blocks given committed context; (3) tokens commit when their confidence exceeds a position-scaled threshold θ_i(t) = clip(θ_b(t)·r_pos, 0.20, 0.98) with r_pos ∈ {0.80, 0.90, 1.05, 1.10}, or when their budget is exhausted; (4) a grinding-phase detector exits a block when the fraction of newly committed tokens stays below 1.5% for K = 4 consecutive steps, force-committing remaining tokens above θ_fb = 0.40. Confidence gating (budgets + force-commit) is enabled for LLaDA and disabled for Dream based on GSM8K ablations. Critical design decisions: (a) using only the first-step confidence rather than re-checking each step (well-justified by the measured stability tiers); (b) model-specific gating ON/OFF (justified empirically but selected on the full GSM8K test set — a circularity the authors acknowledge); (c) four hand-tuned position factors selected on a 200-sample held-out LLaDA GSM8K subset and reused for Dream without retuning (partially justified; transfer is asserted, not validated per-model). Key Results Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct across seven benchmarks (GSM8K, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, MathQA, PIQA, WinoGrande, plus LongBench on Dream only), on a single NVIDIA H200, against no-cache decoding, DualCache (Fast-dLLM), and ES-dLLM under identical generation settings. Headline numbers: 18.2× speedup on LLaDA GSM8K with accuracy slightly improved (77.41% vs. 76.27%); 13.1× on Dream HumanEval with higher pass@1 (48.17% vs. 46.95% ±3.76, treated by the authors as parity); 44.8× on LLaDA BBH with a 4.42-point drop (56.75→52.33, std. err. ±0.53); 28.5× on LLaDA MBPP (40.00→37.00); 23.0× on Dream BBH (61.48→56.95); 19.0× on Dream LongBench (average 23.11 vs. 24.63 no-cache, similar drop magnitude to the caching baselines). Energy falls up to 95.3% (LLaDA GSM8K: 3559→169 Wh). Denoising steps per request drop 39–56% (GSM8K) and 38–47% (HumanEval). Controller overhead is below 2%. Speedups scale with generation length (e.g., Dream-Instruct 15.29× at L=512 vs. 1.60× at L=64). On short commonsense tasks (PIQA, WinoGrande) speedups shrink to 1.4–2.1× with accuracy losses versus ES-dLLM. Baselines are recent (2025–2026) and reasonably strong, though FlashDLM, Sparse-dLLM, D2F, and Spiffy are excluded for missing compatible implementations. The counter-intuitive highlight: accuracy can improve alongside speedup on GSM8K/HumanEval, while the worst trade-off appears on the hardest multi-step reasoning task (BBH), where early commitment locks in wrong intermediate choices. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component). The genuinely novel element is the use of the free first-step confidence as a one-shot, token-level difficulty signal controlling budgets, schedules, and early exit — replacing Fast-dLLM's re-evaluated fixed-threshold rule. The remaining machinery (KV caching, cosine threshold schedules, per-token adaptive computation, low-yield early exit) is a competent combination of known adaptive-computation ideas applied to diffusion LLM decoding; the position-aware multipliers and block-decreasing thresholds are heuristic refinements rather than conceptual advances. Rigor & Reproducibility Component ablations are present and informative on both HumanEval (Table 3) and GSM8K (Table 11), cleanly attributing most throughput gain to adaptive parallel decoding and showing why gating must be disabled for Dream (pass@1 recovers from 40.34% to 46.34%). Standard errors from lm-eval are reported for CAI-DLLM scores (±0.53 to ±3.76 pp); runs are deterministic (temperature 0, fixed seeds) but there are no multi-seed timing runs and no significance tests. Hyperparameter sensitivity for the APD schedule is swept (Figure 5). Code is promised "upon acceptance" — not yet released; models are public HuggingFace checkpoints; ~99.4 total GPU-hours reported with a per-method compute breakdown. Methodological flags: (1) the gating ON/OFF decision for each model is chosen on the full GSM8K test set — the same benchmark used in headline results — a Goodhart risk the authors admit; (2) LongBench evaluation uses a selected 4-task subset (HotpotQA and Qasper removed for high variance), so the long-context result is not the full suite; (3) MathQA uses 500 of 4,475 validation samples; (4) energy excludes CPU/DRAM/system power; (5) baselines are not per-benchmark tuned, but neither is CAI-DLLM beyond GSM8K-derived hyperparameters, which is a partial advantage on the GSM8K-family results. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (an inference method actually run on commercial hardware). - Practical: Yes — training-free, runs on a single commodity H200 GPU with public model weights and standard PyTorch 2.3.1/CUDA 12.4. - Efficient: Very — 2.1×–44.8× wall-clock speedup over no-cache, 2×+ the throughput of the closest caching baselines on most tasks, 95%+ energy reduction in the best case, <1.5% memory overhead on LLaDA (though 5.8 GB over DualCache on Dream due to fuller parallel decoding). - Effective: Yes with caveats — it demonstrably reduces redundant denoising while preserving accuracy on math/code at parity or better, but the evidence also shows real accuracy costs on hard reasoning (BBH −4.42) and short-output tasks, so it solves the latency problem only for settings tolerating moderate quality loss. - Scalable: Claimed and partially demonstrated — throughput grows with generation length up to 512 tokens and across batch sizes 2–16 on one GPU, but nothing tests multi-GPU, batch-size 100+, or longer contexts beyond 4,000-token inputs, so 10×–100× serving scale is extrapolation. Deliverable: a software artifact (inference scripts, configs, evaluation code) promised upon acceptance; currently paper-form only. Strengths - The motivation analysis is the paper's best execution: it quantifies uneven denoising (layer drift, block convergence, first-step-confidence stability tiers) over the full GSM8K test set, turning a heuristic into an evidence-backed control signal. - The controller costs essentially nothing — the difficulty signal rides the mandatory first forward pass, O(L) bookkeeping versus O(L²d) transformer passes — so the speedup mechanism is structurally sound, not an artifact of measurement. - Honest, decision-relevant ablations: the Dream gating result (gate-off recovers 6 points of pass@1 at no throughput cost) is reported prominently rather than hidden, and the model-adaptive conclusion follows from the data. - Energy and throughput are measured end-to-end (nvidia-smi power × wall-clock, warm-up pass, deterministic decoding) rather than estimated from FLOP counts, and the compute-bound regime on H200 is profiled to justify why step reduction converts to wall-clock gains. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state four limitations directly: (1) the model-specific gating choice was selected on the full GSM8K test set rather than a held-out validation split; (2) speedups come with accuracy trade-offs (BBH 56.75→52.33, MBPP 40.00→37.00 on LLaDA), making the method suitable only when latency/energy outweigh quality; (3) all experiments ran on a single H200, so results may differ on other hardware; (4) some evaluations use reduced samples (500 MathQA, 100/task LongBench), increasing variance. This is a candid limitations section — the authors confront the benchmark-tuning circularity and the accuracy-speed trade-off head-on rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No comparison against Spiffy (speculative decoding, claimed orthogonal), D2F, FlashDLM, or Sparse-dLLM — the missing-baselines excuse (no compatible implementations) leaves the speedup ranking among 2025-era accelerators unverified. - The position factors r_pos and budget tiers were tuned on LLaDA GSM8K and ported to Dream unvalidated; the Dream memory anomaly (+5.8 GB) hints that the aggressive parallel-commit behavior may interact differently across models in ways the single-set hyperparameters do not capture. - Only two models, both from the same masked-diffusion family and similar scale (7–8B); nothing tests whether first-step confidence remains predictive for larger or differently trained diffusion models. - The LongBench suite was pruned to four tasks after removing high-variance ones, and the short-output regime (PIQA/WinoGrande, ≤2.1× speedup with accuracy loss) is where most real serving traffic may live — the paper concedes unsuitability only in an appendix. - Error bars exist for CAI-DLLM but not consistently for baselines in the main tables, and wall-clock timings have no reported variance across repeats. Bottom Line A practitioner deploying LLaDA or Dream should read this paper — it delivers the strongest measured throughput numbers for training-free diffusion-LLM inference to date (up to 44.8×, 95% energy cut) with honest trade-off reporting, but its hyperparameter tuning on the evaluation benchmark, missing contemporaneous baselines, and real accuracy cost on hard reasoning mean the gains should be validated per-model and per-task before production reliance.

It Takes Two to Match: Co-Evolving Generative Retriever with Reinforcement Learning (64 ▲ )

Runpeng Dai, Kaili Huang, Changsung Kang, Ciya Liao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 3 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CoGR, a retrieval framework that trains two LLMs — one for queries, one for items — to directly generate keyword sets that serve as the retrieval representations themselves, matched through an inverted index, via SFT followed by alternating GRPO reinforcement learning against each other's frozen index. - Why it's important: Retrieval is the irreversible first stage of search and advertising pipelines, and existing LLM-based methods only tune the query side while delegating matching to a fixed downstream retriever; jointly adapting both sides removes that bottleneck while staying compatible with deployed keyword-bidding infrastructure. - How it does it: Both generators optimize the same query-to-item retrieval F1 objective under GRPO — the query side receives F1 directly, the item side receives a counterfactual marginal reward (the change in aggregate query-side F1 from swapping in its keywords), with the opposite side's index frozen during each update so each generator optimizes against a fixed environment. - The good: Across 10 baselines spanning sparse, dense, and generative retrieval, CoGR-4B achieves the best F1 on both datasets — 0.396 on an internal APP Marketplace set (+10.9% over the strongest baseline, ANCE-Qwen4B) and 0.682 on WANDS (+36.1%) — and the query-frozen ablation (CoGR冻结 item side) confirms the co-evolution itself drives the gain rather than model scale. - The missing: Everything is evaluated at toy-to-small corpus scale (~40k items, 480–15k queries), the internal dataset's relevance labels come from an LLM-as-judge, and no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported, so the headline gains carry irreproducibility risk. - Read it or not: Worth reading for IR/advertising researchers exploring LLM-built retrieval indexes or self-play-style co-training; skip if you need large-corpus evidence or a deployable recipe today, since the scale and evaluation are far from production conditions.

Problem & Motivation: Retrieval systems in sponsored search and app marketplaces must select a candidate set from a large item universe; missed items can never be recovered by ranking, and irrelevant ones burden downstream stages, creating a recall–precision tension. Keyword-based matching persists in sponsored search because advertisers bid on keywords, but lexical representations miss deeper semantics. Prior LLM-for-retrieval work (query expansion, rewriting, DeepRetrieval-style RL) trains only the query side and still relies on a separate fixed retriever, leaving the item-side representation unadapted. The gap addressed: can both sides of the retrieval representation be generated by LLMs and co-trained so the two keyword spaces align? Key Idea: Treat the LLM-generated keywords themselves as the retrieval index on both sides, and align the two keyword spaces through alternating RL where each side is rewarded by its marginal contribution to a single shared objective (query-to-item retrieval F1) evaluated against the other side's frozen index — a self-play structure where the item side's counterfactual reward (F1 delta from swapping one item's keywords into the index) makes the shared objective differentiable-free but credit-assignable. Methodology: Two-stage pipeline. Phase 1 (SFT): a base LLM generates M=10 item keywords per item; for each query, the item keywords of its relevant items are pooled and the top-N=15 most frequent become the query-side SFT target, guaranteeing initial query–item keyword overlap. Phase 2 (co-evolving RL): using verl, GRPO (8 rollouts, no KL loss) alternates between query-side and item-side updates for 5 rounds (10 query epochs, 5 item epochs per round). Query-side reward is retrieval F1 (or 0 if the keyword set exceeds Kmax=30). Item-side reward is the aggregate query-side F1 under a counterfactual index (only item i's keywords replaced) minus the reference F1, or −1 on budget violation; an efficient implementation caches per-query counts (n_ret, n_tp, n_rel) and restricts computation to queries whose retrieval status of item i flips via a symmetric-difference lookup. Retrieval ranking within the retrieved set uses BM25 over the generated keyword bags. Three critical design decisions — (1) marginal counterfactual item reward rather than a symmetric item-centric F1 (ablation: 0.3963 vs 0.3743, justified), (2) separate generators per side rather than a shared checkpoint (0.3963 vs 0.3798), and (3) SFT initialization before RL (0.3963 vs 0.3751) — are each supported by ablations on the Internal dataset, though margins for (2) and (3) are modest (~0.02 F1) and lack variance estimates. Key Results: CoGR-4B achieves F1 0.3963 (Internal) and 0.6819 (WANDS), the best among 10 baselines: BM25, SPLADE-v2, DPR, ANCE, zero-shot and ANCE-finetuned Qwen3-Embedding-4B, DSI, DSI-QG, RIPOR, and DeepRetrieval-4B. The strongest baseline is ANCE-Qwen4B (F1 0.3575 Internal, 0.5012 WANDS), a current, reasonably strong dense baseline at comparable model scale; the WANDS gain (+36.1% relative) is far larger than the Internal gain (+10.9%). Co-evolution matters: query-only variants (CoGR with frozen item side, F1 0.2617/0.4662) trail the full system substantially. Validation F1 rises from ~0.16 post-SFT to ~0.40 over five co-evolution rounds on Internal, with most gain in round one. Keyword analysis shows unigram share dropping from 37% to 13% and 3+-word phrases rising from 12% to 31%, with query- and item-side vocabulary sizes converging after 3–4 rounds. Adding search results to the query prompt raises F1 to 0.4379. Tested scale: ~40k items, ≤15k queries — small corpus, standard academic scale at best; generative retrieval baselines (DSI family, mT5-base) are notably older/weaker than the dense ones. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD. Genuinely novel: co-training both sides of a generative keyword index via alternating GRPO under a shared F1 objective, particularly the counterfactual marginal item-side reward, which is a new credit-assignment trick for index-side RL. Standard combinations: GRPO/verl, SFT initialization, inverted-index matching, and BM25 re-ranking are all off-the-shelf; the framing echoes self-play/self-evolving LLM work (R-Zero, G-Zero) applied to retrieval. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for the three main design choices (marginal reward, separate generators, SFT init) and for input information (description, search results), and the efficient item-side reward computation is derived precisely (Appendix B.3). However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere; the Internal dataset's relevance labels are produced by the authors' own LLM-as-judge (self-labeled evaluation data); baseline cutoffs are tuned on training F1, a reasonable protocol, but DSI-family generative baselines use mT5-base while the proposed method uses Qwen3-4B, so model scale is confounded in that family; and no code, data, or model weights are stated as released. The five-round co-evolution result (Figure 3) is a single training run without variance quantification. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — the output is an index compatible with deployed keyword infrastructure). - Practical: Runs on 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs for RL training with Qwen3-1.7B/4B backbones; inference is two keyword-generation calls plus standard inverted-index lookup, so serving is commercially feasible. - Efficient: Index construction requires one LLM pass per item and per query; the counterfactual item reward is made near-constant-time per rollout via cached counts, but re-indexing the whole corpus after every item-side round is a recurring cost the paper does not quantify. - Effective: Evidence shows it beats strong dense retrieval on F1 over the full retrieved set on two product/app-search datasets — a real metric, but only at ~40k-item scale and with self-labeled internal relevance. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~43k items; production universes are 10^7–10^9 items, and per-item LLM keyword generation plus per-round full re-indexing at that scale is unaddressed beyond a claim of inverted-index compatibility. The paper stops at paper form; no artifact release is mentioned. Strengths: - The counterfactual marginal reward for item-side index optimization is a genuine technical contribution: it converts a global retrieval objective into a per-rollout, credit-assigned reward computable in near-constant time via cached counts and a symmetric-difference query lookup. - The query-frozen ablation cleanly isolates the value of co-evolution (F1 0.3963 vs 0.2617 at 4B on Internal), the paper's central claim, rather than hiding it in the aggregate. - Honest framing of the F1 objective as tied to business semantics (precision → user experience, recall → downstream revenue) and a flexible reward design (weighted F-measure) make the formulation portable to other objectives. - The keyword-evolution analysis (unigram→phrase shift, vocabulary convergence) gives interpretable mechanistic evidence that the two keyword spaces align, not just that metrics improve. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion names two future-work items: extending the reward beyond relevance F1 to downstream business metrics (irrelevant-ads percentage, revenue), and replacing the BM25-over-keywords ranking stage with something stronger. The authors confront these directly but do not discuss scale limits, label quality of the LLM-judged internal dataset, or RL training cost. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Scale: 40k-item corpora are an order or two of magnitude below any realistic deployment; index-build cost, keyword collisions (F1 over the full retrieved set becomes meaningless if a keyword matches thousands of items), and vocabulary growth (Figure 4c shows ~10^5 distinct keywords already at this scale) are untested at 10–100×. - The internal dataset's ground truth is the authors' own LLM judge, so the primary benchmark partially measures agreement with their own labeling model. - No significance testing or multi-seed variance despite modest ablation margins (~0.02 F1) being used to justify design choices. - Only two datasets, both product/app search with dense relevance (~200–1,000 relevant items per query); the claim that this setting 'more faithfully' reflects practice is asserted, not validated, and transfer to sparse-relevance web/ad retrieval is unknown. - Latency and serving cost of a 4B-parameter generator in the query path are never measured, and the BM25 re-ranking stage could dominate real-world ranking quality in ways the full-set F1 metric does not capture. - Counterfactual item reward is computed only against the training query distribution; drift between query-side and item-side policies after several rounds (circularity of the shared objective) is analyzed only descriptively over five rounds. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM-driven or keyword-index retrieval gains a genuinely new co-training formulation with a clever item-side credit-assignment trick worth studying, but should treat the headline numbers as small-scale, single-run evidence on partially self-labeled data and expect substantial engineering before any production claim holds.

Propagating construction-time knowledge quality into medical question answering: A framework grounded in clinical guidelines

J Hu, J Wang, S Lu, Y Hu, G Cheng, Y Liu · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a framework (SEEK-GK + CDG-QA) that computes a per-triple quality score Q(t) during LLM-based knowledge graph construction from Chinese diabetes clinical guidelines and propagates that score into quality-weighted subgraph retrieval and tier-conditioned evidence prompting for medical question answering. - Why it's important: Existing GraphRAG systems discard construction-time quality information and rely only on query relevance, so a highly relevant but unreliable triple can be presented as definitive evidence — a serious problem in clinical settings where unsupported answers carry safety risk. - How it does it: The core move is fusing a schema-conformance score (SchemaConf) and an evidence-support score (EvidScore) into a persistent per-triple attribute Q(t), storing it (plus a tier label and provenance TextIDs) with the graph, and reusing it at inference via a weighted ranking function score(t,q) = α·Q(t) + (1−α)·rel(t,q) and reliability-tiered prompting — with no joint training. - The good: The evaluation is unusually rigorous for this literature: nested ablations with McNemar exact tests and Wilson CIs, blinded two-clinician ratings (full 4.68 vs no-retrieval 4.21 vs oracle 4.80 on a 5-point scale), DeLong-confirmed AUC gains under distribution shift (Q(t) 0.748 vs EvidScore 0.703, SchemaConf 0.645), and a cross-generator replication. - The missing: The QA benchmark is self-constructed from the same KG it evaluates (440 questions built from existing KG evidence paths, coverage guaranteed by design), and there is no comparison against any external GraphRAG baseline (e.g., HippoRAG, GNN-RAG) — the ablations only compare the framework against itself. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building guideline- or KG-grounded clinical QA systems who care about evidence reliability and traceability; skippable for general RAG/GraphRAG researchers, since the core mechanism (a weighted fusion of quality and relevance scores) is simple and the evaluation is single-domain, single-language.
