Problem & Motivation: LLM-based extraction of triples from clinical guidelines produces facts of highly variable structural validity and evidential support, and current practice treats this as a construction-time problem only: quality estimates are used to filter, refine, or report, then discarded. Downstream graph-augmented QA (GraphRAG) ranks evidence purely by query relevance or inference-time confidence. The paper targets the disconnect between these two stages: builders of medical QA systems over clinical guidelines currently have no mechanism to carry per-triple reliability knowledge into evidence selection and answer presentation. The domain is Chinese-language diabetes clinical guidelines — terminologically dense documents where a factually wrong or condition-invariant triple (e.g., a contraindication stripped of its qualifying context) has direct clinical consequences. Key Idea: The single core insight is that construction-time quality should be a persistent, graded graph attribute rather than a binary filter or a one-off report: Q(t) = λ·SchemaConf(t) + (1−λ)·EvidScore(t) is stored with each retained triple alongside a reliability tier (core/extended/exploratory) and source-passage IDs, and is later injected into (a) the retrieval ranking — score(t,q) = α·Q(t) + (1−α)·rel(t,q) — and (b) tier-conditioned prompting that instructs the generator to prioritize core-tier evidence and treat exploratory-tier evidence as reference-only. Everything else in the framework is competent plumbing around this one design decision. Methodology: Two phases connected only by stored attributes (no joint training). Construction (SEEK-GK): rule-based preprocessing of guideline text into ~1,905 passages with stable TextIDs; parallel triple extraction by three LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GLM-4-Plus) under a unified prompt; entity/relation normalization using a hand-weighted synonym score (Eq. 4, weights 0.25/0.30/0.25/0.20) with expert review and Union-Find clustering; SchemaConf as a four-sub-score weighted sum (entity 0.30, relation 0.25, type 0.35, direction 0.10) using a five-level embedding-based matching scheme (text-embedding-v3, cosine thresholds 0.70/0.85) and Domain/Range constraint checks; EvidScore as a weighted sum of multi-model agreement (w=0.30), log-normalized passage support frequency (w=0.20), and human verification (w=0.50), with proportional weight re-normalization when dimensions are inactive; fusion into Q(t) (λ=0.3) and tiering at thresholds θ_core=0.85, θ_ext=0.70 selected on an in-distribution calibration set. Inference (CDG-QA): three-stage entity linking (exact → jieba segmentation → fuzzy SequenceMatcher), two-hop subgraph expansion, Q(t)-weighted triple ranking (α=0.4, top-15 triples) alongside BGE-M3 dense passage retrieval (top-5), tier-grouped evidence presentation, and provenance tracing t→TextID→passage. Critical design decisions: (1) graded tiering instead of hard filtering — justified by showing strict filtering discards roughly half the correct triples near the validation boundary; (2) hand-set rather than learned weights — defensible as transparency, and ablated post-hoc against uniform weighting and type-dimension removal; (3) EvidScore weight re-normalization for inactive dimensions — well-motivated engineering for incremental maintenance. Key Results: On the construction side, the framework's validated class retains 13,244 triples (~6,304 estimated correct) versus 6,378 (~3,155 correct) under the strictest schema hard-filtering baseline — roughly double the correct knowledge preserved; uncertain-class precision is near zero (<1%). Under cross-version, cross-model shift (n=1,888 expert-labeled triples), fused Q(t) achieves AUC 0.748 vs 0.703 for EvidScore alone (DeLong ΔAUC=0.045, p<0.001) and 0.645 for SchemaConf alone (ΔAUC=0.103, p<0.001); in-distribution, SchemaConf adds essentially nothing (AUC nearly constant across λ). In QA on 440 self-built guideline questions (301 KG-anchored), the full framework reduces required-knowledge omission from 16.3% to 5.3% (McNemar p<0.001) and conflict rate from 16.3% to 2.7% versus no-retrieval; evidence-grounded precision is 81.6% with near-zero invalid citations; unsupported-claim rate falls from 72.1% to 28.8%. Ablation isolates quality-weighted retrieval (omission 8.3%→5.0%, p=0.031) and tier-conditioned prompting (conflict 4.7%→2.7%, directional but not individually significant, p=0.180). Blinded clinician ratings: no_rag 4.21 < full 4.68 < oracle_kg 4.80 (Wilcoxon p<0.001; inter-rater Pearson r=0.53–0.65). Cross-generator on a 60-question subset, omission drops for all three generators (GLM-4-Plus 18.3%→6.7%, Qwen-Max 28.3%→10.0%, DeepSeek-V3 16.7%→6.7%). Failure analysis of the 16 remaining KOR failures attributes 15/16 to entity-linking/subgraph activation, not graph coverage. Test scale is a single clinical domain at standard (not stress) scale: ~34,672 triples, 2,275 passages. Baselines are internal ablations only — no external GraphRAG system is compared. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the framing of construction-time triple quality as a persistent per-triple signal propagated across the construction–retrieval–prompting boundary (their Table 1 shows no prior system does this operationally). The individual components — schema-conformance scoring, multi-model agreement, evidence-frequency counting, weighted retrieval fusion, tiered prompting — are standard techniques combined in a new integration; no new algorithm or learning method is introduced. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above-average rigor for an application venue: nested ablations isolate each propagation interface, McNemar exact tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction, Wilson-CC confidence intervals, DeLong tests for AUC differences, blinded dual-clinician evaluation with inter-rater statistics, and a cross-generator replication. Concerns the authors partially confront: (1) the QA dataset is self-constructed and questions were built from KG evidence paths, guaranteeing coverage and inflating the apparent value of retrieval; (2) GLM-4-Plus serves simultaneously as extractor, generator, and evaluation judge in the main results (self-consistency bias cannot be excluded); (3) no inter-annotator agreement statistic (κ) is reported for the gold correctness labels; (4) SchemaConf's advantage rests on a single distribution-shift instance. An anonymized review package (de-identified data, frozen labels, analysis scripts, checksums) is available via a private Figshare link, with public release promised upon acceptance — so currently not fully reproducible by outsiders. No pre-existing external benchmark is used, so all numbers are self-referential to their own labeled sets. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (built pipeline, run experiments; no deployment trial). - Practical: Yes — it uses commercially available LLM APIs (GPT-4/4o, GLM-4-Plus, Qwen, DeepSeek), off-the-shelf embedding models (BGE-M3, text-embedding-v3), and standard retrieval infrastructure. - Efficient: The quality signal is a precomputed scalar; inference adds only weighted ranking and prompt organization over a 34K-triple graph, so marginal cost is negligible relative to alternative quality-estimation approaches that re-verify at query time. - Effective: Evidence supports the scoped claim (better evidence selection and presentation within a KG-anchored evaluation), but the coverage condition is guaranteed by design, so real-world questions outside known KG paths are untested; the remaining failure mode (activation/entity linking) is diagnosed but not solved. - Scalable: Not tested — the corpus is one disease area, ~2,275 passages; behavior at 10–100× scale (larger graphs, noisier linking, tier-threshold stability) is unexamined. The work delivers a framework and dataset/QA evaluation protocol; no public library or trained model artifact exists yet (release promised on acceptance). Strengths: - The propagation framing itself: reframing quality as a persistent per-triple attribute spanning construction and inference is a genuinely underexplored design point, and Table 1 credibly positions it against KG²RAG, HippoRAG, CRAG, Self-RAG, MultiRAG, and construction-side quality systems. - Honest, condition-scoped claims: the paper explicitly evaluates when quality propagation helps (in-distribution vs. shift) rather than claiming universal gains, and the finding that SchemaConf's value only emerges under distribution shift is a substantive, non-obvious empirical result. - Failure analysis that points the right way: tracing 15/16 residual omissions to activation/entity-linking failures rather than quality scoring gives practitioners a concrete engineering priority, and the error-type analysis (factual errors dominate at 58.2% and are invisible to schema checks) correctly limits what the method can fix. - Evaluation hygiene rare in this space: denominator-anchored metrics, oracle upper-bound condition, blinded clinician cross-check, significance testing with multiple-comparison correction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: single-domain single-language scope (Chinese diabetes guidelines) with no evidence of generalization; single primary generator with only a 60-question cross-LLM probe; self-constructed QA set with possible overlap between question construction and KG construction (favoring coverage); SchemaConf advantage demonstrated on a single shift instance; GLM-4-Plus triple role (extractor/generator/judge) creating possible self-consistency bias; missing inter-annotator agreement statistics; and an indirect link between triple quality and answer quality (no monotonic relationship demonstrated). This is an unusually direct and complete self-assessment — the authors confront limitations head-on rather than minimizing them, which strengthens confidence in the reported results. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged issues: (1) the headline QA gains (KOR 16.3%→5.3%) are measured against a no-retrieval baseline that no modern system would deploy; the meaningful comparison — against a competent relevance-only GraphRAG or text-only RAG baseline — is missing, so the incremental value of Q(t) over simply returning any top-ranked relevant evidence is established only via the internal 'no_qt' ablation, and the text_only and kg_only conditions are not prominently reported in the results narrative; (2) the oracle condition (4.80) shows a 0.12-point clinician-rating gap between full and oracle, but the paper does not analyze what that residual gap consists of; (3) EvidScore's human-verification weight (0.50) is prespecified, and the marginal value of the expensive human-review component over model-agreement-plus-frequency alone is not isolated; (4) tier thresholds (0.85/0.70) are tuned on the same calibration set used to characterize precision — a mild Goodhart risk; (5) conflict-rate and clinician evaluation on only 100–301 questions gives limited statistical power for the tier-prompting step (p=0.180), yet the abstract reports the cumulative effect in a way that could be read as the prompting step being independently validated; (6) no cost/latency numbers for the construction pipeline, which requires three commercial LLM passes plus iterative expert review of 94,987 raw triples down to 15,636 — the human-review cost is the real bottleneck and is unquantified. Bottom Line: A practitioner building guideline-grounded clinical QA gains a concrete, lightweight, and honestly evaluated design pattern — persist construction-time quality as a graph attribute and reuse it in ranking and prompting — but the evaluation is self-referential enough that the magnitude of benefit over a well-tuned relevance-only RAG baseline remains unproven; read it for the framing and evaluation protocol, not for a deployable system.

CoDPlacer: A Fast Approach for Digital IC Placement via Consistency Distillation

MA Shalmani, JS Yuan · preprints.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CoDPlacer, a consistency-distilled student of the ChipDiffusion placement model that cuts diffusion-based placement sampling from 1000 denoising steps to as few as 1-128 evaluations, and embeds it in two full-chip placement flows (macro-then-DREAMPlace, and a hierarchical cluster-based flow). - Why it's important: Diffusion-based placement generates many candidate layouts during design-space exploration, and 1000-step sampling makes this loop prohibitively slow; a tunable quality-vs-runtime knob directly addresses that workflow cost. - How it does it: The frozen diffusion teacher performs deterministic DDIM transitions between adjacent noise levels, and a GNN student with EMA targets is trained to map any noisy placement directly to the clean placement (consistency distillation) using a coordinate-wise pseudo-Huber loss. - The good: The inference-step ablation over 5 seeds on 18 clustered IBM benchmarks is thorough, and the 128-step student nearly matches the teacher (HPWL 28.973 vs 28.159 x10^6) at 4.1x lower generation time, with legality above 0.998 throughout. - The missing: There is no head-to-head against a plain analytical placer (e.g., DREAMPlace run flat on the same circuits), so the reader cannot tell whether the learned macro initialization beats simply skipping it; and evaluation is limited to HPWL, legality, and runtime, with no routing, timing, congestion, or power results. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on learned/ generative physical design or on accelerating diffusion samplers for combinatorial layout problems; skip it if you want production-grade placement evidence, since key EDA metrics and the analytical-only baseline are absent.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (67) is the strength — a thorough step-count ablation over 5 seeds with public code — but it is capped by the missing flat DREAMPlace-only baseline, un-ablated design choices, a disclosed survivorship filter on ISPD2005, and preprint status. Novelty (65) is moderate: consistency distillation is transferred, not invented, and Non-Obviousness (52) is limited because applying distillation to a slow diffusion sampler is the move any practitioner would try. Completeness (65) benefits from a genuinely honest limitations section, while Resilience (60) and Impact (60) are dragged down by the un-analyzed counter-intuitive full-chip result, absent post-route/timing metrics, and no released weights. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*67 + 0.15*52 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*60 = 62.

Problem & Motivation: Digital IC placement determines macro and cell locations and strongly influences wirelength, timing, and PPA. Learned generative placers (specifically diffusion-based ChipDiffusion) can place many objects jointly and avoid brittle sequential decisions, but high-quality sampling requires a 1000-step reverse trajectory, which is expensive when placement must be repeated across seeds, legalization settings, and design-space exploration loops. The problem addressed is who pays this inference cost: anyone using diffusion placement for rapid candidate generation or design-space exploration. Prior work offers either fast analytical placers or slow generative ones; no prior approach gives a diffusion placer with controllable, few-step inference. Key Idea: Apply consistency distillation (Song et al., 2023) to a pretrained graph-based diffusion placer: train a student GNN to predict the clean placement x0 from any noisy state along the teacher's trajectory, so one or a few network evaluations replace 1000 denoising steps. The secondary idea is a boundary-aware cluster expansion: for each net cut leaving a standard-cell cluster, insert a fixed external anchor into the cluster-local DREAMPlace instance so interface cells see the direction of external connectivity without being fixed. Methodology: The circuit is a graph G=(V,E); nodes are macros, standard-cell clusters, or terminals with normalized dimensions and pin-offset edge attributes; the target is per-object 2D coordinates x0. Noising uses a cosine schedule (alpha=cos(pi t/2), sigma=sin(pi t/2)). The student uses the EDM-style parameterization f(x_t,t,G)=c_skip(t)x_t+c_out(t)F_theta(x_t,t,G) with sigma_data=0.5, guaranteeing the boundary condition at t=0. Training samples adjacent timesteps from a discretized schedule (N=18 pairs); the frozen teacher predicts noise, a DDIM step produces the lower-noise sample, and the loss is coordinate-wise pseudo-Huber distance (c=1e-3) between the student prediction and a stop-gradient EMA target, with EMA decay ramped linearly from 0.95 to 0.999. Training: Adam, lr 1e-4, batch 64, 1,000,000 steps, teacher weights used for initialization, single RTX 2080 Ti. Inference re-noises between predicted clean placements for multi-step sampling; fixed ports are masked throughout. Two downstream flows: (1) conventional — CD-128 predicts macro positions, macros are fixed, DREAMPlace places/legalizes cells; (2) hierarchical — hMETIS clusters cells into 512 groups, CD-128 places macros+clusters globally, each cluster is expanded with boundary-aware anchors and optimized locally by DREAMPlace, then mapped back and assembled. Design decisions: pseudo-Huber over MSE (justified as reducing sensitivity to large errors, though not ablated), N=18 training timestep pairs (not ablated), hMETIS over KaHyPar (chosen for comparability with ChipDiffusion), and reusing the teacher's GNN backbone (sensible but means architecture contributions are nil). Key Results: On 18 clustered IBM benchmarks (reduced graphs of 512-1298 vertices, 5 seeds), the diffusion teacher averages HPWL 28.159x10^6 in 170.42 s; CD-128 reaches 28.973x10^6 in 41.10 s (4.1x speedup, legality 0.9985); CD-1 collapses to 82.488x10^6 while CD-2 recovers to 38.315x10^6. Macro-only on IBM: CD-128 HPWL 2.79x10^5 vs ChipDiffusion 2.61x10^5 at 0.44 vs 1.37 min (~3.1x speedup). Macro-only on ISPD2005 (first 5 circuits only, those that 'completed successfully'): CD-128 HPWL 41.08x10^5 at 0.56 min vs ChipDiffusion 38.10x10^5 at 4.38 min (7.82x speedup), beating ChiPFormer (41.63) and MaskPlace (50.41) on HPWL while being ~440x faster than both. Full-chip conventional flow on IBM: CD-128+DREAMPlace averages 26.98x10^6, lower than diffusion+DP (28.45), 128-step diffusion+DP (28.80), and MaskPlace+DP (29.91). Hierarchical flow: CD 31.27x10^6 vs hierarchical diffusion 30.25x10^6 (3.4% worse; diffusion wins 15/18 circuits). Baselines are current for learned placers (MaskPlace NeurIPS'22, ChiPFormer ICML'23, ChipDiffusion ICML'25), but no analytical-only baseline (DREAMPlace without learned macros) is reported. Tested at standard academic scale (up to ~278k objects for full ISPD circuits); a counter-intuitive finding is that CD-128's worse macro-only HPWL still yields the best full-chip HPWL after DREAMPlace refinement. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (consistency distillation applied to chip placement — genuinely the first such application, but a transfer of Song et al.'s existing technique to the ChipDiffusion teacher rather than a new distillation algorithm) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION and a modest NEW SYSTEM (the hierarchical boundary-aware expansion flow). The core modeling machinery — consistency function parameterization, EMA targets, DDIM teacher stepping, pseudo-Huber loss — is standard; the domain transfer and the empirical finding that a faster sampler's macro initialization improves downstream full-chip HPWL are the new parts. Rigor & Reproducibility: The inference-step ablation (1,2,4,8,16,64,128 steps) is the paper's rigor highlight, with per-circuit results in an appendix, 5-seed averaging, ratio standard deviations, and legality metrics reported — this directly tests the central claim. Code, configs, and data-preparation scripts are public (github.com/mohammad-AJP/CoDPlacer). Hardware and software versions are fully specified. Concerns: (a) no ablation of design choices (pseudo-Huber vs MSE, N=18 timestep pairs, sigma_data=0.5, EMA ramp); (b) the ISPD2005 macro results cover only 5 of 8 circuits and explicitly only samples 'that completed successfully' — a survivorship filter the authors disclose but do not quantify; (c) the pivotal full-chip comparison lacks the flat DREAMPlace-only baseline, so the added value of the learned stage is unquantified; (d) IBM05 (0 macros) yields identical HPWL (9.07) across all methods, correctly reflecting that the learned stage does nothing there; (e) HPWL ratios are against 'clustered reference placements' derived from original IBM coordinates — a nonstandard reference. Not peer-reviewed (Preprints.org, posted 31 August 2026), so results warrant reduced confidence. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — all experiments ran on a single RTX 2080 Ti (11 GB) with 128 GB RAM, consumer-grade hardware. Efficient: 4.1x generation speedup at CD-128 (170.42 s to 41.10 s on clustered IBM) and 7.82x on ISPD2005 macros; 4-8-step modes run ~6.3-6.5x faster; cluster-local DREAMPlace refinement is parallelizable in principle. Effective: Evidence covers HPWL, legality, and runtime only; no routed wirelength, congestion, timing, or power — so it solves the proxy (HPWL-optimal legal placement), not the stated EDA quality problem end-to-end. Scalable: Scalability of the hierarchical flow is claimed (parallel cluster-local solves) but never demonstrated beyond ~278k-object circuits; the largest full-chip ISPD circuits (bigblue3/4, up to 2.18M objects) were not evaluated, and macro masking failures limited ISPD to 5 circuits. Delivers a software artifact: public code and pipeline, no trained model weights mentioned as released. Strengths: (1) First demonstration that consistency distillation transfers to placement generation, converting a 1000-step diffusion placer into a controllable-step sampler with measured legality above 0.998 at every step count — a clean, well-isolated empirical result. (2) The systematic step-count ablation with per-circuit breakdowns gives the field a usable quality-runtime operating curve (e.g., 2 steps: ratio 1.429 at 6.5x speedup) rather than a single point. (3) The boundary-aware anchor mechanism for cut nets during cluster-local expansion is a sensible, reusable technique for any cluster-then-refine placement flow. (4) Honest reporting of trade-offs — macro-only HPWL degradation versus the teacher is stated plainly, not hidden. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) only HPWL, legality, and runtime are evaluated — routed wirelength, congestion, timing, and power are absent; (2) ISPD2005 results cover only successfully-completed samples, requiring 'improved macro masking for very large circuits'; (3) the hierarchical flow needs stronger global refinement after cluster assembly; (4) longer distillation (beyond 1M steps) would likely close the remaining quality gap. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The most important missing experiment is a flat analytical baseline: DREAMPlace alone on the same benchmarks, which would establish whether the learned macro/cluster stage adds value over the standard engine at all — without it, the 'lowest average HPWL' claim in the conventional flow compares learned initializations against each other, not against practice. (2) The finding that CD-128 beats its own teacher in full-chip HPWL (26.98 vs 28.45) despite worse macro-only HPWL is presented as a plausible initialization effect but is never analyzed; with 5 seeds and no significance testing, this could be noise or a systematic bias in how DREAMPlace recovers from particular macro configurations. (3) The student is trained on the same synthetic data distribution used by the teacher and evaluated on IBM/ISPD — generalization to modern, macro-dominated industrial netlists is untested, and the 2023 ISPD-style critique of learned macro placers applies here unaddressed. (4) The one-step model's failure (HPWL ratio 2.975) undercuts the headline motivation for consistency distillation (few-step generation); the practical operating points are 4-8 steps or 64-128 steps, the latter only a ~4x speedup. (5) Timing/congestion consequences of the hierarchical flow's inter-cluster connectivity approximation are unmeasured, despite that being the flow's main structural risk. Bottom Line: A practitioner in learned physical design gains a concrete, reproducible recipe and honest operating curves for making diffusion placement ~4-8x cheaper, but the absence of a flat analytical baseline and of any post-route metrics means this should be read as a promising acceleration study, not as evidence that generative placement is ready to replace analytical flows.

Lucida: Parse, Generate, and Place for Composable Real-to-Sim Scene Modeling (74 ▲ )

Minghan Qin, Yuang Wang, Xiuyu Yang, Yushi Long, Yujian Zhang, Ruihuan Wang, Kai Ye, Yangang Zhang, Hang Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 1 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Lucida, a pipeline that converts posed RGB(-D) captures of real indoor scenes into simulation-ready scenes of individually editable, generated 3D assets with 9-DoF poses, plus GizmoAct, a VLM policy that casts asset placement as closed-loop multi-turn GUI interaction with a 3D gizmo. - Why it's important: Robot simulation and embodied AI need digital replicas of real environments where every object is a complete, manipulable asset; existing pipelines fail on cluttered captures because each stage demands precision (clean masks, unoccluded views, geometry-matching assets) that real footage cannot supply. - How it does it: The core move is redistributing precision along the parse–generate–place order: parsing only consolidates per-instance multi-view evidence, generation only synthesizes an amodal image from that evidence, and a VLM absorbs residual error at the end by issuing incremental gizmo-frame edits (rotation, translation, anisotropic scale in object-size units) until it decides alignment is reached. - The good: The strongest evidence is the pose-refinement evaluation with matched generated assets across three datasets: ADD-SB@0.05 rises from 57.8% to 83.4% on CA-1M and 79.2% to 92.0% on R2S-Object over the best baseline (RecGen), with 3D IoU gains of ~0.11–0.22, supported by ablations showing each parsing stage and RL training contributes measurably. - The missing: The headline scene-reconstruction comparison (F-Score 0.924 vs 0.794) is evaluated on R2S-Scene, the authors' own newly introduced benchmark with manually annotated poses, and the paper reports no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, so variance and generality beyond their own data are unquantified. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on real-to-sim, scene-level 3D detection, or object pose refinement with generated assets — the GUI-interaction reformulation and gizmo-relative action space are genuinely transferable ideas; skip it if you only need monolithic reconstruction or single-image scene generation.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile (a built real-to-sim pipeline whose deliverable is simulation-ready scenes). Rigor (62) and Impact (52) pull the composite down: the headline scene-level result lives on the authors' own benchmark with self-annotated poses, no error bars are reported, and the system depends on proprietary models with no code or weights released, making it effectively unreproducible. Novelty (74) and Non-Obviousness (75) are the strengths — the gizmo-as-GUI recast of 9-DoF placement with learned termination is a genuinely transferable abstraction — while Resilience (58) suffers from the marginal CA-1M detection gain and view-count asymmetry in the main pose comparison. Weighted composite: 0.15*74 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*58 + 0.30*52 = 62.

Problem & Motivation: Composable scene modeling — recovering a real indoor scene as complete, editable object assets arranged as observed — serves robot simulation, embodied AI, AR/VR, and content creation. Three existing routes each fail: differentiable-rendering reconstructions (NeRF, 3DGS) are monolithic and leave occluded surfaces unrecovered; CAD retrieval-and-alignment real-to-sim systems cap fidelity at database coverage; interactive scene synthesis produces plausible rooms grounded in no actual capture. Multi-stage parse–generate–place pipelines inherit a fatal property: the stages run in fixed order, so each stage's input requirements (precise masks, clean point clouds, geometry-consistent assets) become hard preconditions, and any error in a cluttered real capture propagates forward with no correction mechanism. The authors' motivating observation is that a human modeler from the same footage defers precision to the end — nudging each model against the observation until they agree — and the paper asks whether a system can be organized the same way. Key Idea: The single core insight is to recast 3D grounding/placement as multi-turn GUI interaction: the object is presented to a VLM as if selected in a 3D editor (point cloud, asset overlay, 3D box, and a gizmo exposing the object's local frame), and alignment becomes a sequence of executable edits. Two sub-tricks make this work: (1) all pose updates are incremental deltas expressed in the gizmo's local frame, with translation and scale in units of current object size, so the policy never regresses an absolute pose or a metric scale; (2) the policy predicts its own stop action from renderings alone, removing the external convergence criterion that render-and-compare refinement requires. Once this abstraction is understood, the rest of the system (keyframe selection, evidence bundles, SFT + GRPO on synthetic trajectories with error injection) follows as competent supporting machinery. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Parse: geometry-aware keyframe selection via a covisibility-and-temporal-decay similarity (Eq. 2, harmonic mean of directional covisibility with exponential temporal weighting); a VLM + 3D detector (Boxer) propose instances on keyframes; object-centric full-sequence evidence consolidation propagates objects to additional frames via video segmentation (SAM 2), lifts them to 3D, and validates per-frame boxes against a representative 3D box; relation-aware refinement corrects merges/splits and recovers missing support objects into a scene graph whose nodes carry evidence bundles E_o = {views, masks, partial point clouds, 3D box, referring description}. (2) Generate: reliable, viewpoint-diverse views are selected from E_o, organized via Set-of-Mark prompting into anchor/references plus an editing instruction; an image-editing model synthesizes an occlusion-free object image; an image-to-3D model (Seed3D 2.0) lifts it to an asset. (3) Place (GizmoAct): a VLM policy operates a two-action core space (update_pose, stop) plus switch_obs/permute_axis for coarse rotation (a single action covering all 24 axis-aligned reorientations, avoiding gimbal lock); state updates are R_{t+1} = R_t·R_ZXY(δr), s_{t+1} = s_t⊙(1+δs), p_{t+1} = p_t + R_{t+1}(δp⊙s_t). Training is SFT on synthetic expert trajectories from three data sources (Populated 3D-FRONT, FoundationPose-style scattered assets, CA-1M train objects) with a privileged expert that repairs rotation-first, DART-style error injection with recovery supervision, then GRPO (DAPO-style dynamic sampling, K=8 rollouts, quantized reward on generalized 3D IoU and geodesic rotation error with thresholds at g=0.75/0.85/0.925 and e_R=30°/10°/5°, zero reward until both axes reach the success band, stop bonus; symmetric objects excluded from RL). (4) Optional postprocessing for support, collision, and contact consistency, deliberately kept rule-based and outside the agent. Critical design decisions: gizmo-relative deltas (well justified — removes metric scale regression), orthographic views as pseudo-multi-view evidence for single-view input resolving the scale–depth ambiguity (well justified), and quantized RL reward (justified by noise-robustness argument, but excludes symmetric objects, which is a real coverage hole). Key Results: Three evaluation levels. (1) Scene-level 3D detection: highest mean mAP in all four protocols on CA-1M and R2S-Scene; on R2S-Scene_all, mAP improves from 0.351 (Boxer, all-frame prompts) to 0.592 with keyframe-only prompts — a 69% relative gain — though on CA-1M_all the gain is marginal (0.171→0.180). Baselines are Boxer and WildDet3D in offline fusion mode; reasonably current (2026 arXiv works) but only two prompt-based detectors. (2) Pose estimation: with the same generated asset, GizmoAct (max 4 views) achieves ADD-SB@0.05 of 92.0% on R2S-Object (vs 79.2% RecGen 2-view), 83.4% on CA-1M (vs 57.8%), 90.0% on ADT; 3D IoU 0.719/0.607/0.670 vs baselines ≤0.500/0.434/0.520; baselines are Any6D, SAM 3D, RecGen (current, 2025–26). A single policy handles Boxer, Any6D-style, and SAM 3D initializations without retraining (Table 3). (3) Scene reconstruction on R2S-Scene: scene F-Score 0.924 vs 0.794 (SAM 3D) and 0.351 (SceneGen); symmetric scene CD 0.010 m² vs 0.022; BBox IoU 0.495 vs 0.396. RL over SFT is demonstrated on a hard subset of 110 asymmetric objects: rotation error drops from 45.19° (SFT) to 20.98° (RL). Tested at standard scale (scenes of ~9–10 evaluation sequences; 125–199 objects per pose dataset); no stress-scale test. Notably, GizmoAct receives up to 4 views while RecGen gets at most 2 — a partial input asymmetry in the main comparison. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (GizmoAct's reformulation of 9-DoF asset placement as closed-loop VLM GUI manipulation with gizmo-relative incremental edits and learned termination) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (R2S, a real-world indoor real-to-sim benchmark with scene and object splits) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the full Lucida pipeline). The individual ingredients — keyframe selection, multi-view box fusion, amodal image editing + image-to-3D, render-and-compare refinement, SFT-then-RL sequential refinement — are standard; what is genuinely new is the redistribution-of-precision principle and the GUI/gizmo action interface, which is a non-obvious and reusable abstraction. The overall system is more than a combination, but the detection stage (evidence consolidation + relational refinement) is competent composition of known ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and substantive: three parsing-stage ablations (Table 5, showing keyframe selection matters most, mAP 0.597→0.516 when uniform), RL pose-distribution ablation (Table 6), and RL-vs-SFT-vs-single-step-SFT comparison on a constructed hard subset (Table 7). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere. The R2S benchmark and CA-1M test subset involve manual pose annotation and manual mask filtering by the authors — the central benchmark is self-constructed, and only CA-1M and ADT provide external anchoring. Code release is not stated; only a project page (https://lucida-r2s.github.io/) is given, and key components are proprietary or unreleased systems (Seedream-class image editing, Seed3D 2.0, an unnamed "pretrained VLM" acknowledged in thanks), which makes exact reproduction effectively impossible. Concerns: (a) evaluation partly on the authors' own benchmark with self-annotated ground truth; (b) the CA-1M detection gain is small (0.171→0.180) relative to the R2S gain, suggesting the method's advantage concentrates on their own data; (c) view-count asymmetry (4 vs 1–2) in the main pose comparison, though a 1-view variant is also reported and still wins; (d) RL excludes symmetric objects while evaluation includes them, so RL-trained behavior on symmetric categories rests on SFT alone. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL + SYSTEMS (a built pipeline with experiments; the system output is simulation-ready scenes). Practical: It runs from commodity posed RGB-D captures, but depends on large proprietary VLM, image-editing, and image-to-3D models, so a third party cannot run it as-is on open weights. Efficient: Inference cost is unreported — each placement rollout is up to 12 turns of VLM calls with multi-panel renderings, plausibly minutes and significant GPU cost per object; no throughput or cost comparison against feedforward baselines like SAM 3D, which are orders cheaper. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated problem on three datasets including two not authored by the team (CA-1M, ADT), with the caveat that the headline scene-level numbers come from the authors' own benchmark. Scalable: Not tested — evaluation covers ~9–10 scenes and ≤199 objects; behavior on large multi-room captures or long sequences is claimed by design (full-sequence consolidation) but not measured. The work delivers a system artifact at paper form plus a project page; no code, dataset download, or model weights are confirmed in the text. Strengths: - The GUI/gizmo reformulation is a genuinely new interface for pose refinement: incremental local-frame edits in object-size units remove absolute-pose and metric-scale regression, and the learned stop action removes external convergence criteria — both are clean, transferable abstractions. - The training recipe is careful where it matters: DART-style error injection with recovery-only supervision teaches the policy to recover from its own flawed edits, and the RL reward's all-or-nothing success gate plus per-axis excellence bonuses directly shape the deployment metric. - Evaluation is layered (detection / pose / full scene) with the pose evaluation decoupled from upstream detection to avoid confounding, and the initialization-robustness study (Table 3) shows one policy adapting to three error profiles without retraining. - Honest RL evaluation: symmetric objects are excluded from RL training and the authors say so, and the hard-subset comparison isolates exactly where RL helps (rotation). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states two: (1) objects missed by scene parsing cannot be recovered downstream — a structural single-point-of-failure the authors confront directly; (2) agentic closed-loop refinement currently operates only at placement, and extending it across the whole pipeline is left as future work. These are stated plainly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. The paper does not, however, discuss compute cost, dependence on proprietary models, or benchmark circularity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline scene-reconstruction comparison is on R2S-Scene, the authors' own benchmark with manually annotated boxes/poses; no independent scene-reconstruction benchmark (e.g., ScanNet-based) is used, so the 0.794→0.924 F-Score jump cannot be externally corroborated. - The CA-1M detection improvement is within noise territory (0.171→0.180, single-run, no variance), yet the abstract leads with the 69% R2S gain — the claim generalizes only where they measured it best. - Main pose comparisons give GizmoAct up to 4 views vs 1–2 for RecGen; the 1-view variant wins too, but by smaller margins (e.g., 88.0% vs 79.2% on R2S-Object), and the paper does not report a RecGen variant with matched view counts. - Each CA-1M/R2S pose ground truth required manual filtering of masks and manual 9-DoF annotation; annotation error magnitude is unquantified and directly caps the ADD-SB@0.05 threshold at 5% of object diameter. - Inference cost of the VLM policy (number of VLM calls, latency, GPU memory) is never reported, which matters for the stated robot-simulation use case where per-scene cost is a real constraint. - Symmetric objects are excluded from RL training but included in evaluation; per-symmetry breakdown is absent, so the RL gains on symmetric categories are unverified. - The identity and scale of the base VLM, the image-editing model, and the image-to-3D model are cited but their contribution to the final numbers is not ablated — a reader cannot tell how much of the gain is GizmoAct versus better component models. Bottom Line: A practitioner in real-to-sim, scene reconstruction, or object pose estimation should read this for the gizmo-as-GUI action abstraction and the SFT+RL recipe, which are genuinely reusable and backed by the strongest pose-refinement numbers I have seen against matched-asset baselines — but should discount the scene-level headline pending independent-benchmark validation and treat the system as unreproducible until code and weights appear.

H2Table: Hierarchical Hypergraph-Enhanced Large Language Models for Complex Table Reasoning

J Ling, Y Wang, C Tang, H Tan, Y Yang, Y Guan… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces H2Table, a framework that represents complex tables as hierarchical nested hypergraphs, encodes them with a four-stage hierarchy-aware message-passing encoder, and injects distilled structural embeddings into an LLM via 12 learnable query vectors to improve table question answering. - Why it's important: Real-world tables (financial, statistical reports) have multi-level nested headers that 1D serialization and flat graph/hypergraph encodings destroy, causing severe accuracy collapse exactly on the most information-dense tables — the HiTab/TATQA/AITQA domain where enterprise table QA operates. - How it does it: Headers become hyperedges with explicit parent-child relations (R) alongside cell incidence (I); a four-stage encoder (V2E set-attention, C2P and P2C GAT passes across header levels, E2V with residuals) propagates information both bottom-up and top-down, and a Q-Former-style query block cross-attends to encoder outputs to produce a fixed-size soft structural prompt prepended to the serialized table text, trained end-to-end with LoRA (r=8, ~1% parameters). - The good: On the hardest HiTab depth-4 subset (N=35), Llama3.1-8B+H2Table reaches 0.7143 accuracy vs. 0.6286 for the strongest structural baseline TAMO and 0.5714 for pure-text LoRA, and the gain over TAMO on the aggregated depth-3+4 subset (N=848) is statistically significant by paired McNemar's test (p=0.0079). - The missing: The method assumes the header hierarchy is provided as gold annotation at inference time — real deployment requires a table-structure extractor the paper never builds or evaluates, so the headline numbers measure representation quality, not an end-to-end system. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on structure-aware LLM input (graph-to-LLM alignment, table modality); practitioners wanting a deployable hierarchical-table QA solution can skip it until the structure-extraction dependency is closed.

Problem & Motivation: Complex tables in finance, statistics, and industry reports use multi-level nested headers (e.g., "First Quarter Sales" → "March" → cells), so a cell's meaning is entailed by an entire header path, not a single row/column label. LLM-based TableQA systems almost universally serialize tables to 1D text, which disrupts this topology; full-parameter SFT approaches (TableLlama, TableGPT) are data- and compute-hungry; graph-based encodings (TabPrompt, HeGTa) use pairwise edges that cannot express one-to-many header→cell relations; HYTREL's hypergraphs handle only flat tables; TAMO couples HYTREL with an LLM but flattens nested headers into a single hyperedge level, discarding cross-level dependencies. The gap: a structural representation that preserves header hierarchy while remaining cheaply integrable with a mid-sized LLM. Key Idea: Treat the header tree itself as part of the hypergraph — high-level hyperedges connect only to their direct sub-headers (not to all descendant cells), with parent scope defined recursively as the union of children's scopes — so that message passing naturally decomposes into cell→leaf-header (V2E), child→parent (C2P), parent→child (P2C), and header→cell (E2V) stages, with GAT weighting the cross-level passes. A secondary but practically important move is the Q-Former-style bridging: 12 learnable queries cross-attend to encoder embeddings and prepend a fixed-size soft structural prompt, replacing TAMO's average-pooling projection and keeping the LLM context overhead constant regardless of table complexity. Methodology: (1) Table→hypergraph conversion: nodes V = data cells, hyperedges E = headers plus a virtual root, partitioned into leaf vs. high-level sets; directed hierarchical relation R among hyperedges and incidence I between cells and leaf headers. (2) Encoding: node embeddings initialized from RoBERTa-large (hidden size 1024); a single encoder layer runs V2E (set attention per HYTREL), C2P (GAT, bottom-up along R), P2C (GAT, top-down, adaptively mixing global context with local features), E2V (set attention plus residual). (3) Alignment: a stack of Transformer decoder layers applies self-attention over 12 learnable queries, then cross-attention against encoder outputs (Q(l) = FFN(MCA(MSA(Q(l−1)), H, H))), producing soft structure prompts concatenated with serialized table text. (4) Fine-tuning: LoRA (r=8, α=16) on Llama2-7B, Llama3.1-8B, Gemma2-9B with binary cross-entropy loss, AdamW lr 1e-5. Critical design decisions: (a) restricting high-level hyperedges to direct children only — justified by the recursive scope definition, though never empirically compared against the TAMO-style full-connection alternative in a controlled ablation; (b) GAT for cross-level passes — justified by the ablation showing gaps grow with depth, though the w/o-GAT variant actually wins on depth-1; (c) 12 query vectors — chosen empirically from a sweep (N ∈ {1,4,8,12,16}), differences across N are within noise (~0.6–0.8 points), so this is a weakly justified but low-stakes choice. Key Results: Benchmarks: HiTab and TATQA (TableQA, accuracy), stratified by header nesting depth; OOD test on AITQA. On HiTab (Llama3.1-8B): H2Table avg 0.7415 vs. TAMO 0.7186 and pure-text LoRA 0.6483; depth-4: 0.7143 vs. TAMO 0.6286 and pure text 0.5714. On HiTab with Gemma2-9B: 0.7596 avg, beating zero-shot GPT-4o (0.7011) and DeepseekV3 (0.6659). On TATQA gains are marginal: Llama3.1-8B 0.4595 vs. TAMO 0.4525. OOD (Llama3.1-8B trained on HiTab → AITQA): 0.8220 vs. TAMO 0.7974 and pure text 0.7540. Ablations (Llama3.1-8B, HiTab): removing text is catastrophic, removing the encoder degrades severely, removing GAT or queries costs a small but consistent amount. Baselines include TableLlama and TAMO (the current structural SOTA) plus closed-model zero-shot references — reasonably current for this subfield, though no prompting-based baselines (Chain-of-Table, program-aided methods) are run against the closed models, and the main Table 1 results are single-run (only Table 2 reports three-run averages). The abstract's "22.88% average improvement" on depth-4 is not directly reconstructible from Table 1 (relative gain over TAMO is ~13.7%, over pure text ~25%); the figure's derivation is ambiguous. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel piece is the nested-hypergraph formulation with explicit parent-child hyperedge relations and bidirectional C2P/P2C message passing — prior hypergraph table encoders (HYTREL, TAMO) are strictly flat. The Q-Former-style alignment (from BLIP-2), LoRA fine-tuning, set-attention hypergraph layers, and GAT are all standard components assembled competently in a new setting; the paper is an honest architectural delta on TAMO rather than a new paradigm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and target the right components (encoder, GAT vs. plain set attention, query module, query count). Statistical rigor is partially addressed: a paired McNemar's test on the aggregated depth-3+4 subset (N=848) gives p=0.0079 vs. TAMO, mitigating the tiny depth-4 subset (N=35); Table 2 averages three runs, but the main Table 1 does not state seeds or variance. An appendix honestly quantifies TATQA conversion noise (9% of 100 sampled tables mis-converted; accuracy 52.20% on correct vs. 37.04% on erroneous subsets) and defends the fairness of the shared noisy benchmark. Code is released at https://github.com/lila120/h2table. Concerns: evaluation uses a relaxed-match protocol (currency-symbol stripping etc.) rather than strict EM — applied uniformly to all systems, but it changes the comparability to numbers reported elsewhere in the literature; gold header hierarchies are assumed; closed-source baselines are evaluated only zero-shot with no enhanced prompting; the 4-level TATQA tables were excluded for insufficient sample size (N=12). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored artifact via released code). Practical: Yes — 7B–9B backbones, a 1024-dim hypergraph encoder, RoBERTa-large initializers, and LoRA run on commodity single-GPU hardware. Efficient: Only ~1% of LLM parameters are updated, and the structural prompt is a fixed 12 tokens, so per-inference overhead over pure-text LoRA is small; no wall-clock or FLOP measurements are reported. Effective: Evidence supports the proxy (accuracy on benchmarks with gold hierarchies), but the end-to-end problem — QA over raw real-world tables without annotation — is not solved. Scalable: Untested beyond ~1,700 QA pairs per test set and depth ≤4; behavior on very wide/deep tables or production data volumes is claimed via the fixed-token design but never measured. Deliverable: research code repository; no trained model weights or dataset releases are stated. Strengths: (1) The nested hyperedge scope definition (parent scope = union of children's scopes) is a clean, mathematically well-defined formulation that provably degenerates to flat-hypergraph behavior on flat tables — a genuine backward-compatibility property the paper argues explicitly. (2) The depth-stratified evaluation is the right experimental design for the claimed contribution, and the ablation showing GAT's advantage grows with depth is exactly the evidence that isolates the novelty. (3) The appendix-level rigor is unusual for this area: McNemar significance testing, manual audit of LLM-generated table-structure noise with per-subset accuracy, and uniform relaxed-match evaluation across all systems including GPT-4o. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that gold header hierarchies are assumed as input (isolating representation quality but deferring the extraction problem), and that the LLM still receives serialized text, so structural embeddings may not carry full semantics; both are confronted directly rather than minimized, and the TATQA conversion-noise analysis is disclosed transparently. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The gold-hierarchy assumption is more severe than the paper implies: on messy real tables, LLM-extracted hierarchies at HiTab's depth-4 complexity would likely err far more than the 9% observed on TATQA's shallow tables, and the paper's own data (37% accuracy on mis-converted tables) suggests results would degrade substantially — the headline 22.88%-style claims are unreachable without solving that problem. (2) Closed-source baselines get only zero-shot treatment; tool-use or decomposition prompting for GPT-4o would likely close much of the 0.7011 vs. 0.7596 gap, making the "9B beats hundred-billion models" claim weaker than presented. (3) The 22.88% figure in the abstract cannot be traced to any specific comparison in the tables. (4) Main results lack seed variance; several HiTab/TATQA margins (e.g., TATQA 0.4595 vs. 0.4525) are within plausible run-to-run noise and only the deep-hierarchy comparison is significance-tested. (5) The RoBERTa-large cell initializer is never ablated — it may bottleneck or, conversely, carry most of the semantic signal. Bottom Line: A solid, honestly-reported incremental advance that convincingly shows preserving header hierarchy helps exactly where flat encodings collapse (depth-3/4 tables, significant at p<0.01), but its dependence on gold hierarchies and marginal gains on shallower benchmarks mean practitioners should treat it as a representation contribution to build on, not a deployable solution.

DSpec2Test: Specification -Driven Test Generation in Dafny

SV Pinto, ÁF Silva, JP Faria, A Mendes · archimendes.com · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DSpec2Test, a tool that automatically generates black-box, runnable test cases for Dafny programs directly from formal requires/ensures contracts, without inspecting the implementation. - Why it's important: Existing Dafny test generation (DTest) is implementation-driven, so it cannot support test-driven development, specification validation, or testing before code exists — leaving specification-first workflows in verification-aware languages untested. - How it does it: The tool decomposes the conjunction of pre/postconditions into short-circuit-safe Disjunctive Normal Form branches (Safe DNF), optionally pins one variable at a time to partition boundaries (BVA), and encodes each branch as an assume/assert-false stub so Z3's counterexample yields concrete inputs and expected outputs. - The good: On 131 realistically-killable mutants from DafnyBench, Spec_bva kills 123 (93.9%) versus Block's 108 (82.4%), and uniquely kills 17 mutants that implementation-based testing misses — direct evidence the two strategies reach different fault classes. - The missing: The evaluation covers only 20 hand-selected DafnyBench programs (no mutable state, no non-determinism), relies on mutation testing as the sole effectiveness proxy, and the authors' own manual filtering of 39 mutants as non-compiling/equivalent shapes the headline denominator. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers and tool builders in formal-methods testing — the Safe DNF decomposition and assume/assert-false-to-Z3 encoding are reusable techniques — but practitioners outside the Dafny ecosystem can skim it.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (55) is the main drag — released code, Docker image, and dataset are positives, but single-run results, an author-filtered mutant denominator with no inter-rater reliability, and a single white-box baseline cap it. Novelty (60) is moderate: a new tool for Dafny, but Safe DNF partitioning and SMT-based test synthesis extend 2012-era techniques. Completeness (65) and Resilience (65) benefit from direct confrontation of the vacuity problem and honest limitation lists. Practical Impact (65) reflects a genuinely released, integrated artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*65 = 61.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Developers using verification-aware languages like Dafny get automatic proof of correctness against contracts, but verification failures produce uninformative errors, and Dafny's compilation pipeline to target languages (C#, Java) is itself unverified. Tests help, but the only Dafny test generator, DTest, works from implementation code and targets coverage — it cannot be used before implementation exists, which blocks TDD-style workflows where the specification is written first. The gap: no tool generates Dafny tests from specifications alone, despite specification-driven testing being well established in other contract languages (Eiffel's AutoTest, JMLUnit for Java). Key Idea: Treat each DNF branch of the full contract (preconditions ∧ postconditions) as an equivalence class that jointly constrains inputs and outputs, then coerce the host verifier's own SMT backend (Z3) into a test oracle by inserting `assume <branch>` followed by `assert false` in a stubbed body — the emitted counterexample becomes a concrete input/expected-output pair. The critical refinement is Safe DNF: implications are decomposed into mutually exclusive guarded branches (e.g., A⇒B becomes {¬A, A∧B}) rather than naively expanded to ¬A∨B, so postcondition terms are never evaluated outside their guards (avoiding out-of-bounds crashes like evaluating `s[x]` without 0≤x<|s|). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages integrated into Dafny's `generate-tests` command. (1) The Verifier flags methods annotated with `{:testEntry}` or failing verification and discards their implementations. (2) The Modifier converts the conjoined contract to DNF via a rule table (implication, disjunction, biconditional, if-then-else each map to guarded, mutually exclusive branch sets), computes the cross product, prunes infeasible classes via Z3 UNSAT checks, and optionally applies BVA — pinning exactly one variable per test to interval edges, default extremes (-100, 100) for unbounded numerics, and lengths 0/1/>1 for collections. (3) The Updater supports iterative generation under a `--repeat` flag by appending exclusion assumes (e.g., `assume x != 0`). Generated tests are runnable Dafny methods with expected outputs either solved by Z3 (with `--simplify`, when postconditions uniquely determine outputs) or the postconditions instantiated on known inputs. Design decisions: Safe DNF is well-justified with the ConditionalGet example; the timeout-as-kill convention (300 s budget) is defended by manual inspection showing all timeouts were mutation-introduced infinite loops; the vacuity problem where Z3 picks degenerate models making postconditions hold vacuously is honestly identified but only addressed in future work via a relevance-check encoding. Key Results: Evaluated on 20 DafnyBench programs mutated by MutDafny (up to 10 mutants each, 200 total, Dafny 4.11.0 / Z3 4.12.1). After removing 3 programs unsupported by at least one tool and manually filtering 22 non-compiling and 17 equivalent mutants, 131 realistically-killable mutants remain. Spec_bva kills 123/131 (93.9%) vs. Block's 108/131 (82.4%); the union covers 125 (95.4%); 17 mutants are killed uniquely by Spec_bva, 2 uniquely by Block. Spec_bva generates 6.6 tests per file on average (860 total) vs. ~1.6 for Block, but 52% of explicit-failure kills come from the first test and 73% from the first three. Cost: 1.6× slower wall-clock (7,889 s vs. 4,867 s). Baseline currency is mixed — DTest is the only Dafny competitor, but it is a single white-box mode, not a full test-generation landscape comparison. All numbers are single-run; no variance or significance testing is reported. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (first specification-driven test generator for Dafny) plus NEW METHOD for the Safe DNF contract decomposition preserving short-circuit guard semantics. The core techniques — DNF-based equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, and SMT-based test synthesis — are standard and are direct extensions of Rebello de Andrade et al.'s 2012 Full DNF work on Java generics; the genuine novelty is porting them into the Dafny verifier itself (reusing its Z3 encoding rather than calling a solver externally) and the guard-safe decomposition rules for method contracts. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is moderate. There is a component-relevant ablation of sorts (Spec vs. Spec_bva modes, per-file test yield vs. kill position analysis), but no seed variation, no error bars, and no significance tests — reasonable for a tool paper but the margin (93.9% vs. 82.4%) rests on single runs over 131 mutants. Code (github.com/VeriFixer/DSpec2Test), a prebuilt Docker image, and dataset (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21191158) are released, and a demo video exists — strong artifact availability. Methodological concerns: (a) the 39-mutant manual filtering that defines the 131 denominator was performed by the authors with no inter-rater agreement or published criteria beyond the description; (b) timeout-credited kills (17 for Spec_bva, 9 for Block) inflate headline kill rates, though the justification is plausible; (c) evaluation is confined to the authors' own sampled subset of a third-party benchmark with constraints (no mutable state, no `:|`) that also exclude 3 of 20 programs from one strategy — a narrow slice of real Dafny code. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built and evaluated tool). Practical: Yes — it is a mode of the standard `generate-tests` command, distributed with a Docker image and requiring only Dafny and Z3, both freely available. Efficient: Acceptable — 1.6× the wall-clock cost of the implementation-driven baseline (7,889 s vs. 4,867 s across 131 files), which is real but small per-file. Effective: Strongly supported for mutation kill rate on pure-functional, stateless Dafny methods, but effectiveness on real developer workflows (TDD, fault localization) is claimed, not measured. Scalable: Untested beyond 20 small benchmark programs; the paper itself notes exponential DNF blowup and solver crashes on 3 programs, so 10–100× scale is a known weak point. Delivers a concrete software artifact (tool, Docker image, dataset), not just a paper. Strengths: - The Safe DNF decomposition (Table 1 rules producing mutually exclusive, guard-respecting branches) is a genuine, transferable contribution — naive DNF expansion of contracts is a real failure mode, and the paper demonstrates it concretely. - Reusing Dafny's own verifier as the test oracle (assume/assert-false → counterexample → runnable test) is a clean, low-overhead integration that avoids external solver plumbing and guarantees the tests respect Dafny's type/termination machinery. - The complementarity analysis is the most convincing empirical contribution: 17/19 single-tool kills favor Spec_bva, with concrete evidence (union 95.4% > either alone) that specification- and implementation-driven testing reach different fault classes. - Honest accounting of the vacuity problem (the LastIdx example where Z3's minimal model lets a buggy `a[0]`-returning implementation pass) with a concrete proposed fix, in future work. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: no support for mutable state (arrays, class fields), non-determinism (`:|`), or function inlining in specifications; exponential DNF complexity caused 3/20 programs to crash during test generation; the vacuous-postcondition problem where solver-chosen models under-exercise contract literals; and that the evaluation sample should be broadened. They confront these directly, listing them in Future Work and quantifying the 3-program failure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 131-mutant denominator depends on author-performed manual classification of 39 mutants as non-compiling or equivalent; no inter-rater reliability, no published rubric, and no per-mutant listing cited, so the headline 93.9% is conditional on unblinded judgment calls. - DTest's Block mode is the only baseline; there is no comparison against random/property-based generation (e.g., a QuickCheck-style harness over Dafny preconditions) that would establish whether the DNF machinery — as opposed to any solver-guided input generation — drives the kill-rate advantage. - All 20 programs are drawn from DafnyBench, a benchmark of verified programs; a method tested on contracts from one benchmark family leaves open selection fit, and no industry-scale or AI-generated Dafny code (a plausible real user, given the VeriFixer project context) is evaluated. - Expected-output oracles are only uniquely determined "when --simplify is set" and postconditions uniquely constrain outputs; the paper does not quantify how often this holds, so the fraction of tests with strong vs. weak oracles is unknown. - Timeout-as-kill rewards a tool that generates inputs triggering infinite loops; the manual inspection justifying this is described but not evidenced, and the asymmetry (17 TO kills for Spec_bva vs. 9 for Block) contributes to the headline gap. Bottom Line: A solid, honestly reported tool paper that fills a real hole in the Dafny ecosystem and demonstrates — with artifacts released and complementarity evidence — that spec-driven testing catches faults white-box coverage misses, though its 20-program, stateless, mutation-only evaluation means practitioners should treat the 93.9% kill rate as encouraging direction, not a settled result.

AgenticRag-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Stack Memory for Multi-Step Reasoning, Retrieval and Memorizing

X Jiang, Y Fang, Z Yang, J Gao, Z Zhang, T Feng… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AgentiCRAG-R1, a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs (Qwen2.5, 1.5B–7B) to interleave reasoning, retrieval, and explicit memory-stack manipulation (push/pop actions like <Backtrack> and <Summary>) with action-level process rewards and information-aware trajectory rejection. - Why it's important: Existing RL-based agentic RAG systems use coarse append-only actions and trajectory-level rewards, which accumulate noisy intermediate conclusions into context and bias training toward shallow, templated one-search answers — a core bottleneck for real multi-hop decision-making tasks. - How it does it: The core move is a LIFO memory stack with reversible actions plus a pop-based attention mask that structurally removes popped content from conditioning, combined with a UCB-like score (σ²·r + μ) that globally rejects low-information rollouts across each training batch. - The good: Gains hold across three model scales and out-of-domain tasks — e.g., 33.55 vs. 30.16 average F1 for the strongest baseline (Search-R1) on Qwen2.5-3B, +6.76 on HotpotQA, and improvements to 51.1% success on ALFWorld and 20.42 RACE on DeepResearch Bench — with component ablations showing memory actions and rejection each contribute several F1 points. - The missing: Process rewards come from an unvalidated LLM judge (a general reward model), no significance tests or multi-seed error bars are reported for the main tables, and the long-horizon results contain non-monotonic scores for their own method that undercut the headline "monotonically improving" claim. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on RL-trained search agents or agentic memory design — it is a concrete, ablated recipe for action-granular rewards and reversible memory; skip it if you only need another multi-hop QA number, since the deltas over Search-R1/ARPO are moderate and the mechanism choices (LLM-judged rewards) carry deployment risk.

Problem & Motivation: Multi-hop question answering and agentic tasks require an LLM to decide when and what to retrieve, integrate retrieved evidence into an evolving internal state, and revise earlier conclusions when they prove wrong. Prior RL-based agentic RAG methods (Search-R1, ReSearch, AEPO, ARPO, Mem1) collapse the agent's behavior into coarse append-only action templates and assign a single trajectory-level outcome reward, so (1) noisy or erroneous intermediate steps get implicitly reinforced and propagate through context, and (2) training is dominated by short-horizon trajectories that trivially earn reward on easy multi-hop data, starving long-horizon behaviors like revision and planning of learning signal. The authors formalize this as two challenges: fine-grained memory-aware action/reward allocation (C1) and exposure of RL to diverse, high-information rollouts (C2). Key Idea: Two coupled ideas: (1) represent the agent's internal state as a LIFO memory stack with semantically typed actions — <Plan>, <Think>, <Search>, <Conclusion> push, while <Backtrack> and <Summary> pop-then-push — and pair this with (a) action-aligned process rewards assigned only at action tokens and (b) a pop-based attention mask that structurally excludes popped content from future conditioning, so erroneous steps cannot receive outcome reward; and (2) a cross-input, batch-level rollout rejection rule ˜r = σ²·r + μ that keeps only the top fraction p of rollouts, prioritizing prompts whose rollouts show high reward variance (informativeness) and rollouts that are high-reward within them. Methodology: The pipeline is GRPO-style RL over multi-turn rollouts (K=10 generations per prompt, temperature 0.7, batch 16, lr 1e-6, 300 steps, max context 4096 tokens). Per-token reward r_i = (1−I_mask)·r_out + I_act·r_proc,i: outcome reward is EM (discrete) or F1 (graded) on the <Conclusion> answer, spread uniformly over unmasked tokens; retrieved observations are masked from gradients. Process rewards, applied only at action tokens, sum three terms: a format reward (1.0 for valid Conclusion, 0.5 for other valid actions), a retrieval reward from a large general reward model (GRM, from Wang et al. 2025a) scoring query–document–question relevance, and a memory reward from the same GRM scoring whether a Backtrack/Summary operation improved the stack state; a per-trajectory budget with proportional normalization caps total process reward to prevent reward hacking via action spam. Rollout selection computes per-input reward mean μ and variance σ² across rollouts, scores all B×K rollouts with σ²·r + μ, and keeps the global top fraction p. A pop-based attention mask (M_pop added to the causal mask) prevents tokens popped by a Summary or Backtrack from being attended afterward. Training data is HotpotQA/2Wiki training splits filtered by TC-RAG self-sampling (10 trajectories) to keep only questions needing genuine multi-step retrieval. The appendix includes a Theorem 1 showing outcome-only rewards monotonically amplify erroneous steps and Theorem 2 arguing pop-masking structurally isolates them from the gradient — proofs are short and rest on straightforward log-derivative algebra. Critical design decisions: LLM-judged process rewards (justified only by a heuristic-reward ablation showing a 33.55→29.40 drop, not by validating the judge itself); the specific UCB-form score σ²·r + μ (justified intuitively, no ablation of alternative score forms); stack-based memory with attention masking (the most technically substantive and best-motivated decision). Key Results: On Qwen2.5-3B, AgentiCRAG-R1 averages 33.55 F1 across seven benchmarks vs. 30.16 for Search-R1 (best RL baseline) and 26.00 for ReAct, with +3.02 on 2Wiki (32.92), +6.76 on HotpotQA (44.00), +2.56 on MusiQue, +2.42 on NQ, +1.54 on TriviaQA; it loses to baselines on Bamboogle at 1.5B (−2.16) and NQ at 7B (−6.41). On Qwen2.5-7B it averages 36.60 (+5.58 over TC-RAG). Ablations (3B): removing memory actions drops avg to 27.37, removing rejection to 25.43, both to 24.24; removing the retrieval reward to 25.53, memory reward to 24.39. Leave-one-action-out: removing <Backtrack> costs 3.85 avg F1, <Summary> 3.05, <Plan> 1.95. SFT-init vs cold-start RL: 35.20±0.40 vs 33.55±0.42. Long-horizon step budgets (10→30) show gains on 2Wiki (23.91→47.45) and TriviaQA (37.53→55.28) but non-monotonic dips on Bamboogle (10.03 at 10 steps, 14.29 at 20) and TriviaQA at 15 steps. Out-of-domain: MedQA 92% format / 87% answer accuracy (vs ReAct 56%/79%); DeepResearch Bench RACE 43.60 vs ReAct 42.21, FACT effective-citation 20.42 vs EDR's 12.28; ALFWorld 36.5%→51.1% success; WebShop score 14.7→27.8. Inference latency 10.15 s vs TC-RAG's 11.86 s on 3B. Training: 2×A800 80GB, ~21,582 s (~6 hours). Baselines are current (2025 RL agentic RAG methods), and evaluation scale is standard (benchmarks up to ~17K test questions) but not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (fine-grained memory-stack action space with pop-based attention masking and action-aligned process rewards in RL for agentic RAG) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (action-specific neuron activation patterns motivating action-level decomposition). The stack idea itself is inherited from the authors' prior TC-RAG (prompting-based, same group), Mem1 already does RL memory consolidation, and the rejection score is a UCB-flavored variant of known rejection sampling — the genuinely new elements are the pop-based attention mask for reversible memory inside RL and the action-token-level process reward with budget normalization; the rest is a competent combination of GRPO, LLM-judge rewards, and entropy/variance-based rollout filtering applied to this new action space. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: component ablations (memory actions, rejection), per-reward-term ablations, leave-one-action-out over all six actions, rejection-threshold sweeps (0.2–0.8), step-budget scaling, SFT-init comparison, and a heuristic-vs-GRM-judge reward ablation. However, main tables report single runs with no error bars or significance tests (only the small SFT comparison carries ±values); the GRM judge is never validated against human or ground-truth labels, creating an unmeasured reward-modeling risk; several hyperparameters (rejection fraction p at training time, process reward budget B_proc, reward weights) are not stated in the implementation table. Training data derives from HotpotQA/2Wiki train splits while those datasets are also evaluation targets — standard practice but worth noting for in-domain gains. Anonymous code is released at https://github.com/jiangxinke/Harness-RL/tree/AgenticRAG-R1-Whitebox. Methodological red flags are mild: one inconsistency where the Ethical Considerations section mentions GAIA, a benchmark not evaluated; and the long-horizon table's non-monotonic results (Bamboogle 10.03→31.81→14.29→21.43→35.47) sit awkwardly beside the text's claim of "monotonically improving trends on most benchmarks." Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (RL-trained system with measured benchmarks). - Practical: Yes — trains on 2×A800 80GB in ~6 hours with a Wikipedia dump search tool, all commercially available components. - Efficient: Training adds a real overhead from GRM judge calls (~3.5–4.0M input tokens per run for memory judging alone); inference is actually 14.4% faster than TC-RAG (10.15 vs 11.86 s) despite 12.2% more actions. - Effective: Evidence covers QA F1, format compliance, report generation, and interactive environments — it demonstrably improves multi-hop QA and transfers, but the LLM-judged reward quality and true robustness of backtracking (vs. reward-hacking the judge) remain proxies. - Scalable: Untested beyond 7B and 30-step budgets; the GRM judging cost and stack-management complexity would grow with trajectory length and batch size, and the authors themselves flag scalability and hyperparameter tuning as open problems. Deliverable: anonymous code repository (training framework); no model weights or dataset release stated. Strengths: - The pop-based attention mask is a real technical contribution: it makes popped memory content structurally (not just conventionally) invisible to future tokens, and the appendix theorems give a coherent argument that this prevents outcome rewards from reinforcing erroneous steps — a mechanism-level fix, not just a prompting fix. - Action-token-level process reward allocation with budget normalization is a concrete answer to the coarse trajectory-level reward problem, and the ablations (each reward term, each action) genuinely isolate which components matter rather than asserting it. - Evaluation breadth is above the norm for this line: three backbone scales, seven QA benchmarks plus MedQA, DeepResearch Bench, ALFWorld, and WebShop, with the neuron-activation analysis providing independent (if correlative) evidence that action types engage distinct model resources. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (1) computational overhead from the memory stack and dynamic retrieval may challenge time-sensitive or large-scale deployment, and (2) rejection-based sampling requires careful hyperparameter tuning that may not transfer to new datasets/tasks, calling for self-calibrating strategies. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive — though they do not mention the LLM-judge reliability risk or the non-monotonic long-horizon results. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The GRM judge is the linchpin of both the retrieval and memory rewards, yet there is no measurement of judge accuracy, consistency, or susceptibility to gaming (e.g., an agent learning to write flattering queries/summaries); the heuristic-reward ablation shows judges help but not that they are trustworthy. - No error bars or seeds for the main comparison tables; given reported deltas of +1.5 to +3 F1 on some benchmarks, run-to-run variance could matter. - The long-horizon experiment contradicts its own narrative: the method scores 10.03 on Bamboogle at a 10-step budget (far below ReAct's 15.67), and TriviaQA dips at 15 steps — evidence that the stack mechanism itself can hurt under tight horizons, unaddressed in the text. - No comparison against a simpler ablation in which a standard LLM-as-judge (rather than the specific GRM) provides process rewards, leaving unclear how much of the gain depends on that particular reward model. - The UCB-style rejection score has no theoretical justification tying σ²·r + μ to any exploration objective; the citation of Russo & Van Roy is ornamental rather than load-bearing. Bottom Line: A practitioner building RL-trained search agents gains a concrete, well-ablated recipe for reversible memory actions and action-granular rewards that beats the current Search-R1/ARPO generation on standard multi-hop benchmarks, but should treat the LLM-judged process rewards and long-horizon claims with caution — read it for the pop-mask mechanism and reward design, not as a settled recipe.
