Problem & Motivation: LLM code generation works well on HumanEval/MBPP-style function-level tasks (97.6%/92.7% reported) and SWE-bench (76.8%), but generating complex domain-specific pipelines from scratch fails for three reasons the authors identify: exhaustive manual prompting is needed for domain context; hallucinations and absent validation force human correction; and no mechanism retains knowledge across projects. Medical imaging concentrates all three: multimodal data (CT/MRI, 2D/3D, NIfTI/DICOM), strict domain conventions (HU windowing, voxel-space resampling, patient-level splits), multi-stage interdependent pipelines, and unacceptable cost for hallucinated preprocessing. The beneficiaries are practitioners without deep learning expertise; existing remedies (IDE tools, multi-agent frameworks, AutoML agents, nnU-Net, MedSAM) each address only part of the pipeline or require manual scaffolds, dataset cards, or skeletons. Key Idea: Validation-based context engineering — treat every agent output as gated by a validation function V: O → {pass, (fail, feedback)}, so only verified artifacts propagate into shared memory for the next agent, and failures return diagnostic feedback for targeted retry; combine this with a persistent knowledge base of previously validated pipelines retrieved by hard/soft constraint similarity, so new projects synthesize within a 'validated neighborhood' rather than from scratch. The formal-verification component (CSP# + PAT model checking of architecture designs against LTL liveness/safety templates) is the most distinctive move, though the ablation suggests it adds marginal value because imaging pipelines are mostly sequential. Methodology: A router–subagent hierarchy with an independent Validation Layer runs two phases. Planning Phase: a Dataset Analyser extracts dataset properties (modality, dimensions, spacing, intensity range, case counts), checked semantically against required properties (Eq. 2); an Architect produces a JSON pipeline design validated on two levels — contextual (architecture–dataset compatibility, ISO/IEC 25023 modularity, IEC 62304 conventions) and formal (conversion to CSP# verified by PAT for deadlock-freedom and LTL properties like □(model_initialized → ◇training_finished)). Coding Phase: a Coding Router decomposes the design into Dataset/NN/Training/Inference module specs for parallel Coder subagents; the Tester applies Pylint/Radon static checks with CC/MI thresholds (τ = 80), 30–40 LLM-generated Pytest cases per module (assumption/functional/integration tests), then assembly validation on the integrated pipeline. Context per agent is formalized as ⟨prompt, shared memory (Eion MCP key-value store), domain KB (Cognee knowledge graphs built from nnU-Net dataset cards, Grand Challenge architectures, MONAI docs), adaptive synthesis KB, tool history, validation feedback⟩. Adaptive synthesis: pipelines achieving performance above threshold θ are stored; retrieval requires exact match on hard constraints (modality, task type) plus similarity on soft constraints; retrieved components are adapted for class counts, image sizes, preprocessing differences, and re-validated. Critical design decisions: (1) independent validation layer to avoid self-validation bias — justified by the single-agent ablation (−10.2% performance, +1.33 HI); (2) knowledge bases compiled from general standards, claimed dataset-independent — plausible but the rule content is hand-curated by the authors; (3) LLM-based semantic similarity for retrieval with hard-constraint gating — reasonable but unquantified. Key Results: On six datasets (four supervised 3D segmentation, one semi-supervised 3D segmentation, one 2D segmentation, one 3D classification), AutoMedImg achieves 0 human interventions on every task, with Dice up to 0.9041 (ACDC, Claude-4.5-Opus), 0.8333 (FLARE22, DeepSeek-V3.2), 0.7696 (BTCV), 0.9517 (Promise12), and accuracy up to 0.9938 (OrganMNIST). Baselines under identical configuration require 1–7 interventions: CAMEL (Dice 0.5104–0.8923), MetaGPT X (0.6845–0.9125), MaCTG (0.5104–0.8820), AutoML-Agent (0.6237–0.9752, needs manual skeletons), M3Builder (0.7392 on BTCV but template-bound). Against vanilla tools/LLMs (RQ1), Copilot/Cursor/Antigravity need 5–17 interventions; open-source LLMs fail badly (GPT-oss: 0.0067 Dice on FLARE22 from unrestricted Resize corrupting voxel spacing); proprietary LLMs reach 0.5058–0.9752 Dice with 5–12 interventions. RQ1-style experiments used 15 configurations (6 LLMs × tools). Ablations (Claude-4.5-Opus, averaged over datasets): knowledge base removal is the largest single hit (−13.7% performance); execution testing removal adds +3.50 HI; syntax check removal adds +0.67 HI and +37.2 min; adaptive synthesis removal costs −8.4% and +37 min; formal CSP# validation removal adds +0.10 HI, i.e., nearly nothing. Cost: $20–40 and ~32 minutes per pipeline vs. $200–600 and 4–8 hours manual. Scale is standard (datasets of 50–2,000 cases); all experiments are Pass@3, best-of-three trials — an optimistic reporting protocol. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (AutoMedImg) plus NEW METHOD in the specific combination of validation-gated context propagation and formal CSP#/PAT verification inside an LLM code-generation loop for medical imaging; the cross-project adaptive pipeline synthesis is a case-based-retrieval idea (cf. DS-Agent) applied with domain constraints. Individually, the ingredients — multi-agent orchestration (ChatDev/MetaGPT), execution-feedback loops, RAG-style domain knowledge, case-based reuse — are standard; the genuinely novel elements are the validation-formalized context-propagation semantics (Definitions 1–2) and embedding model checking in the architecture-design loop, neither of which prior coding-agent or medical-imaging-automation work combines. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and component-wise (RQ3), covering all eight components plus the multi-agent-vs-single-agent comparison (RQ4, −10.2% performance for single-agent under identical context engineering) — this is above average for systems papers. However: all results are Pass@3 best-of-three with no variance, error bars, or significance tests; ablations use only Claude-4.5-Opus and report averages that obscure per-dataset spread (e.g., +0.10 HI deltas are within measurement noise given integer intervention counts); no statistical testing is mentioned. Code artifacts are released at https://github.com/SeanCho1996/AutoMedImg. Methodological concerns: the semantic validation criteria and knowledge-base content are hand-curated by the authors, so 'no dataset-specific knowledge' is asserted but the rubrics encode exactly the conventions tested (HU windowing, voxel resampling, patient-level splitting) — a partial Goodhart risk; the qualitative Table 3 comparison with nnU-Net/MedSAM/NAS is author-scored, not measured; 'zero human intervention' depends on the authors' own definition of valid intervention events. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a built multi-agent framework actually run end-to-end on real datasets with trained models and measured Dice/accuracy. - Practical: Yes — runs on a 2×RTX A6000 (48GB) workstation; the framework itself needs API access to a backbone LLM plus PAT/Cognee/MCP tooling. - Efficient: $20–40 and ~32 minutes per pipeline versus $200–600 and 4–8 hours manual development; multi-agent orchestration and iterative validation add cost relative to direct single-shot generation, and the paper does not report total token consumption. - Effective: Evidence supports the autonomy claim on these six benchmarks (0 HI, competitive Dice), but 'production-ready' is only proxied by static-analysis thresholds and held-out test metrics on curated public datasets — no real clinical data, no deployment study. - Scalable: Not tested beyond six datasets and one domain; the knowledge base starts empty, so behavior at 10×–100× accumulated pipelines (retrieval quality drift, knowledge-base contamination) is claimed but unmeasured. Delivers a software artifact: the framework and code are on GitHub; domain knowledge bases and CSP# templates are reusable construction recipes. Strengths: - The validation-as-gate formalization (V: O → {pass, (fail, f)}) is a clean, transferable abstraction that turns multi-agent orchestration from prompt choreography into a checkable pipeline, and the ablation quantifies each gate rather than asserting their value. - Independent Validation Layer separation is empirically grounded: the single-agent control with identical context engineering loses 10.2% performance and 1.33 interventions, isolating architecture from context effects — a control many agentic papers omit. - The evaluation matrix is unusually broad for this venue tier: 6 datasets × 5 backbones × 8 baseline systems, plus a qualitative BTCV design comparison showing generated pipelines match domain conventions (orientation, resampling, spacing-aware patching). - Formal CSP#/PAT verification of generated architectures is a genuinely underexplored integration in LLM code generation, even if the ablation shows its marginal current payoff. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two: (1) generalization — the domain knowledge bases, validation criteria, and agent configurations are medical-imaging-specific; the framework skeleton is claimed domain-independent but adaptation requires rebuilding KBs, criteria, and templates; (2) generation overhead — multi-agent coordination with iterative validation costs more API spend and time than direct generation, which they justify against manual development cost. They confront these directly in a Threats to Validity section, which is a credibility positive, but they do not acknowledge any evaluation-protocol threats (Pass@3, hand-curated validation rubrics). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Best-of-three (Pass@3) reporting inflates both performance and the zero-intervention claim; mean/median across seeds with variance is needed, especially since intervention counts are small integers where ±1 changes the story. - The semantic validation rubrics (patient-level splitting, HU windowing, voxel resampling) are authored by the same team that designed the architecture that passes them; a held-out rubric or third-party-curated criteria would rule out circular validation. - No comparison at matched compute budget against a strong single frontier LLM given a well-engineered domain prompt — the RQ1 'vanilla LLM' baselines get generic prompts, so the framework's advantage over good prompting is not isolated. - The adaptive synthesis mechanism's retrieval threshold τ_sim and LLM-based similarity are never characterized; failure cases of retrieval (wrong pipeline reused) are absent, and with only six projects the cross-project learning evidence is thin. - The knowledge base 'built from general standards independent of evaluation datasets' is asserted; the Cognee KB construction process is not documented enough to verify no leakage from the six benchmarks' conventions. - Ablation deltas for some components (formal validation: +0.10 HI) are small enough that the framework's complexity cost is not clearly justified for sequential imaging pipelines — the paper concedes this indirectly but keeps the component. - No failure-mode analysis: all reported AutoMedImg runs apparently succeeded within 3 attempts; the distribution of near-misses is invisible. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM-driven code-generation agents for specialized domains gains a concrete, well-ablated template — validation-gated context propagation, independent validation agents, and formal design checking — that is likely the most complete demonstration of zero-intervention domain pipeline generation to date, but the Pass@3 protocol and self-authored validation rubrics mean the headline numbers should be read as upper bounds rather than expected performance.

Beyond Retrieval: Progressive Latent Memory Evolution for Streaming Video Understanding (22 ▲ )

Hongyu Qu, Guangming Yao, Ling Xing, Xiaobin Hu, Rongxing Ding, Guibin Zhang, Fan Zhang, Yi Yuan, Xiangbo Shu, Shuicheng Yan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LatentStream, a training-free framework that internalizes retrieved video history into a small set of optimizable latent memory tokens, rather than appending retrieved evidence as external visual context, for streaming video QA. - Why it's important: Streaming video applications (live monitoring, autonomous driving, smart glasses) require bounded-memory, causal processing of unbounded visual streams, and existing store-and-retrieve methods keep history as variable-length context that inflates compute and is never compacted into a working state. - How it does it: It maintains a three-level hierarchical memory built with Jenks natural-breaks consolidation, assigns three groups of latent memory tokens nested expanding retrieval scopes, and iteratively retrieves visual evidence and refines the token embeddings at test time with REINFORCE under a reward that combines absolute predictive confidence with a hierarchical entropy-ordering term (entropy must decrease as the accessible scope widens). - The good: The strongest evidence is the ablation isolating the retrieve-and-internalize mechanism: evolved latent tokens achieve 64.2% on OVO-Bench versus 59.7% for direct evidence injection and 56.5% for unoptimized latent tokens — and retrieved tokens are deleted before decoding, so gains are demonstrably not just context padding. - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests on any headline number, no code release is mentioned, and the test-time optimization adds latency (TTFT rises from 7.63s to 8.41s) whose effect on the real-time streaming setting the paper motivates is never analyzed. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on streaming/long-video MLLM memory management, since the retrieve-and-internalize inversion of the retrieval paradigm is a genuinely distinct design point; practitioners seeking deployable streaming systems can skim the efficiency table and ablations only.

Problem & Motivation: Streaming video understanding demands that multimodal LLMs process continuously arriving frames and answer queries posed at arbitrary times under strict causality and bounded memory. Existing training-free methods manage history via frame selection, token pruning, KV-cache compression, or hierarchical memory banks, and newer methods add query-aware retrieval. The gap the authors identify: retrieved evidence is always re-exposed to the model as external, variable-length visual context, so query-agnostic memory retention and query-conditioned reasoning remain loosely coupled — no compact latent state accumulates task-relevant history and evolves alongside reasoning. The intended beneficiaries are builders of real-time video assistants and embodied agents operating on unbounded streams. Key Idea: The core trick is retrieve-and-internalize: instead of returning retrieved history to the context window, inject retrieved visual tokens into the frozen MLLM's forward pass next to their corresponding latent-memory-token group, score the resulting candidate latent state with a predictive-entropy-based reward, and accept the retrieved evidence only if the reward improves (a reward-gated merge). The latent tokens then guide the next round of retrieval, creating an iterative retrieval–update loop, and the evidence is discarded before decoding so the internalized latent state — not the raw evidence — carries the history. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Query-Agnostic Hierarchical Streaming Memory (HSM): incoming visual tokens fill short-term memory densely; overflow routes to mid-term via three-class Jenks partitioning of temporal importance scores (drop/compress/preserve) and to long-term via two-class Jenks partitioning of spatial token distances (merge redundant pairs), all under a fixed budget (2048 visual tokens; 8 short-term + 64 mid-term frames in the default config). (2) Hierarchical Latent Memory Evolution (HME): K=2 latent memory tokens per group across three groups with nested receptive fields (C_s = short-term; C_m = short+mid; C_l = full bank); each iteration, a group retrieves the top-B=8 visual patches by max cosine similarity to its tokens (query-conditioned via a bootstrap forward pass that contextualizes initial tokens with the query), injects candidate evidence after the group's tokens, and admits it into a retained evidence pool only if the candidate reward exceeds the previous iteration's. (3) Progressive Confidence-guided Latent Memory Optimization (PMO): a REINFORCE-style direct policy gradient — a Gaussian perturbation policy (σ = 10% of scale) over the joint latent state of LMT embeddings and retrieved evidence — maximizes a hierarchical progression reward R = Σ_g(1−E_g) + hinge terms enforcing E_s > E_m > E_l, where E_g is top-δ normalized predictive entropy measured after each group's evidence block. After R=4 iterations, retrieved evidence is removed and the answer decodes from [memory; query; optimized latent tokens]. Critical design decisions: the nested receptive-field grouping (plausible but the group sizes/ratios are not ablated), the reward-gated evidence admission (well justified by the reward-improvement criterion), and entropy-as-reward self-supervision (justified by ablation showing it alone recovers most of the gain: 62.5/65.5 without progression terms vs. 64.2/66.6 with). Key Results: Built on frozen Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, 1 fps sampling, tested on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, Video-MME, MLVU, LongVideoBench. OVO-Bench (7B): 64.2% overall vs. 54.0% for the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline (+10.2), beating recent training-free competitors FluxMem (56.9) and OASIS (60.0), with the largest jump on Backward Tracing (44.7→60.0). 3B variant: 52.2→59.0 (+6.8). StreamingBench: 76.9% overall vs. 73.9% baseline and 76.4% for FluxMem. Offline: Video-MME 66.6% (+3.3 over baseline), MLVU 74.0% (+6.1), LongVideoBench 62.1% (+1.4). Efficiency on OVO-Bench (7B): peak memory 30.80→21.97 GB, TPOT 6.45→3.16 ms (−51%), TTFT 7.63→8.41 s (+10% from test-time optimization). Baselines include 2025–2026 methods (FluxMem, OASIS, QueryStream, StreamForest, ThinkStream), so the comparison pool is current; training-based streaming models like ThinkStream (59.7 on OVO-Bench) are also beaten despite using no task-specific training. Hyperparameter sweeps cover evolution iterations R (0→4: 58.1→64.2, plateau after), candidate budget B (degrades beyond 8), and noise scale σ (degrades beyond 10%). Scale is standard benchmark scale (up to 1,024 frames offline), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus a NEW FORMULATION of the streaming-memory problem (internalize rather than re-expose retrieved evidence, with the latent state both guiding and being updated by retrieval). The individual components are standard: Jenks natural breaks is a 1971 cartography technique, cosine-similarity top-K retrieval is standard, hierarchical multi-level memory follows FluxMem, and REINFORCE over continuous prompts is known from test-time prompt tuning. The novelty lies in the specific coupling — reward-gated evidence admission, nested receptive-field token groups, and the hierarchical entropy-progression objective applied to latent token optimization in a frozen MLLM — which is a non-obvious composition, not a new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a genuine strength: component-level (Table 3), mechanism-level isolating internalization from context augmentation (Table 4, including the crucial negative control that unoptimized latent tokens hurt: 56.5 vs. 54.0 baseline is not shown that way, but initial LMTs score 56.5 vs. evolved 64.2), objective-level (Table 5), and hyperparameter-level (Fig. 3). However: no multiple seeds, no error bars, no significance tests anywhere; a single 7B and 3B backbone (no generality across model families); efficiency is reported on one benchmark only; no code, data, or model release URL is mentioned. The comparison includes the authors' own reproduced baselines (marked †), which is transparent but introduces reproduction risk. Goodhart concern: the reward is predictive entropy on the same distribution the model is evaluated on, so optimizing confidence could partially game the benchmark's answer format — the paper does not test this (e.g., calibration of the final answers). One internal inconsistency: the OVO-Bench baseline for Qwen2.5-VL-7B is 54.0 in Tables 1 and 6 but the ablation tables start from 56.9 (attributed to FluxMem), which is explained but makes cross-table comparisons slightly confusing. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (training-free inference-time method, actually run). Practical: Runs on 8× NVIDIA H20 GPUs with a frozen open-weight backbone, so the hardware is commercially available, though 8-GPU experimentation is a high bar for adopters. Efficient: Memory and per-token decode improve over the baseline (−8.8 GB peak, −51% TPOT) at the cost of ~10% longer time-to-first-token from the test-time optimization loop — a real cost for the interactive streaming use case. Effective: Evidence shows it solves benchmark QA tasks under bounded memory; the paper does not measure anything about true real-time constraint compliance (e.g., answering within a latency budget on live streams), only post-hoc benchmark accuracy. Scalable: Not tested beyond ~1,024 frames / 2048-token memory budget; behavior on genuinely unbounded multi-hour streams, where long-term memory quality dominates, is claimed but unmeasured. Deliverable status: paper only — no software artifact, weights, or code repository is mentioned. Strengths: (1) The conceptual inversion from store-and-retrieve to retrieve-and-internalize is a crisp, well-articulated reframing, and the paper defends it with the right experiment: removing retrieved tokens before decoding and showing evolved latent tokens beat explicit injection by 4.5 points on OVO-Bench. (2) The confidence-progression reward is a clever, annotation-free test-time supervision signal — using the frozen MLLM's own entropy both absolutely and as an ordering constraint across memory scopes — and the ablation shows the ordering term adds 1.7 points over absolute confidence alone. (3) The evaluation spans both streaming and offline long-video benchmarks against a current (2025–2026) baseline pool, and beating training-based streaming models with a training-free method is a substantive result. (4) The efficiency profile (lower memory and decode latency than the baseline) means the method is not merely accurate but removes a deployment bottleneck. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper is thin on explicit limitations. The authors acknowledge TTFT increases due to latent memory evolution and note that excessive evidence budgets or noise scales destabilize optimization (empirically handled by fixing R=4, B=8, σ=10%). They do not include a limitations section discussing failure modes, domain restrictions, or the variance of the REINFORCE procedure. This is a credibility gap: the limitations are surfaced only implicitly through hyperparameter sensitivity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Variance and reliability of the REINFORCE-based test-time optimization are never characterized — policy gradient over a Gaussian-perturbed continuous latent state with a single reward sample per iteration is high-variance, and with no seeds or error bars, the +10.2 point headline could be fragile. (2) The reward (predictive entropy) is optimized on the same distribution it is evaluated on; no held-out calibration or format-robustness check rules out confidence-gaming of multiple-choice benchmarks. (3) Latency analysis is incomplete for the motivating setting: 8.4 s TTFT on a benchmark query is fine, but the cost of running R=4 forward/backward passes per arriving query in a genuinely interactive stream is never modeled. (4) Only Qwen2.5-VL backbones — whether the latent tokens can internalize history in a differently-architected MLLM is untested, so the claim is about a framework demonstrated on one family. (5) The memory hierarchy is inherited from FluxMem, and the ablation (Table 3, row 1: 58.1/65.1 with HSM alone) shows a large share of the total gain comes from that prior component; the marginal contribution of the new machinery is +6.1 on OVO-Bench over FluxMem's memory, not +10.2. (6) No code release is stated, which limits verification of the intricate injection/acceptance mechanics. Bottom Line: A researcher in streaming or long-video MLLM memory should read this — the retrieve-and-internalize formulation and the confidence-progression reward are genuinely new design points backed by a well-isolated ablation — but a practitioner should wait for a code release and multi-seed replication before adopting it, and the reported gains over the strongest baselines (roughly +4 points on OVO-Bench over OASIS, +3 over FluxMem on StreamingBench) are meaningful yet unverified for statistical stability.

#154 — Innovative (61)

SOMTab: Set-Order Mamba for Efficient Tabular In-Context Learning

H Wang, S Zhang, W Ma · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SOMTab, a tabular in-context learning architecture that replaces attention in table-representation stages with a Set-to-Order Mamba encoder (attention retained only for the final query-context reader), plus a DCH-TailMix synthetic pretraining prior. - Why it's important: PFN-style tabular foundation models are bottlenecked by quadratic attention cost as context size grows, so a cheaper architecture that preserves accuracy directly reduces inference time and GPU memory for tabular prediction. - How it does it: Learnable seed slots absorb unordered table tokens via cross-attention (giving a permutation-invariant, fixed-order latent sequence), Mamba-2 mixes along that sequence, and attention is reserved solely for query-to-context retrieval where its query-key routing matters. - The good: On all TALENT classification datasets, SOMTab reaches 0.849 accuracy / 0.054 normalized log-loss versus TabICLv2's 0.854 / 0.029, while running at 0.019s per 1K context samples versus TabICLv2's 0.463s (0.151s with a single estimator) — a 8–24× runtime reduction for a small accuracy cost. - The missing: The controlled ablation trains variants for only 20K steps (the main model uses 400K) and evaluates only early checkpoints on a 15-dataset subset chosen where SOMTab trails TabICLv2, so neither the prior comparison nor the Mamba-reader claim is validated at full training scale. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building tabular foundation models or efficient ICL architectures; practitioners just applying existing models (TabICLv2, TabPFN) can skip it since the released model is not yet accuracy-competitive with the top baseline.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (70) is the strongest dimension — the representation-vs-matching role decomposition and the set-to-order latent-slot trick solving Mamba's permutation-invariance barrier are genuinely instructive — and Completeness (72) benefits from unusually honest accounting of the accuracy gap and ablation weaknesses. But Rigor (52) is pulled down materially: controlled ablations run at 20K steps versus the 400K-step main model, on a post-hoc selected 15-dataset subset, with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, and — decisively — no code, data, or checkpoint release for a 23-GPU-day model, making it effectively unverifiable. Practical Impact (40) is low since the work stops at paper form and the released model is not accuracy-competitive anyway. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*52 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*64 + 0.10*40 ≈ 61.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Tabular prediction is dominated by tree ensembles, and PFN-style tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabPFNv2, TabICL, TabICLv2) have closed much of the gap by amortizing prediction across synthetic tasks via in-context learning. But these models use Transformer attention throughout the pipeline, inheriting quadratic cost in rows/features, so long-context tabular prediction gets expensive. The authors pose a specific architectural question: is attention necessary at every stage of tabular ICL, or only for query-context matching at prediction time? The audience is anyone deploying tabular foundation models where inference cost and memory scale with labeled-context size. Key Idea: Decompose tabular ICL into two computational roles with different operators: representation construction is a structured compression problem on unordered tokens, solvable by linear-complexity state-space mixing once tokens are mapped to a stable latent order; query-context matching needs attention's query-dependent routing and should keep it. The "set-to-order" trick — K learnable seed slots read the token set via position-free cross-attention, producing a fixed-index latent sequence that Mamba-2 can then scan — reconciles Mamba's order dependence with the permutation invariance tables require (Perceiver-style latent bottleneck + Mamba-2). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Cell tokenization: grouped input features (TabICLv2-style circular feature grouping) are linearly projected to d=128 tokens, with label embeddings injected only into context rows. (2) Representation construction via Set-to-Order Mamba blocks applied on two axes: a variable-level encoder (Lv=3 blocks, Kv=64 latent slots) reads only context-row tokens per feature, then reads back to all rows; a sample-level encoder (Ls=3 blocks, Ks=Kr=4 slots) compresses each row's m feature tokens plus 4 learned row tokens into a 4d-dimensional row representation. Each block is set-read (cross-attention, O(NK)) → Mamba-2 → FFN, with an optional readback; the set-read is permutation-invariant and readback permutation-equivariant. (3) An attention-based ICL reader (12 Transformer blocks) where all rows query but keys/values are restricted to labeled context, output by a 2-layer MLP. Pretraining minimizes query cross-entropy (Eq. 1) on DCH-TailMix tasks: a synthetic prior sampling degree-corrected DAGs (sparsity τ, node in/out-degree corrections, module biases, low-rank terms across four graph families) with a three-regime tail mixture (70% independent Student-t, 20% hierarchical Student-t, 10% symmetric Pareto) over graph biases, plus random function families (linear, neural, tree, GP-like, quadratic, EM-like, product) for latent propagation. Training: 28.6M parameters, two-stage curriculum (300K + 100K steps), Muon–AdamW, four A100-40GB GPUs, ~23 days, float32. Key design decisions — the fixed-slot ordering for Mamba compatibility, retaining attention for the reader, and label embeddings at two points — are justified by the role-decomposition argument and the reader ablation, though the slot-count and layer-count choices are not swept. Key Results: On all TALENT classification datasets (all methods rerun on one H200 server, official default configs): SOMTab 0.054 mean min–max normalized log-loss, 0.849 accuracy, 0.785 Macro F1, 0.019s median fit-plus-predict per 1K context samples; TabICLv2 (default, 8 estimators) 0.029 / 0.854 / 0.790 at 0.463s; TabICLv2 (1 estimator) 0.046 / 0.853 at 0.151s; TabPFNv2 0.100 / 0.849 at 0.675s; TabICL 0.105 / 0.846; tree baselines (CatBoost, XGBoost, ExtraTrees, RandomForest) at 0.309–0.716 normalized log-loss. Context-scaling test (fixed nte=1024, m=32, C=10; ntr from 512 to 28,672 rows) shows SOMTab with the lowest runtime at every length and growing advantage, with memory crossing below attention baselines as quadratic attention memory dominates; at small contexts SOMTab uses slightly more memory. Ablation (20K-step budget, 15 TALENT datasets where SOMTab trails TabICLv2): DCH-TailMix beats a Cauchy-graph prior and a TabICL-style 70/30 MLP-SCM/tree-SCM mixture at every checkpoint (5K–20K); a Mamba-reader variant is consistently worse than the attention reader. Baselines are current and strong (TabICLv2, TabPFNv2 are the frontier), run under a common pipeline. Notable honest framing: the accuracy gap to full TabICLv2 (0.054 vs 0.029 normalized log-loss) is real and the paper presents this as a trade-off, not a win. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (SOMTab — a hybrid set-to-order Mamba/attention allocation for tabular ICL) plus a partial NEW METHOD contribution in the DCH-TailMix prior. The genuinely novel element is the stage-selective attention allocation instantiated through the set-to-order latent-slot mechanism; the ingredients themselves (Perceiver/Set Transformer latent slots, Mamba-2, PFN pretraining, degree-corrected graph priors, heavy-tailed bias sampling) are all established, so the contribution is a new and reasonably well-motivated combination applied to a setting (tabular ICL) where it had not been tested, not a new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present but shallow: the controlled prior/reader comparison uses a 20K-step budget versus 400K steps for the main model, on a 15-dataset subset selected post hoc where SOMTab underperforms — reasonable for stress-testing weaknesses, but it leaves the prior claim unvalidated at full scale and no component sweep for Kv, Ks, Lv, Ls, or depth. Timing reports medians of three repeats with a warmup; no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for accuracy metrics. No code, data, or model weights are mentioned as released — a major reproducibility gap given the pretraining cost (~23 GPU-days on 4×A100). Evaluation is largely on TALENT with the TabArena comparison explicitly flagged as not hardware-matched (public baselines on H100, SOMTab on H200/A100), which the authors treat as contextual rather than a speed ranking — appropriately cautious. No Goodhart-style train-on-test contamination is apparent (pretraining is fully synthetic), but the ablation subset selection introduces a mild selection-effect concern. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model benchmarked on public tabular suites). - Practical: Runs on commodity A100/H200 GPUs for both training and inference; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: 0.019s per 1K context samples versus 0.463s for default TabICLv2 (~24× faster) and 0.151s for single-estimator TabICLv2 (~8×), with 28.6M parameters and float32 training; memory grows linearly in representation but the retained attention reader is still O(n_tr²). - Effective: Evidence shows a genuine efficiency–accuracy Pareto point, but not problem-solving parity — normalized log-loss is ~2× TabICLv2's, so it solves the cost problem better than the accuracy problem. - Scalable: Tested to 28,672 context rows on synthetic data and full TALENT; beyond that, linear-representation scaling is measured but the quadratic reader cost is unaddressed, and real-data scaling beyond TALENT/TabArena is untested. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, checkpoint, or dataset artifact is stated as released. Strengths: (1) The architectural decomposition into representation construction vs. query-context matching is a clean, transferable design principle, and the set-to-order mechanism is a concrete, correct-looking solution to the order-invariance barrier that otherwise blocks Mamba on tables. (2) The runtime/memory scaling study is the right experiment for the claim being made — it isolates architecture (single estimator), fixes confounds, and shows the gap widening with context length rather than a single-point speedup. (3) The Mamba-reader ablation directly tests the paper's central hypothesis rather than only the full system: representation stages tolerate state-space mixing, the final ICL stage does not. (4) Honest accounting of the accuracy gap to TabICLv2 and of the non-hardware-matched TabArena comparison; the paper claims a trade-off, not superiority. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that SOMTab only "approaches" rather than matches strong Transformer baselines (visible in every table), that memory is slightly higher than attention baselines at small context, that the TabArena runtime comparison is confounded by GPU generation (H100 baselines vs. H200/A100 measurements), that the ablation uses a non-representative 15-dataset subset chosen where SOMTab trails, and that the ablation covers early training only. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No ablation of the core architectural hyperparameters — Kv, Ks, Lv, Ls, and the readback mechanism — so it is unclear how sensitive the result is to the specific latent-slot bottleneck (Kv=64 vs. m features is a large compression; what happens at 64 slots vs. 16?). (2) No code or checkpoint release is stated, making the 23-GPU-day model effectively unverifiable. (3) The Mamba-reader result is confounded by training budget: a 20K-step early checkpoint may under-detect a Mamba reader that needs longer to converge, and the authors do not test this. (4) Evaluation is classification-only; regression, which TabPFNv2 and TabICLv2 support, is absent, limiting the claimed generality of the "attention allocation" principle. (5) The scaling study uses synthetic data, and the memory crossover point on real TALENT datasets (where feature counts vary widely) is not shown. (6) The claim that attention is "most valuable for query-context matching" would be strengthened by testing other linear operators (e.g., linear attention, cross-covariance) in the reader; only Mamba is tried, so the conclusion may be Mamba-specific rather than a general property. Bottom Line: This is a credible, honestly-reported architectural exploration that establishes a real efficiency–accuracy Pareto point for tabular foundation models and would genuinely inform anyone designing the next generation of them, but with a meaningful accuracy gap to TabICLv2, no released artifact, and ablations confined to early training, practitioners seeking a deployable model should stay with existing frontier models while researchers building efficient ICL architectures should read it.

DeliveryBench: Can Agents Earn Profit in Simulated Worlds?

L Mao, J Ren, J Chen, Z Ma, K Zhou, L Qin · openreview.net · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DeliveryBench, a city-scale embodied benchmark in which VLM agents act as food-delivery couriers in procedurally generated 3D cities and must maximize hourly net profit under spatial, temporal, resource, physical, economic, and social constraints. - Why it's important: Existing embodied benchmarks evaluate short-horizon subtasks (typically ~6–25 action steps) and omit economic and social constraints, so there is no standard testbed for the long-horizon, self-sustaining decision-making that real autonomous agents would need. - How it does it: It instantiates a constrained long-horizon optimization problem (maximize E[income − cost] over feasible policies) in an Unreal-Engine city built on SimWorld, with dynamic order pools, a thermodynamic food-quality model, transportation mode trade-offs, and multi-agent competition/cooperation structures. - The good: The human-versus-model comparison is substantive and diagnostic: humans earn over $50/hour across city sizes while the best model (Gemini-2.5-Pro) earns $38.2–$45.1/hour and several open-source models lose money (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B at −$2.7/h in large cities), with fine-grained metrics pinpointing failures in parallel-order exploitation and proactive resource management. - The missing: The human baseline rests on only three participants, the headline claim of a large human–agent gap is therefore estimated from n=3, and the GPT-4o-as-judge personality analysis has no validation against human judgment. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or benchmarking embodied/planning agents who needs a constraint-dense, economically grounded evaluation environment; skippable if you only care about model architectures, since the agent design itself is a standard perception–planning–action loop.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (68) and Impact (70) are the strongest dimensions — the benchmark is publicly released, the honest negative results (overplanning costs Claude money, ACE hurting Qwen, RL converging to a greedy routine) are credibility positives, and the economic coupling of every constraint to a single profit scalar is a well-executed benchmark-design move (Novelty 62 for a new benchmark, not a new method). The composite is pulled down by Rigor (55) and Resilience (52): the headline human-agent gap rests on n=3 participants with no variance estimate, the personality analysis uses a single zero-shot GPT-4o judge with no agreement study, main tables lack error bars, and fixed order-generation seeds mean the reported run-to-run variance understates true stochasticity — all claims that would buckle under adversarial questioning despite the useful diagnostic decomposition. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*63 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*52 + 0.10*70 = 60.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The authors target the gap between what current embodied benchmarks measure and what real-world autonomous agents would face. Benchmarks like ALFRED (~12 steps), ALFWorld (~6 steps), and VirtualHome (~9 steps) score short instruction-following episodes and largely lack time, resource, economic, and social constraints; even longer-horizon platforms (CookBench, >100 steps) miss several constraint dimensions. The motivating question is whether VLM-based agents can make and execute plans that genuinely improve financial outcomes over multi-hour horizons — a proxy for agents that could sustain themselves economically. Food delivery is chosen as the task domain because it really exists, naturally carries a long-term objective (net profit over hours), and forces simultaneous management of deadlines, vehicle battery, stamina, cash, perishable goods, and interaction with other couriers and customers. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat economic self-sufficiency — maximizing net profit P = E_base + E_rating − C subject to a feasible policy set Π_C — as the primary benchmark objective, and to realize it in a simulator where every constraint dimension is mechanistically coupled to profit (e.g., a discrete heat-exchange model determines whether ice cream melts; a stamina/hospital model charges $5 and 30 idle minutes for collapse; odor transfer between food items in a shared bag degrades ratings). This coupling turns abstract 'constraint-aware planning' into a single measurable scalar (hourly net profit) plus diagnostic decomposition, which is what distinguishes the benchmark from prior urban simulators that offer static scenes without interactive consequences. Methodology: The benchmark is built on SimWorld (NeurIPS 2025) in Unreal Engine, with nine procedurally generated cities across three difficulty tiers (small: 11–15 roads; medium: 16–25; large: 26–30), each populated with restaurants, stores, rest areas, car rentals, hospitals, charging stations, and a single bus route. Episodes last 2 virtual hours or 300 API calls; the simulator pauses world dynamics during model inference to remove latency bias. The agent's formulation is a constrained MDP-style objective: π*ᵢ ∈ argmax over Π_C of E_πᵢ[P], where income combines base salary and rating-based bonuses (±$3 bonus above 3 stars, $2 penalty below). Physical dynamics include a discrete heat-exchange update (equations for air-node and per-item temperature with exchange coefficient α = Δt/τ_ex clipped to ≤0.5), a fragility accumulation score for fragile items under vibration, and odor-mixing dynamics. The evaluated agent follows a perception–planning–execution loop consuming global map, local map, first-person view, and auxiliary queries; it outputs (action, updated plan) conditioned on recent-action memory, the previous plan, and the last failure signal — a lightweight plan-and-execute scheme rather than a new algorithm. Three critical design decisions: (1) waypoint-based navigation delegating path planning to the simulator — justified, since their own ablation shows agents complete zero orders with only low-level step/turn actions; (2) pausing the world during reasoning — pragmatic but acknowledged as unrealistic (listed as future work toward real-time reasoning); (3) a 30-action discrete space mixing high-level commands (MOVE TO), low-level control, resource management, and social actions — reasonable breadth but the action semantics are simulator-mediated rather than physically grounded. Key Results: Nine models (six closed: GPT-5, GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Grok-4, Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro; three open: Qwen2.5-VL-72B/32B, LLaMA-3.2-90B-Vision) were evaluated over eight runs per map. Headline: humans (n=3) average >$50/h on all city sizes ($63.6 small, $51.5 medium, $55.4 large) versus Gemini-2.5-Pro at $45.1/$42.1/$38.2 and most models under $30/h; open-source models go negative in large cities. Diagnostic decomposition shows humans achieve TimeEff 2.90 vs. ≤1.21 for all models, and Prevention ratios of 0.91 vs. 0.53–0.88, while models incur >1 interruption/hour and food/customer ratings stay low (e.g., GPT-5: 3.93/3.96 vs. human 4.29/4.06). Multi-agent results (8 instances on a 20-road map across 1×1/8×1/4×2/2×4/1×8 structures) show most models profit-decline in multi-agent settings and peak in pairs; per-agent profit falls with team size (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Pro: $40.6 → $24.5 from 1×1 to 1×8). Context engineering helps strong models (GPT-5 with Dynamic Cheatsheet: $27.3 → $36.2; Claude-3.7 with DC: $31.7 → $44.5) but not weak ones (Qwen2.5-VL-72B with ACE drops to $0.1). On LLaVA-OneVision-8B, SFT on raw human actions hurts (−$7.2 → −$7.8) while GPT-4o-annotated SFT helps (→ $3.2, with TimeEff 1.51 exceeding GPT-5's), and VAGEN-style RL reaches $14.4 but converges to a greedy single-order routine. A greedy rule-based baseline earns $10.1/h on medium cities, below GPT-5 ($26.5) and humans ($51.5). Baseline models are current frontier systems as of late 2025; the human sample is the weak point of the comparison set. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (primarily) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (secondarily). The genuinely novel elements are the profit-as-objective framing with six mechanistically coupled constraint families, the food thermodynamics/odor/fragility model, and the multi-agent competitive/cooperative team structures. The agent architecture, SFT/RL pipeline, and context-engineering baselines (ACE, Dynamic Cheatsheet, VAGEN) are standard existing techniques applied to the new setting; the simulator itself extends the authors' prior SimWorld platform rather than introducing new simulation technology. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: plan-vs-no-plan (planning raises GPT-5 from $8.6 to $27.3 but Claude's profit drops from $31.7 to $19.2 due to overplanning expenses — an honest negative result), waypoint ablation, and the greedy heuristic baseline. Variance is partially addressed: eight runs per map with fixed seeds, run-to-run standard deviations for two models (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash profit $28.46 ± 2.52), and a three-condition difficulty robustness check showing rank stability. Missing: error bars or per-model variance in the main tables, no significance testing across the nine-model comparisons, and no variance estimate for the three-person human baseline. Code, data, and benchmark are stated as publicly available at deliverybench.github.io. Methodological concerns: (1) the personality/behavioral-style analysis uses GPT-4o as a zero-shot judge over six subjective dimensions with no inter-rater or human-agreement validation; (2) the human baseline's small sample means the headline gap's magnitude is uncertain, though its direction is not in doubt; (3) all evaluation is on the authors' own benchmark — unavoidable for a new benchmark but meaning the claimed 'short-sightedness' finding cannot be cross-checked against an external task suite. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus experiments; the artifact is the environment and evaluation suite). - Practical: Runs on standard API access (OpenRouter) plus an Unreal-Engine simulator; usable by any lab with API budget, no special hardware required for the evaluation harness. - Efficient: Episodes cap at 300 API calls per 2-hour virtual episode; cost is dominated by VLM inference over multi-view prompts — not reported in dollars, but the call cap bounds it by design. - Effective: The evidence supports the stated diagnostic goal — the fine-grained metrics localize the human–agent gap to temporal parallelization and proactive resource management — though 'profit' here is a simulated proxy whose fidelity to real courier economics (surge pricing, multi-platform work, real traffic) is unverified. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 30-road cities, 8 concurrent agents, and 2-hour episodes; the authors themselves flag real-time (non-paused) reasoning as unsolved and defer it to future work, so any extrapolation to longer horizons or larger agent populations is unvalidated. The work delivers a software artifact: a publicly released simulator, benchmark, and evaluation suite (deliverybench.github.io), plus a small human-trajectory SFT dataset (1,627 annotated pairs). Strengths: - The economic-coupling design is the real contribution: every constraint (heat exchange, odor mixing, stamina collapse, battery drain) is wired into a single profit scalar with explicit formulas, which makes failures diagnosable rather than anecdotal — most prior benchmarks cannot decompose a score this way. - Honest negative and mixed results strengthen credibility: Claude earning less with planning enabled due to overplanning, ACE hurting Qwen2.5-VL-72B, RL converging to a greedy routine, and SFT on raw actions degrading performance are all reported rather than buried. - The multi-agent finding that per-agent profit peaks in pairs and declines with team size despite rising communication frequency is a genuinely non-obvious empirical result with implications for agent-team design. - The three-tier difficulty robustness check (varying charging fees, rewards, battery drain) showing rank stability of agents is an evaluation-hygiene practice rarely seen in benchmark papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge (Appendix A) that the simulator pauses during model thinking — a significant departure from real-time embodied decision-making — and that current RL only induces basic delivery workflows, not advanced strategies like proactive recharging or order parallelization. They also note in the ablations that agents cannot navigate at all without the waypoint scaffolding. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The human baseline is n=3, yet the headline narrative ('agents lag far behind humans') quantifies the gap against this tiny sample; no demographic or expertise information about the participants is given, and no variance for human performance is reported. - The planning-style/personality analysis (GPT-5 'adventurous', Claude 'conservative', Gemini 'careless') rests entirely on GPT-4o-as-judge with a single prompt, no agreement study, and possible bias since GPT-4o is itself one of the evaluated models' family. - Weather is fixed to sunny at 22°C across all evaluations despite the paper advertising Unreal weather control as a realism feature, so the 'physical dynamics' dimension is exercised only through the food model, not environmental variation. - Single-seed order generation per map (fixed random seeds for identical orders across runs) aids comparability but means all eight runs per map share the same order draws; order-pool stochasticity across runs is not captured in the reported variance. - Only medium-map multi-agent results are reported (one map, one configuration grid); the interaction between city size and multi-agent coordination is unexplored. - Model access temperature is fixed at 0 and GPT-5 is run at 'minimal' reasoning effort — reasonable for cost control, but the sensitivity of the human-gap conclusion to reasoning-effort settings is not examined. Bottom Line: This is the strongest current testbed for evaluating long-horizon, economically grounded embodied agent behavior, and practitioners building planning or multi-agent systems will get real diagnostic value from it — but the human-gap headline should be quoted with the caveat of a three-person baseline, and the personality findings should be treated as suggestive until validated by human raters.

AUSO: Action-Level Unified Skill Optimization from Internalization to Utilization

H Lin, C Huang, T Gao, T Huang, D Liu, T Li, X Sun… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AUSO, a progressive reinforcement learning framework that unifies skill internalization and skill utilization for LLM agents by reweighting GRPO updates per action using a Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) information-gain signal computed between skill-conditioned and skill-free action distributions. - Why it's important: Existing hybrid skill methods (e.g., Skill0.5) route training objectives at the trajectory level using noisy success-rate thresholds, mislabeling samples near the boundary and applying uniform importance to all actions in a trajectory, which limits both learning efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization of long-horizon agents. - How it does it: The core move is a single counterfactual information operator — JSD between the policy's action distribution with and without skill conditioning at each visited state, requiring no extra environment rollouts — used as a weighted distillation signal in an early teacher-guided phase and as an advantage-modulation weight (gated by p(1-p) rollout variance) in a later utilization phase, all on top of a persistent GRPO backbone. - The good: Consistent gains over the strongest baseline Skill0.5 across three benchmarks under one shared backbone (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), with the largest improvements in OOD settings: WebShop OOD 51.2 vs 40.6, ALFWorld OOD 67.9 vs 58.5, and per-component ablations confirming each module contributes. - The missing: All results are single-run with no error bars, significance tests, or multiple seeds, and only one 7B backbone is tested, so the margin over Skill0.5 (e.g., 1.2 points on ALFWorld ID) cannot be distinguished from run-to-run variance; the stage-ratio and gate hyperparameter K are also selected using the evaluation benchmarks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building skill-based or credit-assignment-aware agentic RL post-training pipelines who want a concrete alternative to trajectory-level routing, but skippable if you only need a production recipe — the evidence is preprint-grade and confined to one small model and three academic environments.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents solving long-horizon interactive tasks (embodied households, web shopping, search-based QA) must decide when procedural knowledge (skills) should guide each action. Prior paradigms either fully externalize skills (retrieval noise, context overhead), fully internalize them (loss of controllability), or — in the hybrid case exemplified by Skill0.5 — route samples between internalization and utilization objectives using trajectory-level empirical success rates. The paper demonstrates empirically that these thresholds are noisy: many samples across ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA sit within one rollout unit of the medium/easy boundary yet receive different optimization objectives. The deeper limitation is granularity: trajectory-level rewards cannot reveal which individual actions benefit from skill conditioning and which are distracted by it, a credit-assignment problem at the actual granularity of agent decisions. Practitioners training agentic RL policies with reusable knowledge face this cost directly in training efficiency and generalization to unseen task categories. Key Idea: Measure skill influence per action as the JSD between the same policy's action distribution at the same visited state under skill-conditioned and skill-free contexts — a bounded, symmetric mutual-information estimator I(C; A|h) with uniform context prior — and use this action-level signal to modulate GRPO advantage magnitudes (preserving sign) so that skill-sensitive actions in successful trajectories get stronger reinforcement and in failed trajectories get stronger suppression. The same operator, instantiated with a privileged skill-conditioned teacher context, doubles as the internalization distillation weight, giving a unified information-theoretic treatment of both lifecycle phases. Methodology: AUSO runs on GRPO (group-normalized advantages, G=8 rollouts, lr 1e-6, 150 optimization steps) in three scheduled phases. (1) Early internalization: for task groups where all rollouts fail (zero GRPO advantage), a teacher distribution computed from the same model conditioned on general skills S_G supervises the skill-free student; token-level JSD over the top-k teacher tokens is averaged over each action span, z-normalized within the task group, passed through tanh and re-centering to give weights u_t ∈ [1-β_int, 1+β_int], yielding loss L_JSD = (1/N)Σ u_t D_t; the coefficient λ(s) ramps up then decays via SmoothStep. (2) Middle phase: plain GRPO. (3) Late utilization: for each visited state, I_t = JSD(π(·|h_t, Skill) ∥ π(·|h_t, No-skill)), standardized to m_t ∈ [-1,1], gated by g(p_q) = K·p_q(1-p_q) (justified in Appendix A.1 via variance analysis showing the precision of the success-failure information contrast is proportional to p_q(1-p_q)), producing weights w_t = 1 + β(s)g(p_q)m_t that multiply the GRPO advantage; the paper proves w_t preserves advantage sign and unit mean within groups. The full objective reduces continuously to GRPO when auxiliary signals vanish. Critical design decisions: JSD over KL for symmetry and boundedness (well-justified, Appendix A.3); top-k union plus tail-category support approximation (practical, small approximation risk unstated); the p_q = 0 indicator restricting teacher supervision to no-signal groups (plausible but the hard indicator itself reintroduces a threshold-like boundary the paper criticizes). Key Results: Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 4×H200 GPUs: WebShop averages 49.7 ID / 51.2 OOD vs Skill0.5's 40.4 / 40.6 (+9.3 / +10.6 points); ALFWorld 94.3 ID / 67.9 OOD vs Skill0.5's 93.1 / 58.5, with the OOD Pick2 task jumping from 33.3 to 54.2; SearchQA average 47.5 vs SkillRL 47.1, Skill1 44.7, Skill0.5 44.2, best on TriviaQA (64.7) and HotpotQA (44.0). Baselines include prompt-based (ReAct, Reflexion, ExpeL, Mem0), RL (RLOO, GRPO), memory-augmented RL (MemRL, EvolveR), and skill-augmented RL (SkillRL, Skill0, SLIM, Skill0.5) methods; the skill-augmented baselines are recent (2026 preprints) and current. Ablations on ALFWorld/WebShop show removing any component degrades performance (e.g., removing action-level internalization drops ALFWorld from 94.3/67.9 to 85.1/54.7). Stage ratio 2:5:3 beats 3:5:2 and equal splits; gate constant K peaks at 4. A notable unremarked result: WebShop OOD (51.2) exceeds WebShop ID (49.7), which the authors do not explain. Case studies show AUSO terminating SearchQA episodes in 2 steps vs Skill0.5's 4-step failure from over-answering. Scale is standard (7B model, three academic benchmarks), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING about the ambiguity of trajectory-level success-rate routing boundaries). The genuinely novel element is the unified action-level JSD information-gain operator serving both skill internalization (as weighted distillation) and utilization (as advantage modulation) within one progressive GRPO curriculum. The constituent techniques — GRPO, teacher-student distillation, curriculum scheduling, uncertainty gating, SmoothStep annealing — are standard; the contribution is their principled composition at action granularity, not any new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover all major components (action-level internalization, action-level utilization, adaptive increase/decrease schedules, uncertainty gate) and hyperparameter sensitivity for K and stage ratios is examined — a strength. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, despite several margins (ALFWorld ID: 94.3 vs 93.1) being within plausible run variance; the SearchQA margin over SkillRL is 0.4 points. Code is released at https://github.com/JordanSancholhz/Action-Skill. Methodological concerns: (1) hyperparameters K and the 2:5:3 stage ratio are selected by comparing ID/OOD evaluation performance on the same benchmarks used for headline results (Goodhart risk); (2) evaluation protocol and ID/OOD splits are inherited from Skill0.5, the direct predecessor and strongest baseline, so the comparison is well-matched but the ecosystem is a small chain of related preprints; (3) only one backbone model and one training budget (150 steps) are tested; (4) this is an arXiv preprint (2608.21292), not peer-reviewed, and several baselines it compares against (Skill0.5, Skill1, SKILL0) are themselves unpublished preprints, so reported baseline numbers are partly self-reproduced or carried over rather than independently verified. Deployability: EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: Yes — a 7B model trained on 4×H200 GPUs is within reach of most academic and commercial labs. Efficient: Training adds teacher/counterfactual forward passes per state (no extra environment rollouts) and top-k vocabulary JSD computation; at inference the internalized policy needs no skill prompts, reducing token cost relative to external-skill baselines — though no throughput or wall-clock numbers are reported. Effective: The evidence shows it improves success on the three tested benchmarks including OOD splits, but whether it solves the general 'when should skills guide an action' problem beyond these environments is untested. Scalable: Untested beyond 7B/150 steps; whether the JSD signal remains informative for larger models whose skill-free and skill-conditioned distributions differ less is an open claim. Delivers a software artifact (code repository); no trained model weights or skill banks are mentioned as released. Strengths: (1) The unified counterfactual JSD operator is a genuinely clean formulation — one bounded, symmetric, information-theoretic measure instantiated in two complementary ways — with the Appendix A.2 reduction proofs showing the whole framework degrades gracefully to GRPO, which is more principled than the heuristic loss-stacking common in this area. (2) The empirical demonstration that Skill0.5's success-rate-threshold routing has ambiguous boundaries (samples differing by ≤1/8 across the threshold) is a concrete, motivating diagnosis rather than a strawman. (3) The uncertainty gate g(p)=K·p(1-p) comes with an actual statistical derivation (precision of the success-failure contrast under homoscedastic approximation) rather than just intuition. (4) Well-matched baseline comparison: same backbone, rollout configuration, and optimization budget as Skill0.5, plus a controlled longer-training check and training-dynamics analysis (entropy, episode length) supporting the sample-efficiency claim. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: There is no dedicated limitations section. The authors acknowledge: (1) JSD measures whether skill conditioning changes a decision, not whether that change is beneficial — usefulness is deferred to the RL reward (Appendix A.3); (2) SearchQA does not support an ID/OOD partition, so it is evaluated under Skill0's original protocol instead; (3) performance is sensitive to the stage ratio and gate constant K (Fig. 4). They confront the JSD-benefit decoupling directly, which is a credibility positive, but they do not acknowledge variance/statistical concerns, single-backbone scope, or hyperparameter selection on evaluation sets. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The hard indicator I[p_q = 0] gating teacher supervision reintroduces exactly the kind of sharp empirical-threshold boundary the paper criticizes in Skill0.5, just moved to the p=0 edge — no analysis of sensitivity there. (2) WebShop OOD exceeding ID (51.2 vs 49.7) is anomalous and unexplained; it may indicate the OOD categories are easier or the split is favorable, warranting scrutiny. (3) The top-k + tail-support JSD approximation's error versus exact JSD is never quantified. (4) No inference-time cost comparison against external-skill baselines (the claimed token-efficiency benefit of internalization is asserted, not measured). (5) The ablation for stage ratios uses ID/OOD benchmark results, so the chosen configuration is fit to the test distribution. (6) The related work and baseline chain (Skill0, Skill0.5, Skill1, plus multiple cited preprints) is heavily populated by the authors' own collaboration network, so the narrative of paradigm gaps should be read with that self-referential framing in mind. (7) Single seed throughout means the 0.4-point SearchQA margin over SkillRL and the 1.2-point ALFWorld ID margin over Skill0.5 should be treated as unconfirmed. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on agentic RL post-training with skill or knowledge conditioning will gain a concrete, well-reasoned alternative to trajectory-level routing that is worth implementing and stress-testing, but the single-seed, single-model, preprint-grade evidence means the headline gains — especially the sub-point margins — need independent replication before being trusted over simply training Skill0.5 longer.

Kang Liao, Yihang Luo, Xiao-Ming Wu, Linyi Jin, Size Wu, Chunyu Lin, Yao Zhao, Fei Wang, Wei Li, Chen Change Loy · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Puffin-World, a unified multimodal model that jointly performs absolute camera perception (roll, pitch, vertical FoV), camera-controllable text-to-image generation, and multi-view 3D world generation with per-view depth reconstruction inside a single LLM-plus-diffusion network, and releases a 16M-sample camera-grounded dataset. - Why it's important: Existing generative world models control cameras only in relative terms and treat the world as RGB, so trajectories drift from real-world orientation (gravity, uprightness) under rotation and long horizons; skip it if you need only single-image calibration (GeoCalib-class tools) or appearance-first video world models with mature baselines.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building spatial intelligence and physical-AI systems need a model that can recover where the camera is in the physical world, simulate new viewpoints, and reconstruct 3D structure — today these are separate systems. Generative world models (CameraCtrl, ViewCrafter, CAT3D-style multi-view diffusion) generate appearance conditioned on relative pose but have no global physical anchor, so the same relative trajectory can yield different absolute orientations, causing horizon tilt and drift under extreme rotation or long horizons. Unified multimodal models (Chameleon, Janus, Show-o) couple understanding and generation but only for 2D semantics. Meanwhile, training data for 3D is thin: most trajectory datasets restrict roll to ±5° and pitch to ±10° and almost none provide absolute camera orientation. Puffin-World targets the researchers who need all three capabilities — perception, simulation, reconstruction — from one model grounded in a persistent physical frame. Key Idea: Make camera physics a first-class, per-pixel conditioning signal rather than a 6-DoF pose vector or a language string. The Omni-Camera representation densely concatenates a gravity-anchored absolute field (pixel-wise up-vector and latitude angle) with the relative Plücker ray map, so one signal supports both single-view text-to-image control and cross-view trajectory generation. The enabling trick for trajectories is physics propagation: the model perceives the reference view's absolute orientation (roll, pitch, FoV) through its own understanding branch, then propagates the gravity vector to every future view via the known relative rotations (g_t = R_rel t←0 g_0), rendering each view's absolute field analytically. This converts an absolute-world grounding problem into a closed-form rotation, avoiding orientation drift without extra modules. Methodology: The architecture follows the unified-LLM-plus-diffusion-decoder recipe (Transfusion/BLIP3-o style): a geometry-aligned vision encoder (C-RADIOv3/v4-H) and LLM (Qwen2.5-7B for Base, 1.5B for Pro) handle autoregressive understanding; LLM hidden states are projected via 64 learnable queries and a 6-layer connector into conditioning for an MMDiT diffusion backbone (SD3.5-Medium 2.5B / Large 8.1B) trained with a flow-matching objective. Three unifications organize the design: (i) appearance and depth share one frozen VAE, with depth encoded as an RGB image via an invertible 3D Hilbert-curve color mapping; (ii) perception and generation share the same LLM; (iii) tasks are selected by input composition plus a 4-channel role mask. Critical design decisions: (1) the Omni-Camera map is fused additively into the noisy latent before patch embedding and re-injected at sparse transformer layers, zero-initialized to preserve the pretrained generator — pixel-aligned injection replacing Puffin's 3-channel VAE-encoded perspective field, justified only qualitatively; (2) depth latents are trained with a separately weighted, time-ramped loss (ω ramping 0→1 over 3,000 iterations) plus asymmetric attention (appearance/text cannot attend to geometry tokens) and a zero-initialized geometry embedding — two safeguards to protect a converged appearance model, sensible but un-ablated; (3) long horizons are handled by chunked autoregression where the carried-over view is passed as a latent, avoiding compounding VAE artifacts. Training is four stages (alignment → single-view SFT → multi-view post-training → joint appearance-geometry), with physics fields for training data pre-computed offline by the Stage-II perception model. There is no explicit objective beyond flow matching plus cross-entropy for the LLM; note that the "physics" state is only gravity and latitude — no dynamics. Key Results: Calibration: best median error on all four benchmarks — Stanford2D3D roll 0.29° / AUC@5° 97.4 (GeoCalib: 0.40° / 91.8), MegaDepth roll 0.28°, TartanAir roll 0.31° / pitch 0.67°, LaMAR roll 0.26°, beating GeoCalib, UVP, ParamNet, CTRL-C, and prior Puffin; it also beats the FoV-specialist AnyCalib on most benchmarks. Camera-controllable generation on the authors' new Puffin-Cam-Bench (600 prompts): 0.96° mean up-vector error and FID 75.93, versus PreciseCam 13.37°/90.89, Puffin 3.86°/80.29, and general generators (GPT Image2, Nano Banana 2, FLUX.2-dev, Qwen-Image2-Pro, Z-Image) at 24-29° error and FID 90-99. 3D world generation: on RealEstate10K (50 held-out clips) PSNR 17.22 / LPIPS 0.318, marginally ahead of MVGenMaster (17.11, which trained on RealEstate10K eval data) and SEVA (17.94 SSIM-best); on the self-built Puffin-Traj-Bench (100 clips), PSNR 18.00 with roll error 0.80° / AUC@1° 0.57 versus SEVA's 1.35°/0.38. The single ablation shows physics propagation improves average PSNR 19.87→20.54 and reduces roll/pitch calibration error on rotated trajectories. Fidelity gains on standard benchmarks are modest; the large margins are in control accuracy, and the strongest evidence comes partly from author-defined benchmarks. Tested scale: 8-view sequences at 640×640, models up to ~8.1B diffusion backbone; preprint, not peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (native physics/geometry/appearance world states with absolute-anchored camera conditioning) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (Puffin-16M with ±45° roll/pitch and 0-360° yaw trajectories, plus 44.5M absolute-camera annotations of 28 public datasets), with an ENGINEERING component (unified system). Genuinely novel: the physics-propagation mechanism and the demonstration that one network can close the loop across perception, generation, and reconstruction without external modules. Standard combination: Omni-Camera is a channel-wise concatenation of two established dense representations (Perspective Fields, Plücker rays); the backbone, flow matching, depth-as-image encoding, and LLM-diffusion unification are all existing techniques applied to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak ablation coverage: exactly one ablation (physics propagation, Table 6) against the many design decisions introduced (latent-space injection, re-injection layers, Hilbert depth encoding, asymmetric attention, loss ramping, latent-space chunk carryover). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere. Two evaluation-integrity concerns: (1) camera-control accuracy on generated frames is measured by re-estimating parameters with Puffin-World's own perception branch — applied uniformly to all baselines, but a model-centric metric invites Goodhart effects and would not detect shared perceptual biases; (2) the headline generation benchmark (Puffin-Cam-Bench) and rotation benchmark (Puffin-Traj-Bench) are self-built, though the calibration evaluation on four public benchmarks excludes Stanford2D3D from training, which is a credibility positive. The 44.5M public-dataset annotations and the dense depth labels (DA3 predictions aligned to sparse GT) are model-generated and unverified against human measurement. Positively, the authors state code, model weights, and datasets are fully released (project page: kangliao929.github.io/projects/puffin-world/ and /puffin-16m), which if accurate makes this among the more reproducible unified world-model efforts. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built and evaluated model system). Practical: Yes — it is assembled entirely from open components (SD3.5, Qwen2.5, C-RADIO), so it runs on high-end commodity GPUs, though the Pro variant's 8.1B diffusion backbone plus LLM is not consumer-hardware territory. Efficient: Not quantified — no inference latency, FLOPs, or memory comparison against baselines is reported; physics propagation is pre-computed offline for training, which caps its cost. Effective: The evidence shows it solves camera control (sub-degree errors) and joint reconstruction, but visual fidelity is only comparable to, not clearly better than, existing multi-view generators (RealEstate10K PSNR 17.22 vs. 17.11), so the appearance-quality claim rests largely on qualitative results. Scalable: Long-horizon exploration via chunked latent carryover is demonstrated qualitatively; drift behavior over very long horizons is claimed mitigated but not measured at 10× the 8-view training scale. The work delivers concrete artifacts: code, model weights (Base/Pro/Caption variants), Puffin-16M, and the 44.5M-image annotation release — not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The physics-propagation idea is a genuinely simple and well-motivated solution to a real failure mode (absolute-orientation drift in relative-pose world models), and the one ablation that exists supports it with consistent gains across roll, pitch, and yaw. (2) Real system-level unification, not a paper claim: understanding, single-view generation, multi-view generation, and depth reconstruction all run through one network with task selection by input composition, enabling closed-loop behaviors (self-calibrated exploration) that per-task pipelines cannot express. (3) Puffin-16M fills a documented data gap — existing 3D datasets confine roll to ±5°/pitch to ±10°, while this provides 1M trajectories with ±45° rotation and 360° yaw plus 15M labeled triplets at multiple aspect ratios. (4) The calibration results are strong against current, specialized baselines on standard public benchmarks, not just author-built ones. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge only briefly, in the conclusion, that the framework is limited to static scenes, restricted horizon lengths, and a narrow physics state (gravity and latitude only), naming dynamic scenes and richer physical states as future work. There is no dedicated limitations section, and the circular camera-evaluation scheme and unverified annotation quality are not confronted; this is a paper that minimizes rather than directly engages its limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The evaluation metric for the headline claim (camera-control accuracy) is produced by the model being evaluated, and no independent verification (e.g., off-the-shelf GeoCalib scoring, or human judgment of horizon alignment) is provided. (2) Dense depth supervision for real-world data is partly DA3-generated, so the reconstruction branch may inherit a specific depth model's biases — an unexamined teacher-student loop. (3) No quantitative comparison against 3D-native baselines such as CAT3D or Gen3C on the 3D modeling task; the comparison set is camera-controlled video generators. (4) Only one ablation despite at least six load-bearing design decisions; the choice of additive injection over alternatives is argued, not measured. (5) The Pro variant uses a 1.5B LLM while Base uses 7B — an unexplained asymmetry that undermines the "scaling" narrative in the title. (6) The 44.5M annotations released as a community resource are self-labeled with no reported accuracy audit on out-of-domain imagery. (7) The "physics" branding overstates scope: the model captures static gravity/latitude, not dynamics, forces, or object physics. (8) The fidelity comparison on RealEstate10K is confounded by MVGenMaster's noted training overlap with the benchmark. Bottom Line: For researchers building camera-grounded or unified world models, this is worth reading for the physics-propagation idea, the unified perception-generation-reconstruction demonstration, and the released rotation-diverse dataset — but single-task practitioners (calibration, novel-view synthesis) already have stronger specialized tools, and the paper's headline numbers lean on self-referential metrics and self-built benchmarks more than the breadth of results suggests.
