TL;DR - What it does: This survey introduces a three-way taxonomy of knowledge-localization claims in language models — representational (R: information can be read out from few units), causal (C: interventions on few units change behavior), and editable (E: restricted native-parameter updates change knowledge) — and reclassifies ~96 papers at the level of individual claims rather than whole papers. - Why it's important: The literature contains apparently contradictory answers to "is knowledge localized?" (knowledge neurons and mid-layer MLP loci vs. distributed, redundant pathways), and this confusion propagates into model editing and machine unlearning, where practitioners assume a causal locus is the right place to edit or unlearn. - How it does it: The core move is definitional disambiguation: the paper argues evidence supports one notion only under a specified unit system, representation system, budget/counting rule, and measurement instrument, and it maps which cross-notion inferences are licensed (mostly none without direct comparative evidence). - The good: The synthesis organizes scattered dissociation results into a coherent "dissociation triangle" — e.g., Hase et al. show causal-tracing scores do not predict best edit layers (C≠E), Sharma & Le show demographic information is encoded early but causally influential late (R≠C), and R↔E is almost entirely untested — giving the field a concrete, checkable map of evidential gaps. - The missing: The survey runs no experiments of its own (not even a small joint R/C/E measurement on one model), so its central thesis — that the three notions dissociate under matched budgets — is assembled from heterogeneous studies rather than demonstrated in a controlled comparison. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone doing model editing, unlearning, or mechanistic interpretability who needs to justify which localization claim their method actually supports; skip it if you already know the Hase et al., Niu et al., and Makelov et al. critiques and want only new empirical results.

Problem & Motivation: Researchers studying LLM interpretability, model editing, and unlearning face a literature that gives conflicting answers about where knowledge resides. Some works report compact loci (knowledge neurons, mid-layer MLPs amenable to rank-one edits); others report superposition, polysemantic neurons, redundant non-contiguous retrieval pathways, and the finding that random-head interventions can match localization-selected ones. The survey's position is that much of this apparent disagreement is definitional: "Is knowledge localized?" conflates three distinct evidential properties (R, C, E), and evidence for one is routinely over-interpreted as evidence for the others. Prior surveys treat localization as a subsection of knowledge editing, mechanistic interpretability, or unlearning; none classifies claims by the logical type of evidence presented. Key Idea: The key insight is that a localization claim is only well-posed relative to five components — knowledge target (with evaluation distribution), model description (units and representation system), localization notion (R/C/E), measurement instrument, and budget with an explicit counting rule — and that cross-notion inference (e.g., from causal-tracing scores to edit-site selection, or from SAE sparse decodability to causal necessity) is an empirical question, not a entailment. This is a NEW FORMULATION contribution, not a method: the paper's deliverables are the taxonomy, a claim-level evidence map (Table A1, 96 papers, 79 with localization labels), a "dissociation triangle" showing evidence is strong for C–E dissociation, moderate for R–C, and weakest for R–E, and a measurement checklist plus seven open problems (joint measurement, description-robust localization theory, beyond-item-level localization, provenance-vs-internal localization, localization-aware unlearning, emergence during training, instrument calibration). Methodology: This is a survey; the methodology is corpus compilation and claim-level coding, not experiments. The paper defines each notion formally: representational localization holds when a readout restricted to S ⊆ U predicts the target on held-out evaluation distribution D_K versus controls; causal localization holds when interventions on S produce specified counterfactual changes in the behavioral score m_K(f); editable localization holds when an update Δθ confined to a parameter region meets efficacy, generalization, and locality criteria (including ripple-effect consistency). Sections 3–5 review evidence per notion (neuron-level encoding and SAEs including the "SAE-skeptic wave" of random-baseline and identifiability critiques for R; causal tracing, circuit discovery, task/function vectors, and DAS for C; ROME/MEMIT-style locate-then-edit, hypernetwork editors, and external-memory editors for E). Section 6 synthesizes pairwise dissociations and attributes them to three sources: model description (superposition makes sparsity coordinate-dependent), knowledge target (paraphrases shift loci; entity vs. relation knowledge differ), and measurement instrument (patching protocol choices, subspace-intervention illusions, editing-criterion choice). Design decisions that are well-justified: coding claims rather than papers, and refusing to label findings as localized/distributed without specifying notion and budget. Weakly justified: no quantitative meta-analysis, no systematic inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond "examines knowledge localization in neural networks," and no inter-coder reliability reported for the 96-paper annotation. Key Results: As a survey, headline outputs are syntheses rather than measured numbers. The three most consequential reported findings: (1) Hase et al. (NeurIPS 2023) found causal-tracing localization scores poorly predict which MLP layer yields best editing success — layer identity was a stronger predictor than the localization score, directly undercutting locate-then-edit logic (ROME/MEMIT). (2) Sharma & Le (TMLR 2026) found demographic information is strongly encoded in early layers while causal influence concentrates in later layers, a matched R≠C demonstration. (3) Korznikov et al. found constrained random baselines match trained SAEs on several interpretability, sparse-probing, and causal-editing benchmarks. The paper also catalogs known editing failure modes: edits fail multi-hop propagation (MQuAKE), break relational consistency (RippleEdits), degrade general capabilities, and accumulate interference over sequential editing. The corpus spans BERT, GPT-2, LLaMA-2, Alpaca 7B, Claude 3 Sonnet, MoE, multimodal, and audio-language models. The R↔E pair is explicitly flagged as nearly devoid of direct comparative evidence. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the R/C/E taxonomy, claim-level coding, and the budget/units/instrument checklist) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in the weak sense of a documented synthesis (the uneven evidence distribution across the dissociation triangle). No new method, dataset, or system is introduced. The individual dissociation results are drawn from existing work; the genuine novelty is the observation that these results have never been jointly organized as cross-notion evidence gaps, and that much prior "contradiction" in the literature dissolves once claims are typed. It is a conceptual reframing of a known landscape, not a discovery of new structure in models. Rigor & Reproducibility: No experiments, ablations, seeds, or error bars apply — none are claimed. The appendix provides a 96-paper evidence table with per-claim notion labels, targets/units, instruments, and findings, which is the survey's main verifiable artifact; however, no annotation protocol, codebook release, inter-annotator agreement, or repository URL is stated, so the coding is not independently reproducible from the paper alone. Notable methodological strengths: the survey consistently distinguishes what an instrument measures from what authors of primary papers conclude (e.g., noting that causal tracing is presented by Meng et al. as one thing and ROME as another), and it flags Goodhart-style risks including SAE benchmark scores failing to track ground-truth feature recovery and patching-protocol sensitivity. Concerns: the corpus selection criteria are informal, coding of borderline papers (e.g., Wang & Veitch's blogpost-track piece) mixes peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed sources without differentiation in the evidence map, and the central claim that "evidence is uneven" is asserted from counts the paper never tabulates quantitatively. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL-adjacent survey (no primary experiments; a formal vocabulary and synthesis). - Sound: The formal definitions in Section 2 are internally consistent and explicitly conditional, but they are definitions, not theorems — no proofs or bounds are offered. - General: The taxonomy is stated broadly (any architecture, unit system, or budget), though all cited evidence comes from transformer LLMs and close relatives; generalization to other architectures is posed as open. - Tight: Not applicable — no bounds; the closest analogue (the dissociation triangle) is coarse (strong/some/weak evidence) rather than quantitative. - Implementable: The measurement checklist (Figure 2) is directly operationalizable as a reporting standard for future localization papers, and the joint-measurement open problem suggests a concrete experimental design; no follow-up operationalization exists yet. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form (a taxonomy, checklist, and evidence table). Strengths: - The claim-level (rather than paper-level) coding is a real methodological contribution for surveys in this space; it correctly handles papers like Meng et al. that bear on both C and E without conflating the two. - The dissociation triangle is a genuinely useful organizing device: it converts a vague "the literature disagrees" observation into three specific, testable pairwise hypotheses with an explicit statement of which pair (R–E) is under-studied. - The treatment of the SAE-skeptic wave (random-baseline parity, L0-sensitivity, compositional-shift failures, identifiability limits) is a current and balanced synthesis that many interpretability surveys omit. - The checklist forcing explicit budget/counting-rule specification addresses a real reproducibility defect in the primary literature, where budgets based on incomparable unit systems are treated as commensurable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that (i) no prior work has measured all three notions concurrently and rigorously, so the dissociations they describe are assembled from pairwise, unmatched studies; (ii) localization conclusions depend on representation system, target, and instrument, so the survey deliberately avoids labeling findings as localized or distributed; (iii) their synthesis covers dense text LLMs primarily, with MoE, multimodal, and audio settings only sketched (Section 7.3); and (iv) direct cross-notion evidence is scarce, so several triangle edges rest on single studies. They confront these limitations directly — the entire Section 6.4 and Section 8 are devoted to them — which is a credibility positive. They do not, however, explicitly acknowledge the absence of any quantitative tally of the evidence distribution or the lack of a released, auditable coding protocol. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No quantitative meta-analysis: the claim that evidence is "uneven" across R–C, C–E, R–E is never backed by counts, effect sizes, or model families, so the survey's central empirical assertion is itself qualitative. - The annotation procedure lacks inter-coder reliability, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and a release, making the 96-paper evidence map unverifiable. - The survey mixes peer-reviewed venues with blogposts (Transformer Circuits Thread), arXiv preprints, and workshop papers in one evidence table without confidence weighting, despite treating primary-source rigor as a theme. - The proposed remedy (joint matched-budget measurement) is stated as an open problem but not prototyped even at toy scale — a small synthetic demonstration would have substantially strengthened the taxonomy's practical force. - The R–E pair is declared under-tested, yet the survey does not identify why (e.g., lack of shared benchmarks between probing and editing communities) or propose a specific protocol, which limits how actionable the gap is. - Potential selection bias: several cited works (Sharma & Le, Hochman et al., Korznikov et al.) are 2026-dated and very recent; the evidence map may over-represent the critiques the authors favor relative to positive localization results. Bottom Line: This is the survey to hand to a new model-editing or interpretability researcher to inoculate them against cross-notion over-claiming, and its checklist is worth adopting as a reporting standard — but it is a preprint with no experiments, no quantitative meta-analysis, and no released coding, so specialists already familiar with the Hase, Niu, and SAE-skeptic results will find the framing useful and the content largely known.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PCoMoE, an MoE inference framework that decomposes each SwiGLU expert into expansion-side and projection-side operators and lets inference execute cross-expert compositions of these sub-operators, yielding up to 1.305× decode speedup and +2.87 points average zero-shot accuracy over matched fine-tuned baselines. - Why it's important: Existing MoE serving systems treat experts as atomic units, so all scheduling, caching, and pruning happens at a boundary that wastes both intra-expert computation and intra-expert redundancy; breaking that boundary expands the efficiency–quality trade-off space for every deployed MoE LLM. - How it does it: Each expert is split at the expansion/projection boundary into an n×n virtual path matrix; a learned per-layer compatibility bias matrix scores paths, iterative pruning shrinks the active path set, and a source-grouped execution engine computes each expansion-side operator once and reuses it across multiple projection targets. - The good: The design ablation is genuinely informative — frozen compatibility biases give 1.286× decode speedup but crater accuracy to 55.50 on Qwen1.5-MoE, while learned biases recover 73.70 with 1.238× speedup, cleanly demonstrating that learned path compatibility is the load-bearing component. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, the headline '+10% accuracy' in the abstract is not reconciled with the +5.8/+2.1/+2.5-point table gains, and the claimed accuracy improvement over fine-tuned vanilla MoE lacks a mechanistic explanation. - Read it or not: Worth reading for systems researchers and engineers building MoE inference runtimes who want to move past expert-atomic optimization; skippable for those seeking rigorous ML science, since the evaluation is single-run, five-benchmark, and single-GPU.

Problem & Motivation: Operators of MoE-based LLMs (Mixtral, Qwen-MoE, DeepSeek) face a gap between theoretical expert sparsity and real end-to-end latency: dynamic token-to-expert routing, dispatch, packing, and scattering overheads dominate, and existing accelerators (expert offloading like MoE-Infinity/HoBBIT, pruning like MoE-Pruner, sharing like ReXMoE/Xshare) all preserve the whole-expert abstraction. The authors profile that whole-expert reduction (top-k to top-(k−1)) has highly layer-dependent quality cost — e.g., reducing one expert across all layers raises Mixtral perplexity by 0.89 while 25% of layers cost only 0.14 — so inter-expert redundancy is non-homogeneous and depletes quickly when compounded. Meanwhile, inside each SwiGLU expert, the gate+up expansion side is two-thirds of expert FLOPs and tolerates cross-expert substitution better than the down-projection side (expansion-side substitution gives lower representation error in 23 of 32 Mixtral layers), exposing exploitable intra-expert structure that no prior framework touches. Key Idea: Reformulate an MoE layer's routing space from n experts to n×n compositional paths Pi,j(h) = Dj(Ui(h)) — expansion side of expert i composed with projection side of expert j — where diagonal paths reproduce vanilla experts exactly and off-diagonal paths are new, zero-parameter execution routes; then a factored gate score s_i,j(h) = g_base,i(h) + b_i,j + λ·g_tgt,j(h) with a learned compatibility bias matrix B, negative off-diagonal initialization, and iterative per-layer pruning confines execution to a compact high-value path subset, and source-grouped dispatch computes each active expansion operator once and fans it out to multiple projection targets. The asymmetry insight (expansion side is both compute-dense and structurally substitutable; projection side is neither) is what makes this middle granularity work where arbitrary operator splitting would not. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Path formulation: each expert e is decomposed into Ue(h) = SiLU(W_gate·h) ⊙ (W_up·h) and De(z) = W_down·z; the layer output generalizes to y = Σ β_i,j(h)·Dj(Ui(h)) over an active path set Π(h), which strictly contains vanilla MoE as the diagonal-only special case — no new weights or storage are introduced. (2) Compatibility-aware routing: a factored gating score combines the pretrained base router prior (frozen expert weights), a target-side prior, and a learned n×n bias matrix B initialized to zero on the diagonal and c+ε (c<0) off-diagonal; during LoRA fine-tuning (rank 16, 25K Alpaca+SQuAD examples, batch 32, expert weights frozen) B is iteratively hardened into a per-layer binary active mask with m_i,i = 1 always, pruning from layer 3 onward. (3) Execution: layer-static metadata (active paths, source/target layouts) is materialized offline; online routing is a fused masked top-k over the pruned set; source-grouped execution computes Ui(h) once per unique selected source i and dispatches to the projection targets Ti(h) — expansion evaluations scale with |S(h)| rather than |Π(h)|. Critical design decisions: the expansion/projection split point (justified by FLOP asymmetry and substitution-error profiling), diagonal-always-active fallback to vanilla behavior (justified as low-confidence safety, well-motivated), and layer-autonomous path density (empirically shown: first two Qwen MoE blocks stay dense, later layers compress to a mean 20.6% expansion-side arithmetic saving). Key Results: On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, PCoMoE raises the five-benchmark macro average (BoolQ, ARC-E, ARC-C, HellaSwag, WinoGrande) from 67.90 (vanilla) to 73.70 and from 70.83 (matched Vanilla-FT) to 73.70 (+2.87); on Mixtral-8x7B it reaches 79.97 (+1.61 over Vanilla-FT); on DeepSeek-V2-Lite 72.48 (+2.14). Against pruning baselines MoE-I2 (69.10 on Mixtral avg) and MoE-Pruner (71.80), PCoMoE's 79.97 is clearly ahead, though these baselines degrade badly relative to vanilla, making them relatively weak comparators; MoEITS (78.02 on Mixtral) is the closest competitor and PCoMoE beats it by 1.95 points. Speedup on an NVIDIA H20: 1.305× decode (26.50→34.58 tok/s on Mixtral) and 1.294× end-to-end (133.43→172.72 tok/s); prefill is unchanged by design. Execution ablations stack routing (+1.15×), fusion (+1.28×), and source-grouped dispatch (+1.45×) to 1.73× over an unoptimized path-compositional reference. Testing scale is standard (7B–8x7B-class open MoE models, single GPU), not stress-scale; no multi-GPU or batched-serving results. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component: the path-compositional reformulation of MoE routing over sub-expert operators is genuinely new — prior expert-reuse work (ReXMoE, Xshare) shares whole experts, and intra-expert low-rank work (MoE-I2) does not compose operators dynamically — while the source-grouped dispatch engine and fused masked top-k are competent but conventional systems engineering applied to make the new formulation real. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and meaningful at two levels (component design and execution optimizations), plus layer-wise sensitivity analyses (active path density, 15–27% per-layer expansion savings). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and given accuracy deltas of +1 to +3 points on four-choice benchmarks this matters. Code is released at https://github.com/gzyyy0/PCoMoE. Methodological concerns: the accuracy-improvement claim rests on a comparison where PCoMoE gets extra learnable parameters (the compatibility matrix B and target-prior gate λ) that Vanilla-FT does not, so part of the +2.87 could be added routing capacity rather than path composition per se — the Router-Only FT ablation (67.51) partially addresses this but does not fully isolate it; the abstract's 'enhancing model accuracy by 10%' is inconsistent with the reported +5.80/+2.10/+2.46-point vanilla deltas; all comparisons are single-GPU zero-shot on five modest benchmarks with no perplexity-on-generation or long-context evaluation; this is an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system actually built and run on an H20 GPU), with a SYSTEMS artifact component. - Practical: Yes — runs on a single commercially available NVIDIA H20 GPU with no new weights or storage, and preserves the vanilla MoE layer interface so it composes with existing serving stacks in principle. - Efficient: Decode throughput improves 1.24–1.31× over vanilla at equal or better accuracy; prefill is untouched, so the benefit is confined to the decode phase the authors identify as the serving bottleneck. - Effective: Evidence supports the speedup claim directly, but the accuracy-gain evidence is proxy-level (five zero-shot classification benchmarks) and confounded by added routing parameters; no long-form generation quality or perplexity deltas are reported for the final system. - Scalable: Untested — all results are single-GPU, single-request-ish throughput; behavior at 10× batch sizes, multi-GPU tensor/expert parallelism, or with 64-expert models under contention is only claimed, not measured (DeepSeek-V2-Lite with top-6 is the largest configuration tested). The work delivers a released code artifact (GitHub repository); no trained model weights or datasets are stated as released. Strengths: (1) The core reframing — routing over an n×n sub-operator path matrix that strictly contains vanilla MoE as a subset with zero parameter overhead — is a genuine conceptual contribution to how MoE inference granularity is defined. (2) The motivation is empirically grounded rather than asserted: the layer-dependent ΔPPL profiling of whole-expert reduction (Figures 3–4) and the expansion-side substitution-error study (23/32 layers) concretely justify both the problem and the chosen split point. (3) The ablation discipline is above average: the Frozen-Bias row (55.50 accuracy at 1.286× speedup vs. 73.70 at 1.238×) isolates the one component that actually matters, and the execution ablation honestly shows that path expansion alone yields no speedup (1.00× base) without the scheduling co-design. (4) The diagonal-fallback design means worst-case behavior degrades to vanilla MoE, which is a responsible engineering choice for deployability. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: the method is demonstrated only on SwiGLU-style experts (with a claim that the principle generalizes to other expert internals by adapting boundaries — asserted, not shown); the system optimizes only autoregressive decoding, leaving prefill and distributed serving unaddressed; and offline calibration is not yet integrated into automated end-to-end compilation pipelines. They confront these directly and frame them as scoped boundaries rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No seeds/variance reporting means the +1.03 (ARC-C on Mixtral) to +3.08 point gains over Vanilla-FT cannot be statistically distinguished from fine-tuning noise. (2) The accuracy-improvement mechanism is never explained — a sparser-or-restructured routing graph beating the full fine-tuned model is counter-intuitive and likely partly attributable to the extra learnable gating parameters, which Vanilla-FT does not receive; a parameter-matched control is missing. (3) The baselines MoE-I2 and MoE-Pruner lose 6–20 points to vanilla, so the headline table mostly demonstrates that PCoMoE avoids catastrophic degradation; the only live comparison is MoEITS. (4) Missing standard MoE-efficiency baselines such as expert offloading (MoE-Infinity, HoBBIT) and expert sharing (ReXMoE, Xshare) that operate on the same decode-latency axis — the related work cites them but never measures against them. (5) No perplexity or long-generation quality metric for the final system, only five multiple-choice benchmarks, so representation-fidelity claims are extrapolated from a narrow proxy. (6) Abstract-level claims ('1.31×', '10% accuracy') slightly outrun the reported measurements (1.305×, +5.8/+2.1/+2.5 points), a self-report inflation pattern a reviewer should flag. Bottom Line: A practitioner building MoE serving infrastructure gains a concrete, code-released, well-ablated technique for squeezing decode throughput out of intra-expert structure that no prior system touches, and should read it despite the thin statistical rigor — but anyone citing the accuracy-improvement claim should treat it as confounded until replicated with parameter-matched controls and multiple seeds.

Why didn't more people see it? Recommendation: Transparency for providers

M Varasteh, R Burke · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a surrogate-modeling approach that explains, at a system level, why items receive different amounts of exposure in a recommender's top-k lists, by training an XGBoost regressor to predict per-item exposure from structural dataset features. - Why it's important: Item providers (artists, rights holders, creators) currently have no insight into why their content gets little or no exposure on recommendation platforms, leading to speculative "folk theories" about opaque algorithmic gatekeeping. - How it does it: The core move is regressing each item's aggregate exposure (fraction of users whose top-10 list contains the item) on a small set of collaborative-filtering structural features — popularity, neighborhood density, related-item overlap, profile size, genre density, and item metadata — using gradient-boosted trees and reading off gain-based feature importance. - The good: The surrogate achieves R² = 0.83–0.93 across three recommendation algorithms (NCF, VAE, BPR) and two datasets (ML-1M, Last.fm), and backward elimination shows a single feature (RI for NCF, POP for VAE and BPR on Last.fm) explains 60–70% of exposure variance. - The missing: No uncertainty quantification (no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests), no validation that the surrogate supports counterfactual or interventional questions providers would actually ask, and the user-facing value of these explanations is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for recsys researchers working on multi-stakeholder transparency, provider-side explainability, or exposure bias; skippable for those seeking deployable explanation tooling or human-subjects evidence.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is the anchor: the shift from local recipient-facing explanation to global provider-facing exposure explanation via an i→U surrogate is a genuine problem formulation, and the released code helps. The composite is dragged down by Rigor (55) — no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere, gain-based XGBoost importance used without SHAP verification, R² on a zero-inflated target unexamined, and no comparison to any existing explanation method — and by Non-Obviousness (58), since 'popularity predicts popularity-driven exposure' for BPR is close to tautological and the single-feature collapse is partly an artifact of the descriptive framing. Completeness (58) is mixed: the circularity objection is confronted honestly, but the no-conditioning ablation that would settle it is missing, and backward elimination runs only on one dataset. Resilience (55) and Impact (55) are limited because the explanations are diagnostic, not actionable, and no human or provider evaluation exists. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*55 = 59.

Problem & Motivation: Recommendation transparency research has focused almost exclusively on local explanations for recommendation recipients ("why item i for user u?"), while item providers — the creators and rights holders whose content the platform distributes — lack any account of why their items receive little or no exposure across the user base. Prior human-centered studies of artists and music-industry professionals document frustration with opaque platform algorithms and reliance on inaccurate folk theories. The gap this work closes is global, provider-facing explanation: explaining the i→U relation (an item's exposure pattern across all users) with veracity (fidelity to the actual recommender) rather than persuasive content-level narratives. The paper restricts itself to purely collaborative filtering models, where exposure is driven by structural data properties (popularity, profile density, neighborhood interactions) that are measurable but largely unexploited as explanation sources. Key Idea: Aggregate item exposure in a trained collaborative recommender is largely predictable from a handful of structural statistics of the training data, so a gradient-boosted surrogate trained to predict exposure from those statistics yields a faithful global explanation, and its feature importances reveal which structural signal (neighborhood density, popularity, item similarity, etc.) drives each model's exposure distribution. The explanatory target is deliberately descriptive, not counterfactual: characterize what structural properties co-occur with observed exposure, conditioned on the set of users U*_i who actually received the item. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Train a recommender on an 80/20 interaction split using RecBole implementations: NCF (nonlinear embedding), Mult-VAE (generative probabilistic), and BPR (matrix factorization with pairwise ranking loss) — three deliberately different learning objectives. (2) Generate top-10 lists for all users and compute each item's exposure E_i = |U_i|/|U|; split items 80/20 into surrogate train/test sets. (3) Train an XGBoost regressor (max depth 7, 200–500 estimators, learning rate 0.01) to predict E_i from item features in three categories: frequency-based (POP = interacted-user proportion; SZ = average profile size of users who received the item), neighborhood-based (ND = target-item frequency in the Jaccard top-10 user neighborhoods of U_i; RI = fraction of related items, by user-overlap Jaccard similarity, in U_i profiles), and item-specific (GD = genre density; YR = release year; AE/INS = Last.fm audio features). Feature importance is XGBoost gain-based importance; a backward elimination study on Last.fm measures R² as features are removed. Critical design decisions: (a) conditioning SZ, ND, RI, GD on U_i — the authors pre-empt the circularity objection by arguing the goal is descriptive characterization of observed exposure, and point out that GD/RI still contribute near zero despite the same conditioning; this is a reasonable but not fully dispositive defense, since ND remains conditioned on the outcome; (b) gain-based XGBoost importance, a known-biased importance metric, is used without alternative attribution methods (e.g., SHAP) for verification; (c) linear-scale exposure regression on a heavily skewed target (most items have near-zero exposure), with no discussion of how the skew affects R² and importance estimates. Key Results: Surrogate fidelity is R² = 0.85 (NCF) and 0.93 (VAE) and 0.83 (BPR) on ML-1M, and 0.87/0.87/0.88 on Last.fm. Dominant drivers differ by model and domain: on ML-1M, ND dominates for NCF (0.8) and VAE (0.7), while POP dominates for BPR (0.5); on Last.fm, NCF splits between RI (0.4) and ND (0.4), VAE is popularity-driven (POP = 0.5), and BPR is strongly popularity-driven (POP = 0.7). Backward elimination on Last.fm shows the R² curve is flat through removal of INS, AE, GD, and YR, degrades moderately when POP, SZ, RI are removed, and collapses to near zero when the last remaining feature (RI for NCF, POP for VAE and BPR) is removed — a single feature explains 0.6–0.7 of exposure variance. Acoustic features (AE, INS) contribute minimally in all models. Scale is modest: ML-1M (6,040 users, 3,953 items) and Last.fm (24,631 users, 6,584 items, 99% sparsity), both standard recsys benchmarks. Baselines are the recommendation models themselves, not competing explanation methods — no comparison to existing global-explanation or counterfactual approaches (e.g., PRINCE, fidelity-aware attribution) is reported. The R² range of 0.83–0.93 as the headline claim is consistent and the finding that exposure collapses to one feature is the most striking result, but it is also partly a consequence of the descriptive framing: for BPR, "popularity predicts popularity-driven exposure" is close to tautological. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the problem formulation — global, provider-facing exposure explanation via a structural-feature surrogate over the i→U relation, a stakeholder perspective the paper correctly identifies as underexplored. The mechanism itself (XGBoost surrogate + gain importance) is a standard combination of existing techniques; the empirical finding that one structural feature carries 60–70% of exposure variance, and that the identity of that feature varies by algorithm (neighborhood density for NCF/VAE, popularity for BPR), is the substantive contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation covers a useful 2×3 grid (two datasets, three architecturally distinct recommenders), and the backward-elimination ablation partially serves the role of showing which components matter. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, so the stability of both R² and the feature-importance split (e.g., ML-1M NCF ND = 0.8 vs. BPR ND = 0.2) is unverified; code is released at github.com/that-recsys-lab/ProviderSideTransparency, which is a strong reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: (a) four of eight features are conditioned on U*_i, the very outcome being predicted — the authors defend this as descriptive rather than counterfactual, and the null results for GD/RI partially support them, but ND's dominance on ML-1M is exactly where this conditioning most inflates fidelity, and a no-conditioning ablation is not run; (b) there is no comparison against any alternative explanation method, so fidelity and usefulness cannot be contextualized; (c) R² on a heavily zero-inflated exposure target can be misleadingly high — no exposure distribution plots or alternative metrics are given; (d) backward elimination is run only on Last.fm. The recommenders are trained and the surrogate evaluated on the same data, but since the goal is descriptive fidelity to a fixed model rather than generalization, this is less concerning than in predictive settings. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a light SYSTEMS flavor via released code). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on standard benchmarks with RecBole and XGBoost on commodity hardware; the heaviest step (Jaccard neighborhoods over ~25k users) is tractable. - Efficient: The surrogate is cheap to train once recommendation lists exist; the dominant cost is generating top-10 lists for all users and computing Jaccard neighborhoods, which scales as O(k·N²) in the user count and could dominate at larger scale. - Effective: The evidence shows the surrogate reproduces observed exposure (a descriptive proxy) — it does not yet show that these explanations help providers act or understand, which the authors concede requires future human-centered work. - Scalable: Untested beyond ~25k users / 6.6k items; neighborhood computation and per-item exposure over all users will strain at 10–100× scale, and the paper only assumes rather than demonstrates applicability to larger or production systems. The work delivers a code artifact (data generation, training, evaluation pipeline) but no tool, library, or trained model packaged for provider use, and stops at paper form as a diagnostic method. Strengths: - Genuine reframing: shifting explanation target from local (i→u) to global provider-facing (i→U) exposure, with a concrete operationalization (surrogate R²) that makes fidelity measurable — this fills a real gap in the multi-stakeholder recommendation literature. - The cross-model comparison is the most informative part: showing that BPR's exposure is popularity-dominated (POP = 0.5–0.7) while NCF's is neighborhood-dominated on ML-1M gives platform engineers model-specific diagnostic signal, and aligns with BPR's known popularity bias [25], lending face validity. - The authors proactively confront the circularity objection about conditioning features on U*_i with both a conceptual argument and an empirical one (GD/RI null results), and candidly classify their explanations as diagnostic rather than prescriptive rather than overselling actionability. - Releasing the full pipeline code supports verification of the modest experimental claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that most identified factors (POP, ND, RI, SZ, GD) are not actionable by providers — only item properties (YR, AE, INS) are — so the explanations are diagnostic, not prescriptive (Table 3). They acknowledge the circularity concern for U*_i-conditioned features and argue against it. They state that additional human-centered research is needed to determine how such global insights should be presented to providers and whether providers would find them usable. This is a credibility positive: the limitations section is direct and does not minimize, though the practical consequence — that the paper's stated motivation (helping providers) is only partially served by the delivered method — is treated lightly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No uncertainty or stability analysis: single runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals on R² or importance scores; with ~4k–6.5k items, train/test splits and XGBoost variance could shift the headline numbers. - The R² metric on a zero-inflated exposure distribution is unexamined; most items likely have near-zero exposure, and a model that simply separates exposed from non-exposed items could score well without capturing graded exposure differences. No exposure histograms or rank-correlation metrics are reported. - The no-conditioning ablation is missing: a variant of ND/RI/SZ computed over all users rather than U*_i would directly test whether fidelity rests on outcome leakage. The GD/RI null-result argument is suggestive but not a substitute. - No comparison to any prior provider-side explanation method (e.g., PRINCE counterfactual explanations), so the contribution cannot be positioned quantitatively against the field. - Zero predictive but nonzero descriptive framing: providers will likely ask counterfactual questions ("what would raise my exposure?"), and a gain-based descriptive surrogate offers no support for interventions; the paper flags this only obliquely via the actionability table. - Backward elimination is confined to Last.fm, so the "single feature explains 60–70% of variance" claim is unverified on ML-1M. - Gain-based XGBoost importance is a biased attribution metric; SHAP or permutation importance would strengthen the model-comparison claims. - The provider perspective is assumed from prior qualitative studies rather than tested: no provider, platform engineer, or user study is included. Bottom Line: A practitioner interested in provider-side transparency or exposure bias gains a cheap, reproducible diagnostic lens and a useful formulation of the global-explanation problem, but the absence of baselines, uncertainty quantification, and any human evaluation means this is a promising workshop-stage formulation rather than a deployable explanation solution — read it for the framing and the model-comparison findings, not for a finished tool.

Generation of Web Apps with Agentic IDEs: An Empirical Assessment

M Marceca, MT Rossi, L Mariani · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a controlled empirical study comparing three agentic IDEs (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf) on end-to-end generation of five full-stack Web applications, evaluating 48 generated project instances across effectiveness, self-correction, efficiency, and model evolution. - Why it's important: Developers and teams adopting agentic IDEs currently lack evidence about whether these tools can reliably produce complete multi-layer applications rather than isolated functions, and how much human verification effort the outputs actually demand. - How it does it: Each IDE generated applications from identical constrained prompts (FastAPI backend, plain HTML/CSS/JS frontend, pytest tests), followed a 4-stage generate-validate-correct-collect protocol with a six-dimension validation checklist, and was measured with automated tools (Lighthouse, SonarQube, coverage) plus manual inspection. - The good: The study isolates a clear, quantified failure mode — test generation accounts for 49.6% of all errors — and its repeated Note Manager experiment across Claude Sonnet 3.5 → 4.5 cleanly shows coverage jumping from 48–63% to 95–99% as models evolve. - The missing: There are no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals on any comparison, samples are small (3 repetitions per configuration), and all tools ran on a single model family (Claude Sonnet), so IDE differences of ~1 error/project may be noise and model-related conclusions are confounded with IDE updates. - Read it or not: Practitioners deciding whether to adopt agentic IDEs and researchers studying agent-based code generation will find concrete, actionable numbers; ML researchers seeking architectural or algorithmic novelty will not, since the paper contributes measurement rather than method.

Rigor (58) is the main drag: zero inferential statistics on 3-repetition cells whose per-project results contradict the per-tool averages, a single model family confounding IDE vs. model effects, and single-lab manual acceptance testing. Problem & Motivation: Teams adopting AI-assisted development face a gap between benchmarks and reality: HumanEval, MBPP, and SWE-bench evaluate isolated functions or issue fixes, while studies of developer perception measure adoption rather than code correctness. Nobody has systematically measured whether agentic IDEs — where the LLM acts semi-autonomously across the whole workspace — can generate complete full-stack applications (backend, persistence, frontend, tests) from natural-language specifications, how many correction rounds this requires, and how much human effort the verification loop consumes. The beneficiaries are developers deciding whether to trust these tools and researchers deciding what to improve. Key Idea: The core move is methodological rather than algorithmic: treat full-stack application generation as a controlled experiment with a fixed, requirement-constrained prompt, a shared six-dimension validation protocol (installation, frontend acceptance tests, backend API contract tests, persistence checks, AI-generated test executability/coverage, project structure), and a bounded validation-correction loop (max 10 iterations) applied identically across IDEs — enabling apples-to-apples comparison of commercial black-box tools, with functional-area error attribution (API, persistence, frontend, tests, structure) revealing where generation fails. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Initial generation: the IDE receives a full natural-language prompt with strict boundaries on API endpoints, entity schemas, and testing requirements (pytest, minimum test counts), producing a multi-file project with a mandated backend/frontend/tests layout. (2) Validation: six checks combine executable scripts (API contract tests, pytest execution, statement coverage, persistence across restarts), manually executed browser acceptance tests, and Lighthouse/SonarQube static audits. (3) Correction: structured corrective prompts list observed deviations; the loop repeats until compliance or the 10-iteration cap (never reached; averages 1.13–1.73 corrective iterations). (4) Data collection of error counts, iterations, regressions, agent time, and manual verification time. Design decisions: fixing Claude Sonnet 3.5 across IDEs isolates IDE effects (well-justified); fixing the FastAPI/plain-JS stack trades realism for control (acknowledged limitation); three repetitions per configuration addresses stochasticity but is a small sample (weak justification for the effect sizes reported). RQ4 repeats the Note Manager task in January 2026 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, holding requirements constant. Key Results: Across 48 generated projects (5 applications × 3 IDEs × 3 repetitions + 3 repeated runs), all applications converged to passing validation. Average errors per project: Copilot 1.67, Windsurf 1.93, Cursor 2.87. Test errors dominate (49.6% of all errors; 1.06 per project on average), while persistence and project structure had zero errors. SonarQube found no security, duplication, or security-hotspot issues for any tool. Coverage averages: Cursor 77.7%, Copilot 71.2%, Windsurf 66.9%; worst case 48.1% (Windsurf, Note Manager). Average agent execution time: Cursor 6:33, Copilot 9:43, Windsurf 14:07; manual verification time was roughly equal (~11:40–12:24) and often exceeded agent time. Distributed architectures (Real-time Chat, especially Task Queue) produced consistently more errors (e.g., 9–11.7 SonarQube reliability issues on Task Queue vs. 0–1.3 on Note Manager). Model evolution (RQ4): errors dropped to 0.00–2.00, corrective iterations fell to 0.00–0.33, regressions went from 8 total to 0, and coverage rose to 95.8–99.6%, though frontend accessibility slightly decreased. No significance testing is reported for any of these comparisons. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (primary) — the first controlled, multi-tool, multi-application measurement of agentic IDEs on from-scratch full-stack generation, with error attribution by architectural layer and a human-effort quantification. The validation protocol and error taxonomy are competent engineering of known techniques (Lighthouse, SonarQube, contract testing, pytest); no new algorithm, dataset, or system is introduced, and the findings (tests are hard, distributed patterns are hard, models drive progress) confirm intuitions with data rather than overturning expectations. Rigor & Reproducibility: The protocol design is careful: identical prompts, controlled stack, three repetitions, explicit iteration cap, exclusion of non-corrective interactions from iteration counts, and a six-dimension validation checklist applied uniformly. However, no statistical tests, error bars, or confidence intervals accompany any comparison despite the small sample; per-project results visibly contradict per-tool averages (the authors note no IDE dominates per-project), which descriptive means obscure. Manual acceptance testing and structure inspection introduce subjectivity, mitigated only by checklists. Threats to validity are discussed honestly and at length, including construct, internal, external, and conclusion validity. Experimental material, prompts, and scripts are publicly released at https://zenodo.org/records/19208143. A confound the authors partially acknowledge: RQ4's improvements conflate model evolution (Sonnet 3.5 → 4.5) with eight months of IDE-side engineering changes, and their claim of attribution is only partially supported by the design. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study of commercially deployed tools; no new system is built). - Practical: Yes — all three IDEs are commercial products running on standard developer hardware; nothing exotic is required to replicate the workflow. - Efficient: Agent time is 2:20–20:31 per application, but human verification (avg ~12 min/application, under-approximated by the authors) roughly equals or exceeds machine time, making validation the true bottleneck. - Effective: Evidence supports near-correct generation for CRUD/authentication patterns but only proxy evidence for complex architectures — validation was functional and static-analysis-based, not production deployment or long-term maintenance. - Scalable: Untested beyond five small standalone applications; the authors explicitly disclaim generalization to monorepos, microservices, and industrial codebases, so 10×–100× behavior is unknown. The work delivers a reusable experimental artifact (prompts, validation scripts, data on Zenodo) but no software tool; the paper itself is the deliverable. Strengths: - Fills a genuine evaluation gap: end-to-end, multi-layer application generation is measured where prior work used function-level benchmarks or perception surveys; the layer-attributed error taxonomy (tests 49.6% of errors, persistence 0%) is a concrete, reusable finding. - The RQ4 repeated-measurement design (same requirements, April 2025 vs. January 2026, Sonnet 3.5 vs. 4.5) is a clean longitudinal probe of a fast-moving ecosystem that most evaluations ignore entirely. - Quantifying the human verification burden (~12 minutes per application, often exceeding agent time) directly challenges productivity narratives that count only generation time — a non-obvious, practice-relevant result. - The observation of systematic generation biases (homogenized frontend templates, blue-violet palettes, Linux command-line assumptions) is a qualitative finding relevant to prompt design that tool vendors do not advertise. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and thoroughly: five applications cannot represent industrial systems (no monorepos, microservices, deployment pipelines, or organizational conventions); the FastAPI/plain-JS stack limits generalization to framework-heavy stacks; the experimental timeline confounds model evolution with IDE updates; LLM stochasticity and evaluator variability affect measurements; conclusion validity is limited by dataset size and descriptive-only analysis; and reported human effort is an under-approximation of real-world validation cost. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No inferential statistics anywhere: with 3 repetitions per cell and per-project results that contradict per-tool averages, headline claims like "Copilot generates fewer errors" (1.67 vs. 1.93 vs. 2.87) may not survive a significance test; the paper reports deltas without uncertainty. - All tools ran exclusively on Claude Sonnet models; conclusions about IDE capabilities are inseparable from one vendor's model family, and the RQ4 "model evolution" finding cannot separate Anthropic's model progress from Cursor/Windsurf/Copilot product changes despite the authors' attempt to attribute it. - Acceptance tests were executed manually in a browser by the experimenters, and only 3 runs per configuration — the validation protocol itself is single-lab, and no inter-rater reliability for manual judgments (structure compliance, frontend behavior) is reported. - The Task Queue and Real-time Chat results are used to claim distributed architectures are hard, but the applications differ in domain familiarity and specification detail simultaneously; the confound between domain rarity and architectural complexity is asserted, not isolated. - SonarQube's default configuration finding "zero security issues" is reported as robustness, but default-config SonarQube has limited sensitivity for FastAPI security patterns — absence of reported issues is not evidence of secure code. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous head-to-head measurement of commercial agentic IDEs on full-stack generation available today, and any team deciding whether to adopt these tools or any researcher studying agentic code generation should read it — but it is an honest snapshot of a moving target, not a definitive ranking, and its findings will age with the next model release.

Problem & Motivation: Deployed ML systems frequently run GPU kernels that exist only as compiled artifacts — AMDGPU code objects, HSACOs from Triton JIT caches, vendor binaries like AITer — where the source is unavailable, generated, or too far removed from the final machine code to expose remaining optimizations. Existing LLM kernel optimizers (KernelBench-style systems, GEAK, KernelEvolve) and tensor compilers (TVM, Ansor, Triton) all assume an editable source/IR and an independent reference implementation; compiled code objects provide neither, since the binary itself is the only oracle of correct behavior. The risk of naive binary editing is real: a local instruction change can corrupt memory, violate the kernarg ABI, desync metadata, or improve timing only by changing semantics. The authors ask whether an agent can safely optimize the exact deployed binary without any source or reference. Key Idea: The core insight is correctness-gated post-compilation optimization: treat the unmodified original binary K0 as a differential correctness oracle, and make every speedup signal strictly conditional on passing empirical equivalence before any timing occurs — so the optimization signal is, as the authors put it, non-hackable. This is enabled by a two-tier oracle acquisition mechanism (synthetic launch inference from metadata when possible; capture-and-replay of a real production dispatch — kernargs, launch geometry, and device memory restored at original virtual addresses — when not), plus a metadata-aware rebuild that regenerates descriptors while freezing the launcher ABI so the result is a drop-in replacement. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) recover editable AMDGCN assembly from the ELF container, re-symbolizing PC-relative control flow and reconstructing .amdhsa_kernel declarations, gated by a one-time byte-level round-trip fidelity check; (2) acquire the differential oracle via Tier 1 synthetic inputs (with canary guard regions to catch OOB writes) or Tier 2 real-dispatch capture and replay; (3) profile with hardware counters, instruction sampling, and static analysis to isolate hot instruction windows; (4) an LLM agent (Claude Opus 4.8) proposes localized edits using failed attempts as memory; (5) candidates are spliced into full assembly, rebuilt with rescanned VGPR/SGPR/LDS/scratch resources reflected in kernel descriptors and metadata (kernarg layout frozen), with a conservative in-place byte-patch fallback restricted to resource-neutral, size-non-increasing edits; (6) GatedEval applies gates in fixed order — assembly validity, static ABI/resource consistency, functional equivalence (cosine ≥ 0.9999 and L∞ ≤ 10⁻³ for FP, byte-exact for integers and guard regions, repeated 3×), then timing. The commit gate is variance-aware: speedup must exceed max((1+max(ε, k·cv))·best, s_floor) with ε=0.002, k=0.85, s_floor=1.0. The agent operates under a deterministic controller owning budget, lineage, and termination; multi-start team mode assigns orthogonal optimization directions to parallel workers branching from diverse verified lineage nodes, and verified composition incrementally combines compatible candidates with re-verification after each step. Critical design decisions: correctness strictly precedes timing (well justified — it prevents rewarding broken-but-fast kernels); tree-structured lineage over a destructive chain (justified — enables backtracking from local optima); empirical rather than formal equivalence (a deliberate, explicitly acknowledged trade-off). The objective is implicit (maximize T(K0)/T(K′) subject to the equivalence and ABI constraints) rather than an explicit training loss — the LLM is prompted, not trained. Key Results: On MI308X, AsmEvo improves 29 of 30 selected KernelBench kernels (15 Level 1, 15 Level 2), reaching 1.35x geometric-mean and 3.88x maximum speedup (depthwise Conv2D); Level 1 shows 1.56x geomean with all 15 improved and a median of 1.31x, Level 2 shows 1.17x geomean with 14/15 improved and a median of 1.10x, consistent with fused kernels having less headroom. Only 5.1% of ~138 attempts per kernel become verified commits, showing edits are sparse. On MI300X production artifacts, all 4 AITer code objects improve (1.09x geomean, 1.31x max on FP8 blockscale MoE) and all 4 vLLM/SGLang Triton JIT kernels improve (1.18x geomean, 1.343x max on vLLM fused_moe_kernel). End-to-end validation confirms drop-in usability: AITer replacements pass unit tests, and vLLM/SGLang cached HSACOs pass framework tests with recompilation disabled. The KernelBench K0 baselines are not weak — the HIP sources were refined by a GEAK-style agent with GPT-5.0 and all were faster than their PyTorch operators before compilation. Scale is modest per kernel (30 benchmark + 8 production kernels) but each search consumed a 12-hour wall-clock budget with 4 GPU workers. Notably absent from the provided text: quantitative results comparing the agentic driver against alternative search drivers, despite the Related Work stating "We therefore compare search drivers within the same harness." Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW FORMULATION: the formulation of source-free, ABI-preserving, correctness-gated post-compilation kernel optimization — with the deployed binary as the only oracle — appears genuinely new for AMDGPU code objects; the recovery/rebuild/verification pipeline is the concrete novel artifact. The constituent techniques are standard combinations relocated to a new setting: stochastic/learning assembly search follows STOKE, CuAsmRL, and RL-for-CPU-assembly; the agent loop is a conventional LLM-as-proposer-under-verifier pattern; differential testing and profiling-guided localization are established compiler-practice ideas. The claim of being "first to combine" agentic search, ABI-preserving AMDGPU rebuild, and binary-oracle differential verification is plausible but only asserted, not systematically demonstrated against prior binary-rewriting work. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partially present but not reported in this text: the harness design holds recovery/rebuild/verification fixed, yet no tables show which agent components (multi-start, composition, memory, anti-stall) contribute to results, and the promised search-driver comparison is not quantified. Commit thresholds are variance-aware (addressing noisy shared-hardware timing), but no error bars, multiple seeds per kernel, or significance tests are reported on the headline speedups. The equivalence check is repeated 3× per candidate with fixed tolerances, and static consistency plus canary guards are sensible defenses. No code, dataset, or artifact release URL is mentioned — reproducibility depends entirely on the method description. Methodological concerns: (a) the KernelBench K0 objects were produced by the authors' own GEAK-style pipeline, so headroom may partly reflect suboptimal upstream compilation rather than universal post-compilation opportunity — though the production results mitigate this; (b) empirical equivalence with loose tolerances (cosine 0.9999) could accept numerically divergent kernels whose behavior degrades at other shapes; (c) hardware clocks could not be locked, acknowledged by the authors. Scalable: Not tested beyond 38 kernels; the paper claims architecture-agnostic harness design but the implementation is calibrated for CDNA-class GPUs, and per-kernel cost does not obviously amortize across large serving fleets without stated. Strengths: (1) The correctness-before-timing gating with a variance-aware commit margin is a genuinely well-engineered answer to the known failure mode of LLM kernel optimizers rewarding fast-but-wrong candidates, and the 5.1% commit rate suggests the gate is doing real work rather than rubber-stamping. (2) Tier 2 real-dispatch capture-and-replay (restoring device memory at original virtual addresses so nested pointers stay valid) is a technically substantive solution to verifying pointer-rich production kernels with no reconstructable signature. (3) The evaluation deliberately includes vendor binaries (AITer) and runtime JIT artifacts (vLLM/SGLang HSACOs) with end-to-end runtime validation, not only benchmark kernels — the strongest form of evidence for the source-free claim. (4) The round-trip fidelity gate (byte-level comparison of reassembled vs. original bodies, descriptors, and metadata) cleanly establishes that edits operate on a faithful representation before any optimization begins. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state explicitly that equivalence is empirical, not formal, and scoped to evaluated inputs and launch configurations; new shapes require new oracle acquisition; the recovery/rebuild implementation is calibrated for CDNA-class AMD GPUs only; complex application state requires real-dispatch capture; and achievable gains depend on optimization headroom remaining in the compiled kernel. They also acknowledge shared hardware with unlocked clocks as a noise source. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No quantitative search-driver ablation appears despite the positioning section promising to compare drivers within the harness — the reader cannot tell how much the agentic machinery matters versus random or heuristic assembly perturbation under the same gates. (2) The FP equivalence tolerances (cosine ≥ 0.9999, L∞ ≤ 10⁻³) are fairly loose for accepting production kernels; an optimized FMHA or MoE kernel could pass on captured dispatches while drifting on other input distributions, and the paper does not test generalization of a committed kernel to unseen shapes. (3) No comparison against a simpler alternative: recompiling from recovered assembly through LLVM/rocprofiler-level reoptimization, or even a scheduling-only pass like CuAsmRL-style reordering, would establish how much gain requires full LLM agentic search. (4) The production set is only 8 kernels, and the AITer results (three of four between 1.007x and 1.049x) suggest marginal gains on vendor-optimized attention code — the aggregate "all 8 improved" phrasing flatters small wins. (5) No artifact release is stated, which limits both verification and community impact for a paper whose central claim rests on tooling. (6) The paper is a preprint (arXiv) from AMD with no stated peer review; the numbers are self-reported and the timing methodology (no locked clocks) cannot be independently checked. Bottom Line: A practitioner shipping AMD GPU inference kernels should read this for its verification-harness design — the two-tier differential oracle and correctness-gated commit logic are directly reusable ideas — but the missing search-driver ablations, loose FP tolerances, unreleased artifacts, and vendor-authored evaluation mean the headline speedups should be treated as promising self-reported evidence rather than independently validated results.

B Liu, S Jin, P Wang, Z Yin, Y Wang, Y Zhou, X Liang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CAFE, a training framework in which a single shared-parameter LLM alternates between search-agent and critic roles, learning to request, generate, and exploit corrective feedback inside an active search trajectory while the critic co-evolves with the policy it guides. - Why it's important: Outcome-supervised search agents get only terminal rewards, so early directional errors go uncorrected and compound over long trajectories; a learnable, in-trajectory corrective mechanism addresses this compounding-failure pain point without deploying a separate critic model. - How it does it: The core move is coupling feedback utility to outcomes: a comparative feedback estimate (CFE) rewards feedback requests by the prompt-level success gap between call-vs-skip rollouts, token-level advantage shaping separates pre-request behavior from post-feedback recovery, and rollout-derived DPO (RDPO) trains the critic on prefix-matched success/fail pairs mined from the latest on-policy rollouts, iterated 100 RL steps × 5 rounds. - The good: The one-sided co-evolution ablation is the most credible evidence: agent-only optimization plateaus at 83.6 mean score on 2Wiki (peaking 84.2) and feedback-only reaches 71.3, while alternating updates reach 86.6, and cross-play shows each agent iteration performs best with the same-iteration critic. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the headline +2.1 EM over the strongest baseline (IGPO, itself reproduced by the authors on their own SFT checkpoint), and no code or data release is mentioned. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building RL-trained search/deep-research agents who want feedback-based credit assignment designs; skippable for practitioners seeking a deployable search system, since gains are modest over a strong GRPO baseline and no artifact is released.

Problem & Motivation: Search agents trained with outcome rewards learn when and how to retrieve, but a binary terminal reward neither localizes which intermediate step went wrong nor intervenes before errors compound in a long trajectory. Prior finer-grained credit methods (information gain, confidence change, state comparison — e.g., StepSearch, IGPO) are evaluative, not instructive: they reweight learning signals but do not redirect the ongoing rollout. Prompted self-correction loops (Reflexion, Self-Refine, CRITIC) are post hoc and untrained. Making in-trajectory feedback learnable raises three coupled problems: the agent must learn when requesting help pays off; the critic must learn useful corrections from outcome-confounded data; and a static critic goes stale as the agent's failure distribution shifts. The authors of this Fudan/Tencent collaboration target RL-based search-agent builders in the agentic QA domain. Key Idea: Treat corrective feedback as an optional learned intervention in the action space (<request_feedback>), and resolve the two confounds it creates — when to request, and how to credit the success it rescues — by comparing rollouts that called feedback against ones that skipped it (CFE), by differentially shaping token advantages before vs. after the request (down-weight the erroneous prefix, up-weight the recovery), and by keeping the critic aligned to the evolving agent through alternating online RL and RDPO on a shared backbone. The design decision to preserve the agent's own failed prefix in SFT bootstrap data (rather than ideal teacher trajectories) is what makes the pre/post advantage split meaningful. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Feedback-augmented SFT: collect failed rollouts from the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent, use teacher Kimi-K2.5 to locate the first erroneous turn, preserve the erroneous prefix, insert a <request_feedback> action, generate corrective feedback plus a successful continuation; keep only repaired trajectories with correct answers. (2) Online agent optimization: GRPO with 8 rollouts per prompt; the CFE-shaped reward is R = r_task + β·C_i·û(x) − γ·[n_fb,i −1]+ (β=0.5, γ=0.05, batch-level fallback when a prompt realizes one route), and advantage shaping splits tokens at the first request into pre/call/post segments, applying Â_t = A_i ∓ λ·clip(û, 0, b) only when A_i > 0 and the gap is positive (λ=0.5, floor 0 on pre-feedback advantages); observation and feedback tokens are excluded from the policy loss. A theorem (Thm. 1) shows the shaped update stays positively aligned with the outcome-only update when the perturbation norm is bounded. (3) Offline RDPO: pair a called-correct and called-incorrect rollout with prefix Jaccard ≥ 0.7 and an LLM-judge quality filter; apply DPO (lr 2e-7, 2 epochs) on the shared checkpoint; alternate 100 online steps with one RDPO update for 5 iterations (500 total RL steps, 8×A100, ~2 days). Well-justified decisions: matched-prefix preference pairs to reduce outcome confounding, and the conservative RDPO learning rate to avoid overriding RL behavior. Less justified: the hyperparameters β, γ, λ, and the 100×5 schedule are tuned by ablation on the same benchmarks used for evaluation. Key Results: On seven SearchQA benchmarks (2WikiMultihopQA in-domain for training; HotpotQA, MuSiQue, PopQA, Bamboogle, NQ, TriviaQA out-of-domain; 500 examples each, 125 for Bamboogle; E5 retriever over a fixed corpus, ≤30 tool calls), CAFE-7B reaches 52.5 EM / 60.7 F1 average — highest EM and second-highest F1 among evaluated methods — beating the strongest RL baseline IGPO by 2.1 EM / 1.3 F1 and Search-R1 by 7.4 EM on the four multi-hop datasets (vs. 1.3 EM on single-hop). Training-stage gains: backbone 38.1/47.9 → SFT 40.8/50.1 → GRPO 49.7/58.0 → CAFE 52.5/60.7, consistent across all six out-of-domain sets and replicated at 3B scale (48.8/57.4, matching several 7B baselines). On BrowseComp-Plus, EM rises 4.4 → 5.3 → 6.8 → 7.7 across stages. Hallucination rate drops from 29.9% (base) to 17.6% (GRPO) to 12.6% (CAFE). Component ablations: CFE alone +1.1 EM over GRPO, advantage shaping alone +1.5 EM, both +2.2 EM; RDPO beats rollout-derived SFT (52.5 vs. 51.2 avg EM after five iterations). Baselines include current closed- and open-source frontier models evaluated under the authors' protocol plus released checkpoints of WebSeer-14B and StepSearch; IGPO was reproduced on the authors' SFT checkpoint, and Search-R1/R-Search numbers are taken from their original papers. Notably, the plain SFT+GRPO variant (49.7/58.0) already beats most published RL baselines, so the full CAFE machinery adds 2.8 EM over the strongest internal control. One-feedback-per-trajectory request budget; testing is at standard 7B/3B scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (primary) with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (one-sided controls plateau while alternating agent/critic updates keep improving). Genuinely novel: CFE's call–skip success gap as a feedback-utility reward, the pre/post-feedback advantage split tied to the retained-failure-prefix SFT design, and in-trajectory (not post-hoc) feedback as a learned, co-evolving intervention — distinct from ECHO's post-trajectory critic. Standard combinations: GRPO, DPO, role-conditioned prompting, teacher-located error turns, and Jaccard/LLJ-judge filtering are all existing tools assembled competently. Rigor & Reproducibility: Component ablations are thorough (CFE/shaping, RSFT vs. RDPO, schedule 50×10 vs. 100×5 vs. 250×2, 3B-scale replication) and the cross-play matrix is a genuinely informative analysis. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests appear for any headline number; the 2.1 EM margin over IGPO is within plausible run-to-run variance for 7B GRPO training; IGPO is a reproduction on the authors' own SFT checkpoint (favorable initialization) while Search-R1/R-Search numbers are imported from other papers (protocol mismatch risk); hyperparameters (β, γ, λ, schedule) are selected on the same benchmarks used for reporting (Goodhart exposure); 2Wiki, the sole training domain, is also in the reported average (84.0 EM there vs. 53.4 best out-of-domain). No code, data, or checkpoint release is mentioned in the paper text. Full hyperparameters, prompts, and an algorithm box are provided, which aids reimplementation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — trained on 8×A100 (~2 days) with Qwen2.5-7B/3B backbones and a local E5 retriever, all commercially available. Efficient: Adds overhead vs. plain GRPO (two-phase training, preference mining, an LLM judge, and a teacher model for SFT construction), and inference pays for feedback-request turns, though the case study shows feedback can cut search calls 25→2. Effective: Evidence supports improved QA accuracy and reduced hallucination on curated benchmarks with a fixed retriever; it does not yet demonstrate solving the stated problem under live, realistic search conditions. Scalable: Untested beyond 7B and five alternation iterations; co-evolution dynamics under much larger policies, corpora, or more iterations are claimed by extrapolation, not measured. The work delivers no software artifact — no library, weights, or dataset release is mentioned; it stops at paper form with reproduction-level detail. Strengths: - The co-evolution claim is backed by a properly controlled experiment: agent-only and feedback-only one-sided controls that both plateau (83.6 and 71.3) versus alternating optimization (86.6), plus a cross-play matrix showing same-iteration agent–critic pairing is best — this directly tests the paper's central thesis rather than asserting it. - The pre/post-feedback advantage shaping is a clean, well-motivated fix to a real credit-assignment boundary (a rescued trajectory and a flawless one get identical rewards), and the advantage-distribution shift (Figs. 2b–2c) plus routing-entropy analysis (0.496 vs. 0.221 bits) give mechanistic corroboration. - The SFT bootstrap design — retaining the agent's own failed prefix rather than replacing it with an ideal trajectory — is a subtle but consequential decision that the paper correctly identifies as the reason shaping is meaningful. - Honest quantification of where gains concentrate: multi-hop datasets benefit most (7.4 EM over Search-R1) versus single-hop (1.3 EM), matching the stated mechanism. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: No explicit limitations section appears in the paper. Implicitly, the authors acknowledge that outcome labels confound feedback quality (motivating RDPO's matched pairs), that feedback learned from stale rollouts misaligns with an evolving policy (motivating alternation), and that a batch-level CFE fallback is needed when a prompt realizes only one route. They do not confront compute overhead, seed variance, benchmark selection, or the single-retriever setting. This is a credibility negative on transparency, though not on the experiments themselves. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No seed variance or significance testing anywhere; the 2.1 EM headline margin over IGPO and the 0.6–1.3 EM margins in the offline ablation table are not statistically supported. - IGPO, the strongest baseline, is reproduced by the authors starting from their own feedback-augmented SFT checkpoint — a potentially favorable comparison that a from-scratch IGPO run would disentangle. - Only one training domain (2Wiki), one retriever (E5), and one teacher model (Kimi-K2.5); sensitivity to retrieval quality and teacher strength is unexamined, and 2Wiki's in-domain 84.0 EM inflates the reported average. - The hallucination metric ("unsupported factual claim") appears to be judged by a procedure not fully specified in the main text, risking self-serving evaluation; no human validation of the criterion is reported. - The request budget is one feedback call per trajectory in training; behavior with multiple interventions, and whether CFE's call–skip gap is even estimable at higher request rates, is untested. - Search-R1 and R-Search numbers are copied from their original papers rather than re-run under the fixed-corpus E5 protocol, mixing evaluation conditions in the main table. - Theorem 1 assumes bounded perturbation relative to the task-update norm — a condition verifiable only post hoc — and the bound parameters (U, K, ν) are not instantiated empirically. Bottom Line: A technically solid and well-instrumented RL paper whose co-evolution analysis genuinely advances understanding of coupled agent–critic training, but whose headline gains (+2.8 EM over its own strong GRPO control) are small, statistically unsupported, and demonstrated only on curated benchmarks without a released artifact — researchers in agentic RL should read it for the CFE/shaping design and co-evolution controls; practitioners wanting a deployable search agent should look elsewhere for now.
