Problem & Motivation: Deductive/SMT-backed verification requires proof engineering — loop invariants, ghost state, assertions, lemmas — that makes specs true but not solver-dischargeable: a fact can match the intended safety argument yet fail because a helper lemma is missing, the query carries irrelevant context, or the obligation is encoded in a hostile theory (e.g., bit-vector promotion semantics in C integer arithmetic). LLM agents placed in repair loops over Rocq/Lean see kernel-checked states but inherit verbose prover contexts, while SMT-backed loops (AutoVerus, KVerus) expose only coarse verifier failures and cannot diagnose why the lowered SMT query returned unknown or timed out. The paper targets verification researchers and tool builders who need agentic verification to scale to feature-rich C programs (SV-COMP-style tasks averaging 1,427 LOC), closing the gap between what the model can write and what the solver can prove. Key Idea: Treat a failed proof as a diagnostic question at the SMT layer rather than a request to rewrite the specification: expose the failing obligation ⟨l, Γl, φl, τl⟩ to the agent, let it test candidate lemmas m1..mk directly via fast unsat entailment checks (Γl ∧ m1..mk ⊨ τl φl, then each mi proven from prior context), and inject a checked policy library encoding solver-theory priors (ghost prefix arrays for aggregates; LIA/NIA for value-level arithmetic, bit-vectors only for truncation/wraparound facts) so the model stops rediscovering formulations that are semantically equivalent but solver-hostile. Snapshots at checked program-point boundaries prevent repair from re-replaying proven prefixes, with a clean-gate end-to-end recheck that discards cached state at acceptance time. Methodology: The system is a trust-split agent/checker harness (~220K lines of non-test Rust). The untrusted agent side runs a plan-generate-repair-review loop: it produces source-level specifications, counterexample proposals, lemma edits on the exposed SMT file, and theory-view selections, guided by theory-aware policies scoped as proof directives. The trusted side lowers anonymized source plus annotations into verification conditions via language-specific front ends (C semantics including pointer validity, malloc/free safety, integer promotion; Rust/Verus with ownership modeled separately), checks each obligation as unsatτl(Γl ∧ ¬φl) with a parallel solver bundle (CVC5 1.3.1-dev, Bitwuzla 0.7.0-dev, Z3 4.16.0), accepts unsafe answers only via concrete witness replay, and routes unknown/timeout outcomes to lemma repair. Three critical design decisions: (1) deliberately short 10–20s default timeouts as a diagnostic signal rather than a completeness measure — justified by the observation that compact, theory-matched obligations discharge in milliseconds; (2) direct SMT-file edits are diagnostic-only and must be lifted back into source annotations the checker can regenerate — this preserves soundness and is well-argued; (3) snapshots are incremental engineering devices, with final acceptance always running a clean-gate full recheck from original source — a sound design choice explicitly defended. Objective structure is standard deductive verification (Hoare triples / weakest preconditions) with the contribution living in the feedback interface, not the calculus. Key Results: On 1,475 tasks: 1,367 direct passes (92.7%). On AutoRocq-ReachSafety: 106/112 (94.6%) vs AutoRocq's 45/112 (40.2%) and CPAchecker's 25/112 (22.3%); AutoRocq-NoOverflow: 47/50 (94.0%) vs AutoRocq 10/50 and CPAchecker 45/50; KVerus-File: 299/313 (95.5%) vs AutoVerus 217/313 (69.3%) and KVerus (paper-reported, not rerun — not open-sourced) 251/313 (80.2%); VariousSVC-ReachSafety (1,000 curated SV-COMP 2026 tasks, avg. 1,427 LOC): 915/1,000 (91.5%) vs CPAchecker 601/1,000 (60.1%). Under the SV-COMP scoring rule (safe +2, unsafe +1, wrong safe −32, wrong unsafe −16): SCHWARZ 1,516/1,672 (90.7%) vs pure-agent baseline (same GPT-5.5 xhigh agent, no formal assistance) 1,212/1,672 (72.5%, with 10 wrong-safe and 7 wrong-unsafe hallucinated labels) and CPAchecker 986/1,672 (59.0%). The 1,000 accepted SV-COMP verdicts split 601 safe proofs / 314 unsafe replays, with zero incorrect SCHWARZ-accepted verdicts. Ablations: no-policies 1,301 (88.2%), no-lemmas 1,146 (77.7%), neither 1,081 (73.3%); lemmas are the dominant contributor, and the combined drop exceeds either single ablation on three of four suites, indicating complementarity. Feature breakdown shows floating point as the weak region (e.g., 12/22 above 5,000 LOC) driven mostly by missing libm models (sqrtf, tanf); only 13/1,000 SV-COMP failures attributed to time exhaustion. Scale is standard-to-stress (up to >5,000 LOC tasks, 4-hour per-task timeout, 8 cores/12GB). Baselines are current (SV-COMP 2026 ReachSafety champion CPAchecker, 2025–2026 agentic tools), though AutoVerus/KVerus/SCHWARZ comparisons cross different proof artifact granularities, which the authors acknowledge. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW FORMULATION: the genuinely novel element is positioning the failed SMT obligation itself (with symbolic context, theory view, and the generated SMT file) as the unit of agent repair, together with checked obligation-local lemmas and a theory-policy library — an interface level that sits below Rocq-kernel-state feedback (AutoRocq, LemmaNet) and below Verus-frontend lemmas (AutoVerus, KVerus) and differs from theory-fragment-specific LLM-assisted SMT work (AquaForte, inductive-lemma solvers) by retaining source-level semantics alongside the lowered formula. The outer plan-execute-review loop, checked-generation pattern, snapshots, and deductive front ends are competent standard components; the contribution is their reorganization around solver dischargeability rather than any new solver algorithm or proof calculus. Rigor & Reproducibility: The two-factor ablation (policies × lemmas) is the strongest methodological element and directly answers RQ2 with per-suite numbers. Missing: no multiple seeds, no error bars, no significance tests — a real concern given acknowledged LLM output nondeterminism, since none of the headline margins (e.g., 915 vs 871 without policies) carry variance estimates. No code, benchmark curation scripts, or model artifacts are stated as released (no URL given), and the underlying agent is a proprietary GPT-5.5 xhigh via Codex CLI, making exact reproduction impossible. Methodological concerns a reviewer should flag: (1) the 1,000-task suite is the authors' own curated subset with stated exclusions (cyclic goto) — the technique is partly developed against and evaluated on a suite whose selection criteria they control (Goodhart risk); (2) KVerus numbers are quoted from its paper (different model, Claude Sonnet 4.0) rather than rerun, so that cell is not apples-to-apples; (3) AutoRocq results require a VC-to-source mapping defined by the authors; (4) the 4-hour wall-clock budget with uncapped model calls means compute cost per solved task is unreported. On the positive side, acceptance is grounded in deterministic checking with a reported zero incorrect-accepted-verdict rate, and the clean-gate end-to-end recheck guards against snapshot caching artifacts. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built harness with trusted front ends, solver bundle, and Docker-scripted deterministic loop, evaluated by running it). EMPIRICAL evidence supports the SYSTEMS classification. — Practical: Runs on commodity hardware (single AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, 128 GB RAM, 12 GB/task), but requires access to a frontier closed-source model (GPT-5.5 xhigh), which is a real deployment dependency and cost. — Efficient: Per-task cost relative to CPAchecker is not reported in compute or dollar terms; the short-timeout diagnostic design and snapshot reuse reduce wasted solver/LLM work, and CPAchecker's cheaper pure-analysis route is not given a runtime comparison. — Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem on the tested suites with zero accepted-incorrect verdicts, but the safe/unsafe balance (601/314) and curated selection leave open whether it holds on an unstratified SV-COMP draw. — Scalable: Tested to >5,000 LOC with maintained high pass rates on control-flow and numeric tasks; behavior at project-level scale (multi-file, interprocedural) is claimed via the KVerus framing but not directly demonstrated. Delivers a paper-described system; no software artifact, dataset, or repository release is mentioned, so it stops at paper form for external users. Strengths: (1) The obligation-local repair formulation is a real conceptual contribution: identifying solver dischargeability as a distinct failure mode and giving the agent a checked, inspectable SMT-level repair target is a sharper interface than prior Rocq-state or Verus-frontend loops, and the motivating C integer-promotion example concretely demonstrates why coarse failures mislead repair. (2) The ablation is well-designed and honest — it separates the solver-facing contribution from generic LLM spec generation and shows a large, consistent effect (73.3% → 92.7% aggregate), with the expected weak result on already-saturated NoOverflow reported rather than hidden. (3) The trust architecture is sound and clearly specified: lemmas must be proven from checked context, SMT edits are diagnostic-only, unsafe verdicts require concrete replay, and a clean-gate full recheck discards cached snapshot state — zero incorrect accepted verdicts over 1,475 tasks substantiates the design. (4) Failure analysis is unusually candid for a systems paper: ~80% of misses attributed to named frontend/solver semantic gaps (libm, unions, layout), with only 13 time-exhaustion failures, giving readers an accurate capability map rather than a uniform success story. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: missing semantic coverage in front ends/solvers (libm functions like tanf, sqrtf, strncmp; union-heavy bit-level layout), long proof routes needing many specifications before the target (partially mitigated, not solved, by snapshots), and frontend scope exclusions (cyclic goto). They confront threats to validity directly in a dedicated section: task-granularity non-comparability across Rocq VCs, Verus artifacts, and C sources (hence per-suite rather than aggregate leaderboard claims), and nondeterminism in model outputs plus incomplete prototype coverage. This directness is a credibility positive; the one place they minimize is benchmark curation, where the stratified 1,000-task selection is described but not defended against selection-bias concerns. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No independent replication surface: no code, no curation script for the "curated" 1,000-task suite, and no release stated — combined with author-controlled task selection and stated exclusions, the 91.5%-vs-60.1% CPAchecker gap invites selection-effect scrutiny; running on the full unfiltered ReachSafety track would resolve this. (2) Cost opacity: with a 4-hour timeout, uncapped model calls, and a frontier proprietary model, the token/compute cost per solved task — the quantity that determines whether this beats just running CPAchecker longer or running the pure agent with majority voting — is never reported. (3) Single-seed, single-model evaluation: all headline numbers come from one model (GPT-5.5 xhigh) with no variance estimate, despite acknowledged nondeterminism. (4) The pure-agent baseline's 17 wrong labels on 1,000 tasks is presented as motivating the harness, but no baseline combines the pure agent with simple self-consistency or verifier-lite checks, leaving unclear how much gain comes specifically from SMT-local repair versus any form of grounded checking. (5) The comparison to KVerus mixes models and reruns versus paper quotes; a rerun of KVerus under the identical GPT-5.5 setup is absent. (6) SV-COMP-style scoring uses their projected local-subset numbers for official tools ("projected to the same local subset"), which is reasonable but means the 90.7% figure is not an official SV-COMP result. Bottom Line: For researchers building LLM-assisted verification or proof-repair systems, this is a genuinely useful read — the obligation-local SMT repair interface and its two-factor ablation make a convincing, quantified case that solver-level feedback is the missing layer in agentic verification, and the soundness architecture is worth imitating; but practitioners seeking a deployable tool should note the absent artifact release, the curated-benchmark selection risk, and unreported compute costs before treating the headline numbers as field-ready results.

Apodex-1.0: A verification-centric agent team for discoverative intelligence

A Team · liangcaisu.github.io · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Apodex-1.0, a deep-research model post-trained from Qwen3.5 (35B-A3B and 397B-A17B MoE variants) via a three-stage SFT → agentic DPO → RL recipe, plus a 'heavy-duty mode' (Apodex-1.0-H) that deploys it inside an asynchronous agent team with dedicated verification agents and a global evidence-graph verifier. - Why it's important: Deep-research agents saturate at a few hundred steps in a single ReAct context window, and long-horizon reliability currently depends on either much larger models or fragile outer scaffolds; this work claims an alternative scaling axis (scaling agents, not parameters) with trained-in team and verification behavior. - How it does it: An orchestrator asynchronously spawns retrieval/verification sub-agents whose reports collect in a shared evidence pool, a three-role verification team audits claims, and a global verifier reasons over an assembled claim–evidence graph — with the team behavior itself instilled by RL over long agentic rollouts (IcePop masking + bypass-mode importance ratios on an asynchronous, partially-colocated training stack). - The good: The within-family ablation is credible and consistent: heavy-duty mode lifts BrowseComp from 75.5 to 90.3 (+14.8), FrontierScience-Research from 28.3 to 46.7 (+18.4), and IMO-ProofBench overall from 30.71 to 57.38 via the generate–verify–revise loop, while general-capability benchmarks show the base model's knowledge/coding/reasoning scores survive post-training within ~1–4 points. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; skippable for anyone wanting rigorous, controlled benchmark comparisons, which this vendor-style report does not provide.

Resilience (45) is low: the 'new SOTA' framing collapses under compute-unmatched comparisons (90.3 vs 90.1 at 16 rollouts/query) and a 41-query self-authored benchmark scored by the authors' own rubrics. Problem & Motivation: The paper targets long-horizon deep-research tasks — multi-step web investigation, cross-referencing, and evidence synthesis — where a single ReAct agent's think–act–observe loop saturates after a few hundred steps because one context window cannot hold the work and self-reflection degrades with turn count. The intended beneficiaries are users and organizations needing auditable, factual research reports rather than plausible-sounding answers. The gap the authors identify in prior work is twofold: (1) multi-agent frameworks (AutoGen, MetaGPT, AgentVerse) impose team topology as an external scaffold around a generalist model rather than training the coordination behavior into the model, and (2) existing verification methods (CoVe, Self-Refine, Reflexion, process reward models) use the generator itself, or a single scorer model, rather than an independent agent with its own context and tools — so a systematic error in the reasoner propagates to every 'verification' pass. Key Idea: The core insight is that verification must be structurally external — dispatched to independent agents that do not share the reasoner's context, prompt, or trace — and that this external-verification behavior, along with sub-agent spawning and asynchronous coordination, can be trained into the model weights (via DPO and RL on agentic rollouts) rather than imposed by an outer framework. At test time this composes into a second scaling axis: heavy-duty mode runs many parallel agent teams and a global verifier that reasons over the union of their evidence as a claim–evidence graph (nodes = atomic findings/claims; edges = support/contradiction), rather than voting over finished answers — so the same verifier weights operate from one team to a swarm. Methodology: The system has three layers. (1) Agent-team deployment: an orchestrator decomposes the query and spawns specialized sub-agents (researcher, data analyst, developer, domain specialists), each with its own context, prompt, and full tool set; sub-agents deposit reports in a shared pool with status flags, and the orchestrator dispatches a conflict reviewer, fact checker, and draft-report reviewer as reports become ready — exploration, verification, and synthesis run as three independent asynchronous control loops. For the hardest tasks, multiple teams run in parallel and a domain-specific global verifier selects/synthesizes: evidence-graph reasoning for research, causal-evidence comparison against 'pseudo-correctness' for coding (three rubric axes: Comprehension, Causality, Empirical Grounding), and generate–verify–revise (GVR: up to K rounds of proof → 0–7 self-grading with written critique, grader blind to reference solution and rubric) for math. (2) Data: two streams — a deep-research stream built by evidence-grounded extraction from research literature, random-walk question synthesis over statement graphs (3–10 hop evidence chains with interleaved reasoning/retrieval sub-steps), and model-in-the-loop difficulty filtering (retain only questions where some panel model fails and another succeeds); and a capability-preservation stream (general knowledge, instruction following, execution-gated coding trajectories). (3) Training: SFT for behavioral initialization (assistant-side tokens only), DPO on complete agentic trajectory pairs labeled by final-answer correctness, then RL on long rollouts using a fully-asynchronous pipeline (ROLL Flash-style persistent rollout worker), partial-GPU collocation (inference engines onloaded to training GPUs during idle windows, per-token weight-version provenance), a bypass-mode importance ratio that reuses inference-engine log-probs (saving the old-log-prob recompute, 5–15% step time reduction), and the IcePop bidirectional mask (zeroing tokens with ratio outside [0.5, 5.0]). Critical design decisions: training team behavior into weights rather than scaffolding (asserted, not ablated against a scaffold-only baseline); grader blindness in GVR (well-justified, prevents oracle inflation); masking vs. truncated IS for MoE stability (claimed as the operative ingredient, supported only by monitoring diagnostics, no controlled comparison reported). Key Results: Apodex-1.0-H reports: BrowseComp 90.3 (GPT-5.5-pro 90.1, Kimi-K2.6 86.3), BrowseComp-ZH 84.1, DeepSearchQA 94.4 (Claude-Opus-4.8 93.1), text-only HLE 60.8, FrontierScience-Research 46.7 (next best 38.3), FrontierScience-Olympiad 87.4 (GPT-5.2 75.0), SuperChem 74.2 (Gemini-3.0-Pro 63.2). Standalone Apodex-1.0 scores 75.5 on BrowseComp and 49.0 on HLE-text. Coding: SWE-bench Verified 79.0 and Terminal-Bench v2 58.4 in heavy-duty mode at 397B-A17B; notably Apodex-1.0-mini (35B-A3B) in heavy-duty mode beats Apodex-1.0 without verifier on LiveCodeBench v6 (77.8+ heavy-duty vs 82.0 single-sample — the claim is heavy-duty mini surpasses verifier-less large). IMO-ProofBench: GVR lifts 12.38 → 34.29 on Advanced and 49.05 → 80.48 on Basic. Open-weights small models: Apodex-1.0-4B-SFT scores 48.8 BrowseComp / 63.5 BrowseComp-ZH, beating open 30B-class models (Tongyi-DeepResearch 43.4, RedSearcher-30B 42.1). On the authors' internal Hard Deep Research benchmark (41 self-authored queries), Apodex-1.0-H averages 63.6 vs 44.0 for Claude-Opus-4.7. Baselines are current frontier systems, but scores are quoted from those vendors' own reports; heavy-duty results use 16 rollouts/query (BrowseComp, HLE) or 8 (others), and the internal benchmark comparison runs baselines in their 'deep research' product modes. Scale: production deployment claims up to 150 sub-agents and 15,000+ steps per task. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Apodex-1.0-H agent-team-plus-global-verifier deployment) + NEW METHOD (verification trained into model weights rather than scaffolded; evidence-graph global verification per Argus; domain-specific verifier primitives) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (4B SFT-only model beating 30B-class open deep-research models; selection quality dominating model scale on coding benchmarks). The individual ingredients — asynchronous orchestration, shared blackboards, multi-agent debate, CoVe-style verification, SFT+DPO+RL pipelines, IcePop/DAPO-style ratio masking, ROLL-style async RL infrastructure — are each established; the genuinely novel element is the claim that team-coordination and external-verification behavior is learned in-weights, enabling verification to compose hierarchically (team → heavy-duty) with unchanged weights, though the paper does not ablate trained-in vs. prompted coordination to substantiate this differentiator. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the within-family progression (mini → 1.0 → 1.0-H) cleanly isolates the heavy-duty contribution (+14.8 on BrowseComp, +18.4 on FrontierScience-Research, +26.7 on IMO-ProofBench overall), and capability-preservation is checked against matched-size Qwen3.5 bases across 11 benchmarks. However: no error bars, seed counts, or significance tests are given (only 'average performance' over agent randomness); competitor numbers are self-reported by other vendors under potentially different harnesses, judges, and tool access; the HLE comparison is confounded (Apodex on text-only subset, several baselines on the full multimodal set); BrowseComp uses Claude-Opus-4.6 as judge; the headline internal benchmark (Hard Deep Research, 41 queries) is small, self-authored, and evaluated only against baselines the authors configured. The differentiating claim — trained-in vs. scaffolded team behavior — is never tested against a strong prompting-only harness on the same base model. Code and weights are released for Apodex-1.0-mini and 0.8B/2B/4B variants (HuggingFace collection 'apodex/apodex-1', GitHub ApodexAI); the 397B model, training data, and AgentOS source availability are not clearly stated. This is a vendor technical report (self-published, with product/API links), not peer-reviewed — treat headline numbers with appropriate discount. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a trained model plus a deployed runtime, evaluated on benchmarks). - Practical: The open 0.8B–35B variants run on accessible hardware, but the flagship Apodex-1.0-H requires a 397B-A17B MoE served with 256K contexts across up to 150 concurrent sub-agents — effectively datacenter-only. - Efficient: Heavy-duty mode multiplies inference cost by 8–16× per query in rollouts alone (plus sub-agent fan-out), and the paper reports no tokens, latency, or dollar cost, so efficiency relative to a single frontier-model call cannot be assessed. - Effective: Benchmark evidence for research and proof tasks is strong and internally consistent, but effectiveness is measured against deterministic-answer proxies; report quality, citation fidelity, and real-user value are not evaluated. - Scalable: Agent-level scaling is the paper's thesis and is claimed up to 150 sub-agents/15K steps, but no scaling curve (performance vs. number of teams/agents), no cost curve, and no failure-mode analysis at fan-out limits are provided — the 10–100× claim is architecturally motivated, not experimentally mapped. Deliverables: open model weights (mini + three small SFT variants), an online service and API, and a described runtime (AgentOS) — the paper artifact itself stops at report form for the flagship model. Strengths: - The heaviest-duty claims are backed by clean within-system ablations: the same trained model is measured with and without heavy-duty mode across four domains, so the test-time-verification contribution is separated from the training contribution. - The external-verification argument is intellectually sharp: the paper correctly identifies that parallel paths sharing one context inherit the reasoner's systematic errors, and the conflict-reviewer/fact-checker/draft-reviewer decomposition maps each verifier role to a distinct failure mode rather than generic 'critique' prompting. - The GVR math recipe's grader-blindness constraint (no reference solution, no rubric in the grader prompt) is an unusually honest design choice that makes the +26.7 IMO-ProofBench gain harder to dismiss as oracle leakage. - The RL infrastructure section contains real engineering substance — per-token weight-version provenance enabling a bypass-mode importance ratio (5–15% step-time savings) with IcePop masking for MoE stability under mixed-version rollouts — that is concretely reusable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that HLE comparisons are not apples-to-apples (text-only subset for Apodex/DeepSeek vs. full multimodal set for others), that BrowseComp uses an LLM judge, that they block benchmark-hosting websites to reduce contamination, and that Apodex-1.0's 397B IMO-ProofBench heavy-duty numbers were 'still in flight' at writing. They also note heavy-duty mode is reserved for the hardest workloads (implicitly conceding cost). These disclosures are direct and specific — a credibility positive — but the report does not confront the absence of statistical uncertainty quantification, the self-reported nature of all competitor baselines, or the unquantified compute cost of heavy-duty mode. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central differentiation claim — that team behavior is trained in-weights rather than scaffolded — is never tested: no experiment runs the same Qwen3.5 base under a prompted orchestration harness to show the trained model is necessary rather than merely sufficient. The related-work section frames this as the key departure, yet the evaluation cannot distinguish it from a well-engineered framework around a good base model. - All competitor scores are quoted from vendors' technical reports under unknown harness, tool, and judge conditions; given that heavy-duty mode itself is a large test-time-compute multiplier, several 'SOTA' margins (e.g., BrowseComp 90.3 vs 90.1) may be attributable to compute-per-query rather than method, and no compute-matched baseline (e.g., GPT-5.5-pro with 16 samples + selection) is reported. - The internal Hard Deep Research benchmark is 41 hand-authored queries scored by the authors' own rubrics and hard-negative penalties — a favorable venue where the authors' rubric design (which rewards exactly the restraint behavior their verification pipeline produces) could itself shape the ranking; case studies confirm the rubric punishes the baselines' enumeration style. - No ablation of the deep-research data pipeline (random-walk synthesis vs. generic tool-use traces) or of the DPO stage's marginal contribution over SFT+RL; the three-stage recipe's component attribution is asserted, not measured. - The 150-sub-agent/15K-step deployment figures come with no latency, token, or cost accounting, and no analysis of how verification quality degrades (or fan-out saturates) as team count grows. Bottom Line: A practitioner building deep-research or coding agents will genuinely profit from the system design patterns (external verification roles, evidence-graph global verification, GVR, the async MoE RL stack) and from the open small-model weights, but should discount every cross-model leaderboard claim heavily: the comparison methodology — self-reported baselines, unmatched compute, self-authored benchmark, no error bars — cannot support the 'new state of the art' framing, and the in-weights-vs-scaffold question the paper stakes its novelty on remains unanswered.

HyQuant: Hybrid-Precision Quantization for LLM Attention

J Ding, B Xing, Y Zhang, D Ding, X Yi, X Ouyang… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HyQuant, a hybrid-precision quantization framework that keeps a small set of vertical-line tokens (top-5% by accumulated column attention mass) plus a 128-token local sliding window in full precision while quantizing all remaining KV states to 4 bits, for both Prefill attention and Decode KV-cache. - Why it's important: Long chain-of-thought inference makes decoding memory-bandwidth-bound over large KV caches, and uniform 4-bit KV quantization causes accuracy drops (e.g., KIVI K4V4 falls 6.91 LongBench points below full precision on Qwen3-8B), so any method that holds near-full accuracy at 4-bit cost directly reduces serving cost. - How it does it: It accumulates column-wise attention scores from a small query buffer to identify persistently-attended key positions online, fuses a full-precision path for those tokens and the recent window with a low-bit path for everything else into a single FlashAttention-style online-softmax kernel, and in Decode fuses dequantization into the attention kernel instead of dequantize-then-attend. - The good: Across four models (Qwen3-8B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B, GLM-4-9B) it stays within ~1 point of the FlashAttention-2 full-precision average on LongBench v1 (e.g., 45.04 vs 44.59 on Qwen3-8B) while beating 4-bit baselines, and decode-kernel latency drops from 6.354 to 1.775 ms/token at 32K prefix (3.58x). - The missing: The throughput-vs-batch-size experiment (Table 6) contradicts the text — it shows HyQuant slower than FA2 at batch 4 (84.2 vs 122.2 tok/s) and OOM at batch 32 — and no prefill speedup is demonstrated, only MSE reduction; error bars and multiple seeds are absent throughout. - Read it or not: Worth reading for systems/quantization engineers building long-context inference kernels who want a concrete fused mixed-precision design, but skippable if you already know MInference's vertical-line patterns and KVTuner's mixed-precision KV caching, since HyQuant is largely their recombination at token granularity.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (method plus Triton kernels run on hardware). Novelty (62) is moderate: token-granularity precision allocation and the fused prefill+decode operator are useful engineering, but the conceptual ground is largely MInference's vertical-line pattern recombined with KVTuner-style mixed precision, which the authors themselves acknowledge. Completeness (55) and Resilience (52) pull the composite down: the Table 6 batch-throughput experiment directly contradicts the text's multi-batch claim, KIVI/KVTuner baselines run on self-implemented kernels with suspiciously poor relative numbers, no eviction/sparsification baseline is tested despite the motivating critique, and the frozen vertical-line set is never stress-tested against the non-stationarity the paper itself argues for. Impact (68) is the strongest dimension thanks to the released kernel code and the only tested method faster than FA2 end-to-end. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*52 + 0.10*68 = 58.

Problem & Motivation: Long-context, CoT-heavy LLM inference stresses Prefill (compute-bound attention GEMMs) and Decode (bandwidth-bound repeated KV reads). Uniform low-bit quantization degrades quality because attention mass is highly concentrated: the authors measure that the global top-1% key positions cover 58.83% (Llama-3.1-8B) and 47.30% (Qwen3-8B) of attention mass, rising above 80% when combined with a W=128 local window. Quantization error at these high-score positions is amplified because many queries repeatedly access the same perturbed K/V states; they show that on Qwen3-8B Layer 28, keeping just top-1%/top-5% positions at full precision with the rest at 4-bit brings the attention-output MSE down near the uniform 8-bit level across 1K–32K contexts. The gap they target: existing eviction/sparsification (H2O, SnapKV, MInference) and KV-quantization methods (KIVI, KVTuner, KVQuant) treat tokens as homogeneous or apply mixed precision only at layer level, not token level, and none jointly optimize Prefill and Decode. Key Idea: Reuse the known vertical-line attention pattern (from MInference/attention-sink literature) not as a sparsity mask but as a precision-allocation signal: compute a cheap running column-mass score S(k) = sum of attention probabilities over recent queries, select the top-rho non-window keys as vertical-line positions, and keep those plus a fixed sliding window in FP16/BF16 while everything else runs/stores at 4-bit. The non-obvious move is retaining the quantized long tail (rather than dropping it as sparse attention does), which the paper shows recovers +13.39 average F1/ROUGE-L over a MInference-vertical-only variant on a 100-case subset. Methodology: Three components. (1) Vertical-line awareness: maintain at most 64 buffered FP16 query vectors, compute S = Q_avg K_pre^T (GQA-native, no materialized KV-head expansion) every 64 tokens, top-k selection over the non-window prefix; the vertical-line set is frozen once at the Prefill-to-Decode boundary (Algorithm 4) rather than recomputed per decode step. (2) Prefill: a segmented FlashAttention-style operator scans quantized-prefix tiles (per-tile INT8/FP8/INT4/FP4 scales, c_B = 127 or 448), then full-precision vertical-line tiles, then the causally-masked window tiles, merging all through a single online-softmax state; KV are reordered so vertical-line keys sit near the window. (3) Decode: hybrid KV cache (quantized prefix + FP vertical-line set + staging buffer of new tokens + FP window), with dequantization fused inside the decode kernel's online-softmax pass so no full-precision cache is materialized; split-K chunks reduce via softmax-state merging. Critical design decisions: freezing the vertical-line set at prefill-to-decode (avoids per-step importance recomputation but assumes importance is stationary during generation — an assumption the paper does not stress-test against its own critique of eviction methods); using a tail-query proxy for column scoring (cheap, but only ~64 recent queries vote on global importance); per-tile rather than per-channel quantization for the prefix. Justification is largely empirical (MSE ablations) rather than analytical. Key Results: Accuracy: on LongBench v1 (11 tasks), Qwen3-8B thinking-mode HyQuant K4V4+top-5% averages 45.04 vs FA2 44.59, KIVI 37.68, SageAttention 38.13, KVTuner 40.45; on Llama-3.1-8B 46.73 vs FA2 46.63; on GLM-4-9B 45.78 vs 44.83; on Qwen3-32B 48.46 vs FA2 48.61 (slightly below). GSM8K/MATH500 on Qwen3-8B: 96.52/78.73 vs FA2 95.88/80.14. Short-context (C-Eval/MMLU/GSM8K avg): 87.82 vs FA2 88.89. Efficiency: decode-kernel speedup over FA2 grows from 1.32x at 1K to 3.58x at 32,768 prefix (0.224→1.775 ms/token FA2 vs 0.170→1.775 HyQuant); end-to-end decode speedup 1.04x–1.17x (KIVI 0.69–0.72x, KVTuner 0.72–0.80x relative to FA2). Prefill: no latency speedup claimed ("comparable to SageAttention"); instead layer-wise MSE reduction factors over SageAttention are reported. Vertical-line identification overhead is 3–5% of runtime; memory overhead vs strict K4V4 is ~17.4% (32K) to ~24.4% (8K prefix). Baselines are current and representative (FA2, KIVI, KVTuner from ICML 2024/2025, SageAttention ICLR 2025), though KIVI/KVTuner kernels are the authors' own implementations. Scale: prefix up to 32K for latency, up to 128K prefill config, batch 1–32 on a single H100-80GB; batch-32 OOMs for all methods including HyQuant. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component). Genuinely novel: token-granularity (not layer-granularity) precision allocation driven by accumulated column-attention mass, and a single fused operator covering both Prefill attention and Decode KV-cache with dequantize-in-attention execution — prior work used vertical lines as sparsity masks (MInference) or sensitivity-aware mixed precision per layer (KVTuner), and prior systems covered only one stage. The vertical-line observation itself, the sliding-window retention, the 4-bit quantization scheme, and the online-softmax fusion pattern are all standard components recombined; the authors are transparent about this in Section 3.3. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and meaningful: top-k ratio sweep (2%–10%, Table 11, though non-monotonic — 6% scores 50.76 vs 10% at 51.91 on a 7-task subset), window size sweep (64/128/256), component-level MSE ablation isolating window vs vertical-line retention, and a MInference-vertical-only ablation quantifying the value of the quantized long tail. No error bars, no multiple seeds, no significance tests; per-task LongBench swings of ±8 points between methods on single tasks (e.g., HotpotQA 44.44–62.65 across top-k values) suggest high variance that is never quantified. Code is released at https://github.com/jerrysfls/HyQuant. Methodological concerns: (i) KIVI and KVTuner baselines run on the authors' own implementations, creating potential for unfavorable baseline kernels (the claimed 0.72x/0.78x end-to-end slowdowns of KIVI/KVTuner relative to FA2 are suspiciously poor versus published numbers); (ii) the prefill contribution is measured only as MSE against SageAttention, not end-task accuracy at matched latency; (iii) some benchmark results where HyQuant exceeds FA2 (GSM8K 96.52 vs 95.88) are correctly attributed by the authors to evaluation variance. Deployability: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile (a method plus Triton kernels actually run on hardware). - Practical: Runs on a single NVIDIA H100-80GB with released Triton code and standard open-weight models (8B–32B), so yes for commodity datacenter hardware. - Efficient: 3–5% runtime overhead from vertical-line identification and ~17–24% extra KV memory versus strict K4V4, but it is the only tested method faster than FA2 end-to-end (1.04–1.17x), whereas KIVI/KVTuner as implemented are slower than FA2. - Effective: Evidence supports near-lossless accuracy at 4-bit on LongBench/GSM8K/MATH500 up to 32K contexts, but Prefill efficiency is unproven (MSE-only) and the accuracy claim rests on benchmark averages without variance estimates. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 32K decode prefix, 128K prefill config, and 32B parameters; batch 32 OOMs on an 80GB H100 for all methods including HyQuant, and the text's claim that "HyQuant is the only method that operates in batch size 32" contradicts its own Table 6 — multi-batch serving at realistic scale remains unvalidated. The work delivers a software artifact: a released GitHub repository with fused kernels (stated, not independently verified here). Strengths: (1) The reframing of vertical-line structure from a sparsity signal into a precision-allocation signal is a genuinely useful conceptual move, and the Table 12 ablation directly quantifies why (sparse vertical-only loses 13.08 average points to FA2 vs HyQuant's +0.31). (2) End-to-end system integration across both Prefill and Decode with dequantize-in-attention fused kernels is real engineering beyond a paper quantization scheme, validated by 3.58x kernel-level speedup at 32K. (3) Honest error accounting: attention-output MSE at the o_proj input gives a sharper instrument than end-task scores alone, and the top-1%/top-5% error analysis cleanly motivates the design. (4) The overhead analysis (Table 14) itemizes memory costs per component rather than hiding them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: gains are mostly visible on long-context tasks with weaker benefit at short context (Appendix B.4); end-to-end speedups shrink at short context on H100 because decoding is not fully memory-bound; models beyond Qwen3-32B (e.g., 80B) were not evaluated due to GPU memory limits; and effectiveness in agent/coding settings is unknown. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. They also explicitly disclaim that HyQuant exceeding FA2 on some datasets is evaluation variance. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The Table 6 batch-throughput experiment is internally inconsistent with its own narrative: HyQuant is 31% slower than FA2 at batch 4 and OOMs at batch 32, yet the text claims HyQuant "is the only method that operates in batch size 32" — this discrepancy is unexplained and undermines the multi-batch claim. (2) No comparison against sparse/eviction baselines (H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV, MInference full) on accuracy, only against a hand-built MInference-vertical variant on 100 cases; the motivating critique of eviction methods is never tested head-to-head. (3) The vertical-line set is frozen from prefill tail queries, but the paper itself argues token importance is non-stationary in long CoT — no experiment measures how often decode-time attention drifts away from the frozen set, which is precisely the failure mode that would break the method. (4) Single-seed, no-variance reporting on LongBench where per-task differences of 1–3 points decide conclusions. (5) Prefill efficiency is asserted only via MSE parity with SageAttention; no prefill latency or end-to-end prefill-inclusive wall-clock numbers are given. (6) The paper cites model families "Gemma4-31B" and "Qwen3.5-4B" in Figure 1 and a 2026 citation (Zheng et al., Visual Intelligence) that postdate typical publication timelines; the provenance of these heatmaps and references cannot be verified from the text. Bottom Line: A practitioner building long-context inference serving should read it for the concrete fused mixed-precision kernel design and honest overhead accounting, but should independently verify the multi-batch and baseline claims given the internal Table 6 contradiction and self-implemented baselines; as an idea, MInference plus KVTuner covers most of the conceptual ground, and the durable contribution is the token-granularity fusion engineering.

H3-World: Turning Language Understanding into World Control (42 ▲ )

Danze Chen, Zeqing Wang, Ziyue Lin, Xingyi Yang, Yeying Jin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 2 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces H3-WORLD, a framework that converts the 33B MiniMax-H3 video generator into an interactive world model by expressing character and camera actions as per-latent-interval natural-language instructions, with only 0.199% of parameters trainable. - Why it's important: Building action-conditioned world models typically requires dedicated action modules and large action-video supervision; this work offers a cheap path that reuses the language interface a pretrained video generator already possesses. - How it does it: Each discrete control state is rendered into a compositional text prompt bound to one video latent interval via mirrored temporal positional encoding, and a deterministic single-egress attention mask restricts each action span so only its matched video latent can read it, with rank-32 LoRA learning the dynamics. - The good: A controlled intervention cleanly separates the mechanisms: frozen H3 with a global instruction fails temporal control (cumulative horizontal flow 0.0/-17.3 across a left-to-right pan switch), a zero-LoRA per-latent interface is unresponsive (-0.1/0.0), while H3-WORLD follows both directions (+52.7/-106.0). - The missing: Evaluation is dominated by qualitative figures on 128 held-out clips with a single hand-rolled optical-flow metric, one unseen action combination, and no comparison against published world-model baselines like Matrix-Game or GameGen-X. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building interactive world models on large video generators — the single-egress routing trick and the negative results on direct additive/FiLM conditioning are practically useful — but skippable if you need quantitatively benchmarked world models rather than a control-interface design pattern.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (50) and Impact (55) pull the composite down: the entire quantitative case rests on a single hand-rolled optical-flow metric on one diagnostic schedule, there are no comparisons against published world-model baselines (only author-constructed conditioning variants), the method is developed and evaluated on the same data source, and the model requires a 33B datacenter-class backbone. Novelty (60) is moderate — single-egress routing is a genuine methodological idea, but the remainder is standard adaptation — while Completeness (65) is a strength thanks to direct, non-minimizing limitation acknowledgment, and Non-Obviousness (65) benefits from the useful negative results on additive/FiLM conditioning. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*50 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*55 = 58.

Problem & Motivation: Interactive world models must generate visual futures that respond to user actions, but pretrained video generators do not expose a precise action interface. Existing systems (Genie, GameGen-X, Matrix-Game lineage, Diffusion Game Engines) learn control through discrete action embeddings, feature modulation, camera geometry, or dedicated conditioning modules, which require extra supervision, add parameters, and risk disturbing pretrained capabilities. The authors observe that MiniMax-H3 already exhibits coarse zero-shot control of character behavior and camera motion from plain text, and ask whether this latent capability can be sharpened into temporally precise world control without building a new control pathway. The target users are researchers and practitioners building playable, action-responsive video world simulators. Key Idea: The core insight is that temporal precision, not a new representation, is what separates coarse language control from world control: represent each action as a compositional text prompt (character clause + camera clause), bind it to its video latent interval via mirrored temporal positional offsets within MiniMax-H3's packed single-stream self-attention, and enforce that binding with a deterministic single-egress attention mask so each action span has exactly one entry point into the video stream while video latents retain full bidirectional attention for continuity. Everything else (the backbone, encoder, VAE) stays frozen; LoRA learns only the action-conditioned dynamics along the permitted routes. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Semantic action interface: discrete control states (eight character/camera keys plus a binary speed flag) are aggregated per VAE latent interval into a state, opposing keys are cancelled, and each state is rendered as a concatenated clause like "the man walks backward and strafes left, camera pans right slowly," yielding a 9×16 character-camera space (135 structurally valid pairs). Each prompt is encoded by the shared H3 encoder plus a two-layer token refiner with block-diagonal attention. (2) Latent-aligned temporal binding: static semantic tokens, action spans, first-frame condition, and noised target latents are packed into one sequence (X = [S; A1..AK; C0; V1..VK; P]), with each action span placed at τ(Vk) − Δ to preserve text-before-video ordering. (3) Single-egress routing + LoRA: when an action span is a key, only its matched video latent (and its own tokens) may read it; as a query it sees static context, the first-frame condition, audio tokens, and its matched latent. Rank-32 LoRA is applied to QKV/output projections and the token refiner; training uses the native H3 denoising objective on 7,872 gameplay clips (124 frames, 832×480, 37 latent-aligned prompts per clip) for 10,000 steps at lr 1e-4. Critical design decisions: grounding actions in the pretrained text pathway rather than learned embeddings (justified by the ablation showing direct additive/FiLM conditioning produces weak, inconsistent responses); single-egress rather than full masking (justified by preserving video-to-video information flow); and LoRA-only adaptation (justified by preserved visual generalization to six out-of-distribution scenes). Key Results: The headline evidence is the controlled camera-switch diagnostic: for a scheduled sharp left pan for 15 latents then sharp right pan, H3-WORLD yields cumulative horizontal flow of +52.7 (before) and -106.0 (after), reversing correctly with instruction order (-58.7/+121.0), versus a frozen-H3 global prompt (0.0/-17.3; -11.9/+24.1 reversed) and a zero-LoRA per-latent interface (-0.1/0.0). With a constant action, H3-WORLD matches global prompting (300.5 vs 301.8), showing adaptation adds temporal binding, not raw motion capability. Qualitatively, on 128 held-out clips the model reproduces recorded character displacement and viewpoint changes; controlled interventions (fixed seed and first frame, only action varied) show distinct strafing, panning, and fast-vs-slow camera responses. Generalization is shown for one unseen action pair (of 52 valid unseen combinations) and six visually distinct initial observations. Testing scale is modest and standard for LoRA adaptation — roughly 8k clips of a single data source — and every quantitative number in the paper comes from one Farneback optical-flow diagnostic; the baselines compared are the authors' own ablations, not published world-model systems. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus a partial NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is single-egress temporal attention routing — restricting per-latent text action spans to a unique direct egress into the video stream within a packed single-stream (no separate cross-attention) bidirectional diffusion backbone. The remainder is a competent combination of known ideas: language-as-action is established (the authors themselves identify Incantation as closely related, differing mainly because Incantation uses local cross-attention rather than packed self-attention), per-latent prompts, LoRA, and mirrored positional alignment are all standard. The empirical finding — that a large video generator's emergent language control can be sharpened into temporally precise world control with 0.199% trainable parameters — is the paper's real contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the three-way comparison (global prompt / zero-LoRA per-latent interface / full H3-WORLD) and the direct additive-bias vs FiLM vs text-interface comparison isolate which components matter. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; the quantitative evidence reduces to a single flow metric on one diagnostic schedule. Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative figures, and the compositional generalization claim rests on one unseen action pair of 52 possible. Code (github.com/Danzer1xxxxChan/H3-World) and model weights (huggingface.co/DANNY621/H3-World) are publicly released, which aids reproduction. Methodological concerns: the method is developed and evaluated on the same ABot-World-Explorer-500h-derived data, the held-out set is only 128 clips from one game distribution, and no external strong baseline (Matrix-Game 2.0/3.0, GameGen-X, Oasis) is run — only author-constructed conditioning variants, which weakens any claim of superiority over existing action interfaces. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — a released, adapted model). Practical: It runs on the open-weight 33B MiniMax-H3, so it requires datacenter-class GPU memory for the backbone, though LoRA training itself is lightweight. Efficient: Extremely cheap to adapt — 10,000 LoRA steps on 7,872 clips, 0.199% trainable parameters — versus training action modules or fine-tuning backbones, but inference inherits H3's cost (50 denoising steps for 124 frames; no real-time claim). Effective: The evidence shows temporally precise short-horizon character/camera control on held-out and intervened cases; the paper does not demonstrate persistent world state, long-horizon consistency, or any downstream use such as planning or policy learning. Scalable: Not tested — long-horizon rollout, streaming, and broader action vocabularies are explicitly future work; the paper claims no 10× scale results. Deliverable: a software artifact (adapted checkpoint, code, project page), not just a paper. Strengths: - The zero-LoRA / frozen-H3 / full-model decomposition is a genuinely well-designed ablation that cleanly attributes the gain to the interaction of temporal binding with learned adaptation, ruling out the trivial explanation that per-latent prompts alone suffice. - The single-egress routing mask is a simple, parameter-free architectural idea well matched to packed single-stream diffusion transformers, where an unstructured mask would either leak control or fragment video-video attention. - The honest characterization of the training action distribution (83 of 135 valid pairs seen; top-40 pairs cover 95.4% of prompts) turns sparsity into a controlled compositional-generalization test bed. - The finding that direct additive-bias and FiLM action conditioning underperform text grounding in this backbone is a practically useful negative result for anyone building on similar architectures. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) the work covers only short-horizon generation, with compositional generalization and visual transfer evaluated through representative examples rather than systematic evaluation across action combinations, scenes, and seeds; and (2) the model generates fixed-length segments with no persistent world state, real-time interaction, planning, or policy learning. This is a direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment that correctly identifies the two biggest weaknesses — the small qualitative evidence base and the gap between "world control" and a deployable interactive world model. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline "effective control" claim is supported by one scalar flow metric on one diagnostic schedule plus figures; no per-action success rates, no human evaluation, no distributional statistics over the 128 held-out clips. - Only one of 52 unseen action combinations is evaluated, so the compositional-generalization claim is anecdotal; failure modes on unseen pairs are never shown. - No comparison against any published interactive world model at matched data or scale — the reader cannot tell whether H3-WORLD is better, worse, or merely different from Matrix-Game or GameGen-X-style systems. - The temporal binding is measured only via horizontal optical flow, which conflates camera pan with lateral object motion and cannot detect control leakage, timing jitter, or drift within an interval; a latency/timing-accuracy metric is absent. - The coarse zero-shot control of vanilla H3 (Figure 2) is claimed as central motivation but never quantified, so the reader cannot measure how much of the final capability was already latent versus learned from 8k clips. - The speed flag is derived from estimated yaw rate at training time and user-specified at inference — a distribution mismatch that is not discussed or ablated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building interactive world models on large video generators gains a concrete, well-motivated design pattern (per-latent text actions with single-egress routing in packed self-attention) and useful negative results on direct conditioning, but should look to systems like the Matrix-Game line for quantitatively benchmarked, real-time interactive world modeling — this paper is a strong proof-of-concept, not a benchmarked solution.

UI-Venus-2 Technical Report

V Team, Z Cai, H Chen, J Chen, W Chen, C Gao, Z Gu… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces UI-Venus-2, a pair of open-source (9B and 27B dense) GUI agents that operate mobile, web, and desktop environments in a unified closed-loop reasoning–action framework, trained through multimodal mid-training, domain-specific offline RL, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation with structured action-aware supervision. - Why it's important: Real-world digital automation needs agents that work beyond a handful of benchmark apps — across multilingual mobile ecosystems, live websites, and full desktop OSes — with trustworthy RL reward signals and safety control over consequential actions; skip it if you want controlled evidence that each proposed technique (vs. scale and data volume) drives the gains.

Problem & Motivation GUI agents that automate digital tasks remain benchmark-oriented rather than deployment-ready. The paper identifies three coupled gaps: (1) environment coverage is narrow — most agents train and evaluate on a small set of apps, failing on multilingual mobile ecosystems, dynamic live websites, and full desktop operating systems; (2) task construction at scale is brittle — generated queries must be grounded in actual application functionality and remain executable under changing interface states; (3) RL reward quality is unreliable — coarse success/failure verifiers conflate partial progress with completion, miss task-critical visual evidence, and are exploitable by the policy. Users are practitioners and product teams (Ant Group's Venus team) who need a general-purpose agent that can pass verification gates (CAPTCHAs) during login flows, operate safely, and run across mobile, web, and OS in one model rather than three specialists. Key Idea The core move is joint scaling of environments, task generation, and verification as one feedback system, plus a GUI-specific fix to on-policy distillation: because the structured action (type + parameters) is the only part of a response that changes the environment, the distillation signal is conditioned on the student's action correctness — suppressed for correct actions, concentrated on parameters when the type is right, and masked at parameters (emphasizing type tokens) when the type is wrong — while the teacher scores student samples with a privileged hint about the correct action type that the student never sees, so inference behavior is unchanged. The rest of the recipe (catalog-driven task synthesis, VLM-judge verification with visual keypoints and voting, CAPTCHA data as a verifiable dense-supervision source) is competent integration of known ideas around this core. Methodology The pipeline has three training stages and a data/verification engine. Stage I: multimodal mid-training (large-scale SFT) on a heterogeneous mixture dominated by Mobile/Web/OS navigation trajectories, validated by human–discriminator collaborative filtering. Stage II: offline RL with step-level trajectories per domain (Grounding, CAPTCHA, Mobile, Web, Computer); CAPTCHA and grounding data come from programmatic synthesis (70 CAPTCHA type rule engines with latent solvable state; synthetic HTML/CSS/JS interfaces with nine-point hit tests for pixel-aligned targets). Stage III: Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), where domain-specialist teachers score trajectories sampled by the student; the distillation advantage (Eq. 1) is a stop-gradient token-level log-prob difference between hinted teacher and student, weighted by the structured action-aware scheme described above. Data generation is a closed loop: (1) capability catalogs built via deep research over documentation/forums and dynamically updated with runtime observations; (2) task construction as executable contracts (domain, capability tags, initial state, resources, expected outcome) with a validity gate; (3) trajectory collection with outcomes written back to the catalog to steer coverage-aware sampling. Web data uses a 4,000+ domain pool (Tranco + benchmark sites, Kimi-scored for quality) seeded with 45,000 InSTA-150k-v3 tasks, executed via a 15-action Playwright interface with step-level sanitization. Desktop tasks are serialized as TaskSpecs with snapshot provisioning, fixture fingerprints against answer leakage, preflight checks, and hierarchical subgoal segmentation for long-horizon tasks. Verification is two-level: trace-level Semantic Guided Verification (SGV) extracts verifiable keypoints, windows the trajectory with red click markers overlaid, judges keypoints in parallel, routes ambiguous cases to a multimodal final judgment, and outputs completed/partial/infeasible/failed labels used for data stratification (not direct rewards); sample-level verification makes a priori per-step judgments (correct/exploratory/ineffective/incorrect) via reasoning–action consistency then task alignment, aggregating into a three-tier trajectory assessment that requires at least one task-specific operation to grant partial credit. Critical design decisions: (1) action-type-conditional masking in distillation — well-motivated by the type→parameter dependency, but no ablation is presented in this report; (2) teacher-side hint never shown to the student — clean design, inference-time cost is zero; (3) treating verification labels as data curation rather than direct RL rewards — a sensible hedge against reward hacking, but its effectiveness is asserted rather than measured. Key Results Tested at standard benchmark scale with two open dense models (9B, 27B) against current general VLMs (Claude-Opus-4.x, Kimi-K2.6/K3, Seed-2.0/2.1-Pro, GPT-5.x variants, Qwen3.5/3.6) and GUI-specific models (UI-Venus-1.5, GUI-Owl-1.5, MAI-UI, Qwen-UI-Agent, Fara1.5, OpenCUA, UI-TARS-1.5). Mobile: AndroidWorld 84.0% (27B, best; prior best 77.6%), MobileGym 60.5% (best; prior best Seed-2.0-Pro 52.0%), VenusBench-Mobile 48.7% (best; Opus-4.6 36.5%), MobileWorld 76.1% at 50 steps (second to Qwen-UI-Agent-27B at 82.1%), KnowUBench 59.7% (best; Seed-2.0-Pro 51.6%), MemGUI 70.3% (best). Computer: OSWorld-Verified 80.5% (second to Claude-Opus-4.8's source-reported 83.4%), DeskCraft 55.5% (best; Kimi-K2.6 41.4%), but OSWorld 2.0 binary accuracy only 2.8% vs. GPT-5.5's 13.0% (partial score 13.2%, below Claude-Opus-4.7's 20.3%). Web: WebVoyager 93.4% (best, +4.1 over Fara1.5-27B), Online-Mind2Web 78.3% (best), REAL 80.2% (best, +5.8), Odysseys 80.4 avg rubric (best, +11.5). Grounding: VenusBench-GD 80.1% (best), ScreenSpot-Pro 74.1% (second to Qwen-UI-Agent-27B 76.6%), OSWorld-G-R 79.1% (best), UI-Vision 66.9% (second). CAPTCHA: VenusBench-CAPTCHA 79.9% vs. 53.0% for Qwen3.6-27B (+26.9); NextGen-CAPTCHAs 54.5% vs. 20.4% for Seed-2.0-Pro; but Open CaptchaWorld is near parity at 56.3% vs. 55.6%. Safety: lowest attack success rates on OSHarm (11.3% for 9B vs. 18.0% best baseline) and OSBlind (47.9% for 27B vs. 79.4–93.6% for all baselines). Many baseline numbers (marked "*") are the authors' own reproductions; some DeskCraft/OSWorld comparisons use author-chosen aggregate splits and differing action scaffolds. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (structured action-aware distillation with teacher-side action-type hinting), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (VenusBench-CAPTCHA, 219 screenshots across 8 types with strict action-level scoring), and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (an open cross-platform GUI agent with a closed-loop data engine and two-level verification framework). The core distillation trick is a genuine, non-obvious adaptation; however, most of the system — SFT mid-training, offline RL, OPD, capability catalogs, VLM-as-judge verification, synthetic CAPTCHA generation — is a strong combination of established techniques scaled to mobile+web+desktop, and the report inherits its training recipe from UI-Venus-1.5. Rigor & Reproducibility No ablation tables appear in the provided text for the novel components — the introduction promises "detailed experimental results and ablations," but the report presents only benchmark comparisons, so the claim that structured action-aware distillation yields "significantly more robust fusion" is unsupported here. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; live-web results (WebVoyager, Odysseys) are inherently date-sensitive. Code (github.com/inclusionAI/UI-Venus), full-parameter model weights (HuggingFace inclusionAI/ui-venus), and evaluation infrastructure are publicly released, which is a major reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: roughly a third of baseline entries are author-reproduced ("*") rather than source-reported; VenusBench-Mobile, VenusBench-GD, and VenusBench-CAPTCHA come from the same team (self-benchmarking risk, though public benchmarks corroborate); OSWorld-Verified baselines use model-specific action scaffolds the authors themselves flag as not strictly controlled; DeskCraft is reported on an author-defined 538-task aggregate differing from the official split-level protocol; and OSWorld 2.0 baselines are copied from the official leaderboard with possibly different tool settings. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model system evaluated across benchmarks; no theoretical claims). - Practical: Yes — 9B and 27B dense open-weight models runnable on a single high-end GPU (the 27B dense model needs roughly 54GB in bf16, so multi-GPU or quantization for the larger variant), with grounding mode at temperature 0 for efficiency. - Efficient: The 9B variant retains most capability (within 1.8 points on CAPTCHA, 3–10 points on most agentic benchmarks), making it the cost-efficient deployment point; no throughput/latency numbers are reported. - Effective: Strong evidence on mobile, web, grounding, and CAPTCHA across independent third-party benchmarks; effectiveness on long-horizon desktop workflows is clearly not solved (2.8% binary accuracy on OSWorld 2.0), and OSBlind attack success remains ~48%, so the stated goal of dependable real-world autonomy is only partially met. - Scalable: Not tested — models top out at 27B, and the report offers no evidence on 10× data/model scale; the closed-loop data engine is claimed to improve over iterations but no iteration-over-time curves are shown. The work delivers a real software artifact: full-parameter open weights, action-space/prompt suite, and evaluation infrastructure. Strengths - The structured action-aware distillation scheme is a real technical insight: masking parameter supervision when the action type is wrong (because parameters are semantically meaningless under a wrong type) exploits the type→parameter dependency structure specific to GUI actions and is not a generic distillation heuristic. - Breadth with honesty: top results on 10+ external benchmarks plus candid reporting of failure on OSWorld 2.0 and a stated loss to Qwen-UI-Agent on MobileWorld builds credibility that pure win-rate tables lack. - The two-level verification framework separates data curation from reward assignment and distinguishes partial credit that requires task-specific operations from generic operations (launching, scrolling), a defensible design against reward hacking. - Full open release of weights and evaluation infrastructure at two scales enables reproduction and follow-up research at a level most GUI agent reports do not match. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors acknowledge: OSWorld-Verified comparisons are "a benchmark-level reference rather than a strictly controlled ablation" due to model-specific scaffolds (e.g., CLI actions for Qwen-UI-Agent); MobileWorld at 50 steps trails Qwen-UI-Agent-27B (76.1 vs. 82.1); AndroidWorld is near saturation; Open CaptchaWorld shows only near-parity with Seed-2.0-Pro, exposing "clear headroom" on heterogeneous CAPTCHA mechanisms; spatial reasoning CAPTCHAs remain below 50% for all models; and safety ASR on OSBlind, while halved, remains high (~48%). This is a credibility positive — the limitations are stated directly rather than buried, though the report does not confront the absence of ablations for its own proposed techniques. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No human-agreement study validating SGV or sample-level verification: the entire data engine's quality rests on VLM judges whose accuracy against ground truth is never quantified — a dogs-not-barking omission for a paper whose thesis is "verification is the bottleneck." - The multi-model voting verification highlighted in the introduction is never specified in the methodology section (which describes single-judge SGV pipelines), so a claimed contribution is undelivered in the text. - No ablation isolating the contribution of structured action-aware distillation or the teacher-side hint relative to vanilla OPD or simple model merging; the claimed "significantly more robust fusion" is anecdotal. - Dual-use risk is unaddressed: the paper trains and open-sources a model that solves CAPTCHAs (the very technology defending against bots), yet contains no discussion of misuse, guardrails, or responsible-release considerations — despite including a safety section on other attack surfaces. - Compute cost, training data volume (beyond the 45,000 seeded web tasks), and iteration counts for the closed-loop pipeline are absent, making cost-of-reproduction impossible to estimate. - CAPTCHA evaluation is single-turn; the multi-action parsing used at deployment is a different regime, and the 1.8-point 9B/27B gap may partly reflect prompt sensitivity rather than capability. Bottom Line For anyone building GUI agents, this is currently one of the most useful open references — a full-stack recipe, honest benchmark tables, and two usable model scales — but read it as an engineering report whose headline training innovations are asserted rather than ablated, and whose verification and safety claims outrun their evidence.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AERIS, an offline centralized-training/decentralized-execution framework for multi-UAV integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) control, with STAR-CRDT, an offline multi-agent RL algorithm that distills critic-vetted, support-constrained action corrections into a shared local Transformer actor. - Why it's important: Online RL for UAV fleets requires exploratory flights that can degrade sensing, disrupt users, or create collision risk before the policy converges, and repeated non-convex trajectory/beamforming optimization is too slow for real-time distributed control; learning purely from a frozen flight log removes that deployment risk. - How it does it: A shared Decision-Transformer-style actor executes from local histories, while a centralized implicit-Q critic scores candidate action corrections near the actor and behavior actions; a trust gate admits a correction only when its predicted joint-action gain is large and its distance from logged support is small, and the approved teacher is distilled into the actor. - The good: The evaluation is unusually broad for this venue class: +29.3% return over the strongest offline baseline (TD3+BC), +69.1% sensing margin, −54.2% collision-risk events under random mobility, first place at all fleet scales (3–6 UAVs), and best return in all 6 scene-scale settings on unseen OpenStreetMap road networks with zero road-specific tuning. - The missing: Everything is simulation-only — the "flight log" is rollouts from a TD3 controller in the authors' own simulator, not real or even high-fidelity flight data, and no seeds/error bars or significance tests are reported for the headline comparisons. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on offline MARL for wireless/UAV control or need a template for converting centralized critic feedback into safe decentralized policies; skip it if you need hardware-validated ISAC results or a general offline RL contribution beyond a domain-specific assembly of known ideas.
