Problem & Motivation: Multi-UAV ISAC in 6G requires UAVs to jointly control trajectories and beamformers so that moving communication users get high sum rate, moving sensing targets stay above beampattern thresholds, and UAVs keep a 30 m safety separation — a long-horizon stochastic, non-convex control problem. Classical model-based methods need repeated global non-convex solves per slot, which is impractical for fast distributed response; online RL needs trial rollouts that are physically risky (sensing loss, collision events); and existing offline RL/MARL methods ported to this setting face a dilemma the paper diagnoses empirically: imitation-style methods stay near the log but inherit residual ISAC violations, while aggressive actor rectification (e.g., OMAR-style) leaves the logged joint-action support and amplifies critic error. The paper motivates this with two diagnostics: TD3 checkpoints during online training trigger collision events, and a k-NN support test shows offline baselines trade ISAC violation cost against joint-action OOD ratio (OMAR at 6.25 violation cost vs. ~2.2–3.0 for conservative methods). Key Idea: Use the centralized critic not as an optimization target to maximize (which invites overestimated out-of-support actions) but as a trust-gated teacher: search a small candidate set of local corrections within a bounded radius of the actor and behavior actions, accept the critic-best candidate only if it beats the anchor, then blend it into a teacher via a trust coefficient that decays with the correction's distance from support, and distill that teacher into the local sequence actor. This is essentially support-restrained, critic-ranked one-step rectification on top of IQL-style advantage-weighted behavior cloning inside a CTDE Decision Transformer. Methodology: AERIS transforms the trajectory-and-beamforming program P0 (maximize λc·Ucomm + λs·Usen subject to sensing thresholds, power budgets, and inter-UAV distance ≥ dmin) into a CTDE offline MARL problem P1 with reward rt = λr·Ucomm + λp·Ppass + λm·Msen − ζ·Nvio − ccol·Ncol, converting hard constraints into penalties (a standard move). Pipeline: (1) a TD3 behavior controller collects a frozen log of 1000 episodes / 200k transitions using only local per-UAV information; (2) a shared return-conditioned causal Transformer actor (6 layers, 8 heads, hidden 256, context 50 slots) is trained on local histories; (3) twin centralized critics Q(s,a) and an expectile value network Vψ(s) (IQL-style, κ=0.8) are fit on global logged states; (4) support-aware rectification builds candidate sets U_i(s) from clipped Gaussian perturbations around actor and behavior actions (Nr=4 each, σπ=0.18, σβ=0.06), scores each candidate in two joint-action contexts, and picks the critic-max candidate; (5) a trust gate τi (max ~0.35–0.45) scales the correction based on critic gain and L2 distance to anchor, producing a teacher that is distilled via an auxiliary loss, with an actor-side Q-regularizer (λQ=0.18). Critical design decisions: local-only actor observation (justified by the deployment requirement of no real-time global exchange), candidate search restricted near support (justified by the OOD diagnostic in Fig. 1b), and IQL-style expectile baseline (justified by known offline overestimation failure). The theoretical result (Theorem 1) shows the post-update actor's expected critic value exceeds the anchor's minus LQ·ε, provided the critic ranks candidates correctly (Assumption 1), the critic slice is locally concave (Assumption 2), distillation error is bounded (Assumption 3), and the critic is locally Lipschitz (Assumption 4) — a modest, honest claim confined to the offline-support distribution, but Assumption 1 (correct critic ranking) does most of the work and is not verifiable in practice. Key Results: All results are from the authors' simulator (500×500 m area, T=200 slots, 4-antenna arrays, 20 dBm). Random mobility, M=3/K=6/L=3: STAR-CRDT improves return by 29.3% over TD3+BC (the strongest non-STAR baseline), communication sum rate by 3.4%, sensing pass rate by 4.8%, sensing margin by 69.1%, and reduces collision-risk events by 54.2%. Baselines: BC, DT, TD3+BC, CRR, OMIGA, OMAR (current, representative offline RL/MARL methods), plus CRDT (the authors' ablation without trust-gated rectification) and online TD3 as the behavior reference — these are appropriate and current for offline MARL, but notably no model-based trajectory/beamforming optimizer is evaluated as a baseline despite being the motivating alternative. Scale study: zero-shot transfer of the shared actor to M=4, 5, 6 UAVs; at M=6, +39.3% return over TD3+BC and +60.8% over CRR, ranking first at every scale. Zero-shot OSM road deployment (three Hong Kong scenes: dense grid 72.6 km/km², arterial 15.5 km/km², sparse 9.8 km/km²): best return in all six scene-scale settings; best in 24 of 30 metric rows, top-two in 29; at M=6, +36.7% (dense) and +132.1% (sparse) return over the strongest baseline. Ablation: CRDT vs. STAR-CRDT shows trust-gated rectification reduces ISAC violation cost (2.19 vs. 2.97) at a controlled OOD ratio (0.066 vs. 0.020), and CRDT trails the full method on return — the components matter. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (STAR-CRDT's trust-gated, support-aware actor rectification for offline MARL) applied to a NEW SETTING (fixed-log multi-UAV ISAC control), plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (offline baselines exhibit a measurable imitation-vs-OOD violation dilemma in this domain). The ingredients are all standard: Decision Transformer, IQL expectile values, twin critics, CTDE, behavior cloning, candidate search resembling OMAR's actor rectification — the genuinely new element is the trust gate that couples critic-ranked corrections to a distance-from-support filter and distills them into a local actor; the theory is a straightforward Jensen-plus-Lipschitz argument, not a new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: CRDT isolates the trust-gated rectification contribution, and the OOD-ratio/violation-cost analysis explains why it helps, not just that it does. However, no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere — the headline percentages rest on single-run point estimates from 50 held-out evaluation episodes. Code, data, or model weights are not stated as released. Methodological concerns: (1) the behavior log is generated by the authors' own TD3 controller in the authors' own simulator, so both the log and the evaluation share the same generative model; (2) hyperparameters (trust range, σ values, λQ) presumably tuned on the same random-mobility distribution used for the main result, though the road-map transfer is commendably tuning-free; (3) Theorem 1 rests on Assumption 1 (critic correctly ranks candidates), which is untestable and partially circular; (4) the strongest motivating alternative — repeated non-convex trajectory/beamforming optimization — never appears as an experimental baseline. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — a framework and algorithm, but evaluated entirely in simulation). Practical: Inference is a 6-layer Transformer per UAV on local history, so it runs on embedded-class hardware, but training requires the centralized critic pipeline. Efficient: Offline training over 200k transitions is modest by modern standards, and all critic/search machinery is dropped at runtime; however, the paper reports no wall-clock, FLOP, or latency numbers. Effective: The evidence shows the method solves the simulated surrogate of the stated problem (return, sum rate, pass rate, margin, collisions) across mobility distributions; no physical or hardware-in-the-loop validation exists, so real-world effectiveness is unproven. Scalable: Tested only at M=3–6 in a 500×500 m area with 2 users + 1 target per UAV — a 2× fleet increase; behavior at 10–100× scale (dense swarms, interference saturation, communication-free coordination assumptions) is untested, though the parameter-sharing design plausibly extends. Deliverable: paper-form framework with full algorithmic detail; no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model artifact is stated. Strengths: - The problem framing is well chosen and the imitation-vs-support dilemma is demonstrated, not just asserted: Fig. 1(b) quantifies the tradeoff (OMAR: 6.25 violation cost; conservative methods: ~2.2–3.0) and the ablation confirms the proposed gate resolves it (violation cost 2.19 at OOD 0.066). - The zero-shot road-map transfer protocol is genuinely rigorous: policies frozen on random-mobility logs are deployed on three structurally different OSM road graphs with no road-specific tuning, checkpoint selection, or early stopping, and still win across scene types — this is the strongest evidence against mere mobility overfitting in the paper. - The theory is honestly scoped: the authors explicitly restrict the guarantee to the offline-support distribution and label the assumptions as local regularity conditions rather than claiming global optimality. - The CTDE information asymmetry (centralized evaluation vs. local execution) is treated as the central design constraint throughout, rather than an afterthought, and the algorithm's pieces each map to one of three stated requirements. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly scope the theoretical guarantee to the offline-support distribution and concede Assumption 1 (critic ranking) is "the usual local ranking condition" — a direct confrontation with the theory's weakness. They acknowledge no public flight-log dataset exists and that their log is a TD3 surrogate for human-pilot or legacy-controller records, retaining "sensing and safety violations." They note the reward-and-penalty reformulation relaxes P0's hard constraints. They do not, however, explicitly flag the simulation-only nature of all results, the absence of variance reporting, or the small fleet scale as limitations — a partial rather than full confrontation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No model-based baseline: the introduction argues repeated non-convex optimization is impractical, but a receding-horizon or SCA-based trajectory/beamforming optimizer is never run; the entire comparison is against RL methods, so the claim of practical superiority over the classical approach is unsupported by experiment. - Single-seed, no-variance results: with 29.3% and 69.1% headline gains, seed variance could plausibly matter; the training curves in Fig. 4 show notable spread for offline methods, and no repeated runs are disclosed. - Simulator circularity: the log, the critics, the reward, and the evaluation all come from the same channel/mobility model; the OSM transfer tests mobility generalization but not channel-model, antenna, or kinematics generalization. - The trust-gate and rectification hyperparameters (τ range 0.35–0.45, σπ, σβ, λQ=0.18) are domain-specific constants with no sensitivity analysis; nothing indicates how they transfer to a different ISAC configuration. - The "flight log" framing invokes human-pilot or legacy-controller data, but the actual log is a TD3 policy sharing the same reward definition used for evaluation — a behavior-engineering choice that flatters offline improvement relative to genuinely heterogeneous human logs. - Collision risk is a distance-threshold proxy in simulation; no communication latency, localization error, or wind disturbance is modeled, all of which directly affect the safety claims. Bottom Line: For researchers in offline MARL for aerial wireless networks this is a solid, well-motivated piece with a genuinely useful trust-gating mechanism and an unusually careful transfer protocol, but the simulation-only evidence, single-seed reporting, and absence of model-based baselines mean a practitioner should treat it as a promising design template rather than validated deployable technology — and a general RL reader will find the ingredients largely familiar.

Problem & Motivation Bioinformatics researchers — especially those with wet-lab backgrounds — must assemble multi-tool pipelines (e.g., VSEARCH, USEARCH, QIIME2, mothur, DADA2) with interdependent Conda/pip dependencies, error-prone environment configuration, CLI mastery, and R/Python visualization skill. Existing solutions split into CLI-driven managers (Snakemake: high extensibility, low usability) and GUI-driven platforms (Galaxy: high usability, but every new tool requires manual mapping of arguments to interface elements, which bottlenecks extensibility). Recently released local agent tools (OpenClaw, Claude Code) and life-science agent kits (ClawBio, BioClaw) automate workflows but center interaction on the user–agent relationship, which the authors argue weakens the user's connection to the underlying software and exposes fragility in traceability and debuggability when the agent fails. The gap addressed is a framework that keeps the rule-based extensibility of CLI tools, gains GUI usability via LLM automation instead of manual interface development, and preserves user access to the underlying scripts. Key Idea The single core insight is to use the LLM as a thin translation layer between CLI and GUI — parsing each tool's actual `--help` output at workflow-creation time into structured parameter metadata that renders as a graphical panel — rather than as a top-down agent that takes over the workflow. Users can always drop down to the generated scripts or the terminal, so the LLM assists configuration without removing knowledge content or hiding computational logic. The same philosophy drives the environment module: the LLM generates `environment.yml`, `install.sh`, `supplies-list.md`, and `MANUAL.md` from a minimal workflow description (steps + software), then enters a bounded self-correction loop that reads failure logs and retries. Methodology The system is a frontend–backend split: a vanilla-JS single-file SPA communicates with a FastAPI + Python-socketio backend via REST and Socket.IO, with an AI layer routing to the OpenClaw Gateway (session key `agent:limbo:{session_id}`, token read from `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`). Five modules: (1) Environment construction — an agent queries software sources and emits four artifacts (`supplies-list.md`, `environment.yml`, `install.sh`, `MANUAL.md`); environment creation via `/api/env-build/create-env-with-fix` triggers an automated diagnosis/repair loop with user-configurable rounds (default 3), submitting the full workflow description, error log, and current `environment.yml` on each attempt. (2) Workflow management — the module executes each tool to obtain real help text, an LLM classifies parameters into the five-tuple, separates required (expanded) from optional (folded, default-filled) parameters, infers I/O continuity between steps, and stores the result as `config.json` + `params.json` + per-step scripts; at execution, scripts are combined with user configuration into complete commands. (3) R data analysis — `VisualizationManager` drives an R session (vegan, ggplot2) via `template.json` panels and `script.r`, supporting α-diversity (Shannon, Chao1, ACE), β-diversity (PCoA, NMDS, PCA), composition, and correlation analyses, with outputs duplicated as RData and PDF/SVG/CSV/TSV. (4) Terminal emulation — Paramiko SSH + Python pty with `terminal_input`/`terminal_output` Socket.IO events for concurrent multitab remote sessions. (5) AI chat — SSE-streamed token responses through `/api/agent/chat`. Validation used a 16S rRNA amplicon workflow (VSEARCH/USEARCH) plus a cross-model benchmark of seven LLMs on two stages (environment-component generation and workflow-panel rendering), scored on format/count correctness and correct classification of Rosetta-emulation-dependent software. No formal objective function exists; this is a systems-integration design, not an optimization method. Critical design decisions: (a) invoking the LLM only for help-text parsing and orchestration rather than full takeover — argued conceptually, supported by the traceability rationale but not by experiment; (b) bounded repair rounds (3) — justified empirically by the 23.33%→93.33% success jump; (c) parsing real executed help text rather than static documentation — well-motivated for accuracy but creates the stated `--help`-parseability boundary. Key Results Functional validation on a 16S rRNA amplicon workflow demonstrates all three stages end-to-end: environment construction (repair success ~23.33% in one round vs ~93.33% with three rounds, Supplementary Table S2), workflow-panel rendering with per-parameter cards (name, label, type, required flag, default, description) and I/O continuity detection (e.g., `--fastq_mergepairs` receiving merged output, `--otutab` feeding R analysis), and R visualization with reusable session objects. The cross-model test (seven LLMs — MiniMax-M3, MiniMax-M2.7, Kimi-k2.6, GPT-5.5, GLM-5.1, Qwen3.7-plus, DeepSeek-v4-pro — on macOS 26.4) found only DeepSeek-v4-pro and MiniMax-M3 had failing instances in the workflow stage (streaming-parsing incompatibility and chain-of-thought context exhaustion, respectively); Qwen3.7-plus was fastest (std = 9.4) but highest in token cost, DeepSeek-v4-pro lowest in tokens but slowest, and MiniMax-M2.7 and GLM-5.1 ranked best on both metrics and are recommended. All numbers come from the authors' own platform and a single test pipeline; baselines are qualitative comparisons against Snakemake and Galaxy (Supplementary Table S7), not head-to-head measurements. Tested scale: one workflow type, one operating system, standard desktop deployment. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an incremental NEW METHOD component. The genuinely novel element is the LLM-as-middle-layer pattern: automatic mapping of live CLI `--help` text to GUI parameter panels plus an AI-driven Conda repair loop, positioning LLM assistance between the extensibility of Snakemake and the usability of Galaxy while keeping underlying scripts user-editable. Everything else — FastAPI/Socket.IO architecture, Conda environments, Paramiko SSH/PTY, standard R visualization templates — is a competent combination of existing components; the system itself is built on the OpenClaw agent framework, and ClawBio/BioClaw already combine agents with bioinformatics pipelines. Rigor & Reproducibility Quantified evidence is limited but present: the environment-repair experiment (Supplementary Table S2, apparently ~30 trials given the 23.33%/93.33% figures — sample size not stated in the main text) and the cross-model test with elapsed-time and token-consumption rankings including significance letters (p < 0.05) and reported standard deviations. No multiple-seed reporting for the repair experiment, no user study, no accuracy benchmark of the generated pipelines' biological outputs against established tools like QIIME2/DADA2. Code is publicly released at https://github.com/Listen-Lii/LIMBO-Less-Is-More-Boosts-Organization, with software versions (Supplementary Table S1) and test templates (Supplementary Table S5) documented. Methodological concerns: the system is developed and evaluated on the authors' own test scenario with self-defined pass criteria; the cross-model benchmark covers only two LLM-involved stages under one fixed workflow text; the authors themselves note model rankings will drift with model updates. The claimed ~93.33% repair success is a single-point estimate on one workflow type under nondeterministic generation, which the authors acknowledge. Deployability: (4-property check)** Profile: SYSTEMS — a built tool evaluated by functional deployment on real infrastructure (local machine + SSH servers). - Practical: Runs locally in a browser on commodity hardware (macOS 26.4 tested), requires only a Conda-capable server and OpenClaw Gateway access with an API token. - Efficient: Adds LLM token cost proportional to workflow complexity — each repair round resubmits the full workflow description, error log, and `environment.yml`, so cumulative input grows across rounds, a cost the authors flag explicitly. - Effective: Evidence shows the environment builds and panels render correctly for one well-structured pipeline, but effectiveness at the stated goal (lowering the barrier for non-experts across general bioinformatics analysis) is demonstrated only by proxy — no task-completion or user-performance data. - Scalable: Not tested at 10×–100× scale; the authors bound scope to workflows resolvable via Conda and tools with LLM-parseable `--help` text, and context-length growth with workflow complexity suggests cost scaling limits for large pipelines. The work delivers a real software artifact (open-source repository, MIT-compatible) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths - The help-text-to-GUI-panel translation is a genuinely clever mechanism for the extensibility/usability trade-off: it automates what Galaxy does manually, applies to any tool with parseable `--help` output, and avoids per-tool interface development. - The restrained-LLM design philosophy is architecturally disciplined — the LLM is confined to parsing and orchestration while scripts, JSON configs, and terminal access remain fully exposed, directly addressing the traceability/debuggability weakness of agent-first tools. - The quantified self-correction loop (23.33% → 93.33% across rounds) is the paper's most credible empirical result and gives practitioners an actionable configuration knob. - The cross-model benchmark (seven LLMs, time vs. token cost, with per-model failure diagnostics such as MiniMax-M3's context-budget exhaustion) is a useful, honest characterization that goes beyond demonstrating the system works with one model. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and at length — a credibility positive. They enumerate four OpenClaw single-dependency risk surfaces (protocol breakage, project discontinuation, licensing shift, credential handling) with concrete mitigations (adapter abstraction, self-hosted fallback, MIT-compatible release branch, least-privilege token handling). They acknowledge: (1) context growth and token cost in multi-round repair; (2) output nondeterminism making repair success a random variable amplified across rounds; (3) that LIMBO does not reduce the need for bioinformatics expertise — users must still know which steps, software, and parameters to use; (4) that the cognitive-burden-reduction claim lacks quantitative data; and (5) cross-model results are version-specific and will change. They also define tool boundaries precisely: Conda-resolvable dependencies and `--help`-parseable CLIs only. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No evaluation of the correctness of the biological outputs: the paper never verifies that a LIMBO-driven 16S pipeline produces feature tables/taxonomies matching those from QIIME2, DADA2, or mothur on the same data — the core scientific-reproducibility concern the design claims to address. - No user study with wet-lab researchers, so the central usability claim (lowered barrier, reduced cognitive load) rests entirely on argument, which the authors admit. - No head-to-head timing/cost comparison against Snakemake or Galaxy on the same workflow; Supplementary Table S7 is a feature comparison, not a measurement. - The repair-success rates (23.33%, 93.33%) lack stated trial counts, seeds, error bars, and workflow diversity — one workflow text may not generalize, and the authors' own nondeterminism caveat undermines the precision of these figures. - The cross-model test measures generation time and tokens, not end-to-end success on harder pipelines (multi-environment, database-dependent annotation steps), where model differences would likely matter most. - Security posture is thin: a browser-controlled PTY/SSH interface executing arbitrary scripts locally is a significant attack surface not analyzed beyond credential-file permissions. Bottom Line A practitioner choosing or building bioinformatics workflow tooling gains concrete, transferable design ideas — LLM-parsed parameter panels and a bounded Conda-repair loop with a measured success curve — but should treat the usability and reliability claims as design hypotheses rather than validated results, since stronger-validated alternatives (Galaxy, QIIME2-based stacks, or ClawBio-class agents) cover much of the same ground.

#177 — Moderately Innovative (58)

Specification Portability Across LLM Development Agents : Cross- Agent Compatibility in Specification-Driven Software Migration

O Grynets, O Ilchuk, D Zatulna, V Lyashkevych · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents an empirical study showing that software specifications produced inside one LLM development agent (Amazon Kiro, Google Gemini/Antigravity, GitHub Copilot/Spec Kit) degrade — sometimes catastrophically — when consumed as implementation input by a different agent, and evaluates rewriting, compression, and retrieval-augmented ingestion as mitigations. - Why it's important: Multi-agent SDD pipelines (ChatDev-style role specialization, agent handoffs) implicitly assume intermediate artifacts are agent-neutral; if that assumption fails, silently swapping or upgrading an implementation agent can destroy output quality with no visible warning. - How it does it: The authors run native (agent consumes its own spec) versus foreign (agent consumes another agent's spec) experiments on an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration task over 1,802 script pairs, scoring six metrics (Token F1, exact match, SQL syntax validity via sqlglot, AST exact match, AST mean similarity, immediate runnability) and defining a directional per-metric compatibility ratio C(i→j) = Q(A_j, S_i)/Q(A_j, S_j). - The good: The single most striking result — Gemini consuming a Kiro-origin specification collapses to Token F1 0.035, SQL syntax validity 2.33%, and AST mean similarity 0.015 — was replicated in a second independent run, and the same spec rewritten by Gemini first restored Token F1 to 0.68, isolating representation (not knowledge content) as the failure locus. - The missing: Almost everything is single-run with no error bars or significance tests, despite the paper itself citing evidence that LLM code generation is nondeterministic even at temperature zero; there is also no no-specification baseline (raw Oracle source directly to the agent) to establish what the specification adds at all. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build or operate multi-agent LLM development pipelines or database-migration tooling, because it documents a real, replicated failure mode with a useful directional-compatibility framing; skip it if you want statistically grounded conclusions or a method you can adopt, since the evaluation does not support either.

Rigor (45) drags the composite down: single runs with no error bars despite the paper citing its own nondeterminism concerns, no no-specification control, inconsistent baselines across tables, preprint status, and no released artifact. Completeness (65) benefits from unusually candid limitation acknowledgment; Resilience (55) is mixed (well-bounded claims but fragile single-run numbers), and Impact (40) is low given no reusable release. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*45 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*40 = 58.

Problem & Motivation: Specification-driven development (SDD) turns specifications into operational artifacts that directly steer autonomous code generation, and modern multi-agent frameworks routinely pass such artifacts between specialized agents. The unstated assumption is that a specification that works for its producing agent remains effective for any consumer. The paper targets practitioners and researchers in heterogeneous agentic development workflows — specifically LLM-assisted database migration, where Oracle-to-PostgreSQL conversion requires preserving procedural semantics across dialects (triggers, packages, cursors, exception handling). Prior work covers specification quality, retrieval, requirements clarification, and multi-agent orchestration, but no prior study measures whether a complete specification retains its implementation effectiveness when the producing and consuming agent environments differ. The paper closes that gap empirically, using migration as a controlled transformation task with ground-truth targets. Key Idea: The core insight is that specification information content and specification operational effectiveness are distinct properties: a specification S consumed by agent A_j must be modeled as Q_code = f(A_g, A_i, S, I_s, C) — quality depends on the spec-generating agent, the implementing agent, the ingestion strategy, and context — and portability is a directional, per-metric ratio C(i→j) that is generally asymmetric (C_Kiro→Gemini ≠ C_Gemini→Kiro). Once this framing is accepted, the natural experiment follows: hold the spec fixed, swap the consumer, and measure. The formalism itself is a ratio and a 4-tuple decomposition S = ⟨K, R, D, G⟩; it is a useful vocabulary, not a deep technical contribution. Methodology: Two stages. Stage 1 validates a specification-first migration pipeline: deterministic preprocessing decomposes PL/SQL source files into database objects, an LLM agent loop (GPT-oss-120b and GPT-o4-mini, ~2,000 tokens/iteration, ~3 iterations average, MCP-based tools, explicit termination conditions) generates an intermediate specification and then PostgreSQL code, with per-object regeneration on failure. Stage 2 is the cross-agent experiment: five environments were initially screened (Kiro, Gemini/Antigravity, Copilot/Spec Kit, Claude Code, Cursor), narrowed to three (Kiro, Gemini, Copilot) due to pricing constraints. Each agent first completed a native single-agent workflow (spec generation, human review, code generation, testing in one environment) as baseline; specs were then exchanged. Three adaptation strategies were tested on foreign specs: (1) rewriting (consumer restates the spec in its preferred format), formalized as T_rewrite(S, A_i); (2) compression/summarization; (3) retrieval-augmented ingestion, where the agent is blocked from reading the full spec and gets retrieval tools with a relevance threshold θ. The objective is empirical comparison across six metrics spanning lexical, syntactic, structural, and operational quality. Critical design decisions: multidimensional evaluation (well-justified, argued from EvalPlus/ClassEval/SWE-bench evidence that lexical similarity is insufficient); object-level decomposition (justified for token economy and isolation); narrowing to three agents for cost (understandable but weakens coverage). A notable weakness: the "tuned" native baselines in Table II differ from the baselines actually used in the cross-agent table (Kiro/Kiro in Table III matches the untuned Table I numbers), making the reference point for the compatibility ratios ambiguous. Key Results: Stage 1: 623/1,006 PL/SQL files (61.9%) regenerated; 380/623 (~61.0%) of those executed successfully in PostgreSQL 16; tables reached ~85% regeneration success while queries performed worst and procedures/functions/indexes remained hard. Stage 2 (1,802 Oracle/PostgreSQL script pairs): specification size did not predict quality — Kiro's ~1,597-line spec underperformed Gemini's ~193-line spec on most metrics. The headline finding: Gemini consuming a Kiro spec scored Token F1 0.035, SQL validity 2.33%, AST similarity 0.015 (replicated in a second run), versus Gemini-native Token F1 0.73 and SQL validity 45.54%. Transfer was asymmetric: Kiro consuming a Gemini spec scored Token F1 0.68 (roughly native level), and Copilot consuming a Kiro spec scored 0.69 versus its native 0.75. Rewriting rescued Gemini (Token F1 0.68, SQL validity 43.62%) but hurt Copilot (Token F1 0.60, SQL validity 14.09% versus 43.4% direct). Compression gave Copilot Token F1 0.72 but 0% runnable. RAG did not dominate any single metric but was the only strategy on the per-agent Pareto frontiers (SQL validity vs. AST similarity) of both Gemini and Copilot. Baselines are commercial agents of current vintage, but native runnability rates are extremely low (0.72%–2.22% untuned, 4.11%–28.75% tuned), so the absolute operating point of every configuration is poor. Tested scale is a moderate industrial dataset, not a stress-scale benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the empirical characterization of specification portability as a directional, agent-dependent, multi-metric phenomenon — including the replicated Gemini–Kiro collapse and the finding that rewriting fixes Gemini but not Copilot. The formal apparatus (compatibility ratio, ⟨K,R,D,G⟩ decomposition) is standard notation over a straightforward idea, and the pipeline combines known techniques (Code–Text–Code intermediates, agentic loops, RAG); the value lies in the measurement, not the machinery. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the three ingestion strategies constitute an ablation over ingestion, but there is no ablation isolating why the Gemini–Kiro failure occurs (no analysis of what in the Kiro spec breaks Gemini), and no no-spec or direct-source-to-target baseline. No error bars, no confidence intervals, no significance tests, and exactly one replication (of the single anomalous configuration), despite the paper citing Ouyang et al. that LLM code generation is nondeterministic even at temperature zero — the paper knows the threat and does not fully counter it. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (a) native baselines are inconsistent across tables (Table I vs. tuned Table II vs. Table III), leaving the denominator of the compatibility ratio ambiguous; (b) runnability is measured against an empty database with generated stubs — acknowledged as a lower bound, but this makes the operational metric weak evidence; (c) several cross-agent cells are marked "not evaluated"; (d) evaluation is confined to the authors' own dataset and one migration domain; (e) heavy self-citation to the authors' own arXiv preprints ([5]–[8]) frames the work without independent validation. The paper appears to be a preprint (IEEE template with placeholder copyright, 2026-dated arXiv references), not a peer-reviewed publication. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs real pipelines and reports measurements; it also ships a described but unreleased pipeline). - Practical: Yes in principle — all components (Kiro, Gemini, Copilot, sqlglot, PostgreSQL 16, GPT-oss-120b/GPT-o4-mini) are commercially available, though the study spans proprietary, version-unstated agent products that a replicator cannot pin down. - Efficient: Costs are only indirectly characterized (~2,000 tokens/iteration, ~3 iterations per object in Stage 1; pricing constraints visibly shaped the experimental design), and no cost comparison against direct source-to-target translation is given. - Effective: The evidence shows the problem exists (the portability failure is real and replicated), but the absolute quality of every configuration is low (best tuned runnable rate 28.75%), so it demonstrates a risk rather than a working solution. - Scalable: Untested — 1,802 scripts is a moderate corpus, and nothing indicates behavior at 10× scale or across domains beyond Oracle-to-PostgreSQL; scalability is not claimed, which is honest. The work delivers no reusable artifact (no released code, dataset, or tool); it stops at paper form plus a conceptual model. Strengths: - The Gemini–Kiro catastrophic transfer failure (Token F1 0.68→0.035, SQL validity 45.5%→2.33%) is the paper's strongest evidence: it is large, replicated, and, crucially, the rewriting experiment (restoring Token F1 to 0.68 from the same knowledge source) cleanly separates representation incompatibility from knowledge loss — a genuinely informative experimental contrast. - The directional compatibility framing C(i→j) ≠ C(j→i), instantiated per metric, is a correct and reusable conceptual contribution that resists the temptation to summarize portability as a single scalar. - The finding that specification size is uninformative (1,597-line Kiro spec vs. 193-line Gemini spec, with no monotone quality relationship) directly undercuts a plausible practitioner heuristic and connects to the authors' earlier token-optimization result that context reduction is not context preservation. - The multidimensional metric suite (lexical, syntactic, structural, operational) is well-motivated by the cited evaluation literature and avoids over-claiming from Token F1 alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually explicit and non-defensive: they restrict all conclusions to the observed agents, specifications, ingestion strategies, dataset, and metrics; they deny any claim that foreign specifications are universally worse; they state that RAG is not universally optimal, only the most robust common Pareto-frontier strategy; they flag runnability as a lower bound measured against an empty database with stubs; and they disclose that pricing constraints reduced the systematic cross-agent stage to three of five environments. They also explicitly invoke the nondeterminism literature to caution against over-reading single runs — while still running mostly single trials. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run results throughout (except one replication) directly contradict the paper's own cited evidence on LLM nondeterminism; without multiple seeds or variance estimates, the 2.33% SQL validity figure and even the milder transfer effects cannot be distinguished from run-to-run noise. - No no-specification baseline: the reader cannot tell whether any specification outperforms simply giving the agent the raw Oracle source, so the entire specification-first premise is untested against the obvious control in the cross-agent setting. - The mechanism of the Gemini–Kiro failure is unexamined — no qualitative analysis of what the Kiro spec contains (formatting, verbosity, implicit assumptions, tool-specific artifacts) that breaks Gemini, which limits the finding's transferability. - Baseline inconsistency across tables (untuned Table I values appear as the Kiro-native row in the cross-agent Table III while Table II reports different tuned values) obscures which reference the compatibility ratios use. - Several AST-exact-match values across unrelated agents are suspiciously clustered (12.76, 12.98, 12.65, 12.87, 12.49, 12.10), which either indicates a data-reporting artifact or warrants explanation. - Confounding in the adaptation experiments: rewriting changes both representation and length/structure simultaneously, so the claimed representation-vs-knowledge separation is suggestive rather than controlled. - One task domain, one proprietary dataset, three agents, and no public artifact together make independent verification impossible. Bottom Line: A practitioner operating multi-agent LLM development pipelines should read this for its replicated, quantified demonstration that specifications are not agent-neutral artifacts and that ingestion strategy matters as much as spec content — but should treat every specific number as a single-run anecdote and look elsewhere for a validated, reproducible method, since none is released.

Extending Security Orchestration Automation and Response to the Cloud

D Abate · webthesis.biblio.polito.it · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This Master's thesis extends an inherited CACAO 2.0 playbook-driven remediation engine (from the TORSEC group at Politecnico di Torino) into a cloud-capable SOAR system for Microsoft Azure, adding Sentinel incident ingestion, a typed Azure action library, MITRE-ATT&CK-driven dynamic playbook generation, and an LLM planner gated by a closed action catalogue and human approval. - Why it's important: SOC analysts face high alert volumes against hand-authored, vendor-locked SOAR playbooks that go stale as cloud attack surfaces change; this work shows how an open, auditable (CACAO-standard) automation pipeline can cover Azure incidents — including technique combinations no human anticipated — without sacrificing operator control over destructive actions. - How it does it: All three execution modes (static file-based, MITRE tactic-technique-action mapping, LLM planner) funnel into one unchanged CACAO 2.0 executor; the LLM mode is constrained by a closed, machine-readable action catalogue with per-action approval flags, and a strictly read-only ReAct enrichment agent supplies evidence before planning. - The good: The safety architecture is coherent and actually exercised: every AI-assisted run ends in a complete CACAO 2.0 report with the planner's reasoning trace archived, destructive actions are parked behind explicit per-action approval, and all 16 test scenarios (including replays of Pikabot, Spalax, SolarWinds, and Lapsus$) produce valid executed reports under all three modes. - The missing: The evaluation is entirely on the author's own single test tenant with 16 self-authored scenarios, using human-judged action correctness with no inter-rater agreement, no comparison against any commercial SOAR or academic baseline on the same incidents, and no reported quantitative plan-quality numbers (validation rate, approval rate, latency) in the evaluated text. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you are building cloud-native SOAR automation or researching LLM planners with human-in-the-loop safety in security operations — the safety-by-construction design (closed catalogue + read-only enrichment + CACAO audit trail) is a reusable pattern; skip it if you want statistically grounded LLM-agent evaluation or multi-cloud generality.

Problem & Motivation: Security Operations Centres that have migrated workloads to public cloud now triage identity-centric attacks, control-plane abuse, and supply-chain compromises, but the SOAR products that automate their response rely on hand-authored playbooks tied to specific vendors (Splunk SOAR, Cortex XSOAR, Sentinel Logic Apps) that cannot be ported between platforms and must be rewritten whenever a new threat shape or platform feature appears. The inherited TORSEC remediator implemented correct CACAO 2.0 execution semantics but had three limits: no Azure control-plane coverage (no Sentinel ingestion, no Graph/ARM actions), only static pre-authored playbooks (unanticipated technique combinations got no response), and no planning layer at all. The thesis closes all three at once, because each limit assumes the others remain unsolved. Key Idea: Treat the CACAO 2.0 executor as a fixed point and vary only how the playbook is sourced, then make LLM-generated plans safe by construction: the planner can only emit actions from a closed, typed catalogue (each entry declaring parameters, required context, risk level, and an approval_required flag), a validator rejects anything outside that catalogue before execution, destructive steps wait for per-action human approval, and a read-only, budget-capped ReAct enrichment agent grounds the planner in live tenant evidence (sign-in failures, user risk state, role assignments, VM criticality, TI lookups). This converts the hallucination problem into a validation problem and keeps every run auditable as a CACAO report. Methodology: The system is a Python package with four layers: web API/UI, a trivial environment-variable router, three front-ends, and a shared back-end (executable graph, action library, CACAO serialiser) inherited unmodified. (1) Sentinel ingestion normalises incidents — flattening MITRE technique codes from additionalData, bucketing typed entities (account, host, IP, URL, file hash), and extracting the Azure scope triple (subscription, resource group, workspace). (2) The action library spans five capability families (Identity via Microsoft Graph, Network and Compute via ARM, Sentinel via Log Analytics REST, plus a Key Vault example), each action declaring entity kinds, required permissions, scope, and passive/destructive status, with a cheap feasibility GET before first SDK call and idempotency where feasible (no transactional rollback — only pre-state logging). (3) The tactic-driven mode resolves the incident's technique codes through a hand-curated tactic-technique-action mapping, deduplicates and orders actions (containment first), binds parameters from the entity dictionary, and compiles a CACAO playbook on the fly. (4) The AI-assisted mode calls an OpenAI-compatible planner (validation used gpt-5; a heuristic fallback exists) to emit a strict-JSON remediation plan, validates it against the catalogue, splits it into an autonomously executed passive half and an approval-gated destructive half, and compiles it to CACAO with structural optimisations (ForEach folding of same-action steps; Parallel_step grouping by a disjoint-non-structural-parameter rule). A read-only enrichment agent (four swappable backends: heuristic, OpenAI single-shot, OpenAI ReAct tool-loop, external claw binary) runs before planning with budgets of 12 tool calls and 8 turns. The safety-relevant design decisions — closed catalogue, package-boundary read/write split, per-action (not per-playbook) approval — are each explicitly justified. Key Results: On a dedicated Azure test tenant (Sentinel workspace, one Linux VM + NSG, Key Vault, Conditional Access named location, three Entra test users, one service principal), 16 scenarios — 12 single-alert (identity compromise, malicious URL click, lateral movement, key-vault lockdown, VM lifecycle) plus 4 multi-stage campaign replays (Operation Spalax C0005, Pikabot C0036, SolarWinds C0024, Lapsus$ DEV-0537) covering the ATT&CK Cloud and Identity Provider matrices — all produced valid, executed CACAO 2.0 reports under all three modes. Cross-run consistency over three independent AI-planner invocations on the same Spalax incident showed the two core containment steps reproduced verbatim with identical parameter bindings, with run-to-run variability confined to how many associated indicators were promoted to active firewall blocks versus passive watchlist entries. The thesis defines metrics for each research question (coverage, regression, generation rate, human-judged action correctness, first-try validation rate, approval rate, auditability, zero safety violations, end-to-end latency), but the provided text does not report the numeric values for most of these metrics. No baselines outside the system's own three modes were compared; scale is a single-tenant lab deployment, not production stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component and a modest NEW FORMULATION (the MITRE tactic-technique-action mapping as a standalone, reviewable artefact driving runtime CACAO synthesis). The genuinely new combination is a CACAO 2.0-native remediator with native Sentinel integration plus an LLM planner behind a formal approval policy — the positioning table plausibly shows no commercial SOAR or CACAO tool combines all three. However, each ingredient is standard: CACAO execution (inherited), MITRE mappings (established practice in detection engineering), LLM planning with catalogue constraint and human approval (the now-conventional guardrailed-agent pattern), and ReAct (Yao et al.). The agent design is deliberately conservative, as the authors themselves state. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the classical sense are absent; the three-mode comparison functions as a partial ablation (legacy vs. mapping-driven vs. LLM planning on identical incidents), and the four-backend enrichment design enables swapping components, but no component-removal study isolates what the enrichment agent actually contributes to plan quality. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; the cross-run consistency check (3 invocations, one incident) is the only repetition. Evaluation is entirely on the authors' own tenant and self-authored scenarios — a Goodhart risk, since the MITRE mapping and scenarios were co-designed with the system. Action correctness is human-judged by (presumably) the author with no rubric or inter-rater detail. Reproducibility is comparatively strong for a thesis: a Docker image, full config captured in config.local.json, scenario JSONs under tests/azure/alerts_test/, user and developer manuals in appendices, and an open-source posture — though the repository URL and credentials handling (secrets "captured verbatim in config.local.json for reproducibility") raise questions about what is actually publishable. The validation chapter text provided is truncated mid-way, so headline quantitative metrics (validation rate, latency figures) could not be verified. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated by running it against a live Azure tenant). Practical: Yes — it runs as a local Docker container against public Microsoft Graph/ARM/Log Analytics endpoints with a single App Registration, on commodity hardware; the only external dependency is an OpenAI-compatible API key. Efficient: Cost is dominated by LLM calls (one planning call plus up to 12 enrichment tool calls per incident); the deterministic modes avoid LLM cost entirely; no latency numbers are reported in the provided text beyond noting the metric exists. Effective: The evidence shows the system produces valid, executed, auditable remediation playbooks for self-authored scenarios on one tenant — it solves the integration and safety-workflow problem, but effectiveness against realistic adversarial incidents (evasion, alert poisoning, prompt injection from attacker-controlled alert fields) is argued by design, not measured. Scalable: Not tested beyond one tenant and 16 scenarios; the authors claim the mapping/catalogue shape extends to new actions and SIEMs, but 10–100× scale (multi-tenant, high alert volume, concurrent jobs on a ThreadingHTTPServer) is untested. Deliverable: a working software artifact (Python package, web UI, Docker image, MITRE mapping, action catalogue, scenario corpus) with user and developer manuals — not just a paper. Strengths: - The safety architecture is the real contribution: the closed action catalogue shared between the LLM prompt and the validator, the package-boundary read-only/write split, per-action approval gating, and heuristic fallbacks on LLM failure together form a defensible, testable safety envelope rather than prompt-level instructions. - End-to-end auditability is genuinely delivered: every mode, including AI-assisted ones, emits a CACAO 2.0 report containing the executed graph, per-step wall-clock durations, the planner's per-action justifications, and the enrichment snapshot — enabling post-hoc reconstruction without runtime logs. - Backward compatibility was treated as a hard contract (legacy mode as regression baseline, untouched executor/serialiser, lazy imports so unconfigured deployments never load LLM code), which is disciplined systems engineering for a thesis. - The worked Pikabot example is unusually transparent — including the honest admission that the compiler's parallelism is structural, not semantic, and that ordering safety is delegated to action-level idempotency. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the system is Azure-specific (Sentinel, Graph, ARM) with only a narrow fifth capability family; the MITRE mapping is intentionally a curated baseline, not exhaustive; techniques not addressable from inside the tenant (Reconnaissance, Resource Development) are out of scope; there is no transactional rollback, only pre-state logging for manual reversal; the enrichment agent is deliberately read-only and budget-capped rather than autonomous; and the AI mode is more conservative than the autonomous-agent architectures in the literature, trading autonomy for verifiability. These are confronted directly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Evaluation on scenarios co-designed with the system, on the authors' own tenant, with human-judged action correctness and no external baseline (SOARCA, Sentinel Logic Apps, or any LLM-agent system run on the same incidents) — the positioning table is a feature checklist, not a measured comparison. - Prompt injection is named as a risk and mitigated by design (read-only tools, allow-listing), but the evaluation never adversarially tests it: attacker-controlled Sentinel alert fields (URLs, descriptions, entity names) flowing into the planner prompt are exactly the injection surface the threat model should stress. - Single LLM (gpt-5), single run per scenario except one 3-run consistency check on one incident; no sensitivity to model choice, temperature, or catalogue size. - The disjoint-parameter parallelisation rule can produce semantically wrong ordering (the paper's own example: revoking sessions before the source IP is blacklisted invites immediate re-compromise, patched only by reactive re-revocation), yet no ordering/dependency analysis of generated plans is performed. - The reproducibility claim that tenant credentials are captured verbatim in config.local.json conflicts with secure publication of the artifact. - The provided validation text does not report the promised quantitative metrics (first-try validation rate, approval rate, latency distribution), so the central RQ3 claims rest on walkthroughs rather than reported numbers. Bottom Line: A practitioner building cloud SOAR automation or studying guardrailed LLM planners gains a concrete, well-engineered reference implementation and a reusable safety pattern (closed catalogue + read-only enrichment + CACAO audit trail), but as an empirical claim about LLM-driven remediation it is a single-tenant, self-authored scenario study with no external baselines — read it for the design, not for the evidence.

AI4AI Survey: From Long-Horizon Agents to Recursive Self - Improvement —Definitions, Reliable Horizons, and Open Problems

K Wu, H Lyu, Z Luo, C Wang, S Ye, J Lin, X Ji, B Jiang… · preprints.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a formal taxonomy and evidence-audit framework for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) — systems that use AI to improve AI artifacts or research processes — and applies it to a 35-record primary-source audit and a 67-entry benchmark inventory to separate demonstrated AI-improves-AI capability from claims of recursive self-improvement (RSI). - Why it's important: The literature on self-improving agents is fragmented across long-horizon agents, AutoML, AI-for-research, and RSI with incompatible terminology and evidence standards, so it is currently impossible to tell how much real progress toward reliable self-improvement has been made; this survey defines the measurement standard for that question. - How it does it: The core move is decomposing any improvement loop along five independent dimensions (target, self-reference, stage ownership, signal grounding, evidence profile G/R/H/T) plus a protocol-conditioned reliability surface R_S,Q(z), so that "autonomy" claims must be reported as per-stage ownership codes (HUM/MIX/SYS) rather than labels. - The good: The stage-ownership audit is brutally concrete: across all 35 audited systems, goal-setting is human-owned in 35/35, feedback is system-owned in 0/35, and a budget-matched human comparison exists in only 1/35 (AIDE) — a quantified refutation of current RSI marketing. - The missing: The paper's central formal object — the reliability surface H_α — is defined and given a reporting checklist but never actually estimated on any real system, so the framework's practical utility remains unproven by the paper itself. - Read it or not: Essential reading for anyone doing research on agentic systems, self-improvement, or agent evaluation who needs a defensible vocabulary and evidence standard; skippable for practitioners who only deploy existing agents and do not need to interpret improvement claims.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the fragmentation of research on AI systems improving AI. As of its writing, frontier labs position models for long-horizon agentic work, and systems (AlphaEvolve, Darwin Gödel Machine, AiScientist, ML engineering agents) claim various forms of self-improvement — but these claims span incommensurable evidence standards: some report a gain on one metric, some report multi-pass gains, almost none report retention, transfer, or budget-matched human comparison. The intended audience is researchers and evaluators of agentic AI systems. The specific gap closed: no prior framework separates (a) what an improvement loop changes, (b) who controls each stage of the loop, and (c) what evidence the outcome establishes — so "automated execution" is routinely conflated with "autonomous research judgment." The survey argues that strong component benchmark scores (browsing, coding, tool use) do not compose into reliable end-to-end improvement, and names this the composition gap. Key Idea: The single core insight is that AI4AI claims must be decomposed into independent, separately reported coordinates rather than a single autonomy ladder. Concretely: (1) the improvement loop is pointed at a target (D1: data, weights, harness, evaluator, research process); (2) self-reference and runtime closure are distinguished from recursion (self-improvement = editing your own components; RSI = editing the successor-producing process); (3) each loop stage (goal/plan/execute/feedback/repair) is coded HUM, MIX, or SYS; (4) improvement evidence is coded on four independent axes — measured gain (G), retention (R), budget-matched human comparison (H), held-out transfer (T) — where passing one does not imply another. A second supporting idea is functional coupling as the definition of long-horizon work (later rounds must consume feedback via carried state), and a protocol-conditioned reliability surface R_S,Q(z) over a six-axis task-pressure vector, whose α-threshold region H_α is the "reliable horizon." The synthesis claim is the composition gap: execution is now system-owned everywhere, judgment is not. Methodology: The survey is structured as: (§2) definitions and taxonomy with formal notation — round u_k = (p_k, a_{t_k:t_{k+1}}, f_k, r_k), carried state m_{k+1} = m_k ⊕ r_k, ownership signature c+ ∈ {HUM, MIX, SYS}^5, reliability R_S,Q(z) = Pr[Y_Q(τ)=1 | Z=z]; (§3) an evaluation methodology (pass@k vs. pass_k, pre-registered success conditions, resource-matched comparisons, a diagnosis table mapping six result patterns to next research targets); (§4–§5) model-side (planning traces, tool learning, credit assignment RL, weight-layer AI4AI) and harness-side (execution, persistence, governance, four harness self-modification regimes) mechanism synthesis; (§6) open problems organized at four failure scales (one pass, across passes, across generations, evidence/attribution). Empirically, it conducts a documented search (Google Scholar plus arXiv/OpenAlex APIs through eight recorded query families, frozen 4 Aug 2026, citation chaining, 369 post-dedup records) yielding a 67-entry component-benchmark inventory with typed scale/extent codes (T/S/B bins) and a 35-record stage-ownership audit coding D1/D3/D5 per system release, with primary-source verification and commercial material assigned to a separate source tier. Critical design decisions: refusing to collapse ownership into one autonomy score (well-justified — the audit shows goal and feedback ownership diverge sharply from execution); coding "not reported" separately from "no" (well-justified, prevents inventing evidence); and keeping the reliability surface multidimensional rather than scalar (justified in principle, but never instantiated). Key Results: The headline quantitative outcomes come from the audit and inventory, not from running systems. Of 35 audited records: goal-setting is HUM 35/MIX 0/SYS 0; planning is HUM 3/MIX 16/SYS 16; execution is SYS 35/35; feedback is HUM 16/MIX 19/SYS 0; repair is SYS 23/MIX 12. Evidence profile: measured gain demonstrated in 33/35, retention 31/35, budget-matched human comparison 1/35 (only AIDE), held-out transfer 14/35 with 20 not reported. Under the paper's strict rule, no audited system is runtime-closed because every one relies on a human-authored success criterion. Illustrative numbers drawn from the synthesized literature: on RSIBench-Data, 58.33% of settings improve over the first valid attempt but 78.26% of searches continuing past their best checkpoint finish below that peak; supplying a dynamic plan raises WebArena-Lite executor success from 9.85% to 44.24%, and joint Planner–Executor training to 57.58%; scaffold choice shifts accuracy by up to 28 points for the same model (preregistered study); a 0.95^100 < 1% independence calculation motivates error accumulation concerns; ResearchArena found none of 117 audited AI-generated papers reached a top-tier bar after artifact inspection. Baseline comparison here is the prior survey landscape (self-improvement surveys, RSI-closure work, AI4Research surveys), which the paper argues lacks the ownership/evidence decomposition. Note: vendor-positioned frontier systems are explicitly marked as non-comparable, and the document is a not-peer-reviewed preprint. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the five-dimension decomposition with separate G/R/H/T evidence codes, the stage-ownership grid crossing editable target layer with loop stage, the composition-gap diagnosis, and the quantified audit showing universal human ownership of goals and feedback. Standard combination of existing ideas applied to a new setting: the formal reliability surface adapts standard success-probability/threshold-region ideas; the mechanism catalogues (§4–§5) competently synthesize known work (ReAct, Reflexion, MemGPT, ADAS, DGM, etc.); the evaluation metrics (pass@k, contamination controls, cost-normalized reporting) consolidate known best practices rather than inventing them. Rigor & Reproducibility: The search process is documented and reproducible (recorded query families, freeze dates, inclusion/exclusion criteria, source tiers), and the audit coding rules are explicit with rationale per record. Ablations, seeds, and significance tests are not applicable to a survey, but the audit includes uncertainty-relevant caveats: counts describe the 35-record sample, not field prevalence; the sample was selected for evidence quality (selection bias acknowledged); one record is blog-only and low-confidence; the audit lacks two completed human annotations (single primary coding pass plus an independent source check, no inter-rater reliability statistics). No code repository, dataset release, or artifact URL is mentioned for the audit data or inventory — the audit appears to exist only as appendix tables. Methodological concerns: (1) several key evidence sources are 2026 preprints and vendor technical reports (Kimi K3, Frontis-MA1, AlphaEvolve) that cannot be independently verified; (2) coding judgments like "design-time artifact = HUM" embed contestable conventions (a human-authored success criterion makes feedback HUM even if no human touches the run), which drives the headline 0/35 result — the conclusion partially follows from the coding convention; (3) the goodharting-adjacent problem of the framework being developed and demonstrated on the same literature it prescribes standards for is unavoidable but unexamined. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL, in the limited sense that the paper runs a structured literature audit and benchmark inventory; the survey itself delivers analysis, not a system. - Practical: Not applicable to a method — the framework is a paper-and-checklist methodology any research group can apply without special hardware. - Efficient: The 35-record audit and 67-entry inventory are modest-effort artifacts, but the prescribed reliability-surface estimation (frozen system, repeated trials per pressure cell, replayable state) is expensive per evaluated system and the paper does not bound that cost. - Effective: The evidence shows the framework successfully discriminates real from inflated claims in the audited corpus (e.g., separating G from H and T), but it has never been validated as a tool — no case study demonstrates two independent teams reaching the same codes. - Scalable: Coding a rapidly growing literature (the paper itself notes 2026 preprint velocity and terminology drift) is a scaling problem the authors acknowledge but do not solve; no automation or community-maintenance mechanism is proposed. The deliverable is paper-form only: taxonomy, checklists (Appendix C), and appendix tables; no library, CLI, dataset release, or maintained inventory is mentioned. Strengths: - The G/R/H/T evidence decomposition and the refusal to merge it into one score is a real conceptual contribution: it converts vague RSI claims into four falsifiable checks, and the audit immediately cashes this out (H demonstrated in 1/35 systems, T in 14/35 with 20 never tested). - The stage-ownership grid (target layer × loop stage) with the HUM/MIX/SYS coding is operationally precise enough that Table 1 can differentiate Kimi K3 and KernelEvolve cell-by-cell — most surveys cannot make claims this checkable. - The diagnosis table (§3.4) mapping six benchmark result patterns (component failure, composition failure, pass@k/pass_k divergence, evaluator overfitting, lost checkpoints, human-owned feedback) to concrete next experiments is immediately actionable for researchers. - Unusual candor for a survey: the authors explicitly report their own search gaps (capped queries, one OpenAlex timeout, incomplete earlier log, no full PRISMA flow), selection bias in the audit, and that no audited system survives their own strict runtime-closure test. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the documented search is reproducible but incomplete (query caps, one timeout, changing terminology, rapid 2026 preprint publication); stage-ownership labels depend on what is counted as one system version; the audit is a non-representative sample selected for evidence disclosure and cannot establish field prevalence; the audit has two coding passes but not two completed independent human annotations; low-confidence and non-peer-reviewed sources are retained for transparency but excluded from strong RSI claims; commercial/vendor material is tiered separately from peer-reviewed evidence; and the reliability-surface estimation requires conditions (frozen systems, repeated trials, replayable state) that most current evaluations do not meet. This is a credibility positive — the limitations section confronts constraints directly rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline conclusion ("no system is runtime-closed; goals and feedback are always human-owned") is substantially an artifact of the coding convention that design-time artifacts (prompts, reward functions, acceptance rules) count as HUM/MIX. Under this convention the result is nearly unfalsifiable — any system trained on human data or evaluated on any metric would fail it. The paper does not test or discuss a relaxation of this convention. - The formal reliability surface H_α — the paper's central measurement object, given a full appendix — is never estimated for even one real system, so the framework's flagship methodology is entirely unvalidated. A single worked example (e.g., computing R_S,Q(z) with uncertainty for one agent on a stress path) would have transformed the paper's practical value. - No inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen's κ, agreement rates) are reported for the audit coding, despite coding judgments (MIX vs. SYS for repair in 12 records) being the paper's core empirical output. - Many load-bearing citations are 2026 preprints and first-party vendor reports; the audit's positive findings (e.g., 33/35 demonstrating gain) inherit unverified self-reported numbers, and the paper's source-tier separation does not fully insulate the synthesis from this. - The benchmark inventory (Appendix E) is truncated in the available document; the full 67-entry inventory's coverage of web/browsing domains is admitted to be incomplete, and no release path for the inventory as a living artifact is described. - No discussion of adversarial gaming of the taxonomy itself — a lab aware of the D5 profile could selectively report G and R while silently omitting H and T, and the "not reported" code rewards nondisclosure symmetrically with honesty. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous attempt yet to turn "can AI improve AI?" from a slogan into a set of independently checkable codes, and anyone researching self-improving agents or evaluating RSI claims should adopt its vocabulary — but the framework's own reliability-surface methodology remains unexercised, and the headline anti-RSI conclusion partially follows from its coding conventions, so read it as an essential measurement standard rather than as final evidence.

The PUR-1 Cyber -Physical Digital Twin

V Theos, J Lau, K Gkouliaras, Z Dahm, K Vasili… · arxiv.org · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds and experimentally validates a real-time, bidirectionally coupled cyber-physical digital twin (PUR-1 DT) for an operating U.S. research reactor, integrating OpenMC Monte Carlo neutronics, COMSOL multiphysics, point-kinetics, Gaussian-process and deep-surrogate models, Kalman-filter state estimation, and PID/MPC control over a live 1 Hz reactor synchronization loop. - Why it's important: Digital twins for nuclear reactors remain mostly conceptual or non-synchronized; this is one of the first validated demonstrations on a licensed, operating reactor, establishing feasibility of sub-second, secure (QKD-capable) physical-virtual coupling in a safety-critical, regulated environment. - How it does it: High-fidelity physics models too slow for real time (Monte Carlo ~2 h, CFD ~8.6 h) are replaced in the live loop by surrogate models trained on ~2,500 simulation runs, while a critical-path latency analysis guarantees end-to-end (transmission + execution + rendering) latency under the 1 s operational cycle. - The good: Hardware-in-the-loop benchmarking against physical experiments — >60 gold-foil neutron activation measurements, pool-temperature campaigns, and full operational-cycle runs — gives concrete accuracy numbers (6.75% mean flux deviation, 1.37% thermal, 9.2% integrated cycle error) rather than simulation-only self-consistency. - The missing: The flux-field surrogate drops to 17.81% average error against the experimental gold foils (vs. 3.62% against its own training simulations), localized errors reach 70%, and no code, data, or model weights are released; anomaly-detection and cybersecurity capabilities are asserted via citations to the group's prior papers rather than evaluated here. - Read it or not: Worth reading for nuclear-engineering digital-twin researchers and I&C/cyber-physical systems practitioners who need a concrete reference architecture and latency budget for real-reactor twinning; ML methods researchers can skip it since every algorithmic component is standard.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Practical Impact (55) and Rigor (65) carry the composite — a validated, bidirectionally coupled digital twin running on a licensed operating reactor with experimental gold-foil benchmarking, kernel ablations, and a genuine latency-critical-path analysis is rare in this space. Novelty (55) is bounded: the contribution is systems integration of entirely standard components, not methodological invention.
