Problem & Motivation: Video generators typically omit audio or generate it in a separate video-to-audio or audio-to-video cascade, in which one modality is a fixed condition and the other the output; this prevents reciprocal co-determination of visual dynamics and acoustic events (e.g., mouth motion and speech, visible impacts and their sounds, camera motion and ambience). Practitioners and researchers in generative audio-video modeling also face an access problem: contemporary joint systems are 22B–114B parameters, often hosted-only, or lack an official local ≥2K output path. The paper additionally identifies four gaps: noisy cross-modal training data (shot transitions, background audio creating spurious correlations), the need to control cross-modal interaction strength per layer/head/token/sample, the fact that flow-matching objectives do not directly optimize perceptual quality or synchronization, and the differing computational demands of latent joint generation versus 2K refinement. Key Idea: The core mechanism is asymmetric, depth-staged cross-modal coupling: keep the two modality streams independent for the first half of the network, then introduce paired A2V and V2A cross-attention paths in the second half, where each attention-head output is scaled by a token- and head-wise sigmoid gate conditioned on both the target hidden state and the cross-modal attention output (following the gated-attention design of Qiu et al., 2025). A per-sample direction mask selects A2V, V2A, or Joint mode with modality-specific noise-ordering and stop-gradients, so interaction strength is learned per head and token rather than fixed. This is a competent adaptation of a known gating idea to bidirectional audio-video diffusion rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Methodology: The system has four stages. (1) Data system: clip construction via PySceneDetect scene segmentation (trimming 3 frames per boundary), silence removal by RMS energy, quality filtering with Q-Align (visual), optical-flow motion magnitude, and Audiobox Aesthetics (audio); synchronization filtering with Synchformer (general) plus SyncNet (visible speech); joint captioning with Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, ASR with Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, and caption fusion with Qwen3.6-27B; clips are organized into four capability pools (speech/dialogue, actions/Foley, ambience/music, general cinematic). Training data is 45.0% speech, 33.4% event sounds, 5.5% music, 5.4% natural sounds, 10.7% mixed. (2) Joint generator training: flow matching with independently sampled noise per modality, token- and feature-normalized losses (L_AV = λv·Lv + λa·La; λv=λa=0.5 in pre-training, λa=0.1 in finetuning), discrete 1,000-timestep schedule with shift 5.0; three stages — rank-256 LoRA pre-training (first halves frozen, cross-modal modules trained directly), full-parameter pre-training, and High-Quality Finetuning on synchronization/aesthetic-filtered clips with OmniShotCut transition detection; AdamW, bf16, gradient clip 1.0. Stop-gradients block the target-stream loss from updating the conditioning backbone through cross-attention while leaving attention parameters trainable. (3) Audio-Video RL: group-based rollout from 1,000 first-frame–prompt pairs; video, audio, and cross-modal advantages are group-normalized and routed as Ãv = Av + Aav, Ãa = Aa + Aav, with a KL/regularization term to the base policy; synchronization-relevant video tokens are up-weighted using frame-normalized V2A cross-modal responses with a warmup coefficient, and shallow-block gradients entering the audio stream are attenuated (depth-dependent gradient scaling). (4) 2K Refiner: a bidirectional multi-step flow-matching teacher trained on a real-world degradation curriculum (including temporally correlated corruptions to handle generated-video flicker), converted to an autoregressive multi-step refiner via teacher forcing, then distilled with DMD/DMD2 into a 1-step student trained under self-rollout (student-generated past chunks as context to avoid exposure bias) with DISTS perceptual and ℓ2 reconstruction losses (both weight 1); audio is unchanged by refinement. Design decisions (gate placement, stop-gradient direction, decomposed rewards, self-rollout distillation) are each motivated in text but none is experimentally isolated. Key Results: Evaluation is on Verse-Bench (Sets 1–3, with Set 3 speech-centric), using VQ (aesthetic/MUSIQ/MANIQA + DINOv3 identity), Audiobox Aesthetics (CE/CU/PC/PQ), WER and LSE-C (speech), and ImageBind similarity plus Synchformer DeSync. Against five research baselines (NAVA 6.3B, UniAVGen 7.1B, Ovi 10B, DaVinci-MagiHuman 15B×2), the 7B RL model achieves VQ 0.6573 (vs. 0.6644 best baseline), WER 0.1232 (Ovi: 0.1053), LSE-C 7.8361 (best in group), and DeSync 0.1351 (best in group). Against larger open systems, the model trails: MiniMax-H3 (33B) leads on CE (5.2776 vs. 4.7463), CU (6.5847 vs. 6.0929), PQ (7.0140 vs. 6.4094), LSE-C (8.7354 vs. 7.8361), and IB (0.3119 vs. 0.2677); LTX-2.3 (22B) leads on the same audio/semantic metrics; the 7B model wins on VQ (0.6930 with refiner vs. 0.6285/0.6429) and DeSync. In the blind user study, the model wins every criterion against Ovi, UniAVGen, NAVA, and DaVinci (video-quality wins 61.7%–73.7%), but loses on AV-align and audio quality against Wan2.7, Kling v3, and MiniMax-H3 (e.g., audio vs. MiniMax-H3: 23.7% win / 30.8% tie / 45.5% lose). In refiner comparison, the 2K refiner posts MUSIQ 0.7073 and MANIQA 0.4382 (best among FlashVSR, SeedVR, LTX-2.5 Refiner), with small LSE-C/IB degradation (−0.1382 / −0.0002 vs. baseline). RL improves DeSync from 0.1902 to 0.1351 but slightly worsens WER (0.1112→0.1232) and PC. Scale is standard-benchmark, not stress-scale; no latency/throughput numbers for the 1-step refiner are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the smallest open-weight native joint A/V generator at 7B with a local 2K path, plus unusually transparent benchmarking against larger systems). The genuinely new pieces are system-level: the combination of directional noise-ordering/stop-gradient training modes with gated bidirectional cross-attention, modality-decomposed reward routing, and autoregressive 1-step 2K distillation under self-rollout. The components themselves are standard: gated attention (Qiu et al., 2025), flow matching, group-relative RL (Flow-GRPO/DanceGRPO lineage, modality-aware feedback from OmniNFT), DMD2 distillation, and teacher-forcing/Self-Forcing-style autoregressive adaptation. The data pipeline is competent assembly of off-the-shelf scorers and Qwen-family captioners. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak on ablation: no component ablations for the gates, direction masks, stop-gradients, LoRA-vs-full staging, RL reward decomposition, regional token weighting, or gradient scaling — the reader cannot tell which ingredients carry the results. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any table. The user study lacks assessor counts and sample sizes. The paper claims both model components are publicly released (Table 1 lists "Open" weight availability), but no repository URL or license is given in the text. Baselines are current and strong (2025–2026 joint A/V systems, including larger open models), and the evaluation protocol (Verse-Bench, MOVA-style metrics) is external rather than self-defined — a credibility positive. Notably, the authors self-report the model's losses to larger baselines rather than cherry-picking. One methodological inconsistency: the Conclusion states the RL and 2K refinement stages are "stated as designs with explicit validation requirements, not as completed empirical claims," which contradicts Sections 4–6 and Tables 3–5 that present RL and refiner results as measured — this needs clarification. Reward-metric coupling is a Goodhart risk the authors themselves flag (synchrony scores can be gamed) but do not experimentally test for. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, released model stack evaluated on benchmarks and a user study). Practical: 7B total parameters with a 1-step-per-chunk 2K refiner target consumer/prosumer GPU inference, and Table 1 claims local ≥2K support, but no VRAM footprint, resolution, or latency figures are reported. Efficient: The 1-step distilled refiner avoids multi-step 2K diffusion sampling, and the paper claims a "comparatively modest GPU-day" training budget, but no inference-throughput comparison (e.g., vs. FlashVSR's ~17 FPS) is provided. Effective: The evidence supports competitive video quality, lip sync, and synchronization at 7B, and explicitly does not support parity on audio aesthetics or cross-modal semantics against 22B–33B open models — the authors say so directly. Scalable: The autoregressive chunked refiner is designed for long videos, but the longest tested duration is not stated, and long-video error accumulation is addressed only by the self-rollout training claim, not by a duration ablation. Deliverable: open-weight 7B generator plus 2K refiner (artifact claimed), not a library or dataset release beyond the data recipe description. Strengths: (1) Honest, disaggregated evaluation — the paper separately reports comparisons with same-scale research baselines and larger open-weight systems, and quantifies exactly where the 7B model loses (audio aesthetics, ImageBind, lip sync vs. MiniMax-H3), which is rare and valuable for model selection. (2) The modality-decomposed RL formulation (Ãv = Av + Aav, Ãa = Aa + Aav with routing, regional token weighting from cross-modal responses, and depth-dependent gradient scaling) is a sensible, well-motivated answer to the real problem that a single global reward cannot attribute improvements across streams. (3) The refiner's degradation curriculum includes temporally correlated corruptions specific to generated-video artifacts (flicker, motion jitter), targeting temporal repair rather than generic spatial sharpening — a thoughtful detail. (4) Self-rollout distillation of the autoregressive refiner directly addresses exposure bias in chunk-wise refinement rather than ignoring it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the 7B model "has not reached across-the-board parity" with LTX-2.3 and MiniMax-H3, particularly in audio aesthetics, cross-modal semantics, and lip synchronization, and call the favorable VQ/DeSync results "a trade-off rather than overall superiority." They note the user study's sampled subset under-represents highly dynamic and compositionally complex scenes, so results show competitiveness "on the comparatively less challenging cases." They name audio fidelity and cross-modal alignment as the main improvement areas. They also warn (in Related Work) that synchrony-reward optimization can exploit evaluator artifacts and that controlled temporal-shift tests and held-out human comparisons are needed — though they do not report running these controls. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting; a clear credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No ablations at all — the architecture has at least five independently ablatable components (gates, direction masks with noise-ordering, stop-gradients, depth-staged coupling, LoRA staging), and none is validated in isolation, so the design reads as a plausible recipe rather than an analyzed one. (2) The RL stage trains on only 1,000 first-frame–prompt pairs — no data-scale analysis, no report of reward curves, reward-model identity, or how the video/audio/AV rewards are computed (model-based? human-derived?), making the RL results hard to audit for reward hacking, which the authors themselves flag as a risk. (3) No inference-cost numbers (latency, VRAM, FPS) for either the generator or the 1-step refiner, despite efficiency being a headline motivation. (4) No release URL, license, or code for the evaluation stack despite "democratization" framing and an "Open" claim in Table 1. (5) The Conclusion's statement that RL and refinement are "designs... not completed empirical claims" contradicts the presented results — either a stale conclusion or an inflated evaluation section; a reviewer must flag this. (6) The refiner comparison omits latency and the strongest recent one-step VSR systems' efficiency claims (e.g., DUO-VSR's ~50× speedup is cited but not compared). (7) Possible circularity: Synchformer and SyncNet are used both for data filtering and as evaluation metrics (DeSync, LSE-C), which could inflate temporal-synchronization scores relative to systems filtered differently. Bottom Line: For anyone selecting or building an open native audio-video generator, this is worth reading as the most transparent small-model data point available — but it is a strong engineering report with honest benchmarking, not an algorithmic advance, and its missing ablations, unreleased URLs, and internal conclusion/evaluation inconsistency mean each claimed component should be treated as unvalidated until the weights and code are actually inspectable.

#207 — Moderately Innovative (52)

A reinforcement learning framework with adaptive psychological state awareness for safe and effective intelligent psychological intervention

Y Li · link.springer.com · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RL-MindFlow, a reinforcement learning framework for psychological intervention that combines a multimodal (text/audio/visual) affective state encoder, a PID-controlled Lagrangian multiplier for dynamic ethical-risk constraints, and a two-stage CQL-pretrain-then-PPO-fine-tune training pipeline. - Why it's important: Counseling agents must make safe long-horizon decisions under non-stationary user states and ethical risk, where static unimodal classifiers and fixed safety constraints are either brittle or overly conservative. - How it does it: The core trick is a PID controller on the constraint-violation signal that modulates the Lagrange multiplier in a constrained PPO objective in proportion to risk deviation, its integral, and its rate of change, so safety boundaries tighten as risk variance rises. - The good: Ablations with 5 seeds and paired significance tests isolate each component's contribution (e.g., removing cross-modal attention drops MELD F1 from 68.4% to 59.7%; removing offline pretraining drops PsyQA reward 21.5%), and the framework is 3.2× smaller and ~2.3× faster to train than the strongest baseline. - The missing: There is no evaluation with real users or any deployed system — safety is measured by the authors' own external BERT risk classifier (94.6% accuracy), training rewards on PsyQA partly come from the model being evaluated, and the long-horizon policy results are text-only even though the framework is sold as multimodal. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on safe RL for dialogue or mental-health agents and want a concrete, ablated recipe for dynamic Lagrangian constraints; skip it if you need validated clinical effectiveness or a strong LLM-era generation baseline — it offers neither.

Problem & Motivation: The work targets builders of intelligent counseling systems and socially interactive agents who need to (a) perceive latent, time-varying psychological states from mixed signals and (b) plan multi-turn intervention strategies without committing ethical harms (self-harm encouragement, manipulation, privacy violation, risky advice). The paper argues prior approaches fail on three fronts: unimodal or static state representations miss verbal–nonverbal inconsistency; static or single-step-adaptive Lagrange multipliers in constrained RL yield either over-conservative or lagging safety behavior; and purely online RL is sample-inefficient and unsafe to explore in psychological settings while purely offline RL generalizes poorly to individual users. No real-world user study motivates the problem empirically — the motivation is framed from the literature. Key Idea: The single transferable insight is the PID-Lagrangian mechanism: treat the cumulative ethical-cost constraint in a CPOMDP as a control loop, updating the Lagrange multiplier with proportional, integral, and derivative terms on the risk deviation (and reacting to the predictive variance of the risk-value estimate) so the multiplier rises quickly when risk uncertainty grows and relaxes in low-risk regions — replacing the static multiplier of standard constrained RL. The rest (InfoNCE-aligned cross-modal attention with text as queries, CQL offline pretraining followed by KL-regularized constrained PPO fine-tuning) is a competent assembly of existing techniques. Methodology: The problem is formulated as a constrained POMDP with strategy-level actions (empathetic response, open-ended questioning, cognitive restructuring, referral) rather than token-level generation; reward reflects affective-support quality and cost comes from an external BERT-based ethical-risk classifier (94.6% accuracy, 93.8% macro-F1, AUROC 0.972 on its held-out set), with the constraint threshold set at the 95th percentile of cumulative risk among ethically acceptable validation samples. The pipeline has three modules: (1) a multimodal psychological state encoder — BERT/DistilBERT text branch, 2-layer Transformer audio and visual branches — fused via scaled dot-product cross-modal attention and trained with an auxiliary InfoNCE loss on paired modalities; (2) a dual-path actor–critic with a reward value network and a risk value network (both TD-learned), coordinated by the PID-updated Lagrange multiplier in a min–max optimization (AdamW on policy/value parameters, gradient ascent on the multiplier); (3) hybrid training — conservative Q-learning (CQL) behavior-cloned offline priors, then constrained PPO with GAE and a KL divergence penalty to the offline policy, run in a PsyQA-derived simulated interaction environment (no real-time human interaction), with a fallback to a safe strategy if cost exceeds threshold. Critical design decisions: strategy-level action space (plausible but makes evaluation depend on strategy-label inference from counselor responses); using the MPSE encoder itself as the training reward estimator on PsyQA (acknowledged circularity, partially mitigated by LLM-as-judge and a small human-rated subset); and a fixed risk threshold shared across all variants (well-justified for fair comparison). Key Results: On MELD (9,989/1,109/2,610 utterances), RL-MindFlow reaches 68.4±1.1% Weighted F1 vs. 64.7±1.2% for TheraMind, 64.5±1.3% for AL-PPO, and 62.3±1.5% for SQL (p < 0.01, 5 seeds); in the verbal-nonverbal-inconsistency subset it cuts error from 23.7% (TheraMind/EvoEmo) to 8.3%. On PsyQA (22,346 Q–A pairs, text-only), average cumulative reward is 28.4±1.2 vs. 24.6±1.8 for TheraMind and 25.1±1.6 for AL-PPO, with Safety Rate 0.982±0.007 and Distinct-2 0.184±0.005; it reaches a reward of 25.0 in 120k interaction steps vs. 195k for TheraMind (38.5% fewer steps) and 90% of final performance in 95 vs. 185 epochs. Efficiency: 58.3M parameters and 21.7h training on 2×RTX 3090 vs. TheraMind's 187.6M and 72.5h. Stress tests: MELD-derived Safety Proxy degrades from 0.982 to 0.891 at SNR = 5 dB while SQL and EvoEmo collapse to 0.712/0.768 at SNR = 10 dB; under modality dropping, text-only F1 is 62.1% (9.2% drop) vs. >20% drops for baselines. Baselines are reasonably current for this niche (TheraMind, RRL, AL-PPO, RCPO, EvoEmo, SQL), though none are frontier LLMs — all tested systems are 45–188M parameter models, so this is standard-scale, not stress-scale, testing. Notably, AL-PPO and RCPO (existing dynamic-multiplier methods) close much of the safety gap, and RL-MindFlow's margin over AL-PPO on reward is 13.1% — real but smaller than the headline margins over weaker baselines. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (partially) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely novel element is the application of PID-controlled dynamic Lagrangian multipliers — responsive to risk-estimate variance — to ethical-risk constraints in psychological intervention, along with an honest model-derived safety-proxy stress-test protocol. The multimodal encoder (Transformer cross-modal attention + InfoNCE), CQL pretraining, and PPO fine-tuning are standard components; PID-Lagrangian schemes themselves exist in safe RL (e.g., differentiable/PID constrained-policy work), so the contribution is a domain-specific integration and system rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above average for this venue tier. Five random seeds with mean±std on all headline numbers, paired t-tests against the second-best baseline (p < 0.01 on most metrics), a systematic ablation table (cross-modal attention, PID vs. fixed λ, offline pretraining, InfoNCE vs. concatenation, text-only), interaction-effect analysis, PID hyperparameter sensitivity, and both failure-case and modality-missing/noise stress tests. Baselines are retrained under identical splits and hardware. Methodological concerns: (1) the training reward on PsyQA is partly produced by the pretrained MPSE model being evaluated — the authors acknowledge reward hacking cannot be ruled out and add LLM-as-judge plus a small human subset, but the human evaluation size is not quantified; (2) the MELD "Safety Proxy" is explicitly model-derived, not a dataset-native metric (the authors are commendably explicit about this); (3) PID gains and threshold are empirically tuned on the same benchmarks used for evaluation. No code repository is released — data are "available from the corresponding author on reasonable request" — which limits reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter reporting. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — a full framework is built and run, but never deployed). - Practical: Yes — the full pipeline trains and runs on 2× RTX 3090 (24 GB) consumer-grade GPUs with a 58.3M-parameter model. - Efficient: Favorable relative to the strongest baseline — 3.2× fewer parameters, 2.4× fewer FLOPs/step (16.4 vs. 38.7 G), 3.3× faster training, and 3× higher inference throughput (128 vs. 42 samples/s) than TheraMind. - Effective: Evidence covers perception accuracy and simulated-policy metrics only; "safety" is measured against the authors' own risk classifier, not against clinical outcomes or human users, so effectiveness at the stated real-world goal (safe psychological intervention) is a proxy result. - Scalable: Not tested — no experiment above ~22k dialogues or 58M parameters, and the claimed edge-device deployability is asserted, not measured; behavior at 10–100× scale or with frontier LLM decoders is unknown. The work delivers no software artifact (no code or weights released); it stops at paper form plus two public datasets. Strengths: - The PID-Lagrangian controller is a clean, well-motivated mechanism for time-varying risk constraints, and the paper demonstrates its operating mechanism concretely (λ rising from 0.1 to 0.34 as risk-estimate variance grows from ±0.08 to ±0.24 under noise). - The ablation and interaction-effect analysis is genuinely informative — e.g., the finding that cross-modal attention and InfoNCE partially overlap (joint removal: −18.3% vs. summed −23.1%) gives practitioners actionable pruning guidance (multimodal branches can be dropped in text-only settings). - Unusually honest metric framing: the paper repeatedly and explicitly labels the MELD safety proxy as model-derived and clarifies that PsyQA evaluates text-only policy learning, not full multimodal intervention — a credibility positive. - Strong efficiency engineering: matching or beating a 187.6M-parameter baseline with a 58.3M-parameter model and near-3× less training time is a real deployment-relevant result. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront several: the workplace-bullying failure case is dissected into three root causes (OOD terminology, γ = 0.99 insufficient for 5–8-step strategy horizons, CQL-inflated risk estimates for rare strategies); the PsyQA evaluation is explicitly text-only, so the multimodal advantage is untested in the long-horizon setting; reward-model bias and reward hacking "cannot be completely eliminated" because training reward partly derives from the pretrained MPSE; PID parameters rely on empirical tuning; and the framework adds computational redundancy in text-only tasks. This candor is above average and strengthens the paper's credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human evaluation with real users or counselors beyond an unquantified "small human-rated subset" — for a paper about psychological intervention safety, the entire evidence chain rests on classifier proxies and simulated environments. - The external risk classifier (94.6% accuracy) becomes the ground truth for safety; classifier errors are never propagated into the safety analysis, and no inter-annotator agreement or demographic bias analysis of the risk annotations is reported. - Missing modern baselines: no comparison against an LLM-based counseling agent (e.g., prompted GPT-class or fine-tuned open LLM) for PsyQA generation quality, which is now the obvious alternative the field would demand; BERTScore ~0.512 is hard to interpret without that reference point. - The multi-modal encoder is evaluated on emotion recognition (MELD) but never inside the RL loop end-to-end — the policy stage is text-only, so the central claim of "multimodal perception integrated with safe long-horizon decision-making" is assembled from two disjoint evaluations rather than demonstrated as a system. - The claimed "Pareto-optimal balance" between safety and reward in the conclusion is not established by any Pareto analysis in the paper. - A minor credibility signal: the funding acknowledgment (a vocational-education teaching reform project) and the author's School of Marxism affiliation are unrelated to the technical content, and no code release despite detailed hyperparameters. Bottom Line: A carefully ablated, honestly reported, compute-efficient integration of known safe-RL techniques whose PID-Lagrangian twist is worth borrowing for constrained dialogue RL, but whose clinical and multimodal claims outrun its evidence — anyone needing a deployable or clinically validated psychological intervention system will need to look well beyond this paper.

Development and Comparison of Conversational Systems for Natural Language Querying of Enterprise Databases (NL2SQL)

F Russo · webthesis.biblio.polito.it · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This Master's thesis (internship at Technology Data Reply with a major Italian insurance company) builds two production-oriented NL2SQL conversational systems over the same Oracle Autonomous Database — a custom LangGraph agentic architecture and Oracle Select AI (database-native) — and compares them on a controlled 100-query benchmark with seven system configurations. - Why it's important: Enterprises face a real architectural fork between custom application-layer NL2SQL pipelines and database-native capabilities, and no prior controlled empirical comparison of these two paradigms on the same schemas and LLM backends existed; the choice carries real engineering and security cost. - How it does it: A shared 100-query benchmark stratified by difficulty over two contrasting schemas, with three LLM backends (GPT-oss-120B, Gemini 2.5 Pro, LLaMA 3.3 70B) instantiated in both frameworks to isolate architectural effects from model effects, measuring execution accuracy, SQL validity, hallucination, latency, and token consumption. - The good: All three LangChain configurations achieved 100% execution accuracy on all 100 queries, with zero hallucination in all seven configurations, and a schema-comment ablation demonstrates a failure class (semantically wrong zero-row results) that execution accuracy cannot detect. - The missing: The benchmark is a self-authored 100-query set over two small schemas (5-table insurance, food delivery) with single runs, no significance testing, and no evaluation on any public benchmark (Spider, BIRD), so the headline 100% EX figures cannot be generalized. - Read it or not: Worth reading for Oracle-stack enterprise architects deciding between a LangGraph/MCP custom build and Select AI, or for the failure-mode and schema-annotation findings; skip it if you want benchmark-comparable NL2SQL methods or generalizable empirical results.
Why this rank

Impact (52) is the modest anchor: the systems work on commercial Oracle infrastructure and the schema-documentation finding is genuinely actionable for practitioners, but no public artifact is released and scalability beyond 5-table schemas is untested. Rigor (42) pulls the composite down — single runs, no variance or significance tests, a self-authored 100-query benchmark with evident ceiling effects (100% execution accuracy), no public benchmark (Spider/BIRD) or external pipeline baseline, and the work is an unpeer-reviewed Master's thesis. Problem & Motivation: Enterprise business users without SQL skills depend on technical intermediaries to query relational data, creating a decision-making bottleneck. LLMs have made conversational NL2SQL feasible in production, but a critical and previously unresolved question is how a production NL2SQL system should be architected: a fully custom application-layer pipeline (fine control, high engineering cost) versus database-native NL2SQL such as Oracle Select AI (simplicity, native security, limited extensibility). The thesis is anchored in a real client engagement — a disaster-recovery insurance database with legacy abbreviated column naming, heterogeneous user roles, and row-level data entitlements — giving ecological validity that synthetic academic benchmarks lack. The stated gap: no rigorous, controlled comparison of the two paradigms on the same schemas and LLM backends existed in the literature. Key Idea: The core move is a controlled cross-architecture experiment: instantiate the same three LLM backends in both a custom agentic loop (LangGraph stateful graph with iterative SQL error recovery via tool-error feedback) and Oracle's single-shot, database-native Select AI pipeline, then attribute performance differences to architecture rather than model. A secondary, arguably more valuable insight emerges as a finding rather than a design trick: the quality of column-level schema documentation (comments), not the architecture or the model, is the dominant determinant of reliability, enabling the universal absence of hallucination. Methodology: Two systems. (1) A custom four-layer architecture: Chainlit presentation layer (auth, session management, streaming, inline Plotly charts), LangGraph orchestration layer (a two-node state graph — llm_call and tool_node — with a conditional-edge cycle implementing a ReAct-style generate/execute/correct loop), tool layer via Oracle SQLcl running as a Model Context Protocol server (per-session MCP connections, ALLOWED_TOOLS whitelist, a custom show_chart tool), and OCI Generative AI inference; cross-cutting Langfuse observability. Context is managed by a sliding-window trimmer (2,000-token budget, cl100k_base counting, trimming applied only to the inference view while full history persists in the checkpointer); access control is enforced at the database engine (role-specific connection profiles plus a stored procedure setting row-level security context), not in the prompt. (2) Oracle Select AI on Oracle AI Database 26ai: four AI profiles (one per OCI-hosted LLM) with enforce_object_list and comments=true, the SELECT AI action set (RUNSQL, SHOWSQL, NARRATE, CHAT, EXPLAINSQL), the DBMS_CLOUD_AI_AGENT Agent Team framework (tools/tasks/agents/teams) extended with custom PL/SQL chart tools, web-search and email-notification experimental teams, and the Ask Oracle APEX frontend. Evaluation: a 100-query benchmark stratified Easy/Medium/Hard (40/40/20) over two schemas (enterprise insurance with legacy abbreviated naming; food delivery with descriptive naming), seven configurations, four metrics (execution accuracy, SQL validity, hallucination, latency) plus token consumption; Cohere Command Plus was excluded from the LangChain side due to four documented integration defects in the langchain-oci adapter (one unresolved). A schema-annotation ablation removes column comments from the insurance schema to measure their impact. Key Results: On the 100-query benchmark, all three LangChain configurations (GPT-oss-120B, Gemini 2.5 Pro, LLaMA 3.3 70B) achieved 100% execution accuracy; among Select AI configurations, LLaMA 3.3 70B and Gemini 2.5 Pro also reached 100% EX, GPT-oss-120B 97%, Command Plus 95%. Hallucination rate was zero in all seven configurations. Latency: SelectAI LLaMA was fastest (mean 2,449 ms/query), LangChain Gemini slowest (mean 19,730 ms; Hard-query average ~46 s). Select AI failures were concentrated in two architecturally unrecoverable modes: ORA-01843 invalid date literals (Command Plus) and an Oracle-internal response-generation anomaly (GPT), both of which the agentic framework's error-recovery loop can in principle correct. The schema-comment ablation showed that removing column comments produces semantically incorrect zero-row results (EX still 1.0, so execution accuracy is blind to this failure) with identical failures in both LangChain GPT and SelectAI GPT. No statistical significance tests or repeated runs are reported. The benchmark is self-constructed and small; no comparison to Spider/BIRD numbers is possible. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the first controlled same-backend, same-schema comparison of application-layer agentic NL2SQL versus database-native Select AI, plus the finding that schema documentation quality dominates both architecture and model choice and that execution accuracy misses zero-row semantic failures) combined with a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the production LangGraph/MCP system and the Select AI Agent Team mappings). The architectures themselves are competent compositions of standard, well-documented components — LangGraph ReAct-style tool loops, MCP servers, profile-based schema grounding — not new methods. Rigor & Reproducibility: The ablation (column comments removed), the disaggregation by difficulty, schema, and failure mode, and the full documentation of the four Cohere/langchain-oci integration defects are genuinely careful and unusual for a thesis. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests; single runs per configuration; the 100-query benchmark was authored by the thesis itself and evaluated only on the authors' own two schemas (Goodhart-style self-evaluation risk); the headline 100% EX invites ceiling effects on a small, self-designed query set; Select AI token data was excluded for methodological incompatibility; Cohere is asymmetrically missing from the agentic side, so the architecture comparison is only three-way. No public code, data, or benchmark release is mentioned. The work is a Master's thesis, not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (two built systems evaluated by deployment and benchmark). - Practical: Yes — both run on commercially available Oracle Cloud Infrastructure services (OCI Generative AI, Autonomous Database) with no exotic hardware. - Efficient: Select AI is markedly cheaper latency-wise (2,449 ms mean for LLaMA vs 19,730 ms for LangChain Gemini); the agentic loop pays in latency and tokens for its recovery capability, and the authors quantified per-configuration token consumption. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem only on the authors' own 100-query benchmark over a 5-table synthetic-schema insurance database; zero hallucination and 100% EX are encouraging but not evidence of correctness at enterprise schema scale or on adversarial/multi-turn inputs. - Scalable: Not tested — both schemas are small (five tables); the authors themselves identify RAG-based schema retrieval as the necessary path for hundreds-of-tables schemas, so 10×–100× scale behavior is claimed, not measured. Delivered artifacts: working custom NL2SQL application, configured Select AI profiles and Agent Teams, and a reusable evaluation methodology, all in paper form (no public repo stated). Strengths: - The controlled design — three identical LLM backends in both frameworks, same database, stratified query set — is the correct experimental structure for isolating architectural effects and was absent from prior literature. - The schema-annotation ablation is the most intellectually valuable result: it exposes a failure class (plausible SQL returning empty but wrong results) that execution accuracy cannot detect, with the identical failure appearing in both architectures — a finding relevant well beyond this deployment. - Failure-mode analysis is concrete and architectural: the two Select-AI-only failure types (ORA-01843 date literals, internal response-generation anomaly) are mapped to the agentic loop's error-recovery capability, giving the accuracy advantage a mechanistic explanation rather than a leaderboard claim. - Production-grade engineering concerns are taken seriously and justified: database-engine-level RBAC/row-level security (correctly argued as necessary because LLM SQL generation is non-deterministic), per-session MCP isolation, tool whitelisting as least privilege, and the documented removal of the profile-extractor node after measuring a ~2× latency cost. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The thesis confronts limitations directly (a credibility positive): it reports the Cohere exclusion and the four adapter defects in full, acknowledges that the two schemas are small and that the RAG mode of Select AI was not exercised, flags that the schema-comment ablation shows execution accuracy's blind spot, and lists limitations including the self-constructed benchmark, single-database (Oracle-only) scope, non-persistent MemorySaver checkpointing, and static (non-RAG) schema grounding. It also explicitly excludes multi-turn conversational evaluation from the benchmark. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Ceiling-effect suspicion: 100% EX on a self-authored 100-query benchmark over a 5-table schema suggests the queries may be well within current LLM capability, making the architecture comparison less discriminative than the perfect scores imply; no queries are calibrated against public benchmark difficulty. - Single run per configuration with no variance reporting; with non-deterministic LLM generation, the 95–100% differences (e.g., SelectAI GPT 97% vs 100%) rest on very few queries and could flip on re-runs. - The 'no hallucination' claim depends on the authors' hallucination operationalization and grading procedure, which is not externally validated (no inter-annotator agreement or independent grader is mentioned). - Latency comparisons are confounded by unequal model reasoning behavior (Gemini's long chain-of-thought) rather than architecture alone; the claimed architecture-vs-model isolation is only partial. - Cohere's absence from the LangChain side means the cross-architecture matrix is incomplete for one of four models, and the defects are in the third-party adapter, not the model — a fairness caveat the comparative conclusions gloss over. - No baseline against a non-agentic, non-Oracle open-source NL2SQL pipeline (e.g., a straightforward DIN-SQL-style prompt chain), so it is unknown how much of the custom system's value comes from LangGraph/MCP versus simple good prompting. Bottom Line: A practitioner building NL2SQL on Oracle infrastructure gains genuinely actionable guidance — including the decisive role of column-level schema documentation and the latency/reliability trade-off between agentic and native pipelines — but as a research contribution the evidence rests on a small self-authored benchmark with single runs, so its 100%-accuracy findings should be treated as deployment experience, not generalizable results.

Editable Visual Design (32 ▲ )

Junyan Ye, Wei Liu, Dongzhi Jiang, Zichen Wen, HaoDong Li, Zhutao Lv, Jiaxin Lin, Jinhua Yu, Jun He, Zilong Huang, Rui Chen, Weijia Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 4 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Editable Visual Design, an agentic system in which a VLM coding agent uses an image-generation model as an on-demand "visual simulator" to produce aesthetic priors and standalone assets, then writes native HTML/CSS/SVG whose output is a layer-decoupled, fully editable design artifact (poster, infographic, etc.) rather than a flat bitmap. - Why it's important: Diffusion models produce beautiful but entangled rasters with unreliable text that cannot be post-edited, while pure code generation is editable but aesthetically flat — designers currently must choose between beauty and maintainability in AI-generated design. - How it does it: An "imagine first, then act" closed loop: the agent calls the image model to synthesize a visual reference before any code exists, generates isolated assets per layer (alpha channel or green-screen matting), writes HTML/CSS, then iterates through deterministic layout checks plus VLM screenshot review until the render matches intent. - The good: The honest treatment of evaluation — the authors explicitly refuse to score aesthetics and instead publish full Agent Design Replay trajectories (e.g., a 120-layer, 13-group infographic where the review loop catches and repairs real layout defects), which is more falsifiable than fabricated metrics. - The missing: There is no quantitative evaluation whatsoever — no benchmark scores, no ablation showing the imagined visual actually improves the coded output, no user study with designers, and all showcased cases are self-selected single-page artifacts. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in agentic visual generation and computational design who want a concrete instantiation of the "generation-as-simulator" pattern (and its honest limitations section); skippable for practitioners seeking validated, deployable tools or measurable quality gains.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile (built pipeline evaluated by demonstration artifacts). Novelty (70) is genuinely decent — the image→code inversion, with the diffusion model demoted to an up-front aesthetic simulator, is a clean conceptual reframing — but Rigor (30) collapses because there is no quantitative evaluation at all: no benchmark, no ablation of the paper's own central 'imagine first' thesis, no user study despite the authors defining success in designer terms, and cherry-picked single-brief comparisons against raw frontier models. Resilience (40) is weak since the system's value may largely re-derive capabilities already inside the proprietary backbone it orchestrates, and Completeness (55) is only rescued by the unusually honest limitations section. Impact (55) reflects the released repo but proprietary-model dependence and unreported cost cap it. Weighted composite: 0.15*70 + 0.15*30 + 0.10*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*40 + 0.30*55 ≈ 52.

Problem & Motivation: Graphic design deliverables (posters, infographics, marketing materials) need both visual quality and engineering maintainability — real text, separable layers, and post-hoc editing by a human designer. Two existing paradigms each fail on one axis. Diffusion-based text-to-image systems (GPT-Image-2, Nano-Banana 2, Seedream 5.0 Pro) produce high-aesthetic rasters with distorted text and entangled pixels unusable for downstream editing. Code-generating agents (Codex/GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Fable 5, Kimi K3 writing HTML/SVG/CSS) yield clean, editable structure but lack 2D spatial and aesthetic intuition, defaulting to templated "headline, card, rounded shadow" layouts with geometric placeholders instead of real illustrations. The paper targets practitioners and researchers in automated design who need an artifact a human can open, drag, and edit. Key Idea: The core move is inverting the role of the image-generation model: instead of being the deliverable (or, as in the predecessor GenClaw, code being an intermediate canvas for image output, i.e., code→image), the image model is promoted to an up-front "visual world simulator" whose output is only an aesthetic prior and a source of standalone assets, while code becomes the final artifact (image→code). This single reframing lets each model do what it is good at — the diffusion model supplies composition, color, and texture priors that code LLMs lack; the code LLM supplies structure, real text, and layer decoupling that diffusion cannot. Methodology: The pipeline has five stages. (1) Understanding and design planning: the VLM parses the brief into content requirements, deliverable size, and visual register, then immediately calls the image model for an "imagined visual" — a finished-looking reference that anchors the plan and is the cheapest point for user intervention. (2) Visual simulation: the VLM visually parses the imagined visual to extract palette, composition, and style as a global reference (explicitly not to be reproduced one-to-one). (3) Structural coding: the agent determines canvas topology, generates standalone text-free assets layer-by-layer (direct alpha-channel generation where supported, otherwise flat-green-background generation plus a matting script), and writes native HTML/CSS with a fixed-pixel canvas, viewport-independent layout, and every movable element tagged as a separate layer. (4) Verification and self-healing: dual checks — deterministic headless-browser rules (overflow, failed resources, malformed DOM) plus a VLM reviewer critiquing a real rendered screenshot against design intent, followed by targeted local patches, typically one or two rounds. (5) Delivery: the DOM artifact plus a serialized Agent Design Replay of the full decision trajectory. The framework is agentic tool orchestration with render-and-reflect loops (related to UI2CodeN's execute-inspect-refine); there is no explicit loss function or training — this is a prompting/orchestration system over proprietary frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol driving Codex; GPT Image 2). Critical design decisions: assets are never cut from the imagined visual (avoids pixel contamination) — justified by the layer-entanglement motivation; layout is forbidden from depending on viewport (makes drag coordinates meaningful) — well-argued; the green-screen fallback for matting is admitted to fail on green subjects — a pragmatic but under-justified hack. Key Results: The paper reports no quantitative results — no accuracy, F1, or benchmark scores on Design2Code, DesignBench, or any other evaluation. Evidence consists of: (1) a qualitative three-way comparison against pure diffusion (GPT-Image-2, which produced disordered Chinese characters and a locked bitmap) and pure code generation (Codex on GPT-5.6 Sol, which produced blank areas and chaotic layout) under the same brief; (2) a scenario showcase spanning event posters, infographics, marketing materials, and long-text layout; (3) a red panda infographic case study showing a replay trajectory that produces 120 editable layers in 13 groups with review catching and repairing real defects, and a travel poster with 6 layers in 1 group passing review unchanged. Scale of testing is small: all demonstrated cases are single-page designs. Baseline comparison is qualitative and on self-chosen briefs, not a standardized benchmark; the baselines are current frontier systems but the comparison protocol is not controlled or repeatable. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel element is the image→code inversion (image model as up-front aesthetic simulator and asset renderer, code as the engineering deliverable), which distinguishes this from both pure UI-code generation and from the direct predecessor GenClaw (code→image). The individual mechanisms — render-and-reflect refinement, VLM-as-critic, asset matting, Design2Code-style HTML generation, idea of recorded agent trajectories — are standard combinations of existing ideas reassembled in a new configuration. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is low by empirical standards, and the authors are candid about it: there are no ablations isolating whether the imagined visual actually improves the coded output versus prompting the image model only for assets, no error bars or seeds (not applicable to a deterministic-pipeline showcase, but also no repeated trials), and no significance testing. The visual quality check is a VLM judgment standing in for a designer's eye — self-referential and unvalidated. Code is released at https://github.com/yejy53/Editable-Design, but the pipeline depends on proprietary, access-gated frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol via Codex, GPT-Image-2), so exact reproduction is impossible even with the code. Methodological concerns: evaluation only on the authors' own showcase cases (cherry-picking risk is high), no standard benchmarks, no blind human ratings, and the "comparison" in Figure 3 is a single-brief anecdote. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built pipeline evaluated by demonstration artifacts, not a trained model or a proof). - Practical: Runs on API calls to commercial frontier models (Codex/GPT-Image-2), so yes, provided one has paid access; no consumer-hardware constraint since nothing is hosted locally. - Efficient: Cost and latency are not reported; each artifact requires multiple image generations, browser renders, and reflection rounds, so per-design cost is likely nontrivial but unquantified. - Effective: The evidence (self-selected showcase cases) shows the system can produce editable, layered, aesthetically competent single-page designs, not that it reliably solves the problem across a distribution of briefs. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the authors themselves state multi-page consistency is open and "the cases in this report are all single-page designs." The work delivers a software artifact (GitHub repo with the workflow) plus example outputs; there is no trained model, dataset, or benchmark. Strengths: - The image→code reformulation is a clean conceptual contribution: it identifies precisely which capability each modality lacks (aesthetic priors in code LLMs, structural rigor in diffusion) and re-routes rather than re-trains, making the approach immediately implementable on top of existing frontier APIs. - The engineering discipline around editability is real: viewport-independent fixed-canvas layout, per-layer asset generation that never leaks simulator pixels into the deliverable, and DOM-native decoupling are concrete, verifiable design commitments rather than aspirations. - The dual verification loop (deterministic layout rules + VLM screenshot critique) grounds the reflection step in an actual render, and the replay case showing repair of genuine defects in a 120-layer artifact is the most convincing single piece of evidence in the paper. - The limitations section is unusually honest — explicitly refusing to score aesthetics and acknowledging the system is "bounded by both" underlying models is a credibility positive. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) the system only routes tasks to better-suited models and is capped by the weaker of the two — a compositionally mediocre reference image gives the coding agent nothing to build on, and clean subject-background separation is required for the asset route; (2) all cases are single-page — multi-page consistency (shared type scale, palette, visual thread) is untested and presumably harder; (3) aesthetic quality admits no ground truth, so they report cases rather than scores and the visual check is a VLM proxy, not a measurement; (4) editability is easy to assert (layer counts, DOM structure) but hard to measure — what matters is whether a designer can achieve their goal, which "does not reduce to a number." This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond what the authors acknowledge: (1) no ablation of the central claim — the "imagine first" step is the paper's thesis, yet nothing isolates its contribution versus simply prompting the image model for assets (a cheap control the authors could have run); (2) no comparison against strong existing structured-design baselines such as COLE/OpenCOLE, PosterCraft, or DesignBench-scored code generation, only a one-brief anecdote against two raw frontier models; (3) no user study with actual designers, despite the authors themselves defining success as "whether a designer who opens the file can get it to do what they want"; (4) heavy dependence on vendor models that the authors' own institution competes with or depends on — the system's value collapses if it is mostly eliciting capability already inside GPT-5.6 Sol; (5) no failure-case analysis or distribution over briefs, so robustness (e.g., the green-subject matting failure, non-Latin text, dense layouts) is unknown; (6) cost and latency per artifact are unreported, which matters for the "production-grade" claim. Bottom Line: A thoughtful, honestly-written systems/position report whose image→code reframing is genuinely worth internalizing for anyone working on agentic or computational design, but with zero quantitative validation — treat it as a well-argued research direction with a reference implementation, not as evidence of a solved problem.

#210 — Moderately Innovative (51)

HarnessEvolve: Learning from Reference Trajectories for Reliable Agent Self-Evolution

W Jiang, M Chu, Y Tian, Q Zhang, H Yang, R Yang… · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HarnessEvolve, a multi-agent self-evolution framework that optimizes an LLM agent's entire harness (prompts, skills, tools, execution logic) by diagnosing failures against reference trajectories generated with ground-truth answers and filtering updates through quality and performance gates. - Why it's important: Reliable self-evolving agents are blocked by three failure modes — credit assignment failure under sparse terminal rewards, shortcut learning (data leakage/prompt bloat), and catastrophic forgetting — which have kept such systems out of real enterprise deployment. - How it does it: The core trick is reference-guided diagnosis: run the execution agent with the ground-truth answer to obtain a verified successful trajectory, align each failed trajectory against it to localize the first action divergence as the root cause, cluster error signals into systematic patterns, and gate every candidate update on leakage/bloat checks and non-degradation over a replay of recent batches. - The good: The ablation on CloudCoreNetwork-QA (Qwen3.6-27B) is convincing: removing reference-trajectory comparison collapses accuracy from 86.9% to 57.8%, showing the headline mechanism, not scaffolding, drives most of the gain. - The missing: No statistical treatment — no seeds, error bars, or significance tests — and ablations are run on only one of five benchmarks with one of two models, while the two in-house datasets are not publicly available for independent verification. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building agentic self-improvement or harness-optimization systems and want a concrete, well-motivated design for gating and failure diagnosis; skip it if you want statistically rigorous comparisons or reusable open artifacts.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (42) pulls the composite down hard: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; ablations confined to one dataset and one model; no code or data release; the +21.6-point headline rests on non-public vendor data; and the baseline comparison is asymmetric (single-component baselines vs. full-harness optimization) without the cited full-harness competitors. Completeness (50) and Resilience (45) are also low — no limitations section, unmeasured quality-gate reliability, unreported cost accounting for a 5×-overhead reference pipeline. The reference-trajectory first-divergence diagnosis is genuinely clever (Non-Obviousness 70) and the decisive ablation (86.9% → 57.8%) shows the mechanism is load-bearing, but the evidence base cannot bear the claims. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*42 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*50 + 0.15*45 + 0.10*40 = 51.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying LLM agents in software engineering and enterprise settings need agents whose harness (prompts, skills, tools, execution logic) improves autonomously from environmental feedback rather than through handcrafted workflows or human-authored skills. Existing self-evolution frameworks (GEPA, ACE, SkillOpt) each optimize only one harness component and operate on sparse binary success/failure feedback, which leaves three documented failure modes: credit assignment failure (cannot localize which action caused a long-horizon failure), shortcut learning (harness updates hardcode answers or bloat prompts with task-specific examples, inflating training accuracy without capability gain), and catastrophic forgetting (updates on one data subset degrade previously acquired competence). The paper targets practitioners who need stable, auditable, generalizing harness improvements rather than instance-level overfitting. Key Idea: The key insight is that credit assignment becomes tractable if you generate a reference trajectory — re-run the same execution agent on the failed task while providing the ground-truth answer — and then align the failed trajectory against this verified successful path: the first action divergence point isolates the root-cause error from downstream cascading failures. Wrapped around this are two defensive mechanisms treated as first-class architecture rather than afterthoughts: a quality gate (LLM-as-judge leakage score threshold η_leak=0.8, in-context-example bloat limit η_blo=5) and a performance gate (accept only if current-batch accuracy improves by ≥δ while accuracy on R=2 recent batches degrades by ≤ε=0.025), with epoch-end validation over an accumulated snapshot pool selecting the final harness. Methodology: The framework is an iterative batch-driven loop over four decoupled agents: (1) the execution agent A_exec runs training tasks to produce trajectories τ_i, and separately, pre-loop, is run with question+ground-truth answer for up to T_att=5 attempts to produce reference trajectories, which the evaluation agent verifies as genuine execution paths (not shortcut answers) before caching them; (2) the evaluation agent A_eval grades final outputs against ground truth and collects the failed set F_j; (3) the optimization agent A_opt produces structured error signals F_i = (severity, error cause, fix hint) per failure — using first-divergence-point localization when a cached reference exists, single-trajectory analysis otherwise — then clusters signals by error cause (with long-tail protection preserving single-member clusters instead of K-Means) and generates candidate edits across the whole harness (∆harness covering prompts, skills, tools, execution logic); (4) the gate agent A_gate rejects updates failing the quality checks (returning rejection reasons for up to T_rev=3 revisions) and applies the acceptance rule: improve current batch by ≥δ with max degradation on the last R batches ≤ε. Accepted candidates enter a snapshot pool V; epoch-end validation on T_val selects the best snapshot; training terminates after E=20 epochs or after P_ep=5 epochs without validation improvement, with early epoch exit after P_batch=10 consecutive rejections. The design is a verbal/analog form of training-with-validation and replay-based regression testing, not a formal optimization method; no loss function is defined — acceptance is a discrete, constraint-based rule. Critical design decisions: reference trajectories must be verified as genuine (justified by the leakage risk of giving the model the answer); error clustering preserves long-tail singletons (cited to long-tail learning literature); and the gate agent is structurally isolated from the optimizer (justified as preventing self-serving evaluation). Justification is mostly empirical via ablation rather than theoretical. Key Results: On five benchmarks — three public (SearchQA, OfficeQA, SpreadsheetBench) and two in-house (CloudCoreNetwork-QA, Wireless-QA) — HarnessEvolve beats GEPA, ACE, and SkillOpt in every setting with two models (Qwen3.6-27B domain-fine-tuned, DeepSeek-V4-Flash). Headline numbers: CloudCoreNetwork-QA/Qwen improves from 43.4% (Base) to 86.9%, +21.6 points over the strongest baseline GEPA (65.3%); Wireless-QA/DeepSeek reaches 92.8% vs. ACE at 90.1%; SearchQA 92.9%, OfficeQA 70.9%, SpreadsheetBench 76.4% (Base 44.3%). Cross-framework transfer: skills optimized under OpenClaw deployed without re-optimization on Hermes, OpenCode, LAMAgent, and DeepSeek Harness match or improve Base everywhere, with the largest gain on SpreadsheetBench/LAMAgent (45.0% → 80.0%). Ablations on CloudCoreNetwork-QA (Qwen only): full 86.9%, without reference trajectories 57.8%, without error clustering 68.6%, without quality gate 80.1%. Baselines are recent (2025–2026) but each optimizes a single harness component, so the comparison is partly confounded with HarnessEvolve's broader optimization scope. No compute/cost figures for the evolution loop are reported. Results are vendor self-reported on in-house data; no significance testing is provided. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (reference-trajectory-guided first-divergence error diagnosis) combined with a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the decoupled four-agent gated evolution pipeline). The genuinely new elements are the verified reference-trajectory cache for root-cause localization and the explicit two-gate anti-shortcut protocol; the surrounding machinery — mini-batch optimization, replay-based regression checks, validation-set snapshot selection, LLM-as-judge filtering — is a competent assembly of known ideas (ReAct-style trajectories, reflective optimization, replay buffers) applied to harness evolution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and target the right components (reference diagnosis, clustering, quality gate), and they are decisive — each removal hurts, with the largest drop from removing reference comparison (−29.1 points). However, ablations cover only one dataset and one model; there are no seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests on any result, despite batch-level stochasticity (random permutation) that would warrant them. The evaluation agent's own accuracy on trajectory verification is never measured, so cache quality is unquantified. No code, data, or optimized harnesses are released (no URL given), and the two in-house datasets are not public, making the largest claimed gains (+21.6 points) unverifiable. Hyperparameters (δ=0.0, ε=0.025, η_leak=0.8, η_blo=5) are listed but not sensitivity-analyzed. The method is developed and evaluated on the same training distribution it gates against, which the quality/performance gates partially but not formally address (Goodhart risk on T_val is mitigated by epoch-end selection, but T_val-based selection across many snapshots can still overfit a small validation set whose size is not reported). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with SYSTEMS elements — an internal pipeline built on the authors' LAMAgent framework and OpenClaw, evaluated on benchmarks rather than by production deployment). - Practical: Yes — it orchestrates LLM API/model calls and standard agent frameworks (OpenClaw, LAMAgent) on commodity hardware, with no training or gradient computation. - Efficient: Likely costly — reference-trajectory generation requires up to 5 full execution attempts per training task before optimization even starts, and every candidate update triggers re-evaluation on the current plus R recent batches; the paper reports no token or wall-clock budgets, so the cost relative to GEPA/ACE is unknown. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on benchmark accuracy (consistent wins across 5 datasets and 4 transfer frameworks), but effectiveness on real production reliability beyond these QA/spreadsheet tasks is untested. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — largest training sets are standard benchmarks; behavior at 10–100× task volume, larger harness files, or many more epochs (batch patience and epoch patience may saturate) is uncharacterized. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, dataset, or model artifact is released. Strengths: - Reference-guided first-divergence diagnosis is a genuinely clever answer to credit assignment in trajectory optimization, and the ablation (86.9% → 57.8% without it) proves it is the load-bearing component rather than decoration. - Treating shortcut learning as a first-class failure mode with an explicit, auditable quality gate (leakage scoring + bloat counting) is a non-obvious and practically important design; most prior harness-evolution work ignores it. - The two-tier acceptance protocol (batch-level replay non-degradation plus epoch-end validation over a snapshot pool) gives a monotonicity-style guarantee that the final agent is no worse than the best accepted snapshot, addressing catastrophic forgetting structurally rather than by hope. - Cross-framework transfer experiments (optimized skills deployed unchanged on four other frameworks, e.g., SpreadsheetBench on LAMAgent 45.0% → 80.0%) provide evidence the learned harness encodes general error corrections rather than framework-specific tricks — an evaluation dimension most competitors omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors do not include an explicit limitations section. Implicitly acknowledged boundaries: tasks without any verified reference trajectory fall back to imprecise single-trajectory analysis (stated in §3.2), and rejected updates are abandoned after T_rev=3 revisions. They confront the shortcut-learning and forgetting problems directly by construction, but they do not explicitly state scope limits such as dependence on ground-truth answers being available for the training corpus, the cost of reference generation, or the absence of statistical testing — the limitations discussion is thin. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The comparison is asymmetric: baselines (GEPA, ACE, SkillOpt) optimize a single harness component while HarnessEvolve optimizes everything; a full-harness baseline such as Self-Harness [Zhang et al., 2026a] or AHE [Lin et al., 2026] — cited in related work as closest competitors — is not compared against, so the +21.6-point margin cannot be attributed to the reference mechanism versus simply optimizing more surfaces. - No measurement of the quality gate's false-positive/false-negative behavior: the LLM-as-judge leakage threshold (η_leak=0.8) could silently reject legitimate generalizable rules or pass subtle leakage; the M3 ablation (80.1% without the gate) shows net benefit but not gate reliability. - Evaluation-agent accuracy on reference verification is never reported; if A_eval mis-verifies shortcut trajectories, the reference cache is polluted at the source. - No cost accounting (tokens, attempts, wall-clock, API spend) for the full loop despite a 5× reference-attempt overhead per training task — a decisive factor for practitioners. - Single-seed, no-variance reporting on stochastic pipelines; hyperparameter sensitivity (especially ε and the leakage judge) unexamined. - All in-house headline results are vendor self-reported on non-public data, warranting reduced confidence relative to the public-benchmark results (SearchQA 92.9%, OfficeQA 70.9%, SpreadsheetBench 76.4%), where margins over baselines are a more modest 1.5–3.9 points. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent self-improvement systems gains concrete, ablation-backed design patterns — reference-trajectory root-cause alignment and explicit anti-shortcut gates — that no compared baseline offers, but the headline enterprise gains rest on non-public vendor data and uninstrumented costs, so treat the public-benchmark numbers as the realistic expectation.

#211 — Moderately Innovative (51)

Prefix-Denoising Consistency: Test-Time Verification for Diffusion Language Models

Y Ichihara, N Iwase, MA Quamar, J Komiyama · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PDC (Prefix-Denoising Consistency), a training-free test-time verification method for diffusion language models (DLMs) that remasks suffixes of an initial generation at keep rates {0.1, 0.5, 0.9}, regenerates them under the fixed prefix, and majority-votes over the regenerated answers only. - Why it's important: DLMs decode at low temperature, so naive self-consistency fails because repeated full generations collapse to near-identical trajectories; PDC provides a DLM-native way to get independent verification signal without more full generations. - How it does it: It exploits the empirical observation that prefix-conditioned regeneration preserves initially correct answers (R+) more often than it repeats the same wrong answer (R-), so structured perturbations of one output act as a cheap reproducibility test. - The good: Under a compute-constrained comparison, PDC beats 4-sample self-consistency (INIT x4, budget 4T vs PDC's ~2.5T) in 13 of 15 model-dataset settings, with gains up to +9.25 accuracy points (LLaDA-1.5 GSM8K). - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, gains are often ~1 point, no code release is stated, and the theory assumes conditionally independent regenerations and a binary answer space, both violated in practice. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on diffusion LLM inference or test-time compute and want a DLM-specific alternative to self-consistency; skip it if you only care about AR-model reasoning methods, since the signal is specific to masked-diffusion decoding.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Two dimensions pull this down. Rigor (48): no seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere, with many reported gains of ~1 point on 300–600-example subsets; the theorem's conditional-independence assumption is contradicted by the method's own design; the key missing control (random-position remasking instead of prefixes) is absent; and no code is released. Impact (45): the deliverable stops at paper form with vote capped at three candidates and effect sizes near-zero on CSQA. Novelty (58) is moderate — an adaptation of a known prefix-consistency signal to the diffusion setting — and Non-Obviousness (55) is limited because why the R+/R- gap exists is never explained mechanistically. Completeness (58) and Resilience (48) are middling: limitations are acknowledged honestly, but 'consistently improves' claims do not survive the sub-point-margin scrutiny the paper's own tables invite. Weighted composite: 0.20*58 + 0.25*48 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*48 + 0.10*45 = 51.
