Problem & Motivation: Diffusion language models (Dream-7B, LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5) are increasingly competitive with autoregressive models, but their strong pass@1 accuracy comes from low-temperature decoding, which makes repeated full generations highly correlated. Standard self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) therefore transfers poorly: agreement among near-identical trajectories overstates reliability rather than providing an independent check. The closest existing DLM test-time method, TIF (temporal information filtering), votes over answers extracted from intermediate denoising steps of a single trajectory and, by construction, cannot branch into a new trajectory once the run is locked into a wrong path. Practitioners deploying DLMs for reasoning need a verification primitive that produces genuinely alternative reasoning continuations at bounded compute. Key Idea: Prefix-conditioned regeneration is a free self-verification signal: hold an exact prefix of a completed output, remask the suffix, re-denoise, and correct trajectories are reproducible while wrong ones are not (R+_rho >= R-_rho). A majority vote over three such regenerated answers — with the initial answer deliberately excluded from the vote — converts this reproducibility asymmetry into an accuracy gain. Methodology: PDC treats the DLM as a black-box generator DLM(x; L, T). Pipeline: (1) generate an initial output y of length l_y; (2) for each keep rate rho in {0.1, 0.5, 0.9}, hold floor(rho l_y) tokens fixed, remask the remaining L - L_prefix positions within the same length-L window, and regenerate with denoising budget T_rho = L_rho; (3) extract answers a(rho) and return the majority over non-null regenerated answers, excluding the initial answer a(0) to isolate the regeneration effect; ties break in fixed rho order. The paper also proves Theorem 2.2 in a stylized binary-answer setting: Acc(PDC) = piV3(R+) + (1-pi)*(1-V3(R-)), where V3 is the three-way majority probability, so PDC beats INIT iff the corrected-wrong benefit exceeds the spoiled-correct loss; a sufficient condition is R+_rho_j >= R-_rho_j for all j with one strict. Critical design decisions: (a) excluding a(0) from the vote — justified as isolating the regeneration effect, though it caps the vote at three candidates; (b) fixed three-rate set {0.1, 0.5, 0.9} — heuristic, justified only as covering weak/intermediate/strong conditioning; (c) the conditional-independence assumption in the theorem — stated but not realistic, since regenerations share the same prompt and prefix. The R+/R- gap measurement is an empirical diagnostic, not guaranteed by any property of the denoiser. Key Results: Evaluated on Dream-7B, LLaDA-8B-Instruct, and LLaDA-1.5 (all 7-8B open checkpoints) at temperature 0.2, full-diffusion setting, generation lengths L = 128/256/512, on GSM8K, MATH-500, SVAMP, CSQA, and SQA. Against length-optimized INIT: PDC improves 14 of 15 settings (one tie, CSQA on LLaDA-1.5), with gains up to +5.68 points (LLaDA-1.5 GSM8K 60.58 -> 66.26) and mean gains of +1.27 (Dream) / +1.73 (LLaDA) points; TIF variants are near-zero or slightly negative on several settings. Versus INIT x4 at L=128 (budget 4T vs PDC's ~2.5T): PDC wins 13/15, ties 1, loses 1 (LLaDA-1.5 CSQA, -0.41). At tau = 1.0, PDC beats INIT x4 by 4.98 points on average, with large GSM8K margins (e.g., +15.77 on Dream-7B). Reproduction-rate tables show R+ - R- gaps mostly positive (up to +73 points at rho=0.5 on LLaDA-1.5 GSM8K), though a few rows are negative (e.g., LLaDA-8B SVAMP 512 rho=0.1: -3.8). Baselines (INIT, self-consistency, TIF Fixed/Linear/Exp) are current and appropriate for DLM test-time work; scale is standard (8B models, 512-token outputs), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (prefix-conditioned regeneration voting as a DLM-specific test-time verification primitive) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the R+ > R- reproducibility gap) and a minor theoretical contribution (Theorem 2.2). The majority-voting aggregation is standard; the genuinely novel element is using partial remasking of one completed output as a structured, compute-cheap alternative to independent resampling, which is impossible in the same form for AR models. The AR analogue (prefix consistency, Iwase et al., 2026) is cited as motivation, so the concept is an adaptation of a known signal to the diffusion setting rather than an entirely new problem. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are reasonably thorough: alternative unmasking rules (random, origin, entropy, low-confidence), semi-AR block length 32, temperatures tau = 0.2 and 1.0, and a full length sweep (128/256/512) in Appendix C showing the best-vs-INIT selection is not cherry-picked for PDC. However: no multiple seeds, no error bars, no significance tests — on datasets like MATH-500 where 1 point = 0.5 problems (500-example subset, and only 300 examples for SVAMP/CSQA-sized sets per the reported decimals), many reported gains of ~1 point are within plausible sampling noise. The cost comparison admits INIT x4 is "a conservative higher-budget baseline rather than an exactly cost-matched baseline," so the efficiency claim is directional, not exact. No code or artifact release URL is stated. The theory is developed on assumptions (binary answers, conditional independence) that the experiments do not satisfy, so it is illustrative rather than predictive. Evaluation is entirely on the authors' chosen standard benchmarks with the authors' own harness — no independent verification. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Yes — training-free, black-box over open 7-8B checkpoints (Dream, LLaDA), runs on standard GPU hardware with existing DLM decoding stacks. - Efficient: Favorable — ~2.5T denoising steps versus 4T for 4-sample self-consistency, since each regeneration costs only the remasked suffix length. - Effective: Evidence supports gains over the initial sample and over compute-heavier self-consistency on math reasoning (up to +9.25 points), but the effect is near-zero on CSQA (+0.00 to +0.98) and slightly negative in one setting, so it partially solves the stated problem with task dependence unexplained. - Scalable: Untested beyond 512-token outputs and 8B models; the paper only claims, and does not test, behavior at larger model or sequence scales, and the vote is capped at three candidates regardless of budget. The work stops at paper form: no code, library, or dataset artifact is mentioned as released. Strengths: - The core insight — that prefix-conditioned regeneration separates correct from incorrect trajectories and can be aggregated by voting — is a genuinely DLM-specific test-time primitive that has no direct AR analogue and is orthogonal to training-side advances. - The compute-constrained ablation against INIT x4 (13/15 wins at ~62% of the budget) is the right experimental design for a test-time method and directly supports the efficiency claim. - The theoretical analysis (Theorem 2.2) is simple but useful: it makes explicit the corrected-wrong versus spoiled-correct tradeoff and yields a testable sufficient condition (per-rate R+ >= R-) that the empirical tables directly measure. - Unmasking-strategy, temperature, block-schedule, and length-sweep robustness checks go beyond a single favorable configuration. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the robustness checks "do not make PDC independent of the DLM" (results depend on the base model's conditional behavior); that INIT x4 is not exactly cost-matched; that the tau=1.0 experiments are secondary checks rather than main claims; and that escaping the same wrong answer "does not by itself guarantee correctness." Tables transparently show the CSQA tie/negative cases and a handful of negative reproduction-rate gaps. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical uncertainty quantification anywhere: single-run accuracies on 300-600 example subsets with ~1-point margins cannot support "consistently improves" claims without seeds or significance tests. - The theorem's independence assumption is contradicted by the method's own design (regenerations share the prompt and, at high keep rates, most of the output); no experiment measures the actual correlation structure that would justify V3. - Missing baselines: no comparison against compute-matched partial-remask resampling variants (e.g., random-position remasking instead of prefixes, which would isolate whether prefix structure matters), against best-of-n with a verifier, or against early-stopping self-consistency methods the paper itself cites. - The near-zero CSQA results (binary/multiple-choice, short answers) suggest the signal degrades when the answer is a small suffix of the output — a boundary condition the paper does not analyze. - Why the R+ > R- gap exists is never explained mechanistically; it could partly reflect answer-format memorization or low-temperature conservatism rather than reasoning-correctness detection. - Effect sizes are small relative to the extra ~1.5-2.5x compute over a single generation; a cost-accuracy frontier comparison (e.g., 2 full generations + vote) is absent. Bottom Line: A practitioner working with diffusion LLMs gains a cheap, training-free, and empirically well-supported decoding-time accuracy primitive — particularly on math reasoning where the +2 to +9 point compute-cheap wins over self-consistency are the strongest evidence — but the sub-point margins on commonsense tasks, absent statistical testing, and missing ablations against random-remasking controls keep this at the level of a promising technique rather than a validated general-purpose verifier.

Metaheuristic optimized deep learning for intelligent intrusion detection in cloud environments

R Farahi, N Derakhshanfard, RA Sarnaghi, A Ghaffari · link.springer.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AQSE-QDST, a three-stage intrusion detection pipeline combining entropy-weighted normalization (EAFN), a quantum-inspired swarm feature selector (AQSE), and a dual spatial-temporal deep classifier (QDST-Net), reporting 99.69% accuracy on NSL-KDD, 98.86% on CIC-IDS2017, and 98.65% on UNSW-NB15. - Why it's important: Cloud operators need IDS that detect both high-volume (DoS/DDoS) and rare (R2L, U2R) attacks under heterogeneous, imbalanced traffic without static preprocessing pipelines that degrade under distribution shift. - How it does it: The core move is chaining three adaptive components — z-score scaling weighted by per-feature Shannon entropy, a PSO-style binary swarm search with Gaussian 'quantum-inspired' perturbation over feature subsets, and a dual-branch CNN + LSTM with adaptive temporal gating and scaled dot-product attention — into a single leakage-controlled training loop. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough for this subfield: 10 independent runs with mean±SD and 95% CIs, paired t-tests and Wilcoxon tests against baselines, a component-wise ablation on all three datasets, inference latency/memory benchmarking, and an honest cross-dataset transfer experiment (accuracy drops to 86.85–87.42%). - The missing: There is no comparison against modern architectures (transformers, GNNs, self-supervised IDS) that the authors themselves name as the current frontier, the ablation deltas are small (0.24–0.52 percentage points), and Table 9's UNSW-NB15 statistics are verbatim copies of the CIC-IDS2017 table, undermining confidence in dataset handling. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on metaheuristic-plus-deep-learning IDS and want a template for rigorous benchmark evaluation and honest generalization caveats; skip it if you seek a genuinely new algorithmic idea or a comparison against the current state of the art.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (65) and Resilience (60) benefit from an unusually candid limitations section and honest reporting of an ~11-12 pp cross-dataset drop, while Impact (30) is low because no artifact ships. Weighted composite: 0.20*35 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*35 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*30 = 50 — meets minimum publishable expectations through execution discipline, not invention.

Problem & Motivation: Cloud environments face a broad attack surface (DDoS, probing, privilege escalation, multi-stage intrusions) and generate massive, heterogeneous, imbalanced traffic. The paper targets three specific gaps in prior cloud IDS work: (i) preprocessing, feature selection, and classification are usually built as loosely coupled sequential stages with fixed normalization (min-max, z-score) that ignores feature informativeness; (ii) classic metaheuristics (PSO, HHO, Firefly) converge slowly or stagnate in high-dimensional feature spaces; and (iii) deep IDS models typically model either spatial feature correlations (CNNs) or temporal dependencies (LSTMs) but rarely both. The intended users are cloud security engineers and IDS researchers working with benchmark network-traffic datasets. Key Idea: There is no single sharp algorithmic insight. The closest thing to a core trick is entropy-guided feature weighting: after z-score standardization, each feature is multiplied by a scaling factor proportional to its Shannon entropy (normalized by the maximum entropy), so features with more across-class variability get amplified before feature selection and classification. The rest is a competent assembly of known parts — quantum-inspired binary encoding of swarm solutions (superposition-style probability vectors), a centroid-plus-best-solution update rule with Gaussian perturbation, dual-branch (local/global) convolutional spatial extraction, LSTM temporal modeling with a learnable convex interpolation gate between current and previous states, and standard scaled dot-product attention. The authors explicitly acknowledge that "quantum-inspired" refers to algorithmic metaphor, not quantum hardware. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) EAFN: z-score standardization, per-feature entropy estimation over class-conditional frequencies, an adaptive scaling factor in [0,1] computed from normalized entropy, and multiplicative rescaling. (2) AQSE: binary feature vectors, a weighted multi-objective fitness (detection rate, false alarm rate, fraction of selected features; sensitivity-optimized weights 0.6/0.3/0.1 selected by grid search with cross-validation), population-centroid computation, a swarm-guided update combining the global best (exploitation coefficient 0.4) and centroid attraction (0.6), then a Gaussian quantum-inspired perturbation with radius 0.1; population 30, max 100 iterations, convergence threshold 10⁻⁵ over 5 iterations. (3) QDST-Net: 128-dim feature embedding, two parallel 4-layer convolutional branches (local + global) whose outputs are concatenated, 2 recurrent layers, an adaptive sigmoid modulation gate interpolating current and previous hidden states, 4-head scaled dot-product attention, temporal pooling, and a softmax classification layer; trained with AdamW (lr 5×10⁻⁴, cosine annealing, weight decay, dropout 0.3, batch 32, categorical cross-entropy, early stopping at epoch 48). The paper reports O(N·M) preprocessing, O(P·T·C_fit) selection cost (~18.9 min per training cycle, 52% above gradient-based selection), and O(L·h·N) network cost; selection runs offline so inference is preprocessing + network only. Critical design decisions: entropy as an informativeness proxy (theoretically questionable — higher class-conditional entropy usually signals less discriminative power, and the paper's justification is asserted rather than analyzed), the fixed fitness weights (justified by a reported sensitivity analysis), and the offline-only feature selection (well-justified for deployment cost). Preprocessing and selection are fitted per-fold on training data only; official dataset splits are preserved. Key Results: On NSL-KDD, AQSE-QDST reports 99.69% accuracy (95% CI [99.54, 99.82], SD 0.07 over 10 runs), precision 99.66%, recall 99.70%, F1 99.68%, AUC 0.9992, versus PSO+LSTM (99.41%), SVM+HHO+PSO (99.28%), and GKDPCAs+ACD+BNS (98.93%). On CIC-IDS2017 (2.49M flows), 98.86% accuracy, F1 98.63%, AUC 0.9863, versus OptiClass (98.41%), N-CNN (98.14%), EFS-DL (97.81%). On UNSW-NB15 (257,673-sample subset), 98.65% accuracy, F1 98.66%, AUC 0.9885, versus AIDF (98.45%), MEFS-IDS (98.32%), HIDM (98.10%). Statistical tests (paired t-test, Wilcoxon) report p < 0.05 against all baselines; proposed model also has the lowest reported FPR (0.008–0.015), highest MCC (0.967–0.989), and lowest detection latency (5.2–6.3 ms). Ablations show removing QDST-Net costs the most (−0.51 to −0.52 pp), then EAFN (−0.21 to −0.28 pp) and AQSE (−0.25 to −0.33 pp). Per-class analysis claims U2R recall above 78% on the most skewed setting. Efficiency: 29.3 s/epoch training, 0.51 ms/sample inference, 702 MB peak GPU memory (better memory than the LSTM baseline at 768 MB), near-linear processing-time scaling from ~2.6 s for 20K flows to ~12.8 s for 100K flows. Cross-dataset transfer (trained on CIC-IDS2017 → tested on UNSW-NB15 and vice versa) yields 87.42% and 86.85% accuracy with F1 above 84.6% — a ~11–12 pp drop from intra-dataset results. Baselines are 2022–2024 hybrid metaheuristic/DL methods reproduced on the same splits; they are reasonable but not the current frontier (no transformers, GNNs, or self-supervised approaches). Evaluation is standard-benchmark scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (incremental) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. Genuinely novel: nothing at the component level — EAFN is entropy-weighted z-scoring, AQSE is a PSO variant with Gaussian perturbation and quantum-evolutionary encoding (a well-worn metaphor), and QDST-Net is a standard CNN+LSTM+attention stack with an added gating term. What is a standard combination applied to a familiar setting: the entire framework. The paper's real differentiator is the tight integration, the leakage-controlled evaluation protocol, and the breadth of statistical validation, which exceeds typical practice in this subfield but does not constitute a new formulation or new problem. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and cover all three components on all three datasets, though the deltas (0.21–0.52 pp) are small relative to the SDs of some baselines (±0.11–0.47), so component contributions are not clearly separated from noise. The paper reports 10 independent runs with mean±SD, 95% CIs, paired t-tests, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests — better than typical for this area — and describes a leakage-free protocol (per-fold fitting of normalization and selection, official splits, internal 10-fold CV for tuning). No significance intervals are given for the ablation deltas themselves. Code is available only "upon reasonable request" — no public repository; datasets are public benchmarks with URLs given. Methodological concerns: (i) NSL-KDD and CIC-IDS2017 are saturated legacy benchmarks where 99%+ accuracy is routine, so headline numbers mainly confirm parity-with-saturation; (ii) Table 9, which purports to describe UNSW-NB15, is an exact copy of the CIC-IDS2017 statistics table (identical sample counts, 78 features, 8 attack categories) — a serious data-reporting error; (iii) the discussion sections attribute performance to mechanisms ("quality-driven selective transfer," "adaptive structural adjustment," "dynamic sampling") that are never defined in the method, suggesting partially generic result narration; (iv) several baseline comparisons may rely on numbers transplanted from original papers rather than uniform reimplementation — the text is ambiguous; (v) the conclusion states cross-dataset transfer "was not explicitly investigated" while Section 4.10 reports exactly that experiment — an internal inconsistency. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark experiments with measured runtime; no live deployment). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single RTX 3080/4090-class GPU (24 GB VRAM) with commodity PyTorch 2.x software. - Efficient: Moderate — 52% offline feature-selection overhead (~18.9 vs 12.4 min) and 29.3 s/epoch training (above a 21.4 s baseline), but inference at 0.51 ms/sample and 702 MB memory is competitive with or better than LSTM baselines. - Effective: The evidence shows strong benchmark discrimination (98.65–99.69% accuracy) and degraded but functional cross-dataset transfer (~87%), which is a proxy for — not a demonstration of — real cloud intrusion detection under drift and adversarial adaptation. - Scalable: Only claimed at 100K flows in a processing-time plot showing near-linear growth; no experiment at 10–100× that scale, no streaming or distributed test. The work delivers no software artifact: no released code, library, or trained model — it stops at paper form plus public-dataset URLs. Strengths: - Evaluation protocol: the combination of official splits, per-fold leakage prevention, 10-seed repetition with SD/CI, dual parametric/non-parametric significance testing, and a component-wise ablation across three datasets is a model of hygiene for a subfield where single-run accuracy tables are the norm. - Honesty about generalization: Section 4.5.4 and the conclusion explicitly warn that 99%+ benchmark accuracy may reflect dataset-specific statistical regularities, that legacy benchmarks oversimplify production traffic, and that cross-dataset transfer and concept drift remain open — the cross-dataset experiment reporting an ~11 pp drop is a credibility positive. - Deployment-cost accounting: reporting selection overhead, per-epoch training time, per-sample latency, peak memory against named baselines, and a processing-time-vs-volume curve addresses the practical dimension most hybrid-IDS papers omit. - AQSE's quantum-inspired perturbation is a defensible, if minor, mechanism for escaping local optima in binary feature search, with a stated convergence threshold and reported stable fitness trajectories. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront: (i) high benchmark accuracy may partially reflect dataset-specific characteristics of NSL-KDD/UNSW-NB15 (stable distributions, predefined attack categories, limited temporal variability); (ii) absence (initially) of cross-dataset validation and the need for transfer/continual-learning extensions; (iii) real deployments involve concept drift, encrypted traffic, adversarially adaptive threats, and latency constraints not captured by offline evaluation; (iv) AQSE's training-time overhead; (v) increased architectural complexity (listed as the framework's own limitation in Table 2); and (vi) lack of comparison with transformer/GNN/federated/self-supervised IDS due to resource and time constraints. This is an unusually candid limitations discussion for this genre — a credibility positive — though the contradiction between Section 4.10 (cross-dataset done) and the conclusion (cross-dataset not investigated) suggests the limitations text was not reconciled with the final experiments. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The entropy-informativeness premise is theoretically shaky: for a feature's class-conditional distribution, higher Shannon entropy typically indicates weaker class discrimination, yet EAFN amplifies high-entropy features. The paper asserts rather than demonstrates the sign of this relationship, and no analysis isolates why the mechanism helps beyond the small ablation delta. - Baseline comparability is unclear: it is not stated whether baseline numbers were re-run under the identical pipeline or transcribed from original publications, and the baselines (2022–2024 hybrid metaheuristic models) omit the stronger modern architectures the authors themselves identify. - Table 9 (UNSW-NB15 characteristics) duplicates the CIC-IDS2017 table verbatim (2,491,689 total samples, 78 features, 8 attack categories), which contradicts the correct UNSW-NB15 description given in Section 4.2.3 — a reporting error that casts doubt on the dataset pipeline as executed. - Ablation deltas (0.21–0.52 pp) are within or near the reported baseline SDs; no per-component error bars or significance tests are provided for the ablations, so component attribution is not statistically established. - The minority-class claims (U2R recall > 78%) are presented in figures without the underlying per-class confusion-matrix counts in text, and no comparison to imbalance-specific baselines (resampling, cost-sensitive loss, focal loss) is made. - Scalability is extrapolated from a 20K–100K-flow timing curve; no experiment covers the cloud scale the motivation invokes (millions of concurrent flows, streaming drift). - No code release means the leakage-prevention and per-fold selection claims cannot be independently verified. Bottom Line: A methodologically careful but algorithmically conventional hybrid IDS paper whose real value is its evaluation discipline and candid generalization caveats; practitioners seeking a genuinely new detection technique will find stronger and more current alternatives (transformer- and GNN-based IDS), but researchers designing benchmark studies in this subfield will benefit from copying its protocol rather than its architecture.

Clinic-in-a-Box: A Portable, Software-Defined Cyber Range for Realistic, Scenario-Based Cybersecurity Training

E Chumley, A Nair, R Yaezenko, J Payne, V Kyles… · digitalcommons.kennesaw.edu · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the design and implementation of Clinic-in-a-Box, a portable cybersecurity training platform housed in a travel case (three Intel NUC 10s with i7-10710U/32GB/1TB each, a GL.iNet Beryl AX router, UniFi PoE switch and Wi-Fi AP, and two Raspberry Pi 4Bs) that clones, isolates, and resets lab environments on demand, with scenarios grounded in generated organizational profiles and ATT&CK-aligned attack paths. - Why it's important: Realistic hands-on cybersecurity training has historically required fixed lab hardware, recurring cloud subscriptions, or permanent connectivity, which locks out classrooms, workshops, field exercises, and resource-constrained academic programs that cannot afford a permanent cyber range or dedicated range-engineering staff. - How it does it: The core move is packaging Proxmox type-1 hypervisor virtualization, a Docker Compose orchestration control plane driving the Proxmox VE REST API, and software-defined network segmentation into a self-contained commodity-hardware enclosure, paired with a scenario methodology that selects and places vulnerabilities only where they support ATT&CK-traceable attack transitions justified by the network's trust structure. - The good: The scenario-construction methodology is well-grounded and defensible: vulnerabilities are drawn from CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and NSA/CISA misconfiguration advisories, mapped to ATT&CK techniques, and retained only when every attack-path transition is justified by reachable services, credentials, and trust relationships — and the same scenario is designed to produce defender-visible telemetry for blue-team training. - The missing: There are no quantitative results of any kind — no concurrent-VM counts, reset times, deployment durations, cost figures, or user counts from testing — and no controlled evaluation of learning outcomes; all evidence is internal testing and informal instructor feedback, which the authors explicitly acknowledge. - Read it or not: Worth reading for educators building low-budget, offline, or field-deployable cyber ranges who want a concrete architecture and a disciplined ATT&CK-aligned scenario-design recipe; skip it if you need empirical evidence of training effectiveness or deployment-scale benchmarks, which it does not provide.

Problem & Motivation: Cybersecurity educators and trainers outside well-funded institutions cannot deliver realistic hands-on exercises because traditional labs assume stable local infrastructure, controlled network boundaries, known endpoint configurations, and instructor oversight — assumptions that fail in classrooms, workshops, field exercises, and temporary venues where learners have heterogeneous hardware, intermittent networks, and no admin rights. Cloud platforms (TryHackMe, Hack the Box) remove setup burden but introduce recurring per-VM costs, internet dependence, and provider lock-in unsuited to academic budgets and offline settings; fixed labs are hard to replicate across venues. The gap the paper targets is preserving realism, reproducibility, safe isolation, and low-friction access simultaneously when the training environment must be portable rather than permanently installed — a problem framed against NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 and the NIST/NICE cyber-range guide, which treat practical exercises as core to role-based training programs. Key Idea: Two ideas, tightly coupled. (1) Infrastructure: a software-defined, fully automated lab lifecycle (clone from templates → attach to per-user isolated networks → provision → reset/teardown via the Proxmox VE REST API) compressed into a commodity travel-case form factor, so one physical system serves repeated events without manual rebuilding. (2) Scenario design: a weakness is included in a scenario only if it enables a plausible, ATT&CK-mapped attack transition that is justified by the network and trust structure (external reachability for initial access, locally exposed credentials for lateral movement, share permissions for collection) rather than inserted as an exercise shortcut — with the same environment engineered to emit defender-visible artifacts per phase so one scenario serves red, blue, and purple training. Methodology: The paper is a systems design report, not an algorithmic contribution. Pipeline: (1) organizational profile generation — size class (EU SME definitions: micro 1–9, small 10–49, medium 50–249 employees) plus sector (drawn from CISA's 16 critical-infrastructure sectors, plus K-12 and small-business profiles) produce roles (named individuals with concerns and constraints), asset inventories per NIST SP 1800-5, and a layered core/distribution/access network design with subnets, VLANs, and trust levels; (2) vulnerability selection and placement — candidates screened against the CISA/FBI/NSA routinely-exploited-vulnerabilities advisory and the KEV Catalog, placed by attack function (initial-access weaknesses on externally reachable hosts, post-compromise weaknesses where they support progression), reproducible from CVE details; (3) ATT&CK behavior mapping — NSA/CISA misconfiguration guidance maps conditions to techniques (T1190, T1059, T1552.001, T1021.002, T1135, T1039, Kerberoasting, etc.); (4) scenario assembly — a walkthrough scenario chains public-facing exploitation → command execution → local credential discovery → SMB lateral movement → network share discovery and collection, with each transition gated by an environmental precondition; (5) deployment — orchestration clones VMs from templates, attaches per-team networks, and automates reset/teardown. Control plane (Docker Compose) is separated from student lab traffic; isolation is enforced at network, host, and administrative layers. Critical design decisions: lifecycle automation as the core mechanism (well-justified by the observation that manual lab management fails as concurrency grows); scenario complexity scaled to cohort size given fixed hardware (justified, but with no published thresholds); defender-visible telemetry treated as an exercise requirement per NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (well-justified for dual-perspective training). No loss function or formal optimization framework applies — this is infrastructure engineering. Key Results: The paper reports essentially no quantitative outcomes. The hardware bill of materials is concrete (3× Intel NUC 10 with i7-10710U, 32GB DDR4, 1TB NVMe; GL.iNet Beryl AX travel router; UniFi USW Lite 8P PoE switch; UniFi U6 Lite AP; 2× Raspberry Pi 4B for admin and network control), but there are no measured figures for concurrent users, VMs sustained, provisioning or reset latency, transport-to-ready time, or cost savings versus cloud. Pre-built environments demonstrated include GOAD (Active Directory attack lab) and OWASP Juice Shop, plus custom K-12-profile machines (e.g., a student information system with SQL injection and default credentials). The representative walkthrough demonstrates a bounded intrusion path supporting offensive and defensive training in one scenario. "Initial testing" found that lifecycle automation is operationally necessary, that portability introduces power/cooling/recovery concerns absent in fixed labs, and that scenario complexity must be matched to cohort size — qualitative observations only, with no numbers, baselines, or comparisons. Baselines: none evaluated; cloud ranges and fixed labs are discussed qualitatively in related work but never benchmarked against. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the travel-case-integrated platform) plus a NEW FORMULATION of scenario design (organizational-profile grounding + adversarially justified vulnerability placement + defender-telemetry co-design). The individual infrastructure components — Proxmox virtualization, Docker Compose orchestration, software-defined networking, template cloning and snapshot reset — are all standard, well-documented techniques; the genuinely novel elements are the physical integration into a self-contained, off-grid-capable travel case and the systematic methodology that derives attack paths from network/trust structure rather than inserting artificial shortcuts. The scenario-design discipline is the more intellectually interesting contribution, though it formalizes practices already common in commercial and academic range engineering. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no significance tests — appropriate to the genre, but the paper also lacks the deployment benchmarks a systems paper needs (VM counts, reset times, concurrency limits under load). No code, configuration repository, dataset, or model release is mentioned anywhere, so the platform is not currently reproducible by others despite the paper emphasizing "replicable pattern" and reproducibility. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation consists of internal testing and informal instructor feedback — no independent or controlled evaluation, and the authors say so plainly; (2) no comparison against any baseline platform (cloud range, fixed lab, or another open-source range such as those surveyed in the paper's own cited comparative analysis); (3) claimed cost and setup-overhead reductions are asserted, not measured. Two figures were generated with ChatGPT (disclosed and reviewed by authors). Positive: the paper is unusually honest about the absence of learning-outcome evidence and refuses to equate exercise completion with skill transfer. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS — a built platform, validated only through internal deployment and walkthroughs, not yet through real instructional deployments at scale. - Practical: Yes — built entirely from commercially available commodity hardware (NUCs, travel router, PoE switch/AP, Raspberry Pis) operating on standard power with no cloud or facility dependency, and even usable over facility guest Wi-Fi or LTE via cascading-NAT VPN. - Efficient: Likely favorable versus recurring cloud VM costs and fixed-lab staffing, but the paper provides no cost figures, no power draw, and no capacity ceiling, so efficiency cannot be verified from the reported evidence. - Effective: Deployment viability and dual red/blue scenario support are demonstrated by walkthrough; whether it improves learning is explicitly unevaluated — the authors state formal outcome measurement "remains future work." - Scalable: Untested and plausibly limited — 96 GB aggregate RAM across three NUCs bounds concurrency, and the authors themselves note that resource-intensive scenarios must be reserved for smaller groups; no 10×/100× path exists without the proposed cloud extension. The work delivers a physical system and design methodology in paper form; no software artifact, configuration repo, or scenario library is publicly released. The scenario-design methodology (ATT&CK-justified path construction with defender-telemetry co-design) is reusable independently of the specific hardware. Strengths: - The scenario-construction rule — a weakness is admitted only if it enables an attack transition justified by environmental preconditions (reachability, credentials, trust) — is a genuinely useful, articulable design discipline that avoids the "isolated vulnerable machine" anti-pattern common in training labs. - Dual-perspective design: the same ATT&CK mapping defines both the red-team path and the defender-visible artifacts, enabling offensive, defensive, and comparative (purple) training from one scenario — a coherent and economical instructional design. - Grounding vulnerability selection in CISA KEV, the routinely-exploited-vulnerabilities joint advisory, and NSA/CISA misconfiguration guidance ties training content to demonstrably exploited, real-world weaknesses rather than synthetic curiosity exploits. - Honest framing: the paper distinguishes claims from evidence throughout, explicitly refusing to treat exercise completion as a proxy for durable skill transfer, and supplies a credible (if briefly sketched) quasi-experimental evaluation plan with IRB requirements. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length — a credibility positive. They state: (1) no formal evaluation of training effectiveness or engagement exists yet; (2) portability imposes a fidelity ceiling that cannot reproduce every operational dependency of large enterprises; (3) deployment variability, platform maturity, and constraints in concurrency, administrative ease, and observability remain; (4) the evaluation methodology is limited because ATT&CK traceability and reproducibility do not establish long-term effectiveness; (5) representational scope is bounded — weak support for social-engineering-heavy, insider-driven, long-dwell, and cloud/hybrid-identity scenarios. Lessons learned (lifecycle automation as necessity, intentional rather than incidental realism, portability-versus-scale competition) are candid and specific. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No quantitative deployment data at all: for a systems paper whose core value proposition is "reduced setup overhead and cost," the absence of any measured reset time, provisioning time, transport-to-ready time, concurrent-user ceiling, or dollar cost is the single largest evidentiary hole, and the authors do not flag it as such. - No head-to-head comparison with any alternative — cloud ranges (TryHackMe/HTB are discussed but never benchmarked) or open-source ranges the paper itself cites (ref. 29) — so the claimed cost and portability advantages remain untested assertions. - The organizational-profile generation is described at specification level (sizes, sectors, roles, assets) but the generation process itself is never shown as a tool or procedure with inputs/outputs; it is unclear whether profiles are hand-authored, templated, or automated, and no generated-profile corpus or validation of realism is reported. - No release of orchestration code, VM templates, or scenario definitions, which undermines the "replicable pattern" claim — reproducibility is asserted but not enabled. - Pilot-testing details are absent: how many events, how many students, which venues, what failures occurred — "initial testing" is reported only as distilled conclusions. - The walkthrough is a single hand-designed scenario; no evidence that the methodology generalizes across the advertised profile space (IT, OT, small business, K-12) is provided. Bottom Line: A well-motivated, honestly reported systems-design paper whose portable hardware recipe and ATT&CK-justified scenario methodology are genuinely useful to cyber-education practitioners building low-cost or offline training capability, but whose complete absence of quantitative deployment or learning-outcome evidence means it complements rather than replaces the stronger empirical literature on range effectiveness it cites.

Towards a Systems Foundation for Agentic Skills: Architecture, Lifecycle, and Security

S Badhe, D Shah, P Tiwari, N Kathrotia · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a unified systems-level survey and reference architecture for "agentic skills" — modular, externalized procedural packages for LLM agents — formalizing them as a six-tuple s = (A, I, C, T, π, E) and organizing the field across a nine-stage lifecycle (discovery, authoring, storage, retrieval, composition, execution/repair, adaptation, evaluation, security). - Why it's important: LLM agents fail on long-horizon tasks and re-derive procedures every session; a shared conceptual framework for how skills are authored, retrieved, executed, and secured could standardize a rapidly fragmenting subfield that now spans marketplaces with 10^4–10^5 third-party packages. - How it does it: The core move is a definitional formalism — a six-tuple skill representation plus three "triad membership criteria" (encapsulated modularity, late-binding invocation, procedural state transformation) — used to systematically disambiguate skills from prompts, tools, workflows, and episodic memory, then mapped onto lifecycle stages and threat vectors. - The good: The verifiability–portability trade-off analysis (§3.2.3) is genuinely sharp: no existing representation format verifies natural-language instructions (I) or activation conditions (A) pre-execution, which the paper correctly identifies as the root of the prompt-injection attack surface, corroborated by cited audits of 49,943 and 98,440 real-world skills. - The missing: The paper reports no primary experiments of its own; all quantitative evidence is second-hand from cited works, several of which are the authors' own (SKILL.state, SkillSec-Eval), and many citations carry implausible 2026 dates with the arXiv stamp reading August 2026, undermining verifiability of the evidence base. - Read it or not: Read it if you are entering the agentic-skills/tool-use area and need a map of the design space and security threat model; skip it if you want primary empirical results or rigorous analysis — it is a synthesis, not a study.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents deployed on complex, long-horizon tasks suffer two compounding bottlenecks: (1) reliability degradation, where early-stage execution errors propagate downstream and agents rarely detect or recover from them, and (2) non-accumulation of procedural knowledge — successful task execution leaves no durable advantage because routines are locked in transcripts discarded at session boundaries. Existing remedies are inadequate: stuffing procedures into context inflates token cost with no selective loading, and fine-tuning writes procedures into weights that cannot keep pace with fast-changing tools and APIs. The practitioners affected are agent-platform builders, and the specific gap is that the emerging "skills" paradigm (modular, externalized, on-demand procedural artifacts) lacks a unified formal foundation, lifecycle architecture, and security taxonomy — the paper aims to supply all three. Key Idea: The central organizing insight is to treat agentic skills as externalized procedural memory — a non-parametric, persistently stored, late-binding executable abstraction — and to define it precisely enough that boundary cases (prompt vs. skill, atomic tool vs. skill, workflow vs. skill, episodic memory vs. skill) resolve mechanically via three criteria. A second, more original insight emerges from the representation analysis: pre-execution verifiability and cross-harness portability trade off monotonically across representation formats (natural language → structured → executable → formal contracts), and no format verifies natural-language instructions or activation conditions — a structural security blindspot that the paper then uses to organize its entire threat taxonomy around the six-tuple components. Methodology: This is a survey/systematization paper, not an experimental system; its "method" is formalization plus structured literature synthesis. It defines a skill as s = (A, I, C, T, π, E) (activation condition, instructions, constraints, tools, execution policy, effects), with skill activation A(x_t, g) → {0,1} gated by a capability-based permission constraint T_s ⊆ T_permitted(x_t) to formalize privilege-escalation prevention. The lifecycle is organized into nine stages, each formalized with operators: skill discovery as D(H) mapping trajectory histories to candidate skills with pre-admission verification V(s) = 1; memory updates M_{t+1} = (M_t \ Ev(M_t)) ∪ {s} with a counterfactual utility function U(s) balancing performance gain against retrieval/token cost; two-stage retrieval (hybrid BM25+dense candidate generation, then cross-encoder reranking under activation and permission constraints); sequential/DAG composition with compositional preconditions E_1 ⊆ C_2 and locality-bounded O(d_h) subtree repair; and a policy-skill co-evolution objective with alternating updates. Ten comparison tables organize ~150 cited systems by modality, verification rigor, retrieval paradigm, threat vector, and defense stage. Critical design decisions: (1) the capability-subset permission formalism is well-motivated and maps cleanly to real defenses; (2) the verifiability/portability monotonicity claim is a qualitative ordering, not measured, though it is internally consistent; (3) the six-tuple is useful but components like I and π overlap in hybrid formats — the paper acknowledges this via the hybrid format class. The PDF text is truncated mid-Section 6.6, so the final open-challenges discussion is incomplete in the provided document. Key Results: As a survey, the paper's "results" are synthesized empirical findings from cited works, not measurements it ran. The most consequential numbers it aggregates: a 34,000-skill in-the-wild audit (SkillsInWild) showing end-to-end task success degrades severely when agents must autonomously retrieve from open pools versus oracle skill sets; a 49,943-skill audit (BehavioralIntegrity) reporting 80.0% of skills deviate from declared behavior; HarmfulSkillBench's audit of 98,440 registry skills finding weaponized skills that bypass frontier safety guardrails; a null result (OffensiveCS-Eval, 120+ CTF tasks) where skill injection yields zero statistically significant gain over raw tool use (8.9 pp spread, p = 0.71), yielding the "Environment-Feedback Bandwidth Hypothesis"; SkillRouter's 80K-skill retrieval at sub-second latency with a 31–44% routing-accuracy drop under metadata-only indexing; TaskBench showing tool-composition accuracy decays exponentially with DAG depth; SandboxEscape showing non-trivial container breakout rates for frontier LLMs; and the authors' own SkillSec-Eval (327 enterprise skills) and SKILL.state (O(T²) → O(T) token complexity). Benchmarks covered span OSWorld, SWE-bench, WebArena, BIRD-Bench, and TaskBench. These are quoted findings of varying provenance — most are recent arXiv-era preprints, not peer-reviewed results, and none are independently verified here. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW PROBLEM framing — the six-tuple skill abstraction, the triad membership criteria for disambiguating skills from adjacent abstractions (Table 1), the nine-stage lifecycle decomposition, and the mapping of threat vectors onto unverified tuple components (I and A) constitute a genuine conceptual synthesis. The paper introduces no new method, dataset, or system of its own beyond formalizing; nearly all techniques surveyed (retrieval pipelines, DAG orchestration, RL option discovery, trajectory distillation) are combinations of known ideas applied to the skill-packaging setting, and the value lies in the taxonomy and the security blindspot analysis rather than in any single technical mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations, seeds, and significance tests are not applicable to the survey itself; the paper does reproduce detailed per-system experimental parameters from cited works in its tables. No code or artifact release is associated with this paper (the surveyed systems' releases are "Not stated" in the provided text). Methodological concerns a reviewer must flag: (1) the citation record is anomalous — nearly all references carry 2025–2026 dates, the arXiv identifier reads 2608.29596 dated 30 Aug 2026, and some citations (e.g., "SkillTracer (Li et al.)") are incomplete, which makes the evidence base impossible to audit against known literature; (2) the authors cite their own artifacts (SKILL.state, Badhe et al. 2026; SkillSec-Eval, Badhe & Tiwari 2026) as headline evidence, a self-citation loop where their formalism and their benchmark mutually validate; (3) the qualitative claims ("substantial gains," "substantially reduces") are frequently unquantified even where the underlying studies presumably report numbers; (4) the verifiability–portability ordering is asserted, not measured. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL (formalisms and synthesis with no primary experimental claim by this paper's authors). — Sound: The formalism is definitional rather than axiomatic; there are no theorems or proofs, so soundness reduces to internal consistency, which mostly holds, though the activation/execution equations (e.g., x_{t+1} = π(x_t, I, T)) are notation, not analysis. — General: The abstraction is deliberately broad, covering five domains (SWE, GUI/OS, robotics, science, meta-skills), which is realistic but means the formalism constrains little — almost any packaged procedure fits the tuple. — Tight: No bounds are derived; the O(T²) → O(T) and O(N) → O(d_h) complexity claims belong to cited systems, not to this paper's analysis. — Implementable: Yes in spirit — the lifecycle decomposition and threat-component mapping are directly actionable for platform engineers designing registries and sandboxes, and the paper reads as an implicit design checklist; no follow-up operationalization exists within the paper itself. The work stops at paper form; the artifacts it references (SKILL.state, SkillSec-Eval) are separate works whose availability is not stated here. Strengths: - The security analysis is the strongest section: mapping attack surfaces (indirect prompt injection, trojaned policies, credential exfiltration, compositional escalation, dependency squatting) onto specific unverified components of the six-tuple converts a scattered threat literature into a coherent, checkable model, and the claim that no format verifies natural-language instructions is a real, non-obvious insight. - The Table 1 disambiguation of skills against prompts, episodic memory, workflows, and tools — including the honest admission that skills are uniquely unverifiable before invocation — is a crisp conceptual contribution that could become standard vocabulary. - The paper engages seriously with negative results (the CTF feedback-bandwidth null result, open-pool retrieval fragility, the single-agent capacity phase transition, co-adaptation drift), which is unusual and valuable in a survey claiming a paradigm's maturity. - The observation that the verifiability/portability trade-off is monotonic across representation classes gives practitioners an explicit design dial rather than a list of options. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are direct about field-level weaknesses: RL-based discovery assumes dense rewards and cheap simulation and is sample-prohibitive outside simulators; inductive AI synthesis produces brittle, overfit skills without execution grounding; LLM judges exhibit sycophancy and miss stealthy injections; unguided discovery fails the zero-to-one gap in sparse environments; skill proliferation floods retrieval indices; policy-skill co-evolution drifts and breaks downstream planners; lifelong benchmarks suffer evaluation contamination via shared tool APIs; current skills depend on frontier models and fail on 3B–8B SLMs; and sandboxing is porous (container breakout under misconfiguration). The paper confronts these limitations candidly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive — though the provided text truncates before the full open-challenges treatment. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The citation corpus is internally suspect: pervasive 2026 publication dates, a future-dated arXiv stamp, an incomplete citation ("SkillTracer (Li et al.)" with no year or venue), and citation families that appear only in this paper's own framing (e.g., dozens of "Skill*" systems) — a reviewer cannot distinguish a genuine nascent literature from an unvetted or partially fabricated evidence base, and the paper never addresses source verifiability. - Self-referential evidence: the formalism's security claims lean on SkillSec-Eval, authored by two of this paper's authors, so the threat taxonomy and its empirical support are not independent. - The survey claims to "establish agentic skills as a foundational paradigm" but never tests the six-tuple against a system that resists classification — the triad criteria are illustrated only on handpicked cases the authors choose. - The monotonic verifiability–portability ordering is asserted for four format classes and then the fifth (hybrid) is declared off-gradient; no measurement, dataset, or operational definition of "portability" is provided. - Missing critical perspective: no comparison against the alternative that better base models or fine-tuning simply subsume externalized skills — the paper dismisses fine-tuning on agility grounds but cites no head-to-head evidence. - The quantitative figures quoted from cited audits (80.0% deviation, >90% scanner evasion, 33.6% ASR) are reported without confidence intervals or methodology summaries, and the truncation means the security-governance conclusions cannot be fully checked. Bottom Line: As a conceptual map and security threat model for the agentic-skills paradigm this is the most structured synthesis I have seen of this space and is worth a practitioner's time for its formalism and Table 7–8 threat/defense taxonomy alone — but the anomalous, largely unauditable citation record and the authors' self-referential evidence base mean every quantitative claim should be treated as provisional until traced to a verifiable source.

DataFoundry: Evolving Data Preparators via Recursive Self - Improvement

C Yang, X Wu, X Lin, C Xu, X Jiang, H Xiong, J Guo · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DataFoundry, a framework that recursively self-improves an LLM-driven data-preparation pipeline — represented as an evolvable runtime specification — on small pilot sets before full-scale synthesis of domain SFT data. - Why it's important: Existing synthetic-data pipelines apply quality control only post-hoc, discarding 50–90% of generated samples instead of fixing the upstream construction stages that repeatedly produce bad data, wasting generation compute and capping data quality. - How it does it: A coding-agent controller orchestrates three modular skills — compile the specification into an executable runtime, assess a ~100-sample pilot set against six domain-appropriate quality criteria, and design a component-level adapter that revises the specification while preserving stable module interfaces — iterated for two rounds. - The good: Controlled same-backbone comparisons (GPT-5.6 Sol) isolate framework-level gains — e.g., +14.4 points on Finance and +11.1 on Medical domain averages over an agent-based generator with the identical backbone — and the gains transfer to a different downstream model (Llama-3.1-8B). - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and the generator comparisons are confounded by wildly different synthesized dataset sizes (DataFoundry: 87,566 samples vs. DataFlow: 509,242 vs. GPT-5.3-codex agent: 4,796), so the headline margins of 1.3–3.3 points may not be robust. - Read it or not: Worth reading for engineers building LLM data-synthesis pipelines who want a concrete, component-traceable self-improvement architecture; skippable if you already follow AutoData/DataMaster-style iterative recipe optimization closely.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (50) is the main drag: single-run evaluation with no seeds or error bars, a 3–6× dataset-size confound across compared generators that is never controlled, T=2 chosen with a Goodhart-adjacent criterion, no ablation isolating the adapter/frozen-baseline mechanism, and no artifact release. Novelty (55) is a well-differentiated NEW METHOD, but AutoData/DataMaster-style iterative recipe refinement covers adjacent ground; Non-Obviousness (45) is modest since the constituent ideas are standard. The same-backbone controlled comparison and the honest non-monotonic RSI-round dynamics are the paper's best features, supporting Completeness (55) and Resilience (45); Impact (45) reflects a practical architecture pattern that practitioners could adopt, but nothing is released. Weighted composite: 0.20*55 + 0.25*50 + 0.15*45 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*45 + 0.10*45 = 50.
empirical Novelty 55 Rigor 50 Non-Obv 45 Completeness 55 Resilience 45 Impact 45
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Teams adapting LLMs to specialized domains (math, finance, law, medicine) rely on pipelines that restructure raw corpora into SFT data. The dominant construction-then-filtering paradigm generates a large candidate pool and then discards 50–90% of it via post-hoc filters, which wastes generation cost and never repairs the root causes of bad samples. The authors identify two obstacles to intervening upstream: (1) pipelines are implemented as long, standalone code programs that are hard to diagnose and update, and (2) there is little actionable, domain-specific guidance on which pipeline component to optimize and how. The gap they target is a systematic way to trace output-level quality failures back to specific construction stages and fix them before scaling production. Key Idea Represent the data preparator not as fixed code but as an evolvable runtime specification, and run a bounded recursive self-improvement loop on it: compile the specification into a working pipeline, generate a small pilot set, diagnose deficiencies against domain-appropriate criteria, and express fixes as an adapter — a delta document that revises individual components (chunk manager, instruction builder, response generator) while the baseline specification is preserved to prevent drift or specification collapse. Isolating domain-specific changes in adapters, rather than rewriting the whole pipeline each round, is the load-bearing trick. Methodology The formal loop is φ(t) → Compile → R(t) → Construct (pilot set P(t) on corpus K_d with budget Ñ) → Assess(P(t); C_d) → assessment report a(t) → Evolve → φ(t+1), run for T=2 rounds, after which the final specification is compiled and used for full-scale generation. A Skills-as-Modules architecture implements three skills driven by a coding agent (GPT-5.6 Sol via Codex CLI): (1) the Construction-Runtime-Compiler enforces four stable component interfaces — corpus chunk manager (1200–3000 char chunks from markdown headings), instruction builder, response generator, and a batch generation service (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, max concurrency 32) — plus smoke tests and structured logging; (2) the Contextualized-Data-Assessor selects domain-appropriate criteria from a six-criterion library (instruction alignment, self-containment, information density, factual grounding, domain utility, numerical correctness) and produces a structured report with attribute statistics and priority deficiencies; (3) the Evolution-Adapter-Designer traces deficiencies to responsible components and writes an adapter Δ(t) that may revise prompts, policies, configurations, or add modules, applied as φ(t+1) = Adapt(φ_base, Δ(t)). Critical design decisions: (a) adapter-based deltas against a frozen baseline — justified as preventing specification collapse, though no ablation isolates this mechanism alone; (b) fixing T=2 — justified by observed deterioration of pilot assessments after round 2, but Figure 3 shows downstream benchmark performance also peaks at round 2, creating an ambiguous selection criterion; (c) LLM-judged pilot assessment with agent-selected criteria — plausible but unvalidated against human labels. Downstream evaluation fine-tunes Qwen2.5-7B (and Llama-3.1-8B in ablation) with full-parameter SFT (LlamaFactory, 3 epochs, lr 5e-6, ZeRO-3) on Dolly-15k jointly with each generator's synthesized data. Key Results On DataPrep-Bench settings adopted from Liang et al. (2026), DataFoundry (GPT-5.6 Sol) achieves domain-level averages of 28.8 (Math), 66.1 (Finance), 78.6 (Law), and 46.0 (Medical) with Qwen2.5-7B, exceeding the strongest competing generator by 3.3, 1.3, 1.4, and 2.2 points respectively. Against the same-backbone GPT-5.6 Sol agent-based generator the margins are larger: +3.4 (Math), +14.4 (Finance), +4.8 (Law), +11.1 (Medical); against same-backbone DataPrep-Skill: +3.8, +6.2, +7.9, +5.9. With Llama-3.1-8B downstream, DataFoundry is best on Math (13.6), Finance (41.3), and Medical (39.9), beating the best generator by 2.6, 4.8, and 3.8 points, but is not best on Law (71.1 vs. GPT-5.2's 76.4). RSI-round ablation: Math rises 25.6 → 28.4 → 28.8 then falls to 26.1 at round 3; Finance peaks at 66.1 (round 2) then drops to 58.3. Baselines span DataFlow/DataFlow-Skill workflows, direct LLM generators (Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.0 Pro, GPT-5.2), agent-based generators (Qwen3.5-Plus, GLM-4.7, GPT-5.3-codex, GPT-5.6 Sol), and skill-based generators — a broad and reasonably current set, though several agent configurations visibly collapse (e.g., Law averages of 56.5–57.0), inflating relative averages. Scale: 4 domains, ~7k–509k synthesized samples per generator (DataFoundry: 87,566 total), two 7–8B downstream models, 16 benchmarks. Notable non-headline finding: no generator wins every sub-task; DataFoundry wins on domain averages. All numbers are single-run with no variance estimates. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING on evolution dynamics). The genuinely novel piece is the adapter-isolated, interface-preserving specification-evolution loop applied upstream of data production — recursive self-improvement applied to the executable preparation runtime rather than to prompts or data filters. The constituent ideas (agent skills, coding-agent orchestration, LLM-judge assessment, iterative recipe refinement) are standard; AutoData and DataMaster already iterate over data recipes with feedback, so DataFoundry is best read as a well-differentiated instantiation of a known trend — the stable-interface + frozen-baseline adapter mechanism is the main differentiator over DataPrep-Skill-style skill evolution. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations cover RSI round count and downstream base-model swap (Llama-3.1-8B), plus case studies tracing component-level changes — good coverage of the framework's dynamics, but there is no ablation of the adapter mechanism itself (e.g., adapter vs. free-form spec rewrite), no criterion-library ablation, and no human validation of the assessor. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; several claimed margins (1.3–1.4 points on Finance/Law) are within plausible single-run noise. No code, data, or specification artifacts are stated as released. Methodological concerns: (a) the number of RSI rounds (T=2) was chosen partly by observing downstream benchmark behavior, a mild Goodhart risk; (b) all corpora and evaluation settings are adopted wholesale from DataPrep-Bench (Liang et al., 2026), so no independent held-out evaluation; (c) generator comparisons are not controlled for dataset size (87,566 vs. 350k–509k samples for DataFlow variants), leaving a data-volume confound the paper does not address; (d) this is a preprint and has not undergone peer review. Deployability: (4-property check)** Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework run end-to-end with downstream training experiments; closest to a SYSTEMS contribution evaluated by experiments). - Practical: Yes — runs on 8× NVIDIA H800 with API access to GPT-5.6 Sol (Codex CLI) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, all commercially available. - Efficient: The pilot-set-first design (≈100 samples per assessment round) keeps RSI overhead low relative to full-scale generation, but no token/cost accounting of the loop is reported. - Effective: Downstream benchmark gains over same-backbone baselines support the claim on 7–8B models, though size confounds and single runs weaken attribution; effectiveness on larger models is untested. - Scalable: Only claimed — production ran at ~87k samples total across 4 domains; behavior at 10× corpus scale, larger downstream models, or more RSI rounds (which degrade at round 3) is untested. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, dataset, or trained-model release is mentioned. Strengths - The controlled same-backbone comparison (GPT-5.6 Sol across agent-based, skill-based, and DataFoundry conditions) is the right experimental design for attributing gains to the framework rather than the model, and the resulting margins (+5.9 to +14.4 domain-average points) are large enough to be meaningful even without error bars. - The adapter-based evolution with a frozen baseline specification is a concrete, inspectable mechanism against the well-known failure mode of iterative agent self-modification (specification collapse), and the Finance case study (84/100 instructions with deictic references traced to the instruction builder, with targeted fixes per component) demonstrates genuine traceability from output failure to component fix. - The RSI-round ablation honestly documents non-monotonic dynamics — performance degrades at round 3 (Math 28.8→26.1; Finance 66.1→58.3) — providing a rare empirical characterization of when recursive self-improvement stops helping. - Cross-model validation (Llama-3.1-8B) shows the prepared data's utility is not tied to the fine-tuning target used in the main results. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that excessive evolution degrades performance and that the framework requires controlling the number of RSI rounds (fixed at 2), and they concede DataFoundry does not win every individual sub-task, only domain averages. They confront the over-evolution failure mode directly, which is a credibility positive. There is no dedicated limitations section addressing statistical rigor, cost, or dataset-size confounds, so coverage of limitations is partial rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The synthesized-data volume varies by 3–6× across generators (Table 7: DataFoundry 87,566 vs. DataFlow 509,242 vs. DataPrep-Skill 307,252 samples), yet no size-matched control is run — downstream gains may partly reflect a different data-quality/quantity operating point rather than better data. - Single-run evaluation with no seeds or confidence intervals: the 1.3–1.4 point Finance/Law margins over the best baseline are not established as significant. - The pilot assessor and the evolution designer are the same family of frontier LLMs judging their own pipeline's outputs; no inter-rater agreement, human audit of assessment reports, or calibration of the six criteria against human labels is provided. - Selection of T=2 is justified via pilot-assessment deterioration, but the reported evidence (Figure 3) is downstream benchmark performance — the paper does not disentangle whether round selection used test information. - No ablation isolates the adapter/frozen-baseline mechanism, the central claimed innovation, from generic iterative refinement. - No cost/latency accounting of the RSI loop versus a single-pass generator, which matters for the claimed upstream efficiency advantage. - No code or artifact release is stated, limiting reproducibility of an otherwise well-specified framework. Bottom Line Practitioners building LLM-driven synthetic-data pipelines gain a concrete, well-documented architecture pattern — pilot-set assessment plus interface-preserving component adapters with a fixed evolution budget — but the evidence is single-run and size-confounded, so treat the headline margins as directional rather than precise; within this emerging subfield it is currently the most carefully instrumented instantiation, ahead of DataPrep-Skill-style baselines, though AutoData-style work covers adjacent ground.

Harness- RL : Black-Box Reinforcement Learning with Action-Args Decoupling for Central- Agent Multi- Agent Harnesses

X Jiang, Z Zhang, Z Yang, J Gao, R Qiu, S Chen, X Chu… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HARNESS-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that trains the central policy of a multi-agent LLM harness by (a) reconstructing branched, multi-session harness interactions into token-aligned RL trajectories via a black-box interface-capture mechanism and (b) a Conflict-Aware Policy Optimization (CAPO) method that routes Action-token and Args-token gradients to separate activation-derived parameter partitions. - Why it's important: Training the coordinating policy of a multi-agent harness (rather than just architectures) is an underexplored problem, and standard GRPO/DAPO-style sequence-level optimization assumes linear trajectories and treats all response tokens as one decision type — assumptions that break under dynamic sub-agent scheduling. - How it does it: The framework captures per-call input/output tokens and log-probs from every agent-model interaction, builds session-level prefix trees with outcome and process rewards attributed to token positions, and splits gradient updates by masking parameters selected via forward-activation statistics for Action vs. Args tokens. - The good: Consistent first-place results on all seven benchmarks across two model scales — average token-level F1 of 42.93 (Qwen2.5-1.5B) and 47.79 (Qwen2.5-3B), 14–15 points above the strongest reported baseline — with code released on GitHub. - The missing: The headline margins conflate the multi-agent harness itself (Search Agent + Conclusion Agent) with the proposed optimizer; the CAPO ablation contributes only 1.57–1.89 average F1 and is inconsistent across datasets, and no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building RL training pipelines for multi-agent LLM systems and need concrete machinery for trajectory construction and reward attribution in branched harnesses; skip it if you want a clean causal analysis of why the decoupled-gradient idea works, which the paper does not provide.
