Problem & Motivation: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve reliably under RLVR in mathematics and code because correctness can be checked automatically, but extending this to open-ended and agentic tasks fails because reliable rewards are hard to obtain and per-instance human judgment cannot scale with the volume, length, and difficulty of model-generated experience. Practitioners building self-improving training loops face a structural gap: as models produce more of their own training signal, no established framework exists to say which parts of the loop still depend on humans, what new failure modes autonomy introduces, or what evidence should accompany claims of 'human-free' improvement. The paper targets the research community working on post-training, reward modeling, and self-generated curricula. Key Idea: The core intellectual move is the 'receding-supervision ladder' — a five-level decomposition (L0 per-instance human supervision, L1 reusable human-grounded evaluators, L2 rewards beyond human evaluation, L3 experience beyond human design, L4 autonomous co-evolution) that separates the question of where feedback comes from (reward axis) from who supplies tasks and environments (experience axis), and classifies methods by which loop component loses continued human dependence rather than by training pipeline or optimizer. This decoupling — e.g., noting that TTRL and EM-RL change the reward source but not the task distribution — is the insight that lets a reader reconstruct the entire taxonomy. A secondary, equally load-bearing idea is the three-object evaluation principle: held-out capability scores alone cannot certify that training feedback was faithful or that generated curricula remained valid, so each ladder level demands source-matched audits. Methodology: This is a survey/position paper; its 'method' is framework construction plus systematic literature organization, not an algorithm. It first establishes a unified MDP (single-turn) and POMDP (sequential agentic) formulation with a single discounted-return objective (Eq. 1), and reviews the policy-optimization machinery (PPO, GRPO with group-relative advantages, entropy/surprisal measures) needed to discuss reward sources. Section 3 organizes reward acquisition by evidence provenance: human-grounded evaluators (outcome/process reward models, generative verifiers, LLM judges, adaptive rubrics, self-trained evaluators), then model-derived signals (entropy minimization à la EM-RL/Intuitor, majority-vote consensus à la TTRL, trajectory-level consensus à la CoVo), reference-anchored signals (variational/likelihood rewards à la VeriFree/RLPR/JEPO, perplexity rewards à la NOVER, reconstruction/cycle consistency), and environment-grounded signals (execution, game outcomes, formal Lean verification). Section 4 organizes the experience axis from fixed human-designed experience through task generation in fixed environments (proposer-solver self-play with learnability reward p̄(1−p̄), corpus-grounded self-play), environment construction (UED/regret objectives, executable environment synthesis, world models), to integrated pipelines and co-evolution (CURE, AZR, SPIRAL, GenEnv). Sections 3.4/4.5 analyze coupled failure modes, and Section 5 builds an evaluation taxonomy mapping benchmark suites (RewardBench, ProcessBench, WebArena, etc.) to the three evaluation objects. Critical design decisions: (1) classifying by operational human dependence rather than historical artifact origin — explicitly justified and repeatedly defended; (2) placing optimizer choice (online/offline, PPO/GRPO) outside the ladder — well-argued; (3) treating self-trained evaluators as a boundary regime — sensible but somewhat fuzzy. Key Results: Not stated — the paper runs no experiments and reports no quantitative results of its own. Its contribution is qualitative synthesis: e.g., the claim that environment-grounded rewards offer the strongest separation between policy and scoring evidence but remain vulnerable to specification error; that consensus and certainty rewards show a recurring rise-then-collapse pattern (cited from Shafayay et al. 2025, He et al. 2026); that internally generated supervision may plateau below oracle supervision (Qi et al. 2026b). All empirical numbers in the paper belong to the surveyed systems and benchmarks, not to any new measurement by the authors. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the receding-supervision ladder and the three-object evaluation framework) plus a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL in a weak sense (a maintained GitHub tracking repository). The genuinely novel element is the operational classification of methods by which learning-loop component retains human provision, combined with level-specific minimum evidence requirements (Table 6) — prior surveys treated reward-centric or environment-centric design separately (the paper itself cites model-centric Gao et al. 2025a, Fang et al. 2025a and environment-centric Huang et al. 2025b surveys as predecessors it unifies). Everything else is competent organization of existing, mostly 2024–2026 published work. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a survey, ablations, seeds, and significance tests are not applicable. The intellectual rigor is in the definitional hygiene: consistent notation (Table 1), explicit equations for the canonical reward constructions it surveys (Eq. 10, 14, 16, 18, 20), and repeated disambiguation of terms that other papers conflate (intrinsic-as-confidence vs. intrinsic-as-novelty; tool access vs. reward grounding; reward cost vs. reward independence vs. reward validity). A continuously updated GitHub repository is maintained. Methodological concerns: the ladder placement of individual methods is the authors' judgment call with no inter-annotator validation; the taxonomy is developed and illustrated on the same literature it evaluates, so there is no out-of-sample test of its classifications; and the paper cites a very large volume of 2026-dated preprints, meaning several classifications rest on non-peer-reviewed sources. Deployability: Profile: this is a survey/position paper — closest to THEORETICAL in the given trichotomy, though it proves no theorems and runs no experiments; the four-property check is applied in that adapted sense. - Sound: The formalism (MDP/POMDP, GRPO, Jensen bounds for variational rewards) is standard and stated correctly, but the ladder itself is a definitional scheme, not a derived result, and its level boundaries are acknowledged to be non-sharp. - General: The framework is intended to cover single-turn RLVR through multi-turn agentic POMDP settings and is applied across math, code, GUI agents, games, and formal proving — broad in scope, though its L4 level is admitted to be an idealization with no current inhabitant. - Tight: Not applicable to bounds (none are proven); the closest analog is that the taxonomy's categories are mutually informative but the paper provides no test that the levels are exhaustive or that level transitions predict training outcomes. - Implementable: The deliverable is immediately actionable as an evaluation checklist: Table 6 tells a practitioner exactly which audits (reward-source-matched fidelity tests, task-diversity audits, closed-loop stability ablations) a claim at each level requires, and the GitHub repo serves as a living index. The work delivers a paper, a reusable evaluation framework, and a maintained repository; it produces no code, model, or dataset. Strengths: - The operational-responsibility framing (classifying by which loop component needs continued human provision, explicitly excluding historical data provenance) resolves real ambiguities that plague prior 'self-improvement' and 'self-rewarding' taxonomies. - Table 3's per-method annotation of which of R, (S,P), and Π are filled/half-filled/empty circles is a genuinely useful artifact — it makes boundary cases (ZeroGUI, CuES, Genie) auditable rather than hand-waved. - The failure-mode analysis is unusually concrete: it distinguishes consensus collapse, entropy-driven overconfidence (rise-then-decline), verifier false-positive exploitation, coupled policy-judge drift (SPELL), and co-adaptive reward hacking in generated environments, and names the mitigation mechanism for each. - The insistence that capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality are three independent evaluation objects — and that a GSM8K gain says nothing about reward fidelity or curriculum health — is a substantive methodological contribution to how this subfield should report results. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state directly that the ladder measures operational supervision sources, not capability, reliability, alignment, or historical human contribution; that level boundaries are not sharp (methods may reduce human involvement in one component while retaining it in another); that 'Human-free' labels in figures do not imply absence of human influence; and (per the paper's structure, Section 7) that the analysis covers scope and limitations of a qualitative account. They confront the taxonomy's idealization of L4 openly, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 'path toward superintelligence' framing in the title is not earned by the content: L4 is empty of realized systems, and the paper provides no argument that the ladder's final level is reachable, only that it is definable. - The framework is never stress-tested: no worked case study applies Table 6's L3/L4 audit requirements to an actual co-evolving system (e.g., an AZR or Agent-World run), so the practical usability of the evaluation protocol is asserted, not demonstrated. - No inter-rater reliability or disagreement analysis for ladder placements; several placements (e.g., self-trained evaluators as a 'boundary') are defensible but arbitrary, and a second taxonomy could reorganize the same material. - The survey's classification of rapidly published 2026 preprints means many method descriptions cannot have been independently verified, and the continuously updated repository will age unevenly across subsections. - The paper identifies that models may improve at producing answers faster than at checking them (generator-verifier asymmetry) but offers no synthesis of what verifier-training objective would close that gap — a dogs-not-barking omission given the framework's own emphasis on feedback fidelity. Bottom Line: A practitioner designing RL post-training or self-improvement pipelines gains a genuinely useful map — method positioning, failure-mode checklists, and evaluation protocols — that no existing survey matches, but should read it as a rigorous taxonomy and evaluation rubric rather than as evidence about, or a demonstrated path to, superintelligence.

#223 — Moderately Innovative (49)

Fast Weight Attention for Continual Learning (20 ▲ )

Yifan Zhang, Steve Ta, Jasper Zhang, Jichen Feng, Shuzhen Li, Yongxin Zhang, Yifeng Liu, Huizhuo Yuan, Mengdi Wang, Quanquan Gu, Andrew Chi-Chih Yao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Falcon family of fast-weight attention update rules (Falcon-1/2/3 for regression and Falcon-1A/2A/3A for inner-product writes) derived as normalized online gradient descent on an instantaneous ridge/inner-product objective under a shifted read-after-write alignment that pairs φ(k_{t−1}) with v_t. - Why it's important: Linear-attention and SSM models compress context into a fixed-size state whose update rule acts as an implicit online learner; the temporal alignment and normalization of that rule determine both long-context quality and stability, yet most prior architectures leave these choices implicit and ad hoc. - How it does it: The core move is a one-step index shift — writing the newly revealed target v_t under the prefix feature φ(k_{t−1}) that was available when it was predicted — combined with NLMS-style step sizes η_t = β_t/(‖x_t‖² + λ_t + ε) matched to the local smoothness of the objective, plus sliding-window mini-batch variants and chunk-parallel (WY/SSD-style) kernels. - The good: At 124M–130M parameters on a 50B-token FineWeb-Edu run, Falcon-1.3 reaches 17.10 FineEdu validation perplexity versus 17.32 for the strongest baseline (Gated DeltaNet), and Falcon-3A.3 achieves 87.2 mean teacher-forced accuracy extrapolating 33–48-digit addition versus 65.8 for a Transformer and 75.2 for Mamba-2. - The missing: Several proposed variants (Falcon-2, Falcon-2A, Falcon-3) are defined but never benchmarked in the main tables, no error bars or multi-seed results are reported, and no wall-clock/throughput comparison against DeltaNet-style baselines is given despite efficiency being a core motivation. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers designing linear-attention or fast-weight state updates who want the alignment/normalization design space made explicit; skippable for practitioners seeking a deployable long-context model, since evidence stops at 130M parameters.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Rigor (40) is the main drag: single seeds with sub-1% perplexity gaps, three of six proposed variants never benchmarked, the central alignment-shift claim never isolated in a table, the closest baselines (DeltaNet/Gated DeltaNet) omitted from the experiment where Falcon's margins are largest, and a broken table reference — all in an unrefereed preprint. Completeness (55) suffers from a title ('Continual Learning') whose framing is never operationalized in any metric, though the authors' honest 'not a uniform win' characterization helps. Novelty (55) and Non-Obviousness (55) are moderate: the prefix-aligned pairing and NLMS normalization taxonomy are a useful conceptual cleanup, but built from existing ideas. Impact (40) is limited to a code link, no weights, and no throughput measurements despite efficiency being the core motivation. Weighted composite: 0.20*55 + 0.25*40 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*40 = 49.

Problem & Motivation Transformers externalize fast memory as a growing KV cache with O(N²) attention cost; SSMs, linear attention, and fast-weight programmers instead compress context into a fixed-size recurrent matrix state, making the state transition an online learning rule. Prior work (DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, RWKV-7, Titans/ATLAS) presents these update rules at the architectural level, leaving the local objective and, critically, the temporal alignment between write feature and target implicit. Most recurrences bind the same-step pair (φ(k_t), v_t); the authors argue that under autoregressive prefix prediction, the causally revealed example is the prefix-aligned pair (φ(k_{t−1}), v_t) — the target paired with the feature that was actually available when it was predicted. The same-step pairing is still causal but optimizes a different internal fast-memory objective. The paper asks what update rules follow when this alignment, plasticity (step size), forgetting (ridge shrinkage), and bounded rehearsal (sliding window) are made explicit. Key Idea The single core insight: under read-after-write autoregressive semantics, the fast-memory state is an online linear predictor trained on the pair x_t = φ(k_{t−1}), y_t = v_t, and the write rule should be a single normalized gradient step on an instantaneous objective whose local smoothness (‖x_t‖² + λ_t, or the window covariance's top eigenvalue λmax(C̄_t)) sets the step size — reducing the design of linear-attention state updates to classical NLMS/online-ridge regression with an explicit one-step key shift. Methodology The paper derives two families from Online Gradient Descent on per-step objectives: (1) squared-error ridge regression ℓ_t(S) = ½‖S⊤x_t − y_t‖² + (λ_t/2)‖S‖²_F, whose gradient step yields Delta-style updates with residual r_t = v_t − S⊤_{t−1}x_t; and (2) a negative inner-product objective −⟨S⊤x_t, y_t⟩ + (λ_t/2)‖S‖²_F, whose step yields additive Hebbian writes (linear-attention/Mamba-2 style). Each family comes in three forms: Falcon-1/1A (scalar normalized gain), Falcon-2/2A (per-value-channel gain vectors η_t ∈ R^{d_v}), and Falcon-3/3A (sliding-window mini-batch step over the last B causal pairs, with residuals evaluated at the pre-update state). Forgetting is λ_t-driven multiplicative shrinkage, with a clamped log-space positive-decay renormalization for numerical stability. Implementation contributions include three equivalent views (recurrent scan, masked-parallel via WY/TriSolve, chunk-parallel SSD-style) for each variant: Falcon-2 uses a shared key Gram matrix with d_v batched channel-wise triangular solves, Falcon-1 merges these into a single multi-RHS solve, and Falcon-3 maps to the ParallelFlow/tensorInv framework as an exact rank-B low-rank affine recurrence. A per-step descent lemma (standard L-smoothness argument, Lemma 3.1) justifies the β ∈ (0,2) gain regime; the descent guarantee is pointwise and explicitly does not cover the clamped surrogate or the cumulative loss. Critical design decisions: the index shift (motivated by causality of the revealed pair, but its isolated benefit on LM metrics is not isolated by a shipped-vs-unshipped ablation table in the main text), RMSNorm (vs ℓ2-norm) of Q/K features (ablated, favorable), and context-conditioned η over β (ablated, favorable). Key Results All headline experiments are at toy-to-standard scale: 124M–130M-parameter models trained for 100K steps on ~49.2B FineWeb-Edu tokens (seq len 1024, batch 480). On FineEdu validation perplexity, Falcon-1.3 scores 17.10 vs Gated DeltaNet 17.32, DeltaNet 17.84, Mamba-2 17.70, RetNet/LightningAttn 18.79, and a RoPE Transformer 17.38; Wiki/LMB perplexities are mixed (Transformer 33.25/47.43, Gated DeltaNet 30.99/46.70, Falcon-1.3 33.00/48.70 — the authors themselves call the outcome "not a uniform win"). Zero-shot 8-task downstream averages: Falcon-1A.2 best at 49.30 vs DeltaNet 48.88, Mamba-2 48.80, Transformer 48.16; one-shot best is Falcon-1.3 at 49.54 vs Transformer 49.67. On variable-digit addition (train widths 1–32, extrapolate to 33–48, following Kaiser & Sutskever), Falcon-3A.3 reaches 87.2 mean teacher-forced accuracy (100.0/69.0 at d33/d48) vs RetNet/LightningAttn 82.9, Mamba-2 75.2, Transformer 65.8; notably, DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet — the closest related methods — are absent from this comparison. Baselines are current and representative for the LM experiments. No throughput, memory, or wall-clock numbers are reported for any model. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (modest) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new elements are the explicit prefix-aligned (φ(k_{t−1}), v_t) write pairing and the objective-matched NLMS/spectral normalization taxonomy (scalar/per-column/sliding × regression/inner-product) applied to fast-weight states; the descent lemma, WY/chunk-parallel machinery, delta-rule regression view, and sliding-window internal-memory idea (Titans/ATLAS, test-time regression) are existing ideas recombined and engineered into SSD-compatible kernels. Rigor & Reproducibility The theory is thin but honest: a one-paragraph L-smooth descent lemma with explicit caveats that the guarantee is per-step, unclamped, and does not bound the cumulative or outer objective. Some ablations exist within the family (QK-RMSNorm vs QK-ℓ2; context-conditioned η vs β), but the central alignment-shift claim is not ablated against the unshifted pairing in a reported table, and three of six proposed variants are never benchmarked. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are mentioned, and perplexity/downstream gaps between best Falcon and best baseline (17.10 vs 17.32; 49.30 vs 48.88) are within plausible seed noise at this scale. A GitHub project page is given (github.com/yifanzhang-pro/fast-weight-attention); no model weights are mentioned. Methodological concerns: the paper contains a broken table reference ("Tables 2 and ??"), the arithmetic-extrapolation table omits DeltaNet/Gated DeltaNet baselines, and the continual-learning/interference framing in the title and introduction is never measured with any interference or memory metric. The LM evaluation conflates several changes (shift + normalization + context-conditioned gains), so attribution of gains is fuzzy. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL (new update rules with training and evaluation runs; kernels described and pseudocoded but no deployment measurements). - Practical: Yes — training used a single 4-GPU node of H100/H200s, and the kernels are standard chunked GPU primitives (Gram matrices, batched triangular solves). - Efficient: Asymptotically O(N) with O(1) inference state and chunk-parallel training like Mamba-2/DeltaNet; Falcon-1 reduces per-chunk triangular system builds from d_v to 1, but no measured speedup or memory throughput versus baselines is reported. - Effective: Partially — perplexity and downstream accuracy are competitive (roughly parity with Gated DeltaNet at 130M), and extrapolation on synthetic arithmetic is clearly better than the tested baselines, but the evidence is small-scale and partly confounded. - Scalable: Untested — nothing beyond 130M parameters and 50B tokens, no long-context (e.g., 8K–128K) perplexity, and the sliding-window boundary-state requirement (last B−1 pairs must be carried for exact continuation) complicates scaled streaming use, as the authors note. The work delivers algorithms with pseudocode plus a code repository link; no trained model or dataset artifact beyond the benchmark protocol is stated. Strengths - The alignment analysis (RAW/RBW timing conventions, Figure 11's 2×2 pairing design) is a genuinely useful conceptual cleanup that disentangles causality from index convention — a distinction most prior fast-weight papers blur. - Importing NLMS/smoothness-matched normalization from adaptive filtering into fast-weight states is well-grounded: the step size denominator (‖x_t‖², λmax of window covariance) is derived from the objective rather than tuned, and the β ∈ (0,2) sign-flip connection to state tracking is a nice observation. - The implementation appendix is unusually complete and exact: WY reductions for ridge decays, log-space chunk-local renormalization with precise statements of when clamped updates stop being exact gradient steps, single-vs-two TriSolve merges, and exact ParallelFlow mapping with boundary-state requirements — reproducibility-grade algebra. - The sliding-window Falcon-3/3A formulation with window-averaged statistics is designed so neither the injection nor the decay fraction grows with nominal window size B, a subtle and correct scaling property. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that the language-modeling result is "not a uniform win" and characterize the arithmetic experiment as "supporting evidence rather than the paper's primary result." They explicitly flag: the descent lemma does not cover cumulative loss or clamped updates (which become "numerically safe surrogates" with effective ridge coefficients); signed-feature normalized reads can produce zero/negative denominators, so denominator-free reads are the default; Falcon-3/3A matrix state alone is not Markov for exact segment continuation (requires a B−1 pair tail); and sliding windows control a memory horizon without giving strict locality. They also note Falcon-2/2A and Falcon-3 are not separately benchmarked. This is a comparatively direct confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The headline conceptual contribution — the shifted (φ(k_{t−1}), v_t) pairing — is never isolated empirically: no table compares shifted vs same-step pairing under otherwise identical normalization, so the reader cannot tell whether LM gains come from alignment or from NLMS normalization/RMSNorm/context-conditioned gains. - DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet, the closest methods, are missing from the length-extrapolation table where Falcon's largest margins appear — a dogs-not-barking omission given those baselines appear in the LM tables. - No compute-cost measurements despite the motivation being O(N²)-attention cost; the O(d_vC²) Falcon-2 batched-solve overhead is acknowledged in an appendix but never measured end-to-end. - The "continual learning" framing (catastrophic interference, binding new evidence online) is never operationalized — no interference, recall, or associative-memory metric is reported, so the title overstates the evaluated scope. - Single-seed results with sub-1% perplexity gaps and a broken cross-reference ("??") suggest limited statistical hygiene typical of a fast-moving preprint (arXiv 2608.27763, dated March 2026, apparently not yet peer reviewed); results should be treated as preliminary. Bottom Line A technically careful, well-engineered reformulation of fast-weight state updates that makes alignment and normalization explicit and is worth reading if you design linear-attention mechanisms, but its empirical case rests on 130M-parameter parity results and a synthetic extrapolation task with missing key baselines, so it does not yet displace Gated DeltaNet/Mamba-2-style recipes in practice.

InsightSR: Refining Symbolic Regression Search Spaces via Parallel Semantic and Structural LLM Guidance

Y Ling, W Cun, Z Chen · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces InsightSR, a framework that wraps the PySR genetic programming engine with LLM-driven guidance along two parallel pathways — dimensionally consistent seed skeletons and accumulating nonlinear feature transformations — plus a closed-loop feedback mechanism, achieving 95% exact recovery on the Feynman benchmark and 80.18% Acc0.1 on LLM-SRBench's LSR-Transform task. - Why it's important: Symbolic regression suffers from a combinatorial search space that grows exponentially with expression complexity, and existing methods frequently return numerically accurate but physically meaningless expressions; LLM-guided search-space shaping could make automated scientific discovery more sample-efficient and physically grounded. - How it does it: The LLM never generates final expressions; instead it (a) proposes physics-consistent seed skeletons and per-operator complexity biases injected into PySR's parsimony penalty, (b) recommends nonlinear feature transforms that accumulate across generations into an augmented input matrix, and (c) critiques Pareto-optimal candidates into a knowledge base that steers the next iteration. - The good: The headline result is a large, specific margin on a current benchmark — 80.18% Acc0.1 on LSR-Transform versus 50.45% for the best prior method (LaSR), with NMSE orders of magnitude below LLM-based baselines on Oscillator 1/2 (9.55e-11 and 2.45e-9 ID). - The missing: There is no ablation isolating the contribution of the Semantic Seed Pathway, the Structural Feature Pathway, or the feedback loop — the paper cannot show which component drives the gains, and no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-assisted symbolic regression or equation discovery and want the current best numbers on LLM-SRBench and a concrete dual-pathway design pattern; skip it if you need component-level attribution, noise-robustness guarantees, or released code, none of which are here.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners doing automated scientific discovery (physics, chemistry, biology) need symbolic regression methods that recover parsimonious, physically consistent closed-form laws from noisy observational data. Purely data-driven GP and neural approaches (DSR, uDSR, NeSymReS, E2E) waste samples on dimensionally inconsistent expressions, overfit noise, and generalize poorly out of distribution. First-generation LLM-assisted SR methods (LLM-SR, SR-LLM, LaSR, PiSR) inject scientific priors but along a single dimension only — either structural skeleton generation or input-space feature engineering — and incur heavy inference overhead from frequent LLM queries. The paper targets the gap: nobody combines structural priors and feature engineering synergistically, even though priors could inform which features to engineer and engineered features could simplify the required structural forms. Key Idea: Shift the burden of symbolic search from constructing deep expression trees over raw variables to assembling shallow trees over an LLM-curated, physically constrained feature space: the LLM shapes the search space (via seed skeletons, operator complexity biases, and accumulating feature transforms) rather than the expressions themselves, with a knowledge-base feedback loop converting each generation's Pareto-front outcomes into refined guidance for the next. This is a competent synthesis of two existing LLM-guidance strategies (LaSR-style feature engineering and LLM-SR-style skeleton generation) unified around one engine rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Methodology: Four-phase iterative loop per generation. (1) Contextual initialization: the LLM infers physical units for ambiguous variables from problem metadata, producing dimensional constraints used throughout. (2) Parallel guidance: the Semantic Seed Pathway proposes dimensionally audited functional skeletons with symbolic constants, plus per-operator complexity biases ω_o that modify PySR's parsimony penalty to C′(f) = Σ_o (c_o + ω_o) — recommended operators get discounts, implausible ones get penalties; the Structural Feature Pathway recommends nonlinear transforms φ(x) (power laws, sin, etc.) appended to form X_aug = [x_1,...,x_d, φ_1(x),...,φ_k(x)], with features accumulating across generations. (3) Guided PySR search over the constrained manifold with warm-starting (previous best retained as elite). (4) Strategic feedback: the LLM evaluates Pareto-optimal candidates on accuracy, interpretability, and variable completeness, categorizes features as effective/ineffective by residual contribution, and writes insights to a knowledge base that informs the next iteration's seeds, biases, and feature priorities. Objective is the standard GP multi-objective loss MSE + λ·complexity (λ=0.003, parsimony), with early stopping at loss < 1e-10. Critical design decisions: (a) querying the LLM between generations rather than per-step (justified by cost, though no cost numbers are given); (b) accumulating rather than replacing features (plausible but untested in ablation); (c) LLM-based unit synthesis for variables with missing metadata (acknowledged as a sensitivity, not empirically stress-tested). Key Results: On the Feynman 100 benchmark: 95% exact recovery rate, average R² = 0.9999, against baselines including NGGP, GP-GOMEA, gplearn, PySR, QLattice, PSRN, E2E, PhySO, and SR-LLM (reported graphically; exact baseline numbers not in the text). On LLM-SRBench (240 problems, 5 categories): LSR-Transform Acc0.1 = 80.18% vs LaSR 50.45% and LLM-SR 39.64%, with NMSE 1.3e-14; per-domain Acc0.1: Chemistry 66.67%, Biology 50.00%, Physics 40.91%, Material Science 92.00% — beating LLM-SR everywhere except Physics (40.91% vs 36.36%, a narrower margin). On four real-world datasets (LLM-SR's), best or comparable NMSE in most ID/OOD cells, e.g., Oscillator 1 ID 9.55e-11 (vs LLM-SR 4.65e-07), though on Stress-Strain ID it is 2.00e-02 vs LLM-SR's 2.10e-02 (essentially tied) and OOD 5.32e-02 vs 5.16e-02 (slightly worse). Noise robustness degrades sharply: Acc0.1 falls from 97% at zero noise to 79% at noise 0.001 and 37% at noise 0.05 (Feynman). Baselines are current and strong (LaSR, LLM-SR are 2024–2025 LLM-SR methods; PySR is the standard GP reference). Testing is at standard SR benchmark scale (100–240 synthetic problems plus 4 small real datasets), not stress-scale. The Feynman case study (Table 6) shows the discovered forms sometimes differ meaningfully from ground truth (e.g., II.6.15b recovered sin θ cos θ plus an extra term rather than sin(2θ)/2, and Oscillator 1 deviates in several coefficients), suggesting 'exact recovery' claims rest on the aggregate metric rather than uniformly faithful rediscovery. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (primarily) — the genuinely new element is the explicit dual-pathway architecture that couples top-down semantic seeding with bottom-up accumulating feature engineering around a single GP engine, mediated by a shared knowledge base; the individual ingredients (LLM skeleton proposal à la LLM-SR, LLM feature engineering à la LaSR, complexity-biasing in GP, warm-starting, operator weights in PySR) are all established, and the contribution is their integration and the closed-loop refinement over it. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent: no experiment isolates the Semantic Seed Pathway, Structural Feature Pathway, feedback loop, or operator-biasing mechanism, so component attribution is impossible. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for any headline number, despite stochastic GP and LLM components where run-to-run variance is expected to be substantial. Hyperparameters are listed (Qwen-3.5 27B, temperature 0.3, 30 populations of size 50, 3–30 LLM generations), which aids reproduction, but no code, data, or configuration release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (a) LLM-based methods evaluated on Feynman and LLM-SRBench face plausible training-data contamination — the LLM may have memorized Feynman Lecture equations, which would inflate exact-recovery rates, and the paper does not address this; (b) the LLM is used both to generate guidance and to judge candidates (interpretability scoring), creating self-evaluation circularity; (c) the noise experiment has a single accuracy number per noise level with no variance estimate. Baselines themselves are current and appropriately chosen. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the framework is built and run on three benchmark suites). Practical: Yes — it needs only a 27B-parameter LLM (runnable on a single commodity GPU) plus PySR, no exotic infrastructure. Efficient: The design deliberately limits LLM queries to inter-generation intervals, but no wall-clock, token-count, or total-compute comparison against PySR alone, LaSR, or LLM-SR is reported, so the cost of the accuracy gains is unquantified. Effective: Evidence supports strong benchmark performance and modest OOD gains on real data, but effectiveness on genuinely novel physics (where the LLM's priors are wrong or absent) is untested, and clean-data dominance shrinks under noise. Scalable: Not tested beyond 240-problem benchmarks; behavior as variable dimensionality, dataset size, or number of accumulated features grows is unexamined — unbounded feature accumulation could degrade PySR's search. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, dataset, or trained artifact is reported as released. Strengths: (1) The dual-pathway framing is a real conceptual contribution — articulating why structural priors and feature engineering are synergistic (priors inform features; features simplify structure) and instantiating both against a shared knowledge base. (2) Search-space transformation rather than direct expression generation is a smart division of labor: it keeps numerical optimization with a proven GP engine and confines LLM involvement to what LLMs are actually good at (domain priors, critique). (3) The operator complexity-bias mechanism (Eq. 4) is a concrete, implementable interface between soft LLM judgments and hard GP dynamics. (4) Evaluation spans three benchmark families including held-out OOD splits on real-world data, and the reported margins over 2024–2025 baselines (e.g., +29.7 points Acc0.1 over LaSR on LSR-Transform) are large enough to be interesting even with single-run caveats. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the framework is sensitive to problem metadata: when variable semantics are ambiguous, the accuracy of the LLM-based unit-synthesis module becomes critical, and they flag robustness in the absence of explicit textual metadata as an open issue, proposing multi-modal priors as future work. They also note the feedback loop is kept computationally viable only by querying the LLM between generations rather than at every step. This is direct but partial acknowledgment — they confront the metadata dependency honestly but do not quantify it or mention contamination, variance, or component attribution at all. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No ablation studies — with three interacting mechanisms (seeds, features, feedback) plus operator biases, the reported gains cannot be attributed to any component, and it is possible that feature accumulation alone or PySR tuning alone explains most of the improvement. (2) No multiple-seed variance for stochastic GP+LLM search; single-run comparisons of methods with high variance are weak evidence. (3) Train/test contamination for LLM-guided methods on the Feynman benchmark is a known field-wide concern (Feynman equations are in every physics textbook the LLM trained on) and is not discussed or mitigated (e.g., no synthetic-only or perturbed-equation evaluation). (4) The LLM acting as both guide and judge (interpretability/completeness scoring) invites self-confirmation; no human or independent evaluation of discovered expression quality is provided. (5) The noise study (Acc0.1 dropping from 97% to 37% between noise 0 and 0.05) suggests substantial fragility that the framing 'remains high under moderate noise' understates. (6) LLM inference cost is claimed to be managed but never measured against baselines. (7) The 95% Feynman recovery claim coexists with Table 6 cases where discovered expressions deviate from ground truth in structure and coefficients, and the paper does not reconcile these. Bottom Line: For researchers in LLM-assisted symbolic regression this is worth reading as the current best-performing design pattern on LLM-SRBench and a clean articulation of the seeding-plus-feature-engineering synergy, but the missing ablations, single-run evaluation, unaddressed contamination risk, and absent code release mean its headline margins should be treated as promising rather than established until independently replicated.

Solving In-Table Prediction Problems by Deep Neural Networks with Performance Evaluation Using Synthetic Data

X Zhao, D Oelke · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces In-Table Prediction (ITP), a machine-learning problem formulation for tabular data in which the model must predict arbitrarily masked column values — including 'NaN' empty values as legitimate prediction targets — and delivers an embedding layer with dedicated learnable vectors for numeric, empty, and masked states, evaluated across MLP, Resnet, and Transformer architectures on synthetic data. - Why it's important: Real table workflows involve rows where a user enters only some fields or columns are lost to technical failures, and existing missing-value-imputation methods cannot handle the case where the correct output is itself 'empty' rather than a number; a working ITP method would support row-completion suggestions, data recovery, and consistency checks during table creation. - How it does it: It trains self-supervised (BERT/MLM-style) with randomly inserted masks but no fixed masking ratio, using a per-column embedding layer where numeric inputs multiply a learnable vector (following Gorishniy et al. 2021) while NaN and mask tokens get their own learnable vectors, and a 3-way output head (empty-probability, non-empty-probability, regressed value) trained with cross-entropy plus masked-position MSE. - The good: A rigorous full grid search over dataset type, missingness mechanism, masking count, architecture, training size (100–50,000), and embedding dimension (32–512) yields a coherent and honest set of findings: attention-based models win once training data reaches ~10,000 rows, larger embeddings (D ≥ 256) help the Transformer but not MLP/Resnet, and MNAR is measurably harder than MAR. - The missing: All evaluation is on synthetic tables with exactly three columns and two predefined functional relationships (linear and exponential), with no real-world datasets, no MVI or classical imputation baselines (missForest, MICE, GAIN, etc.) for comparison, no error bars or multiple seeds, and no hyperparameter tuning of the architectures themselves — so every conclusion is untested beyond a toy setting. - Read it or not: Worth a skim for researchers working on tabular self-supervised learning or missing-data modeling who want to see the empty-value-as-target problem articulated and a clean experimental template; practitioners seeking deployable imputation or completion tools can skip it since nothing here is validated on real data.

Novelty (62) is the best dimension: the empty-value-as-target problem formulation and three-way numeric/NaN/mask embedding are a clean, distinct contribution, echoed in Non-Obviousness (55). Completeness (60) earns credit for unusually candid scoping, and Resilience (55) survives mainly because claims are deliberately narrow. Practical Impact (25) is minimal — a paper-only proof of concept on three-column synthetic tables with no artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*35 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*25 ≈ 49.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations continuously create and maintain tables in which some cell values are missing (NaN) and others are simply not yet entered by a user. The paper distinguishes this from Missing Value Imputation (MVI): MVI replaces NaNs so downstream pipelines can run, whereas the proposed In-Table Prediction (ITP) task predicts values at user-defined masked positions, where the ground truth may be a number or an empty value. The authors motivate three usage scenarios: suggesting values during new-row creation, recovering lost columns, and verifying whether a position of interest conforms to learned column relationships. The claimed gap is that prior tabular deep learning treats the target column as fixed and supervised, and prior pretraining work (Rubachev et al. 2022; Gorishniy et al. 2021) uses masked reconstruction only as a representation-learning step with a fixed masking ratio and no notion of empty values as recoverable targets — nobody, per the authors, has solved ITP directly with neural networks. Note the framing: standard MVI could already handle ITP on categorical tables by treating NaN as a class; the authors argue MVI cannot handle continuous features with empty-value semantics, though they never test this claim against an MVI method. Key Idea: The core trick is to treat 'NaN' as a first-class, learnable state rather than something to impute away: each continuous column gets three trainable embedding vectors — one scaled by the numeric value (as in FT-Transformer), one for the empty value, and one for the mask — and a per-column 3-dimensional output head that jointly classifies 'empty vs. numeric' and regresses the numeric value, trained only on masked positions. Everything else (MLP, Resnet, Transformer encoder without positional encoding, BERT-style masking) is standard machinery from Gorishniy et al. (2021) and Vaswani et al. (2017). Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) masking layer inserts mask tokens ζ at training-selected or inference-time unknown positions; (2) the proposed embedding layer (Eq. 1) maps each cell to a D-dimensional embedding — x·e_i,1 for numerics, e_i,2 for NaN, e_i,3 for masks; (3) the embeddings pass through one of three backbones (MLP/Resnet consume a flattened KD vector; a 2-block 4-head Transformer encoder processes the K embeddings without positional encoding); (4) a linear head per column outputs (y_0, y_1, y_2), interpreted as empty-probability, non-empty-probability, and regression. The loss (Eq. 2) is cross-entropy on the empty/numeric decision plus MSE on the regressed value, computed only at masked positions; unlike BERT, the number of masks per row ranges from 0 to n_max ≤ K−1 rather than a fixed ratio. Synthetic data is generated from two known 3-column relationships — a linear function x2 = x0 + x1 + τd (Dataset A) and an exponential function x2 = e^{−(cos x0 + cos x1)/16} + τd (Dataset B) — with empty values inserted under MAR (row-dependent) or MNAR (value-dependent, x ≥ 0) mechanisms. Test data uses a distinct 'masking for deterministic relationship' (MFDR) strategy so masked values are exactly determined by the unmasked ones. Critical design decisions: (a) excluding MCAR (justified — nothing to learn), (b) no positional encoding (justified — column order is meaningless), (c) fixing all network architectures, learning rate, and skipping hyperparameter tuning due to 'limited computational capacity' (weakly justified — it confounds architecture comparisons with capacity differences). Key Results: The paper reports NRMSE and empty-value classification accuracy across a full grid: {linear, exponential} × {MAR, MNAR, NoNaN} × {MLP, Resnet, attention} × {mask ≤ 1, mask ≤ 2} × N ∈ {100, 1000, 10000, 50000} × D ∈ {32, 128, 256, 512}, at noise level τ = 0.01. The specific numeric values in Tables 1–2 are not recoverable from the text, so findings are reported qualitatively by the authors: (1) the attention model outperforms MLP and Resnet on NRMSE for training sizes ≥ 10,000 in most cases (with one exception: linear/MNAR/N=50,000), and consistently on accuracy for the exponential dataset above N = 1,000; (2) performance saturates at N = 10,000 for the linear dataset but not for the exponential dataset; (3) mask ≤ 1 beats mask ≤ 2 in most cases at N ≥ 10,000; (4) missingness mechanism barely matters for the linear dataset at N = 50,000, but on the exponential dataset MNAR yields significantly lower empty-value accuracy than MAR — the authors attribute this to MNAR requiring a two-step inference (predict the latent value, then decide missingness); (5) under NoNaN, MLP and Resnet 'are unable to learn effectively' while the attention model remains competitive; (6) increasing D improves the attention model's NRMSE (saturating at D = 128 for linear, ≥ 256 for exponential, no saturation up to D = 512 under MNAR) but has negligible effect on MLP/Resnet. Scale is toy: three columns, two functions, up to 50,000 rows. No comparisons against any external baseline (GBDT, MVI methods, or published pretraining results) are run. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (partially) plus a small NEW METHOD component. The genuine novelty is the ITP problem formulation — predicting masked positions whose ground truth may be an empty value — and the three-way embedding (numeric/NaN/mask) with the joint empty-classification-plus-regression head. The masking scheme, architectures, and MLM-style training are standard combinations of Gorishniy et al. (2021), Devlin et al. (2018), and Vaswani et al. (2017); the problem itself sits close to prior tabular masked-reconstruction pretraining, and the authors' differentiation from MVI rests on an argument they do not empirically test. Rigor & Reproducibility: The experimental design is careful within its scope: a full grid search (each combination trained), random initialization per run, early stopping on a validation set, MFDR test masking designed so ground truth is derivable, and complete architecture and training hyperparameter documentation in Appendices A–B. However: no error bars, no multiple-seed variance reporting, no significance tests; no ablation isolating the contribution of the NaN/mask embeddings versus a naive NaN-imputed baseline; no external baselines of any kind (a serious omission for an architecture-comparison paper); and no code or data release is mentioned. The architecture-comparison conclusions are drawn with fixed, untuned network sizes, so 'attention wins' may partly reflect capacity or LR-sensitivity differences rather than inductive bias. As the authors themselves stress, the method is developed and evaluated on the same two synthetic generators, so the headline findings have Goodhart exposure — they characterize the benchmark, not the problem in general. This is an arXiv preprint (2609.01262); no peer review status is indicated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (small-scale methods-and-experiments paper). - Practical: Yes — the models are tiny (128-wide MLP/Resnet, 2-block 32-dim attention with D ≤ 512 embeddings) and run on commodity hardware. - Efficient: Training appears cheap given the model sizes and N ≤ 50,000 rows, though no wall-clock or FLOP numbers are reported. - Effective: The evidence shows the models learn two specific 3-column relationships and NaN status under controlled conditions; it does not show ITP works on realistic tables, so effectiveness is demonstrated only on a proxy setting the authors construct. - Scalable: Untested — real tables have tens to hundreds of columns with mixed types, heterogeneous noise, and unknown relationships; the authors explicitly disclaim transfer of their conclusions to larger tables, and the fixed architectures would likely need redesign at 10–100× the column count. Deliverable: paper only; no code, dataset generator, or trained model artifact is mentioned as released. Strengths: - Articulates a genuinely distinct problem formulation (empty values as prediction targets rather than artifacts to impute) with a clear operational distinction from MVI, and enumerates concrete use scenarios. - The three-way embedding (numeric / NaN / mask) with a joint classification-regression output head is a simple, clean mechanism for making missingness itself learnable on continuous features. - The MFDR test-masking strategy is a thoughtful methodological move: by ensuring test targets are exactly determined by unmasked values, it isolates whether the model learned the column relationship rather than marginal statistics. - The grid-search findings — attention wins at scale, embedding dimension matters only for attention, MNAR > MAR difficulty, mask ≤ 1 preferable — are internally coherent, non-obvious in places, and stated with appropriately hedged scope. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct: they state that conclusions are drawn from a deliberately controlled setting limited to two synthetic three-column relationships; that trends (attention advantage, embedding-length effects) may not transfer to larger or real-world tables; that the work is 'an initial, narrowly-scoped investigation'; that categorical features are excluded by design; that network structures, learning rate, and hyperparameters were fixed due to limited computational resources; and that MCAR was excluded because it contains no learnable relationship. This candid scoping is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison against any MVI baseline (missForest, MICE, kNN, GAIN, VAE-based methods) despite the paper's central claim being that ITP cannot be solved by standard MVI approaches — the claim is argued, never tested, even in the regime (NoNaN) where MVI-style methods should work. - No ablation of the proposed embedding layer: a baseline that imputes NaN with a constant or mean before a standard FT-Transformer would show whether the dedicated NaN embedding is what drives the empty-value accuracy, or whether it is incidental. - Single runs per grid cell with no variance reporting: several conclusions rest on small NRMSE differences (e.g., the 'one exception' at linear/MNAR/N=50,000) that could be seed noise. - Fixed architectures conflate architecture identity with capacity and tuning; the conclusion 'attention needs larger D' may partly be 'attention was given 2 blocks at width 32 while MLP/Resnet get width 128 with 16/8 blocks.' - The third usage scenario (verifying correctness of existing table positions) is never operationalized or evaluated in any experiment. - Only one noise level (τ = 0.01) is tested, leaving robustness to noise — central to the linear-vs-exponential saturation story — unexamined. Bottom Line: A carefully scoped, honest, but narrow proof-of-concept: a researcher entering tabular self-supervised learning will find the empty-value-as-target formulation and the three-way embedding worth borrowing, but anyone wanting evidence that ITP matters or works in practice will need to wait for real-data evaluation against actual MVI baselines, which this paper does not provide.

Granularity Patterns for Programming Cyber-physical Systems with Business Processes

R Seiger, O Zimmermann · alexandria.unisg.ch · business process mining or process mining - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces four design patterns — Fine-grained Sensing in Processes, Coarse-grained Sensing via Transformation Services, Fine-grained Actuation in Processes, and Coarse-grained Actuation via Controllers — that guide architects in deciding what to model in executable BPMN business processes versus what to leave to code-level CPS control software. - Why it's important: Applying BPM engines to cyber-physical systems raises safety- and real-time-critical questions that standard BPM practice has no answer for, and a wrong granularity choice (e.g., closing a control feedback loop through a BPM engine) can make safety-critical behavior unimplementable or models unmaintainable. - How it does it: The core move is a qualitative force field analysis over eight decision forces (model complexity, understandability, reusability, observability, API ownership, communication overhead, real-time/safety, sensor data complexity/velocity) mapped onto a fine-grained-to-coarse-grained granularity spectrum, with the primary decision drivers being sensor data characteristics for sensing and safety-critical feedback loops for actuation. - The good: The patterns are grounded in more than a decade of the authors' hands-on CPS lab experience (smart factory, robots, ROS2 controllers) and are anchored in an explicit, worked BPMN example where the same activity ('Burn material', 'Check Product Quality') is shown at both granularity levels, making the trade-off concrete. - The missing: All evidence is qualitative (known uses, force field indications); there are no quantitative measurements of the claimed costs — e.g., BPM engine round-trip latency in feedback loops, model-size/understandability metrics, or communication overhead — so the guidance cannot be calibrated against project-specific thresholds. - Read it or not: Worth reading for software architects and BPM engineers orchestrating CPS/IoT with BPMN who face exactly this abstraction decision; skip it if you want measured performance data or a formal decision model, since it delivers neither.

Problem & Motivation: Teams automating cyber-physical systems (smart manufacturing, smart homes, logistics robots) increasingly want to use business process management systems to gain explicit, traceable, analyzable, and executable process models across multiple CPS components. BPM engines provide versioning, state management, connectors, and process mining, but they are not built for high-frequency sensor streams, near-real-time reactions, or closed safety-critical control loops. The central gap the paper targets is the granularity decision: how much sensing and actuation detail belongs in the business process model versus the CPS controller code. The authors cite Beerepoot et al. (2023) identifying granularity of BPM-related tasks as one of the major open BPM problems, and note that CPS introduces decision forces (real-time, safety, data velocity, feedback loops) absent from traditional enterprise BPM. Key Idea: The key idea is that sensing and actuation granularity should be decided by different primary drivers — sensor data complexity/velocity drives sensing granularity (simple, low-frequency data can be evaluated in-process via decision tables; streamed, complex data must be abstracted by an external Transformation Service), while safety-critical feedback loops drive actuation granularity (non-critical actuation decomposes into fine-grained BPMN service tasks; safety-relevant actuation is encapsulated behind a single coarse-grained API call, effectively a Facade, keeping the control loop inside the CPS controller out of the BPM engine). The paper crystallizes this into a pattern map with explicit compatibility relations (e.g., fine-grained sensing is incompatible with coarse-grained actuation for one action; coarse-grained sensing can be part of coarse-grained actuation). Methodology: This is a pattern paper following a modified EuroPLoP template: per pattern it gives Context, Solution, Example, and Known Uses; Decision Forces Resolution and Related Patterns are discussed jointly per pattern pair. The vehicle is a smart-manufacturing laboratory (smart factory with oven and gripper robot under a Python control stack, a quality-control station with two Dobot arms and conveyor, and a ROS2-based delivery robot) orchestrated by an executable BPMN 2.0 process; the same subprocesses are re-modeled at both granularities (Figs. 5 vs. 7 for sensing; Figs. 10 vs. 2 for actuation) to illustrate each pattern. The analytical instrument is a force field analysis (Figs. 8 and 12) scoring each of eight forces with +/-/o per pattern. Three critical design decisions: (1) the binary fine/coarse framing with an acknowledged intermediate spectrum — justified as a simplification but potentially coarse; (2) elevating real-time/safety and data velocity as CPS-specific forces beyond classic BPM trade-offs — well-motivated by the domain; (3) purely qualitative force resolution — the authors admit quantification is 'strongly dependent on the specific decision cases'. Key Results: No quantitative results are reported; the deliverables are the four patterns, the pattern map with compatibility relations, and two force field tables. The qualitative outcomes: (a) shifting sensing/actuation detail into the process model improves observability, reusability (fine-grained case), and initially understandability but increases model complexity, communication overhead, and is infeasible for high-frequency streams; (b) BPM engine round trips per feedback-loop iteration make fine-grained actuation unsuitable for high-frequency safety control, so safety-critical actuation must be encapsulated in the CPS controller (illustrated by ROS2-based robot navigation with obstacle avoidance); (c) API ownership of legacy/brownfield CPS constrains achievable granularity. Known uses are drawn from the authors' CPS labs, prior publications by the group, and literature across smart manufacturing, smart homes, healthcare, HVAC, drones, and elevator control. No baselines, benchmarks, or measurements exist because none are claimed. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD (pattern-level): the genuinely novel contribution is the explicit mapping of CPS-specific decision forces — real-time/safety with feedback loops and sensor data complexity/velocity — onto the BPM granularity decision, plus the compatibility relations among the four patterns; the underlying ingredients (fine-vs-coarse abstraction trade-offs, Facade, Aggregator, Data Abstractor, event-driven consumers, transformation services) are standard patterns recombined and contextualized for the BPM-meets-CPS setting, as the Related Patterns sections themselves make clear. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a pattern paper, traditional rigor criteria (ablations, error bars, seeds, significance tests) do not apply, and none are present. The evidence base is experience-anchored: the patterns were shepherded through the EuroPLoP 2026 writer's workshop (shepherd Uwe Zdun), which provides community review but not archival peer review — treat as a workshop-reviewed preprint. Known Uses cite ~15 independent literature sources plus the authors' own lab systems, which strengthens applicability claims; however, the force field analyses are self-assessed (+/-/o scores with no measurement or inter-rater validation), and the motivating testbed is the authors' own laboratory. No code, process models, or tooling artifacts are reported as released. The patterns were distilled partly from the same lab systems used to illustrate them, a mild self-confirmation risk, though the literature known-uses partially offset this. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (experience-based pattern guidance with a physical lab testbed; no primary experiments run in this paper). - Practical: Yes — the patterns assume commodity BPM engines (BPMN 2.0) and standard CPS stacks (Python, ROS2, MQTT/CoAP/HTTP connectors), all commercially available. - Efficient: Not measured; the paper argues directionally that coarse-grained patterns reduce BPM-to-CPS communication and move high-frequency processing off the engine, but provides no latency, throughput, or overhead numbers. - Effective: The evidence shows the patterns are applicable and have known uses across domains, but only a proxy for effectiveness — no evaluation that following the force-field guidance yields measurably better models or safer systems than ad-hoc choices. - Scalable: Not tested; the paper flags cloud-vs-edge BPM deployment and connector configuration as open technical questions for 10×-100× scale (more sensors, faster streams), and the lab is small-scale (roughly a handful of robots and stations). The work stops at paper form: no library, tool, dataset, or reusable formal artifact is delivered, though the authors state the patterns will feed an emerging formal model of architectural requirements and decisions. Strengths: - The identification and naming of two CPS-specific decision forces — real-time/safety with closed feedback loops, and sensor data complexity/velocity — as primary granularity drivers is a genuine conceptual contribution that distinguishes CPS-BPM from enterprise BPM granularity concerns. - The side-by-side re-modeling of identical activities (quality check, burn material) at both granularity levels in a real executable lab setup makes the abstract trade-off inspectable and teaches the pattern faster than prose alone. - The pattern map's explicit compatibility and coexistence relations (e.g., fine-grained sensing is incompatible with coarse-grained actuation for one action; coarse-grained sensing can nest inside coarse-grained actuation) go beyond a flat pattern catalog and support actual composition decisions. - Honest epistemic framing: the authors repeatedly qualify the force analysis as indicating trends only, non-quantifiable in general, and acknowledge emergency-stop-style behavior as an exception to their own sensing rule of thumb. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) the force field analysis provides only indications/trends, with quantification 'strongly dependent on the specific decision cases'; (2) the discussion focuses on the two ends of a granularity spectrum, acknowledging intermediate levels exist but are not analyzed; (3) error handling, timeouts/retries, and compensations — process aspects also affected by granularity — are deferred to future work; (4) deployment topology (cloud vs. edge BPM), connector configuration (MQTT, CoAP, HTTP), and process-mining implications are listed as future technical work. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens the paper's credibility as pattern documentation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The claimed hard technical constraint — 'BPM systems are not designed for real-time control' and engine round trips make in-model feedback loops infeasible — is asserted, never measured; a single latency benchmark comparing BPM-engine loop iteration against controller-internal loops would substantiate the paper's most load-bearing claim. - Process understandability is treated as uniformly improved by fine-grained modeling 'until the model becomes too complex' (citing Schreiber et al.), but the paper provides no way to detect that tipping point, leaving the key human-facing force unoperationalizable. - The incompatibility claim between fine-grained sensing and coarse-grained actuation (Fig. 3) is stated but not justified in the text; a reader cannot reconstruct why these two cannot coexist for one action. - Known Uses rely heavily on the authors' own prior publications (roughly a third of cited known-uses are self-citations), and there is no evidence any pattern was applied by an independent industrial team. - Safety is used as the decisive actuation force, but the paper offers no discussion of how BPM-level orchestration interacts with formal safety verification or certification of the controller side (e.g., IEC 61508-style arguments), which is where the real deployment cost lies. Bottom Line: For architects and BPM engineers who must decide how to wire sensors and actuators into executable BPMN processes for CPS, this is a useful, experience-grounded decision aid worth a careful read; for everyone else, the same fine-vs-coarse abstraction territory is covered more rigorously by the cited IoT and process-execution pattern literature, and nothing here is measured.

Problem & Motivation: Generating Dafny programs that actually pass the Dafny/Z3 verifier from natural-language descriptions is hard because it requires simultaneously producing a tight specification, a correct implementation, and auxiliary annotations (loop invariants, decreases clauses). Existing approaches fail in characteristic ways: one-shot generation has no repair mechanism; naive iterative repair conflates all error types into undifferentiated retries and oscillates; ReAct/CodeAct-style agents waste budget on open-ended next-action reasoning in a domain where the error space is finite; and tree-search methods (MCTS) scale combinatorially. The target users are researchers and practitioners in LLM-based formal code synthesis, and the gap the paper targets is the absence of a deterministic, structured repair pipeline that uses the verifier as an active oracle rather than as a passive pass/fail signal. The paper cites concurrent benchmarks (VeriCoding, Verina) reporting only 3.6–4.9% proof success for top models on hard tasks as evidence of the gap. Key Idea: The single core insight is that formal verification is a domain where the oracle's error output is structured, finite, and categorizable, so the open-ended "what should I do next?" decision of an agent can be replaced by a closed, deterministic mapping from error category to repair skill — with zero reasoning overhead and unconditional soundness (the harness never returns an unverified program). Each skill is a triple (prompt template, tool binding, decidable success criterion), and decidability of skill success is what enables bounded termination and principled routing. This is a real, well-articulated idea, though it is close in spirit to Agentless's non-agentic-workflow finding and classical CEGIS counterexample-guided repair. Methodology: The pipeline has two phases. Initial synthesis: INFERSPEC extracts (types, preconditions, postconditions, construct type) from the NL description, validated by the Dafny type checker; SYNTHBODY generates the body with specification anchoring (prompt forbids weakening postconditions). Repair loop (Algorithm 1, budget N=5): the Dafny verifier (4.5.0 + Z3 4.12.2) judges the candidate; DIAGNOSEERROR classifies failures into four categories via regex patterns (handling ~84% of cases) with LLM fallback; a fixed routing table maps invariant_missing→GENINVARIANT, spec_gap→STRENGTHENSPEC, body_error→REPAIRCODE, type_error→SYNTHBODY. The loop maintains best-state tracking with stagnation detection and rollback when the error count increases for two rounds; on stagnation it regenerates at temperature 0.3. Termination soundness is stated formally: any returned program satisfies Verify(d*) = ⊤ regardless of skill correctness. An equivalence-verification stage additionally checks interface matching, spec equivalence, and behavioral equivalence against reference implementations via auto-generated Dafny lemma wrappers. Critical design decisions: (1) deterministic routing over agent reasoning — well-justified by the ablation (−11.8 pp when routing is randomized); (2) specification anchoring preventing postcondition weakening — justified qualitatively but not ablated against a free-to-weaken variant; (3) hybrid regex/LLM diagnosis — pragmatic, with an acknowledged 11.8% misclassification rate. Key Results: On the authors' 178-example benchmark (62 simple / 71 medium / 45 hard; drawn from the Dafny standard library, DafnyBench, and 8 GitHub repositories), SKILLFORGE achieves 91.6% verification rate (VR) and 86.5% equivalence rate (ER) with GPT-5.5, versus Proof2Silicon 85.4%, MCTS-Repair 84.3%, ReAct-Verify 82.0%, Clover 81.5%, Laurel 80.3%, CodeAct-Dafny 79.2%, and traditional baselines 62.4–77.5%. The advantage widens with difficulty: on Hard tasks 77.8% vs. 66.7% for Proof2Silicon (+13.4 pp), driven by the GENINVARIANT skill (−22.2 pp on Hard when ablated). Cost: 4.6K tokens, 2.8 verifier calls, 14.2 s per example versus ReAct-Verify at 8.9K tokens / 22.4 s and MCTS-Repair at 14.2K tokens / 38.7 s. Convergence: 71.3% verified on the first attempt, 83.1% within two iterations. Multi-model: Claude Opus-4.7 89.9%, Claude Sonnet-4.5 84.3% (matching the strongest GPT-5.5 agentic baseline). Baselines are recent (2023–2025 methods) but all were re-implemented by the authors on a new benchmark, so absolute numbers are not comparable to any published leaderboard. Scale is small (178 examples); this is a standard-scale, not stress-scale, evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (skill-decomposed harness with verification-error-conditioned deterministic routing) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 178-pair NL–Dafny benchmark, though partially derived from DafnyBench). The genuinely novel element is the explicit framing of decidable per-skill success criteria plus a fixed error-category→skill routing table as a replacement for agentic next-action selection in domains with perfect oracles; the components themselves (structured repair prompts, verifier-in-the-loop iteration, invariant synthesis prompts, error-taxonomy routing à la CEGIS) are standard ideas competently combined, and the closest prior work (Laurel's error-guided assertion placement, Proof2Silicon's RL repair, Agentless's anti-agent finding) covers much of the same ground. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the strongest element: every skill is removed individually with quantified deltas, and per-skill invocation statistics, error-category distributions, and per-difficulty skill usage are all reported. Weaknesses: results are single-run (temperature 0.0 mitigates but does not eliminate variance; the 0.3-temperature stagnation retry and LLM nondeterminism are unaddressed); no confidence intervals or significance tests for the 6.2 pp margin over Proof2Silicon; no code, data, or model release is mentioned anywhere; the benchmark is the authors' own curation with author-written NL descriptions, and baselines are author-adapted implementations — a Goodhart risk since the method was developed on the same benchmark it is evaluated on; the paper itself concedes that baseline implementation differences may affect absolute numbers. The Appendix J "thirty application systems" claim is supported only by citation of unrelated papers and no experimental evidence, which is a serious integrity red flag alongside a bibliography containing many entries (Hu 2025a–e, Zhu 2025a–e, Xie 2025a–c, Zhang 2025a–e, Tu 2025a–e, etc.) that are plainly irrelevant to the paper's topic. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — the harness is a built Python 3.11 pipeline around the Dafny CLI). - Practical: Yes — runs on an 8-core CPU / 32 GB RAM box plus API access to a frontier LLM; Dafny and Z3 are open-source, though the primary backend (GPT-5.5) is a paid closed API. - Efficient: Best in class among iterative methods tested — 4.6K tokens and 2.8 verifier calls per example, roughly half the tokens and latency of ReAct-Verify. - Effective: Evidence supports the verification claim directly (machine-checked proofs), but the 5.1 pp VR–ER gap means some "verified" programs deviate semantically from the reference — the paper measures and acknowledges this rather than hiding it. - Scalable: Not tested; 178 curated, self-contained single-file examples are far from repository-scale, multi-function programs, and cited work (Xu et al., 2025) shows verification success does not compose across multi-function programs — the paper claims but does not test generalization. The work delivers a methodological recipe and prompt templates (Appendix A) in paper form; no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model artifact is stated as released. Strengths: - The deterministic-routing thesis is falsifiable and was actually tested: randomizing routing (−11.8 pp) reproduces agentic-baseline performance, giving the paper a genuine causal story rather than just a leaderboard win. - Cost-quality analysis is unusually honest for this genre — the method wins on VR while using fewer tokens (4.6K) than every iterative baseline, and the convergence table shows 71.3% first-pass success, so the result is not bought with extra compute. - The difficulty-stratified results localize the advantage precisely: GENINVARIANT drives the Hard-subset gain (−22.2 pp when ablated), and per-difficulty skill invocation frequencies corroborate the mechanism. - Soundness is architectural, not statistical: the harness provably never emits an unverified program, and the equivalence-checking pipeline (interface, spec, and behavioral equivalence as verified Dafny lemmas) goes beyond pass/fail verification rate as a metric. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the 178-example benchmark is small; the skill library is Dafny-specific and transfer to Lean 4/Coq requires reimplementation; only closed frontier models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus-4.7, Sonnet-4.5) were tested, not open-source models; the 5.1 pp VR–ER gap indicates some verified programs are semantically wrong; GENINVARIANT has the lowest skill success rate (64.7%) with quantifier-heavy loops as the main failure mode; skill templates are hand-crafted; and agentic baselines were author-adapted, so implementation differences may affect absolute numbers. A dedicated Discussion section analyzes the 15 failure cases (7 complex inductive proofs, 5 quantifier-heavy specs, 3 diagnosis cascades) and explicitly scopes the harness-over-agent conclusion to domains with finite error taxonomies and perfect oracles. This is direct, non-defensive limitation handling — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run evaluation with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; a 6.2 pp margin on 178 examples could plausibly be within run-to-run variance given LLM nondeterminism. - All six agentic/search baselines were re-implemented by the authors on the authors' benchmark; without released code, neither the baselines' fidelity nor the headline margin is independently checkable. - No comparison on the original DafnyBench protocol or against its published numbers, so results cannot be positioned relative to the broader literature the benchmark was drawn from. - The benchmark's NL descriptions were written by the authors who also designed the skills that consume them — a possible distributional fit between prompt authoring style and skill prompt templates that no external annotator validation rules out. - Appendix J claims evaluation "across thirty application systems" spanning advertising, 5G networking, financial risk, and urban design, supported only by citations to papers with no apparent connection to Dafny verification; combined with the many off-topic bibliography entries, this suggests citation manipulation or compromised authorship and should trigger reviewer scrutiny of the entire evaluation. - The routing table handles exactly four error categories; compound failures (which the paper says constitute 16% of diagnoses) and multi-error programs are handled by an LLM fallback whose 11.8% misclassification rate is reported but whose effect on the 15 failure cases is only partially analyzed. - Scaling behavior is asserted (language-agnostic harness, applicability to Lean 4) but never tested; multi-function/compositional programs — where cited work shows failure — are absent from the benchmark entirely. Bottom Line: A practitioner in LLM-based formal code synthesis gains a concrete, well-ablated demonstration that deterministic verifier-feedback routing beats open-ended agentic repair on cost and reliability for single-function Dafny tasks — but given the author-implemented baselines, small self-curated benchmark, unreleased artifacts, and the serious citation-integrity concerns in the appendix, the 91.6% headline should be treated as an unverified claim pending independent reproduction.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper (presented as a Journal-First talk; slides only) introduces Radiant, a domain-specific language with an editor and code generator that lets domain experts specify start/end/intermediate sensor patterns for process activities, and compiles them into complex event processing (CEP) applications that detect activity executions from raw IoT sensor streams at runtime. - Why it's important: In IoT-enhanced processes without a BPM system orchestrating them, low-level sensor events must be mapped to process activities before process mining can be applied, and prior fully automated signature-based detection degraded when sensor data varied. - How it does it: Experts author declarative pattern definitions (conditions over sensor values with optional time constraints, multiple cases per pattern) in Radiant; a Langium-based VS Code tooling parses these and generates Siddhi CEP queries that segment unlabeled sensor streams into labeled activity start/end events. - The good: Evaluation on two real instrumented environments—a smart-factory dataset (181.4 minutes, 424 activity instances, 77 sensors, workflow-engine ground truth) and a smart-healthcare blood-donation dataset (65.31 minutes, 240 activity executions, 31 sensors, manually recorded ground truth)—with public data via the Zenodo iopt community. - The missing: The slides report no quantitative detection performance (precision/recall/F1) for Radiant versus the prior automated approach or any baseline, so the central claim that expert-encoded patterns fix the quality problem is not evidenced here. - Read it or not: Worth reading for process-mining and IoT researchers seeking sensor-to-activity event abstraction tooling, but only via the underlying journal article (Internet of Things, Elsevier)—these slides alone lack the quantitative results needed to judge it.
